en: Salutation to Śiva.
[In the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā, the Section on Debate.]
I bow to the illustrious True Guru, by whose glances even the dull-witted attain omniscience as well as the capacity to expound all things. (1)
Having clarified the intellect that wanders in all directions under the sway of doubt, unable to reach the further shore amidst the dense thickets of various systems of measurement,
and having established it in the reality of the six excellent points;
I daily honor him who acts as my own preceptor. || 2 ||

The followers of Brahmā say it is Śaṅkara; others, the Pāśupatas, say it is Paśupati; the Pāñcarātras say it is Viṣṇu; the followers of Jaimini say it is Karma; the followers of Kaṇāda say it is Īśvara; the followers of Gautama say it is the Unmanifest; and those who know the doctrine of the Serpent (Patañjali) say that Īśvara is the cause of that [Unmanifest].
I praise the glorious Mahāliṅga, which is in a state of aesthetic oneness with the manifestation of its own non-different, inconceivable power. || 3 ||
O Master! By means of the entire section on ritual action (*kriyākāṇḍa*) issued from Your mouth, all that is to be known has been attained; consequently, an excellence of joy arose in my heart.
[I have now] longingly [received] the sequence of words of the great Siddhānta of the Vīraśaiva.
My mind desires to understand the doctrines of various disputants as well as the methods for refuting them.
O King Basava, I shall proclaim to you the established doctrine, as well as the views of other schools and their refutations;
fix these in your mind, for they are difficult even for the wise to comprehend.
One whose inner self is exceedingly purified by the excellence of worshiping Miśra. || 5 ||
Indeed, among these four aims of human life— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—

which are established as desired by all through the Vedas, Āgamas, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and common worldly experience, the last one (mokṣa) consists essentially in cessation, which eradicates the root of all misfortune.
Because its essential nature is the state of non-dual Śiva— the ripening of the waves flowing without restraint from the ocean of nectar consisting of an unobstructed mass of gentle bliss—
and because it is the most desired object for the world of living beings, whose life is solely the light of continuous experience perpetuated by a succession of unsurpassed cessations.
In that regard, the direct means for the immediate realization of unconditioned non-dual Śiva is [the guru];

and therein, the three— namely hearing (śravaṇa), reflection (manana), and meditative absorption (nididhyāsana)— which are established as occurring in a sequence where each serves as the means for its respective successor, function as causes both directly and indirectly.
Establishing the lack of authority and the authority, respectively, of the words of the Vedas, Āgamas, Dharmaśāstras, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas,
[there are] the Cārvākas, Sautrāntikas, Vaibhāṣikas, and Yogācāras.

The fourfold Buddhist schools, namely the Mādhyamika and the Rūpa; the non-Vedic schools known as the Hārta; the Pāśupata school comprising the fourfold divisions of Lākula, Kāpāla, Bhairava, and Kālāmukha;
and the dual forms of the Pañcarātra—divided into the Mādhva and Rāmānuja branches, each further subdivided into six internal sects—and the two types of Śaiva Tantras.
The non-Vedic systems consist of the two types of logicians—the Akṣapādas (Nyāya) and the Kāṇādas (Vaiśeṣika)—and the Sāṃkhya in its two forms, with and without a Lord; as well as Yoga;
and the Vedic systems, consisting of the fourfold group of Jaimini’s followers and the Ṛṣis.
In the removal of doubts, misconceptions, and contradictions arising from a critical examination of the methodology of the Vivarta-vāda (theory of illusory manifestation) doctrine:

first, [this work establishes] the Vīraśaiva [position], which is consistent with the intent of the venerable sage Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā-śāstra, who brings about the attainment of a single coherent system of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[He acted] with a heart single-mindedly intent on bestowing unrestrained grace upon those eminent Vīraśaiva scholars— who, though they have worshipped the essence of the Śiva-siddhānta through faith connected to the reality of the six points (*ṣaṭsthala*) and the specific method of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) characterized by the doctrine of the transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) that is the very core of the [Śaiva] tradition— are being troubled [by others].

By him who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of words, sentences, and means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) contained within the entirety of the *Nigamas*, *Āgamas*, histories (*itihāsa*), law-codes (*smṛti*), and *Purāṇas*;
who was intent on providing replies that brought joy to the heart of the illustrious Keladi Basava, the lord of the earth;
and who had attained the majesty of stainless wisdom through the grace of Siddheśvara.
By the venerable Maritoṇṭadārya— an incarnation of the stainless Nirañjanajaṅgama and the preeminent leader of the empire of Nirābhāra Vīraśaivism—
this work was composed to establish the state of essential identity between the Liṅga and the body, and to generate an awakening to the reality of the six locations (ṣaṭsthalatattva).

It dispels the various conceptual constructions imagined by the minds of those possessed of doubt; it awakens the majesty of devotion through the sixfold marks; it accomplishes the unsurpassed goal of human existence; it destroys all defilements;
it cuts away the very root of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra; and it gladdens the hearts of all learned Śaiva-vīras.
First, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is set forth.

[Objection: But how can discerning persons engage with this treatise, given that its subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), qualified audience (*adhikārin*), and their mutual relationship (*sambandha*) are not perceived? For according to the maxim, "even a fool does not act without aiming at a purpose," [the answer is: no, it is not so.

Since the subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), qualified practitioner (*adhikārī*), and relationship (*sambandha*) are present here as well, engagement [with this work] is indeed justified. To explain:
[the subject matter is] that which is delimited by the pure internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) characterized by the definitions to be stated hereafter, and denoted by the term "limb" (*aṅga*).

The subject matter of the scripture is the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from Śiva, whose essential nature consists of existence, consciousness, action, bliss, and so forth—terms denoted by the word "liṅga. This occurs through the cessation of the principle of ignorance (avidyātattva), which resides within the category of the person (puruṣatattva) as regulated by the power of the Lord’s will; this cessation takes the form of the soul's abiding in the state of equilibrium with the power of omniscience, which is its own cause.
The purpose is the glory of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), characterized by the state of one's own self as Śiva.

The qualified candidate (*adhikārī*) is one who, through the power of virtuous deeds such as the worship of Śiva accumulated over many births, is established in the fivefold conduct (*pañcācāra*) and the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*), and is endowed with the four means beginning with tranquility (*śama*). [This applies] to both the subject matter and the scripture.

The relationship between the subject to be explained and the explainer, and the relationship between the object and the subject regarding the direct realization of the non-duality of Śiva— these constitute the fourfold preliminary conditions (anubandhacatuṣṭaya).
The fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), however, consists of: (1) the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities; (2) dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter;

(3) tranquility, self-control, contentment, endurance, faith, and concentration; and (4) the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*). Among these four means, each preceding one is the cause for each succeeding one. For example, as it is said: "In this world, that which is produced by action..."
"Even so, the world of one who has accumulated merit perishes in the hereafter," according to the Śruti.
"Those learned in the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having worshipped Me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven.
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, when their merit is exhausted, they enter the world of mortals."

Thus, from the statement in the *Bhagavadgītā*, and from the statement in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*— "Even in heaven, there is no peace for one who fears a fall and whose eyes are weakened"— it follows that the fruits of actions prescribed by injunction, such as cattle, houses, gardens, and fields produced through activities like royal service, [are not the ultimate goal].

Since even heaven and the like are taught to be perishable and to produce the sufferings of birth, death, and so forth— consisting of the union and separation of the body and the vital breaths— that which is higher than that is formless, free from affliction, the eternal, the true, and the supreme.

When that was darkness, there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone existed— partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless, the supreme bridge to immortality,
like a fire whose fuel has been consumed— by reflecting upon such numerous scriptural statements, [He is known] by virtue of His freedom from affliction.

Furthermore, because the Śiva-tattva— designated by such terms as Virūpākṣa and Śiva— is heard to be eternal by virtue of its truth and its nature as the immortal bridge, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities arising therefrom constitutes the first means. Through that, by way of a lack of interest in the fruits of this world and the next, dispassion (*vairāgya*) becomes the second.

The means of accomplishment arises. By that, there is tranquility (*śama*), which consists in the internal organ, the mind, turning away from its objects; by that, there is self-control (*dama*), which consists in the eyes and other senses turning away from their respective objects; and by that, there arises the notion that other objects are obstacles, born from attaining the object of the practice of merely sustaining the vital breath (*prāṇadhāraṇa*).

Contentment; by that, forbearance (*titikṣā*), which consists of the desire to endure the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat; and by that, faith (*śraddhā*), which consists of conviction in the words of the Guru and the Vedānta;
and by that, [the mind's] abiding in the reality of Śiva—established through the words of the Guru and the Vedānta—by abandoning other objects.

A concentration (*samādhāna*) arises in the form of a specific mental disposition (*manovinyāsaviśeṣa*). Thus, the third means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), consisting of the sixfold group beginning with tranquility (*śama*), which culminates in the eight coverings and the five conducts, arises through detachment (*vairāgya*), the second means of accomplishment. By that [detachment], there arises the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*), characterized by the wish to abandon the entire multitude of sufferings.

The fourth means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). One who is endowed with these four such means of accomplishment is qualified for *śravaṇa* (listening) and *manana* (reflection), which consist of inquiry into the spiritual scripture of Śiva-monism (*śivādvaita*) as favored by the Vīraśaivas. By such a qualified person, *śravaṇa*—which consists of inquiry into the reality of Śiva-monism—is [to be performed].
And reflection must be performed. This very point was stated by the blessed sage Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the Sūtras: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*).
Here, *atha* (=) ...
After the attainment of the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) through virtuous deeds such as the worship of Śiva performed over many lifetimes,

and for the reason that the Vedic and non-Vedic doctrines will subsequently be refuted according to the method to be described— because they are devoid of logical justification— the Brahman is [established] as consisting of independent vision and action.

The nature of the Great Liṅga is non-dual Śiva-consciousness; the desire to know that is "taj-jijñāsā," where the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). The remainder of the sense is that its investigation—consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*)—must be performed.
"Hearing" (*śravaṇa*) means [the inquiry] from the mouth of the Guru regarding all the statements of the Vedas and Āgamas concerning non-dual Brahman.
Reflection (*manana*) consists of the examination of the meaning that culminates in the intended purport (*tātparya*);

it serves to remove doubts regarding impossibility and contrary notions concerning non-dual Brahman, by means of the reasonings set forth in the *Brahmasūtras*, which are augmented by the logic of the *Pūrvatantra*, applied to the sentences of the Vedānta scriptures.

The contemplation of the meaning that determines the firmness of its intended purport (*tātparya*) is *nididhyāsana*. It consists of setting in motion a continuous flow of homogeneous cognitions preceded by the suppression of heterogeneous cognitions. And this is termed "concentration" (*samādhi*) in the Yoga Śāstra. Furthermore, it is of two kinds.

It is both conceptual and non-conceptual. The conceptual is helpful for the non-conceptual; those who are dull-witted and unable to directly realize the supreme Brahman without conceptualization are shown compassion through descriptions of the qualified (saviśeṣa).

Thus it is stated in the *Kalpataru*. And the conceptual [meditation] (*savikalpaka*) is accompanied by restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Restraint (*yama*), moreover, is fivefold, consisting of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), truthfulness (*satya*), non-stealing (*asteya*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*).
The five observances (niyamas) are purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord.

Postures such as the lotus posture (padmāsana), the svastika posture (svastikāsana), the perfected posture (siddhāsana), the cow-faced posture (gomukhāsana), the eagle posture (garuḍāsana), and the hero posture (vīrāsana) are to be understood according to the methods well-known in Patañjali’s Yoga and as described in the *Haṭhayogapradīpikā* and other such works.
When the mastery of the postures is achieved, there follows the perfection of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Breath control is characterized by the interruption of the movement of inhalation and exhalation. It is threefold, distinguished as exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*). Exhalation is the outward movement of the breath; inhalation is the inward-moving breath.

The internal suspension of the breath is *kumbhaka*. It is of three kinds, characterized by locations such as the nose or the *dvādaśānta*, and characterized by durations of time such as thirty-two *mātrās*.
Furthermore, the fitness for mental concentration (*manodhāraṇā*) is the fruit of *prāṇāyāma*. This has been stated by the learned authorities:
Detachment from the body, the senses, and so forth is called *yama* by the wise;
devotion to the supreme reality is proclaimed as *niyama*.
Maintaining an attitude of indifference toward all objects is called *āsana*;
the realization that this entire world is illusory is *prāṇāyāma*.
The inward-turning of the mind is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra);
the purification of the mind is declared to be concentration (dhāraṇā).

"Thus, 'I am indeed pure consciousness alone'—this is called meditation (*dhyāna*), which is contemplation. But where there is non-mingling (*amiśraṇa*) [of that], it is celebrated as *samādhi*," and so forth.
Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is the drawing back of the senses from their respective objects.
When withdrawal is practiced, the senses become subject to one's control.
Dhāraṇā (concentration) is the stabilization of the mind upon a specific location, such as the tip of the nose or the navel-cakra. Where...

When the mind is held upon the prāṇa-liṅga or other objects established within the heart-lotus, the continuity of that object—achieved by avoiding dissimilar transformations of the cognition—is meditation (dhyāna).
Samādhi is the appearance of the object alone, as if devoid of its own nature; the "object" here refers to the desired liṅga and so forth.

Among the eight [limbs] beginning with *yama*, *yama* and *niyama* are included within the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) as appropriate. By means of each preceding means, each succeeding goal is produced. And thus, for one established in the Vīraśaiva doctrine, the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) is indeed the means.
There is no yoga without knowledge, nor is there knowledge without yoga.

From this statement, it should be understood that for the Vīraśaivas, knowledge conjoined with such yoga alone is the means to liberation (*kaivalya*). Thus, according to the sequence described, because hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) are the specific causes for meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), [the practice] consists of hearing and reflection.

An inquiry into the Śiva-principle (śivatattva) must be undertaken; that is, an investigation into the Śiva-principle must be performed by means of the reflective awareness of one's own self as non-different [from Śiva].
The meaning is that this reflective awareness as non-different from one's own self must be carried out.

In this sūtra, by the word "ataḥ" (hence/therefore), the entire subject matter of the subsequent chapters on reconciliation (samanvaya), non-contradiction (avirodha), and the fruit (phala) is indicated.
It is concise. By the word "atha" (now/thereupon), the subject matter of the *Sādhanādhyāya* (the second chapter) is summarized.

By the word "brahma," it should be reflected upon that its intended meaning (*tātparya*) is the state of being distinct from the insentient and the individual soul (*jīva*), characterized by self-luminosity, independence, and the nature of power (*śakti*).

Now, one might object: how can the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is unattached and indifferent consciousness (*asaṅgodāsīnacitsvabhāva*), possess independence or the possession of powers such as consciousness?
For there is no evidence for its possessing powers.
Nor can it be argued that [the scripture] says, "His supreme power is indeed manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are His inherent nature."
As it is heard in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"There is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there Śiva devoid of Śakti;
they are mutually dependent like the fragrance of a flower and the wind, or like the air and the sky."

Thus, by virtue of such corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), Śiva’s possession of power (*śaktimattva*) is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇasiddha*). For this very reason, the compositions of the learned, such as "If Śiva is joined with Śakti, he is capable of exercising power," and so forth, are also consistent. This should be stated [in response to the objection] regarding the Vedic passages from the *Śvetāśvatara* and other Upaniṣads concerning *māyā*.

One should know that Prakṛti is Māyā and Maheśvara is its possessor; for this is established by considering the preceding context beginning with "When there was darkness, neither day nor night," and also by considering the subsequent context beginning with "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas. Thus, Māyā is Tamas and Pradhāna.

Because it is concluded that the purport of those words lies solely in establishing *avidyā*—which is insentient and non-different from ignorance (*ajñāna*) in its positive form. Furthermore, is the power (*śakti*) you accept non-different from Śiva or not?
In the first case, there is a loss of the non-duality (*advaita*) of Śiva. In the second case, [the scripture states]: "In the beginning, there was darkness; this world was enveloped by darkness."

The nature of Śiva as non-dual with the Power (śakti)— which has been established as having the character of a concealer, like the darkness being perceived through such descriptions as "consisting of darkness," "unknowable," and "without characteristics"— is [the subject].
Because it would be impossible to state [otherwise]; furthermore, according to the Vīraśaiva doctrine,

after describing the *puruṣa* as the twenty-fifth principle among the thirty-six principles, and then designating five principles as its five "sheaths" (*kañcuka*)— namely, *kalā*, *vidyā*, *kāla*, *rāga*, and *niyati*— thereafter...
Even for you, who accept the six principles known as Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Sadāśiva, Maheśvara, Śakti, and Śiva,
there exists the thirty-first principle, the Māyā-tattva, which is distinct from the Śakti-tattva.

Since an insentient (*jaḍa*) power must be admitted, it is impossible for that power— which consists of the obscuring ignorance (*āvaraṇājñāna*)— to be identical with Śiva, whose nature is consciousness (*cit*). Nor is the existence of power established by such passages as "His supreme power," for by synonyms such as "power," "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), "natural disposition" (*nisarga*), and "essential form" (*svarūpa*), it is the essential form itself that is intended.

Because it is incapable of being defined either as distinct or as non-distinct, the conventional usage such as "my power" (*mama śaktiḥ*) or "Śiva's power" (*śivasya śaktiḥ*) ultimately results in non-difference alone— just like expressions such as "the head of Rāhu," "my self" (*mama ātmā*), "my nature" (*mama svabhāvaḥ*), or "my own form" (*mama svarūpam*); therefore, she is not a separate ontological principle (*tattvāntara*).

It is capable of being established. Therefore, if it is argued that the usage of the term "power" (*śakti*) in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other texts ultimately refers only to our accepted *māyā*—namely, insentient ignorance (*avidyā*) denoted by the word *māyā*—[we reply:
no, because of the impossibility of a relationship between that which is designated as *māyā* (insentient ignorance) and Brahman.

Because it is impossible to express [it otherwise], the very power (śakti) favored by us is the intended object of the Śruti and Smṛti; furthermore, there is no proof for the existence of ignorance (avidyā). To explain: what is the means of knowledge (māna) for the existence of ignorance?

Is it perception, inference, scripture, or internal experience? Not the first, because we do not observe a subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya) such as "I directly perceive ignorance," in the way that one might have "I directly perceive a jar.
Nor the second, because there is no mark (liṅga) pervaded by it [ignorance]. Now, even though it is not visible to the eye...

If it is argued that there exists some beginningless, indefinable, positive entity called ignorance (avidyā), which is dependent on Brahman and concerns the individual soul (jīva)—since otherwise the observed effects could not be accounted for—we say no; for if the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding this ignorance were itself real, non-duality (advaita) would be lost. It is for this very reason that the scripture states: "He rules over both knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā)."

The claim that the experience "I am ignorant" is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been refuted. If that were the case, one must consider whether that means of knowledge and ignorance (*avidyā*) are distinct or non-distinct. It cannot be the first [option], because it would entail the consequence of a triple reality (*trisatyatva*): namely, that Brahman, ignorance, and its means of knowledge would all be real by virtue of being a means of knowledge. Nor...
It should not be argued that there is no fault because the difference [of the means of valid cognition] is accepted as being an effect of ignorance;

for if there were a difference between cause and effect, they would possess distinct natures like a thread and a jar, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that [ignorance] is not the cause. If, on the other hand, there is non-difference, then by virtue of having a single nature, it cannot be called an "effect."

Because it is impossible for there to be a distinction [between cause and effect], if difference alone were intended, then since identity would be impossible, the cessation of the phenomenal world— which is the effect— would not occur even upon the cessation of its cause, ignorance, just as a jar remains even when its cause, the stick, has been destroyed. If such an undesirable consequence were accepted, liberation itself would not exist.

Because bondage is included within phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*). Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because there would be no possibility of distinguishing "this is the means of knowledge" from "this is the object of knowledge" due to the non-difference between the means of knowledge and its object.
If it were itself the means of knowledge for its own existence, then it would follow that it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatā*).

Because it appears as independent of anything else, just like the Self (*ātman*). Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), for if ignorance were [itself] knowledge, then the very term "ignorance" would be meaningless. Therefore, since it would follow that there are two truths, and because there is no possibility of postulating some form of ignorance existing apart from Brahman, [the opponent's position] is untenable. It is not so.

Nor can it be argued that there is no such fault because existence (*sattā*) residing in the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) appears within ignorance (*avidyā*) and its effects; for this is impossible. For does that existence appear while ignorance exists in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), or while it does not exist? Not the first; for if it were already established as having the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), what further [appearance] could there be of it?

Because it does not depend on a connection with another existent (sattāntara). Nor is the second [alternative] possible, because a connection is impossible for that which is non-existent, due to the contradiction between the existent and the non-existent. Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because ignorance (avidyā) is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent; for even in that case, the same dilemma arises: is it existent or non-existent in its own form?
Because the aforementioned defects remain as they were.

Furthermore, even if ignorance (*avidyā*) is accepted in some manner or other, the relationship of locus and located between Brahman and ignorance is not possible; for instance, regarding Brahman and ignorance:

What is the relation? Is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), a relation of essential nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*), or something else? Not the first, because ignorance (*avidyā*) is not a substance (*adravyatva*). Not the second, because the relationship of part and whole (*avayava-avayavibhāva*) and so forth is untenable. Not the third, because there is no essential nature possessing the same level of reality (*samasattāka*) as Brahman. Nor is it a relation consisting of superimposition (*ādhyāsika*).

In the case of the error "this is silver" regarding a mother-of-pearl shell, [the theory of residual impression (saṃskāra) is untenable] because there is an absence of an impression produced by a prior valid cognition of the superimposed object— unlike the impression produced by a valid cognition of silver found in a marketplace— and because, in any instance other than Brahman, ignorance (avidyā) is not admitted, there is an absence of a cognition of the object present before one, and an absence of a cognition of similarity.

Therefore, neither ignorance (*avidyā*) nor illusion (*māyā*) can be superimposed upon Brahman. Furthermore, because Brahman is of the nature of light and ignorance is of the nature of darkness, a mutual relationship between them is not tenable. Nor is it the case that there is no universal opposition between light and darkness, as the eye-light of an owl is itself pervaded by darkness.
It should be stated that it is possible in that manner:
"Some living beings are blind by day, others are blind at night;
some living beings have limited vision both by day and by night."

According to this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), because of his limited vision and being overwhelmed by the solar radiance, he lacks the proficiency to perceive objects of knowledge; otherwise, since he would be devoid of even the sight of the moon and its light at night, he would be perpetually blind, and the designation "blind by day" would not apply to him. Nor is it the case according to the analogy of the lunar spot.
A relationship is not possible [between them],

because Brahman, being partless, is devoid of upper, lower, and lateral divisions. If there were no contradiction between the two, then ignorance would never cease even through the vision of reality (tattvadarśana).

Since it has been stated that "action does not remove ignorance because it is non-contradictory [to it]," it would follow that Brahman is ignorant. Nor can [ignorance be removed] partially, because Brahman is partless.
Furthermore, even a distinction of parts imagined by ignorance is impossible, because of the nature of imagination itself.

Because its prior state is impossible; because there is no location external to Brahman at all; and because, according to the reasoning already stated, its persistence in that very place is impossible. Furthermore, its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) is also not possible, since it can be defined as being an unoriginated positive entity (*anādibhāvarūpatva*). Nor is its beginninglessness (*anāditva*) possible.
Because, like a jar or similar objects, it possesses parts and is insentient, its self-establishment is impossible;

and if that were admitted, it would follow that it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). If its establishment were dependent on another, then, like a jar, it would be an effect, which would lead to an infinite regress by necessitating yet another cause.
Furthermore, even the nature of being an existent entity is not possible, because it is the object of a cognition that reflects the meaning of a negation (*nañ*).

Likewise, its being the material cause of the universe is also not possible, because it is devoid of its own existence and, due to its insentience, lacks the capacity to impel. Nor is it possible for the conscious Brahman to be the impeller, because of its state of non-attachment (*niḥsaṅgatā*). It is not.

It should not be argued that, by the analogy of the magnet, the causality of ignorance is possible through the power of proximity (*sānnidhya*) to consciousness; for proximity is restricted to those things situated in different locations, and in this case, there is no location external to Brahman. Rather, [ignorance] resides in Brahman itself.

It is like a needle inserted into iron or a gem; because it is devoid of independent activity, the process of transformation into the form of the universe becomes possible. If that [Māyā] were to produce an effect without any substratum, then, by virtue of its independence, it would become impossible to restrain. If such a consequence were accepted, liberation itself would not exist.

Nor is it possible for ignorance (*avidyā*) to have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its object; for, since ignorance is insentient (*jaḍa*), it is the object, whereas the soul, being sentient (*cetana*), is the subject.
Therefore, because of this reversal, even if that [relationship] were accepted, the soul would have its heart overwhelmed by ignorance.

There would be no discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities; nor could it arise from a teacher or from scripture, because the heart of even a teacher is overcome by ignorance, and because scripture, being an effect of ignorance, is of the same nature as it. Therefore, there is a lack of evidence for the existence of ignorance. As follows:
Furthermore, even if that [consciousness] were admitted as a constituent part [of Brahman], it would follow that there are two truths.
Moreover, because Brahman and ignorance are as contradictory as light and darkness, the relationship of locus and located (the substratum and the superstratum) is impossible.
If, however, they were not contradictory, then the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (that which is removed and that which removes) would likewise be impossible.

Furthermore, it would follow that Brahman is ignorant; therefore, it is impossible for ignorance (*avidyā*) to be beginningless or to be a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*). Since it is impossible for Brahman to be its instigator, [ignorance's] status as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe and its relation to the individual soul (*jīva*) are refuted. Otherwise, for the soul—

It would be improper to say that "all the Vedāntas are commenced for the sake of abandoning the cause of evil, because of the impossibility of discriminating between eternal and non-eternal entities," since there could be no relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*nivartya-nivartaka-bhāva*) between the Vedāntas and their commencement, as both would be of the same nature as ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, the definition of superimposition (adhyāsa) as "the appearance elsewhere of something previously seen, having the form of memory," is not possible; for instance,
[it would fail] in the case of a snake perceived previously in an external location such as an anthill, appearing [now] upon a rope or similar object situated in front.
[Superimposition occurs] upon something present before one, such as a rope; however, in this case, since there is no location external to Brahman, superimposition is impossible.
For in the world, we never observe the superimposition of that which is seen in one place onto that very same place.
Even in the illusory attribution of yellowness to a conch shell, the yellowness has been seen elsewhere [in a karṇikāra flower]; otherwise, the conch would not appear yellow.

Thus, there would be no such cognition, because yellow was not previously perceived; otherwise, there would be no distinction between error and valid cognition, since it is accepted that what is superimposed must have been seen in that very same place.
Nor should it be said that being sublated by a subsequent moment is itself the definition of error, for [otherwise] there would be no difference between [the cognition of] a jar and a cloth.

Furthermore, since even the mother-of-pearl and the silver cannot stand in the relationship of sublated and sublator by virtue of being real entities, nor can there be a sublation of the cognition of silver by the cognition of mother-of-pearl;
for, like the cognitions of a jar and a cloth, those two [cognitions] possess different times and different objects. Otherwise, the cognition of a cloth would be sublated by the cognition of a jar.

It would be sublated. Nor should it be said that the subsequent cognition, "This is not silver, but only mother-of-pearl," is the sublater of the previously arisen cognition of silver; for even in the case of a cognizer who, after the cognition of a jar, leaves the jar and sees a cloth, there arises the certain conviction, "This is not a jar, it is a cloth."

It might be argued that there would be a sublation of the previously arisen cognition of a jar; however, because every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consists of a determination preceded by the negation of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such a conceptual construction—being of a different nature (*bhinnadharmika*)—lacks contradiction, and thus no relationship of sublated and sublater exists therein. This is not the case here.

It must be stated that, since it is impossible for two contradictory appearances— namely, "this is silver" and "this is not silver"— to both possess validity with respect to a single substratum (*dharmin*), the sublation (*bādha*) of the previously arisen cognition of silver is admitted by means of the subsequent cognition of the absence of silver.
Because the relationship between the sublated and the sublator depends on mutual connection— like the maxim of the staff and the vessel—

and because that [connection] is absent due to the two occurring at different times; for indeed, by the rule that cognitions persist for only three moments, at the moment the cognition of the absence of silver arises...

If it is argued that because the previously arisen cognition of silver— which has reached a state of perishing— is still present, a mutual connection between the two is possible, we say no; for cognitions, being qualities (*guṇa*),
lack mutual connection through either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), owing to their insentience (*jaḍatva*).
Furthermore, because it lacks such an orientation [toward the object], the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is not possible.

Rather, for a cognizer who, having abandoned the jar, perceives a cloth, by the power of his own desire, there is the closing (*nimeṣa*) of the cognition of the jar and the opening (*unmeṣa*) of the cognition of the cloth; thus, within a single substratum (*dharmin*), [these two states occur].
This is because the two cases are equivalent: for one who perceives specific qualities such as a blue back due to proximity, there occurs the closing of the eyes;

and for one whose prior cognition of silver has been manifested by distance and other factors, there occurs the opening of the eyes in the form of a subsequent cognition, "This is not silver, it is only mother-of-pearl. Thus, the necessity of accepting this [subsequent sublation] is the same in both instances.

If it is argued that "error" (bhramatva) is simply the incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), we say no; for even a "sky-flower" (*gaganakusuma*) and the like possess the capacity for grammatical operation, since, by virtue of the rules of grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*), they enter into compounds characterized by "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) through the power of such semantic capacity. Thus, they would [erroneously] possess substantiality (*vastutva*).

It must indeed be accepted that [the object] is not to be admitted [as real], because it would follow that even the cognition of it would be erroneous; and consequently, even things like a sky-flower would,
like mother-of-pearl silver,
fall within the range of the eyes as "this," due to the lack of distinction between what is capable and what is incapable [of being perceived].
Because the Lord’s creative emission is diverse, it is based on a gradation of powers (*śakti*) imagined through His sovereignty.

This is because of the Śruti, "Both the real and the unreal became the Real," and the Smṛti, "I am both being and non-being, O Arjuna," which shows that everything is a mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānandaghana*). Therefore, [it is] ignorance (*avidyā*).
The doctrine that the world is illusory (*mithyātva*) has been refuted by the statement that [Brahman] is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the world.

For this very reason, the distinction between the insentient and the sentient produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), as expressed in the passage beginning with "of the object and the subject within the spheres of the notions of 'you' and 'I'," is also untenable. To explain:
Because no object of that [self-consciousness] is perceived— just like pleasure and so forth which are experienced apart from the notion "I"— and because the notion "I" is false;
for if it were inferred on the grounds that a cognition cannot otherwise be accounted for except by having an object, then [the self] would be unperceivable even to the inferrer.
Therefore, because that which [the opponent] considers to be consciousness is like the son of a barren woman,
and because it has been stated that the inner self (pratyagātman) is well-known— since it is the object of our own cognition and is directly perceived— such [an objection] is utterly trivial.

Furthermore, insentience (*jaḍatva*) is also impossible for that which is the object of the notion of "you" (*yuṣmat-pratyaya-gocara*), because when a dispute arises between Caitra and Maitra, it is observed that their cognition takes the form of "I" (*aham-prakāraka-bodha*) directed toward each other through the use of the second-person pronoun; thus, it has consciousness as its object. This...

This is also established by the force of such scriptural authorities as: "He created all this; this body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field (kṣetra). Furthermore, if the object of the notion of "you" were insentient, the instruction "That thou art" would apply only to something insentient. Therefore, since the notions of "you" and "I" have consciousness alone as their object.

Even one who argues that the inclusion of the word "you" (*yuṣmad*)—when it should have been said "this I" (*idamaham*)—is for the purpose of indicating absolute difference, is refuted; for there is no absolute difference between those two, since their object is the same, namely, consciousness. As it is said: "Never was I not, nor you, nor these lords of men; nor indeed shall we all ever cease to be hereafter."

Furthermore, because the Blessed One has subsumed all three persons— known as the highest, the middle, and the lowest— within the "we" (vayam) by including them within the scope of the notion of "I" (asmat-pratyaya),
there is consequently no relationship of object and subject between the spheres of the notions of "you" (tvam) and "I" (aham).
This is because it is impossible for there to be a difference in kind (*vaijātya*), since consciousness cannot be an object of another consciousness;

otherwise, it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), like a jar or other objects which are the objects of consciousness. Nor should it be argued that this rule does not apply because the validity of the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) with respect to the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) is accepted.

Because the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) rests within the cognizer, and because knowledge—unlike a jar or similar object—is never perceived as "this is it," it always transcends the status of being an object of cognition (*prameya*); for both the determinative cognition and the subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) have the jar alone as their object. This is the case with the subsequent reflective cognition.
Because it takes the form of becoming an object of the heart through the manifestation of determination (*vyavasāya*), one thinks, "This jar has been known by me.
Otherwise, one would have to admit the validity of another jar with respect to that [first] jar.
If this [cognition] were always restricted to the jar as delimited by the property of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), then it would never reside in the locus of the term "knowable" (*prameya*).

If it is argued that another pot is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [the perception of] a pot because it lacks the state of transcending it, this is equally applicable here as well; for since consciousness rests upon the knower, it never enters the category of an object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Therefore, the relationship of object and subject cannot possibly exist between two entities of the same class; otherwise, there would be no distinction at all between "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) and "object of knowledge" (*prameya*), because one would have to admit that even the valid cognition (*pramiti*) which constitutes the nature of the means of knowledge is itself an object of knowledge, and it is also accepted that valid cognition is the means of knowledge.

In this way, it is also impossible for the self (*ātman*) to be an object of knowledge (*prameya*), because it is the knower (*pramātṛ*). Otherwise, if it were also an object of knowledge, there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to its dependence on another knower; for the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower is constituted by their difference. For this very reason, there is also a contradiction between the objects of the cognitions "you" (*tvam*) and "I" (*aham*).

This is not possible, because consciousness is of a single nature and lacks the contradiction found between light and darkness. Even if you intend to imply that the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya) has the form of "this" (idaṃrūpa) through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), then [the object] which is the domain of the "this-notion"— being insentient— would be seen by me as "it is being observed by me" or "it appears to me."

Thus, because they appear as being mounted upon the self-luminous Self (*ātmaprakāśa*), there is no contradiction between them. In the same way, there is no contradiction even between light and darkness, for both of these also appear by depending upon the self-luminous Self. Otherwise, if there were a contradiction between them, their very manifestation would not occur. "By His light all this... [is illumined].
And because of the Vedic scripture: "It shines; everything shines only after it has shone.

Nor is there an impossibility of the mutual relationship between those two [the object and the cognition], since it must be accepted that the object of knowledge (prameya) comes to rest in the knower (pramātṛ) by way of the means of knowledge (pramā), as otherwise recollection (smṛti) would be inexplicable. It is not the case that recollection arises from latent impressions (saṃskāra) alone.
If that were so, then because that [cognition] also possesses an object, it would rest within itself (the self) together with that very object.
Furthermore, since it is impossible for a cognition of a perceived jar to rest within itself while the jar has already perished,
memory— which takes as its object a thing previously experienced— cannot exist merely by virtue of being accompanied by the objectivity of that [past] thing.

It must be stated that [consciousness] arises from the mental formation (*saṃskāra*), because objectivity (*viṣayatā*) is a property of the object, and without that [object], its coexistence [with consciousness] is impossible. If the identity of those two were not established, then the cognition "this is a jar" would not manifest, because it would be external to illumination, like darkness outside of light. Nor is this the case...
It cannot be argued that, like a pot external to light, [the self] can be an object of illumination;

for according to such scriptural passages as "from the Self, space was produced," each subsequent element is the effect of its preceding element, and thus, by the analogy of the clay and the pot, there is an identity between those two through a continuous causal series.
Moreover, if consciousness (*caitanya*) is delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),

then because it would reside only in the region occupied by the internal organ, and because the consciousness delimited by an object would reside only in the region occupied by that object, there would be no connection between the two. Nor can this be resolved through the medium of a mental modification (*vṛtti*).

It must be stated that a connection is possible because, although there is a state of complete unification (*ekalolībhāva*) between the consciousness delimited by the mental mode (*vṛtti*) and the consciousness delimited by the object upon accepting the threefold nature of consciousness, there is no such unification between the embodied self delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the consciousness delimited by the object.
Because that [consciousness], being non-transformable, cannot go outside along with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
and because consciousness is a quality of the self, even if a distinction is perceived due to a difference in location— arising from a division in consciousness—
it cannot [be related] through conjunction or inherence with substances that are qualities belonging to another.

Because, due to the absence of contact, it is impossible for blue and other objects to possess the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*) and for cognition to possess the status of being a subject (*viṣayitva*).

Furthermore, according to the aforementioned reasoning, since [the self] would be devoid of the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, it would follow that one’s own scripture is rendered useless; and because Brahman is without distinction, [one might think]: "I am," "I shine," or "I am joyful."

Thus, because [the mind] is insentient— like the light of a crystal and so forth— due to its being empty of the radiance of a mind that possesses its own existence and the sequence of non-objective activity within the ultimate, and because the sublation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by means of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is accepted;
Because it would result in the subversion of the proposition taught in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad that the knowledge of all things arises from the knowledge of one thing,

and because, in the passage "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman," Brahman alone devoid of attributes is indicated as the object of inquiry, and since that [Brahman] is devoid of agency and other such qualities...

Because the authors of the treatises do not accept a definition of the subject matter that has not been specifically indicated, and because for that very reason, the unique definition of "the origination of the world" and so forth mentioned in the immediately preceding sūtra is also incoherent.

In brief, because the subsequent scripture begins with the words "Since [Brahman] has the sacred teaching as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*), and because [the opponent's position] is thus rendered ineffective, that which was stated by them is to be disregarded by learned authorities.
Regarding this, the authors of the *Kriyāsāra* further describe it as follows: "Now, therefore, by some... [and so on].

In the phrase "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*), superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is indeed elaborated as being based on the Sūtras themselves. Nor should it be argued that because the first Sūtra indicates the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), and because the subject matter— characterized by the identity of the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—
and the knowledge thereof depend upon superimposition, therefore that [superimposition] must likewise be based on the Sūtras here.

Because the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman does not exist at all, it cannot be accepted as the subject matter [of the inquiry]. Indeed, the identity of the essential nature of the *jīva* and Brahman is nowhere aphorized (*sūtrita*); on the contrary, in the sūtra "A part [of Brahman], because of the designation of multiplicity" (*aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt*), the *jīva*— [Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated. The translation reflects the available portion.]
It has been stated that a portion (*aṃśa*) of Brahman is both distinct and non-distinct, like sparks from a fire.

For there is no identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) between fire and its sparks, such that by that analogy the same [identity] could exist between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. Nor is it the case that...

It must be said that because difference and non-difference are contradictory and cannot coexist in one place, what is stated there is merely a false difference produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) characterized as ignorance (*avidyā*); for [the scripture] provides both designations, like a serpent and its coils, or like light and its substratum, or due to its being luminosity— as in the previous case— there are both permission and avoidance.

Because of the connection with a body, there is an attainment of the nature [of the deity] like that of light and so forth, as is logical; and there is an "entering" (āveśa) like that of a lamp, for thus the scripture shows— since both difference and non-difference are established by valid means of knowledge and are clearly observed in the illustrative examples, it is precisely non-contradiction that is established.
And so it will be stated in that very same place:

"If it be argued that there would be no distinction because of the eater's becoming [the eaten], it is not so, for it is as in the world. Here too, the absence of contradiction is established. For this sūtra has been explained by them in this manner, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, the doctrine of Brahmā as the cause is refuted by the power of reasoning alone. Although scripture is authoritative with respect to its own domain, nevertheless, when that domain is sublated by another means of valid cognition, it must be understood as having another purpose, just as is the case with mantras and arthavādas.

Reasoning (*tarka*) too would be non-conclusive regarding anything other than its own specific object, as is the case with *dharma* and *adharma*. What follows from this? If it is so, then it is improper that the Veda should subvert an object established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But how can an object established by another means of valid cognition be subverted by the Veda?

To this it is replied: This distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is indeed well-established in the world; the enjoyer is the conscious embodied self, and the objects of enjoyment are sound and the other sense-objects, just as Devadatta is the enjoyer and the rice is the object of enjoyment.
And the non-existence of this distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed would follow [as a consequence] if the enjoyer...
The object of enjoyment would attain the state of the enjoyer, or the enjoyer would attain the state of the object of enjoyment;
for these two, the mutual attainment of each other's states would result from the absence of non-difference from Brahman, the supreme cause. And this well-known distinction [would not exist].

Obstruction is logical; for just as the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is observed in the present, so too must it be postulated for the past and the future. Therefore, it is untenable [to deny this], as it would entail the non-existence of this well-established distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
If someone should raise the objection that this establishes Brahman as the sole cause, one should say to him:

"It may be so, as in the world. This distinction is indeed possible even in our view, because it is observed to be so in the world. For instance, although [the foam] is non-different from the ocean, which consists of water, [it still appears distinct].

The mutual distinction and the worldly transaction characterized by mutual conjunction and so forth among its modifications— such as foam, waves, and the like— are indeed perceived; yet this is not the case even though those modifications are non-different from the ocean, which is of the nature of water.

The foam, waves, and so forth undergo mutual transformation into one another; yet, even though they do not undergo mutual transformation, they do not cease to be non-different from the ocean, which is essentially water. It is the same here as well:
there is no mutual transformation between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, nor is there any difference between them and Brahman, whose nature is Being.
"It will be so. But is this justification for non-contradiction not merely a *abhyupagamavāda* (an argument based on a provisional admission),

since it contradicts the Sūtra, "The non-difference [of the effect from the cause] follows from such words as 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*)," and the scriptural passage beginning with "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*)?

If it is argued that this is because the sublated nature of the entire manifold of difference (*bhedaprapañca*) has been established, we say no; for by this sūtra, the sublated nature of the entire manifold is not established. To explain:
the manifold of difference established by means of valid cognition such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) cannot be sublated by scripture (*śruti*).

Because when there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is observed that the scriptures themselves have another purpose; for example, in the injunction "one should cook a *kṛṣṇala*," since the literal sense of a gold bean is sublated by direct perception, the injunction has the purpose of merely making it hot; or as in "one should sacrifice with *soma*," [the word *soma* refers to the act] of sacrificing.

Since it is accepted that "one should bring about [the result]" is the meaning, when there is a grammatical coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "by means of Soma" and "by means of sacrifice," the identity between the Soma-plant and the sacrifice is contradicted by direct perception. Therefore, in the expression "by means of a sacrifice possessed of Soma," the word *Soma* is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to that which is related to it; this is precisely why others also [hold this view].

In the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), because the identity of the literal meanings (*vācyārtha*) is contradicted by perception, it is accepted that the sentence intends the identity of the indicated meanings (*lakṣyārtha*).
Furthermore, if the sublation of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were admitted, then [the sublation] of the very nature of the Śruti itself would follow.

Since the recollection of the objects produced by that [sublation] and the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence are themselves included within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), if they too are sublated, how can the sublation of the phenomenal world be established? Or how could there not be a contradiction—like saying "my mother is barren" or "I have no tongue"—even when the phenomenal world is sublated? Nor is it the case that...
It must be stated that its own nature (svarūpa) indeed persists, and therefore its effects also arise;

for the designation "non-existence" (abhāva) regarding that which does not negate its counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is merely a technical convention (paribhāṣā). Nor is the nature of the phenomenal world (prapañca) sublated by scripture, such that there would be a contradiction; rather, [it is only its reality that is negated].

It must be stated that [the world] possesses reality; for since the absence of sublation of its own nature entails the acceptance of reality—in the form of being unsublated—even with respect to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the sublation of its reality is likewise untenable. Therefore, it is not by this [argument] that the sublation of the phenomenal world is established, but rather its non-difference [from Brahman]; thus, there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference.
It has been established.
Likewise, in another place as well, [it was argued] that "because of the designation of the other, there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial, and so forth.
However, because of the designation of non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), [the world] has Brahman as its agent.

Anticipating the objection that since creation is performed by the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, the soul would create only what is beneficial for itself and not what is harmful, such as hell and the like, it is stated [in the Sūtra] "But more than that, because of the designation of difference" (*adhikaṃ tu bhedanirdeśāt*) that the soul is not the agent; rather, the agent is Brahman, who is superior to it, and He indeed creates even that which is harmful to the soul. If this is so—

If there is no difference [between the Lord and the individual souls], how can there be a state of inferiority and superiority? Furthermore, how could the Lord—who, through omniscience, perceives all living beings as his own self—create sorrow, delusion, and so forth in them? For it would follow that he himself would experience sorrow and the like as his own states. Anticipating this objection, [the author says]: "And like a stone, etc. (aśmādivacca).
By the phrase "the impossibility of that," it is meant that just as in the case of stones such as lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) and sun-crystals (*sūryakānta*),

although there is no difference in their common nature as being stone, there is a diversity of intrinsic forms and a diversity of effects due to the differences between individual instances— consisting of inferior, middling, and superior natures— in the same way, this applies to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) as well.
It has been stated that the relationship of deficiency or excess and the diversity of effects are possible due to the difference between individuals (*vyakti*).

Nor should it be argued that because the generality (*sāmānya*) of "stoneness" is non-different while the individuals are indeed different, there is no coexistence of difference and non-difference in a single locus.

This is because non-difference, in the form of the absence of difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the generality of "stoneness," as well as difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by "lapis lazuli-ness" and so forth, are both admitted to reside only in individual instances (*vyakti*).
Nor does it follow that there would likewise be the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even between a diamond and lapis lazuli.

Because that [cognition] which expresses non-difference through a universal must necessarily be accepted, and because there is no non-difference of particulars; for this very reason, even in the case of God, the vision of non-difference from the individual soul is established as "by way of selfhood alone," as in the statement: "They approach Him as the Self, and they cause others to grasp Him as the Self. And for this same reason, it has been stated by others as well:
Setting aside the aspect of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) which corresponds to the individual,

the non-difference of consciousness alone— which corresponds to the universal— is accepted. And thus, although the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is characterized by the absence of difference, [it nevertheless occurs].

Alternatively, the object is the specific nature (*svarūpa*). Nevertheless, where there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apprehending difference in every respect, identity of nature is the object, as in cases such as "This is that Devadatta.
However, where there is a means of valid cognition apprehending difference, as in the case of cause and effect and so forth, [the object is the specific nature].

The object [of knowledge] is either the two natures characterized by the absence of difference in their delimiters of existence (*pṛthaksattāvacchedaka*), or the two natures characterized by the absence of generality (*sāmānya*). And in the present context, through the statement that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" in the passage "Did you ask for that instruction? (*uta tam ādeśam aprākṣyaḥ*), the state of being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*) [is established].

Just as the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), though repeated nine times in the explanatory text following the initial proposition— "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*)—
does not take as its object the identity of the essential natures (*svarūpa-ekya*) of Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), so it is with the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

As for the designation [of difference], since the designation of both difference and non-difference is equal in both cases, there is the negation of difference in such passages as "There is no other seer than this," "Where one sees nothing else," and "From which nothing higher exists. This [negation] occurs through the distinctions of sentience and insentience, and of being in saṃsāra and not being in saṃsāra.

Furthermore, since the possession of contradictory properties is equal in both cases, both difference and non-difference are established through the negation of difference and the demonstration of difference respectively. Therefore, there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference.
As for what was said—that the false distinction is produced by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) characterized as ignorance—that is not correct;
for nowhere has it been stated in the Sūtras that ignorance is such an adjunct, nor that its status as an adjunct is illusory.

Nor can it be argued [that this is implied] by the Sūtra "And [the self is] inferable for some," because [the Sūtra] shows that [the self] is grasped through the metaphorical representation of the body. And [the Sūtra] further demonstrates [this].

Regarding the statement "But that [Self] is subtle because of its fitness," it should be stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) was indicated by the aphorism. In that context, concerning the passage "The Unmanifested is beyond the Great," there may arise the doubt that by the word "Unmanifested" (*avyakta*) the *pradhāna* consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) is meant; therefore, by the phrase "because of the grasping of what was set forth as the metaphor of the body," [it is shown that] the Self is the chariot-rider.

Having stated that in the mantra "Know the body to be the chariot itself," it is the body alone that is designated as the chariot and not *pradhāna*, [the author] addresses the inquiry: "Since the body is manifest (*vyakta*), how can it be unmanifest (*avyakta*)? In response to this, he says: "But it is subtle (*sūkṣma*) because of its fitness for that."

By this [statement], it is said that the subtle body alone is grasped by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*), and not the gross body; for the three-guṇa *avidyā* is not grasped by the word "unmanifest," since when a well-known subtle body is available, it is improper to resort to an unfamiliar *avidyā*. Regarding *avidyā*:

Furthermore, since you accept that [the Self] pervades the cosmic egg by virtue of being its material cause (*upādāna*), and since it is perceived by everyone as "I am ignorant," it is untenable for it to possess subtlety or to be worthy of the designation "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). Otherwise, if it were stated in the subsequent [sūtra] that "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is grasped by the term "unmanifest," after having previously stated in the preceding sūtra that the "body" is grasped by that same term; [then there would be a contradiction].

Because that would lead to a contradiction and result in the doctrine of Pradhāna [being primary]. Nor should it be argued that the distinction was stated by the phrase "it is purposeful because it is dependent on that," implying that Pradhāna is independent while Ignorance (avidyā) is dependent on Īśvara;
for such is the view of the Sāṅkhyas who accept a Lord (Seśvara-sāṅkhya) and of the Yogins.

Since it is admitted that even *pradhāna* is dependent upon the Lord, its distinctness [from the Self] is not established by that much alone; for just as objects are superior to the senses because the activity of the senses is dependent on the objects,
so too the body is superior to the Self because the activity of the Self is dependent on the body.

This is because the meaning of the sūtra is precisely "otherness" (*paratva*). Furthermore, if ignorance (*avidyā*) were intended here by the sūtra, then the subsequent section would not need to be commenced, since that very [ignorance] is also addressed in the *ajā* mantra.

Because there is no specific reason for the primary [meaning] to be grasped when it could be grasped in a secondary sense, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) does not arise; on the contrary, since it was stated previously that "the power of the divine Self is concealed by its own qualities" (devātmaśaktiṃ svaguṇairnigūḍhām), and later that "one should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara" (māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyān māyinaṃ tu maheśvaram).

Because the dependence of *prakṛti* upon Īśvara is established by the passage beginning with "Maheśvara," it is logical that even in the *ajā-mantra* (the verse concerning the unborn), the reference must be to that very same [Īśvara]. Likewise, [the Sūtras] state: "But because it begins with light, for thus some read; and because there is instruction through metaphorical representation, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth."

In every respect, [this interpretation] would be untenable; for since ignorance (*avidyā*), which has been without beginning, can be grasped by the word "unborn" (*ajā*) both because it is the primary meaning and because it is the subject under discussion, one should not abandon that and instead take the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) characterized by fire, water, and food as the referent of the word "unborn" merely in accordance with another Vedic branch.

In response to the objection that the word "Unborn" (*ajā*) is inappropriate because it lacks birth (*ajani*) and thus lacks the state of being unborn (*ajātvābhāva*), [the answer is: just as the sun, though not actually honey, is metaphorically conceived as honey in the passage "That sun is indeed the honey of the gods," so too is it with the Unborn.

Since it is impossible to conceive of the "unborn" (ajā) as being like the "unborn" [Brahman] when its nature consists of fire, water, and earth, primordial ignorance—which is beginningless—cannot be intended by the Sūtra as something distinct from the nature characterized by fire, water, and earth; nor does it exist, for there is a lack of evidence. Furthermore, without ignorance, [the creation] of that which is partless...

It should not be argued that the transformation of the world from Brahman is untenable, because this very objection has been raised and refuted by the Sūtra itself in the passage beginning with "If [Brahman were to transform], it would follow that the whole [is transformed], or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding its being partless" (BS 2.1.26).
For indeed, what is called "transformation" (pariṇāma) consists in the abandonment of the previous form of things...

Regarding this transformation into another form, it must be stated: does Brahman transform in its entirety, or does it transform with one part while remaining as it is with the other parts? In the first case, Brahman would not exist at the time of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because the whole would have abandoned its own nature and assumed the form of the effect. In the latter case...

Having raised the objection that this would contradict the scriptural texts concerning partlessness (*niravayavatva*), it is resolved by the principle that "Scripture, however, is rooted in the Word" (*śruteḥ śabdamūlatvāt*). Thus, while such reasoning has scope regarding matters accessible through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
when a matter is to be understood solely through Scripture, its true nature must be established by Scripture alone, and not by reasoning.

There is a purpose for this, as it has been said: "Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be joined with logical reasoning. Furthermore, the Śruti declares that Brahman, being partless, undergoes transformation while abandoning its solid nature.
For instance, after describing the creation of fire, water, and food (earth), the scripture immediately thereafter states: "This [was then]..."

The Deity thought: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms. And thus, apart from the transformation characterized by fire, water, and food, there exists the Supreme Lord who is the seer.

A separate state has been described. Even in the world, transformation (*pariṇāma*) is not the assumption of another form through the abandonment of a previous form; for when the material cause (*upādāna*) has perished, a transformation that lacks a substratum is impossible.
Rather, while the material cause remains exactly as it was, [the effect] is non-different from it.

It has been stated that transformation (*pariṇāma*) is simply the arising of an effect capable of practical function (*vyavahāra-yogya*), just as motion and so forth occur in an arrow; and this is likewise the case for the Self, as expressed in the phrase "and thus manifold indeed. Just as in the individual soul (*jīvātman*), there are various specific transformations such as intellect (*buddhi*), desire (*icchā*), and so on, without any sublation of the essential nature of the soul itself.
Just as jars, cloth, and so forth arise from clay, threads, and the like, there is this distinction:

where another effect exists at the time of production, it exists there precisely as something capable of being produced; and in that case, the production of the jar and so forth occurs through the destruction [of the cause]. But where...

There is no other effect that is contradictory [to the cause]; rather, in that case, the production of another effect occurs precisely through the sublation of the absence [of the previous state], just as the production of a cloth from threads occurs precisely through the sublation of the absence of the cloth [in the threads]. Even in the case of a sprout and so forth, the seed and such are not the material cause (*upādāna*), because they do not persist in the effect; for only that which persists in the effect is the material cause.

Rather, they are merely parts permeated by both. Thus says the Śruti: "O dear one, it is from this very subtle atom that such a great banyan tree stands. And these [parts] possess the capacity to produce sprouts and so forth precisely without the destruction of their own essential nature. And this was stated by the Author of the Sūtras in the Tarkapāda:

"Because it is not seen [to arise] from what is non-existent. This has been explained by them in exactly that same way. Thus, the transformation of the world from Brahman—which is partless—is logically established without any impairment to its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, the refutation of the opposing position has been stated [in the verse]: "And because of the faults in our own position," as well as regarding the *pradhāna* and the qualities such as *sattva*.

If transformation were total, it would entail the destruction of the original nature; if, on the other hand, partial transformation is admitted, it contradicts the admission that [the cause] is partless. This same defect applies equally to ignorance (*avidyā*), since ignorance is equal in status to *pradhāna*. Nor can it be said of ignorance...
It should not be said that transformation is impossible for Brahman because of its association with diverse powers;

for the scripture states, "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold," and the Sūtra, "And [Brahman] is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen," establishes that Brahman alone possesses diverse powers. As for ignorance (avidyā) [it is as follows]:...
And because there is no evidence for such a power.

Thus, even though the meaning of the Sūtra is established as the transformation of Brahman (*brahmapariṇāma*), the statement that "ignorance transforms" (*avidyā pariṇamate*) and "Brahman undergoes illusory appearance" (*brahma vivartate*) is untenable; furthermore, it contradicts the Sūtra: "Because of the self-made [nature], [it is] a transformation" (*ātmakṛteḥ pariṇāmāt*). If only ignorance transforms and not Brahman, then [the Sūtra would have to say] "na... [and so on].

The section [of the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*] stating that "because this [world] is of a different nature, its being such [as Brahman] is known from scripture" would be untenable, because there would be no difference between ignorance (*avidyā*) and the world; furthermore, it is not accepted that Brahman undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Moreover, if some so-called ignorance established from beginningless time were to be resorted to, then of that—
Since there would be no non-difference from Brahman due to the absence of being a modification of Brahman, even if Brahman were known, that [avidyā] would not be known;
thus, the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" would be contradicted.
Therefore, avidyā does not exist at all, nor is the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) merely adventitious (aupādhika). And for this very reason...

It should not be said that the fact of being conditioned (*aupādhikatva*) is indicated in some places by the comparison "as from the sun" (*sūryakādivat*); for in that context, it is not the conditioned nature of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) that is indicated, but rather the atomicity (*aṇutva*) of Brahman itself through such passages as "smaller than the smallest" and "greater than the greatest."

In response to the doubt that both [attributes] exist because of the perception of greatness and so forth, [the Sūtra] states: "Not even on account of place does the Supreme possess both characteristics;

for everywhere [it is one]. Having stated that two contradictory forms cannot possibly exist in this Brahman due to its unity, [it continues] that because the fields (kṣetra) have different dimensions, even though [Brahman] has entered within them...

The example "like the sun [in water]" is adduced regarding the appearance of the Supreme Self as having a different dimension. In this case, because both the water and the sun are material substances and possess color-form (*rūpa*), the reflection is possible there; however, because Brahman is immaterial and lacks color-form, a reflection is impossible.

Having raised the objection with the words, "But [the soul] is not like that, because its perception is like that of water in a vessel" (*pattiriti ambuvadagrahaṇāttu na tathātvaṃ*), [the author replies:

"For here, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is not intended to be based on the relationship of original object and reflection; rather, the meaning is precisely this: that there is merely the appearance of Brahman itself having a dimension corresponding to the dimensions of the various fields (*kṣetra*)."

It has been made clear by the presentation of the illustration that what is intended is the participation in increase and decrease through internal inclusion, because of the consistency of both [cases] in this way. Therefore, there is no state of being qualified by difference. For this very reason, there is a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), who have entered within one and the same [reality].
