For it is established in passages such as "The two, the individual self and the Supreme Self, are indeed taught therein because they are seen there" that the distinction between the individual self (jīva) and the Supreme (para) is innate;
therefore, there is no identity of essential nature between the individual self and the Supreme, nor is such identity the subject matter of the scripture.

Furthermore, if the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) were the subject matter of the scripture, then that alone would be established in every section (*adhikaraṇa*). But it is not so established; rather, in each section, given the doubt as to whether the individual soul or the Lord is being taught by this or that statement, it is the individual soul that is [initially] presented.

Having established the prima facie view, it is then demonstrated that because the attributes taught by those respective passages cannot possibly belong to the individual soul (jīva), a Lord distinct from it is what is being taught; for "it cannot be another, as that is untenable" (na itaraḥ, anupapatteḥ).

"And [the Self] is other [than the individual soul] because of the designation of difference. If it be argued that [it is] not so because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), we say no; because of the threefold nature of meditation, because [the soul] has resorted [to the vital breath], and because of the connection with those [marks] here [in this context]. "Because of the distinction in deep sleep and departure [from the body].
"But because of the impossibility [of the attributes], it is not the embodied soul. "And because of the designation of the object and the agent of action. "And because of Smṛti."

[The opponent argues: "No, because of the distinction in terms, because of its having a small abode, and because of the designation as such. [The reply is: "If this is said, it is not so; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like space (the ether). [The opponent says: "In that case, there would be the attainment of enjoyment [of the world]. [The reply is: "No, because of the difference in nature. "It cannot be the other [the individual soul], because of non-abiding and impossibility. "And the embodied soul [is not the Self], for both [recensions] indeed teach him as distinct."
And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, [the two others] are not [the Self]; nor is the individual soul (prāṇabhṛt). Because of the designation of difference;
because of the context; and because of abiding and eating. He is [Brahman] because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing.

If it be argued that "He is [the individual soul] because of the reference to the other," we say no, because of impossibility. If it be argued that it is from what follows, [we reply] that his true nature has indeed become manifest.

And the reference [to the soul] has another purpose. If it is argued that "the soul is not atomic because of scriptural statement to that effect," we say no, because of the context of something else. Furthermore, "because of the designation of difference," and "because of the teaching of something greater, Bādarāyaṇa's view is thus, for that is seen," and so forth. Nor is it the case that the soul, being conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is taught merely in that conditioned form.

It is being negated; however, it must be stated that this is not by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*). For if it were so, since the Lord is characterized by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), He would not be established even in that form. Only His essential nature (*svarūpamātra*) would be established as being intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). Yet, He is not established in that manner; for in the case of establishing Him...

Because of the impossibility of such a cause; rather, [the Self] is taught solely in the form of Lordship (īśvaratva) as distinguished from the individual soul (jīva), by such means as "because of the teaching of its attributes within" and "because of the designation of those attributes in the passages concerning the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) with respect to the divine and so forth. Therefore, the identity of the essential nature of the individual soul and Brahman is not the subject matter of the scripture.

Nor is this the purpose [of the treatise], because it has been stated otherwise— namely, that [the Lord's activity] is excluded from the world-activity due to the context, its non-proximity, and the indicative mark of similarity in only a portion, and so forth. Therefore, it is established that superimposition (adhyāsa) is not enshrined as a topic in the aphorisms, because it is of no utility regarding either the subject matter or the purpose.
Thus, by the aphorism "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]," the characteristic of Brahman as the cause of the world was stated.

When the question arises as to what kind of causality that is, it was stated— by the aphorism beginning with "And [it is] the material cause, because of the consistency with the promise and the illustrative examples"— that it possesses both the nature of an efficient cause (nimittatva) and a material cause (upādānatva).
Thus, while it has been stated in the Sūtra that Brahman alone is the twofold cause, some have asserted that ignorance (avidyā) is the material cause (upādāna);
others that the five subtle elements (sūkṣmabhūta-pañcaka) are the material cause; and still others that primordial matter (prakṛti) is the material cause.
Thus, this mention of another [type of] appropriation is disconnected from the Sūtra.

Therefore, since the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) appears merely superficially attractive due to its lack of consistency with the context of the aphorisms of Vyāsa— which are directed toward non-duality as their ultimate purport—
it must indeed be disregarded by the Vīraśaivas who know the truth and understand the connection between words and their meanings.

Now, since the Vīraśaiva Siddhānta must be established as being distinct from all forms of dualism, it consists of the non-duality of Śiva qualified by Śakti, which is of the nature of a transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*) characterized by the perfect identity (*sāmarasya*) of the Liṅga and the body (*liṅgāṅga*).

Since the non-dual framework propounded by the proponents of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) is dependent upon superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and has been refuted, and since no means of establishing a non-duality other than that [superimposition] is perceived, the very establishment of the non-duality one intends would not be achieved; for [such a non-duality depends on] ignorance (*avidyā*), which consists of false cognition and serves as the material cause of the universe.
Because it is not accepted [that Brahman is the material cause], because transformation is impossible given that Brahman is changeless,
because it would entail defects such as being subject to modification,
because there is no other external material cause for illumination, and because it would contradict the doctrine of non-duality (advaita).
In this regard, here is the *Sārasvatasūtra*, which illuminates the heart by way of its essential conformity with the path of Śivādvaita as favored by the Vīraśaivas.
"The agent becomes dependent upon the act of becoming;
that very act of reflective awareness (vimarśa), whether abiding in itself or agitated, is the expansion of the universe. Thus [it is said].

This is its meaning: being the light of the heart, it is to be accepted. For the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* states, "One should know that heart to be the great abode of the universe"; here, by the word "heart," the Self manifesting within the heart is intended. (As stated in the *Chāndogya*: "He is within the heart.")

Keeping in mind the etymological derivation of the word *hṛdaya*, the author of the *Śivādvaitamañjarī*, while commenting on this sūtra, cites the scriptural passage: "One should know that as the heart. [He explains that] it is the Supreme Lord who shines forth within the heart.

The commentator has provided the explanation that "it exists as having the nature of Being. By the two words "Being" (*sat*) and "the illumination of the Heart" (*hṛdayaprakāśa*), both its nature as Being and its nature as Consciousness (*cit*) are encompassed. Otherwise, if its nature as Being were not admitted, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the loss of existence for the speaker himself—for it is his own [existence]...

Because there is no difference from Brahman. The meaning of the *Ṭīkā* is that if one does not accept the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa-rūpatva*), there would be a state of ignorance regarding the world—a lack of apprehension with respect to any object whatsoever. A scriptural passage in support of this is: "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent; if he knows that 'Brahman exists,' him [the knower] they regard as existent."
Regarding the phrase "then [it is] known": one should not be deluded into thinking that no scriptural citation was provided for the aspect of luminosity (*prakāśa*);

for the previously cited scripture, beginning with "That is the heart," intends to show its nature as luminosity in accordance with the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*. For this very reason, blissfulness (*ānandatva*) is established through the state of consciousness (*cittva*) in the root aphorism.

Since it has already been largely stated that the *Ānanda-śruti* was cited in the *Ṭīkā*, there is no inconsistency with the present context. The *Ānanda-śruti* states: "Other beings subsist on only a fraction of this very bliss.

Now, regarding the point that one becomes an agent by being dependent upon the action of becoming—that is, one becomes the substratum (*āśraya*) of the action of becoming—[this is explained as follows].
The intention of the commentator is stated: [the word] *asa* is derived from the verbal root *as* (to exist) with the suffixes *śn* and *as*, where by the rule *allopo 'naḥ* the *a* is elided;
then, by the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāv aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied, resulting in the form *sann*.
Thinking that this word *sann* serves as a reminder (*pratyabhijñāpaka*) of the Vedic scripture, "If one knows that Brahman exists" (*asti brahmeti ced veda*), [he says] *asa*.
The word "on earth" (*bhuvi*) has been explained as being the locus for the action of becoming (*bhavana*), which is established by its meaning in the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*).

Now, one might object: "By the commentator who desires to establish the non-duality of Śiva (*śivādvaita*), duality itself has been established—this according to the maxim: 'While intending to fashion an elephant, he instead produced a monkey. This is seen in cases such as *pacati* ('he cooks')."

If it is argued that— since the mutual distinction between the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), the action (*kriyā*), and the agent (*kartṛ*) is established through linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), this distinction must necessarily be asserted even in the present case of the word *asti*— we say: not so, because [this rule] applies elsewhere.

In cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), although there is a distinction [between the meanings of the root and the suffix], in the present context—such as in *asti* ("it exists") and so forth—one must assert the non-difference between the action denoted by the verbal root and the agent denoted by the suffix, because that difference is sublated by the lack of empirical observation; otherwise, there would be no way to account for the usage, and thus there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*). For this very reason, in expressions such as *kūlaṃ pipatiṣati* ("the bank wishes to fall"), [the same principle applies].

The meaning of the suffix *san* has been abandoned; in examples such as "he knows" (*jānāti*), the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has been abandoned. Bearing this in mind, he says: "The suffix *san* exists only as a manifestation of the heart," and so forth. By the explanation "because it is the locus of the action of becoming" (*bhavanakriyāśrayatvāt*), the distinction between the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) in the present context is resolved. [The agent (*kartṛ*)...]
By the word "bhavati" (it exists), the difference between the meaning of the verbal root and the operation denoted by the verb suffix is set aside.

Now, what is the proof for the non-duality of Śiva? The proof is the experience of existence, consciousness, and bliss through their co-referentiality with the "I-consciousness," expressed as: "In this light, I rejoice."

Otherwise, there would be no distinction between Brahman and inert matter (*jaḍa*). For instance, in such expressions as "fire exists" or "it shines," the fact that inertness is established by experience— due to the lack of reference to the inner self (*pratyagātman*)— is the very nature of inertness.

And since difference exists in fire and other such things, the experience must be stated as "I am manifest" in order to distinguish [the self] from insentient objects. This being the case, the knowledge whose object is manifestation would be merely a distinct cognition— just like the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that has the knowledge of a jar as its object— and not [the manifestation itself].

When the doubt arises as to whether there is the establishment of the non-duality of Śiva (*śivādvaitasiddhi*), that very same [doubt] is resolved by the commentary beginning with "the action itself is established in its own state" (*svasthā ca*), which addresses the distinction caused by reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).

This is because the reflective awareness, which is of the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*), encompasses the action through the use of the pronoun "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "there is the action, that very [one]."

The purport of both the *Ṭīkā* and the root text is that there is no difference between the meaning of the word (*śabda*) and the performance of action (*arthakriyā*). By this very mode of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) accompanied by verbal expression, the fact that the non-duality of Śiva (*śivādvaita*) is supported by valid means of knowledge has already been stated;
thus, the non-duality of Śiva is established in this *Prakāśa* through such statements as "I rejoice" (*nandāmi*) and so forth. Likewise...

Furthermore, the ultimate conclusion of both the *Ṭīkā* and the root text (*Mūla*) is that during the state of the Supreme Self’s composure, it abides as the very nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), and even the powers such as Consciousness (*cit*) abide in their causal form. If [the power] is agitated and oriented toward creation, it is indeed perceived—as the text says: "it is seen" (*dṛśyate tu*).

Just as a scorpion or other creature may arise from cow dung by virtue of the presence of the *brahmasūtra*, so too does the manifestation of the manifold universe—consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) from Śiva down to the Earth—come into being.
For it is said: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are His inherent nature."

And because of the charm of the particle *ca* (and) situated in the scripture, which illuminates meanings not explicitly stated, we understand that the supreme power (*parā śakti*), which constitutes the very nature of Maheśvara,
possesses various forms such as consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). Nor is it the case that...

Because of the Vedic scripture stating, "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear— all this is indeed the mind," desire and the other qualities are attributes of the mind; for this very reason.
It might be asked: "Since [desire and so forth] are experienced as being inherent in the body, how can they be the very nature of the Self?
To this we reply: even the Naiyāyikas and others accept that desire and other qualities belong to the Lord (Īśvara) even though He is bodiless; otherwise, [their system would be inconsistent].

Furthermore, it would follow that [the Self] is non-distinct from jars and other such objects. Moreover, because there is a rule of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between inquiry, bondage, and liberation, it would follow that liberation belongs either to the mind or to that which is qualified by it;
for both of these are false with respect to the substratum (*viśeṣya*) qualified by inquiry and bondage. Regarding the part qualified by inquiry and bondage...

Even "liberation" (mokṣa) cannot be predicated [of the Self], because that would entail the fallacy of attributing distinct substrates (vaiyadhikaraṇya). For if the qualifier and the qualified were identical, liberation would be impossible due to its being characterized by falsity (mithyātva).
Therefore, in the demonstration of the manifestation of the mind through the desire and other attributes of the artificial knower (kṛtrima-pramātṛ):

Since it must be accepted that this is the intended meaning of the scripture, there is no contradiction; furthermore, because another scriptural passage— “In Him all desires are contained”— uses the prefix *sam-* with its inherent force, it is understood that [desires] constitute the very nature of the Self.

This being the case, there is never any agitation (*vikṣobha*) in that state regarding consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*), because their nature is non-sequential (*akrama*). This is because the powers such as Will (*icchā*) and the rest possess a sequential and non-sequential nature, and thus are subject to agitation. Nor should it be said that there is a contradiction between the sequential and the non-sequential, for to say so would involve a self-contradiction (*vyāghāta*). There is indeed a contradiction between difference (*bheda*) and non-difference (*abheda*).

Thus, it must be stated that this is known precisely because, upon its cognition, both the objects in the form of difference and non-difference appear; for that [cognition] possesses an object. Otherwise, there would be no manifestation of contradiction at all. Therefore, due to the absence of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the manifestation itself—

Furthermore, it is only a difference based on mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) that is contradicted by non-difference; we do not assert such a difference, because it is impossible. For in that case, it would be untenable for otherness (*anyatva*) to be the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a category (*padārtha*), as it would entail the absurd consequence that a category is different from itself. Nor...
It should not be argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because the nature of a thing consists in its difference from other things;

for since that [nature] is constituted by specific qualities, it is not the subject of the question, whereas it is precisely the "difference" that constitutes the general definition of distinction which is the subject of the question. Furthermore:

The specific cognition that "the nature of the cloth is its difference from the jar" and "the nature of the jar is its difference from the cloth" is only possible once the difference between the jar and the cloth has been established; therefore,

because that [difference] remains something whose nature is yet to be desired [as proven], [the argument] cannot [be sustained] by means of such properties as being composed of threads or being made of clay.

It must be stated that the difference between these two is established, because even the certainty that "the jar alone possesses the nature of being made of clay" and "the cloth alone possesses the nature of being made of threads" occurs only after the difference between the jar and the cloth has been established. Furthermore, there is indeed a difference between the nature of being made of threads and the nature of being made of clay, owing to the difference between their respective constituent parts.

The distinction between its parts [arises] from the distinction between those parts; thus, when one investigates down to the limit of atoms, because they are partless and beyond the senses, no distinction can be apprehended therein. Consequently, since this would lead to the destruction of the root [of the argument] and the fallacy of infinite regress, there is no otherness.
Difference is not based on some limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because since difference would then be merely a mental construction, it would entail fallacies such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
Rather, we maintain that difference is simply division, according to the analogy of gold and a bracelet. In that case, the bracelet is the gold.

Because it is impossible to avoid the conclusion that "it does not exist," for we observe that one who desires gold engages with the earring; likewise, it is improper to avoid the conclusion that even gold never becomes an earring,
because of its suitability for being an earring, since it is precisely the gold itself [that takes] the form of an earring.

Because it is manifest. Furthermore, it cannot be said that "the earring does not exist in the gold," because in common usage such as "the gold becomes an earring," there is the activity of arising established in the present tense.

Because it would follow that [the effect] is without a substratum; because at the time of its birth, there is no existence of the object such as the earring; and if it were to exist [then], its production would be impossible.
Furthermore, if one were to accept the existence of the object while it is being produced even though there is no existence of the object once produced, then [it would have to be] manifest.
Because persistence is impossible, because of the aforementioned fault, and because one must admit that objects such as earrings persist through their own causes despite their unmanifest state;
this being so, there is no contradiction between non-difference and difference based on division, for that very reason.

Because [the latter] depends upon that which is being analyzed; for, just as there is the appearance of an elephant and a bull in a particular painting due to the skill of the painter, so too Brahman, by virtue of its autonomy, appears in the form of both power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), as in the case of the expression "the serpent's coil. This is because the suffix in the word *cetana* [indicates this relationship].
Because, by virtue of having "being" as its primary meaning, it manifests the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) whose form as an action is unmanifest;
and because action is necessarily possessed of a substratum, its substratum—the agent—is also implied by that very [meaning];

and because the action contained therein is of the nature of volitional effort (*kṛti*), and volitional effort has an object, [the agent is implied] by virtue of its being of the nature of consciousness (*cit*).

Because action is self-luminous; for such independent power of manifestation is of the sole nature of light. Precisely for this reason, since division is preceded by conjunction, [it does not exist] in Brahman.

Since there is no possibility of the stain of doubt that a distinction among Vaibhāṣikas could exist due to the absence of connection with conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) or because of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), for the Vedic scripture "Not here,
not manifold" is intent upon the negation of worldly distinctions.

Because the power of reflection (*vimarśa-śakti*) consists of the state of equilibrium with all things, it cannot exist as something distinct; furthermore, since that power would require a relationship of either inherence (*samavāya*) or conjunction (*saṃyoga*),
and since inherence is impossible— given the non-acceptance of categories such as quality and qualified— the [relationship] must be conjunction.

Since conjunction preceded by action— and specifically that produced by the action of one or both— is only possible for two things situated in different locations, it is impossible here due to the absence of any location external to Brahman;
for a conjunction not preceded by action is unestablished.
From this are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses;
as well as space, air, light, water, and the earth which sustains the universe.
Thus, since space and the other elements are included within the category of effects according to scripture,
even the example of the conjunction of atoms with space is cast far aside; for it is not established for either disputant, as [space] always bears the burden of others.
Because it would entail the loss of independence; because, since a relation is a single entity, it is impossible for it to reside in two things;

because it is partless; and because, if it were to have parts, it would follow that it is a substance, which would lead to an infinite regress by necessitating the search for yet another relation for that [relation] by virtue of its being a relatum.

This is because scriptures such as "He is partless" (*niṣkala*) intend to convey that [the Self] is devoid of the parts (*kalā*) and other such qualities belonging to primordial matter (*prakṛti*) that are distinct from itself and subject to rejection;

otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of its being insentient, since it has been indicated that, like the light of a crystal or similar objects, it would lack self-reflective awareness (*nirvimarśatva*).

Therefore, because Brahman is conscious, it is stated in scripture: "He, being alone, did not rejoice; He desired a second; He was so great; having created that, He entered into it; having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)," and this is also established by the Brahma-sūtra: "But as in the world, [His action] is solely for the sake of sport."
If, for the sake of His own play, He were dependent on some other external cause for the construction of the universe—

as is the case with a potter and the like— then, by losing His orientation toward His own Self and being oriented elsewhere, He would necessarily be subject to factors such as *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), which would result in the undesirable consequence of Him not being the Supreme Lord (*anīśvaratva*).

By being independent of any other cause external to itself, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) that grants desired objects, like a yogin, or like a spider; and by virtue of its nature as the pervasion of consciousness through identity— according to the principle of the diversity of colors in the feet and wings found within the fluid of a peacock’s egg— it possesses the characteristic of autonomy in the form of vibration (*spandana*).

The universe— consisting of both the insentient and the sentient, characterized by the fourfold nature beginning with the "All" (viśva), and comprising the five objects of knowledge such as space, which are embraced by the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti) that has attained identity with the stainless mirror-surface of one's own Self through its nature as the radiance of consciousness, its nature as the nourishment of consciousness, and its nature as consciousness itself— [is thus established].
Having diversified Himself by means of the chisel of *apohana*, which is the form of His own power of will, into the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth,
He becomes the connoisseur of the great drama consisting of the fivefold cosmic acts characterized by creation, maintenance, withdrawal, bondage, and liberation.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that [the Lord] plays, because the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) must have an object; for without the universe abiding within [Him], its manifestation would be impossible.
Now, one might object: since the universe possesses existence through its non-difference from Brahman, it is eternal.

Since the bondage contained within that [unmanifest] would likewise be of the same nature, liberation could not occur because it would be impossible for that bondage to cease even through the knowledge of reality; furthermore, there would be a persistence of bondage even for one who is liberated,
because the phenomenal world (prapañca) is subject to the six modifications of being.

If it is argued that there would follow the consequence of Brahman being non-eternal due to its non-difference from that [destruction], it is replied: in the case of the statement "the jar perishes," the act of perishing cannot reside in the jar by itself, because destruction is impossible through its own nature;
rather, it depends on time and instruments, since instruments depend upon the organs of action. Of those...

Because they depend upon the sense organs (*jñānendriya*), because those [sense organs] depend upon the internal organ (*antarindriya*), and because that [internal organ] depends upon an artificial knower (*kṛtrimapramātṛ*),
it lacks independence due to its dependence on space, time, and other such factors.

It is not possible [to maintain that the effect is non-existent], because since that [effect] is defined by that [cause], its subsistence within it must be accepted even against one's will; for the agent is of the nature of Maheśvara, and according to the direction shown,
it must be accepted that effects such as earrings exist in the form of their causes, such as gold.

Since the effect, namely the destruction of the effect, consists in its abiding in the nature of the cause, there is no consequence of defects such as mutability (*vikāritva*). This is because, in the case of milk and so forth, the action of transformation is observed to depend upon time, instruments, and an agent; therefore, it possesses the nature of an agent (*kartṛ-svabhāvatva*).
This is because even qualities and defects possess the nature of being identical with the self.
Furthermore, in the world, among things that undergo transformation, there is not in every case a total abandonment of one's own essential form;
for instance, when a substance such as gold that undergoes transformation changes into the shape of an earring.

This is because we experience that gold and other substances do not abandon their essential nature; furthermore, since there is no possibility of even a trace of modification— due to the transformation of an independent entity following the logic of the contraction and expansion of a tortoise's limbs— the action indeed finds its rest in the object (*karman*) alone, and not in the agent (*kartṛ*).

Furthermore, according to logic, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation at all. "O Bhārata, beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, and indeed unmanifest again in their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this?"

Thus, according to the statement of the Blessed One, because the universe— between the prior and posterior limits characterized by enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*)— is of the single essence of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*), it lacks any obstructive nature as its own true form (*svarūpa*). Consequently,
like a jar or other objects that have entered the plane of desire (*icchā*) and so forth, it is devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) except in the intermediate state.
It is an obstacle because it is characterized by causal efficiency;
for the conceptual cognition produced by you, which consists of the means of proof and takes the form of "the knower and the known," arises [only as such].
O Goddess, because his own nature— which is yours— is perceived by him as being without blemish, that wise one does not attain liberation.

Thus it is stated by Kālidāsa in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*. Since it is the will of the Lord alone that acts as the regulator, there is no possibility of the liberated soul being bound again; therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
This should be reflected upon by the learned whose hearts have been purified by the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*).

This being the case, in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, in the first sūtra, [establishes the inquiry] based on the Vedic scripture: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; it thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" according to the etymological derivation of the verbal root *īkṣ* as meaning both "to see" and "to intend."
Because it is distinct from the insentient due to its nature as perception characterized by seeing, and because it is "great" (*bṛhat*);

and because it is augmented by bliss characterized by the agency of seeing— which is independent of other characteristics of the individual soul (*jīva*) whose nature is seeing, and which consists in the reflection on the act of becoming many in the form "May I become many"— it is [the Supreme Self].

And because of this reality, it is also appropriate that Brahman—which is independent in respect to knowledge and action—is indicated as the object of inquiry; thus, the definition of its unique characteristics, such as being the cause of the birth of the universe, as stated in the immediately following sūtra, is likewise justified.
For instance, in the context of "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*), [it is said] "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, is to be heard..."
"One should reflect upon it; one should meditate upon it"—this is the subject sentence (*viṣayavākya*).

The doubt is whether the scripture (*śāstra*) is not to be commenced or is indeed to be commenced. For it has been sung by the Blessed One himself: "Therefore, in this world and in the Veda, I am celebrated as Puruṣottama. Regarding this:
Worldly renown is not established by means of inference, because common people and others lack knowledge of the necessary concomitance (*vyāpti*) and so forth;
rather, it is known even by children through the realization "I am. This is also found in the Veda:
"I am Brahman," "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite is Brahman," and "I am the first-born of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), prior to the gods, of the Immortal."

Because Maheśvara is well-known from such scriptural passages as "The navel," he cannot be the subject of inquiry due to the absence of doubt; furthermore, since the ignorance (avidyā) residing in the individual soul (jīva) is of the same nature as Brahman, its cessation is impossible; and because there exists no other entity external to Brahman.

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that the scripture need not be commenced, because the attainment of produced bliss is to be rejected due to its impermanence, and because eternal bliss is neither something to be attained nor has it ever been unattained, and thus there is no purpose [for such a treatise].

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that Brahman is indeed well-known as the "I" in both cases. Nevertheless, in this world, among those who are non-Vedic and analytical, the proponents of consciousness (*vijñānavādins*) maintain that— relative to the stream of momentary cognitions— there exists no eternal conscious being, nor indeed any Lord (*īśvara*) who impels those cognitions.

Because, while being distinct from cognition, there is no evidence for their existence as external to cognition; for if there were such evidence, they would necessarily be equivalent to cognitions—just like jars and other objects—by virtue of being included within cognition. Thus, even regarding Vedic [entities], the followers of Kapila [cite] such scriptural passages as "the unborn" (*ajā*).

Because the *pradhāna* is heard in scripture to be the cause of the universe, they assert that there is no Lord (*īśvara*) other than *puruṣa* and *pradhāna*. The followers of Jaimini (*jaiminīyāḥ*), however, maintain that with respect to heaven characterized by pleasure, it is ritual action such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* alone that is enjoined; [the attainment of heaven occurs] solely through the force of the unseen merit (*apūrva*) residing in the sacrificer, which is produced by that [action].

Because it is possible for the entities that serve as the means to achieve those [results] to arise, they argue that the Vedāntas are concerned with the agent, the deity, and the substance; since they possess purposefulness by being useful for performance, they are merely subordinate to ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*) and not concerned with Brahman. Therefore, because there is disagreement even regarding the Veda among such disputants, [the following is stated].

Thus, for the sake of attaining liberation—characterized by the expansion of power (*śakti*) that will be described hereafter—by means of refuting the doctrines of those who have entered heterodox paths, both Vedic and non-Vedic, this scripture must be commenced.
And so, the meaning of this aphorism (*sūtra*) is as follows: *atha* (=)
For the qualified seeker— who has acquired the means such as tranquility and self-control through the power of virtuous deeds like the worship of Śiva accumulated over many lifetimes—
following the manifestation of the power of an extremely intense desire for liberation, [it is said] "therefore" (ataḥ), which means "hence" (atha).

Because rites such as sacrifices and yoga—characterized by the worship of deities distinct from oneself, as in the inquiry into dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) and so forth—are to be rejected due to their impermanence, as evidenced by scriptural passages such as "this world acquired through action perishes" (*eṣa karmacito lokaḥ kṣīyate*); and because action, being insentient, lacks the capacity for the exertion required to produce the *apūrva*; and because the deity consists of sound (*śabdamaya*).

Because [the self] is insentient, for that very reason the means and the end [of action] would be like flowers in the sky; by this same reasoning, the Sāṃkhya doctrine which asserts the Pradhāna as the cause is also refuted;
and because the Vedāntas, being read in distinct contexts, have Brahman as their sole purport according to the six marks that determine such purport.

Because the nature of the self, as accepted here, consists of a plurality of mutually exclusive forms, and because each [cognition] is restricted solely to its own object and its own nature— thereby being, with respect to the objects and natures of others,
almost like one who is blind and deaf— it follows that Caitra is distinct from Maitra, and Maitra is distinct from Caitra.

Since there is no possibility of internal synthesis— such as "I know Caitra" or "I know Maitra"— among the manifestations of Caitra and others who are differentiated by the connection of mutual distinctions (e.g., "Caitra is happy," "Maitra is suffering"), [there can be no such thought as] "I am Caitra."
Because light illuminates only its own self as its object,
so too, for the non-Vedic proponents who accept a momentary consciousness as the self, there is a multiplicity due to the forms of blue and so forth,
and the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by those [forms] are likewise manifold.

Because they terminate at different times, they are devoid of mutual connection; for this very reason, according to the aforementioned method, because they reside solely within their own respective objects, they are like those who are blind or deaf with respect to the objects and essential natures of others. Thus, "blue is distinct from yellow."
Yellow is distinct from blue; "I know blue," "I know yellow";
"I, who experienced my parents in childhood, am that very same person experiencing my great-grandchildren now"—thus, by virtue of being attached to a single consciousness of "I."
Because the connection between the external and internal is untenable,
due to the absence of any intervening consciousness that could grasp both moments; and because, in states such as deep sleep,
there exists the vibration of the prāṇa-vāyu characterized by rejection and appropriation.

Because it is preceded by an agent— that is, preceded by the knowledge of an agent— and because the memory of pleasure experienced by one who has awakened, such as "I slept happily," is rooted in an experience and an experiencer via the medium of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*),
and because the experiencer is independent and self-luminous, so too is the manifestation of the void [expressed in] "I was not aware of anything."
Because it exists; because it is accepted that the aspect of the self’s self-luminosity remains unmanifested even when freed from its qualifiers;
and because, according to the direction shown, actions such as cutting cannot occur in the world without resting in a supreme subject.

By the logic already stated, [He is] the one who has embraced within the sphere of His own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*) the manifold circle of both existence and non-existence through His identity with His own Self;
He is the singular convergence of the many kinds of powers such as knowledge, memory, and exclusion (*apohana*); [He is] the experiencer and the rememberer...

For this reason, Maheśvara— whose nature consists of the conceptualizer and the recognizer, whose form is the self-luminous autonomy of the vibration of the full "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃsphuraṇa*) consisting of the synthesis of pure experience, and who is self-manifesting— must be accepted; because [the world] is regulated by the power of the will of such a Maheśvara.

Aiming for the fruit characterized by one's own self as Śiva, by means of cessation— which consists in the state of equilibrium with the power of omniscience that serves as its own cause— the reality of ignorance [attains] the reality of the Puruṣa (= Brahman).

[The inquiry] is augmented by an undivided reflective awareness (*amarśa*) characterized by its own independence and self-luminosity; the desire to know that [awareness] is indicated by this word, and by implication, the investigation (*vicāra*) is what must be performed. The meaning is that one should perform the reflective awareness as non-different from one's own Self, since the duality asserted by others has been refuted.
In this sūtra, by the word *ataḥ*, the entire subject matter of the subsequent chapters on Concordance (*samanvaya*), Non-contradiction (*avirodha*), and Fruit (*phala*) is summarized.
By the word *atha*, the subject matter of the chapter on Means (*sādhana*) is included. By the word *brahma*—

One should investigate with subtle vision that the intended meaning [of this teaching] is the nature of self-luminosity, independence, and the power [of consciousness], which is distinct from both the insentient and the individual soul (jīva).
Thus, by the mere reflection upon the meaning of this aphorism, one of the highest qualification becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
This is the ultimate conclusion.

In this way, the meaning of the subsequent sūtra, "janmādy asya yataḥ," is also consistent. Indeed, the meaning of that sūtra is as follows: when the analysis (vigraha) is made as "that of which birth is the first" (*janma ādir yeṣām*), it is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* bahuvrīhi compound. And thus:

The defining characteristic of Brahman culminates in its agency over the fivefold functions known as creation, sustenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace. Thus, the agency of creation belongs to Brahman;
the agency of both creation and sustenance belongs to Viṣṇu; and the agency of creation, sustenance, and dissolution [belongs to Rudra].

Rudra possesses the agency of creation, maintenance, destruction, and concealment; Īśvara possesses the agency of creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace; and Sadāśiva possesses the agency of creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace.
This nature of being the agent of these fivefold activities constitutes the extrinsic definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa) of Sadāśiva.
This is possible only for the presiding lord of the five elements, who is distinguished by the five faces beginning with Sadyojāta;

[it belongs] to him who is the director of this performer of the fivefold cosmic acts (pañcakṛtya), who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), unattached, indifferent, eternally liberated, and pure by nature.

The defining characteristic of Paramaśiva— who is designated as the Great Liṅga (mahāliṅga), whose nature consists of the powers of consciousness and so forth belonging to the Supreme Brahman, and whose primordial essence is the six limbs and the ten immutable states— is indeed the very nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda),
because He is of that single essence. Therefore, His status as the cause who presides over the fivefold cosmic functions (pañcakṛtya) [is established].
Just as a magnet possesses another characteristic in its action upon iron, so too does Paramaśiva possess another defining characteristic.
Since the causality of Brahman with respect to the phenomenal expansion of objects has been established, for that very reason,
His causality with respect to the phenomenal expansion of words is also effectively proven.
To demonstrate this immediately, the subsequent sūtra, "Because He is the source of the Śāstras" (*śāstrayonitvāt*), has been set forth.

Here, by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of "the source of the Śāstras," His status as the progenitor of the Vedas and other scriptures is established. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "because He is the source of the Śāstras," [one may refer to] such passages as, "I ask about that Person who is known through the Upaniṣads" (*tantvaupaniṣadaṃ puruṣaṃ pṛcchāmi*).

Even through a critical examination of the scriptures (*śruti*), the meaning results in [Brahman] being that which is propounded by the scripture (*śāstra*). Alternatively, "Teacher" (*śāstṛ*) refers to Brahman; because of its "not being born from a womb" (*ayonitva*), that is, because it lacks a cause like the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
Brahman, as indicated by the word "which" (*yat*) in the preceding sūtra, is the instructor of the scripture.

Since the status of being a teacher of Viṣṇu and others is not established by either worldly experience or the Vedas, it is agreed upon by both that this belongs to Śiva alone; likewise, the previously mentioned causality regarding the birth and so forth of the universe belongs to Śiva alone.

Thus, it is implied by this Sūtra that He alone is the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*). Alternatively, because of His being "not born from a womb" (*ayonitvāt*), [He is] that which is denoted by the syllable *A*.

The syllable *a* belongs to Viṣṇu, Brahmā, or Rudra, according to the lexicon which states: "The syllable *a* [is used] for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa; in a courtyard (*kamaṭha*), in a limb (*aṅga*), and in battle (*raṇa*). Because it is the source (*yoni*), that is, because it is the cause (*kāraṇa*).
For by reflecting upon the sūtra to be stated later—"And it is indeed called the source" (*yoniśca hi gīyate*)—it is determined that the word *yoni* signifies causality.

And thus, by reflecting upon the meaning of that [text], the previously stated conclusion is established: Śiva alone is the instructor of the scripture, as he is the cause for encompassing the meaning of such Vedic passages as, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra— they are all produced from him."

But is it not the case that by the sūtra *śāstrayonitvāt*, the fact that Brahman is the subject matter propounded by the Vedānta was stated? That is not possible, because those [Vedānta texts] are devoted solely to the performance of the aforementioned ritual acts. To explain:
among those [Vedic texts] which propound Brahman...

The fact that certain sentences have as their purport deities who are constituent parts of yoga; that some sentences which set forth creation and maintenance have as their purport substances that are constituent parts of sacrifice; and [those] which set forth the individual self (jīvātman)...

If it is argued that since the texts are possible to be directed toward the sacrificer—that is, since they are directed toward injunctions concerning ritual action—how can Brahman be the subject matter taught by the scripture? To this, it is replied:
[Brahman is established] by means of the sixfold marks that determine the purport, such as the introduction and conclusion, and by the distinction of context.

Since it can be stated with the clarity of a ringing bell that [the Upanishads] have Brahman as their subject matter, everything you have said is merely for the purpose of deluding a few common folk. To illustrate: having begun with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," [it continues] "That which is this subtle essence (aṇimā), all this has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is..."
The conclusion is "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). The fact that both [passages] have Brahman as their object is one mark [of identity].

The frequent repetition of "That thou art" is the mark of repetition (*abhyāsa*). The possession of great sovereignty inaccessible through other means of knowledge is the mark of novelty (*apūrvatva*).
[The mark of fruitfulness is shown by: "By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known."

The knowledge of all things through the knowledge of one is the result, as expressed in the passage beginning with "Being" (*sat*). The meaning is that just as when clay is known, its effects—such as jars, bowls, and the like—are known to be non-different from it because they are its products, so it is exactly thus [in the case of Brahman]. The five declarations of purpose are: creation, maintenance, dissolution, entry, and governance.
The examples of clay and so forth are logical justifications; for by these marks, [the texts] have Brahman as their ultimate purport.

Nor is there a lack of purpose without inference, because there exists a great fruit consisting in the emergence of the perfect "I-ness" (ahantā) through the submergence of the "I-ness" [associated with] the body and other such [limited identities].
But even if the Vedāntas have Brahman as their ultimate purport, they do not terminate in Brahman alone;

rather, having first established the reality of Brahman through indirect means—such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—they subsequently effect its direct realization. This being so, because the Vedāntas possess the nature of instruction (*śāsana*), [they are indeed scriptures].

The status of being a scripture (śāstra) is established because it leads to the comprehension of an as-yet-unapprehended object. Furthermore, having enjoined "listening" (*śravaṇa*)—which consists of the knowledge of words—in the injunction "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*), the subsequent [injunctions] "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavya*) and "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*) enjoin experience, which consists of direct knowledge. Therefore, the Vedāntas are prescriptive of realization.

If it is argued that [the injunction of realization] is not possible because it is not a human goal— since it is impossible to perform, not to perform, or to perform otherwise— that is not so. There is no fixed rule that a scripture possesses its status as a *śāstra* solely through the teaching of what is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*), for that status is established even by means of establishing an already existent reality (*siddhavastu*).

Nor is it reasonable to say that after an object is known through verbal testimony, mental reflection (*manana*) and so forth— which consist of direct experience— are subsequently enjoined; for, as in the case of the statement "You are the tenth," the word itself generates immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*), and thus, prior to the verbal comprehension, the agent must [apply effort] in order to remove doubts such as improbability (*asambhāvanā*).

Because of the prescription of [inference] and so forth for the purpose of contemplating the nature of other things; because the sole purpose of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the removal of delusion; and because it is experienced as such in cases such as "this jar before me exists, because it is perceptible. In this context, the jar is not being produced, because it is already established (*siddhatvāt*); nor is it being made known.

Because it is being made known by perception itself; however, through the means of establishing "being foremost," the delusion that it is not foremost is removed. Likewise, by the means of establishing "possessing fire" through the mark (liṅga) of smoke, the delusion consisting of the form "not possessing fire" is dispelled. Thus, the Vedāntas culminate in Brahman alone. For this very reason:

Because of the Vedic teaching that "all this has that as its self; that is the Truth," and because one observes the persistence of an intrinsic existence— distinct from the universal *sattā* (existence)— in all things, such as in the forms "the jar exists" and "the cloth exists," even within universals and the like.

The aforementioned moment is established because the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*); for it has been shown that an insentient entity cannot maintain its existence through its own power, as such independence would lead to the impossibility of maintaining an existence established by another.

It must be accepted that there is only one thing which is a mass of existence-consciousness (saccidghana); for action, being insentient, is devoid of any effort to produce unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), and unseen merit, likewise being insentient,
is devoid of any effort to produce heaven or the substances that serve as its means.
The established conclusion is that Brahman alone— which is the nature of the existence of all conceptual proliferation, independent, and self-luminous— is what is propounded by all the Vedāntas.

This being the case, since the Vedāntas are in harmony with Brahman by means of the six marks that determine their purport (*tātparya*), the sense is that Brahman possesses the aforementioned characteristics and is accessible through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its great sovereignty.

Thus, by means of these four sūtras, which concern the necessity of inquiry, the characteristics [of Brahman], the means of valid cognition, and the harmony [of the Vedāntas], [the subject matter is established].
Having established those various duties of reflection and so forth, and having preceded this with the determination of the meditations on the qualified, the unqualified,
and the symbols, as well as the refutation of the Sāṅkhya doctrine, [the text establishes] all the Vedāntas in Brahman.

The nature of the creation of the five elements and the ten sense organs, preceded by the refutation of the doctrines of the Sāṅkhya, Pātañjala, Kāṇāda, Akṣapāda, Sautrāntika, Vaibhāṣika, Yogācāra, Mādhyamika, Ārhata, Pāśupata, and Pāñcarātra schools, [contained] in the first chapter which determines the connection.
Following the second chapter which determines [the nature of transmigratory existence],

and having first established that the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) and other such teachings are intended to strengthen dispassion (*vairāgya*) by focusing on the perishability of the fruits of action and the experience of various sufferings;

And [the commentary on] the third chapter, which establishes the fourfold means (sādhana-catuṣṭaya) that facilitate the inquiry into Brahman by first determining the nature of the attributes of the dream state, deep sleep, fainting, the individual soul (jīva), the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and the body; and [the commentary on] the fourth chapter, which determines the fruits of those respective meditations (upāsanā).

Because this [work] has as its primary purpose the exposition of the doctrine of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) characterized by the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*); and because, having reached that conclusion,
[it is established] in the *Kriyāsāra* and other [texts].
Because it is presented in the form of a *kārikā*, its specific details should be understood from that very source;
they are not written here for fear of excessive length.
As for the method of meditation (*upāsanā*), however, it is as follows: "Neither gross, nor subtle, nor short, nor long," and so forth.
According to the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:

"That which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet— eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and imperishable— that source of all beings they perceive."
"The wise," according to the statement of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:
"Partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, stainless,
the supreme bridge to immortality, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed."
When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather,
then, without knowing Śiva, there will be an end to suffering.
Thus, by the statement of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"Neither inwardly cognitive, nor outwardly cognitive, nor cognitive of both, nor a mass of cognition, nor cognitive."

They consider the Fourth to be non-discernible, invisible, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without characteristics, unthinkable, indefinable, the essence of the realization of the one Self, the cessation of phenomenal proliferation, peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual;
that is the Self, that is to be known. It is without measure, the Fourth, beyond conventional usage, the cessation of phenomenal proliferation.
Śiva is non-dual; thus, the syllable Om is the Self itself. He who knows this enters the Self by means of the Self.
Thus, according to the statement of the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad:
"The supreme reality, which is of the nature of consciousness, is indeed called Śiva, the cause of the universe;
it is free from all worldly impurities, partless, and beyond conceptual construction."
Consisting of the subtle power that causes the radiant expansion of the bliss of existence,
it is immeasurable, ineffable, and worshipped by those seeking liberation.
The Great Liṅga of the Supreme Brahman is beyond the phenomenal world and imperishable;
it is the object perceived within the inner abode of all living beings.
According to the statement in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"The *praṇava* is the designator of that Śiva, the Supreme Self;
the letter *A* is the great seed, the quality of passion (*rajas*), and the four-faced creator."
The syllable *U* is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the womb; it is goodness (*sattva*), the protector Hari.
The syllable *Ma* is the person (*puruṣa*), the seed-sower; it is darkness (*tamas*), the destroyer Hara.
The Nāda is the Supreme Person, the Lord, devoid of qualities, actionless, and auspicious;
thus, by these three measures alone, everything is threefold.
Intending the Self that is Śiva, one awakens it by means of the half-mora;
for this Śiva is indeed the Praṇava, or the Praṇava is remembered as Śiva.
Furthermore, because of the statement in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* of the Śaiva tradition: "The distinction between the signified and the signifier is never entirely separate," and because Paramaśiva—
who is synonymous with the Supreme Brahman that is the signified by the *praṇava*— is established as the Great Liṅga (*mahāliṅga*).

Because the *praṇava* consists of the forms of the *tāraka*, the *daṇḍa*, the *kuṇḍala*, the half-moon, and light, and because it consists of the forms of the syllables *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, the *nāda*, and the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*),
[it is the source] of those mantras such as the *kāra*s that encircle such a *praṇava*.

Because the *praṇava* is of the nature of the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*), and because such a *praṇava* itself is the very essence of the Great Liṅga (*mahāliṅga*), the worship consists precisely in the contemplation of the Great Liṅga— known as the Bhāva-liṅga— preceded by a firm mental cultivation within the gates of the senses, through the inclusion of the five Liṅgas of conduct and so forth which are its constituent parts.

The intended meaning belongs to the distinguished Advaitic Vīraśaivas, who are knowers of the meaning of the Brahma-sūtras and experts in logic; therefore, in accordance with that, the definitions of the Mahāliṅga and other [categories] are stated as follows:

[they consist of] the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*), the form (*rūpa*), the orientation toward bliss (*ānandaunmukhya*), the subtle (*sūkṣma*), the outward-facing (*bahirmukha*), the gross (*sthūla*), the exertion (*udyama*), and the activity (*kriyā*)—[these being their inherent natures].

While being the determiner of the fivefold cosmic functions (pañcakṛtya) conceived as the states beginning with Śāntyatītā— consisting of will, knowledge, and action, along with withdrawal (ava) and descent (apara)—

and while being the state of non-dual equilibrium (samarasa) beyond Śāntyatītā, which is of the nature of consciousness (cinmaya) in the form of the Praṇava that is the totality of the five syllables;

[He is] the one who has attained the sixfold play, beginning with the Great Liṅga, through the threefold play characterized by the vital breath of all states—namely, the formless (niṣkala) Sādākhya characterized as Śiva known as Mahāsāda which is non-different from Ānanda, Jñāna, and Satya; the embodied (mūrta) Sādākhya; the formless (niṣkala) Sādākhya-form; the embodied (sakala) Sādākhya-kartṛ; the embodied (sakala) Sādākhya-karma; and the formless (niṣkala) [state] characterized as the desired object (iṣṭa).
While being the Self (*ātman*), while being the one who synthesizes all categories of existence and whose facial expressions are hidden within the heart,

and while manifesting the playful facial expressions of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta— produced by the synthesis of specific objects such as sound and the rest— while being thus, [he is the Lord].

The state of being the Great Liṅga (mahāliṅgatva) consists in its eternality, its perfection, and its being free from the stain of all disturbances; that alone is the definition (lakṣaṇa) of Brahman-hood. For a definition is a property that is exclusively negative (kevalavyatireki), and it is that which distinguishes [the subject] from others.
If it is objected: "Since the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has Brahman as its essence, how can there be an exclusion of others?"—the answer is no;

for although the phenomenal world is non-different from the qualified Brahman because it has the qualified Brahman as its material cause, it is possible to exclude it from others by treating it as something other than the pure [Brahman]. For that purpose...
Since a definition is necessary, the purpose of a definition is either exclusion or conventional usage.

In this regard, some describe a threefold nature of consciousness as the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśa*), and pure consciousness (*viśuddhacit*). We, however, speak of it as the triad of *aṅga*, *liṅga*, and *sthala*. Therein, the word *sthala* denotes the substratum;
the power (*śakti*) eternally connected to that [substratum], through the play of the worshiped and the worshiper, assumes states of deficiency or excellence.

We state that the purpose of the definition is to exclude [the category of] *aṅga-tattva* (the reality of the subordinate), since it brings about a twofold division of the *sthala* by way of the relationship between the *liṅga* (the indicative mark) and the *aṅga* (the subordinate).

In this definition, although each suffix denoting a verbal action (*bhāvārthaka-pratyaya*) serves as a differentiator, it has been established in the scriptures that there is a rule requiring the possession of all attributes for those [meditations] read within the context of specific meditations (*viśiṣṭopāsanā*). Therefore,
just as there is a qualification by all attributes as an auxiliary to the Vaiśvānara meditation and others, so too for as many...

The significance of the qualifiers: The proponents of the doctrine of the attributeless Brahman (*nirviśeṣa-brahmavādin*) maintain that meditation characterized by attributes (*guṇaviśiṣṭopāsanā*) is auxiliary to the meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇopāsanā*). [As it is said: "This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true."
"The mind delights in truth, self, and life, and finds its bliss therein. Furthermore, from such scriptural declarations as, "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold;
knowledge, strength, and action are His inherent nature," it follows that the Lord is the singular mass of infinite auspicious qualities, whom the virtuous call Śiva.

Furthermore, according to the traditional teaching that "by those who know the true meaning of the Śiva-tattva," the reality is this: meditation characterized by all the qualities offered through scriptural injunction is, in itself, a means for achieving the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha).
The letter *na* is the position of the star; the letter *ma* is said to be the staff (*daṇḍa*).
The letter *śi* is shaped like a earring (*kuṇḍala*), and the letter *va* is a half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
"The letter *ya* is of the nature of the *bindu*, and the syllable *ūṃ* consists of five colors"—

such passages [occur] in the detailed description of the divisions of the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) as the constituent parts of the five-syllabled mantra, beginning with the letter *na*: namely, the *tāraka*, the *daṇḍa*, the *kuṇḍala*, the *ardhacandra*, and the *bindu*.
This is the authoritative source. A detailed account should be sought in the *Cidambaropaniṣad* and other such texts. In the *Yogapātañjala* as well, it is stated:

"The Lord (Īśvara) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent dispositions. In Him, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed. He is the teacher even of the ancients, for He is not limited by time."

The *praṇava* is its designator. Furthermore, through the method of the five aphorisms beginning with "Its repetition and meditation upon its meaning," the eternal relationship between the *praṇava* and the reality that is its designated object has been described. This is also stated by the Śruti: "That sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the end of the Vedas..."
"For him who is dissolved in primordial nature (prakṛti), he who is beyond that is Maheśvara.
Thus, by means of the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, his manifestation through the play of the five faces has been described.
"He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving; his austerity consists of knowledge"—thus his omniscience has been described.
And that is the state of being the object of an entirely stainless, direct, and eternal experience that does not depend upon external instruments;
by this—
It has been stated that [Brahman] possesses the capacity to fashion various bodies suited to the manifold karmic experiences of all sentient beings.
From the scriptural text "Bliss is Brahman," its state of eternal satisfaction is established;
and this consists in being completely filled with unsurpassed bliss, from which every stain of affliction has been removed.

The state of being eternal consciousness and the state of being beginningless awareness are established through the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the Vedic text: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. Sovereignty is established by the Śruti: "He who rules over both knowledge and ignorance is another [than these]. And that sovereignty consists in being devoid of subservience to another and of dependence.
Its nature consists of having brought all things other than itself under its control. Its supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold:

"Brahman has space as its body," "It has truth for its self, delighting in breath, with the mind as bliss, enriched by peace, and immortal"—by such passages, its possession of infinite powers is established.

And that [nature] consists in being characterized by immeasurable and infinite powers. In this manner, other groups of meanings as well, which enter into the body of the definition, are to be seen in their respective places.
The characteristics contained within the Great Liṅga and other such features are to be contemplated in this manner:

while there is a state of equilibrium (*samarasya*) with the *kalā* that transcends the Peaceful (*śāntātīta*), which is a synonym for the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*)— the material cause of the subtle expansion of the world of effects that is non-different from the Root Praṇava.

Mahāliṅgatva is the state of possessing the playful manifestation of the secret face characterized by the heart, which is the synthesizer of all pure categories of existence, while remaining non-different from the Liṅga of the partless state known as Mahāsāda, and being the director of the fivefold cosmic functions (pañcakṛtya). || 1 ||

When there is a state of essential identity (*samarasatva*) with the *yakāra-mantra*, which is a synonym for the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) whose nature is bliss (*ānanda-rūpa*) and belongs to the level beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta-kalā*),
there occurs a continuous contemplation (*anusandhi*) upon the objects of specific words that are non-different from the *liṅga* of the partless (*niṣkala*) state of Śiva known as Sādākhya.
The state of being the playful manifestation of the face of Īśāna, who is revealed as the Father, is the characteristic mark of grace. || 2 ||

When there is a state of equilibrium with the peaceful *kalā*, which consists of mantras inseparable from the form [of consciousness] that is non-different from the powers characterized by orientation (*aunmukhya*) and so forth;
and when there is the specific object of touch, inseparable from the formless, the *sādākhya*, the partless (*niṣkala*), and the whole (*sakala*) *prāṇaliṅga*.
The state of being manifested through the face of the Puruṣa who is the unifying observer is the nature of the mobile liṅga. || 3 ||

Śivaliṅgatva is the state of manifesting as the playful manifestation of the face of Aghora, while remaining in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*samarasya*) with the *vidyā* and *kalā* kalās, which consist of mantras and the *śikhā*— the latter being a synonym for the power of will (*icchāśakti*) characterized by subtle activity— and while being non-different from the formal *sādākhya*, the partless (*niṣkala*), the whole (*sakala*), and the vital *prāṇaliṅga*, as the perceiver of objects that possess their own specific, determinate forms. || 4 ||

When there is a state of equilibrium (*samarasatva*) with the *kalā* of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), which consists of the mantra *A*— a synonym for the power of outward-turned cognition (*bahirmukhajñānaśakti*)—

there arises the [consciousness] that discerns the specific objects of experience (*rasapadārtha*) as non-different from the agent (*kartṛ*), the *Sādākhya*, and all desired *liṅgas*. This is the manifestor...
Your state of being the playful manifestation of the faces of Atri, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu is the nature of the Guru-liṅga. || 5 ||

The state of being the Ācāra-liṅga consists in the manifestation of the face of Sadyojāta, which is the discerning subject of specific objects such as fragrance— non-different from the *sakala-iṣṭa-liṅga* (the desired liṅga with parts) known as Karma and Sādākhya— and which exists in a state of *samarasya* (equilibrium) with the *nivṛtti-kalā*, which is composed of the mantra *na* that is synonymous with the root-exertion (*mūlodyama*) and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). 6.

And there is a concomitance of these characteristics with every instance of the characterized object (*lakṣya*). Now, is the reality of the logical mark (*liṅgatattva*), as defined by these characteristics, well-known or unknown? In the first case, this treatise should not be commenced for the purpose of investigating an already established subject, because that would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

If it is argued that even in the second case, a treatise should not be commenced for the purpose of investigating an object that is like the horn of a hare, because such investigation would be futile— we say no;

for one who has studied the Vedic scriptures according to rule and has grasped the connection between words and their meanings, [the inquiry into] Brahman leads to the attainment of the Knower of Brahman.

By the words beginning with "param," when the nature of reality (*tattva*) that is the means to the supreme human goal has been generally understood—as in such passages as "Food is Brahman; breath is Brahman; mind is Brahman; consciousness is Brahman; bliss is Brahman"—even though there is a general understanding of the reality of the signs (*liṅga-tattva*), the sign of being (*bhāva-liṅga*) [remains to be specifically discerned].
Because many categories of *liṅga* are heard of— namely, the *prāṇaliṅga*, the *iṣṭaliṅga*, the *prasādaliṅga*, the *śivaliṅga*, the *guruliṅga*, and the *ācāraliṅga*—
it is likewise [taught that] the Supreme Brahman alone, characterized by supreme bliss, is the *śivatattva*, according to the *Śivācāryas*.
Furthermore, because of such scriptural declarations as "They call it the abode with reverence," which proclaim non-duality,

a doubt arises as to whether the nature of the *liṅga* is one or many; likewise, by statements such as "Or rather, the Lord is a single mass of infinite auspicious qualities," [the nature of] auspiciousness—

Because of hearing of the perfection of qualities, and because of hearing of the state of being devoid of qualities through such passages as "devoid of qualities, devoid of action, peaceful," the mind— mounted upon the swing of various doubts such as whether the principle of the subtle body (*liṅga-tattva*) is with qualities or without qualities— is rendered unstable; [the scripture provides] the fruit of non-contradiction which bestows steadiness.
The exposition of the subject matter should now be commenced.

Thus, [this work concerns] the supreme, non-dual majesty characterized by the Supreme Power (paramaśakti), which consists of the six-syllabled mantra manifesting the entire expanse of sentient and insentient beings;
it is the treasury of the secret essence of all the Nigamas.
To him whose supreme majesty is manifested through the play of his eightfold powers— known by the names Bhava, Śarva, Rudra, Paśupati, Ugra, Mahādeva, Bhīma, and Īśāna—

and who bestows upon all conscious beings the fruits of their respective worship according to their specific capacities through the grace arising from his own sovereign manifestation; [The city] granted by the favor of his own self, which has arisen in accordance with the worship performed by all sentient beings through the particularities of his own divine manifestations...

The restriction established by the scriptural statement "that which is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) is that the investigation into the meaning of the scriptures— which demonstrates the non-difference between the state of being the limbs (*aṅgatva*) and the state of being the possessor of the limbs (*aṅgin*), as well as the reality of the gendered signs (*liṅga*)— must be performed solely through the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*. Consequently,
[the seeker becomes] free from sorrow when he perceives the Lord as distinct, thinking, "I behold Him who is adored, and His majesty."
Because of such scriptural passages, there arises the possibility of the delusion that liberation results from the knowledge of a distinct self;
consequently, one might proceed to study other treatises that propound a distinct self in order to gain the knowledge that is the means to liberation.
Thus, the exclusion of such [erroneous] activity is established as the purpose [of this work].

If it is argued that the exclusion of inquiry into scriptures propounding a differentiated self is already established by the fact that all the statements of the Vedas and Agamas are harmonized with the non-dual reality through the indicators of purport such as the opening and closing passages (*upakrama-upasaṃhāra*), and therefore that restriction is not the result [of the inquiry], then [the answer is] "no," because [this is achieved] by the mantras alone.

Just as the injunction to remember the meaning of the mantra excludes from the scope [of the injunction] the ritual manuals (*kalpasūtra*), one's own private notes, and the like— even though these might also be included under the category [of things to be remembered]— so too here, the injunction to "listen" excludes from the scope of the injunction compositions by human authors and works in vernacular languages, even though these might also be included under the category [of things to be heard].
"It accomplishes" refers to the fruit of the rule governing that [practice].
As for the fruit of human compositions, linguistic treatises, and so forth,
it consists in producing mental purity, detachment, and the like for one who is incapable of grasping the meaning of the Vedas and Agamas.
The actual state of affairs is that liberation is achieved through the investigation of the secrets of the meaning of the Vedas and Agamas belonging to successive periods.
The subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this scripture is the state of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) between the reality of the *liṅga* and the reality of the *aṅga*.
Therefore, following the determination of the reality of the *liṅga*, the reality of the *aṅga* is now described. Its characteristics are as follows:
the transformation into bliss through the acceptance of grace—which is the supreme object to be attained—arising from the knowledge of the identity between the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama*.

That which has as its characteristic the oneness of the witness to yoga and enjoyment— consisting of the sequential and necessary renunciation of body, speech, mind, and wealth pertaining to that [object],
and which brings about the play of the Śaraṇa, Prāṇaliṅgin, Prasādin, Māheśvara, and Bhakta [categories].

[He is] characterized by the sixfold devotion consisting of equanimity (*samarasa*), bliss (*ānanda*), experience (*anubhava*), attentiveness (*avadhāna*), steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*), and faith (*śraddhā*); [he is] the pure knowledge of the sixfold internal organ consisting of feeling (*bhāva*), intellect (*jñāna*), mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), thought (*buddhi*), and consciousness (*citta*); [he is] the satisfaction of the six objects of the six sense organs; [he is] the true knowledge of the sixfold existence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the organs of action denoted by the six syllables; and [he is] the well-knowing, beautiful mind free from egoism.
Being a limb consists in possessing the power whose nature is the sixfold group of pure consciousness and intellect. || 1 ||
In that regard,

when the mental space— which possesses a subtle form whose nature consists of the powers of consciousness and so forth contracted by the play of Maheśvara— is conditioned by earth, water, fire, air, and ether;
