The state of being a practitioner (*upāsaka*) consists in being illuminated by *śuddhavidyā*, which bestows the distinction that serves as the basis for the differentiation of the upward creation.

The classification of that practitioner into categories such as "devotee" (*bhakta*) and so forth is as follows: [it begins with] taking refuge in Śiva through the marks of Śiva—such as sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads—preceded by the realization of the identity between the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama*.
Devotion (*bhaktatva*) consists in possessing unsurpassed and firm love, which is produced by the knowledge of the greatness of that very object [of devotion]. (1)

Māheśvaratva (the state of being a devotee of Maheśvara) consists in the quality of being presided over by the identity established through the relationship of tādātmya (essential identity) as defined by Śiva, which resides in the oneness of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama. || 2 ||

The state of being graced (*prasāditva*) consists in possessing a lack of mindfulness and an absence of attentive concentration regarding the eight enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) and the five conducts (*pañcācāras*), which have as their subject matter the Guru, the *liṅga*, the *jaṅgama*, the water from the feet (*pādodaka*), the grace (*prasāda*), the sacred ash (*bhasma*), the *rudrākṣa* beads, the mantras, and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*). || 3 ||

Prāṇaliṅgitva (being marked by the vital breath as the liṅga) consists in possessing a specific form of intense attachment to the identity with the liṅga of the vital breath, while being characterized by the grace of the water used for washing the feet—which has not been transgressed by obstacles such as disease—and while not enjoying anything other than that [liṅga]. || 4 ||
While possessing the state of being a *satī* (faithful wife) established through the relationship between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the *liṅga* (the object of devotion),
while possessing the cessation of the enjoyment of another *satī* through a cognition characterized by the absence of any other *satī* to be enjoyed by oneself,
and while being filled with the bliss of the union with one's own power of consciousness (*cicchakti*),...
Refuge-hood consists in being filled with devotion, knowledge, and dispassion, which take recourse in the path of cessation (nivṛtti). || 5 ||

It is the state of oneness with the single, inward-turned Great Liṅga, which consists in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the identity of all things with Śiva—attained through non-conceptuality, the absence of objective support, the absence of appearance, and the manifestation of that which arises immediately after the cessation of the semblance of the contemplation of reality; it is comparable to the union of fire and camphor. || 6 ||

By means of [the scriptural passage] beginning with "The Self is to be seen," the knowledge of the non-different Self— which is established as being in accordance with the systematic harmony (samanvaya) indicated by the marks of purport such as the introduction and conclusion regarding the means to liberation— is shown to take the form of meditative worship (upāsanā) consisting of hearing, reflection, and contemplation.

Having explained the essential nature of the reality of the *liṅga* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is to be meditated upon according to that [text], and having also established the status of being a meditator (*upāsaka*) toward it by way of defining its constituent parts, the method of meditation is now set forth for the reality of the *liṅga*.
The limb of the reality of refuge is the characteristic of refuge, which is *prāṇa*; through the analogy of the seed and the tree,
there is a continuous realization of non-difference by means of contraction and expansion.

The initial form of worship consists of the cultivation of the identity with the sixfold characteristics of the state of being an "Aṅga" (limb) in a general sense. For one who has thus taken refuge, there arises the recognition of one's own true nature (*svātmapratyabhijñāna*), which takes the form of worship attained through the glance of the Guru characterized by self-reflection.
For one who is diligent, the experience of all objects such as sound— which are the respective domains of each external sense organ characterized by the ear and so forth—
is the means for the internal-turning tree of the mind; it is the seed known as the Great Liṅga, whose characteristics have been described as being in the form of the Praṇava.
And the first [stage] consists of the uninterrupted practice of the realization of non-difference and the meditation on the specific [form]. || 1 ||
Through the cause of the successive grace of *paśyantī* and the others— consisting of the intention to speak,

determination, and utterance— there arises, by means of the *nāda*, *sunāda*, and *mahānāda*, a continuous realization of non-difference between the ear as the instrument for hearing the scripture characterized by the words of the teacher and the *yakāra*-form of the *prasāda-liṅga*, just like [the non-difference between] a seed and a tree.
The second is the worship with specific distinctions. || 2 ||

The special form of meditation (*viśeṣopāsanā*) consists in the continuous realization of non-difference between the mobile *liṅga*— which is presented through synonymous terms such as "the mobile *liṅga* born of the *cāra-liṅga*"— and the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*), which pervades all limbs and serves as the means for perceiving objects of touch such as cold and heat, and which is composed of the form of speech (*vākāramaya*).
The third [verse]. || 3 ||

The fourth special form of worship consists in the continuous realization of non-difference, namely that the eye itself is the Śiva-liṅga composed of the syllable *Śi*, for it is the great light that serves as the means for illuminating all objects of form that have entered the pupil of the eye. 4.

The fifth special form of worship consists in the continuous practice of non-dual realization, wherein the tongue itself— the instrument for the tasting of the flavor arising from the recitation of the six-syllable mantra, whose very nature is the embodiment of the Guru manifested as the six flavors beginning with sweet— is perceived as the *liṅga* of the Guru composed of the syllable *ma*. 5.

The nose itself— the means for practicing prāṇāyāma produced through the sequence of exhalation (recaka) and so forth, which consists of the purification of the body that serves as the basis for the movement of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) through the two channels named iḍā and piṅgalā, and which is the cause for performing virtuous deeds— is the linga of conduct consisting of the letter *na*; this constitutes the uninterrupted realization of non-difference.
The sixth is the meditation on specific attributes.
Thus, since both types of meditation—those concerning the universal and the particular—are each sixfold, all six types of meditation have been elucidated.
Now, one might ask: by relying on these sixfold meditations, immediately after the cessation of the limiting adjunct of the body—

Regarding the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*)—which consists of the seventeen principles and comprises both the gross limiting adjunct (*sthūla-upādhi*) and its root cause, the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*) consisting of name and form—what is meant by their "oneness"? Is it a dissolution, as in the case of bracelets, crowns, and so forth into gold, or like jars and other objects into a lump of clay; or is it something else, such as that which is imagined through defects like cataracts?

Is sublation [of the world] like that of silver in mother-of-pearl and the like due to the influence of sleep, or like that of the dreamy manifold in the individual self (*jīvātman*) due to the direct realization of the reality of the substratum? It is not the first, because [sublation occurs] in the cause, such as gold or clay.

For one who has ceased [from transmigratory existence], there would be the recurrence of saṃsāricity for the liberated one— who abides in the form of the cause— just as there is a renewed birth at a later time for the world-expansion consisting of name and form (nāmarūpa), such as bracelets, crowns, jars, and potsherds, which depends upon the operations of their respective makers like goldsmiths and potters. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.

In your system, because the direct realization of the reality of the *liṅga* is based on the cessation of the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna-kāraṇa*) that is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), [it would follow] that the power (*śakti*) which transforms the phenomenal world is of the nature of an attribute of the supreme reality (*paramatattva*).

Because the admission of [their] destruction is impossible. Nor should it be said that there is a cessation of the prior state, as in the case of the contact between fire and camphor; for even in that case, the specific element (bhūta) which is the camphor would necessarily undergo cessation within its own cause, namely heat (tejas), and thus it does not differ from [the view of] subsisting in the form of its cause.

The analogy of the seed and the tree is also established in the demonstration of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), concluding with the statement, "O gentle one, all these creatures have their root in Being," through nine successive repetitions of illustrations given to Śvetaketu, beginning with, "Bring a fruit of this *nyagrodha* tree," and ending with, "There stands a great *nyagrodha* tree."
Thus, since it is impossible to say that the state of being qualified by the reality denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) is sublated, one might ask:

"What then is this 'sāmarasya' (perfect equilibrium)? If so, [the answer is: having accepted the theory of indeterminable manifestation (*anirvacanīya-khyāti*), it refers to the transformation of the beginningless but finite connection with the qualification of Māyā into the form of the world.
Even if this is accepted, since the thirty-first principle, Māyā-tattva, and its specific form,

Avidyā, exist, then through the arising of Vidyā— which is their opposite— there occurs the cessation of Avidyā (designated as a "bond"). This results in the state of *sāmarasya*, wherein both the insentient and the sentient abide as the True Self (*sadātman*), which is their causal ground.

Furthermore, the cessation of the bonds (*pāśanivṛtti*) consists precisely in the nature of the substratum itself. By this [inquiry], one asks: what is this cessation of the bonds—is it of the nature of existence, of the nature of non-existence, or of the nature of both existence and non-existence? Not the first, because it would entail the loss of the state of non-duality (*advitīyatva*).
Not the second, because if the cessation of the bonds were of the nature of non-existence, it would entail the absence of any fruit for knowledge (*vidyā*).

The third [alternative] is not tenable; for the consequence of there being no distinction between the bound and the liberated would follow from the persistence of an indefinable relationship, and so forth—this has already been refuted. And thus, regarding the six sense organs characterized as mind, ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose:
The insentient instruments of knowledge [attain their status] through the sentient,
according to the analogy of the seed and the tree, within the characteristics of the Mahāliṅga, Prasādaliṅga, Jaṅgamaliṅga, Śivaliṅga, Guruliṅga, and Ācāraliṅga.
By teaching that the means of realization consists in the contemplation of the equilibrium of forms existing as the essence of their cause,
the ultimate goal is the attainment of sentience once again by those insentient things produced from the sentient; therefore,
even the linguistic usage of the term "liṅga" (the subtle body) applies to the six insentient organs.

This is intended to indicate the intention that, through the aforementioned method, when the inert limiting adjuncts (*jaḍopādhi*) of the various limited consciousnesses (*caitanya*)— which are termed "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇacaitanya*)— are removed, they attain their prior state. Then,
by means of the six [stages] beginning with *nivṛtti*, *pratiṣṭhā*, *vidyā*, *śānti*, *śāntyatīta*, and *śāntyatītottara*.
Together with the *kalās*, there are the *ācāraliṅga*, *guruliṅga*, *śivaliṅga*, *jaṅgamaliṅga*, *prasādaliṅga*, and *mahāliṅga*, along with the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, ears, and mind.
Having attained the state of oneness with the refuge of the devotees of Maheśvara, the Prasādins, and the Prāṇaliṅgins,

they have come to possess sixfold distinctions by virtue of being the perceivers of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound, and by virtue of being the smeller, taster, seer, toucher, and hearer— thus comprising all objects of perception.

The first stage consists of a specific meditation concerning the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) in general, [viewing it] as non-different from the nature of the *liṅga*. In this way, the six meditations on the non-difference of each specific cognizer— from the olfactory faculty onwards— should also be performed according to possibility in the order already described.
They are to be inferred by virtue of being qualified by that.

The fruit of these meditations, however, is the cessation of bondage (*pāśa*). Bondage, moreover, is the characteristic of the bound soul (*paśu*). The state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), while possessing a distinction brought about by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*)—like a spark of fire residing within wood—is [the condition from which liberation arises].
Being reflected in the latent impressions (vāsanā) enveloped by the Māyā of the Lord, and being veiled by the impurities of Āṇava, Kārma, and Māyika,
[the soul] possesses only limited agency, distinct from [the attributes of] omnificatory power, omniscience, perfection, eternity, and omnipresence.

While being enveloped by the five-fold sheaths (*kañcuka*) consisting of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*, and *niyati*— which bring about [respectively] the states of knowing nothing, incompleteness, impermanence, non-pervasiveness, and limitation— there arises the experience of pleasure and pain reflected through *māyā*, which is characterized by the mutual differentiation of knowledge and action as they manifest from the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) pregnant with intentionality.

Bondage consists of the state of being bound by the twenty-five principles (tattvas), characterized by the equilibrium of the qualities of delusion (moha), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas). That very state is what constitutes the condition of being a transmigrating soul (jīvatva).

Now, is this individual soul (jīva), denoted by the term *paśu*, one or many? In the first case, there is but one soul, and only one body is possessed of that soul; all other bodies, however, are devoid of a soul, like the various and more diverse bodies fashioned in the state of dream. Furthermore, the entire world is a construction of that ignorance, like the perception of objects in a dream.

As long as there is the state of ignorance, just so long does all worldly transaction (vyavahāra) exist. Some say that even the transaction regarding one who is bound or liberated is merely imagined—like the liberation of another person in a dream—because the individual soul (jīva) is one; but that is not so, for there is a further teaching of distinction.

Because of the contradiction with such sūtras as "The world-process is the sport of the Lord" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.33) and "The part [of the Lord] is not [identical to Him], because of the designation of multiplicity" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.43);

thus, Hiraṇyagarbha alone is the primary individual soul (jīva), while others are like the reflections of that [primary soul], resembling the appearance of a cloth superimposed upon human bodies painted on a canvas.

"The appearances of the individual soul (jīvābhāsa) partake in saṃsāra and so forth"—this is the view of those who maintain the doctrine of a single soul in multiple bodies with specific distinctions. But even that is not [correct], because Hiraṇyagarbha—who is regarded as the primary soul and serves as the archetype (bimba)—is distinct in every kalpa; therefore, of which Hiraṇyagarbha... [is it said]?
Because there is no determining factor for [the distinction] regarding suchness (*tathātva*), those who maintain the doctrine of a single,
undifferentiated soul residing in all bodies argue that thus there is only one soul presiding over every body.
And this being so, even though there is a difference of bodies due to the difference in the limbs of the body, [the soul remains one].

There would follow the consequence of mutual sharing of pleasure, pain, and so forth; for even though the individual souls (*jīva*) are one, it is possible that there is no mutual sharing of pleasure, pain, and so forth, just as there is no such sharing across different births. [Objection: But surely, by virtue of the yogis’ manifold bodies (*kāyavyūha*),...

If it is argued that, because we observe the recollection of pleasure, pain, and so forth even when the body has changed, the soul must be eternal since it possesses this capacity for the recollection of pleasure, pain, and so forth—this is not so; for that [recollection] is not a valid example, as it is like the perception of distant objects through the power of yoga. Therefore...
The doctrine that there is one single living soul (jīva) inhabiting many bodies without distinction is also charming only at first sight;

for it is equally subject to the absence of any established distinction between the bound and the liberated. This is because of such scriptural passages as, "Whosoever among the gods awakened to that, he alone became That," and so forth. If it is argued that this is not so because of the prohibition [of plurality], we say no, on account of the section beginning with "Not from the embodied soul" (*Śārīrād adhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, this is because it contradicts the Bhāṣya which establishes that Śuka was liberated. By this, the doctrine of a single jīva—whether in the view that the jīva is a reflection of ignorance or in the view that the jīva is delimited by ignorance—is refuted.

In the second [view] as well, having accepted that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), and following the doctrine of the plurality of souls (*anekajīvavāda*) regarding the distinction between the bound and the liberated, some [teachers] hold the view concerning whether the ignorance (*ajñāna*) to be removed by the knowledge of Brahman for those souls is one or many.

Ignorance (*ajñāna*) has as its sole locus and object the pure Brahman, and liberation is simply the destruction of that [ignorance]. Even if this were so, there would be no contingency of universal liberation occurring when one person becomes perfected through the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) and the consequent destruction of ignorance; for we accept that this single ignorance possesses parts (*sāṃśatva*), such that during the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*), [only those parts corresponding to that individual are destroyed].
Since it is possible to assert that— because one accepts the persistence of a trace of ignorance— the partial ignorance, being composed of parts,
ceases only in part when the realization of Brahman arises in some limiting adjunct such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
while it continues to persist as before in other limiting adjuncts.
Therefore, some say that ignorance is indeed one and partless;

that is not so, because if one accepts that a single ignorance has multiple parts, there is the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating the destruction of many parts. The position that ignorance is one and partless should be maintained as follows:

According to the view of a portion of the Nyāya school, the absence of contact with a jar (*ghaṭasaṃyogābhāva*) is the restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*) for the occurrence of the absolute absence of a jar (*ghaṭātyantābhāva*) on the ground; and this being so, the absolute absence of a jar, which exists by being conjoined across many locations, [is restricted] to a particular location.

Just as [the ether] does not become conjoined when the conjunction with a jar arises because its own [prior state] has not ceased, so too, since the mind is the regulator of ignorance’s manifestation within consciousness, ignorance— which exists by being conjoined to specific regions of consciousness through that limiting adjunct (upādhi)—
is severed at the heart-knot upon the arising of the vision of Brahman.
According to the method stated in such scriptural passages as the *Rigveda*, when the mind ceases [its activity], one is no longer bound;

otherwise, one remains as before. Since bondage and liberation consist respectively in the association with and dissociation from ignorance (*ajñāna*), and since ignorance is indeed partless, that [position] is incorrect, because [one perceives]: "Ignorance exists in me."

Since ignorance is experienced as having a positive (bhāva) nature, the assumption that the mind's connection acts as the regulator for the manifestation of positive ignorance is untenable due to a lack of parallelism with the illustrative example; furthermore, because it is experienced as residing in the individual soul (jīva)—as in "I have ignorance"—it cannot reside in Brahman. And if [it were to] reside in Brahman...

Since there is no distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, it would follow that Brahman, too, is bound. For Brahman’s being the locus of ignorance by virtue of being its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) does not entail bondage; rather, the soul’s status as bound is established because its being the locus of ignorance occurs through its agency in the form of "this is mine. Therefore, ignorance [does not belong to Brahman].
However, it has pure consciousness as its substratum, yet resides in the individual soul (jīva) and has Brahman as its object;
and existing in all individual souls— which are the forms of reflections in the internal organ— as a universal residing in each particular instance, it remains present until knowledge arises.

Just as a genus (jāti) abandons one individual (vyakti) that has perished, it likewise abandons a certain person; and liberation, characterized by the severing of bonds, occurs precisely through the abandonment of ignorance (ajñāna). Elsewhere, among other limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and other individuals, it resorts [to them] just as before, like a genus; thus, because the illustrative example is dissimilar, ignorance must be of a positive nature (bhāvarūpa).

"It is partless and indeed one. This too is not [the case], because in the example, since the universal (*jāti*) is eternal, even when it abandons a perished individual (*vyakti*), it remains everywhere devoid of connection with that [individual] due to the destruction of its own substratum, and does not perish.
Likewise here as well, when the life of its own substratum is destroyed, it abandons it; being eternal, it [remains] itself.

Since it is impossible to say that [the bondage] persists, there too the illustrative example is dissimilar. Therefore, having accepted that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is distinct for each individual soul (*jīva*), the distinction between the bound and the liberated must be established; thus, the actual state of affairs is that even the bond denoted by the term "ignorance" is manifold.

If it is asked, "In this view that there is a plurality of *pāśas*, by which individual soul's *pāśa* was this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) created?", [the answer is: due to the absence of any determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), this phenomenal world is created by all the *pāśas*, like a cloth woven from many threads.
Just as when one *pāśa* is severed—like the destruction of a single thread—the cloth common to them all is destroyed.

There is the destruction of the manifestation common to that [individual soul]. In the same way, just as there exists another cloth produced by other threads, it is logically possible that there exists another manifestation common to both the bound (sakala) and the liberated (itara), produced by other bonds.
Let us return to the subject at hand.

Thus, by demonstrating through the perspective of the diversity of bonds (*pāśanānātvapakṣa*) that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is imagined by the ignorance (*avidyā*) of all individual souls (*jīva*), and by the possibility of establishing bondage and liberation on the basis of an ignorance that is distinct for each soul, [the author] establishes that... [of that].

Furthermore, since it is inappropriate to establish that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is eternal like a genus (*jāti*), bondage and liberation consist solely in its association with or dissociation from [the self]. Thus, ignorance, which is a single positive entity, resides in the individual soul (*jīva*) as its agent and has Brahman as its object; the individual souls are manifold as being delimited by that [ignorance].
The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*); the soul conditioned by that is the bound one (*paśu*).

And the fetter (*pāśa*), according to the definition already stated, consists of the fivefold equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which manifests as the bestower of pleasure, pain, and delusion through the reflection of *māyā*.

It consists of the nature of the twenty principles (*tatvas*). The cessation of bonds (*pāśanivṛtti*), however, is based on the aforementioned twelvefold worship directed toward the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*. Through that means, liberation consists of the substratum characterized by the five conducts (*pañcācāra*) and the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*).
Thus, the entire path of the Vīraśaiva Siddhānta, which maintains that the material cause undergoes transformation through its inherent power (śakti), is entirely consistent and coherent.

[Thus, the *Ṣaṭsthala*— divided into one hundred and one unsurpassed sections produced by churning the ocean of the *Śāmbhava-āgama*, which was obtained through the grace of Tōṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the mobile form of the glorious, beginningless, and stainless [Lord],]
In the work composed by the eminent teacher Śrī Maritoṇṭadārya— who bestows a mass of bliss from the tasting of the nectar of the realization of reality—
[entitled] *Yaḍavamurārikoṭekolāhalaikāṅgivīravairisaptāṅgaharaṇapaścimasamudrādhī*...

In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, composed through the instruction of Basava— the thunderbolt to the earth, who gladdened the heart of Mallāmbā, the lawful consort of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth and moon over the milky ocean of the Nāyaka dynasty, the preceptor who established the pure Vedic non-dual doctrine of Śiva— [The section on] the purification of the corpse.
The First Chapter in the Section on Debate.
[The Second Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O Master, treasury of the knowledge of the secrets of the meaning of all scriptures,
[I shall act] in the midst of the assembly of Vīraśaivas, preceded by the throwing of a handful of rice.
What did Bhṛṅgī say at the very beginning to the most excellent Śīlavat, who was establishing the Śrī Vīraśaiva Siddhānta?
Spreading laughter among the members of the assembly and revealing the opposite of the virtuous man's words through modulations of voice, facial expressions, gestures, and so forth.
O Teacher, out of compassion for me, please explain all of this: how did he, being virtuous, fail to console him with appropriate words?
O King, because he was a guest, the virtuous Bhṛṅgin first spoke words of welcome to his preceptor; I shall relate that to you.

Because the Śrī Guru is the most venerable of all— being the unique cause for liberation, which is the most highly esteemed among the four aims of human life— and because he bestows the knowledge of qualified non-duality characterized by the state of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium) between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, [there follows] the approaching of him (*tadupasadanasya*).

Because of the superior status of the teacher—characterized by being a master of the limbs [of knowledge], a worthy recipient, and the proper locus—as prescribed in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: "For the sake of knowing that, one should approach a guru alone, with fuel in hand, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) who is established in Brahman," and as it is said: "He for whom [there is] the supreme [devotion] toward the God..."

"Devotion toward the guru should be the same as toward the deity; for to that high-souled one, these truths thus declared become manifest"— thus, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, by means of the contemplation of the identity between the guru and one's own worshipped chosen deity, the meaning not yet taught becomes revealed just like that which was taught by the guru.
And because he is described as the means for illumination, the Guru alone is to be worshipped first by the Vīraśaivas who seek liberation and desire the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
Regarding his definition, it is stated in the *Śivasūtravārtika*:
Bestowing grace as a guiding star upon the fathomless ocean of doubt,
the Guru alone is Supreme Śiva, because he is the very embodiment of supreme knowledge.
In the Śivadharmottara, it is said:
"He alone is to be saluted, he alone is to be fully worshipped; he alone is the mother and the father of the worlds."
He alone is a kinsman, he alone is a teacher, and he alone is Śiva,
who bestows the supreme nectar of knowledge.
In the Sūtasaṃhitā and the Śaivaratnākara it is said:
"O Lord of the Gods, Śiva himself is directly present in the form of the Guru, and not otherwise;
the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, abide within his two feet."
By this statement, [he is established] as the one who,

through his role as the bestower of grace— manifested by a special affection that removes all doubts regarding the meaning of the entire scriptures (which are otherwise difficult for ordinary people to dispel due to their lack of knowledge of the reality of various objects)— is [the Lord of] all...
Because he is to be worshipped as the very kinsman of embodied beings,
because he possesses a pair of feet that serve as the support for the three worlds with all their mobile and immobile inhabitants, and because he is established as non-different from Śiva,
the Guru alone is the supreme of all.

Is it not the case that knowledge— characterized by having the Supreme Self as its qualificandum and the distinctness from others as its qualifier, and preceded by the knowledge of the true nature of categories— is the means to liberation, which consists in the destruction of suffering that does not coexist with the prior non-existence of the twenty-one kinds of suffering residing in one's own continuum?
The logicians think thus.

The knowers of the tradition of Nirīśvara Sāṅkhya maintain that the knowledge of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*— caused by *sāttvika* virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty— is the means to liberation, which consists of a gradual upward ascent with unimpeded progress resulting from the dissolution of *prakṛti*.

The followers of Patañjali, however, maintain that knowledge— even of Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the self of the collective and individual totality of all the senses by virtue of presiding over both Prakṛti and Puruṣa— is a means to liberation, provided it is a knowledge [of him] as distinct from those two.

The Pūrvamīmāṃsakas maintain that the knowledge of the distinction between the body and the self— attained through the performance of dharma characterized by Vedic injunction— is the means to liberation, which consists in the preservation of the prior non-existence of suffering.

Devotion preceded by the knowledge that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme among all gods and is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)— this devotion being itself preceded by the knowledge of the non-difference between the state of the served and the server, which is produced by the gradations [of spiritual progress] based on the prior knowledge of the reality of the world composed of fivefold divisions—
is the means to liberation, which consists in the experience of one's own innate bliss free from all veils.
The Mādhvas are proponents of difference.
Having attained the status of a Vīra-Vaiṣṇava through the application of the five purificatory rites beginning with *tāpa*,

one [realizes] by means of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) that the Supreme Vāsudeva— whose body is the entire phenomenal universe and who exists in the forms of the Para, Vyūha, Vibhava, Arcya, and Antaryāmin— is the ultimate substratum (*sarvaśeṣatva*) of all.
The knowledge of qualified non-duality (viśiṣṭādvaita), characterized by devotion as being the very self of all bodies,
[is attained] in the non-material Vaikuṇṭha above the shell of the cosmic egg, within a pavilion of a thousand non-material pillars,
presided over by many *prapannas* such as Nammāḷvār, the author of the Drāviḍa Prabandhas.
Having emerged from the cosmic egg through the Sudarśana gate and having crossed the Virajā river,

it consists of remaining in a state of uninterrupted experience of service characterized by complete similarity with the Lord of Lakṣmī— except for the specific status of being her husband— due to its being purified by the touch of the hands of non-human beings.
The followers of Rāmānuja, proponents of qualified non-dualism (viśiṣṭādvaitavādinaḥ), maintain that the means of proof is verbal testimony (ukti).
[He is] endowed with a permanent, divine, and auspicious form characterized by having a blue throat, three eyes, being accompanied by Umā, and having the moon as His crest-jewel;

He is filled with the six limbs, the ten imperishable [powers], and the sixfold sovereign excellences; and He possesses the eternally pure, unsurpassed, and all-pervading powers of knowledge and action, which are established by His own nature and transcend the thirty-six categories of existence.

Through her, by means of devotion born from the grace of Śiva, there arises the knowledge of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*), characterized by the state of being the ultimate remainder of everything, regarding that Supreme Śiva— who is designated as the Lord, who governs the five cosmic acts, and whose body is the phenomenal universe— outside of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

Those who follow the doctrine of Nīlakaṇṭhācārya maintain that liberation consists in abiding in a state of equality with Paramaśiva— free from the status of being the husband of Pārvatī— in the non-material Kailāsa known as the Supreme Abode (Paramapada), which is adorned by hosts of Pramathas such as Nandin.

Through the realization of the non-difference of the individual soul— which is a reflection in the internal organ— from the non-distinct Brahman, by means of the falsity of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) consisting in its being indefinable (*anirvacanīyatva*), there occurs the attainment of one's own true nature as the immutable (*kūṭastha*) essence of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), via the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The proponents of non-duality (Advaitavādins) maintain that this is the means for achieving liberation (kaivalya).

If it is asked, "Since there exist many gurus who teach the knowledge that produces liberation characterized by such various forms of difference and non-difference, how can it be determined that the guru Vīramāheśvara alone is the most excellent of all?"— it is replied as follows:

Because the contemplation of that state of identity— which consists of the perfect fusion (*sāmarasya*) of the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*— is the uncommon means for attaining liberation, it is the cause of *mokṣa*; therefore, [this work] imparts the knowledge of the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*), divided into one hundred and one distinct varieties, which bestows such specialized non-dual knowledge and was propagated by the founder of the Vīramāheśvara tradition.

Of one who is perfected in the limbs [of yoga], who is established in the specific mental contemplation consisting of the eightfold offering— namely, the limbs, signs, face, hands, power, devotion, mantra-words,
and the meaning of the names— and who is characterized by the unique qualities of a Guru such as tranquility and the rest.
The Guru is more venerable than all others;
for it is said in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"One approaches [the Guru] who is world-renowned and free from greed and delusion."
One who knows how to investigate the reality of the self and is liberated from the delusion regarding sense objects.
One who knows the reality of the Śiva-siddhānta, whose doubts and delusions have been severed,
who is skilled in the application of all tantras, righteous, and truthful in speech.
One who follows the conduct inherited through family lineage, avoids the practices of evil paths,
is devoted to the meditation on Śiva, is tranquil, and possesses discernment regarding the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).
One who is proficient in smearing oneself with ashes, who discerns the true nature of ash,
who is eager to wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and who wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads.
One who is engaged in the wearing of the *liṅga*, devoted to the worship of the *liṅga*,
who knows the reality of the yoga of the *liṅga* and its limbs, and whose latent impression of non-duality is firmly established.

"A disciple endowed with devotion should serve the illustrious Guru, the proponent of Śiva, who knows the distinctions between the *liṅga*, the *aṅga*, and the *sthala*, as his supreme teacher. Thus it is said.
And like stones and so forth, that [oneness] is untenable; moreover, because of the designation of difference,

as in the sūtras beginning with "A part, because of various designations," just as in the case of stones such as lapis lazuli and sun-crystals, even though there is no difference in their nature as stone, [there is a distinction].

It has been stated that, due to the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*), there exists a diversity of essential nature and a diversity of effects characterized by inferior, intermediate, and superior qualities;

likewise, for the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), a state of inferiority and superiority as well as a diversity of effects are established on account of the distinction between their individual instances. Furthermore, the universal (*sāmānya*) of "stoneness" is not non-different [from its instances].
It should not be argued that since individuals are indeed distinct, there can be neither difference nor non-difference in a single locus;

for it is universally accepted that among individuals themselves there exists both non-difference— in the form of the absence of difference whose counter-positive is delimited by the generality of "stoneness"— and difference, whose counter-positive is delimited by "lapis lazuli-ness" (*vaidūryatva*) and so forth.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of treating diamond and lapis lazuli as co-referential, because such usage must necessarily be admitted only when it refers to the non-difference of universals, whereas there is no non-difference of particulars in their case.
For this very reason, even with respect to God, the vision of His non-difference from the individual soul is taught by the Sūtra through the term "the Self" (*ātmeti*).
[They] approach and cause [the meaning] to be grasped. Thus,
although there is non-difference— consisting in the absence of difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the state of being a solid ground (sthalatva)—
because this exists in both the linga and the aṅga grounds, even though they are non-distinct;
Since the difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the states of being both a limb (*aṅga*) and a sign (*liṅga*) exists in both [the individual and the universal], the two are distinct;

thus, difference and non-difference exist in one and the same thing. In this way, with reflection and with reasoning, there is the knowledge of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*), which consists in the perfect harmony (*sāmarasya*) of the sign and the limb.

Because it is the means for attaining liberation in the form of non-difference from the Great Liṅga, such knowledge and liberation [are superior] in comparison to the knowledge and liberation propounded by the multitude of teachers mentioned previously.
Since he is most highly honored because his teaching is supported by logical justification, it is established that the Vīraśaiva Guru alone is transcendent.

[Thus ends the section on] the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*), which are distinguished by one hundred and one unsurpassed divisions arising from the churning of the ocean of the Śāmbhava Āgama— attained through the grace of Toṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the venerable, beginningless, stainless, and mobile Aparā.
[This work is] composed by the eminent teacher Śrī Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows a mass of bliss from tasting the nectar of the realization of non-reality;
[it concerns] the seizure of the seven constituents of the enemy of the sole hero whose body was the tumultuous roar of ten million Yādava Murāris, [and] the lord of the western ocean...

In the instruction of Basava, the thunderbolt for the earth, who brought joy to the heart of Mallāmbā— the lawful wife of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth and the full moon to the milk-ocean of the lineage of Keladi Sadāśivarāya Nāyaka, the preceptor who established the doctrine of non-duality according to the pure Śiva-Vedic tradition.
The Second Chapter in the Section on Debate within the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*.
The Third Chapter in the Section on Debate within the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*.
O Lord, having heard the excellence of the Vīraśaiva gurus through the extensive discourses on the teachings of the Guru, I became joyful; tell me whatever else there is beyond that.
Listen, O King, as I shall today declare the majesty of wearing the *liṅga*,
which is pleasant to hear in the form of a discourse and endowed with the authority of the Vedas and Āgamas.
Since for those who have entered the Vīraśaiva system, the contemplation of the identity between the *liṅga* and the body (*liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya*) alone is required as the generator of liberation,
and because the wearing of the chosen *liṅga* is considered an internal and most venerable practice therein, [there are] many [reasons] for its wearing...
Since the means of valid cognition are awake, the wearing of the marks must necessarily be performed.

For it is said in the Vātula-tantra: "That which consists in bearing the *liṅga* of Śiva, the Teacher of the World, with an extremely steady mind for as long as one lives— that indeed is the supreme vow."

In the Pārameśvara [Tantra]: "Through constant contact with divine manifestations, through the constant wearing of rudrākṣa beads, and through the wearing of my liṅga, he is indeed myself; of this there is no doubt."
O Goddess, he on whose forehead there is the *vibhūti* mark, on whose neck the *liṅga* consisting of me resides, and who wears *rudrākṣa* beads upon his body—he is myself; of this there is no doubt.
O Īśānī, he on whose body these three—the vibhūti, the rudrākṣa, and the liṅga—are present, is Rudra himself; he is none other than I, without a doubt.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara, the liṅga is said to be threefold: gross, subtle, and beyond the supreme.
This gross one is the chosen liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga), which one should wear externally upon the body.
But that subtle *prāṇaliṅga* is that which consists of internal contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
That which is declared as higher than the highest is called the Linga of Contentment;
it is beyond all conceptualization, unmanifest, the Supreme Brahman known by the name Śiva.
This auspicious emblem directly wards off what is undesirable;
therefore, the wise person should always wear it upon their body with focused attention.
In the Vātula-tantra, it is said:
"One should wear the Īśvara-linga on the head, or in the region of the throat, or in the armpit, or on the chest, or in the belly, or even on the hand."
Always remaining pure while discharging urine and other excretions, while traveling, and while eating, one should maintain the sacred and divine Linga in a restrained place.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, opening or closing his eyes,
whether pure or impure, he should wear the *liṅga* everywhere.
In accordance with the authority of such scriptural statements as these,
the Guru [removes] the three impurities (mala) residing in the three bodies for those seekers of liberation who are devoted to the Vīraśaiva vow.
Having consumed the three marks with the three initiations, he taught [the doctrine of] the three marks.

Thus, by means of the threefold initiation— distinguished by the differences in its forms as piercing (*vedha*), mantra, and ritual action— as understood from this statement, one effects the abandonment of the three bodies after first uprooting the three impurities (*mala*)— namely the *āṇava*, *māyeya*, and *kārmika*— which are inherent in the triad of gross, subtle, and causal bodies; thereby bringing about their status as the limbs of abandonment (*tyāga-aṅga*), enjoyment (*bhoga-aṅga*), and yoga (*yoga-aṅga*).

In those statements which establish that the wearing of the *liṅga* is the means for achieving the supreme human goal— stating that the Guru taught the true nature of the *iṣṭaliṅga*, the *prāṇaliṅga*,
and the *bhāvaliṅga*— one must, with faith, recognize the necessity of wearing the *liṅga* and its [significance].

It is understood that the wearing of the *liṅga* must necessarily be maintained because it brings about perpetual purity; that one who is steadfast in the observance of the vow of wearing the *liṅga* is the very embodiment of Śiva; and that this vow is to be observed for as long as one lives. Thus, the wearing of the *liṅga* is essential.
It must be performed.
Indeed, the internal wearing of the *liṅga* alone is more highly esteemed; for it is said in the *Siddhāntasāra*:
"I worship the jewel-like *ātma-liṅga*, situated within the lotus-heart of the city of *māyā*."
With the constant consecrations of the water of the pure mind from the river of faith, and with the flowers of meditative concentration, for the sake of non-rebirth.
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"The supreme Liṅga of Śaṅkara, which is the nature of consciousness and the cause of all—
fixing that within the mind is declared to be the internal [form of worship]."
For the supreme reality, known as Śiva, is of the nature of consciousness, the cause of the universe,
free from all worldly impurities, partless, and beyond conceptual construction.
Consisting of the subtle power that causes the radiant manifestation of the bliss of existence,
it is immeasurable, ineffable, and worshipped by those seeking liberation.
The Supreme Brahman is the Great Liṅga, beyond the phenomenal world and imperishable;
it alone is the object within the range of the inner abode of all beings.
In the mūlādhāra, in the heart, and between the eyebrows of all embodied beings, the liṅga of light shines eternally; the scriptures declare that to be Brahman.
The small, stainless lotus that serves as the dwelling of another, situated in the center of the city—
within that too is a small, sorrowless sky.
That which is within it is what should be worshipped.

By such statements as these, it is well known to all people that the bestower of liberation is the *jyotir-liṅga* residing within the heart-lotus, which is maintained through the form of meditation and worshipped by seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*), gods, sages, and yogis using purely mental offerings.
If it is argued that external wearing of the insignia (*liṅga*) should not be performed because the desired goal is accomplished by wearing [the internal insignia] alone, we say no;
for it is precisely the object experienced externally during the waking state that appears internally,
exactly as it was perceived, during the state of dreaming.
Likewise, the internal sacrifice is always preceded by the external sacrifice;
if one is devoid of the external sacrifice, the internal sacrifice is not accomplished.
Wise men should perform the worship of their chosen *liṅga* with supreme devotion, both in its external and internal aspects.
The clarified butter residing within the bodies of cows does not nourish themselves;
yet once extracted through their labor and placed outside, it becomes their very medicine.
Thus, although the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, resides within the body,
He does not bestow welfare upon men without external worship.

According to this statement, following the principle that one should first rely upon the *saguṇa* (with attributes) and subsequently resort to the *nirguṇa* (without attributes), there are the *iṣṭaliṅga*, *prāṇaliṅga*, and *bhāvaliṅga*, which correspond respectively to the *sakala*,
*sakalaniṣkala*, and *kevalaniṣkala*.

Since the *iṣṭaliṅga* is the substratum for both the experience of bliss and the worship of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) through one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), the wise practitioner should worship by unifying the *iṣṭaliṅga* with the *prāṇaliṅga*.
Furthermore, he should recite the mantra by unifying the *maṇimālā* with the *mātṛmālā*.
Because of the statement, "Of the *iṣṭaliṅga* [made of] jewels and of the *mātṛkāprāṇaliṅga*," the worship of both the *prāṇaliṅga* and the *iṣṭaliṅga* must be performed in combination.
Since such worship is not possible without wearing the *iṣṭaliṅga*, there is the wearing of the *liṅga*.
It must be performed.

Now, one might object: since the wearing of the *liṅga* and other such practices are to be performed by Tantrikas alone according to these [Tantric] statements, and since they are not taught in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, or Purāṇas, they are non-Vedic;
therefore, they cannot be practiced by those who follow the Veda. To illustrate this:
For those who have fallen away from the Vedic path, there is entry into the path of Tantra;
women, Śūdras, and Brahminical outcasts possess the qualification for the Tantric path.
Indeed, Tantra is for those men who have strayed from the path of the Vedas;
it should never be practiced by those who are devoted to the path of the Vedas.
A person who has fallen away from the Vedas and feels fear regarding the expiatory rites prescribed therein should,
for the sake of gradually achieving success in the Vedas, take recourse to the Tantra.
A mortal initiated into the Tantras should never touch that which is Vedic;
and one who is Vedic should also never touch one initiated into the Tantras.
But the king, most wise, should always establish all those who follow the Vedas and all those who follow the Tantras in their respective, unmixed states.

If it is argued that the wearing of sectarian marks (*liṅgadhāraṇa*) should not be practiced by those following the Vedas because of such scriptural remembrances (*smaraṇa*), we say no; for there exist many declarations from both Vedic and Puranic sources. To illustrate this, it is stated in the *Śivarahasya*:
When the Śiva-liṅga is established within the body, one attains the state of being like Śiva;
therefore, one who desires to attain that experience of Śiva should indeed wear the Śiva-liṅga.
In the Śāṅkara-saṃhitā: "Whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, is committed during the time of sleep,
that becomes false of its own accord at the time of awakening."
Whatever great sin was committed previously through the wearing of the *liṅga*,
all of that goes to dissolution by means of the supreme wearing of the *liṅga*.
Having placed my male organ upon their heads and other limbs, the gods, led by Śakra,
worshipped me residing within that linga and returned to their own abodes.
Furthermore, in that very place,
one should hold the *liṅga* on the lion-throne of the hand with vigilance;
if the *liṅga* falls due to negligence, one should abandon one's life along with it.
In another context,
all noble ancestors desire that their sons, having come together, be endowed with devotion to Śiva.
If there should be virtuous ones whose dispositions are completely pure,
then among them, one may bear the outward mark.
In the *Gāruḍa*, it is said: "For those of the lowest-of-the-low nature, for sinners, and for practitioners of malevolent magic,
there is always no fear of the world of Yama due to the wearing of the *liṅga*."
In the Skanda [Purāṇa]: "Ūṃ Mit— Maheśvara, the supreme Brahman, whose form is the Liṅga,
[is present] in all states and at all times, even for half a moment."
Desiring both enjoyment and liberation without separation from it, the best of the twice-born,
with his mind fixed upon this, should wear [the mark] on these five places.

Thus, by such statements from the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, the *Śivarahasya*, the *Garuḍapurāṇa*, and other Purāṇas— which serve as supplements to the meaning of the Vedas— it is established that the wearing of the *liṅga* effects the continuous contemplation of Śiva, removes previously committed sins, and [is ordained] for the gods...

Because it is established that wearing the *liṅga* leads one to one's own respective state, is desired by one's ancestors for their own deliverance, and results in undesirable consequences for oneself through negligence, the wearing of the *liṅga* is indeed Vedic;
surely, there are many statements in the Purāṇas themselves that prohibit the wearing of the *liṅga*.
Since [the practice] exists, how can it be said that the wearing of the *liṅga* is Vedic? For instance, in the *Prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa* of Hemādri, citing the *Nāradīya*:
"O King, wherever a person has his body marked with the discus, or even marked with the *liṅga*..."
And one should recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta; otherwise, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"The twice-born who joyfully wears a *liṅga* upon his own body, being devoid of fear,
shall remain in hell until the dissolution of all beings."
In the Skanda [Purāṇa]: "If a twice-born man, out of his own desire, wears a *liṅga* upon his own body,
he shall experience terrible hells and in the end attain the state of an outcaste."
In the Śiva Purāṇa:
"O King, for that twice-born man who joyfully wears upon his own body a linga offered by a Śūdra,
there is indeed no atonement, even through many purificatory rites."
In the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"Listen, O mighty-armed Rāma! For those who wear the *liṅga*, the discus, and other such marks, and who are devoted to the duties of *śūdras*, there is no liberation from rebirth."
Because this act is censurable for a Brahmin, an expiation has been declared:
having first performed a mental act [of repentance], one should practice the *kṛcchra* penance for six years.
If a twice-born man, out of desire, accepts gold or even a quarter-measure of it from them,
he should perform a Prājāpatya penance for the sake of purifying that acceptance.

If it is argued that the non-performance of wearing the *liṅga* is established because of such statements, because of the prescription of penance for wearing the *liṅga* and the discus-mark (*cakrāṅka*),
because of the prescription of penance for those who accept [gifts] from them, and because of the association with the prohibited marking of the discus, we say:
no.

When there is a mutual contradiction between the statements prohibiting the wearing of the *liṅga* and the statements enjoining the wearing of the *liṅga*, the statements enjoining the wearing of the *liṅga* possess greater authority because they are rooted in the Veda; whereas the statements prohibiting the wearing of the *liṅga* are weaker because they lack a basis in the Veda.
This is because [the mention of] "branding with a heated discus" can be construed as referring to the branding with a heated *liṅga* prescribed by the Pāśupatas due to their association;
as it has been stated in the *Pūrvatantra*: "In case of contradiction, however, there should be no reliance [on Smṛti], for there is no inference [of Vedic basis] when such a contradiction exists."

"And because of the observation of a reason. For in that case, there is the scriptural injunction (*śruti*), "One should chant the *udgītha* while touching the *audumbarī* pillar," and the traditional law (*smṛti*), "The *audumbarī* pillar must be entirely covered. When these two are in conflict, is there an option (*vikalpa*) due to equal strength, or is there a sublation (*bādha*) of the matter prescribed by the *smṛti* because of the superior authority of the *śruti*?

When this doubt has arisen, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is as follows: because the Smṛtis are remembered by those learned in the Vedas, and because their acceptance is firm, it is possible that they are rooted in the Veda;
therefore, since the Smṛti regarding the "veiling of all" (sarvaveṣṭana) is also rooted in the Veda, the veiling of all [the sacrificial post] must be performed.
Since touching the *audumbarī* pillar is prescribed by the Vedic injunction, "Having touched the *audumbarī*, one should chant the *udgītha*," that touching must also be performed.

When it follows that both [the chanting and the touching] are to be performed simultaneously, and a conflict arises, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, like the case of *vrīhi* and *yava* grains, there is an option (*vikalpa*) because they possess equal force. To this, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:
A Smṛti that contradicts direct Śruti does not possess independent authority;

rather, its authority must be asserted by postulating an underlying Śruti. In that case, when there is a contradiction with direct Śruti, there is no authority regarding its own subject matter due to the lack of expectancy for an underlying Śruti. Therefore, even an option (vikalpa) is not possible.

It is consistent; for the authority of *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) regarding its own object is established immediately through its independence. Therefore, the sublation of *smṛti* (tradition), which functions with delay, by *śruti* is self-evident.
As it was stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda:
As long as one action is perceived in the Śruti and another in the Smṛti, when there is a conflict between the two, the performance of the Śrauta rite is desired.

Thus, by that same principle, since the authority of wearing the *liṅga* has been established here as well through its being ordained by direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), those statements that directly prohibit the wearing of the *liṅga* lack authority. Or else—

Due to their association with the branding of the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*), these [passages] refer to the branding of the heated linga (*taptaliṅgāṅkana*) performed by non-Vedic Pāśupatas; or alternatively, they refer to the lack of entitlement to wear the linga as prescribed in the Āgamas because of being devoid of the Vīraśaiva initiation (*dīkṣā*).
If it is objected: "But was it not stated that the wearing of the *liṅga* is ordained by Śruti?
Since such a Śruti is not perceived, how can it be considered Vedic?"—if this is asked, we say no, because the *Paiṅgāyana-Śruti* serves as its source. And thus says the Śruti:
Those wise ones who here bind the nectar with truth in the world of good deeds— whether at the neck, the armpit, or the mouth—
they cross over evil and beyond death.

The meaning of this Vedic passage is as follows: those who are wise in the world of good deeds—that is, in the world of men—[attain] through truth—that is, by means of an oath—the immortal: namely, the *liṅga*, Brahman, procreation, the sacrificial grass (*kāṭa*), the purifier, the immortal, the waters, the ritual grass-bundle (*prastara*), birth, breath, and likewise the god; these are synonyms for the *liṅga*.

"These are indeed the marks of the Supreme Self," according to the Vedic Nighaṇṭu. "Bound" (*baddhā*) means binding; the word "also" (*api*) has the sense of "or"; the ellipsis is "they exist. They cross over evil (*pāpmānam*), that is, sin; they cross over death (*mṛtyum*), that is, ignorance.
In the word *baddhāḥ*, the suffix *kta* is used in place of the suffix *śatṛ*; this is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

For the sake of the complete cessation of all sins and for the sake of the total removal of beginningless ignorance—the root of transmigratory existence—at one or another of the locations such as the throat, the wearing of the *liṅga* is absolutely necessary.

This is the purport of the Vedic scripture stating that "it must be performed by those desiring liberation. Therefore, the wearing of the *liṅga* must necessarily be performed by followers of the Vedas.

If it is objected that, although the Paiṅgāyana Śākhā has been cited by the authors of the Kalpasūtras as authoritative, there is no reason to trust it because it is not heard among the currently recited Vedic traditions, we say: no;
for even within the currently recited Śākhās, such as the Taittirīya and others, there are specific indications (liṅgas) that are uniquely devoted to the wearing of the [sacred] marks.
These words are heard:
"O Brahmaṇaspati, your purifier is spread out; as the Lord, you encompass our limbs on every side."
"One whose body is not heated does not enjoy that; only those who have been cooked [by austerity] and are bearers [of the burden] attain it. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this Vedic verse is as follows: O Brahmaṇaspati—O Mahādeva, the controller of the four-faced one—for the Śruti says, "He is the lord of Brahman, the supreme ruler of Brahman. You are the Lord (prabhuḥ) over all (viśvataḥ)—here the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe*). Your purifier (*pavitraṃ*) is the Liṅga.

Regarding the word *pavitra* having the meaning of *liṅga*, the Vedic Nighaṇṭu has been cited previously. "Spread out" (*vitata*) means expanded, that is, pervaded by the form of the *liṅga* consisting of Śiva and Śakti. Therefore, "limbs" (*gātrāṇi*) refers to the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, as well as the senses and so forth.

One who has not heated his body—that is, one devoid of the purificatory rite of Vīraśaiva initiation—is for that very reason raw, meaning unripened and lacking in refinement. Such a person does not attain—that is, does not reach—that Liṅga, which exists in the form of the *iṣṭaliṅga*, the *prāṇaliṅga*, the *bhāvaliṅga*, and so forth; he does not pervade it.

He is not qualified for its wearing; therefore, the meaning is that he is not fit for liberation in the form of the identity (*sāmarasya*) of the *liṅga* and his own limbs. "The cooked" (*śṛtāsaḥ*) means ripened by the purificatory rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is to say, accompanied by the ripening of impurities (*mala*).
"Carrying" (*vahantaḥ*) means wearing the desired *liṅga* in the aforementioned locations. That...

"The *liṅga* is all-pervasive; they attain it by fully embracing the *liṅga*. Therefore, because it is enjoined by the Śruti as recited directly before one's eyes, and because it is Vedic in nature, the wearing of the *liṅga* must be performed."

Now, one might object: this Śruti passage does not establish the wearing of sectarian marks (*liṅga*), but rather establishes the necessity of branding with the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*). For instance, the meaning of "pavitrante" is as follows: "O Viṣṇu, Lord of the Veda (*brahmaṇaspati*), being the Sovereign, [protect us] from all sides..."

You pervade and encompass all limbs. That is the extended, wide-spread, purifying wheel (*cakra*), the purifying movement (*caraṇa*), the wheel, the gate of the world, the Sudarśana. For these are synonyms for the *cakra* which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), according to the lexicon: "That which exists by it is 'one whose body has not been heated' (*ataptatanu*); for that very reason, it is raw (*āma*)."
One whose evil has not been exhausted does not attain liberation from that. Carrying such a wheel in this manner, those who are cooked—that is, fully ripened—attain its fruit.
On this point, another mantra also serves as authority:
The foot is a sacred, far-reaching, ancient means by which, when purified, one crosses over evil deeds;
purified by that pure, sacred [foot], may we be cleansed.
May we cross over the most wicked enemy.
By that mark of the wheel, being purified, may we overcome evil, misfortune, and the enemy; by which mark of the wheel, being purified,
they cross over evil deeds and sins— that wheel, the foot-mark, is pure, the cause of purification, spread wide, and ancient, having come down through a beginningless stream.
The meaning of the second mantra.
And another mantra:
"The door of the world, radiant, purifying, luminous, shining, and glorious;
milking the stream of immortality in many ways—may it establish us as well-placed in this world. Thus.

The meaning of this is: the door to this world—that is, the means to the heavenly world; the stream of immortality, being milked in many ways—that is, serving as the means for liberation in various modes; radiant—that is, beautiful;
luminous—that is, endowed with the light of flames and rays; and blazing.

May the wheel, which is the foot— the purifier and cause of complete purification— that is intensely enveloped in flames immediately after being heated by fire, establish us in a state of well-being within this world.

If it is argued that since even the *pavitra* scripture among these [scriptures] is devoted to the branding with the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*), how can this scripture be applied to the wearing of the *liṅga*? We say no;
for instance, in the animal sacrifice prescribed by the scripture: "One should offer a *babhrukarṇī* [cow] to Brahmaṇaspati."
How can the meaning of a prescribed mantra be determined as being intended for the branding with the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*)?

And how is there a logical consistency of meaning in its being intended for the branding with the heated discus? For instance, even though the mantra employed here lacks the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), or gerundive (*tavya*) suffixes, its prescriptive character must be inferred.

Furthermore, setting aside the well-established meaning of the word *pavitra* as "purification" according to grammar and other sciences, one would have to postulate an entirely unknown meaning—namely, "a circle"—based on the fabrication of an unattested lexicographical definition (*nighaṇṭu*).
This would be required in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the injunction immediately following, which states: "One should sacrifice a brown-eared animal to Brahmaṇaspati."
Based on the Vedic revelation, "O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), may I be perfected through prayer," it must be stated that [the deity] has Brahman as its ultimate referent.

Furthermore, in the second book of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, at the beginning of the third chapter, it says: "One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice to Brahmaṇaspati. In this context, [the deity] is likewise intended to be Brahman.

Because it has been explained as being supreme over the four-faced one (Brahmā), its reference is to Brahmā; moreover, its reference must necessarily be to him due to the greatness of the immediately following scriptural passage, "brahmā devānām. To set aside that [meaning] and establish a practice of one's own fabrication, one might imagine it refers to Viṣṇu, [claiming] "that which exists is by him."

There is the ellipsis of three words. Regarding the phrase "taptatanu" (one whose body is heated), since there is an expectancy for an instrument (*karaṇa*), and because a wheel alone cannot burn the body, the word "agni-taptena" (by one heated by fire) must be supplied. If the word *tanu* were intended to mean the body alone, then upon the burning of the mere body, life itself would not persist; therefore, the word *tanu* [must be understood in its broader sense].
It would entail the assumption that [the word] indicates the base of the arm, which is merely a part of that [whole], and thus it is marred by numerous such defects.

In the *Kāṭhaka*, regarding the sacrifices (*iṣṭi*) of the *apāghā* [and other] *anāmikā* [sacrifices], there occurs the word *caraṇa* in the well-known phrase "the fifth *caraṇa*" and so forth; and since this word *caraṇa* is established as denoting action in the sense that "it is practiced" (*caryate*), [as in the passage]: "Those of pleasant conduct (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*) quickly [attain] a pleasant [rebirth]."

Regarding the passage, "They would enter a foul womb; for those who perform foul deeds, they would quickly enter a foul womb," if it is argued that this refers to conduct (*caraṇa*), [the answer is] no, because according to the two *sūtras* in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*: "Kārṣṇājini says it is for the purpose of indication" and "Bādari says it is merit and demerit alone."

Furthermore, in the commentary on that [text], one would have to assume an unfamiliar meaning for the word *caraṇa*— which has been determined to refer to ritual action (*karman*)— namely, that it denotes a *cakra*. Moreover, there would be redundancy between the words *caraṇa* and *pavitra* as denoters of the *cakra*, by which [the person] is purified.

In this case, one must also assume that the focus is on the irrelevant matter of marking with the discus-sign (*cakrāṅkana*). Here too, one must supply the ellipsis as "the foot heated by fire," "purified by that which was heated by fire," and "by him who was heated by fire";
furthermore, even though there is no suffix indicating an injunction (*vidhi*) to restrict the application of the mantra, its injunctive force (*vidhāyakatva*) must be assumed.

This is common to all mantras. Whosoever might imagine such a connection with [the Lord's] feet, they would incur faults such as the acceptance of matters forbidden by all the *smṛtis*, *purāṇas*, *itihāsas*, and so forth; these are the faults that would accrue to those who advocate the wearing of the heated seal (*taptamudrā*).
Therefore, there is an inconsistency with the meaning of the scriptural passages cited as being devoted to the wearing of the discus.

Furthermore, there are many statements in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas that prohibit the marking with the discus (*cakra*). For instance, in the *Prāyaścittakāṇḍa* of Hemādri’s work and in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, it is said:
"He whose body is seen marked with a heated conch and discus..."
While still alive, he should be abandoned like a corpse and excluded from all religious duties.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "He who has no entitlement to the Vedas or to shares in the sacrifices,
having heated the discus and other [emblems], should wear them upon his two arms."
If a Brāhmaṇa, out of delusion, should wear heated seals,
one should look upon the sun merely by the sight of him.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa], it is stated:
"The body of a Brāhmaṇa is to be known as consisting of all the gods;
therefore, if that [body] is tormented, what can I say of his great sin?"
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"If a Brahmin, being deluded in mind, should heat [the fire] with the fire-seal (vahnimudrā), he is not fit for ritual action here; he is indeed designated as a heretic (pākhaṇḍa)."
In the *Parāśara-upapurāṇa*:
"O best of the twice-born, one should not burn [the body] of such a person; nor should one burn it with [implements] preceded by the discus.
The king should quickly banish from his own country anyone who is marked [with these signs]."
He who is branded is disqualified from teaching and studying, from performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, and from conversation or social association.
In the *Ātreyadharmaśāstra*, Viṣṇu states:
"Just as wood found in a cremation ground is unfit for all ritual acts,
so too is a Brahmin marked with the discus censured for all ritual acts."
He who makes a conch and a discus out of clay or heated iron shall be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra.
Bodhāyana also says:
"One should neither brand nor burn the body; even if one should burn it out of personal whim, one must not employ a person with a branded limb in rites prescribed by the Śruti or Smṛti."
In the Bāṣkala-saṃhitā:
"A Brahmin should not mark his limbs with the emblems of divine weapons;
if he should mark them out of delusion, he falls from his status—of this there is no doubt."
Marking the body with the conch, the discus, and so forth, as well as dancing, singing, and the like—this is the dharma of the low-born; it should never belong to one of the twice-born.

Upon seeing a heretic, one who follows the conduct of the fallen, a twice-born man bearing a heated discus, a wearer of the sacred thread, or one who has offered fire, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
A twice-born man should not even look upon those who bear the heated discus.
Furthermore:
"The cock, the boar, one marked with the heated discus,
a woman in her menses, and a eunuch— these five are defilers of the *śrāddha*."
Those Brahmins who are husbands of prostitutes, those who bear the heated discus,
atheists, and slaves to Shudras— these indeed have their lineage ending in ashes.
There were those with matted hair, those with shaven heads, those with cropped hair, and those carrying skull-bowls;
likewise, there were those bearing the heated discus and those devoted to reviling the Vedas.
These have strayed from the path; a twice-born man who falls through association with them becomes pure by bathing after touching these impure ones and consuming clarified butter.
Whatever offerings to the gods (havya) or ancestors (kavya) are given to one who bears the mark of the wheel,
the Rākṣasas indeed seize them— not the gods, nor the ancestors.
Those who are known as heretics and those people who bear the mark of the discus—
their presence shall not be permitted anywhere during meritorious rites.
One should not look upon a Brahmin marked with the heated wheel during a meritorious rite;
likewise, the ground does not become pure immediately due to contact with him.
A Brahmin who marks his limbs with symbols such as the conch and the discus—
even if they are connected to Viṣṇu and other deities, whether by engraving or by branding— becomes an outcast.
If one wears the Sudarśana [mark] out of ignorance, greed, or passion, he is a destroyer of his lineage; seeing him, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
Whoever suddenly draws the Sudarśana on the tip of his arm—
even if he possesses knowledge of the Vedas and the sacred fires— burns his lineage down to the seventh generation.
In the Vahni Purāṇa it is said:
"Having burned their own bodies with the conch, discus, and other [emblems],
their ancestors truly fall from every twice-born duty."
Indeed, there is no atonement for him through bathing, giving, recitation, and the like;
yet an atonement for him has arisen as enjoined by Parāśarya.
Having shaved his hair and removed the tuft, one should perform the consecration again,
having extracted him from the womb-vessel and beginning with the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) and the others.
"The expiation for [these] kṛcchra penances is declared to be performed by means of sixfold repetition.

Thus, those marked with the heated disc (taptacakrāṅkita) attain purification after performing the kṛcchra penances for six years, preceded by appearing before an assembly (pariṣad). Even in the case of accepting gifts from them, [if they have not performed the expiation],...
The expiation has been stated.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Where a Brahmin, out of ignorance, [accepts] gifts from those who have been burnt by their own seals, with devotion..."
One who accepts gold alone should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
"Having again reduced that by half, fasting for the duration of a single meal leads to purification; no other means of purification is seen. Thus it is said.

Thus, the unfitness for wearing heated discs and other such marks, as well as the state of being fallen (pātitya) and the requirement for expiation (prāyaścitta), have been extensively established in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas.
Furthermore, among the recited lexicons (kośas), it is read: "The foot is the purifier, the disc."

Since the statement regarding the treasury (*kośa*) as you have described it is nowhere to be seen, it was fabricated by you yourself for the purpose of deluding the world through a blind faith in the untruthful meaning of the Tantras that you propounded. Even if you maintain the conceit that it was not fabricated, nevertheless, the point you intend to establish is not proven.

On the contrary, there is a contradiction for you yourself. For instance, regarding the word *caraṇa* found in the mantra "Having purified [them] from their feet with the Pāvaka [mantras], I purify them again," which is recited among the mantras in the *Ṛgveda-Parिशिष्ट* (*Ṛk-pariśiṣṭa*) as removing all sins— if one were to determine its meaning according to the lexicon cited by you:
The meaning of the mantra culminates in the conclusion that an expiation must be performed for wearing the heated seal (*taptamudrā*).
For it is thus: from the feet—that is, from the wheels—the fifth case ending is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).
"I purify" those sins which are caused by the branding of the heated wheel (*taptacakrāṅkana*), [committed] by those who despise the true reality (*tattva*).

The meaning is: "having turned oneself away from evil, one purifies [it]. Since the verbal root is transitive, the cessation of evil by the self is obtained through the sense of the word. Furthermore, if the word *pavitra* were taken to mean the *cakra*, another contradiction arises; for [this would conflict with] those engaged in the application of mantras.

If, without the ritual application (*viniyoga*) of the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* such as Baudhāyana and others; without the commentaries (*vivaraṇa*) of those devoted to explaining the meaning of the mantras, such as Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, Vidyāraṇya, and others; without the statements of well-known lexicons (*kośa*); and without supplementary elaborations (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), [one were to proceed]...

If one were to imagine a different meaning according to one's own intellect and based on the pride of one's own particular doctrine, then there would be yet another meaning for this sacred *śruti*. For instance: "O Brahmaṇaspati"—that is, O best of Brahmins; for according to the lexicon, "Brahmā" means "the wise one" (*vipra*) and "the Lord of Creatures" (*prajāpati*). You, [O] such one...
The genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative. "Viśvataḥ" means everywhere; "prabhuḥ" means you are capable, meaning that you do not fall into delusion through the words of the Tantrikas.
Furthermore, "pavitram" means as it becomes pure, and "vitatam" means expanded or extensive.

The change in word order is Vedic (*chāndasa*). You encompass—that is, you reach—the limbs; for the purity of the limbs is established by the scriptural statement: "As many deities as there are, all of them dwell in the Brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda. In the phrase *ataptatanūḥ*, the syllable *a-* denotes Viṣṇu; [the syllable] *a-*...
