According to the lexicon *Aṅgādi-kośa*, which states "in Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, Kamaṭha, a courtyard, and battle," [the word *āya* refers to Viṣṇu]. One whose body is scorched (*taptatanuḥ*)— meaning one whose body is burnt at the base of the arms—
and who is therefore raw (*āmaḥ*), meaning lacking in self-restraint, tranquility, dispassion, and so forth, does not attain, that is, does not reach, that supreme state (*tatparam padam*).

*Śṛtāsaḥ*: cooked by the heated wheel; from the root *śrai* (meaning "to cook"), the suffix *kta* is applied, with the augment *asun* added according to Vedic usage. Carrying the callus produced by that burning—meaning the aforementioned action of the root, "cooking," which refers to the *Kumbhīpāka* hell. [This is an instance of] referring to a whole by a part of its name.

The mention of the name is like the word "Bhāma" used for Satyabhāmā. "They obtain [the result]" means that a man who wears the heated conch and discus attains Kumbhīpāka; this is the extracted meaning.
Therefore, since the Śruti is intent upon the branding with the heated discus, it describes what is favorable to its own position.
Because it is corrupted by many defects, the assumption that our stated intention is the wearing of the marks (liṅga-dhāraṇa) alone is more excellent.

It might be argued that, although the *pavitra* scripture cannot be taken as referring to the branding with the discus (*cakrāṅkana*) because it is tainted by numerous defects already established, it is nevertheless quite possible to interpret it as referring to the branding with the heated trident (*taptaśūlāṅkana*), which is the duty of the non-Vedic Śaiva heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*).
For it is said: "The trident is pure; the trident is the supreme, great weapon, the purifier of sin, the armament of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva).
These are declared to be the unique names of the trident, the weapon of Śiva."

The fact that the trident is denoted by the word *pavitra* (purifier) is well known from the words of the *Pāśupata-āgama*. O Brahmaṇaspati, Śiva— whose status as the Lord of Brahman (*brahmapati*) is established by the Vedic text "Brahmādhipati, the lord of Brahman"— that which belongs to you (*te*), by that trident heated by fire.
Those whose bodies have not been heated, who are unrefined and unripened, do not attain that state of Pāśupata.

Those who have been cooked—ripened by the branding of the heated trident upon the base of their arms, and for that very reason bearing the callus produced by the wound resulting from the burn—attain, that is, reach, that state of Pāśupata. This is the meaning.

The rest is clear. Furthermore, according to the application of the meaning thus established, even the branding with a heated trident (*taptaśūlāṅkana*) becomes something to be performed by those who follow the Vedas (*vaidika*).
Branding with a heated trident is to be performed by the followers of the Veda, because it is set forth in the wording of a mantra (*mantravarṇa*), just like a particular knot of *darbha* grass.
If it is argued that this inference is also favorable [to our position], it is said in response:
"A Brahmin should not mark his limbs with the weapons or emblems of the deities;
if he should mark them out of delusion, he falls from his status—of this there is no doubt."
One should not brand or burn the body; even if one burns it out of one's own will, one should not accept a branded limb for the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
A person marked on the body with the weapons of the deity, such as the conch and the discus,
is purified simply by wearing the triple mark made of sacred ash.
A Brahmin devoted to the Śrauta and Smārta rites should not brand his body with marks, even those associated with Viṣṇu and others; otherwise, he becomes fallen.
O King, whether his body is marked with the discus or even marked with the linga,
he should be known as ineligible for the rites prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis.

Because there exist such prohibitive statements regarding branding, and because we observe the application of the mantra "pavitram te" in the consecration of the *daśāpavitra*—that specific cloth capable of filtering the Soma juice—as indicated by the rule: "The sacrificer consecrates [it] while it is being spread out. In this sense...
Due to the absence of scriptural injunction (*viniyoga*) and the absence of corroborating explanatory texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*),

the assumption that one is intent upon branding oneself with a heated trident is indeed improper. For this very reason, even the wearing of the branded insignia of a heated trident, which is to be practiced by certain non-Vedic Pāśupatas, is likewise [untenable].
Refuted.
The sacrificer consecrates this being spread out with this purifying *śruti*,

because it has been enjoined by the venerable author of the Sūtras, the sage Āpastamba, for the consecration of the specific cloth known as the *daśāpavitra*, which is capable of filtering the *soma* juice.

Furthermore, because the author of the *Vaijayantī-nighaṇṭu* employs the term *daśāpavitra* with reference to cloth, stating: "The word *pavitra* [is used] for fire, for the pure Hari, for the neuter [gender], for copper, for water, for cow-dung, for a mantra, for curd, for the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), for the Sāman, for the sun, for a water-pot, for *kuśa* grass, for the *daśāpavitra* cloth, for a trident, and for deities."
If the primary intent were the wearing of the *liṅga*, how could the meaning be explained?
Furthermore, it is appropriate to explain the meaning as referring to the *daśāpavitra* cloth; for instance:
"O Brahmaṇaspati, O Soma!"—for Amarasimha states that "Veda," "truth," "austerity," and "Brahman" are synonyms.

Alternatively, according to the teaching that "Brahmā, the sage, and Prajāpati [are derived from] *brahman*," [the term refers to] the Lord of the Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*). By reflecting upon the traditional law (*smṛti*) which states: "He whose Veda and sacrificial altar (*vedi*) are severed for three generations is to be known as a base Brahmin, excluded from all ritual acts."
"One should sacrifice an *indrāgni* animal that has been released again; for him whose Soma-drinking is severed up to the third generation— namely, that Brāhmaṇa who, being a Brāhmaṇa,
does not drink Soma up to the third generation," and so forth, according to the Śruti, [this applies] up to the third generation.

Furthermore, because an expiation is prescribed for the absence of Soma-drinking, it is established that Soma possesses the status of a Brāhmaṇa, as it brings about an excellence of Brāhmaṇahood by means of removing the state of being a fallen Brāhmaṇa (*daurbrāhmaṇya*). For this very reason, another Śruti states: "Therefore, King Soma is our Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, O...

O Brahmaṇaspati, Lord of the Brāhmaṇas, O Soma! Your filter, known as the *daśāpavitra*, is spread out and extended; you, the Lord, having been drunk, pervade and encompass all the limbs [of the body]. For it is said: "There is no austerity higher than fasting."

Because fasting is prescribed as consisting merely of drinking water through the act of remembrance, it is called austerity (*tapas*). Therefore, one whose body has not been heated—that is, one whose body has not been purified by austerity consisting of fasting—is "one of unheated body" (*ataptatanū*);
such a person, who does not perform the vow of subsisting on milk, is like one who is unworthy, being devoid of the Soma initiation, and thus does not enjoy the fruit of that ritual action.

They obtain [it]; being "cooked" (śṛtāsaḥ)—that is, fully ripened—by the milk-vow (*payovrata*) and thus carrying out their ritual action in this manner, they attain (*samāśata*), that is, they obtain, the fruit of that action. For this very reason, the venerable Āpastamba, the author of the Sūtras, speaks a praise regarding the consecration (*dīkṣā*): "When indeed..."

"The initiated one becomes emaciated; thus he becomes fit for sacrifice. If it is asked, "How can this scriptural passage concerning purification (*pavitra-śruti*) be interpreted as referring to the wearing of sectarian marks (*liṅga-dhāraṇa*)," we say: it cannot be so, because the determination of the meaning of scripture must necessarily be made in accordance with its supporting explanatory texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*).

This is because many Purāṇic statements that elucidate the meaning of the mantras are heard to be devoted to the wearing of the *liṅga*. Nor should it be argued that a corroborative statement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) cannot be asserted as having equal authority to a mantra when that mantra has been directly enjoined by the author of the Sūtras.

Since the *upabṛṃhaṇas* (elaborative texts) are included within the fourteen branches of knowledge (*caturdaśa-vidyā*) just like the *sūtras*, they possess equal authority in determining the meaning of the Vedas. For this very reason, the authors of the *smṛtis* have declared: "One should elaborate upon the Veda by means of the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*; the Veda is afraid of one who has heard little, thinking, 'He might lead me astray.'"
For this very reason, the Chāndogya Śruti also establishes the Vedic status of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas:
"The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda as the fourth; and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth among the Vedas."

Therefore, it is established that even the *upabṛṃhaṇa* (explanatory supplements) possess the capacity to determine the meaning of the Veda, just like the *kalpasūtras*. Nor should it be argued: "How can a mantra that has been assigned to a specific ritual action by a *sūtra* be subsequently assigned elsewhere by an *upabṛṃhaṇa*?"

In the section on the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), regarding the oblation of goat’s milk to be performed upon the final brick in the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*), there are the *Śatarudrīya* mantras employed for that oblation;
"He who, meditating upon Maheśvara, recites the *Śatarudra*... [and so forth].
[He saw] the earth bounded by the seven oceans, together with its mountains, islands, and forests.
One might give land endowed with gold and medicinal herbs;
yet the merit arising from a single recitation of the Rudra-mantra would be ten million times greater than that.
Those who bathe the Great Lord, the God, with the Rudrādhyāya,
and those who perform their own ablutions with that water, cross over death.
By the consecration of the Śatarudra, a man becomes a hundred years of age;
liberated from all sins without exception, he shall become beloved of Śiva.
A drinker of liquor and a stealer of gold, by standing in water and reciting the Rudra-hymn and the Sahasra-śīrṣa hymn, is liberated from all sin.

Since the application [of this mantra] is observed in both recitation (*japa*) and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) by virtue of such corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), even though the *pavitra* mantra in the present context is applied to a different ritual act, its application to the wearing of the *liṅga* is established through the force of those corroborative texts. To explain: Thus, by the power of such corroborative texts, since its application in recitation and consecration is observed, even though the *pavitra* mantra in the present case is applied to a different rite, its application to the wearing of the *liṅga* is consistent due to the force of those corroborative texts. For instance:
Brahmaṇaspati is indeed the Lord; this is called the Linga of Brahman.
It is renowned as pure, and through contact with it, the body becomes pure.

Thus, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, the statement establishing the purification of the body through lifelong connection with the *liṅga* possesses the unique quality of being an explanatory expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the *pavitra-śruti*. In accordance with this expansion, [the address] "O Brahmaṇaspati, O Lord" is formed; the *sa*-sandhi occurs according to the rule for the *kaska-* group.

"Brahmādhipati" means the lord of Brahmā, according to the sacred scripture (śruti). The genitive case in "te" (of you), however, denotes non-difference, as in the expression "the coldness of Rāhu. The purifying *liṅga* is Brahman, the source of procreation.

"Kāṭa, Pavitra, Amṛta, Srapa, Prastara, Janima, Prāṇa, Deva, and likewise Liṅga—these are indeed synonyms for the Liṅga, which is the Supreme Self," according to the *Vaidika-kośa*. That which exists spread everywhere, pervading all—that is "viśvataḥ"; by the word "viśva" (the universe), those existing within the universe [are meant].

The term *paśu* (animal/soul) indicates the individual souls beginning with Brahmā; for it is possible to apply the word *viśva* (universe), which denotes the entire complex of sentient and insentient things, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to its single constituent part, namely the sentient. This has been stated in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*:
From Brahmā down to the immovable beings, all who are subject to the cycle of transmigration are proclaimed to be the "bound souls" (paśus) of the trident-bearing God of gods.
Because he fell upon them, Śiva, the Lord of Devas, is remembered as Paśupati. Thus it is said.

"He is called Paśupati because he is the lord (pati) of those who have fallen (paśu), because he protects all beings (paśu), because he delights in them, and because he is their lord as well"— this is from the etymological explanation (*nāmanirvacana*) in the Śatarudrīya chapter of the Droṇaparvan; [the term] *pati* is derived from the verbal root *pā-* in the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣaṇa*), with the suffix *ḍati*.

This should be understood because the derivation of the word *pati* is established by grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and because its meaning— namely, the state of being a protector— is made clear by the very statement already cited;

furthermore, it is supported by the *Skanda Purāṇa*, which functions as an explanatory expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) directed toward determining the meaning of the word *prabhu* found in the sacred revelation (*śruti*).
By virtue of the lexicographical definition in the Amarakośa— "Īśvara is the lord (pati), for he rules"—

which establishes that the word *īśa* signifies sovereignty (*ādhipatya*), and because, according to the Mahābhārata and the Nirukta, the word *pati* necessarily shares the same meaning as a term signifying both a protector and a ruler, [the term *īśvara*] denotes both sovereignty and protection.

It must be stated that this is the meaning of the word "Lord" (prabhu). You are the Lord, the sovereign, and the protector of those living beings, manifesting in the form of the Liṅga denoted by the word "Pure" (pavitra). The manner in which such living beings—denoted by the word "animals" (paśu)—are to be protected is revealed through the limbs [of the ritual].

By [the words] beginning with "those," etc.: "limbs" refers to the gross, subtle, and causal bodies; the word "limbs" (*gātra*) is indicative of the organs of knowledge, the organs of action, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and so forth.
Having withdrawn these from their objects such as sound and the rest, [the practitioner] himself—
Having remained among them in the form of the presiding deities through signs such as conduct,
and having appropriated those objects— sound and the rest— he subsequently [bestows] those objects, which consist of grace, upon them who are designated by the word "limbs" (aṅga).

Having given [it] to living beings whose internal organs are pure, you cause them to become enjoyers of perfectly pure serenity. Regarding this point, the authority is found in the Vātula-āgama: "Whatever pleasure has arisen from the senses, that is offered to Śiva."
Having established faith, one should enjoy [the offering] through the gateway of that sense faculty.
The *iṣṭaliṅga* is in the external limb, the *prāṇaliṅga* likewise within;
the *bhāvaliṅga* is always well-established in this limb of the Self.
The Great Liṅga is in the limb of the heart; the Suprasādaka Liṅga is in the limb of the ears;
the Caraliṅga is in the limb of the skin; and the Śivaliṅga is in the limb of the eyes.
The Guru-liṅga is indeed on the organ of the tongue, and likewise on the organ of the nose;
the Ācāra-liṅga is perpetually well-established.

"Just as the subtle body (liṅga) is established in the limbs of the organs of cognition in their respective order, so too is the subtle body established in the limbs of the organs of action in their respective order. Thus it is said.

He states with the words "ataptā" and so forth that there is no attainment of the supreme state for those who lack mastery over the senses and are devoid of austerity, because of the absence of connection with the [auspicious] marks (liṅga). This is supported by the Taittirīya statement, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity," and by the Brahmopaniṣad statement, "The knowledge of the Self has austerity as its root."

"One whose body is unrefined" (*ataptatanūḥ*): since there is no "body" distinct from the senses such as the ears and eyes, the word "body" (*tanu*) here refers to the senses. He by whom the "body"—that is, the senses—is "unrefined" (*atapta*), meaning unrestrained, is one who has not conquered his senses; this is the meaning of "ignorant. "Raw" (*āmaḥ*): due to the absence of the ripening of impurities.

A person devoid of Śiva-initiation does not attain that Liṅga. Those who have been cooked— meaning those ripened by Vīraśaiva initiation and freed from sin— carrying their chosen Liṅga and wearing it on the aforementioned places, attain— that is, they reach— that all-pervading Liṅga.

The meaning is that others who are devoid of austerity, lacking the purificatory rites of Śiva, and bereft of the wearing of the *liṅga*, do not attain the supreme state. On this point, in the Skanda Purāṇa, it is said: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and indeed Īśa—this is called the *liṅga*."
For that is renowned as the purifier; its Lord himself is omnipresent.
Through contact with that [knowledge], it spontaneously makes the limbs pure;
for one whose body is not heated by austerity is indeed ignorant, raw, and devoid of refinement.
One devoid of initiation shall not directly attain the supreme *liṅga*.
Those who have taken refuge in the Dharma of Śiva, who are tranquil, and who are devoted to the conduct of Śiva [attain it].
"Those who always carry the *liṅga* go to the supreme state;
otherwise, O Goddess, it is not possible to attain me—so says the sacred revelation (*śruti*)."
In that very place, in another section, it is said:
"The supreme sky, free from evil and praised, is situated within the body;
transcending birth, death, and old age, they declare it to be pure."
Because it protects one from falling into the ocean of hell,
that Liṅga, the divine light, is the most sacred among all sacred things.
Through contact with it, it will bring purity to the very limbs of the body;
O Goddess, this is that supreme light-liṅga which is identical with me.
Śivānanda is the supreme abode, difficult to attain by those who have not disciplined themselves;
thus, having taken refuge in the Liṅga, they always carry it with constant devotion.
All of them indeed attain Me alone in this matter; there is no doubt.
Thus says the Rigveda: "O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), your purifier is spread abroad."
Therefore, that pure Śaiva liṅga, which is free from all ailment, should be worn. Thus it is said.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"He whose body has been heated by the performance of austerity is called 'taptatanu' (one of heated body).
Matured for the sake of liberation, he attains the wearing of the liṅga."
"He who does not first perform austerity is said to be one whose body has not been refined; being unripened for liberation, he does not attain the wearing of the *liṅga*. Thus it is said.

Therefore, by a careful consideration of the sacred Śruti texts augmented by the Skanda Purāṇa and the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, the wearing of the Liṅga must indeed be respectfully adopted by Vedic seekers of liberation. On this point, the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad and other scriptural authorities serve as proof. For instance:
Homage to Brahmā! May there be retention for me, may there be no forgetting; may I be a retainer.
What has been heard by my ears, let that not depart from me—of such-and-such a person, Om. Thus.

The meaning of this mantra is as follows: "Obeisance to Brahman" (*namo brahmaṇe*). According to the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, "Brahmāṇaspati is indeed the Lord; this is called the Liṅga," and according to the statement in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, "Brahman is declared to be the Liṅga, and Brahmāṇaspati is the Īśvara," [it refers to] the one unmanifested Liṅga.

From the statement in the *Īśvaragītā*, "The *liṅga* is Brahman," and from the statement in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, "To Brahman, whose form is the *liṅga*," it follows that "Brahman" is a name for the *liṅga*. Thus, preceded by an act of salutation, the Person of the Veda requested the wearing of the *liṅga* with the words, "Salutations to Brahman, whose form is the *liṅga*. This is the wearing (*dhāraṇa*).

"May there be for me the wearing of that Liṅga of Śiva whose nature is Brahman. Now, one might object: "Since the word 'tat' (that) is absent here, how can it be understood that it is Brahman which is to be worn? Nor [is this a valid objection], because the word 'Brahman' is expectancy-laden, and its syntactic connection with the act of wearing must necessarily be asserted.
It must be stated that what is obtained is "the wearing of the mark denoted by the word *brahman*";
however, if it is argued that this is not so because there is no expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) since the word *brahman* is construed with the word *namaḥ*, we say no,
because the word *dhāraṇa* (wearing) denotes a thing that necessarily involves a correlative term.

Since it is appropriate for the word *namaḥ*— though already construed with [the word] *brahmaṇe* as requiring another related term— to be construed with the word *dhāraṇa* by the force of an aroused expectancy, the meaning is "the bearing of Brahman," that is, the bearing of the *liṅga*.
When a word denoting an object is specified as depending upon a counter-correlative (pratiyogin), it is logical that what is proximate should be construed as that counter-correlative; for example:
"one should be given," "six should be given," "twelve should be given," "twenty-four should be given," "a hundred should be given," "a thousand should be given," or "an unlimited amount."
The word "unlimited" (*aparimita*), which is heard in the various injunctions regarding the sacrificial fees for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)—

meaning that which expresses a general plurality dependent upon its counter-correlate— is restricted to a plurality exceeding one thousand due to its proximity [to that number], or else it means "more."

Since it has been determined in the *Pūrvatantra* that "it may be so because of the multivalence of other [terms] due to their proximity," there is a connection between the wearing and the mark denoted by the word "Brahman" on account of their proximity;
this non-exclusion applies to the wearing of the mark at any one of the six locations mentioned in the Purāṇas and Āgamas.
"Never abandoning" means non-separation; the use of the *loṭ* (imperative) mood expresses a prayer: "May I be the bearer.

According to the principle that seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) must repeat this statement even a hundred times for the sake of strengthening their adherence to the wearing of the marks (*liṅga*), he repeats it; thus, there is no tautology. It was heard by the ears.

At the time of Vīraśaiva initiation, the wearing of the chosen *liṅga* (iṣṭaliṅgadhāraṇa) must be performed preceded by the instruction of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarīmantra*). Since that mantra exists in the form of sound, it is perceivable by the sense of hearing; thus, by the phrase "heard in the ears," the mantra is indicated. And that [mantra]—

Because it is suitable for the section concerning the wearing of the *liṅga*, it takes the form of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*). Regarding the phrase "heard from the ears" (*karṇayoḥ śrutam*), the meaning is "heard by means of both ears. Although only the right ear is suitable for receiving instruction, [the text mentions] both ears as well.

The use of the dual number is justified because there exists fitness for hearing [the Veda]. In the expression "ghṛtasya yajati" (he sacrifices with ghee), the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental. But is it not the case that the genitive case is prescribed for meanings such as "remainder" (śeṣa) and so forth, and not for the meaning of the instrumental? Indeed, the genitive case-ending is used here in the sense of the instrumental.

If it is asked how this is established, [the answer is: "The *svaru* is produced from many [pieces of wood], because it is a word denoting its own action," as stated by the Blessed One in the section of the second quarter of the fourth chapter (*adhyāya*), regarding the passage "he makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya svaruṃ karoti*).

In that context, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established as: "He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpāt svaruṃ karoti*), or "He takes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpāt svarum ādatte*).

The venerable Śabarasvāmin, the author of the commentary on the *Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra*, having raised the objection as to how the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīvibhakti*) can have the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyartha*), states: "In the case of non-living things, the genitive occurs in the sense of the ablative, as in: 'He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post' (*yūpasya svaruṃ karoti*)."

Regarding the statement "he makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpāt svarum karoti*), in some cases it is used in the sense of the instrumental case, as in "he sacrifices with ghee" (*ghṛtasya yajati*) or "he sacrifices with ghee" (*ghṛtena yajati*);
or in the sense of the ablative case, as in "he sacrifices from ghee" (*ghṛtād yajati*) or "he sacrifices of ghee" (*ghṛtasya yajati*).

In some cases it is used in the sense of the accusative case, as it has been stated: "he drinks of the Soma" (*somasya pibati*) or "he drinks the Soma" (*somam pibati*), or "he drinks from the Soma" (*somāt pibati*). By that same principle, it is so here as well.

The genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental. For this person of mine, who recites the five-syllable mantra taught by the guru as heard from the ears, may [the obstacles] not fall away, may they not depart;
for the root *cyu* (to fall, to move), in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *dhvam*, there is the elision of *sij*, the substitution of *guṇa*, and the change of *dha* to *ḍha*.

The change in the person of the verb is Vedic. The meaning is: "May the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra always be mine; may it not fall away. *Ūṃ* marks the conclusion of the mantra. Alternatively, [the meaning is]:
"O Brahman, do not cast down, do not cause to fall away from me, the five-syllabled mantra taught by my Guru."

The causative sense (*ṇij-artha*) is inherent [in the root]. The change in verbal number (*vacanavyatyaya*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In the context of the mantra, "May Indra, through peace and wisdom, deliver me," it is firmly illuminated that non-forgetfulness depends upon the Supreme Lord.
This is corroborated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O God, salutations to You, the Brahman, the Teacher, the Great Soul;
for its negation is indeed by Death alone, because [the Brahman] is common to all."
O Supreme Teacher, may there be for me no rejection [of this teaching], but rather its retention;
it is well-known in the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas, and has been heard by my ears.
Do not cause my linga, which is the refuge of Śiva, to fall;
for that which was taught by my gurus into my ear possesses a divine form.
One should always recite the five-syllabled jewel of mantras, which is established in the Vedas. Thus it is said.

Now, according to the Vīraśaiva doctrine, the established conclusion is that the wearing of the *liṅga* must be performed preceded by the instruction in the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarīmantra*). In this mantra which establishes that [practice], the wearing of the *liṅga* is first set forth; thereafter, the instruction in the five-syllabled mantra follows with the words "heard in the two ears."

If it is asked, "Why is the instruction of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī-mantra*) not performed immediately after the wearing of the marks (*liṅgadhāraṇa*), given that this [instruction] is established by a consideration of the mantra itself?", do not say so; for the instruction of the five-syllabled mantra is more appropriate at the very outset, because the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) takes precedence over the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

Because of its greater strength. This has been stated in the *Pūrvatantra*, in the second section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the first quarter (*pāda*) of the fifth chapter, in the sūtra "And because of the purpose" (*arthācca*). When there is a doubt as to whether the cooking of the barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) should be performed after the *agnihotra* oblation or before it—given that, in comparison with the textual order (*pāṭhakrama*), the [temporal] sequence [is stronger] regarding the five fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*)—...

Since it is impossible for the directly perceived recitation being heard to be set aside by the mere sight [of the text], one might argue that after performing the Agnihotra oblation with a different substance, the cooking of the gruel (yavāgū) must be performed immediately thereafter.
To this, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: when the Agnihotra oblation has been performed with a different substance, immediately thereafter—
Since the cooking of the gruel being performed lacks an observed purpose, an unobserved purpose must necessarily be postulated. And that is improper,
because when an observed result is possible, one should not postulate an unobserved result.

Because it would be unjust. Therefore, setting aside the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*), on the basis of the functional requirement (*arthavaśa*) that the cooking of the gruel (*yavāgū*) serves to accomplish the *agnihotra* oblation, one must assume an alternative textual sequence: "He cooks the gruel; he performs the *agnihotra* oblation. Even if this were the case...
The assumption of an alternative reading is one obstacle; furthermore, there is the assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭaphala*),
the uselessness of the prepared gruel substance, and the effort required to produce another substance not present when the gruel is already at hand.
By virtue of the three defects, the assumption of a different reading in accordance with the sequence of meaning is accepted as a single defect, according to the maxim:

"A single defect is outweighed by a collection of virtues. By that same logic, here too, [the phrase] "heard in the ears" refers to the wearing [of the ashes] preceded by the instruction of the five-syllable mantra: "May there be for me [this wearing]."
One must assume an alternative reading according to the sequence of meaning that "the wearing of the *liṅga* must necessarily be performed."
Now, one might object that this investigation into sequence is not applicable here,
because there is no relationship of primary and subordinate between the instruction of the five-syllable mantra and the wearing of the sectarian mark (*liṅga*),
according to the Mīmāṃsā principle that it is only the sequential auxiliaries that assist the principal act.

If you say this is not so, [we reply]: upon examining the Śruti and Smṛti, it is established that the wearing of the *liṅga* alone is intended, for when one becomes weary of bearing the burden, one sets down the burden and returns home; likewise, if the *liṅga* falls through negligence, one would abandon one's life along with it.
Due to its preeminence, the instruction of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī-mantra*), which brings about the fitness for wearing the *liṅga*, constitutes an ancillary part (*aṅga*);
for this is established in both the section on explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the section on mantras, as it is an ancillary part of every mantra whatsoever. Nowhere else... [is this not so].

Since there is an absence of predominance [in anything else], and because it is repeatedly observed that predominance belongs to action alone— such as sacrifice and the like— it must necessarily be stated that the wearing of the *liṅga* also possesses predominance by virtue of its being an action.
Now, since the auxiliary rites must necessarily be performed at the very time of the performance of the primary rite,

and because it is observed that the *prayāja* offerings and others are performed at the same time as the primary *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, [the result] of what was performed prior to the wearing of the sectarian mark [is as follows].

If you ask, "Since there is no performance of the instruction on the five-syllable mantra at that time, how can it be said to be an auxiliary [aṅga]?"— then your objection is indeed appropriate for one who is ignorant of the principles of logic (nyāya).
How [could it be otherwise] regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), which is performed prior to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice?

The status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Jyotiṣṭoma is accepted. Furthermore, by virtue of the authoritative instruction of the venerable Pāṇini— that "the object most desired by the agent of an action prescribed as 'one should establish the fires' (*agnīn ādadhīta*) is the *karman*, and likewise that which is not desired [but is connected to the action] is also [the *karman*]"— the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) [is applied].

It should not be said that, by virtue of its conjunction [with fire], it lacks the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma for the purpose of producing fire; for, as stated in the section of the third chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "And because qualities are for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality," and "In whatever [action] there is pleasure for a person, the desire for that is for the sake of the object."

Regarding the phrase "because it is not distinguished by its characteristic marks," this is because the status of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) rite was established in the second sūtra of the fourth chapter, in the fourth section (*varṇaka*). This was stated by the commentators, Śabarasvāmin:
"It cannot be like the *ādhāna*, for in that case there is an explicit scriptural statement [specifying] 'in spring'."

"A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires"— and this [fire-establishment] is not an auxiliary part [of the Vājapeya]. Alternatively, according to the injunction, "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya,

one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," since the Bṛhaspatisava— which is performed in the spring— has the Jyotiṣṭoma as its archetype, [the rule] "one should sacrifice with the Vājapeya in the autumn" [applies].

Just as the Vājapeya performed in the autumn season is a subsidiary of that [autumnal] time, or just as the Vaimṛdha sacrifice— performed after the completion of the Full Moon sacrifice by virtue of the scriptural injunction "having concluded the Full Moon sacrifice, he subsequently offers the Vaimṛdha"— is a subsidiary of the Full Moon sacrifice, so too it is in the present case.
Even though the instruction of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*) is performed at a different time,

its status as a constituent part of the subsequent practice of wearing the *liṅga* is consistent with the scriptural statement: "Having received the five-syllabled mantra from the Guru, the wise man should thereafter wear the *liṅga*."

Nor should it be doubted how the performance of the preceding subsidiary (pūrvāṅga) could possibly occur at a time other than that of the principal (pradhāna), given that in both the cited instances, the performance of subsequent subsidiaries is observed later on;
for this very principle concerns the performance of subsidiaries at a time other than that of the principal.
Since there is no decisive factor [to determine] whether it is the prior subsidiary or the subsequent subsidiary, the prior subsidiary is to be performed.

Alternatively, since it is observed that the *ādhāna*— which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice called the *jyotiṣṭoma*— is performed prior to the principal rite (*pradhāna*), it is already established that its performance as a preliminary auxiliary also exists. Nor is it the case that, by virtue of the accusative case ending, the *ādhāna* has the purpose of producing fire (*agni-niṣpatti*), and not [the purpose of qualifying the agent].

It should be stated that it was previously mentioned [that the fires] serve the purpose of the sacrifice; for the venerable teacher Bhaṭṭapāda has explained in his commentary that since the word *ādhāna* (consecration) indicates the Āhavanīya and other fires by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the fires can indeed be auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice. Thus, regarding the fires...

Since it is possible for those [rites] performed at the same time as the principal [rite] to be subsidiary parts of that principal rite, this principle applies here as well; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
Regarding this point, there is another scriptural passage in the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad: "Salutation to the Lord of the End;
salutation to Him who is near the Lord of the End; salutation to the Upward One; salutation to the Upward Liṅga.
Having begun thus, it continues: "This establishes the all-pervading Liṅga of Soma and Sūrya."
The purifier is the size of a hand. Thus it is said.

In this context, within the discussion defining the nature of the *liṅga*, the injunction to "establish the *sarvaliṅga*" means that one establishes the *liṅga* which consists of the powers (*śakti*) and Śiva in the form of the moon and the sun; having thus prescribed the wearing of the *liṅga*, and when the question arises as to where it is to be worn, [the text states] "the mantra in the hand," because it protects by being contemplated (*manana*) in the hand.
Thus, by this etymological derivation, it is established that the hand itself is the support for the *liṅga*,
because among the six locations suitable for wearing the *liṅga*, the palm of the hand is also enumerated as being fit for wearing it. As it is said in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*:
He who, having placed his own chosen *liṅga* upon the palm of his hand, directs the movement of his mind toward it,
and whose soul is free from desire for the multitude of external activities;
"O dear one, that Vīraśaiva performs worship in this manner. Thus [it is said].

Nor should it be said that this [instruction] regarding placing [the hand] is merely for the purpose of worshipping a clay linga made according to one's own desire; for there is no evidence for restricting the word "all" (*sarva*) in the phrase "all lingas" (*sarvaliṅgam*), which refers to every [linga] without limitation. And thus, its corroboration is found in the Skanda Purāṇa:
This is the form of power of Soma, and this is the auspicious (śiva) nature of Sūrya;
because it protects everything through contemplation (manana) in the hand, the entire Liṅga is the abode of Śiva.
"One should always establish it within the body as a sacred thread (*pavitra*). Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that it is called "pure" (*pavitra*) because it brings about purity even at a time when one is impure, just like the sacred thread (*upavīta*) which is always pure.
Regarding this matter, there is another Vedic scripture in the Ṛgveda:
"This hand of mine is blessed; this hand of mine is more blessed.
This is the universal healer for me; this is the one whose touch is auspicious."

"This is my mother, this is my father"—this is the meaning of this Śruti, derived from the arrival of life. "This is my hand; Bhagavān" means he possesses *bhaga* (fortune/majesty); that is to say, he is one who possesses greatness. [He is] most blessed (*bhagavattara*).

The meaning is that he possesses ultimate greatness. *Viśvabheṣajaḥ*: the medicine for the entire phenomenal world of *māyā*, or one who possesses medicine—a physician; the suffix *ac* is applied here because it belongs to the *arśas* group. *Śivābhimarśanaḥ*:
the word *abhimarśana* does not denote mere touch alone, but rather [touch] on all sides (*abhitaḥ*) or completely (*paritaḥ*).

"Touching" means *abhimarśana*; the meaning is that he touches every limb of the Liṅga-form with the fingers of his own palms. "This is the mother, this is the father, this is the life-giver"—that is, the medicine for life. Regarding this point, there is an explanatory supplement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*):
"This hand of mine is the Blessed One; this [other] hand of mine is even more blessed, because of its constant touch of Śiva and its bearing of the Śivaliṅga. Thus it is said.
Regarding this matter, there is another Vedic text:
"The sacrificial thread is the supreme purifier,
which was born together with Prajāpati in the beginning."
"Bestow the foremost longevity and the pure sacrificial thread; may there be strength and splendor for you. Thus.

The meaning of this Śruti is as follows: "That which is the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread); 'yajña' is Viṣṇu," according to the Śruti, "Yajña is indeed Viṣṇu. Furthermore, there is the statement by the author of the *Caturvedatātparyasaṃgraha*: "You are the Lord of Sacrifice (*yajñeśvara*), for they praise that sacrifice. [The term *upavītam* means] "near" (*upa*) to the form of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) attained through Viṣṇu, who is the sacrifice (*yajña*).

"Vīta, āvṛta, śaṃvīta, ruddha, and āvṛta" [are synonyms], according to Amara. Thus, the meaning is that the *yajñopavīta* is the *liṅga* consisting of Śiva and Śakti; for, by the Vedic text "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb," Viṣṇu is a portion of Śakti. [This applies] to the *liṅga*.
Because Viṣṇu consists of both Śiva and Śakti, and because the Liṅga— being the object of his presiding presence— is essentially the Pīṭha (the seat),
the Śivaliṅga is referred to by the term "sacrificial thread" (*yajñopavīta*) due to its status as that which presides over it. Paramam-...
The most excellent, pure, and completely purified [Being], prior to Prajāpati Brahmā— He who in the beginning generated Hiraṇyagarbha, He who ordains Brahmā in the beginning,
and who indeed bestows the Vedas upon him; so says the Śruti.
The existence prior to Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha is well known.

"Innate" means established by its own nature (*svabhāvasiddha*). Alternatively, it means "innate to Prajāpati," that is, born together with Prajāpati, who is Brahman—as in the phrase "he sacrifices with ghee," where [the quality belongs] to the ghee.
In this context, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental, as in the expression "he sacrifices" (*yajati*). That is to say, [He] was born together with Prajāpati.

Now, one might object that a certain fearful person approaches Him simply as the "Unborn," according to the Śruti: "O Rudra, protect me forever with that face of Yours which is the southern one," [and thus He is the cause of all].

Given the statement in the Droṇaparvan of the Mahābhārata, "The unborn, the sovereign, the unmanifest, the causal self, the imperishable," which describes Śiva— who is devoid of birth— in his *liṅga* form; how can the mention of his "origination" (*utpanna*) by means of the word "born together" (*sahaja*)— in the sense that he "is born together with" (*sahajāyate*) Brahmā, who possesses birth, as stated in the cited scripture, be logically justified?

If it is argued that [the mention of Tvaṣṭṛ] is contradictory, we say no; for in the third chapter, in the section concerning the *bhakṣa* (consuming) formulas, it is stated that one should indicate Tvaṣṭṛ by way of secondary indication (*upalakṣayet*).
Thus, in the mantra for the *pātnīvata* cup—"O Agni Pātnīvān, drink the Soma together with the god Tvaṣṭṛ"—although Agni Pātnīvān is the deity, he is mentioned along with him.

Regarding the doubt as to whether Tvaṣṭṛ possesses the status of a deity or not— since, like Agni, the Vedic mantra "O Tvaṣṭṛ, drink the Soma" (RV 3.55.19) mentions him as a drinker, it follows that he has deity-status— the established conclusion is as follows: just as in the case of the statement, "The she-ass carries the burden together with her ten sons," [the sons are merely figurative].

Just as in the case of sons unfit to carry burdens, even though the word "together" (*saha*) is heard expressing their coexistence, there is no connection with the act of carrying in relation to the she-ass; likewise, here too, although there is coexistence with Tvaṣṭṛ, because there is no connection with the act of drinking, it is stated that he lacks the status of a deity. By that same logic, it applies here as well.

In the mantra that establishes the simultaneous birth (*sahotpatti*) of Prajāpati, although Prajāpati possesses birth, Śiva’s lack of birth does not preclude his being denoted by the word "born-together" (*sahaja*). This is because [Śiva] is life-giving (*āyuṣya*),
bestowing longevity (*āyuṣkara*), and foremost (*agrya*)— as the Veda declares, "I alone existed first"— and he is radiant (*śubhra*), meaning stainless (*nirmala*).

Therefore, put on—that is, wear—this mark of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), since the root *muc* preceded by *prati* is established to have the meaning of "wearing. May you possess strength and splendor. Regarding this matter, there is the following corroborative text (*upabṛṃhaṇa*):
Then, having summoned and seen the sages, he said: "O best of sages, you who are proficient in the use of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, worship [the Lord] with [rosaries made of] crystal or stone."
The eternal sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), consisting of the essence of Śiva and Viṣṇu, composed of three strands, is the supreme purifier; [one should wear it] together with faith.
"O you who are learned in the Vedas, worship Him upon the seat of His lotus-hand or upon a pedestal.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Brahmā departed for Satyaloka.
Because it is woven together within all things at all times,
and because it indicates the Supreme Lord, the Linga is remembered as the "Sūtra" (the thread).
"One should maintain that the supreme Brahman, which is the Imperishable (akṣara), is this Sūtra.
By wearing this Sūtra, one shall neither be rendered impure by food remnants (ucchiṣṭa) nor unclean (aśuci). Thus it is said.
Regarding this matter, in the Śatarudrīya [it is said]: "O Rudra, that body of yours which is auspicious, not terrible, and free from the appearance of evil—
with that most peaceful body, O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with favor."
The meaning of this is: O Rudra, the Lord who causes that which is obstructed—namely suffering or the cause of suffering—to flow away for us, Śiva, the supreme cause, is called "Rudra" by the wise.
Thus, from the statement in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"Because you cause all living beings to weep at the time of the end by your own will,
therefore you are designated as Rudra by the wise and best of sages."

And from the statement in the Śiva Purāṇa: "Rudra" is so called because you cause the suffering consisting of the three-fold affliction (*tāpa*) of your devotees to melt away (*drāvayasi*) and pass away (*yāpayasi*). Regarding the phrase "your auspicious body" (*śivā tanūḥ*): according to the Śruti, "This fire is indeed Rudra;
these two are his bodies—the one terrible and the other auspicious. Thus, the *liṅga* is the auspicious body.

It has been stated: "The form [of Śiva] is declared to be the Ghoratanū; among those two, the Śivā-tanū resides within sinless devotees. In accordance with this supporting statement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), the form of the body that is the *liṅga* is the Aghora, whose nature is eternally auspicious; it shines (*kāśate*) within those who are sinless—that is, within those whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) have reached maturity—hence it is called "shining among the sinless" (*apāpakāśinī*).
O Giriśanta, with that most peaceful (śantamayā) body of yours, which is of the nature of ultimate bliss and takes the form of the *liṅga*,
look upon us; that is to say, by means of wearing the *liṅga*, grant us the supreme bliss consisting of the state of identity between the *liṅga* and the limbs of the body, and reveal it.
Regarding this point, there is a supporting statement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*):

"O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is non-terrible and does not appear as evil, because it is sung with the *Yajus*, therefore one who belongs to Śiva (*śaiva*) is free from sin. Thus it is said.

Regarding this matter, there is another scriptural passage (*śrutyantara*): "You are the goad of Brahman; you are the yoke-pole of Brahman; you are the receptacle of Brahman. By Brahman this earth is supported; by this [Brahman] the great [earth] is supported; [so too are] the great intermediate space and heaven."
He has supported the earth together with the gods. "What I have known, may I maintain;
may the Veda not slip away from me. May wisdom and insight enter me from both sides for the attainment of what has been and what is to be.
May I attain a full span of life—may I attain a full span of life! Thus.

The meaning of this scripture is as follows: because of the explanatory expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) stating that "the sign of Brahman is declared to be Brahman," and from the statement in Vedic lexicons such as "the procreative organ of Brahman is the *kāṭa*," etc.;
and because [the term] *codanī* is derived from the root *cud* (to impel) with the suffix *lyuṭ* followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, it means "the impeller" of that sign.

O Earth, you are [the support]; furthermore, you are the *aṇi*—meaning the pin or wedge (*kīlaka*)—of the *liṅga* of Brahman (according to Amara: "the two terms *aṇi* and *kīlaka* are synonyms"). Although the singular is used here, the dual and plural forms are seen in other mantras; thus, the dual form is used in the sense of the singular as a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). You have taken your stand.

*Āṅ* is a prefix (*upasarga*). The separation [of the prefix] by an intervening word is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). You are the vessel for the sowing of the subtle body (*liṅga*) of Brahman; you are the support, for scripture declares that "the earth is the great vessel. This status as a support is by virtue of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). By this [statement], [the suitability of the earth] for the fiery subtle bodies...
The cessation of wearing [the linga] is indicated. By the phrase "you are the goad of Brahman," the wearing of a linga that has been joined to a pedestal (pīṭha) is indicated;
by this, the cessation of wearing crystal lingas that have not been so joined is indicated. By the phrase "you are the goad of Brahman,"...
Since it is impossible for an accomplished *liṅga* to be impelled [by a command], its associated activity is indicated;
and that activity consists in the form of the *vīraśaiva* initiation (*dīkṣā*). The meaning is:
"You are the impeller of initiation. Therefore, by means of these three sentences, the earthly [element] alone is joined through the gateway of *vīraśaiva* initiation.

It has been described that the *liṅga* is fit for wearing. The meaning is that this earth is worn as the earthly *liṅga*; thus, by means of the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*), which denotes the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*) and ends in the feminine gender, it is referred to as the "earthly *liṅga*" (*pārthivaṃ liṅgam*).

A modification is prescribed because it is observed in another mantra; for instance, in the passage "May the earth, being purified, purify me," the term *pṛthvī* (earth) appears in the feminine gender, and it is observed that by this word one refers to the earthly body. By this [mantra] held by this practitioner...
The meaning is that the earth becomes a *pārthiva-liṅga* (an earthen linga) sustained by Brahman.

Thus, just as it is said that "the knower of Brahman, who wears the linga denoted by the word 'Brahman,' becomes Brahman itself," the meaning here is that he becomes non-different from Brahman. By this [phrase], [it refers to] the worshipper who performs the act of wearing [the linga].

Furthermore, because it is taught by means of the word "Brahman," the word "Brahman" is intended solely for the purpose of attaining identity; otherwise, the word "Brahman" would be redundant. By the three preceding statements and by the word "Earth," the wearing of the marks of Prāṇa and Bhava is indeed preceded by the wearing of the desired marks.

It is indicated that the attainment of Brahman, which consists of the state of perfect identity (*sāmarasya*) between the *liṅga* and the body, is not achieved merely by wearing the *prāṇaliṅga* or the *bhāvaliṅga*. Now, one might object:
even so, by the use of the word "Brahman" in grammatical apposition with the word "this" (*idam*) in the phrase "by this," [it refers to] the practitioner...

If it is argued that the designation [of the state of liberation] as the primary meaning is untenable— because the state of being liberated while living (*jīvanmuktatva*) occurs only after the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma following the attainment of Brahman,
and thus cannot be designated by the word "Brahman" in its primary sense due to its merely figurative nature— the answer is no; for this is not the case in the *Pavamāneṣṭi*.

Regarding the statement, "One pours out the oblations with the *agnihotrahavaṇī*," how is it possible for the word *agnihotrahavaṇī* to denote a specific vessel that serves as the instrument for pouring? [The answer is: because immediately after one has established the two fires through the *ādhāna* and *pavamāna* rites, the *agnihotra* sacrifice is subsequently performed by means of this [vessel].
Because the Agnihotra has not been performed at the time of the Pavamāna-iṣṭi— since it is to be performed with the vessel used for the offering (nirvāpa) of the Pavamāna-iṣṭi—
and because the term *agnihotrahavaṇī* lacks conventional status (*rūḍhi*) due to its being merely etymological (*yaugika*), meaning "the specific vessel by which the Agnihotra is offered."

When [the time] has arrived, since there is no lack of fitness because the connection with the oblation is possible through the future state in that particular vessel, its mention is possible even at a time prior to that.
By that same principle, here too, [this applies] by means of wearing the marks of the desired [deity], the marks of the vital breath, and the marks of existence.

It is possible to designate by the word "Brahman" a practitioner who is fit for liberation in the form of the identity (*sāmarasya*) of the *liṅga* and the body. Following that, the praise of the practitioner who bears the *liṅga* is made by means of the passage beginning with "the Great," on account of his being the sustainer of the entire world: "The Great—the intermediate space—is supported by the Great; by the Great..."
The status of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) as the supporter is figurative, because that which is placed upon it is above and its support is below.
[It supports] the intermediate space, which is the sky (*ākāśa*), and the heaven (*div*), the celestial realm (*svarga*) together with the gods— that is, the earth accompanied by many deities.

Regarding *dādhāra*: although it should have been stated as *dadhāra*, the form *dādhāra* is a Vedic (chāndasa) form. Here, since there is a requirement for an agent (*kartṛ*) for the verbal root, it is precisely the agent of the action of maintaining the desired gender previously indicated by the word "this" (*idam*).

It follows [the preceding] by virtue of its proximity as something worthy of praise; a change of case-ending (vibhaktivipariṇāma) is to be imagined. Therefore, "this" (ayam) is a designation of the agent. The practitioner (upāsaka) sustains the three worlds;
by this term "sustaining the three worlds," the wearing of the desired insignia (liṅga)—namely, the prāṇa-liṅga and the bhāva-liṅga—is [intended].

It has been indicated: "That liṅga which I know as being characterized by the previously mentioned characteristics—that liṅga I shall wear. Now, an objection may be raised: since the wearing of the earthen liṅga was already established by the previous statement, "This earth was worn [as a liṅga]," why is the wearing of the liṅga being established again?

If it is asked, "For what purpose?", [the answer is: there is no fault whatsoever, as this repetition is intended to demonstrate that the fitness for wearing the *liṅga* belongs only to one who possesses the previously mentioned knowledge and not to anyone else, and also to state that there is a fruit pertaining to this world (*aihika*). He demonstrates that very fruit pertaining to this world with the words, "medhām anīṣā. Here, *medhā* consists of retention (*dhāraṇā*).

"Buddhi" means "manīṣā," that is, pure intellect (*kevalā buddhiḥ*). Your "medhā" and "manīṣā" are "samīcī"—the singular number is Vedic; it means they are "harmonious" (*samīcīne*), acting by turning toward the Inner Self through the renunciation of sense-objects and the like. May they enter into me.
May [the two] always sit upon me from all sides. From me, let the King of Mantras consisting of five syllables—the Veda—not fall away or be lost;

for in the root *sraṃsu* (meaning "to fall" or "to slip"), the augment *aṭ* is prohibited due to its connection with the prohibitive particle *mā*, and there is elision of the *n* due to its being marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter. And furthermore:
He states another result with the words beginning "of what has come to be" (*bhūtasya*). By "of what has come to be," preservation is meant;

by "of what is to be" (*bhavyasya*), acquisition (*yoga*) is meant, because it has been said that "acquisition is that which is not obtainable through other means, and security (*kṣema*) is its protection. For the sake of securing—that is, for the attainment of—both acquisition and security, one should practice the entire span of life.

"May I attain the full lifespan; may I obtain the hundred-year life span declared in the Vedas. Therefore, for one who has made a firm resolve through this Vedic injunction, the attainment of liberation—characterized by the state of essential identity between the *liṅga* and the body (*aṅga*)—following the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the wearing of the *liṅga* as a symbol of the earthly king, constitutes the fruit pertaining to the hereafter.

It is determined that the fruit [of this practice] consists of the non-forgetting of the five-syllable mantra and others, the attainment of right knowledge preceded by the renunciation of sense objects, the achievement of security (yogakṣema), and the attainment of the full lifespan prescribed in the Vedas.
He takes the *prastara* bundle from the front; he thereby makes it the principal. He inserts the two strainers (*pavitra*) into it.
The *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer, and the two strainers are the out-breath and the in-breath; thus, he bestows out-breath and in-breath upon the sacrificer himself.

Thus, by this Vedic text as well, the wearing of the *liṅga* is enjoined. For it is said: "The *prastara* is a specific stone having the form of a *liṅga*; [it is] the *prastara*, the source of birth, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the *liṅga*"—according to the *Kośa*.
First, the Guru takes hold of it; upon that he places two *pavitra*s. Regarding the word *pavitra*:

Since the *Vaijayantī* lexicon establishes that [the term] denotes deities in general, Śiva and Śakti are understood as the two deities in the *pavitra*. These two, moreover, the Guru creates at the time of initiation through the sequence of invoking the *kalā*s upon the *pīṭha* and the *golaka*; the word "also" (*api*) is displaced in its order, and the construction is "he creates them also."

The meaning is that he also "joins" [it]. This has the sense of conjunction with the verb "grasps" (*gṛhṇāti*). By this, the meaning is that he grasps—that is, he should wear—the *liṅga* consisting of Śiva and Śakti, which was given by the Guru after the preliminary rite of invocation (*āvāhana*). Now, one might object: since there is an absence of suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), or gerundive (*tavyat*) in the word "grasps," [how can it be an injunction?]

If it is argued that maintenance is not enjoined by the present-tense suffix *laṭ* because it merely indicates a current state, this is not so; for, as in the cases of "the sacrificial post is made of udumbara wood" (*audumbaro yūpo bhavati*) and "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), its injunctive character is possible through the transformation of the suffix into *leṭ*.
Now, let it be granted that there is an injunctive suffix.

Since there is no word expressing "retention" (*dhāraṇa*), but rather the hearing of the root *gṛhṇāti* which expresses "grasping," how can retention be enjoined? Nor should it be said that retention is indicated by implication through the word "grasps," according to the maxim: "In an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not [to be set aside] for another. Therefore, how is retention enjoined?

If this is argued, [we reply: no; because in the subsequent injunction prescribing the encircling—"while holding the *prastara* he lays down the *paridhis*"—the act of holding is restated by means of the present participial suffix (*śatṛ-pratyaya*). Since a restatement (*anuvāda*) requires a prior statement (*purovāda*), the act of holding [is understood] from the [earlier passage] "he takes [the *paridhis*]" (*gṛhṇāti*).

It is indeed prescribed; otherwise, the restatement (anuvāda) would be without cause. Therefore, by the force of its presentation as an established fact, it must be admitted that holding (dhāraṇa) is indeed prescribed. Now, according to the maxim "in an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not [to be set aside]," the root *gṛh* [is understood] through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) as having the sense of holding.

If it is asked, "How is this to be conceptualized?"— do not say so. In the injunctions, "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu" (*vāyavyaṃ śvetamālabheta bhūtikāmaḥ*) and "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a pap (*caru*) to Sūrya" (*sauryaṃ caruṃ nirvaped brahmavarcasakāmaḥ*),

although the roots *ālabhati* ("to touch/sacrifice") and *nirvapati* ("to pour out/offering") do not themselves denote the act of sacrificing (*yajati*), sacrifices are enjoined by conceptualizing the appropriate expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*) as required by the context.
Otherwise, when the acts of *ālabhati* (touching) and *nirvapet* (offering)— which consist of the meanings of touching and separating— must be performed in connection with one another,

it would follow that they are redundant (*vaiyyarthya*), because they could not possibly serve as injunctions for substances already established in the sacrifice due to the impossibility of them being otherwise [established]. Rather than redundancy, [the former view is preferable].

The assumption of a meaning in any way whatsoever [is not permissible]. Therefore, it was determined in the third pāda of the second adhyāya that when [the meanings of] *ālabhati* ("he slaughters") and *nirvapati* ("he offers") are already established by their own inherent sense, these words merely restate (*anuvāda*) those meanings and indicate the assumption of a sacrifice (*yāga*).

By that same principle, here too, since the mere act of "taking" (gṛhṇāti) would be impossible to perform as a "holding" (dhāraṇa), and because it is already established [as such], it is unfit to be prescribed; therefore, "holding" is inferred. Furthermore, in the second pāda of the fifth adhyāya, the subject matter is heard in the scriptural text: "He cuts off the oblation twice. In that regard, what...

When the doubt arises as to whether there should be a performance by items (*padārthānusamaya*) or a performance by sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*), the conclusion reached is that it must indeed be a performance by items, because only the act of cutting (*avadyati*) is explicitly heard in the scripture. Therefore, having performed the cutting of the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni and having executed the sacrifice, [one should proceed] again...

Having performed the cutting-off (*avadāna*) from one oblation and having also performed another sacrifice, it would follow—according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that the same should be done for other oblations as well. However, if the injunction were to enjoin merely the act of cutting-off, which is already established by the sense of the context, the injunction would be redundant; furthermore, the cutting-off would then serve only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, the cutting-off [is not [enjoined]...].

However, the number two is prescribed; whereas the act of cutting (avadāna) is a constituent part of the primary sacrifice. According to the principle that "when a visible result is possible, it is improper to assume an invisible one," the cutting is for the sake of the sacrifice. Therefore, because the performance of the mere cutting constitutes a single part [of the whole],...

Since the performance of the ritual act itself has already occurred when the sacrifice is not performed, the sacrifice must be performed without taking a further portion of the oblation; thus, it is said that there is "performance by sections" (*kāṇḍānusamaya*).
By that same principle, here too, in the injunction for the mere grasping of the sign (*liṅga*), [the same applies].

Since mere grasping (*grahaṇa*) lacks the status of a ritual act (*padārtha*) as it constitutes only a single part [of the process], it is necessary to pursue it until its culmination in retention (*dhāraṇa*); otherwise, the grasping would be for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, grasping conjoined with retention constitutes a single ritual act.

Therefore, even the fact that it has a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatā) is established. Consequently, holding (dhāraṇa) is enjoined for the sake of accomplishing a single ritual act. Furthermore, a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of "holding" is accepted for the root *grah* (to take). Nor should it be argued that "in an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not [necessarily] intended," as stated in the fourth chapter regarding the passage "he brings the eastern direction."

Because, in the second section (pāda) of the second chapter (adhyāya), under the heading "On account of its being the primary factor in the branch," the acceptance of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) for an injunctive sentence is established. Indeed, the determination there is as follows:
by means of the sentence existing within the context of fetching the branch, namely, "He fetches the eastern [branch],"...

When the doubt arises as to whether the bringing of a branch is being enjoined, or whether it is the primary purpose [of the injunction] that is being enjoined, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is reached: according to the maxim "in an injunction, the literal meaning of the word [is primary]," the bringing of the branch should not be performed;
rather, it is the primary purpose that is being enjoined. To this, the final conclusion (siddhānta) is: if it were for its own sake...
If this were the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of this sentence, then, like the statement "one should sprinkle with fire," it would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*) by conveying an impossible sense;
therefore, having set aside the primary meaning—

The primary meaning must be adopted. Even if a non-primary meaning were to be assumed there, if one were to assume a meaning based on the context such as "he brings a branch toward the eastern direction," then a great fault would arise because it would necessitate the supply of two additional words. If...

Since the branch is obtained by virtue of the context, the word denoting it need not be supplied; even so, the fault of supplying the word *prati* remains unavoidable. Therefore, one must accept that the word *prācī* (eastern) functions as a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for a branch facing the east, in the sense of "he brings a branch facing the east."

The previously mentioned defects must be avoided. By that same principle, since the root *grah* here culminates in its own primary sense, it would result in extreme futility; therefore, one must necessarily accept indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to avoid the burden of postulating an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Alternatively, [it may mean] "holding the prastara-grass-bundle."

The injunction for wearing the marks is postulated only in the subsequent sentence, "He puts on the enclosing sticks" (*paridhīn paridadhāti*). Now, one might object: since the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is present in the word "wearing" (*dhārayan*), and since that suffix denotes the sense of the present tense (*laṭ*), which lacks injunctive force, how can there be an injunction for wearing here?

Or rather, it is "to be spoken" (*vācya*) because it can be stated; for a direct injunction (*vidhi*) is possible here, just as in the case of the statement, "May Agni and Soma sacrifice for us with clarified butter alone in a low voice at the full moon.
Alternatively, an injunction is accepted here as well, just as in the case of the statement, "For he holds [the ladle] above for the gods. And it is not so in that [other] case.

Since the verbal suffix *tiṅ* is heard in the word "dhārayati," it is possible there to transform it into the *leṭ* mood, whereby an injunction (*vidhi*) is possible; however, one might object that since there is no verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) here, how can it be established that an injunction exists? To this it must be said: for [the text continues] "upari hi devebhyaḥ... [and so forth].

For in the case of the word *dhārayati*, since the particle *hi* is heard, even though the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) is present, its expressive power is blunted; and because it is impossible for it to undergo the transformation into the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, how could an injunction (*vidhi*) be accepted there?
Yet, it is indeed accepted. By that same principle, an injunction is also accepted in the phrase *dhārayan prastaram*.

This was stated in the second chapter (*dvitīyādhyāya*) in the passage, "And those with which one sacrifices to the gods and gives," where it was demonstrated that the relative pronoun (*yat*), the vocative, the particle *hi*, and the first person verb forms lack the capacity to constitute an injunction; therefore, it is improper to assume an injunction there. But even so—
There is an inequality because [the suffix] is heard as ending in a *sub* (nominal) affix, and thus there is an absence of an injunction altogether.
If it is argued that, since a form ending in a *tiṅ* (verbal) affix is heard there, an injunction can somehow be postulated, we say no;
for just as a pot cannot be produced by a broken stick which is inherently unfit for that purpose, so too [an injunction cannot arise from such a form].

Similarly here as well, although it appears to be a verbal form (*tiṅanta*), because there is no injunction whatsoever in the phrase "he holds [the debt] for the gods" (*devebhyo dhārayati*), there is no difference at all between the two cases of "holding" (*dhārayan*) and "holds" (*dhārayati*); this is the counter-argument (*pratibandī*). Now, one might object:
If it is asked how there can be a resolution in that case since the counter-objection (*pratibandī*) is not answered, the response is as follows:

in the fifth section of the fourth quarter of the third chapter, regarding the phrase "wearing" (*dhārayan*), there arises the doubt whether this is an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*). [The conclusion is that] because of the hearing of the word *hi* (for/since), it is not an injunction.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "it is possible" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), [the opponent replies] that this is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*), because a restatement depends upon a prior statement (*purovāda*),

and the act of holding the *samidh* fuel-stick over the substance intended for the deity is not established by worldly practice. Nor can it be argued that "whatever substance is covered must be concealed."

It should not be said that holding the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) above [the fire] is established by logical inference (*nyāya*), because there is no injunction (*vidhi*) for it anywhere. Therefore, even though the word "for" (*hi*) is heard [in the text], the conclusion is that an injunction exists because it is something new (*apūrva*) and has not been previously established. Thus...

Since such a state of retention is equally applicable here even in the case of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), an injunction must indeed be postulated. For this very reason, taking such retention as an illustrative example,
the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā-sūtras, [discusses it] in the fourth pāda of the third adhyāya.

In the statement, "Established in Brahman, one attains immortality," the injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is established by the sūtra, "Or [it is] like the holding [of the prastara], because it is an injunction" (*vidhirvā dhāraṇavad iti*). Therefore, in this present context as well— in the phrase "holding the prastara"—
by means of the word "dhārayan," which ends in the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), there is a transformation into an injunction, as in the case of the *rātrisatra*.

Just as in the sentence "Those who perform these nights indeed find firm support," the injunction is that those who wish to find firm support should perform these nights— where the suffix *san* (desiderative) is transformed [into an injunctive sense]— so too in the case of "holding the *prastara*," it means "one should hold the *prastara*."

There is no obstacle whatsoever to the transformation of the suffix *vidhi* into the suffix *śatṛ*. Therefore, it is established that by this scriptural statement as well, the wearing of the *liṅga* must necessarily be performed by Vedic Vīraśaiva seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*). [The text continues: "He takes up the *prastara* grass-bundle; he thereby makes it the principal. Regarding the *prastara*...

The Guru takes up the *liṅga* for the purpose of wearing it; because it is to be worn for as long as one lives, he treats it as primary, just like the *ukhā* (sacrificial fire-pot)—this is the meaning. Within that *liṅga*, he creates the two deities, Śiva and Śakti, by means of the ritual of invoking the *kalās*; [he likewise creates] Śiva and Śakti within the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*).

The subsequent sentence praises the very meaning already stated in "he invokes," because the injunction for invocation depends upon an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), according to the maxim that "a single sentence [should consist of] an injunction and its purpose. "The sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is indeed the sacrificer"—the sacrificer is the one who wears the *liṅga*, and the *prastara* is the *liṅga* itself; [this refers to] the relationship between the *liṅga* and its constituent parts.
Because the state of *sāmarasya* (equilibrium) has been brought about by the Guru;
the two, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, are the two purifiers (*pavitra*), which are Śiva and Śakti. Since the two, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, exist above the *liṅga*, they possess the nature of *prāṇa*.

Because it is situated below the pedestal (*pīṭha*), it has the nature of the downward breath (*apāna*). Therefore, by means of the invocation of such a deity into the *liṅga*, the sacrificer himself establishes both the upward and downward breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) therein. Consequently, the invocation of the deity into the *liṅga* is praised as being equivalent to the sacrificer’s maintenance of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. Thus [it was said] by the Guru.

One should wear—indeed, one ought to wear—the stone (prastara), that is, the *liṅga*, which has been rendered as consisting of the nature of Śiva and Śakti preceded by the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Vīraśaiva. Just as it is said, "at the silent full moon," so here is the rule for wearing the *liṅga*. He places the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); like an enclosing stick, that is, like a surrounding enclosure.

Because it exists [there], it is called a *paridhi*; this is a figurative usage (*gauṇaprayoga*), like saying "the boy is fire. It encircles, that is, it binds around the neck; the natural sense of the word *paridhi* indicates binding around the neck.
The plural number in *paridhīn* is used for a single object, as in the mantra: "May the goddess Aditi release the bonds."

Since the excellence of wearing the *liṅga* is possible, it is established that, by virtue of the meaning of the words in this scriptural passage and by virtue of the meaning of the sentence as reinforced by the previously stated reasoning,
the wearing of the *liṅga* must necessarily be practiced.
Regarding this matter, another scriptural passage (*śruti*) is also an authority:
"Being the supporter, he supports while being supported; the one God has entered into many forms.
When he becomes weary of bearing the burden, having laid down the burden, he returns again to his setting. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this Vedic passage is as follows: "Being the supporter" (*bhartā*), that is, being the protector; the verbal root *ḍubhṛñ* means "to support" and "to nourish. According to Amarasimha’s *Nānārthavarga*, "supporter" (*bhartā*) has multiple meanings, including "creator" (*dhātṛ*) and "nourisher" (*poṣṭṛ*). "Being supported" (*bhriyamāṇaḥ*) or "being maintained" (*dhriyamāṇaḥ*); [this is formed] from the root *bhṛñ* with the suffix *śānac* in the sense of the object (*karman*). "Alone" (*ekaḥ*).

"God is Mahādeva; Rudra is indeed one alone, he does not stand with a second," according to the Taittirīya Śruti; "For Rudra is one alone, they do not stand with a second," according to the Śvetāśvatara Śruti; and "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the maker of auspiciousness," according to the Arthaśikhā.

And because of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* stating "Brahman is one only, without a second," and because it is well known in many places that the word "one" (*eka*) has the sense of "Śiva alone" through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Śiva," and because the word "deity" (*deva*)— just as in the case of "Satyabhāmā" where "Bhāmā" is used— should be understood here as "Mahādeva."

By mentioning a portion of a name—such as "Deva"—to refer to the whole name, the intended meaning is "Mahādeva," which results in the sense of "Śivaliṅga. He is called "Deva" because he plays (dīvyati) or shines (prakāśate);
he is established and situated in many ways and in manifold forms, and he sustains and nourishes his devotees.
In the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, it exists in the form of the desired vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the *bhāva-liṅga*;
