in the forms of the sixfold *liṅgas* beginning with conduct (*ācāra*) and ending with the great *mahāliṅga*, which have attained the nature of its manifestations; and within the circles of the organs of knowledge, the internal organ, the vital breaths, and the bodily constituents, it exists as their illuminating light.

The sense is that, having settled down, he perceives each collection of objects as they arrive at their respective sense organs, remaining fixed upon them each time. Since the root *bhṛ* (to bear) is transitive, when there is a requirement for an object (*karman*), the devotee (*bhakta*) is presented as the object;
and in the phrase "being borne" (*bhriyamāṇāḥ*), he is presented as the agent of the act of bearing (*dhāraṇa-kartṛ*). [He bears] the burden (*bhāram*).

By the etymological derivation from the root *bhṛ* ("to carry"), the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). When—that is, at which time—the practitioner (*upāsaka*) becomes weary or negligent due to laziness and the like, being unable to bear or maintain the "burden" (*bhāra*), namely the *liṅga* that is being carried; [the meaning is] "again," he should set down the deity who is the burden being carried.

Having separated [the soul] from the body and deposited it somewhere, he sets; that is, through the non-perception of the body, he attains *kaivalya*. The intended meaning is this: for the Vīraśaiva who possesses the state of identity between the *liṅga* and the body, the *iṣṭaliṅga* itself constitutes the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
In the event that, due to negligence, a deficiency such as cutting or piercing occurs which results in the loss of those constituent parts,

one should attain invisibility by means of withering the body in order to achieve liberation (*kaivalya*) in the form of union with the Great Liṅga (*mahāliṅga-ekya*). Regarding this matter, the authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*) are as follows:
Śiva, in the form of sound (nāda), is directly designated as the liṅga;
the supreme power (śakti) is the pedestal (pīṭhikā), and she indeed has the form of the point (bindu).
O Goddess, from the union of those two, the *kalā* is established therein;
that *kalā* is supreme and subtle, pervading everywhere at all times.
Just as oil shines within sesame seeds and fragrance within flowers, so too,
in the *Kāmika*,
the entire world— both stationary and moving— is of the nature of *bindu* and *nāda*.
The drop (bindu) is Śakti, and the resonance (nāda) is Śiva; the universe consists of the essence of both Śiva and Śakti.
Nāda is the support of Bindu, and this world has Bindu as its support;
for indeed, Bindu and Nāda are established as the foundation of the world.
Everything joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda* constitutes the process of *sakalīkaraṇa*;
through this *sakalīkaraṇa*, the world undoubtedly attains birth.
The Bindu is the altar, Nāda is Śiva, and the Śivaliṅga is thus described;
this is declared to be the Vīraśaiva tradition, which is free from the need for expiation.
One should wear with great attention the *liṅga* bestowed by the Guru;
should the *liṅga* fall through negligence, one should even give up one's life.
In the Vātula-tantra:
when the fear of losing one's life has arisen— whether from thieves, spirits, seizing demons, or water—
in both heedfulness and heedlessness, one must not abandon the *prāṇaliṅga*.
If the *prāṇaliṅga* is severed, the vital breath will depart from the *liṅga*;
if the *prāṇasaṃsthā* occurs while it is out of sight, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
If the vital-force-linga is severed, one should abandon the breaths within that linga;
having received initiation again while remaining [in that state], one shall go to the Raurava hell.
Therefore, one should worship the subtle body (*liṅga*) composed of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) as long as life lasts;
when that has perished, O high-minded one, you may abandon your vital breaths.
In the *Candrajñānāgama*, it is stated:
"The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) indeed reside in the *iṣṭaliṅga* of the Vīraśaivas;
therefore, one must protect [the *liṅga*] with effort by means of the unwearied vital breaths."
If [the vessel] falls or breaks through negligence, no expiation exists;
therefore, one should hold it with great care until death.
If one, out of delusion, should wear another's linga even when one's own has been lost,
he becomes fallen and deprived of his linga, and shall go to the Raurava hell.
The male organ is called the "liṅga," and it is declared to be the limb of the woman;
he who has fallen from the sight of his own liṅga is like a widow who has gone to another man.
In the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara:
"If one is devoid of the *liṅga* connected to the body, one becomes like a *piśāca*;
by being separated from it for even half a *nimeṣa*, one becomes especially a sinner."
He of deluded intellect who places his vital breaths into a *prāṇaliṅga* should be known as a *caṇḍāla*; he is a traitor to Śiva, without a doubt.

If one who possesses the *prāṇaliṅga* gives up his life while minor faults such as the loss of the *liṅga* or the neglect of the observances (*vrata*) and practices persist, he sinks into blinding darkness.
If that linga is destroyed by fate, another linga should not be worn;
rather, once that very same one is recovered, one should wear it again, provided it is free from defects.
If one born of yoga possesses a desired *liṅga* that is fragmented, and desires to enjoy it further, [the following occur]:
drinking from a sacred ford (*tīrthapāna*), drinking liquor (*surāpāna*), and eating the flesh of a cow (*gomāṃsabhakṣaṇa*).
One should never wear that liṅga which has a head-shaped base, a cow-faced base, a circular middle, or a pedestal-base, provided there are holes at these six locations.
Nevertheless, even a yogi who practices concentration (dhāraṇā) shall go to the Raurava hell if,
through negligence, [the breath] is interrupted for the duration of a grain of rice, half a grain, or as long as it takes to pull out a hair.
O daughter of the mountain, one should abandon the vital breaths from the seat (pīṭha) up to the liṅga.
In the *Candrajñānāgama*,
it is said: "O Maheśvarī, when the *liṅga* has been pierced to the measure of a barley grain,
one should cast off the body through the complete withering of the self for my satisfaction."
If it is pierced at the location of the pedestal (pīṭha), or if it is pierced at the location of the circle (vṛtta);
if there should be a piercing at the cow’s mouth (gomukha), or at the womb (yoni), or at the sphere (golaka) itself.
Whether it be the size of a hair-tip, subtle like a mote of dust in a sunbeam,
or even the measure of a grain of dust, there is no fault in cutting or piercing it.
Having seen this, O Goddess, one should maintain it; this is the definitive conclusion in all scriptures.
In the *Kiraṇāgama*, it is said:

"O daughter of the Mountain, one should abandon the vital breaths [from] the pedestal (*pīṭha*) up to the linga, whether it has been cut to the measure of a barley grain, or half of that, or even a quarter."

Half a grain of rice [in measurement] should be placed in the center of the pedestal (pīṭha), half of that in the circular cow-mouth (gomukha), and the size of a sesame seed in the womb (yoni) and the linga; if these exceed those measurements, one should give up one's life.
If a linga made of rice has two parts, or if it is shaped like a cow's mouth or a sphere, or if it has three parts, or if it is cracked, one should certainly not wear such a linga.
He who would give up his life solely for the sake of the *liṅga*, having firm oneness with me—O fair-faced one, he attains [the goal], there is no doubt; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Or likewise for the sake of the *liṅga*, for the sake of the Guru, or even for the sake of right conduct.
The renunciation of the body is prescribed either for the sake of wandering or for the sake of [divine] grace;
likewise, even a householder who possesses such steadfastness is liberated.
If there is a deficiency in his chosen emblem, he should perform the renunciation of life,
avoiding weapons, mountains, water, nooses, meditation, and fire.
Having renounced food, wearing ashes and rudrākṣas while observing the prescribed rules,
and having performed the recitation of the Śaiva mantra, one should unite the body with Rudra.
The intended meaning of these statements heard in the Śrutis, Āgamas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas is as follows:
after the excellent Guru has effected the union of the Pīṭha and the Golaka, which are of the nature of Bindu and Nāda, respectively...

Having brought the digit of consciousness (citkalā) situated in the Brahma-randhra by the disciple into its own essential nature (svarūpatā) through the path of the Suṣumṇā by means of the door of mental vision directed toward that state, and having established it—
because that very [consciousness] is designated as the "liṅga" when it has been fully integrated (sakalīkṛta), and because it alone is the cause of the world— of that liṅga...
At the time of initiation, the disciple's existential liṅga (*bhāvaliṅga*), the vital breaths' liṅga of life-force (*prāṇaliṅga*),
and the body's preferred liṅga (*iṣṭaliṅga*)— whether partless (*niṣkala*), both partless and with parts (*sakalaniṣkala*), or with parts (*sakala*)—
becomes that very liṅga of the disciple from the moment it was joined [to him] by the Guru.

It becomes the *prāṇaliṅga*. Therefore, in the event of the impairment of that *liṅga*, the separation from life for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) Vīraśaivas is indeed appropriate. For this very reason, it is said to be "exempt from expiatory rites" (*prāyaścittavivarjita*). Consequently, the *liṅga* must be worn with an attentive mind; [otherwise], due to negligence or some other cause—

In the case of one who has been separated from his *liṅga* and, for the sake of saving his life, wears another *liṅga*, even though there is a threat to his life due to the fear of thieves, tigers, and the like— arising from the fact that the wearer of such a [new] *liṅga* is considered a traitor to Śiva and a *caṇḍāla* by virtue of his [former] karma— for the purpose of wearing it again with a state of non-negligence;
Since another initiation (*dīkṣā*) is not to be performed, and because that [initiation] would be a cause for hell;

and since the Vīraśaiva who bears the *liṅga* is the husband of the *liṅga*, such that upon separation from the *liṅga* he would be like a widow separated from her husband; and because defects such as cutting or piercing the *liṅga* might occur—[the following is stated].

Even if there occurs a violation of the observances and rules of the vow due to delusion, forgetfulness, or the like, because one who continues to sustain his life would otherwise be fit for entry into blinding darkness; and because that very same prescribed [vow], though lost through negligence, must be maintained once it is seen again; [this applies] in the event of a deficiency in the desired emblem (*liṅga*).

Even when food and drink have been obtained for one who eats and drinks, [the sin] is equal to that of eating beef and drinking liquor; and when a mark (*liṅga*) is joined with an opening at any one of the six locations, such as the head or the forehead, by wearing that which is not to be worn,
the wearer becomes subject to falling into the Raurava hell— thus, according to the specific location on the *liṅga*.

By means of the discernment of whether the *liṅga* is to be grasped or not grasped according to the specific measure of its dimensions such as cutting (*cheda*) and so forth; and because the abandonment of life preceded by the emaciation of the body— performed for the sake of the *liṅga*, for the sake of the Guru, for the sake of Śiva’s conduct, for the sake of a spy (*cara*), or for the sake of divine grace— is prescribed by rule and leads to the attainment of identity with Śiva (*śivasāmarasya*).
The renunciation of life must be performed— without the means of weapons and the like— by first relinquishing food,
by withering the body through emaciation,
and by following the observances of Śaiva dharma, such as the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣa beads.
And from this hearing [of the scripture], it is established that the wearing of the *liṅga* must necessarily be performed by Vīraśaivas who seek liberation.
This wearing of the *liṅga* was also approved by the venerable Vedavyāsa;
thus, the author of the *Kriyāsāra* has demonstrated its consistency with the meaning of his sūtras:
"And for one who is devoted to that [liṅga], liberation is ordained here through instruction."
For those who are established in that are indeed established in Brahman; they are truly the ones qualified for liberation.
Therefore, that which was stated regarding "injunction" would be false;
for Brahman is the cause of the world and is indeed to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation.
By the statement "This is not the Self," there is the relinquishing of the body of Śiva;
"relinquishing" (varaṇa) means assuming that [divine] form according to the path of ritual injunction (vidhi).
The wearing [of the mark] is established by the statement "liṅgāṅga... and so forth for those solely intent on the path to liberation, and by the statement "amṛtasya... [it is established].
Only those humans devoted to that [Truth], who take delight in being beyond the castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśrama),
have their wearing of the insignia (liṅgadhāraṇa) firmly established by such statements as "Om" and so forth.
"That merit which is the means to liberation should be held within the lotus of the heart. Thus [it is said].

Likewise, in the sūtra beginning with "Because of the designation of the meters" (Chandobhidhānāt), it is stated: "The fixing of the mind and its concentration are in the middle of the lotus of the heart. Similarly, in the sūtra beginning with "On account of the marks of the individual soul and the chief vital breath" (Jīvamukhyaprāṇaliṅgāt), it begins: "I am that which is designated by the term 'consciousness,' the lotus of the heart, which is exceedingly difficult to attain."
"Therefore, the Brahman-linga, which is higher than the highest and superior even to the vital breath (prāṇa),

because from it the supreme good arises, should be held in the heart-lotus by one seeking liberation; that is the Prāṇa-linga"— thus it is established at the end of the first section of the first chapter.
In the *Kriyāsāra*, regarding the aphorism "Because liberation is taught for one who is intent upon That," the intended meaning of the statements composed in the form of *kārikās* is as follows:

in the section on the "Contemplation" (*īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*), which introduces the refutation of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause, it is stated that "It [the Self] contemplated" (*tadaikṣata*).

If it is argued that the statement "May I be many, may I procreate" is a figurative expression applied to the *pradhāna*—just as one says "the bank desires to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*) when the bank is about to collapse—[we reply: no, because [the scripture] speaks of the agent of seeing, saying:
"He is this subtle essence; all this has that as its self; That is Truth; He..."

It is because of the conventional usage of the word "self" (*ātman*) [in the sense of "I"]. Nor should it be argued that the word "self" is also used figuratively— just as when a king says, "Bhadrasena is my self," the word "self" refers to his general Bhadrasena— because for one who is devoted to that [Self], [the usage is primary].

"Because of the teaching of liberation for one who is intent upon that. Having thus explained the meaning of this sūtra—namely, that liberation is taught for one who is intent upon that [Brahman] denoted by the word "Self," as the Śruti says: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united"—it follows that the cause of the world is to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation, and that such meditation culminates in being intent upon Brahman.

And that [attainment] consists in the choosing of Śiva; for thus says the Śruti: "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Only he whom this Self chooses, by him is He attained; to him this Self reveals His own form. And that revealing of Śiva occurs by way of the path prescribed in the injunctions.

The wearing of that [liṅga]— and that liṅga is declared to be the body of Śiva, and it is remembered as the Aghora-body— is the wearing of the liṅga in accordance with such corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*). The non-dual Śiva is the fourth state; He alone is to be meditated upon, He alone is to be worshipped, and through meditation on Him, they become liberated. [The Fourth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O glorious Guru, having heard you fully describe the majesty of wearing the *liṅga* in all its detail, I am pervaded with joy.
Thereafter, that which is to be described shall be explained by me in detail;
listen, O King, as I today clearly proclaim the majesty of the mobile [creation].
An inquiry into the stainless reality consisting of consciousness, which resides in the heart at the end of the stream of beginningless devotion, is now commenced.

By means of the words of the Āgamas and Purāṇas, [He is revealed] as the consciousness situated in the center of the three maṇḍalas of consciousness within the hearts of the devotees of ancient times;

as the void-liṅga (śūnyaliṅga) residing within the praṇava of consciousness at the heart of the lotus; as the partless liṅga (niṣkalaliṅga) and the liṅga of the praṇava; and as the one who initiates the liṅgas and so forth, possessing a form imagined for the sake of the worship of those devoted to the formless and attributeless (nirguṇa-nirākāra), yet encompassing the entire phenomenal world of sentient and insentient beings.

The excellence of the stainless, mobile reality (*jaṅgamatattva*), which is endowed with the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the power of consciousness that has mastered the creation of [divine] forms, is now established; for it is said: "Thereafter, within the lotus of the heart of one who has been devoted from time immemorial..."
He resides in the center of the seat of the Praṇava, which is endowed with the three circles of consciousness.
Here, the stainless one, whose nature is the *praṇava*, is described;
that which is called "staining" (*rañjana*) has been cast off—that which is the manifestation of the delusion of *māyā*.
By means of that established intrinsic nature, he indeed becomes stainless;
this is declared to be his supportless intrinsic nature.
The four Vedas are his womb, and the Purāṇa is his middle;
all the yogis and sages are supported by his moving feet.
Within his body are all fourteen worlds:
one should know that *atala* is in his feet, and likewise *vitala* is above the feet.
Sutala is to be known in the shanks; Mahātala is in the region of the knees;
Talātala is in the thighs; and Rasātala is in the secret place.
The netherworld (pātāla) is said to be at the waistband, and the seven worlds are thus described:
the world of the earth (bhūrloka) is in the middle of the navel, while the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka) is in his belly.
The world of the gods (Svarloka) is in the heart, Janaloka is situated in the head;
Tapoloka is in the palate, and Satyaloka is on the forehead.
The great world is upon his head; fourteen [worlds] are said to be there.
The cosmic egg is his crown; hear that the sky is his face.
His arms are all the directions, his two eyes are the moon and the sun,
his body is the form of space, and the netherworld is his lotus-feet.
The void-linga is situated in the palm of the hand; the cloud and all matted locks are auspicious;
the moonlight and the sacred ash, as well as all the gods, consist of action.
The stars are flowers, the Rudrākṣas are the principal mountain ranges,
the ocean is the water-vessel, and the patched garment is this world composed of creation.
The earth is his seat, and day and night are his caves and monasteries;
O Dear One, the six seasons are the six sacred sites, possessing the good fortune of knowledge of the three times.
The remainder is his waist-thread; the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) consists of speech. Mount Meru is the staff, the quality is the thread, and his lineage shall be the family of Śiva.
The Vanaspati tree is his body hair; thus, O Pārvatī, these have been proclaimed as his embodied form.
Thus, according to the collection of scriptural statements,

in the center of the seat of the *praṇava*, which is endowed with three circles of consciousness (*cinmaṇḍala*) situated in the rear part of the hearts of those who have been devoted since beginningless time,
there resides He who is designated by the term "the stainless mobile one" (*nirañjana-jaṅgama*), because He seeks to dispel the expansion of *māyā*.
This is because he has demonstrated the sequence for joining all categories of objects in accordance with the two natures— the formless and the formed— and because,
upon careful consideration of the very words spoken in the treatise titled *Sṛṣṭyuddharaṇa*, which describes the ten-limbed creation mentioned in the section on ritual action (*kriyākāṇḍa*).

From Brahman, whose nature is consciousness (citsvarūpa) and who is designated as the "Untainted Moving One" (nirañjana-jaṅgama)— a term for the beginningless devotee situated within the heart-center of those for whom Nirguṇa-Brahman is another synonym— arises the Nirguṇa Reality (nirguṇatattva) designated as the "Void Linga" (śūnyaliṅga);
from that [arises] the Nirguṇa Reality designated as the "Partless Linga" (niṣkalaliṅga).

From that [arises] the Nirguṇa Tattva, which is designated as the Great Liṅga whose nature is light and whose form is an indivisible sphere consisting of the *cinnāda*, the *acidbindu*, and the *citkalā*;
from that [arises] the Nirguṇa Tattva, which is designated as the *praṇava-liṅga* of speech known as the *anāhata-nāda*.

Therefore, [one should meditate upon] the reality of the attributeless Śiva (nirguṇa-śivatattva), which is characterized by the five attributes of being, consciousness, bliss, eternity, and omnipresence; which is entered by the six limbs and the ten states; and which is to be meditated upon by the host of lords of the Pramathas, headed by Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Vīrabhadra, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Gajakarṇa, Reṇuka, Dāruka, and others.
Therefore, [He is] the totality consisting of the five *sādākhyas*, the five *kalās*, the five *śaktis*, the five mantras, and the five *brahmans*;
He is the one who transcends all parts (*niṣkalātmaka*), and is worshipped by the assembly of the foremost among yogins, such as Sanaka, Sananda, Sanatkumāra, Sanatsujāta, and others.

Of the reality of Sadāśiva— who is worthy of worship by the assembly of great ṛṣis such as Vasiṣṭha, Agastya, Nārada, Bharadvāja, Atri, Gautama, Bhṛgu, Kaṇva, and Dadhīci— and who is distinguished by his five faces beginning with Sadyojāta; therein,
because the powers of consciousness (cicchakti) and so forth are formless, [the distinction applies] to those two who possess them.

Since the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) consist of qualities that bring about the possession of form for Sadāśiva and Mūrta-Sadākhya, who are otherwise partless (*niṣkala*), it follows that those associated with them—namely Mūrta-Kartṛ, Karma, and Sadākhya—belong to the category of the "with-parts" (*sakala*). Thus, it is established that the principle of Sadāśiva possesses both aspects: being both with-parts and partless (*sakalaniṣkala*).

Therefore, [salutation] to the Three-eyed One, who is accompanied by Umā, who resembles pure crystal, whose hands hold the deer, the axe, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and who is the initiator of the twenty-five playful forms (līlāmūrti) ending with the great form of the Holder of the Moon (Somadhārī).

Of the principle of Maheśvara, who is worshipped by all the gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; of Rudra, who is the controller of the eleven Rudras and whose manifestation consists of the group known as Bhava, Mṛḍa, and Hara; and of Him who is distinguished by the ten incarnations beginning with the Fish and the Tortoise.

Of Nārāyaṇa, the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha, whose four arms are resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus; who is praised by tens of millions of Vaiṣṇavas;
and [of the one] from whom [proceeds] the four-faced [Brahmā], the ruler of the nine Brahmās, who dwells in Satyaloka accompanied by Sarasvatī.

From that Brahman, through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) of the five elements, there arises the manifold of sentient beings— consisting of those born from eggs, sweat, sprouts, and wombs— as well as the manifold of insentient things, such as mountains, rivers, stones, and so forth.

Since it is heard that the stainless, moving [deity] is the cause of the origin of all reality, his status as the supreme of all and his being attainable by the Vīraśaiva seekers of liberation are understood.

If it is asked: "How can the creation and the state of being created of the stainless moving [liṅga], the void-liṅga, the partless liṅga, and so forth—extending up to the Śiva-tattva, which are devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), partless (niravayava), and all-pervading (vyāpaka)—be logically consistent? it is replied:

As for the statement that the production of partless entities—such as the mobile reality (*jaṅgamatattva*) and the partless lingas of emptiness (*śūnyaliṅga*)—is untenable, that is extremely weak. [For it is said:
"The venerable Mahānāda is devoted, self-luminous, and non-dual."
He who is proclaimed as Brahman by those who know the true meaning of the Śiva-tattva.
Therefore, he, the stainless moving one, manifested himself;
from his crest, the Linga of the Void, the cause of the universe, was born.
From that partless liṅga, the Great Liṅga (Mahāliṅga) arose spontaneously;
from that, the Praṇava-liṅga was born, intent upon creation.
From this [Prakṛti] arose the principle of Śiva, and from that, Sādākhya;
from that Maheśvara was born, and from him Rudra emerged.
From him Janārdana was born; from him the Grandfather (Brahmā) was born;
and from the Grandfather this entire world, both moving and unmoving, came into being.
Thus,

in accordance with the statement found in the work titled *Sṛṣṭyuddharaṇa*, which summarizes the ten limbs [of initiation] from the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas: "From the partless, stainless mobile [deity], [the partless [mantras are extracted]]."

The production of the Śūnya-linga and other such forms must necessarily be accepted on the strength of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, even animal sacrifices and the like would constitute acts of violence (*hiṃsā*). For instance, regarding the eleven portions of the sacrificial animal, it is stated:
"He cuts these twice: the heart, the tongue, the breast, the liver, the kidneys, the left foreleg, and both sides."

If there are eleven portions to be cut, including the third from the rectum (*gudatṛtīya*), how could there be non-violence (*ahiṃsā*)? However, according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "The initiated one should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," it is said that animals were created by the Self-existent One (*Svayambhū*) himself for the sake of sacrifice; for sacrifice leads to the prosperity of all.

Therefore, by the Smṛti text, "In a sacrifice, killing is non-killing," he accepts its status as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). For this very reason, having established that in the inference— "The violence occurring within a ritual (*kratu*) does not bring about demerit because it is violence,
like violence outside of a ritual"— the property of being prohibited (*niṣiddhatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*), [he refutes] the reason (*hetu*).
Logicians maintain that because [the reason] is *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition), it indicates deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and thus fails to prove the probandum (*sādhya*).

For this very reason, we observe that practices such as ritual impurity (*āśauca*), which are performed by all people, are accepted by all cultured persons (*śiṣṭa*) despite being based solely on verbal authority (*vacana-mātra-pramāṇaka*) without any underlying logic (*yukti*). Therefore...

The inference that "the hell-guardian is pure because he is a part of a living being, like a conch shell" has been accepted by logicians as being sublated by the force of the scriptural statement: "Having touched a human corpse or a bone with marrow, one should enter the water with one's clothes on."

Since it is established that conch shells are purifying while human bones are impure, the authoritative words of the learned (*abhiyukta*) serve as our ultimate refuge; by the force of those very words alone,
it is determined that conch shells are purifying and human bones are impure.
Therefore, the notion that one must provide logical reasoning regarding a matter that is to be understood through the words of a more authoritative source is merely a groundless conceit.

If this were so, then since the moon's being the size of a thumb-span is not experienced by all people, it would follow that those who propound the lunar orb to be eighty-eight thousand *yojanas* in extent [would be correct] because their view is supported by reasoning.
Otherwise, the statements of the *jyotiḥśāstra* and other sciences would lack authority. Therefore, even in this case,
regarding the production of the partless from the partless,
the very words of the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas composed by the supremely authoritative Paraśiva serve as the proof.

Furthermore, because the self (*ātman*) is partless and space (*ākāśa*) is also partless, there could be no origination of the latter from it. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion, for it would result in a contradiction with the scriptural text: "From this very self, space was produced. Moreover, sound does not originate from space.

It may be so. Therefore, by the force of such reasoning, one must necessarily admit the production of partless, stainless, and mobile entities—such as the Śūnya-liṅga and others—from that which is itself partless. Consequently, [the Lord] transcends all principles (tattvas).

The stainless *jaṅgama* alone is that which is to be attained by the liberated; therefore, he alone is to be served by all. In the *Nandipurāṇa*: "Because he is devoid of the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and because he maintains the singular form of innate awakening (*nijabodha*), having himself become the Self (*svayaṃbhū*), he moves about; thus he is remembered as *cara*."
In the Pārameśvara [Tantra],
those who are liberated from the three impurities, devoted to knowledge and realized wisdom, and endowed with firm dispassion— those steadfast ones are the Śiva-yogins.
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"One who is endowed with the knowledge of his own true nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*), whose forms of 'I-ness' and 'mine-ness' have been destroyed,
and who moves about having himself become the Self— such a one is designated as a *cara*."
Having concealed the moon of his eye on the forehead and having closed [the other],
the Supreme Lord moves about, sporting in his left side.
O Maheśānī, in the arising of the heroes, I alone, assuming a mobile form,
wander upon the surface of the earth for the sake of bestowing grace upon my devotees.

Because of the similarity in their hands, feet, and other limbs, the unwise do not recognize those who possess the form of Rudra as being truly divine, but instead imagine them to be merely ordinary mortals.
O child, one should wear the patched garment called equanimity, the ash-bag called patience,
the water-pot of compassion, and the beautiful staff of knowledge.
He begs for the alms-bowl of dispassion and the alms of devotion; his patched garment is his water-pot, his staff is his mendicant’s bowl, and his ashes are his leather bag.
These are the five great mudrās and the characteristics of mobile beings.

By the force of such various statements as these, [the state belongs] to the stainless wandering ascetic (nirañjana-jaṅgama), who is distinguished by the fivefold conduct (pañcācāra) and the eight enclosures (aṣṭāvaraṇa), and who is endowed with the five inner and outer mudrās known as the necklace (kaṇṭha), water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), staff (daṇḍa), bowl (pātra), and ash-bag (bhasmabhastrikā).
The non-difference of the "moving" (cara)—meaning the sentient being who possesses the knowledge and action of qualified non-duality—is accepted.
Therefore, the "moving" one alone is the most excellent of all;
[this is established] through such acts as seeing, touching, conversing with, worshipping, and serving his feet, his sacred water, and his grace.
Thus it is established that [this] is the means for attaining liberation.
[Thus,
from the venerable Tōṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the moving form of the beginningless and stainless Aparā,
and who obtained the grace of the Śāmbhava Āgama ocean churned by him— resulting in the division of one hundred and one unsurpassed *sthala*s...]
[This is] the [work] composed by the eminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows the mass of bliss arising from tasting the nectar of the awakening to that reality,
[and which describes] the seizure of the seven constituents of the final ocean-kingdom of the enemy of the sole hero whose body was the tumultuous roar of ten million Yaḍava Murāris...

In the instruction of Basava, the joy of the heart of Mallāmbā— the lawful consort of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth and the full moon to the milky ocean of the lineage of Keladi Sadāśivarāya Nāyaka, the preceptor who established the doctrine of Śiva-purified Advaita Vedānta— [who was] like the bull of Dharma.

[The Fifth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O Guru, having heard this excellence of the moving world, which causes extreme joy,
my heart has become completely filled with the flavor of wonder.
That which is to be described hereafter, proclaim that to me today;
listen, O Indra among kings, as I speak of the supreme greatness of the water from the feet.

In all the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Itihāsas, the grace of Śiva is established as the supreme means for attaining the highest good because it is served by the hosts of gods and sages; likewise, the water from Śiva’s feet is likewise established as the means for attaining all auspicious goals through the removal of every impurity.
For thus it is:
whatever sacred fords and auspicious, merit-bestowing rivers exist upon the earth, they are eternally established within my feet; therefore, that water from my feet should be worn [as an amulet].
In the *Śivarahasya*, it is said: "The meritorious water from my feet should always be worn by those who have taken refuge in me;
they should be known as three-eyed and ten-armed, possessing prowess equal to mine."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "O beloved, one should daily drink the consecrated water every morning;
it is the remedy for colic, leprosy, epilepsy, fever, and other ailments."
O Sage, the great holy site Himodaka, the Gaṅgā, and the river Yamunā are always present within the water used for washing the feet of Śambhu.
Even those who have approached women who should not be approached and those who delight in sinful conduct become purified instantly by bearing the water from the lotus feet of Śiva.
Whoever carries the water used for washing the feet of Śiva in his linga-form,
it washes away their sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Those auspicious regions such as Kurukṣetra and Naimiṣa do not equal even a sixteenth part of the water from the foot-tirtha."
The auspicious water from the feet of Śambhu destroys untimely death, annihilates all diseases, and pacifies all sins.
By wearing [this] upon one's head, one immediately attains that which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the purifier of all purifiers, and the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
Taking up with their shell-like hands the supreme water from the feet of the Destroyer of Cities, which removes the snare of bondage, the lords of the Gaṇas drank their fill as they desired.
If, after drinking the water from the feet of Śambhu, one sips water again out of delusion due to a suspicion of impurity, one should know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"O lotus-eyed one, having washed the feet of the deity with both hands,
one should sprinkle [the water] upon one's own head, as well as that of the guest and the guru."
In the *Śivarahasya*, it is said: "Those who have taken refuge in me should always carry the meritorious water of my grace.
They should be known as three-eyed and ten-armed, possessing prowess equal to mine."

Because the water from Śiva’s feet is prescribed with its specific ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) by such statements from the Bodhāyana-sūtra, the *Śivarahasya*, the *Āditya-purāṇa*, the *Skanda-purāṇa*, and other Purāṇas;
because it is the locus of all holy fords (*tīrtha*) situated upon the earth; and because it is the means for attaining identity of form (*sārūpya*) with Śiva.

Because it is the embodiment of the medicine that removes all diseases, because it removes all major and minor sins (*mahāpātaka* and *upapātaka*), and because it is served by the entire host of *pramatha* attendants, it is established that those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) should wear it upon their heads and drink it. Therefore, the water from the feet of Śiva must necessarily be used by those seeking liberation.
Is it not true that the water from the Sālagrāma stone especially removes sins;
it is prescribed as an expiation for sins committed since birth?
In the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*, it is said that one should daily drink the water from the feet (*pādodaka*) and eat the food offering (*naivedya*) of Hari;
for the food he has eaten, the water from his feet, and the water used for his flowers [are sacred].
The offerings to Śiva— leaves, flowers, fruits, and water— which are themselves ungraspable, bring about dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa in succession.

"Through contact with the *sālagrāma*, everything attains purity"—from such scriptural statements, one hears that the *nirmālya* (remnants) of Śiva and the water from his feet (*pādodaka*) are to be accepted only when accompanied by what has been offered to the *sālagrāma*. Therefore, the *nirmālya* and so forth should not be accepted at all on their own. Likewise:

A prohibition against accepting the water from the feet of Śiva alone is heard [in the scriptures]. For instance: "That which has been offered by means of a *sālagrāma* stone or other such objects to Śambhu, who is surrounded [by them], should always be consumed by the twice-born; they should also wear that water."
Food offered to Śiva that has been encircled by a *sālagrāma* stone or similar object must be rejected;
there is no doubt that one who consumes it must perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.

Otherwise, by such statements as "that water would be equal to meat" and "it would be the same as blood," it is heard that the water from the feet of Śiva alone is not to be accepted because it is established as a cause of sin; [this being so], [what need is there to mention] the water from the feet of Viṣṇu?
If it is argued that because it is heard [in scripture] as removing all sins, it is established that the water from the ablution of Śiva accompanied by a Śālagrāma stone is to be accepted,

whereas the water from the ablution of Śiva alone is unacceptably like blood and thus the water from Śiva’s feet (*śivapādodaka*) should not be accepted— [we reply: no, for regarding the water from Śiva’s feet alone, by Bodhāyana...
Because it establishes [the water] as something to be taken up. For instance:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the water from the feet of Mahādeva.
Having washed the feet of the Blessed One, one should fill a conch shell or a vessel [with that water]."

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should then consecrate [the water] with the mantra beginning "imaṃ me gaṅge yamune. If it is argued that the previously mentioned defect remains because the scriptures declare that the water from Viṣṇu’s feet is to be accepted, while the acceptance of water from Śiva’s feet alone is a cause for sin, we say no;

And when this has been firmly established by the words of many Purāṇas and Āgamas,

Since subordination is necessarily required, it follows—on the analogy of the *vrīhi* and *yava* [grain] options—that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the *Śatarudrīya-homa*. To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since it is improper to assume separate sentences when a single sentence is possible, and because an option is extremely improper as it is afflicted by the eight defects (*aṣṭadoṣa*), [the two texts] must be taken as a single sentence.
It must necessarily be admitted that only goat’s milk serves as the means for the oblation (*homa*). [Objection:

Since there is the scriptural injunction, "One should offer with wild sesame gruel (*jartila-yavāgvā*)," and since there is the censure, "Wild sesame and *gavīdhuka* seeds are indeed unfit for offering," how can a single coherent statement (*ekavākyatā*) be possible?

It must be stated that an injunction cannot be accepted merely by hearing the verbal suffix (liṅ), but rather through a consideration of whether the matter has already been established or not. For this very reason, in the case of "he sacrifices in a low voice between [the two offerings]," the suffix *liṭ* is transformed into *leṭ*.

Having accepted their injunctive character, [one considers] those injunctions heard as direct Vedic commands (*pratyakṣavidhi*), such as: "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice for the sake of avoiding redundancy; Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to in a low voice for the sake of avoiding redundancy; Agniṣṭoma is to be sacrificed to in a low voice for the sake of avoiding redundancy."
The status of being a restatement has been accepted for all three as well.

For this very reason, in the *Bhāmatī* commentary on the *Samanvaya-sūtra* of the *Uttara-tantra*, the teacher Vācaspati Miśra [explains] the suffix *-tavya* in the passage "it is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon,

The capacity to enjoin [the means] is like that of the suffix -tavya in "yājatavya"; for,

just as the direct perception of the notes *ṣaḍja* and so forth results from the study of the science of music (*gāndharva-śāstra*), it is established that hearing and the other [means] alone are the instruments for direct perception, while other methods are excluded therein.
It is accepted that this is because there is no possibility of such an application.

Similarly, in this case, even the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the statement "one should offer with wild sesame gruel" must be accepted as being intended for the purpose of praising [the prescribed act]. Furthermore, the statement regarding its not being a valid oblation (*anāhuti*) does not aim at censuring the enjoined matter; rather, it serves to praise the nearby offering of goat's milk by way of censuring other alternatives.
It has excellence as its primary purpose. For this very reason, Vācaspatimiśra stated:
"Indeed, when Somaśarman is the subject under discussion, the description of his qualities does not imply that Viṣṇuśarman possesses those same qualities."
For this very reason, at the beginning of the *Harivaṃśa*,

when it was necessary to offer praise to the *Harivaṃśa*— which consists solely of discourse concerning Viṣṇu— with the words, "We purify our speech, which has become dusty from wandering through the wilderness of talk with the wicked, by means of the Gaṅgā that is the conversation about the deeds of Śauri," there occurs in the *Mahābhārata* a censure of its being like a wilderness of talk with the wicked.

From the merit of studying the *Bhārata*, one studies even a single quarter-verse; through the gift of faith, all sins are purified without remainder. He caused the Vedas, with the *Mahābhārata* as the fifth, to be taught: the four Vedas on one side and the *Bhārata* alone on the other. It was placed upon a scale by the celestial sages who had assembled there.

Because of the contradiction with many statements establishing the excellence of the *Bhārata*—such as: "In its greatness and its weight, it is even greater than that; because of its greatness and its weightiness, it is called the *Mahābhārata*"—the passage [in question] is intended as a praise of the *Harivaṃśa*, and not as a censure of the *Bhārata*. By that same logic, it applies here as well.
The censure of the water from Śiva’s feet—
contrary to the numerous statements in the Bodhāyana Sūtras and their followers— is intended to praise the water of the Śālagrāma stone,
rather than being solely intended as a censure of the water from Śiva’s feet; such is the water from Śiva’s feet.
It is established that this must be accepted by those seekers of liberation who follow the Vedic path.

Now, one might object: since within the collection of scriptural passages establishing the excellence of receiving and drinking the water from Śiva’s feet (*śivapādodaka*), we do not hear any statements establishing the excellence of the water from the feet of the Guru’s attendants (*gurucara*) in the same way, it follows that, in the midst of those [passages], it is only the water from Śiva’s feet that is [intended] with its superiority emphasized and supported by reasoning.

Regarding the statement "it is to be accepted": how can there be such acceptance on the grounds of similarity between the water from the feet of the Guru’s attendants (*gurucara*) and [the water from the feet of the Guru himself], given that it is not heard in scripture that the Guru’s feet are equal to Śiva? If this is asked, the answer is no; for we see in many scriptural passages the teaching that the Guru’s attendants are non-different from Śiva. To illustrate: [The text continues with citations.]
In the *Kiraṇāgama*, one should know that the Guru, the Lord, and the Living Liṅga (jaṅgama) are Being-Consciousness-Bliss;
one should constantly contemplate their perfect grace as being identical with one's own self-nature.
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"Śiva alone is the manifest Lord who bestows grace upon all;
existing as the soul of the Guru, the Jaṅgama, and the Liṅga, he grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
In the *Śivarahasya*, it is taught that the *liṅga* has three forms: the mobile *liṅga* is the *prāṇaliṅga*;
the teacher (*guru*) is declared to be the *bhāvaliṅga*. These three are said to be one.
Salutations to you, the moving soul, that supreme Lord who, for the benefit of the entire world, wanders in the form of a guest.
Since the non-difference between the Guru and Śiva is established by such Purāṇic statements,
it is proven that the water from the feet of the Guru’s attendant (carapāda) is likewise fit to be received, just like the water from the feet of Śiva.
The manner of grasping that [mantra] is as follows; in the *Pārameśvara-tantra*: "Having bowed once more to what is within oneself, one should perform the washing of the feet.
First, one should worship [it] in due order with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth."
One should worship again with perfumes and flowers, and then rinse [the vessel].
One should drink the rinsed water, and having drunk it, one should hold it upon the head.
One should not let a drop fall below the water used for washing the feet;
one should contemplate Rudra upon the big toe and remember Śaṅkara upon the index finger.
One should worship Mahādeva on the middle finger, Tryambaka on the ring finger, Īśāna on the little finger, and Kapardin on the top of the foot.
Having meditated upon five faces beneath the feet, Rudra and Bharga at the two ankles, and everything as consisting of the *liṅga*, one's feet become possessors of the moving *liṅga*.

By means of such a collection of statements, after meditating upon the various specific forms of Śiva— such as Rudra and others— as non-different from the individual parts of the feet and toes of the Guru and the Caru, one should, preceded by worship with the sixteen offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra), proceed to receive the water from their feet.

Having carefully collected the water from the foot-washing in a single vessel and having worshipped it with perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and other offerings, one should [offer] that water from the single vessel to those initiated into Vīraśaivism, in accordance with the tradition of the *pramatha*s headed by the ancient Lord Basava.
The devotees of Maheśvara should drink [the offering] one by one in sequence, saying "Ṛtam" and "Satyam.

In that regard, there is no fault of being left-over (ucchiṣṭa), according to the statement in the Āpastamba-sūtra: "Just as by drinking soma-juice they do not become impure from soma," [this applies] when many officiating priests [partake] in a single [vessel].
Since the Soma juice contained in a specific vessel in the shape of a *camasa* is drunk in turn [by all], there is no fault of being "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*) in that case.
But is it not said: "One should not eat what is stale, nor what is leftover"?
Since the prohibition of accepting leavings is heard in such statements as "having rendered [the food] useless," it must be stated that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of prohibition.

Because a prohibition is preceded by a prior possibility (*prasakti*), and because a prohibition is impossible where there is no possibility, that possibility must necessarily be stated. And that possibility may be either worldly or Vedic.

Thus, it exists in both ways. In that regard, if it is worldly (*laukikī*), it culminates in the absolute cessation of the prohibited act, as in "one should not drink liquor" and so forth. If it is scriptural (*vaidikī*) and concerns a contingent application (*prasakti*), it does not culminate in a prohibition, as for example: "At the *atirātra* sacrifice, one takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup."
"Just as one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* [sacrifice], so too here,

since the possibility of leaving a remnant (*ucchiṣṭa*) is based on a scriptural injunction and does not exist in common worldly practice, how can there be a conclusion in the form of absolute cessation?"

Therefore, an option (*vikalpa*) must be accepted. If it is argued that this is improper because it is vitiated by the eight faults (*aṣṭadoṣa*), we say no; for when a scriptural injunction applies to a single object in the absence of a relationship between general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), an option is indeed appropriate, as in the case of [the rules regarding] the taking up or not taking up [of the *camasa*]. This is due to the relationship between general and particular.

When both the application (*prasakti*) and its negation (*pratiṣedha*) exist, there is no alternative option (*vikalpa*), because of the absence of a [mere] negation. This is as in the case: "In the *yajati* sacrifices one performs the *ye yajāmahe*; not in the *anuyāja* sacrifices. In the statement "one does not become impure by means of Soma," the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), not the sense of prohibition (*niṣedha*); so it is here as well.

Even in the case of partaking of the water used for washing the feet (*pādodaka*), the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—which removes the defect of being "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*)—and not the sense of prohibition (*niṣedha*). Therefore, it is established that the *pādodaka* must always be received, one after another in turn, in a single vessel by all seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*), including Vīraśaivas. By this very [rule]...

And it should be understood, on the basis of the strength of many authoritative traditions rooted in scriptural evidence, that there is no fault of consuming leftovers when receiving [food] out of faith according to the rule; thus, everything is consistent.

[Thus ends the section on] the six *sthānas*, distinguished by one hundred and one unsurpassed divisions (*sthala-bheda*) produced from churning the ocean of the *Nāgabha* scriptures, obtained through the grace of the venerable Toṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the beginningless, stainless, and mobile *Aparā*.

[This work] was composed by the eminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows the mass of bliss arising from tasting the nectar of the awakening to the reality of that [Lord], [and which is dedicated to] the pure Vaidya...
[of the Lord of the Western Ocean, who seized the seven constituents of the enemy of the solitary hero Kolāhalaikāṅgi at Yaḍavamurārikoṭe].

therefore, describe to me whatever else is worthy for my ears to hear.
Having reflected with reason according to the views of the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, O protector of the earth, establish this in your mind; it is said that the highest state is serenity.
By the virtuous, who seek the supreme human goal consisting of liberation, whose intellects have been purified by the ripening of the merit accumulated over many previous births,
and who are preeminent in the performance of the traditional practices of all the learned;
The acceptance of Śiva’s grace must be performed. For it is heard in the Jābāla recension:
"They eat what has been eaten by Rudra; they drink what has been drunk by Rudra; they smell what has been smelled by Rudra.
Therefore, Brahmins with tranquil minds consume only the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering)."
Likewise, in the Skanda-purāṇa, it is said: "The disciplined and tranquil ones eat only what has been eaten by Rudra;
they smell only what has been smelled by him, and they drink only what has been drunk by him."
Thus is the corroborative statement, which has the same meaning as the Śruti:
"In this way, one who eats what is forbidden by the three Guṇas, or eats what has not been offered to Śiva—that sin he shall eat;
he shall eat worms, he shall eat filth, he shall eat evil, he shall go downward, downward."
"Go.

Its meaning is as follows: he who has three cows, that is, three eyes, is *trigu*—the "three-eyed one" (*trinetra*). By him, the "three-fold one" (*triguṇa*), it was *psātam*, meaning eaten or appropriated; for the root *psā* means "to eat."

The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*). "One should eat" means one should consume. If one should eat—that is, consume—what is offered by Śiva, [but is actually] by means of evil (*pāpmanā*), that is, by means of sin (*pāpena*), then one would experience (*bhuṅkṣva*) or consume (*bhuñjīyāt*) great transgression (*enaḥ*, *mahāpāpam*). One would experience or consume misfortune (*agham*), that is, a minor offense (*upapātakam*). There is frequent irregularity (*vyatyayo bahulam*) [in the application of these forms].

According to the rule "mityanuśāsana," there is an interchange of the *lakāra* (tense marker) and person (*puruṣa*) in Vedic usage; the same applies hereafter. Because of the repetition of the sentence "go down, go down," it is intended to express going downwards repeatedly.
Likewise, it is heard in the Śatarudrīya:
"Whatever [sacrifice] Manu, our father, performed with faith and devotion—may we attain that under your guidance, O Rudra."
The meaning of this is as follows: O Rudra, I have worshipped you with that mantra characterized by five syllables which is the *manu* among your progeny produced through your creative guidance.
Since I was born from eating the middle *piṇḍa*, which is of the nature of Rudra’s grace, therefore you are my father.
Therefore, may I attain your grace; by that, may I obtain well-being characterized by heaven and the like, as well as happiness, and may I reach the Supreme Self.
Likewise, it is heard in both the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda:
"O Rudra, with these most auspicious [weapons] taken up by you... may a hundred medicines come to me."

The meaning of this Vedic passage is as follows: "O Rudra, through these most peaceful (*śantama*) favors granted by you—consisting of water for the feet, flowers, and food—which are primarily medicinal remedies (*bheṣaja*), may I attain a hundred [years]; that is, may I reach a lifespan of a hundred years. Therefore...
The grace of Śiva is to be cultivated according to tradition by all refined seekers of liberation.

But surely, in many Smṛtis, Āgamas, and Purāṇas, the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) are censured; for instance, in the Vāsiṣṭha-saṃhitā: "Whatever substance has been offered, whether it be a flower or even a fruit..."

"One should not touch, offer, or step over the remains of an offering (*nirmālya*). Why?
Because the *nirmālya* of all the gods is traditionally held to be impure."
Also in the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa: "One should not even use the light of a lamp offered to Me."
In the twenty-fifth chapter, the *Jīrṇoddhāra-paṭala*, of the *Pāñcarātra-saṃhitā*,
that which is irreproachable and prescribed for the worship of the Deity—
That very same thing, once subsequently defiled, is censured as "nirmālya" (the remains of an offering).
"My food offering, water for the feet, flower, and leaf are unworthy [of you]," he said.

And in the *Manusmṛti*: "One should avoid the food of a Śūdra, the food of one in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), food offered as a sacrificial oblation (*naivedya*), food from a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), the food of outcasts (*patita*), food from a communal gathering, and the food of a king. Thus it is said.
In the Śiva Purāṇa it is said: "There is fault in stepping over the remains of offerings (nirmālya), and especially so in wearing them."
Likewise, in the *Śivarahasya* it is also said:

"One should especially avoid both the *nirmālya* (remnants of worship) and the *nivedya* (food offerings). The *nirmālya* used by Rudra is not so [to be treated] as that which has been used by other deities."
The food offering (naivedya) has been consumed by Viṣṇu, and the nectar (amṛta) by the other deities;
having consumed the remains of the offering (nirmālya) and the food offering (nivedya), one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

By this collection of statements beginning with "iti," the unfitness for touching, wearing, eating, and so forth of both types known as *nirmālya* and *naivedya*—those consumed by Śiva and those consumed by Viṣṇu—is established. Furthermore, the fact that the *nirmālya* of Śiva specifically must not be accepted is clearly demonstrated. For instance, in the *Hemādri*:

In the section on expiations (Prāyaścittakāṇḍa), Devala states: "A Brahmin should never eat food offered to Śambhu, nor the water from his sacred site (tīrtha), nor even a mere vegetable; having eaten [any of these], he should perform the Kṛcchra penance."

"In the *Mārkaṇḍeya* and the *Śiva*, it is stated: 'If a twice-born man, out of ignorance, eats food that has been offered to each deity individually [without first offering it to Śiva], he must then perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.'"
In the Kālikāpurāṇa:
"Having touched the remains of Rudra's offerings (nirmālya), one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Those who consume the remains of Śiva’s offerings (nirmālya), those who step over the remains of Śiva’s offerings,
and those who give away the remains of Śiva’s offerings— their touch does not bestow merit."
Out of greed, one should not wear the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of Śambhu, nor should one eat them;
nor, O Nārada, should one even touch them with the foot or step over them.
If a person worships a linga other than a Jyotirlinga,
he incurs the Taptakṛcchra penance by consuming its food offerings and floral remains.

If it is argued that the unacceptability of the *nirmālya* of Śiva is established through this application of many conflicting authorities, we say no; for here there exist scriptural and *purāṇic* statements concerning both the injunction for accepting the *nirmālya* and the prohibition of it.

Since it would be improper to accept invalidity when the contingency of invalidity arises from mutual contradiction, the validity of both must be established by postulating a distinction between their respective objects. And that distinction is not merely logical, but is rooted in the Āgamas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas. To this effect are the scriptural statements:
It is stated in the Śaiva Tantra that *nirmālya* (remnants of worship) is of six kinds:

the property of the deity (*devasva*), the substance belonging to the deity (*devatā-dravya*), the food offering (*naivedya*) that has been presented, the substance for Caṇḍa (*caṇḍa-dravya*), and *nirmālya* [itself]; thus *nirmālya* becomes sixfold.

The property of a deity belonging to a village, a field, and so forth; the substance of a deity such as a cloth and the like; the offering intended for that deity; and what has been offered as the leavings of the deity.
"That fierce substance (caṇḍadravya) which was offered [to Caṇḍeśvara] is discarded outside as *nirmālya*;
however, even the *nirmālya* remaining on the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is discarded once the deity has been dismissed. Thus it is said.

The Piṇḍikā-pīṭha (the pedestal-base); therefore, the learned unanimously accept that whatever is situated upon the pedestal, such as sacred bathing sites (*puṇyatīrtha*) and so forth, is *nirmālya* even after the dismissal of the deity (*devavisarjana*). Here, the term *nirmālya* refers generally to any substance related to the deity, and specifically to its particular [manifestation] outside.

And it proceeds in the sixth division, which is of the nature of being impelled. Therefore, Śiva’s *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) is specifically not to be accepted by the learned in any way whatsoever. Herein it is investigated: why is Śiva’s *nirmālya* unfit for consumption? Is it because it is prohibited by the *Śruti*, or because it is prohibited by the *Smṛti*, the *Purāṇas*, and the *Āgamas*?

Nor is it due to the absence of an injunction; for the first [alternative] is not correct, as no scriptural prohibition is seen stating that the grace of Śiva should not be accepted. On the contrary, in the previously cited scriptures, the acceptance of Śiva’s *nirmālya* is established as necessary by way of its excellence. Nor is it the second [alternative], because of the *smṛti*.

For it must be postulated that the prohibition applies specifically to those who lack the qualification [for initiation], lest one have to resort to the invalidation of numerous scriptural statements whose purpose is to demonstrate that the acceptance of grace (*prasāda*) must necessarily be undertaken. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, [regarding the rule]: "The remains of the garland (*nirmālya*)."

O Rudra, with these most auspicious medicines of yours, may I attain a hundred years of life. Drive far away from us hatred, drive away distress, and scatter our maladies in all directions.

In order to explain this very meaning, the following words of Vyāsa are found in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, within the *Śaiva Saṃhitā* during the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini: "I shall now respectfully declare the hidden meaning of this *Ṛk* hymn."
O Rudra, having eaten with you, he respectfully maintains [the food] by means of these [vows].
By means of these most peaceful and most blissful [teachings] which have been bestowed and propitiated,
they serve as medicines and remedies for the disease known as saṃsāra.
O Lord, through these hundred months of such exceedingly pure blessings granted by You— which are the remedies for saṃsāra as declared because they are its very opposite— [I have been purified].
For a hundred years,
protect without fail and without deviation your own exalted Vīraśaiva devotees together with yourself.
Apply yourself to this [path], being free from hatred for us and devoid of egoism; being free from distress, free from sin and evil, and endowed with devotion, be one who is free from disease.
"O Treasure of Compassion, may he likewise become free from all spreading diseases. Thus it is said.
In the Yajurveda, it is said: "By means of the Rudra [mantra], food becomes nectar; indeed, the gods desire to eat, and the Vedas desire [it as well]. Thus.

The meaning of this is as follows: by Rudra, the Supreme Lord, [the term] "annam" is used; from the verbal root *ad* (meaning "to eat"), the form "anna" is derived through the passive past participle (*niṣṭhā*). That which has no death—that is, no dying—is "amṛta.
For that reason, the gods indeed desire to enjoy it, and the Vedas also long for it.
The meaning is that Viṣṇu and the other gods, as well as the Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda, long to experience that nectar which is His grace. Likewise, in another Śruti:
"O Lord of Beasts, today I bind this beast before You, in the midst of my good deed; grant Your approval for the well-performed sacrifice."
"Let us sacrifice; may this oblation be pleasing to the gods. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the fact that what has been consumed by Śiva is to be accepted by all people, the Vedic scripture prescribing the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation serves as the authority:
"In that he cuts off a portion for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, he thereby satisfies Rudra with his own share."

"He cuts off [the portion] once, for Rudra is, as it were, single. He cuts off from the northern part; this indeed is the quarter of Rudra. Thus he propitiates Rudra in his own quarter. So it is said.
The meaning of this is:

because—for that reason—the Agni Sviṣṭakṛt (the "well-sacrificing" fire), who makes the previously offered substance well-offered and sacrificed, [is] Rudra; he cuts off [the portion]; he performs the severance of the oblation (*havis*). *Do* = ...

The suffix *laṭ* is applied to the verbal root *ava-ṇḍ* (to cut off). Therefore, by performing the role of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and thereby making the previous oblation meaningful, he satisfies (*samardhayati*) Rudra—that is, he fulfills him—by means of his "portion" (*bhāgadheyena*), where the suffix *dheya* is added to the word *bhāga* in its own sense. This is done repeatedly (*sakṛt sakṛt*).
He cuts off and divides [the portion] only once,

for Rudra is indeed the master of all things performed only once; from the northern part— that is, from the northeastern portion— of the oblation he cuts off, since the northeastern direction is the very quarter of Rudra.

The meaning is that it is well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddha*). And thus, because of its being the *sviṣṭakṛt* [offering], because of the single portioning (*sakṛd-avadāna*), and because of the portioning toward the northeastern direction (*aiśānī-diś*), its being consumed by Rudra is established.
Immediately after the *sviṣṭakṛt*, [the consumption] of all the oblations (*havis*) by all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) [is established].
And because of the injunction for consumption, the partaking of Śiva’s grace is mandatory.

Now, one might object: since the sentence enjoining the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering here refers to Agni, and the subsequent sentences concerning Rudra are merely explanatory (*arthavāda*), how [can they be authoritative]?
If it is argued that the determination is made on the basis of Śiva being the supreme [deity], we say no; for in the section beginning with "But when there is doubt,
[the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.4.29), just as in the case of the statement "One places the smeared pebbles," where,
upon the expectation of what substance serves as the means of smearing, [the context determines the answer].
Since there is no definitive determination due to the fact that ghee, oil, fat, and other substances used as ointments are all perceived [as possible], the conclusion is reached—

based on the supplementary statement "Ghee is indeed light" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*)— that the ointment must be made with ghee alone and then applied. Similarly, by means of the word *rudra* found in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the same applies to the word *agni*.

The supremacy of Rudra is established. For it has been demonstrated that Agni is Rudra in the passage, "This Agni is indeed Rudra," and because of his capacity to perform the role of the *sviṣṭakṛt* (the maker of good offerings).

Now, one might object: since there is no word indicating sacrifice (*yāga*) or oblation (*homa*) in the phrase "by means of his portion" (*bhāgadheyena*), how can there be the state of being enjoyed by Rudra?

If it be asked how this applies to the oblation (*havis*), [the answer is: because in the passage "Pūṣan has the ground portion" (*pūṣā prapiṣṭabhāgaḥ*), the word "portion" (*bhāga*) was established in the *Pauṣṇādhikaraṇa* of the third chapter as denoting a sacrificial offering (*tyāga*); by that same principle, the word "portion" here also refers to the sacrifice. Furthermore:

In the *saṃsrāva-homa*, although the mantra and its constituent parts are directed toward the Viśvedevas, it is by the word "portion" (*bhāga*) itself that [the text] states: "All the Rudras and Ādityas have the *saṃsrāva* as their portion;
this is their allotted share; he gratifies them alone with that."
Because it is determined by virtue of having the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas as its presiding deities.

If it is objected: "Since sentences such as 'This fire is indeed Rudra,' which are heard in many places, are of the nature of *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) and thus lack *tātparya* (intentional focus) regarding their own literal meaning, how can they have Rudra as their ultimate purport?"—we reply: No; for when there is repetition (*abhyāsa*), there is a greater weight (*bhūyastva*) of the meaning.

Not even [the status of] being minor, let alone having a figurative meaning; thus it was stated by the teacher Vācaspatimiśra in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya* within the *Uttaratantro* [section]. Regarding the great sentences (*mahāvākya*):
Because it is established that statements such as "That thou art" have non-duality as their ultimate purport.

If it is objected: "Since the mantra that is an auxiliary to the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice is directed toward Agni, and because the word 'Agni' alone is heard therein, how can this oblation have Rudra as its deity when considering the Brāhmaṇa passage?"—we reply: no, for even though the mantra that constitutes an auxiliary to the *saṃsrāva-homa* is directed toward the Viśvedevas...

Because the Brāhmaṇa section determines that [the term] refers to Vasu, Rudra, and Āditya, and because such is observed to be the practice in the world, so too here the word *agni* is determined to refer to Rudra;
for a mantra whose meaning is not explicit is determined according to the method of the Brāhmaṇa.

It is necessary [to apply figurative indication]. For in the case of the injunction "one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse," since it has been determined in the relevant section (adhikaraṇa) that— even for one incapable of performing the worship of the Gārhapatya according to the Brāhmaṇa—
the Aindrī verse may be used in a manner not literal to its meaning on account of the direct scriptural statement (*vacana*).
Because it is the Brahmana alone that determines the meaning.

If it is argued that, in this way, since every occurrence of the word "Agni" found in various *ṛc* verses would—according to the stated reasoning—refer to Rudra, there would be no reference to Agni at all, we say: No; for only in those instances where there exists a direct statement (*āhatya-vacana*), an indicative mark (*liṅga*), or a context (*prakaraṇa*) establishing that the word "Agni" refers to Rudra, does it indeed refer to him.

Because there is no over-extension [of the term] through such a determination; otherwise, in the latter Tantra (the *Uttara-tantra*), words such as "ether," "breath," "light," and "Vaiśvānara"— which have been determined to refer to Brahman by means of their introduction and conclusion, their unique characteristic marks (*liṅga*), and their intended purport— would [contradict that determination] in that [context].

In that *ṛc*, these [mantras] would not have their respective referents in those particular deities. Furthermore, regarding the obligatory (*nitya*) rite prescribed by the Smṛti, within the seven *pākayajñas*, the venerable seer Vāstavya states:
"One should feed the Brahmins with the *sthālīpāka*; they consume the portion for Kṣetrapati."

After establishing the bali offerings for all the various hosts of Pramathas, such as Skanda, Pārvatī, Nandikeśvara, and the Kṣetrapālas, [he considered] the remaining food to be fit for the feeding of Brāhmaṇas, and for himself—
And because it is enjoined as something to be consumed.

Now, one might object: since in the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation only the four-fold portion (*caturavatta*) is offered, and that alone belongs to Rudra—rendering it unfit for consumption—the remainder, which is fit for consumption, lacks a connection to a deity; thus, due to this disparity with the food offered to Śiva, how can this serve as a logical argument to establish the eating of food offered to Śiva?
If it is asked how this was presented—namely, that by this [argument] the matter of the *īśāna-bali* is also almost refuted—it is not so;

for in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, when only the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) is offered into the fire, the remaining sacrificial material (*havis*) still maintains its connection with the deity. Even in common worldly practice, such a connection exists in cases like the remnants of a woman’s meal or the remnants of a Śūdra’s meal.

The negation proceeds precisely because [the substance] exists; therefore, there is a connection between the remaining oblation (*havis*) and the deity. On the contrary, regarding the connection of the remaining food with the deity, there is indeed an explicit scriptural statement (*śruti*). The presentation of examples such as the remnants of women and the remnants of Śūdras, however, is merely illustrative.

This has been written as an additional clarification for the benefit of all people. For instance, it is prescribed that "one divides the cake dedicated to Agni into four parts. This division into four parts is for the purpose of the priests' consumption;
thus says the Śruti: "For these four are the officiating priests (ṛtvij) of the Haviryajña—the Brahman..."
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Agnīdh—[the sacrificer] should touch that [portion], saying: "This for the Brahman; this for the Hotṛ;

this for the Adhvaryu; this for the Agnīdh. Regarding the statement, "He divides the portion for Agni into four parts," since it is only the fourfold portion that has been offered to Agni, there is no connection with the remainder.

In order to justify the scriptural statement that establishes the connection with Agni as the deity, one must necessarily admit that such a connection exists. Nor does the *taddhita* suffix *-ya* (as in *āgneyam*) fail to apply when there is a connection with a deity; rather, it is stated everywhere that the suffix *ḍhak* [which becomes *-eya*] is to be prescribed after the words *agni* and *kali*.

From the *vārttika*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied in the sense of the relationship expressed as "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*). However, it must be stated that while a mere relationship can exist even through a succession—such as being the original material for the fourfold cutting (*caturavatta*)—this *taddhita* suffix is used specifically in the sense of a deity, as in "this has that as its deity" (*sāsya devatā*). For this very reason, [it applies] to the *agniṣomīya*.
Even though the *puroḍāśa* possesses a connection with Agni,

because it lacks a connection with [the specific] deity [of the ritual], there is no fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*). This is because, under the governing rule "a grammatical operation concerning words applies only when they are semantically capable," [the division occurs] only when the deity is exclusively Agni without dependence on others.

Because it is impossible to say "this belongs to Agni" (*āgneyam*) with respect to the *agnīṣomīya* [sacrifice]— which has Agni as a deity only in a dependent sense— by means of the application of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-pratyaya*),
there is no fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) of the *puroḍāśa* cake dedicated to Agni-Soma; this is established in the third chapter.

This was established in the section concerning the division into four parts (*caturdhākaraṇādhikaraṇa*). Therefore, the remnant indeed possesses a connection with that deity; moreover, that connection is a direct one, and not an indirect connection consisting in being the source-material for the fourfold portion-offering (*caturavattāvadāna*).

In the view of Śabarasvāmin, the author of the Bhāṣya, it is determined in the *adhikaraṇa* beginning with "Because it is heard as such, *juhuyāt* would be [an act] consisting of pouring with an addition" (*śravaṇāj juhotir āsecanādhikaḥ syāt*) that *homa* is precisely the act of throwing [into the fire] preceded by renunciation (*tyāga*). Consequently, [the action] is characterized by being the object of a mental operation (*mānasavyāpāra*) in the form of renunciation, which constitutes a part of that [act of *homa*], in every instance.

Because it exists within the *puroḍāśa* cake. According to the view of the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda, the sacrifice (*yāga*) is simply the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), and that alone is the primary element.

Merely the act of throwing [the offering] into the fire is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the relinquishment; thus, it is clear that the entire *puroḍāśa* is the object of relinquishment. Therefore, the connection with the deity belongs to what remains [after the relinquishment].
It exists directly and precisely as it is.

[Objection: "But surely, since the sacrifices (yāga) and oblations (homa) prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti exist, your stated method applies to their very core; however, what does that have to do with the case of offerings presented to Śiva (śivanivedana), given the absence of sacrifice, oblation, and so forth? [Reply: This is not so, because the word *nivedana* (offering/presentation) has the meaning of *yāga* itself; otherwise, the meaning of the word *nivedana*...

Because it is impossible to carry it out. For instance: what is the meaning of the word *nivedana*? Is it the placing of food before the deity? Or is it the recitation of a mantra qualified by that [act]? Or is it a specific hand gesture qualified by that? Or perhaps the sounding of a bell qualified by that?
Is it the closing of eyes distinguished by that [object], or is it some mental intention?

Not the first, because the status of being "offered" (nivedita) is not established merely by placing [the object] before [the deity]. Otherwise, [the status would follow] merely from the placing of an object before a deity performed by women.

If [the rite were completed] by the mere act of offering, the other ritual activities would be rendered useless. Nor is it the second [alternative], for if that were the case, one who—due to the influence of illness—is incapable of reciting mantras, even if possessed of constant devotion, would lack the status of being the performer of the offering.
