Nor is it the third, as in the case of a person whose hand is impaired by illness...
If it were being performed, it would not constitute an announcement because of the absence of a specific hand gesture;

even the movement of the hand for the purpose of brushing away flies, gnats, mosquitoes, and the like from the food present at that moment would have to be considered an announcement. Nor is it the fourth [alternative], as in the case of one who has lost his bell or is walking along a road.

Due to the absence of the sound of a bell, there would be no agency in the act of offering. Nor is it the fifth [alternative], for one whose eyes are afflicted by disease, or one who has closed their eyes at that moment for fear of a mosquito landing on them—even if possessed of devotion—would lack the agency to offer. Therefore, this is characterized as follows:
Or rather, the meaning of the word "offering" (nivedana) is precisely this mental intention: "This is not superior to me; it is yours; you may eat it."

If it is argued that, in that case, the words *nivedana* and *yāga* would be synonyms—just like the words *ghaṭa* and *kumbha*—we reply that this is not so, because a difference in terminology can occur through a difference in perspective, as in the case of the words *yāga* and *homa*. What is called *yāga* is a specific mental intention (*abhisandhi*) directed toward a deity, characterized by the thought "this is not mine. What is called *homa* is...

[Offering] (*nivedana*) is the casting of a substance into the fire, preceded by a mental renunciation of that substance intended for a deity, which serves as the physical support for the fire. It is a specific action characterized by the renunciation of a substance intended for a deity, which accomplishes the satisfaction of the deity who is the agent [of that action].
A specific mental intention characterized by the form of non-attachment to enjoyment.

Therefore, it is established that the grace of Śiva is to be accepted through the statements of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Āgamas, which are reinforced by reason. Regarding this matter, numerous statements from the Āgamas, Purāṇas, Smṛtis, Āyurveda, and so forth, which serve as corroborative expansions (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), are heard. For instance:
In the *Śivadharmottara*, it is said: "One should wear the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) upon one's head and also consume the food offering (*naivedya*);
by drinking that water of grace (*prasādodaka*), one shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The meritorious water [consecrated] by my grace should always be worn by those who have taken refuge in me;
and especially by the sick, and by those consumed by disease, with great effort."
Whoever, out of devotion and without greed, wears upon his head the remains of offerings (nirmālya),
by him I myself am worn— the Moon, the bearer of the lunar digits.
In the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"The remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of Śiva alone should be worn with devotion by the twice-born;
the nirmālya is supremely meritorious, and the food offering (naivedya) destroys sin."
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon celibate students, householders, and ascetics, the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* states:
"One should eat food that has been eaten by Rudra; one should drink water that has been drunk by Rudra."
"One should always smell that which has been smelled by Rudra"—thus says the Jābāli Śruti.
In Āyurveda,
it is said that by drinking the water used for washing the offerings (*nirmālya*) of the trident-bearing God of gods,
one is liberated from consumption, leprosy, fever, asthma, and even from sins.

Since such statements in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Āyurveda declare that there is prosperity in accepting the grace of Śiva and a transgression in not doing so, it must always be respectfully accepted by the devotees of Śiva who are devoted to Him.

Now, although the acceptance of Śiva’s grace is mandatory by the force of such statements from the Śrutis, Āgamas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth, since no scriptural injunctions for the acceptance of the grace of the Guru and the Caru are observed, how can that grace be accepted?

If it is argued that [this is not so], we say no; for in the acceptance of water from the feet (pādodaka), just as with the water from Śiva’s feet, the water from the feet of the Guru’s attendants must also necessarily be accepted, according to the authority of numerous scriptural statements establishing the mutual non-difference between Śiva, the Guru, and the attendants. By that same logic...
Faith is said to be threefold: pure, accomplished, and well-established.
Pure faith is obtained from the mouth of the guru; likewise, accomplished faith is obtained from the mouth of the *liṅga*.
"Grace is well-known to be of three kinds, as received from the mouth of a mobile [preceptor].
In accordance with such specific statements, it is established that the threefold grace— known as *śuddha*, *siddha*, and *prasiddha*—
which is enjoyed by the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Caru, must always be accepted by the Vīraśaivas.
Without dispute.

[Thus ends the section on] the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*), which are distinguished by one hundred and one unsurpassed stages (*sthalabheda*) produced from churning the ocean of the Śāmbhava Āgama, obtained through the grace of Toṇṭada Siddheśvara— the incarnation of the supreme moving form of the glorious, beginningless, and stainless [Lord].
[This work] was composed by the eminent teacher Śrī Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows the mass of bliss arising from the taste of the nectar of the realization of ultimate reality;
[it concerns] the seizure of the seven constituents of the enemy of the sole hero whose body is the tumultuous roar of ten million Yādava Murāris, [and] the [conquest of] the western ocean...

In the instruction of Basava, the thunderbolt of the earth, who brings joy to the heart of Mallāmbā— the lawful consort of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth, who is like the full moon to the milky ocean of the Nāyaka dynasty, and who is the preceptor Śrī Keladi Sadāśivarāya, the master in establishing the pure Vedic non-dual (advaita) doctrine— [this work was composed].
The Sixth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*.
[The Seventh Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O Lord, having heard the majesty of your grace as proclaimed by you out of compassion, I am exceedingly gladdened, as if I had already attained that very grace.
O King of kings, with love make that which is to be known a guest in the path of your ears; listen vigilantly as I proclaim the glory of Bhūti’s prosperity.

The wearing of sacred ash (*bhasmadhāraṇa*) must be performed, as it brings about the purification of the mind—which is an internal means for the knowledge of Brahman, the sole instrument for the supreme good—and because it is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the Vedic worship of Śiva. Regarding this, there is a scriptural authority (*śruti*).
In the *Taittirīyopaniṣad*, [it says] concerning the disciple of gurus...

In the section on the instruction for practicing the essential duties (*pratyāvaśyakadharma*), beginning with "Speak the truth, practice dharma," [the text] states that those actions which are blameless (*anavadya*) are to be cultivated; having thus stated that blameless actions are to be practiced, it says, "not others."

Having stated that practices such as the wearing of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* as propounded by non-Vedic systems like the Pāñcarātra are not to be followed and are therefore to be rejected, [the author] further states in that very same work, within the section on the rules for necessary conduct: "One must not neglect truth;
one must not neglect what is beneficial; one must not neglect prosperity. By this [he means the following].

Because the injunction that the wearing of ashes must be performed without negligence is established; and as for the objection that in the passage "one should not be negligent regarding prosperity" (*bhūtyai na pramaditavyam*), the word *bhūti* can be explained as referring to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), how then can it be said to refer to ashes? [The answer is: *bhūti* refers to both ashes and prosperity.

It should not be argued that the meaning of "attainment" (*sampad*) can also be expressed by the word *tri-kośa*, for the Blessed Sūtrakāra Bodhāyana has defined the word *bhūti* specifically as referring to ashes. To explain: [he states as follows:]...

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the application of the sacred ash (*bhasma*). It is known from scripture: "One must not neglect prosperity (*bhūti*). Furthermore, they cite this: "The triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) made with ash using the middle, ring, and thumb fingers—that *tripuṇḍra* is auspicious and the destroyer of great sins."

Then, with the mantra "O Triyambaka," he should wipe his entire body; he becomes purified. He purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, himself as the twenty-first, and the row [of guests]; he attains union with and residence in the same world as Brahman. Now, this smearing with ashes from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head is [prescribed] for all rites.

"One must perform [these]," so said the venerable Bodhāyana. Thus says the Śruti: "One should not be negligent regarding truth and dharma, nor regarding wholesome conduct, nor even regarding the smearing with ashes, nor the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), nor the study of one's own Veda, nor the rites for the gods and the ancestors."
Thus [it is said].

Likewise, in the Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad: Then Sanatkumāra questioned the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra: "Teach me, O Blessed One, the rule for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) along with its true nature; what is the substance, how many are the places, and what is the measure?"
"What are the mantras of the lines? What is the power? What is the deity? Who is the agent? And what is the fruit?
To him, the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra said: "Whatever substance is that ash is of the nature of fire;
having taken it up with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, [one should purify it] with the mantra 'Agni is ash'."

Having consecrated [the water] with the mantra *mā nastoke*, and having drawn it up with *mā no mahāntam*, and having mixed it with water using *triyāyuṣam*, one should draw three horizontal lines across the head,
forehead, chest, and shoulders with three *triyāyuṣa* mantras, three *tryambaka* mantras, and three *triśakti* mantras.
This Śāmbhava vow is declared by the exponents of the Vedas in all the Vedas;

therefore, one who desires liberation should practice it for the sake of non-rebirth. Then Sanatkumāra asked: "What is the authority for this triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) application, and why are there three lines?"
The first line extends from the forehead up to the eyes, up to the crown of the head, and up to the middle of the eyebrows;

it is the Gārhapatya fire, the letter *A*, the *rajas* quality, the earthly realm (*bhūrloka*), one's own self, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the *Ṛgveda*, the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), and Maheśvara as its deity. As for its second line...

The southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) is the syllable *U*, the quality of passion (*sattva*), the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), the inner self (*antarātman*), the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), the Yajurveda,

the midday libation (*mādhyandina-savana*), and Sadāśiva as the deity. That which is its third line is the *Āhavanīya* fire, the syllable *M*, the quality of darkness (*tamas*), the heavenly world (*dyu-loka*), the supreme self (*paramātman*), the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), the Sāmaveda, and the third libation (*tṛtīya-savana*).

"Mahādeva is the deity. Thus, the wise man—whether a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic—who applies the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with ashes, becomes purified from all major and minor sins;
he has bathed in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*); he is known by all the gods; he...

He has studied all the Vedas; he becomes one who constantly recites the entire mantra of Rudra; having abandoned his body, he enjoys all pleasures and attains union with Śiva; he does not return again, he does not return again—thus said the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra. And whoever studies this [text], he too is exactly like that.
"It exists; Om, it is truth"—this is the Upanishad.
Indeed, numerous scriptural statements from the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas are heard that establish the necessity of wearing this very ash. For instance, in the Śivarāghava-saṃvāda:
"The wearing of that ash is praised; all of it possesses the three marks."
It is the means for accomplishing Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the three sacrifices.
By that [rite], indeed, the maintenance of the three worlds and their qualities is accomplished;
the pure ash, consecrated with mantras, is to be maintained in fifteen locations.
Sin committed above the throat is destroyed by wearing [the amulet] on the face;
and by wearing it on the throat, the sin committed regarding the enjoyments of the throat and so forth is destroyed.
May it take away the sin committed by the two arms, that committed by the chest, and that committed by the mind;
may it take away the sin committed by the navel and that committed by the back.
O Rāma, because he maintains [his practice] at his sides, he is born from the embrace of another's wife and so forth;
he is one whose seat is ashes, whose bed is ashes, and whose body is smeared with ashes.
By bathing with ashes, one is always liberated from sins; there is no doubt about this.
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
"A learned twice-born man covered in ashes is freed from the consequences of great sins."
A person is immediately liberated from the defects; there is no doubt about this.
Therefore, in all the worlds, the one endowed with vigor who is joined with ashes is preeminent;
that which is the supreme virility of the fire of Rudra is celebrated as ash.
The defects of one who is devoted to ashes are burnt away by contact with fire;
having his self purified by the bath of ashes, he is known as one "devoted to ashes."
A person whose entire body is smeared with ashes, who wears the radiant triple-ash mark (tripuṇḍra),
who bathes in ashes, is known as one who is established in ashes (bhasmaniṣṭha).
Spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and diseases that are exceedingly difficult to endure flee away without a doubt from the mere presence of one who is established in the sacred ash (bhasman).
It is called *bhāsaka* because it illuminates, and *bhasita* because it has been spoken; it is *bhasma* (ashes) because it terrifies away impurities (*kalmaṣa*).
It is *bhūti* because it brings prosperity to men, and it is *rakṣā* because it provides protection.
The ash of Śiva is the supreme weapon of the devotees of Śiva; it belongs to the Supreme Lord.
As stated in the *Laiṅgya*, just as sin is destroyed by the mere remembrance of Rudra, so too [is it destroyed] by this ash.
Likewise, by the mere retention of this, all evil is destroyed.
If one bathes with ashes after having committed thousands of improper acts,
that ash burns it all away, just as fire consumes a forest by its heat.
Even if he has committed incomparable sin, that twice-born man who, even at the time of death,
becomes one who bathes in ashes, is liberated from all evil.
One whose self is purified by the ash-bath, who has conquered anger and subdued the senses,
having come into my presence, does not return again.
A person who has applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) becomes purified in soul and conquers death;
however, whatever rite one performs without applying the triple mark is in vain.
The smearing with ashes and the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are the means to liberation;
this is declared by the supreme sages to be the "Agni-bath" (the fire-bath).
For the sake of the successful accomplishment of all rites, a wise person should perform this at the very beginning;
otherwise, all rites will never bear fruit.
In the Smṛti of Kātyāyana:
"At a Śrāddha, a sacrifice, a recitation, a fire-oblation, a Vaiśvadeva rite, or the worship of the gods,
a person who has applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) becomes purified in soul and conquers death."

The application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing with ashes has been proclaimed with reverence by the Jābālas for all castes and stages of life, whether performed with mantras or even without mantras.

One who desires liberation should likewise apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark crosswise with ashes using the mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, and perform the smearing (*dhūlana*) for the sake of attaining knowledge.

From such scriptural, traditional, historical, and Puranic declarations as these, it is understood that the wearing of sacred ash (bhasma) effects the removal of all sins, brings about the fulfillment of all ritual actions, and renders those actions futile if it is not performed.
Indeed,
he who carries on the plowshare the earth produced on the banks of the Ganges bears the form of the sun; it is traditionally held that this is for the destruction of darkness.
He on whose forehead the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) made with clay is seen—even if he is an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*), he is a pure soul and is worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt.
O best of Brahmins, sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors—
all become fruitless if performed without the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
At the time of worship and during the fire-oblation, being composed in mind both morning and evening,
one should duly apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) while pronouncing the names [of the deities].
O best of Brahmins, wherever a mortal dwells wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra),
that very land becomes equal to the sacred field of Kāśī.
Regarding the greatness of Mārgaśīrṣa:
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall declare the threefold method of wearing [the marks],
together with the clay of the Tulasī plant and the sacred Gopīcandana.
The wise should apply the *puṇḍra* mark there using yellow sandalwood;
now learn from me as I speak of the greatness of *gopīcandana*.
Taking the earth from the root of the sacred Tulasī of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the devoted person should apply the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra); Hari is pleased with him.
The man who, taking clay produced at Dvāravatī in his hand, applies it here as a perpetual vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) upon the surface of his forehead;
Then the fruit of the action shall become ten millionfold.
If one applies the clay of the Gopikā on the forehead even after having performed the rite devoid of action and deprived of the proper time,
one always obtains the eternal fruit of that ritual act.
Through the most meritorious grace of the Lord of the Gopīs.
If a twice-born man, having prepared the beautiful *gopīcandana* paste, always wears it on his forehead every day and at all times,
even at night— whatever merit is gained at Kurujāṅgala, at Ravigṛha, or likewise at Prayāga during the month of Māgha; [that merit he obtains].
One obtains that, and even more than that; it remains in my house like a deity.
In whatever house a person keeps Gopīcandana and wears it upon his forehead,
I always dwell in that house.
Endowed with splendor, the four-faced one was delighted.

Whoever would constantly wear upon their forehead this merit-born, purifying mark originating from Dvāravatī— which removes the defilements of the Kali age and is sanctified by my mantra— [shall attain liberation].
Even one joined with sin shall not see Yama.
He on whose forehead a straight and gentle vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is seen is a purified soul worthy of worship, even if he be a Caṇḍāla; of this there is no doubt.
One who performs a ritual action while not having bathed, being impure and joined with sin, becomes worthy of worship through contact with Gopīcandana; of this there is no doubt.
Whether he be impure, lacking in proper conduct, or burdened by great sins,
a man marked with the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* shall always remain pure.
The face of one who is devoid of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is like a cremation ground;
having beheld their faces, one should look toward the sun.
Wherever the worship of Rudra and the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are seen,
that is declared to be the rule for Śūdras, and never for the twice-born.

"A Brahmin shall not wear ashes even when fallen into the greatest distress," and so forth; for by such statements from the Purāṇas, it is heard extensively that the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, along with its prescribed ritual procedure, brings about prosperity and removes all sins.

If it is argued that because the application of ash is prescribed for those such as Śūdras, one should perform only the wearing of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and not the wearing of ash— this is not so;
for the wearing of the vertical mark and other such practices are [enjoined] by Gautama, Dadhīci, Durvāsas, Bhṛgu, ...

Since it is frequently heard in the *Sūta-saṃhitā* and other scriptures, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas that the domain of those twice-born who have been consumed by the curses of gods and sages— headed by Brahmā, Upamanyu, and Nandikeśvara— is restricted to the lowest of the twice-born who are non-Vedic Tantrikas, the wearing of the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) belongs only to them.
Thus, it is established that this applies to the followers of the Vedas. Regarding the prohibition against wearing the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, Parāśara states:
"One devoted to the Vedas should not wear the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), the trident (*triśūla*), the circular, the square, the half-moon, or any such other sectarian signs."

One who has received the birth-rite by virtue of his lineage and has taken recourse to the path of the Śrutis should never wear another sectarian mark (puṇḍra) on the forehead, even if it were out of delusion.

Even for the sake of achieving fame, profit, and other such successes, a person following the Vedic path should never wear any other type of sectarian mark (puṇḍra) than those prescribed in the Viṣṇu Āgamas and similar texts.
One should not burn a preeminent twice-born man, nor should one burn him with the discus and other such marks;
the king should swiftly banish from his own country anyone who has been branded.
For it is prescribed that men who have fallen [from their status] should be marked with their own specific insignia, but those who are pure should not; therefore, one should not mark a pure person.
Indeed, one who bears the mark [of initiation] is entitled to teaching and studying, to performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti,
and to engaging in conversation by virtue of that connection.
Marking the body with the conch, the discus, and so forth, as well as dancing, singing, and the like—this is the dharma of the low-born; it should never belong to one born of the twice-born.
In the Skanda [Purāṇa], in the Muktikhaṇḍa, in the Pāñcarātra, in the Kāpāla, and likewise in the Kālāmukha;
in the Buddhist, in the Ārhata, in the Vāma, and also in the Pāśupata.
"And you shall be initiated into the Śākta [tradition], O lowest of Brāhmaṇas!"—
thus was the curse of Gautama. In the thirty-second chapter of the Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa of the Sūta-saṃhitā, Sūta says:
Today, O Mahādeva, I shall declare the cause of the state of faith;
listen with devotion, O best of sages, regarding human beings.
Having begun thus, the illustrious sage Gautama, the best of sages, having learned that,
was seized by great wrath and cursed those lowest of brahmins.
In the very nature of Mahādeva, in the physical form of Mahādeva,
in devotion to Mahādeva, and in the name of Mahādeva.
In the wisdom of Mahādeva, in the acceptance by Mahādeva,
in the abode of Mahādeva, and in the glories of Mahādeva.
In the preeminence of Mahādeva, in the hermitages of Mahādeva,
and in the exaltation of Mahādeva— such as the application of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana)— [one should remain devoted].
In the wearing of rudrākṣas, in the worship of the liṅga of Rudra itself,
in the desire to behold the temple of Rudra, and in rites such as the rudrayātrā;
Whatever is related to Rudra, in each and every instance, you wicked ones—
you lowest of Brahmins— shall always be averse to it.
If you should turn away from all matters whatsoever declared in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas,
you would be the lowest of Brāhmaṇas in every respect.
"All deities beginning with Viṣṇu are superior to Śaṅkara"—
those base Brahmins who possess such deluded cognition are truly the lowest of their kind.
Those who bear the marks of a circular emblem, a half-aśvattha leaf, a crescent moon, a lamp, and so forth,
shall always be the lowest of Brāhmaṇas, even if they possess faith.
"You have been initiated into the Pāñcarātra, the Kāpāla, as well as the Kālāmukha, and the Śākta; you are the lowest of Brahmins!"
Having been initiated with faith in heretical sects and other paths that are outside the Vedic tradition, you have become the lowest of Brahmins.
What is the use of saying much more? [Salutations] directly to Śiva, the liberator from saṃsāra, and to all those connected with him who are proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti.
"May the state of faith always remain within you and likewise within those born of your lineage; thus has a severe curse been pronounced by me."
In the *Āditya Purāṇa*, regarding the curse of Dadhīci upon the brahmins at Dakṣa’s sacrifice:
"Since all these brahmins hate Maheśvara,
may they be excluded from the Vedas, their minds struck down by sin."
All those devoted to heretical practices go to hell;
this is the curse of Dadhīci at Dakṣa’s sacrifice in the Sāmbapurāṇa regarding the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the smearing with ashes, and the consecration with Vedic mantras.
May you and those born of your lineage likewise turn away from existence.
O twice-born ones, if you should ever be initiated into tantras outside the Vedas, such as the Pāñcarātra and others,
you will always be the lowest of brahmins.
Marked upon your limbs with the conch, discus, mace, and other symbols,
you have become outsiders to the Vedas and the lowest of the twice-born, along with your misplaced faith.
Those who bear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the trident, or marks that are circular or square—
marks contrary to the Vedas— are the lowest of Brahmins.

In the second chapter of the *Parāśaropapurāṇa*, within the section concerning the mutual curse of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Brahmā speaks to Viṣṇu: "Overcome by great anger, Brahmā, the lord of the entire world..."
He cursed Viṣṇu: "Become an embryo, utterly deluded."
Your devotees would constantly turn their faces away from the Brahmins who apply the ash-triple-mark (tripuṇḍra), even though it is established by the Vedas and bestows liberation.
Furthermore, those who are initiated into your Pāñcarātra Tantra as well as the Bhāgavata [Tantra] shall always be fearless in relation to Hari.
In the *Kālikākhaṇḍa* of the *Skānda-purāṇa*, there is the curse of Bhṛgu upon Viṣṇu for killing his own wife, and [the curse] directed toward his devotees:
"Those who are your devotees, O Hari, whether they carry a single staff or three staves— "
May they today become heretics, bringing hell to those who behold them.
Due to the curse of the great-souled sage Durvāsas when he was enraged,
and from the curses of Kaṇva, Bhṛgu, and Upamanyu.
O Brahmin, likewise, due to the curse of Brahmā and the curse of Nandikeśvara,
the minds of the southern twice-born were afflicted by sin.
There is not even a slight degree of faith in auspicious ashes or rudrākṣas.
In the *Vaidikācāranirṇaya*, within the section concerning the greatness of ashes, [it says]:
"Those who hate Śiva, the Rudrādhyāya, the rudrākṣas, and the ashes prescribed in the Vedas..."
In the Kali age, they will fall away from the path of the Vedas.
O wise ones, for those beings who were guilty of great sins (mahāpātaka) in their previous births,
a very firm aversion toward the application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing with ashes arises.
In that very same *Brahmagītā*: "For men burdened with great sins, in the pursuit of the knowledge of Śiva,
[the practice consists of] smearing all the limbs with ashes and wearing the horizontal *tripuṇḍra* mark."
Constant aversion arises toward the wearing of rudrākṣas, toward the worship of the liṅga of Rudra itself, and even toward the chanting of the word "Śiva."
In the Muktikhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"A wise man should infer that there was a mixture of castes at the very birth of one who feels aversion toward sacred ash and even toward the application of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra)."
A wise person should properly conceal their birth from a Caṇḍāla when it concerns the Śruti,
Mahādeva, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), or being smeared with ashes.
A mortal devoid of even a trace of merit does not have faith in the application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing with ashes as prescribed in the Śruti for the most sinful of men.
Indeed, hatred toward Mahādeva arises spontaneously;
so too does the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes established by the Vedas.

Those who follow the conduct prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis, yet perform their rites while omitting the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), act for the sake of worldly gain rather than spiritual purpose.
Everything performed by him is in vain and a cause for misfortune;
the face of a Brahmin devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is like a cremation ground.
Prohibition of Branding in the *Smṛticandrikā*:
"A Brahmin devoted to the Śrauta and Smārta rites should not brand his limbs with marks, even those connected to Viṣṇu and others; by doing so, he becomes fallen."
If one wears the Sudarśana [mark] out of ignorance, greed, or passion, it destroys one's lineage; seeing such a person, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
O King, whether his body is marked with the wheel or even marked with the linga,
he should be known as ineligible for the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and the Smṛtis.
That fool who bears the conch, the discus, and the linga upon his body should be known as a heretic, excluded from all sacred rites.
One should not transgress, even in thought, the practice of smearing ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), since these are ordained by the Śruti; one who abandons them becomes fallen.
A person marked with the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, bearing the circular *liṅga* of the *aśvattha* leaf,
is purified by the mere wearing of the triple horizontal lines (*tripuṇḍra*) made of sacred ash.
Therefore, what is the use of conch shells, discuses, and other weapons of the deities on the body?
One should mutter the Rudra-hymn and the Puruṣasūkta, and apply the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Then, by wearing it with ashes, a Brahmin dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
O best of the twice-born, this ash is proclaimed to be of many kinds, though it is but a small amount.
O best of scholars, there is one type of ash that is Śrauta and another that is Smārta;
O twice-born ones, the Śrauta ash is declared to be primary, while the Smārta is proclaimed to be secondary.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, there is also the purely worldly ash,
as well as the Vedic (śrauta) and the Smārta ash, which is proclaimed for the twice-born alone.
For all others indeed, another kind of ash is prescribed,
both for smearing over the entire body and likewise for applying the horizontal *tripuṇḍra* marks.
"It has been declared by the sages that ash should be worn by all human beings;
O best of sages, for the twice-born, its application with mantras has been prescribed."
O Brahmin, the mere wearing [of the sacred thread] by others is also proclaimed,
using the mantras beginning with "Agni" found in the Jābāla Upaniṣad.
O twice-born ones, one should perform the smearing with water and ashes seven times,
and apply the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with the Triyāyuṣa mantra.
The best of the twice-born, who are righteous and have mastered the Vedas,
have declared that the student (brahmacārī) should wear it day after day with mantras beginning with "medhāvī."
One should also wear the Tripuṇḍra with ashes mixed with water,
using the Tryambaka mantra, the Praṇava, and the Śiva mantra.
Both the householder and the forest-dweller should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
applying the triple mark with the syllable Om uttered three times along with the Praṇava (the *sa-haṃsa*).
"A wise monk should always wear [the mark] on the forehead, on both arms, and likewise on the chest; such is the Jābāli Śruti."
One should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
indeed, both the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) and the triple mark exist solely as limbs of knowledge.
The best of the twice-born who follow the Śvetāśvatara branch declare:
"This is the dharma that transcends all stages of life (atyāśrama), which has been joyfully practiced by them."
For them alone is the knowledge of Śiva the cause for severing the cycle of transmigration;
and the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are for the cessation of the bond of Māyā.
The best of sages, established in the Atharvaśiras,
declare that by which the wise have properly practiced the Pāśupata vow.
For him, that knowledge shall arise by which there is liberation from sin;
the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) exist solely as limbs of that knowledge.
The best of sages, who are the manifest trees of absolute liberation (kaivalya),
prescribe this for the sake of attaining the knowledge that severs the bonds and for the attainment of perfection.
One who desires liberation should properly perform the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
indeed, both the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark.
Vedic scripture prescribes the smearing of the body with ashes and likewise the wearing of the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the destruction of great sins.
The Vedic word ordains for all that very austerity which consists of smearing oneself with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Vedic scripture prescribes for all [these acts] precisely as a religious vow (vrata):
namely, the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The Vedic word prescribes for all these very acts the status of sacrifice:
namely, the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
For the sake of knowledge alone, the Vedic word ordains for all the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The ash was worn by Śiva, Viṣṇu, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), and likewise by Brahmā,
as well as by the gods, in the form of the triple-tilaka and the smearing of the body.
The ash, consisting of the triple-tilaka and the smearing of the body, was worn by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others, as well as by sages.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those of mixed castes,
as well as those of degraded speech, have maintained the sacred ash by means of the triple-mark and the smearing of the body.
O best of sages, only those by whom the smearing with ashes is joyfully practiced are truly refined and wise; no others.
For those who do not perform the smearing with ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with faith,
there is no liberation from saṃsāra even through ten million births.
Those who do not perform the smearing with ashes and the triple mark with faith are possessed of great sins; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Whatever is performed with faith by those who do not practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) leads indeed to contrary results.
O Brahmins, the greatness of wearing the sacred ash cannot be described by me, nor even by a Guru, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
O lords of sages, even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra,
the majesty of wearing the sacred ash cannot be fully described.
That man who desires liberation while abandoning the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) truly makes his own self eternal by drinking poison.
Aversion toward the application of the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra) and the avoidance of its performance,
as well as the failure to wear rudrākṣa beads, are causes for the non-arising of knowledge.
In the *Skānda Purāṇa*, within the *Muktikhaṇḍa*, in the chapter on the causes for the non-arising of knowledge, Śiva says:
"Hostility toward the Vedas and Vedānta, the avoidance of their study,
and the adoption of non-Vedic systems such as the Vāma and Pāśupata."
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, the Pāñcarātra and other such systems are causes for the non-arising of knowledge, as are Umā-devī, Lakṣmī, Vāṇī, and others.
The sacred ash held by all women, consisting of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing (uddhūlana), is supreme Brahman; these two are the means of crossing over saṃsāra.
One of these two should be served by those who fear the terrors of saṃsāra;
by him [who serves it] has been studied, by him has been heard, and by him has everything been practiced.

That by which the *tripuṇḍra* is worn on the head by a Brahmin— indeed, it is stated in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* that only those who wear ashes possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman: "One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the 'head-vow' (*śirovratam*) has been performed according to the rules."
The expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of this Upaniṣadic statement is found in the Purāṇa:
"One who is devoid of the Śirovrata, even if endowed with all other duties, has no eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman and the Self; of this there is no doubt."
In the Saurasaṃhitā:
"With the six mantras beginning with 'Agni' and with pure ashes,
one should perform the smearing of all limbs, which is called the Śirovrata."
This head-vow has been performed with faith by those who know the ritual procedure;
for it is the sacred revelation that the supreme knowledge belongs only to them and not to others.
This is known as the Śirovratam, heard in the Atharvaṇa Śruti;
in the Muktikhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa it is said:
"One should perform this Śirovratam with devotion during the periods of the Sandhyās."
As long as knowledge arises, so long indeed are his knowledges supreme.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the Creator, under the guise of creation, proclaimed the excellence of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*):
"He indeed created it on the forehead as horizontal, neither vertical nor circular."
In this ocean of the nectar of the essence of Dharma,
one should always apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ash purified by mantras;
by following the procedure prescribed in the Vedas, one shall attain union with Śiva.
When the moon has entered the constellation Vanaspati and the sun is in Śruti, one whose body is smeared with ashes is liberated from all sins by beholding that Śaṅkara even once.
In the *Śrutisārasamuccaya*:
"Whether one is impure or of improper conduct, even if one commits sin with the mind,
one shall remain eternally pure by wearing the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*)."
In the Mahābhārata:
"O King, whether a man desires long life, or desires prosperity,
or indeed a twice-born man desires liberation, he should always wear the sacred ash."
In the Nāradīya-smṛti:
"The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is the supreme Brahman, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Those terrible Rākṣasas, Pretas, and other small creatures [are repelled by it]."
Upon seeing one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), [evil beings] flee without a doubt;
the birth of that person who does not wear the triple mark is in vain.
Bhūti brings prosperity to men and destroys their sins;
by even a mere particle of Vibhūti, the fruit of all ritual bathing is obtained.
One should abandon like an outcaste that person on whose plowshare there is no prosperity, who does not wear rudrākṣa beads on his body, and who does not chant the five-syllable mantra.
In the *Candrikā*, in the daily section (*āhnika*):
"The ash-bath possesses innumerable qualities more than the water-bath;
therefore, having abandoned the Vāruṇa bath, one should perform the Āgneya bath."
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices—all that fruit one obtains from the ash-bath; of this there is no doubt.
There is no splendor equal to ashes, and there is no austerity equal to ashes;
for those highly fortunate ones who are devoted, as well as those twice-born ones who are evildoers.
Even they, their limbs distinguished by ashes, attain the supreme goal— those who,
during the time of the *phāla*, are without ashes and without the wearing of *rudrākṣa* beads.
That brahmin, the lowest of outcastes, is not to be honored in the abode of Śambhu;
it is said that [this knowledge] bestows wisdom upon ascetics and detachment upon forest-dwellers.
It likewise promotes the increase of dharma for those engaged in the householder stage of life,
and it bestows the practice of sacred study upon those established in the stage of celibate studentship.
It is said that for Śūdras it bestows merit, and for others it destroys sin,
provided that in his row a twice-born man who is a devotee of Śiva and who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) eats.
A single person among the virtuous purifies an entire assembly, just as the four-faced Brahmā does;
yet, were one to write out the greatness of wearing the sacred ash in its entirety, it would be impossible to finish.

"The three worlds are its palm leaves; the life-span of men is but a hundred years"—by the force of such scriptural and Puranic statements, [it is established that] because the wearing of ashes bestows longevity, prosperity, and liberation, it serves as the means for those desiring longevity, prosperity, and liberation; thus, [the objection] regarding hatred toward the wearing of ashes [is refuted].
The fact that [the practice] is rooted in a confusion regarding its origin; that, in the absence of faith in the wearing of ashes, it is rooted in great sins accumulated over many previous births;
and that the performance of all ritual acts becomes futile if preceded by the abandonment of the wearing of ashes.
Because it serves as an expiation for averting great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin,

it takes the form of the performance of all vows, charities, austerities, and sacrifices; and because it is conducive to the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra*, the Creator’s intended purpose was the fashioning of the forehead with horizontal lines.
Even in states where actions that cause impurity occur, it possesses the quality of bringing about purity;
in the absence of the wearing of ashes, it serves as the cause for the non-arising of knowledge;
and by virtue of warding off Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and the like, it acts as the dispeller of all fears.
Of its being worn by all the deities, such as Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā; of its being worn by all the sages;
of its being worn by the celestial women headed by Umā, Lakṣmī, and Vāṇī; and of its rendering birth fruitless except through its own wearing.
Because it has as its sole means of accomplishment the Vedic mantras,
and its procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is that which is prescribed in the *Atharvaśiras*, *Rājābālakaivalya*, and *Kālāgnirudra* Upaniṣads;
and because it is established as the *Śāmbhava-vrata*, the *Pāśupata-vrata*, and the *Śirovrata*.
Furthermore, because it is established that [the Lord] possesses a majesty that cannot be fully described even by all those who are extroverted, headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
the wearing of sacred ash must certainly be performed.

But is it not stated in the *Atharvaśiras*, within the section on the Pāśupata knowledge: "Having taken ashes with the mantra 'Agni' and so forth, and having rubbed them, one should touch the limbs; this is the Pāśupata vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (*paśu*)"? Thus, the smearing with ashes is prescribed.

By virtue of the context, it is an auxiliary to that [specific] meditation alone, and not an auxiliary to all meditations on Brahman. For instance, one might object: "Is it not the case that eating before guests—which is enjoined in the section on the Vaiśvānara-vidyā by the words 'one should not eat before guests'—is an auxiliary to all meditations on Brahman? If this is raised, we say no.

The smearing with ashes (*bhasmoddhūlana*), which produces the auxiliary benefit of destroying sins in the form of purification of the mind required for all *brahmavidyā*, is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of all *brahmavidyā*. For it is stated in the *Jābāla-śruti*: "It destroys all sin, even that accumulated over hundreds of births," and so forth.

Because it has been determined that [the smearing with ashes] is a cause of assistance for the destruction of evil; the smearing with ashes, which is enjoined by the mantra beginning with "Agni," is an auxiliary to all Brahmavidyās, because, while being an auxiliary to a Vidya,
it generates the required assistance for all Brahmavidyās, just like tranquility (śama), self-control (dama), and so forth.
Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of a guru, having committed theft, and even having committed the murder of a Brahmin—
one who recites the Rudrādhyāya, covered in ashes and lying on a bed of ashes, is liberated from all sins.
In the *Śātātapa-smṛti*, within the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa*),

regarding the recitation of the *Śrī Rudra* prescribed as an independent expiation and its ancillaries such as the smearing with ashes (*bhasmoddhūlana*) which produce assistance required for knowledge, the phrase "provided it is an ancillary to knowledge" (*vidyāṅgatve sati*) is included in order to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

The qualifier [is provided] for the purpose of excluding deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding such cases as eating before the guests; the qualificand is for the same purpose. Nor should it be suspected that the qualifier is unestablished (asiddha), on the grounds that the cited Jābāla-śruti might possibly refer to the independent practice of smearing oneself with ashes.
Since the mantras for smearing with ashes— beginning with "Agni is ash" and "Vāyu is ash," which are recited in the *Atharvaśiras*—
are recorded in the *Jābāla-śruti* as having the purpose of smearing with ashes,
it follows that smearing with ashes is indeed a constituent part of the *Pāśupata-vidyā*.
Since it is understood from the recognition of the mantra that the state of being the door to the destruction of evil is stated in the Jābāla Śruti.

Now, it may be argued that the smearing with ashes, being restricted by its specific context, cannot be subject to promiscuous application (*pāriplava*) merely on the basis of mutual requirement (*apekṣā*), in the absence of a relationship such as that between an archetype and an ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*).
For such a requirement is not included among the means of valid knowledge consisting of direct injunction (*upadeśa*) or extended application (*atideśa*), nor is it the Pāśupata lore itself.

It cannot be said that [this text] is the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), because it does not enumerate the auxiliary sciences (*vidyāṅga*), the auxiliary sciences of the *vidyā* (*vidyāṅga-vidyā*), the auxiliary rituals (*sahakāri-karma*), the contemplation of the destinies (*gati-cintana*), and so forth. For something becomes an archetype only through a complete prescription (*kṛtsna-vidhāna*). Nor is there any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here [to establish such a claim]. Therefore, [the reason you have given] is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

If it is argued that "your inference—that the smearing with ashes is not an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the entire Brahma-vidyā because it is restricted to the context of a specific vidyā, like the eating before a guest—is incorrect," [we reply:

what was stated does not fall within the scope of the authorities of direct injunction (*upadeśa*), extended application (*atideśa*), or other means of knowledge; nor is there [such a restriction] here.

The claim that there exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is incorrect; for the capacity of *apekṣā* (expectancy/requirement) is included within the category of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), since it is rooted in the consideration of functional efficacy. Indeed, it is by that very [capacity] that threshing is established as being common to barley and other grains; otherwise, how could that which is prescribed with rice as its objective referent [be applicable to others]?

There would be a commonality regarding the sacrificial grass (*yavasa*); and by that same [principle], there would be a commonality for those [acts] such as sacrifice, charity, and austerity, as well as tranquility, self-control, and so forth, which are taught in the specific context of particular branches of knowledge, as well as for the stages of the path beginning with the *arcis*, and other similar things.

It is common to all branches of the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Therefore, the capacity for mutual requirement (*apekṣāsāmarthya*) is indeed one means of proof here. Likewise, the scriptural text, "This Pāśupata vow is for the sake of liberation from the bonds of Paśu," is also an authority in that regard; for there, by the word "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), the means to liberation is intended.

It is said that knowledge alone [is the means], just as in the passage, "Verily, this much, my dear, is immortality," the word "immortality" denotes the means to immortality. For in liberation, which is to be accomplished solely by knowledge, the application of sacred ash cannot possibly be a direct means. Thus...

The statement from the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, "One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the head-vow has been performed according to rule," is also an authority in this regard; for there,
by the term "head-vow" (*śirovrata*), the *Pāśupata* vow mentioned in the *Atharvaśiras* is identified.

Therefore, my inference is not inconclusive. As for your inference regarding "being restricted by the context" (*prakaraṇaniyantritatva*), does it mean merely being mentioned in the context, or being governed solely by the specific knowledge (*vidyā*) of that context? In the first case, the reason is inconclusive, because the sacrificial implements (*yajñapātra*) mentioned in the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) are made of *vāraṇa* wood.

Just as the term "yajñāvacara" (used for a sacrificial implement made of *vaikaṅkata* wood) implies its status as a constituent part of the sacrifice by virtue of the sentence (*vākya*), so too, by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and sentence (*vākya*), the smearing with ashes is established as a constituent part of all meditations (*vidyā*). Furthermore, [the reason] would be inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*) with respect to tranquility, self-control, and other such auxiliary rites that accompany the meditations which are themselves constituents of knowledge. In the second case...

The reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). This is because, by virtue of the context, the stronger *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya* [authorities] establish that it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to all meditations (*vidyā*). Now, if it were the case that something bound to one place becomes applicable elsewhere (*pāriplava*) merely through a requirement, then the investigation into the authority of the *codaka* [transfer-rule] would be useless; therefore, this is not so.
That alone is the means of valid cognition. Furthermore, the commonality [of the threshing] does not arise from mere requirement;

rather, since the fact that the rice grains are to be accomplished by threshing—understood through the direct statement of the accusative case—is impossible for rice grains already established in their form as rice, [threshing must be performed].

Therefore, "being for the sake of the *apūrva*" (*apūrvīyatva*) must be indicated by way of being the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, if the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) in the injunction regarding threshing were to refer to rice in general— common to both worldly rice and that which is for the sake of the *apūrva*— then [the injunction would apply] even to worldly rice that lacks any past or future application.

If threshing were considered a primary act (*arthakarma*), it would result in a contradiction of the injunctions, because it would simultaneously be a secondary act (*guṇakarma*) by virtue of being a purificatory refinement applied to rice grains intended for the *apūrva*. Furthermore, if it were restricted solely to ordinary (non-sacrificial) rice, it would entail the subversion of the primacy of the substance as understood through the direct scriptural statement of the accusative case.

For the purpose of avoiding that [objection], the state of being for the sake of the *apūrva* must also be indicated by secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*). In that case, if the generic property of "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) were also intended to be expressed, there would be the fault of a qualified reference (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*).

Therefore, because the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is one and the same, there is commonality [of the term] with respect to both [the specific and the generic]. This applies to sacrifices and the like, as well as tranquility, self-control, and so forth.
In passages such as "They desire to know through sacrifice," the instrumental *śruti* establishes that [tranquility and self-control] are common to all forms of knowledge;

and in the passage "Having become calm and composed, one should see the Self in the very Self," the *ktvā*-suffix *śruti* likewise establishes their commonality to all knowledge. For in those cases, there are the words "desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*) and "should see" (*paśyet*).

Only the knowledge (*vidyā*) itself is taken up [as the subject]. Furthermore, the fact that the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-gati*) is common to all meditations (*sakala-vidyā-sādhāraṇya*) is established by such scriptural passages as, "Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (*tad ya itthaṃ vidur ye ceme 'raṇye śraddhā tapa ity upāsate*). And a direct scriptural statement (*śruti-vākya*) is more authoritative than the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, there is no instance whatsoever where [the path] is not required [by the meditation].

Regarding the application (*viniyoga*): in the phrase "for the sake of liberation from the bonds of *paśu*," the word "liberation" (*vimokṣa*) is not common to all [vidyās] by virtue of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), because it denotes final release (*mukti*). If knowledge (*vidyā*) is to be introduced as a means (*dvāra*), then, in accordance with the context (*prakaraṇa*) and without contradiction, it is appropriate that the very *pāśupata* knowledge under discussion be introduced in that manner.

The statement, "For them alone this [is prescribed]," describes the vow consisting of carrying coals on the head, which is an ancillary part of the study of the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, and not the Pāśupata vow mentioned in the *Atharvaśiras*. In that regard, for the followers of the Atharva Veda...

This is because the term *śirovrata* is well-known [to refer to a specific vow]. Therefore, your inference is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). The second meaning alone is the correct sense of my reason (*hetu*), because, in the absence of any contradiction with *śruti*, *liṅga*, or *vākya*, it is logical that the smearing with ashes (*bhasmoddhūlana*) is governed by the specific knowledge (*vidyā*) within its own context (*prakaraṇa*). If you object to this, we reply: there is the capacity for mutual requirement (*apekṣāsāmarthya*).

It is indeed of that same measure. Precisely because of that, there is the acquisition of properties from elsewhere for those [rites] whose procedure is not fully prescribed; and the postulation of the *codaka* (transfer) statement is rooted solely in that dependence.
However, the discussion on specific extended application (*viśeṣātideśa*) in the eighth book is intended for the purpose of establishing the specific relationship with the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Even for that which is independent [of a specific ritual], if it were to adopt the properties of another, it would follow that *soma* would also adopt the properties of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice. Furthermore, the commonality of *avaghāta* (threshing) with barley is based on dependence alone, not on the definition of being "for the sake of the *apūrva*" (*apūrvīyatva*). This is because the two reasons you have proposed for [resorting to] figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) are untenable.

For instance, the first reason is untenable; because even when the delimitor of the probandum is not present, it is possible for the verbal cognition of the relation between the end and the means to occur, as in the case of rice and threshing, just as it does in the case of heaven and the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. The second [reason] is also untenable.

Although the verbal cognition produced by the sentence regarding threshing has "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) as its qualifier, the threshing enjoined as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) of the rice specified by the heard accusative case-ending cannot appropriately pertain to ordinary rice that lacks utility either for a past or a future purpose.

Because it is possible to understand that the grains intended for the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) constitute the objective domain immediately after the verbal cognition, due to the force of what is to be performed (*vidheya-sāmarthya*). This is as in the case of the text: "For him whose two fires have both gone out, whether by the sun setting or rising, the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is the expiation."
By the principle of the section concerning the failure of the oblation (*havirārtyadhikaraṇa*), since the duality of the fires is not intended to be significant,

although the mere disappearance of the fire is understood to be the occasion (*nimitta*) at the time of verbal comprehension, the establishment (*ādhāna*) enjoined upon that occasion is capable of producing only both fires together, and not each individual fire.
Because it is accepted that, by the force of the grammatical injunction (*vidheya-sāmarthya*), the cause is ultimately restricted to the following of both fires;
for although the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding the statement "one pours curd into heated milk" has as its qualifier only the nature of milk (*payastva-mātra-prakāraka*),
[this is overridden] by the subsequent sentence, "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas."

Furthermore, since it must necessarily be stated that when the connection of milk (*payas*) with the sacrifice is enjoined, by the force of that [injunction], there arises a subsequent verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) through which one understands that the milk related to that *apūrva* is the object [of the injunction];

and because the commonality of sacrifices and so forth, as well as tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth, is not [established] by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)—[as in the case of] "this very [Self]... [the injunction of the means of knowledge is required].

"By the recitation of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, and by austerity, the Brahmins seek to know [Him]," so it is stated in the Śruti; "seeking to know this very one. Therefore, having become thus—tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated—one should see the Self in the self alone; thus it is stated in the Śruti.
And because the phrase "one should see" indicates a connection with the specific vidyā under discussion, [the attainment of Brahman] occurs only through that [vidyā].
Since the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi-gati) is established as being common to all [vidyās] only by way of such dependence, the statement "those who in the forest...
serves as an illustration for the existence of the path beginning with light within the Pañcāgni-vidyā.

[The passage] concerning the coming and going of the individual soul (*jīva*) does not refer to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), because there would otherwise follow the non-existence of the path of the gods (*devayāna-gati*) for that [knowledge], due to the absence of the fruit consisting in the attainment of the divine state. Therefore, in order to establish its existence, when the statement "those who know thus" (*tadya itthaṃ viduḥ*) is to be introduced, [the author] employs the figure of speech *dīpaka* (the illuminator) as an illustration.

The knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is also included [in this context] for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (*paśupāśavimokṣa*); here, the word "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), by the very force of the scripture (*śruti*), is common to all forms of knowledge. This is because the suffix denoting the abstract state (*bhāvārthapratyaya*) has its power present not only in liberation but also in knowledge, since it possesses the suffix denoting the instrument (*karaṇārthapratyaya*). [This applies even to] the head-vow (*śirovrata*).
The statement, "By those by whom it has been performed according to the rule," refers exclusively to the Pāśupata vow described in the *Atharvaśiras*,

because it is explained as such in the *Saura Purāṇa* and other texts; for the meaning of a Vedic revelation (śruti) is to be understood in accordance with its supporting exegesis (upabṛṃhaṇa), and the authority of the Purāṇas is stronger than mere traditional usage among teachers.
Therefore, my inference is not lacking in a logical warrant (*aprayojakatva*), whereas your inference suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished reason (*hetvasiddhi*).

Consequently, it is established that the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*) and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*)—by virtue of removing all sins and, through the purification of the mind, serving as ancillaries to the knowledge of Brahman—are to be worn by the Vīraśaiva seeker of liberation. Thus, everything is concluded.
Thus, the doctrine of the wearing of ashes is established as correct.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Section on Debate within the Śrīvīraśaivānandacandrikā.]
[The Eighth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O Lord, contemplating the extraordinary excellence of your ashes, which inspires such wonder,
I have attained a most profound bliss through your compassion.
Whatever else is to be stated by you, let that be spoken;
listen, O Indra among kings, as the great excellence of the rudrākṣa is proclaimed.

Furthermore, it has been extensively established in all the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Āgamas that the wearing of Rudrākṣas serves as an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman by means of purifying the mind, as it wards off all major and minor sins; therefore, Vīraśaivas who desire liberation must certainly wear them.
It must be performed.
In the Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad: Then Bhusuṇḍa questioned the Blessed Lord Kālāgnirudra, "How did the Rudrākṣa originate, and what is the fruit from wearing it? The Blessed Lord Rudra said to him:

Long ago, at the time of the destruction of Tripura, drops of water fell from his opened eyes onto the earth; these became the Rudrākṣas for the sake of bestowing grace upon all. By the utterance of their names, one obtains the fruit of giving away a thousand cows; by seeing and touching them, the merit is doubled and tripled respectively.
This is the result. Beyond this, I am unable to speak further.
Regarding this, there are these verses: From what is it born? What is its name? And how is it sustained by men?
How many faces do they have here, and what are their mantras? Tell me.
For thousands of divine years my eyes have been open;
from both of them, with their beautiful lashes, drops of water have fallen.
There, the drops of tears became great rudrākṣa trees,
having attained the state of stationary beings for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees.
It destroys sin committed at night during the day, and removes sin committed during the day at night;
by merely seeing it, one gains a hundred thousand merits, and by touching it, ten million.
By upholding it, a person obtains a hundred crore merits,
as well as thousands of lakṣakoṭis and hundreds of lakṣakoṭis.
A person obtains merit from the recitation [of mantras] by wearing rudrākṣa beads;
indeed, there shall be great fruit from wearing auspicious rudrākṣas.
The size of an *dhātrī* fruit is declared by the wise to be the best; that of a *badarī* fruit is said to be the middling.
The lowest [measure] should be the size of a chickpea; this procedure is now being told by me.
By the command of Śiva, there are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Trees born upon the earth that belong to those species have auspicious eyes;
those that are white should be known as Brāhmaṇas, while those of red color are Kṣatriyas.
The Vaiśyas are to be known as yellow, while the Śūdras are declared to be black;
a Brāhmaṇa should wear white [garments], but a king should wear red.
A Vaiśya should wear yellow ones, while a Śūdra should wear black ones;
those that are copper-colored, glossy, firm, thick, and provided with thorns are auspicious.
One should avoid six types of rudrākṣas: those bitten by insects, those that are split or cracked, those devoid of thorns, and those whose circular shape is marred by scars.
During an eclipse, at the equinoxes, likewise at the solstices and during the sun's transition,
on the new moon, on the full moon, and on other auspicious days.
"By wearing rudrākṣas, there shall be the immediate destruction of all sins"—
from such statements in the Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad [it is known that] rudrākṣas belong to Mahādeva, whose gaze was fixed solely upon the destruction of Tripura.

[This refers to] the fact that its extreme purity is established by the water droplets flowing from his three eyes— which possess the quality of being produced [from them]— and that its fruit is of immeasurable extent, since the mere utterance of its name, the sight of it, or the touch of it yields a thousandfold the merit of a gift of a cow, and because its ultimate purpose culminates in the attainment of union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*).

Since it is established that this [text] is a means for achieving the supreme human goal by way of the destruction of all sins, its necessity as something to be retained by those seeking liberation is proven.

But surely, it is heard in scripture that for other [beads] as well—such as lotus seeds and so forth—there are specific individual fruits resulting from their use as means for counting the number of mantra recitations, just as there are for *rudrākṣa* beads. For instance:
"Conch-shell beads bestow prosperity; crystal beads grant liberation."
Lotus seeds bestow nourishment and fortune; rudrākṣas grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Those made of putrajīva bestow an abundance of sons, cattle, and grain;
those of coral grant subjugation and wealth; and those of pearl bring about good fortune and prosperity.
Rosaries made of kuśa grass destroy sins and grant desires; those made of gold and silver likewise do so;
while those made of coral, pearl, and crystal bestow the fruit of ten million recitations.
Even that which has been counted with a Tulasī bead becomes inexhaustible;
for the twice-born who wears a garland produced from Tulasī wood, [the merit is likewise infinite].
Even if one is impure or lacks proper conduct, there is no doubt that he belongs to me alone,
provided he wears a garland made of dhātrī fruits or fashioned from tulasī wood.
That man in whose body these are seen is indeed a devotee of the Lord—
he who wears a garland produced from Tulasī wood.
I bestow upon him a fruit arising from Dvārakā every day,
having offered with devotion a garland made of Tulasī wood to Me.
For that man who carries [this] with devotion, there is no sin here;
I am pleased with him, for he is indeed my foremost devotee.
A mortal, whether a Śūdra or anyone else, who wears a garland made from Tulasī wood upon his chest, or on his arm or hand, becomes equal to a Brāhmaṇa.
Adorned with garlands of Tulasī wood, one should perform meritorious deeds;
for the messengers of the King of the Dead [are terrified] by the garland of Tulasī wood.
Those who see a piece of Tulasī wood— whether dry or fresh— in someone's house flee far away, like grass blown by the wind.
In that house, no sin shall ever arise even in the Kali age;
a rosary fashioned with lotus seeds or with dhātrī fruits out of devotion bestows merit.
And she is adorned with vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), conch shells, and so forth, as well as with tulasī leaves.

This is because of the statements written by authors of the Dharmaśāstras, such as [the one beginning with] "Thus," which declare that the wearing of lotus-seeds (*padmākṣa*) and other [rosaries] is for the purpose of attaining specific fruits; furthermore,
by the Supreme Lord in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, in the meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrti...

By the statement "a crystal rosary, the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), and a book," she is shown to hold them; and by the description "endowed with four arms, holding a rosary made of crystal gems," and so forth, her act of holding them is established; [as it is said] by the sage Nārada: "Shining with a rosary of pure crystal..."
By such [verses] as these, her state of being upheld is described in the *Ambāstava*:

"She who is as bright as the autumnal moonlight, whose crown is a mass of matted hair joined with the moon, and whose hands hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a shield, a crystal rosary, and a book."
Having bowed and offered praise even once, the words of the virtuous— sweet as honey, milk, and grapes— somehow draw them near.

He who meditates upon you in his heart— you who are as white as the autumnal moon, seated upon a lotus throne, your hands marked by the gestures of teaching and holding a crystal rosary, a string of beads, a book, and a water-pot— [attains liberation].
O Mother, he is the emperor of all poets and logicians.

Thus, the divine nature of the goddess is affirmed, and its status as a bestower of liberation is heard from the explicit statement that "the crystal [bead] is the giver of liberation. Now, if it is asked how the wearing of rudrākṣa beads alone can be the means for attaining liberation, the answer is: because of the rudrākṣas...

For among the lotus seeds and other materials enumerated as being produced from the multitude of drops from the eyes of the Supreme Lord himself, as objects to be worn, and as means for attaining specific fruits,
their supreme excellence is heard [in scripture]. Thus, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
For the sake of slaying Tripura and for the protection of the gods,
she assumed the supreme form of the Mother of the Gods, consisting of the science of archery (Dhanurveda).
Having extracted the Gāyatrī as an arrow upon a chariot composed of all the Vedas,
he kept his divine eye perpetually open for a thousand celestial years.
From her two beautiful eyelids, drops of water fell;
those drops of water became great rudrākṣa trees.
Like Śiva, who is worthy of worship by the hosts of gods and asuras,
he shall be invulnerable to all beings and may roam the earth like Rudra.
He who wears the fruits of the rudrākṣa tree upon his limbs,
on whom a line resembling a streak of gold appears when tested on a touchstone—
One should know that lotus-stalk to be supreme; it should be worn by the worshippers of Śiva.
Brahmā is on the back, Hari is in the stalk, and Sadāśiva is at its tip.
And all the gods reside in the filaments; therefore, the rudrākṣa is supreme.
One should wear ten Rudrākṣas on the neck, thirty-six on the head,
six on each ear, twelve on each of the two hands,
sixteen (the digits of the moon) on the two arms, and one single-eyed bead on the crest-lock.
He who recites one hundred and eight [names] upon his chest is himself Nīlakaṇṭha.
A Brahmin should wear Rudrākṣa beads during the Sandhyā rites and other ceremonies;
he always obtains all of that [merit] multiplied by ten million times ten million.
During bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, fire offerings, the Vaiśvadeva rite, worship of the gods, penance, as well as at a Śrāddha ceremony, and especially at the time of initiation;
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, performs any Vedic rite without wearing rudrākṣa beads, he does not obtain the fruit thereof.
Even while eating meat, drinking liquor, or associating with those of the lowest castes,
one’s soul becomes instantly purified if a rudrākṣa bead is placed upon the head.
Therefore, a mortal should wear that rosary of Rudrākṣa beads around his neck for the fulfillment of all rites, even if he is devoid of devotion.
Even a mortal who has committed evil deeds is glorified in the world of Rudra if he wears a rudrākṣa around his neck; even a dog, if it dies while wearing one, attains that same state.
Even he attains the state of Rudra; how much more so, then, humans and others?
In the *Pārāśaropapurāṇa*:
"Mahādeva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are their manifestations;
indeed, all other gods always wear rudrākṣas with devotion."
And all the ancestral sages (gotrarṣis), who are the immovable pillars of their lineages,
are indeed constant wearers of rudrākṣas according to the path declared in the Vedas.
All the sages born in their lineage were indeed pure,
devoted to the Vedic dharma, and wearers of rudrākṣa beads.
Faith does not arise in the most wicked of men toward the wearing of rudrākṣas, which are directly established by the Vedas and grant liberation.
O best of men, by their very nature, a desire for a path independent of the Vedic way arises in those people who are intent on sinful deeds.
Many of the best of sages, being attached to doctrines other than those of the Vedas,
have gone to hell by the command of Śiva, the God of gods.
Many people, devoted to the conduct prescribed by the Vedas,
were liberated from the bonds of worldly existence solely through the grace of Rudra.
Just as a mother is the protector of her own children solely out of compassion,
so too is this Veda the protector of all people.
Just as an enemy person is a direct source of harm to all embodied beings,
so too is any path other than the Veda to a person who follows the Vedic way.
The Tantras are protectors for those established in the Tantras,
yet they are specifically obstacles for those who walk solely upon the path of the Vedas.
Therefore, a follower of the Vedas should certainly adopt the ritual action prescribed by the Śruti;
he should never, even out of delusion, adopt a Siddha-tantra.
One should abandon that which is taught in accordance with [specific] mechanical devices and rituals.
In the Sūtra of Satyāṣāḍha: "Now, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Apabhraṃśas, or those of mixed caste—for all of them..."

The wearing of rudrākṣa beads should be performed with diligence in all rites; if one desires liberation, one should wear them constantly, for they effect the release from the bonds of the individual soul.

According to such scriptural, traditional, Smṛti, and Purāṇic authorities, the wearing of Rudrākṣas is established by virtue of their being produced from the collection of drops of water from the eyes of the Supreme Lord himself,
by virtue of their presiding over all deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and by virtue of their being distinguished by their respective numbers.

Because the retention (*dhāraṇa*) of each respective location brings about non-difference from Śiva; because there is a necessity for retention at the time of performing obligatory and occasional duties (*nitya-naimittika*), as it accomplishes the completeness of the fruit; and because [the fruits] of those [duties] performed without that [retention]...

By virtue of its capacity to render all phenomena fruitless, by virtue of its capacity to effect complete purification through the cessation of all major and minor transgressions, and by virtue of its status as an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman through the accomplishment of success in all ritual actions;

The wearing of rudrākṣa beads is [enjoined] because it is established as a means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) by virtue of its power to liberate from the bonds of *paśu* (the bound soul), because it has been practiced by all the gods and sages beginning with Rudra, and because it is not to be trusted by non-qualified tantric practitioners.

This must necessarily be performed by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), because it is heard in scripture that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in its non-performance, and prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is heard to result from its performance; thus, it is obligatory (*nitya*). Nor is there any excellence [in the gems] due to their being worn by deities, as suggested by the cited statements regarding crystal and other jewels.

It must be stated that [the practice] is distinguished; for it is appropriate to demonstrate that the bearing of those [images], as well as the bearing of Nārada and others, is intended for specific divine pastimes (*līlā*), by virtue of the specific qualities of the respective objects of meditation which bring about specific fruits.
Nor [is this contradicted] by the statement "The crystal bestows liberation," nor by the bearing of the sages such as Nārada who follow that [teaching].

And it should not be said that the quality of bestowing liberation is equal [in both cases], for while the crystal gems' capacity to grant liberation is mentioned in the Purāṇas, even there it is merely occasional; whereas the wearing of Rudrākṣas is extensively practiced and enjoined in numerous Śrutis, Āgamas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas. Therefore, one should follow that [latter authority].
The actual state of affairs is that the very means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which establishes the holding of a crystal is weak.
Thus it is said in the *Uttara-tantra*: "For when there is repetition, there is an abundance of the object's meaning, not even a diminution;
how much less [could there be] a previously expressed meaning? Through the ninefold repetition of 'That thou art,' non-duality alone [is established]."

This is the meaning of the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*). Since it is impossible to claim that its subject matter is anything else, one cannot even postulate that it refers to qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) through the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "you are that" or "by that you are that. Furthermore, the elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktilopa*) is not even present [in the original text].
It must be so conceived. Through repeated practice, as in the case of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) being the Supreme Lord, [the texts state]:

"He reaches this Self consisting of bliss," "He understood that bliss is Brahman," and "The knower of Brahman as bliss fears nothing from anywhere; for who indeed could breathe, who could live, if he were not this [Brahman]?"
