Just as the supreme lordship of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) was determined through repeated practices such as "there would be no bliss in space," so too here, liberation is established through the wearing of rudrākṣas by means of the numerous scriptural, traditional, and puranic statements presented immediately prior, through repeated practice.
The weakness [of the Vedic injunction] is established, as is the frailty of the excellence attributed to crystal gems, due to their being only occasional and thus lacking in repeated practice.
[Thus,

the *Ṣaṭsthalopadeśa*, which is distinguished by one hundred and one unsurpassed sections produced from churning the ocean of the Śāmbhava Āgama obtained through the grace of Tōṇṭada Siddheśvara— the incarnation of the supreme mobile form of the glorious, beginningless, and stainless [Lord],]
[This work was composed] by the eminent teacher Śrī Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows the mass of bliss arising from tasting the nectar of the realization of ultimate reality;
[it concerns] the seizure of the seven constituents of the enemy of the sole hero who caused a tumult among ten million Murāris of the Yādavas, and [the conquest of] the western ocean...

In the instruction of Basava, the Indra of the Earth, who brings joy to the heart of Mallāmbā— the lawful consort of Vīrabhadra, the Lord of the Earth, who is the full moon to the milk-ocean of the Nāyaka lineage, and who is the preceptor for establishing the Śiva-purified Vedic Advaita Siddhānta.
The Eighth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*.
[The Ninth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O Guru, the greatness of the rudrākṣa has delighted my mind in many ways;
therefore, let that which is to be explained hereafter be undertaken by you once more—
namely, O King, the majesty of the jewel of a mantra known as the five-syllabled one (pañcākṣarī).
I shall speak; listen to the *praṇava*, which is preeminent for bestowing the desired goal.

The five-syllable mantra, situated within the middle section of the fourth book (*kāṇḍa*) of the *Yajurveda*— specifically in the eighth section (*aṣṭaka*) of the recited fifth chapter (*prapāṭhaka*)—

is so called because it results in the granting of the fruits desired by all gods, seers, perfected beings (*siddha*), those striving for perfection (*sādhya*), demons (*dānava*), and humans, as well as the attainment of enjoyment and liberation.

The six-syllabled mantra, accompanied by the *praṇava*, is to be worshipped by all; among the seventy million great mantras, it is preeminent as the revealer of the supreme reality (*paratattva*). For it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"There is no other great reality higher than the reality of Śiva."
Likewise, there is no other mantra greater than the five-syllable mantra.
The Śaiva word, which is subtle in its arrival, endowed with few syllables yet of great meaning, is undoubtedly the essence of essences and the sole means to liberation.
O Goddess, having obtained this primordial seed-syllable in its entirety, which bestows all accomplishments, is divine, and illuminates all principles, one [attains the goal].
Just as a banyan seed on the ground is subtler than the subtlest, so too he who possesses this mantra in his speech is none other than I; of this there is no doubt.
In another text: "Among the sciences, the Veda is supreme; among the Vedas, the eleven [Rudra-hymns];
among those, the five-syllabled mantra; and within that, the two syllables of Śivī."
In the *Śivarahasya*: "Having worshipped the *liṅga* with this mantra, one should recite it eight hundred times;
by that, all great mantras are as if already recited—of this there is no doubt."
One should apply ashes consecrated with this mantra after first performing a bath;
by doing so, a person becomes as if bathed in all sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others.
The syllable *Ūṃ* is proclaimed as the king of all mantras;
joined with the five syllables, O Goddess, it is the direct cause of union (*sāyujya*).
In the world, five designations are particularly well-known;
all of these should be understood as being composed of the five syllables.
Through yoga practiced for a long time consisting of the six syllables,
one should be known as liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and shall become a recipient of my grace;
therefore, abandoning everything else, one should mutter the auspicious five-syllabled mantra.
The Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, the Purāṇas, and likewise many mantras;
the various Āgamas, O Goddess, and whatever other seats of knowledge there may be.
They dissolve into the five-syllabled [mantra] and emerge from it again;
they have taken refuge in this heart-pleasing five-syllabled vidyā of mine.
Even in the Kali age, high-souled ones of firm vows are liberated;
for the destruction of great sins, there are these two syllables: "Śi-va."
"The mantra joined with salutation is sufficient and intended for liberation"—
by such statements from the Purāṇas and Āgamas, [the mantra] possesses the status of being the most excellent of all mantras due to its equality with the supreme reality of Śiva.

Because it is contained within the *Rudrādhyāya* recited in the midst of the most excellent of all branches of knowledge (*sarvavidyā*), it is endowed with the word "Śiva"; because by its own recitation it bestows the fruit of reciting all mantras;
and because by bathing in ashes consecrated with it one attains the fruit of bathing at all sacred fords (*tīrtha*). Of this [mantra]...
By virtue of being distinguished by five colors and distinguished by the number five,

[it represents] the five great elements, the five subtle elements, the five principles, the five Brahma-mantras, the five faces, the five fires, the five vital breaths, and the five organs of cognition, as established in the Vedas, Āgamas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas.
[It possesses] the nature of the five organs of action, the five digits (kalā), the five powers (śakti), and the five sheaths (kośa);

it is the locus for the arising and dissolution of all branches of knowledge, beginning with the Vedas; and it is the means for achieving liberation even during the Kali age, which is preponderant in evil.

Since it is heard that the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī) is the means to liberation because it is joined with the word "Śiva" uttered together with the word "Namaḥ," which destroys great sins, it is superior to all mantras and should be worshipped by Vedic seekers of liberation.
Now, an objection may be raised:

since great mantras such as the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa, the six-syllabled mantra of Rāma, and the Narasiṃha mantra— which reside within the Vedas— are heard of as objects of worship for those seeking liberation (mumukṣu), how [is it that they are not considered Śrutipramāṇa]?

The excellence of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarīmantra*) is as follows: among the thirty-two Upaniṣads, in the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, which is distinct from the ten Upaniṣads included therein, it is said: "Ūṃ" is one syllable, "namaḥ" is two syllables, and "nārāyaṇāya" consists of five syllables.

This indeed is the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa. Whoever studies this eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa, being free from falsehood, reaches a full lifespan; he obtains the abundance of offspring, the increase of wealth, and lordship over cattle, and thereafter attains immortality—thereafter he attains immortality. Thus it is said.
Because it is heard that [this knowledge] is a means to liberation, as it is stated: "He who knows this attains immortality," since it is the subject matter expounded in the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad.
In the *Māghamāhātmya*:
"A man who constantly remembers Nārāyaṇa is never afflicted by the bonds of saṃsāra— the sufferings of conception, birth, old age, and disease."
Recite the Nārāyaṇa mantra from this most excellent of histories; chant His auspicious names. Protect the people who have sought refuge in You, and speak what is true and beneficial for humanity.
Meditating on Viṣṇu, who is threefold in relation to the Gāyatrī, one should recite the eight-syllable mantra after bowing to the gods, the brahmins, and the preceptors who stand by the side of Hari.
In the *Rāmatāpanīya*, it is said that the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) recited the mantra of Śrī Rāma in Kāśī,
as well as a thousand other mantras, through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava:
"To you who are about to die and who dwell in half-water at Maṇikarṇikā,
I shall impart the mantra known as the Tāraka-Brahman."
"O Śrī Rāma, Rāma, Rāma—this indeed is called the saving mantra (tāraka).
Therefore, O Lord of Jānakī, you are certainly the Supreme Brahman."

By such statements as these, the Nārāyaṇa-aṣṭākṣara is shown to be the most excellent, because it is enjoined as the remover of all sufferings such as birth and death, and because its necessity for recitation is established through the analogy of the Gāyatrī; and the same applies to the Rāma-ṣaḍakṣarī.

For it is universally acknowledged by all people that this sacred field of Vārāṇasī bestows liberation; indeed, according to the Śruti: "When the vital breaths of a living being are departing from here, Rudra explains the liberating Brahman (tārakaṃ brahma), whereby he becomes immortal and attains liberation. It is in this very place that the Blessed One...

Furthermore, because of the *Laghujābāla-śruti* stating, "Rudra explains the *tāraka-brahman*," and because that [explanation] is finalized by the statement in the *Padma-purāṇa*— which serves as its supplement— that it is the *tāraka-mantra* suitable for instruction into the ears of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) as a means to liberation, it is exactly so.

If it is asked, "Since the *Nṛsiṃha-mantra* is also established in the *Pūrvatāpinī* as a means to liberation, how can it be said that the five-syllabled (*pañcākṣarī*) mantra alone is superior to all?"— to this we reply: [It is so] because of Bodhāyana, Āpastamba, Satyāṣāḍha, Bharadvāja, Vaikhānasa, and others who stand at the very head of all the authors of the Sūtras.

Because it is found in the Taittirīya Śākhā, which is to be studied preceded by the observances (*niyama*) for the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and conclusion (*utsarjana*) of the sections (*kāṇḍa*), and by the performance of the *Āgneyavrata* as prescribed by the six Sūtra-authors known as Gṇiveśya;
and because one who knows the Dharma, having repeated the eleven-fold Rudras, even if touched by great sins—
"He is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. By reciting the Veda once, one is purified on that very day;

by reciting the Rudraikādaśinī, one is purified at that very moment"—thus [it was declared] by Yama, Atri, Aṅgiras, Śātātapa, Yājñavalkya, and others, the sovereigns among the authors of the Smṛtis, regarding Dharma.

Since the authors of the legal treatises have prescribed the "Eleven Rudras" as the expiation for averting great sins (mahāpātaka), and since commentators such as Vijñāneśvara, Mādhava, and Hemādri have likewise explained it in this way, the supreme excellence of the "Eleven Rudras" is established.

If it is asked, "In that case, according to the reasoning already stated, what follows for the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī) regarding its status as the most excellent, since it is the Rudraikādaśanī?"— you are mistaken; for once the excellence of the entire Rudraikādaśanī is established,
the excellence of the five-syllabled mantra recited within it follows by the very logic of "how much more so" (kaimutika-nyāya).

This is established as being like the head upon the body. On the contrary, it is precisely through the application of the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*) that the supremacy of the eleven Rudras is demonstrated. For instance:
the five-syllabled [mantra] shines forth with the word "Śiva," while the Rudras—
Through that meditation it vibrates, and by that vibration the fourth section [of the Veda] shines forth;
through that section all the Yajus-mantras shine, and with that central gem of the Ṛk and Sāman, the Vedas themselves shine resplendent.
Among the sciences, the Vedas are supreme; among the Vedas, the Rudraikādaśinī;
therein, the five-syllabled mantra; and therein, the two syllables "Śi-va."
"This very five-syllabled knowledge resides within the Śatarudrīya;
in the five syllables, Mahādeva is forever perfectly established. Thus it is said.
Therefore, the five-syllabled mantra possesses the state of being supreme among all. Indeed, no such greatness belongs to the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa and others;
nor do the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad, the Rāmatāpanīya, the Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya, and so forth, possess such [greatness] regarding their introductory and concluding sections.
Since the authors of the Kalpasūtras, such as Bodhāyana and others, have not prescribed study preceded by initiation (*āma*), there is no requirement that it must necessarily be studied;
this applies even to a Vīra-Vaiṣṇava who has been consecrated by the five sacraments (*pañcasaṃskāra*).

Furthermore, in the absence of the study of the five-syllable mantra (*pañcākṣarī-mantra*), there is the undesirable consequence that one would be excluded from the company of the twice-born (*apāṅkteya*), due to being counted among the forty-nine types of persons unfit for the company of the twice-born, such as thieves, eunuchs, outcasts, nihilists, those who perform censurable acts, and those who have been expelled from their caste.
Because there is no injunction for the study of the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*, the *Rāmatāpanīya*, or the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya*,

and because there is no sin incurred by not studying them, on the contrary, he who abandons his own Vedic branch (*śākhā*) and takes refuge in another is to be known as a "branch-impotent" (*śākhāṣaṇḍa*).

The phrase "excluded from all ritual acts" (*sarvakarmabahiṣkṛtaḥ*) refers to the fact that by abandoning the study of the *Yajurveda*, one would incur the status of being a "branch-stump" (*śākhāṣaṇḍa*) regarding the study of the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*. Therefore, because the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*) must necessarily be studied and because the commission of sin (*pratyavāya*) is prescribed for its non-study, its status as supreme among all is established.

Now, even if the five-syllabled mantra must necessarily be studied with great effort according to the method already stated, how [can it be considered the cause of liberation], given that— like other mantras recited in the *karmakāṇḍa*— it is merely an auxiliary to sacrifice and serves as a means to achieve perishable fruits such as heaven, and thus lacks the quality of being a cause for liberation?
If it is argued that this [practice] is for the sake of excellence, we say no;
for one should sit in a secluded place that is faultless, fearless, and free from disturbances,
seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), facing either east or north.
With body, head, and neck held straight, free from haste, laziness, and other such faults,
the yogi who meditates on Śiva while reciting the mantra is undoubtedly liberated while living.
Just as Śambhu is the liberator from the fear of *saṃsāra* for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*),

because it is heard in scripture that [the mantra] is the means of accomplishing liberation (*mokṣasādhaka*), it is distinct from the mantras of the *karmakāṇḍa*; nor is it the case that in the Śruti alone, one attains immortality through the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa and others.

If it is argued that because [the five-syllabled mantra] is heard in such passages as these to be a means to liberation (*mokṣasādhanatva*), whereas the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī-mantra*) is not so heard in the Śruti, its status as a means to liberation is therefore merely doubtful—[we reply: No;
for [it is said], "Then the students (*brahmacārin*) said to him: 'Tell us, by what recitation (*japya*) does one attain immortality (*amṛtatva*)? He..."

Yājñavalkya said: "By means of the Śatarudrīya. Indeed, these are the names of the immortals; by means of these, one becomes immortal. According to this statement from the *Laghujābālopaniṣad*, he who studies the Śatarudrīya becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind.
One becomes purified from drinking liquor; one becomes purified from what should and should not be done; one becomes liberated from all bonds.
Therefore, one who has taken refuge in the Unliberated (Avimukta) should always, or at least once, recite [this].
By this, one attains the knowledge that destroys the ocean of saṃsāra. Having understood it thus, therefore...
He attains the state of absolute liberation; he attains the state of absolute liberation.

Furthermore, because it is clearly heard in the statement of the Kaivalyopaniṣad that the Śatarudrīya is a means to liberation, there is no dispute whatsoever regarding the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī) being a means to liberation. Moreover—

The five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī) possesses the status of being supreme among all [mantras] because it is uttered in conjunction with the word "Śiva," which reveals the reality of the supreme Śiva— who is devoid of qualities and transcends all principles— and which makes known its unique greatness that is not shared by others.

In this context, the word *śiva* signifies "beautiful" (*śobhana*), according to the *Amarakośa*: "The words *śreya*, *śiva*, *bhadra*, *kalyāṇa*, *maṅgala*, and *śubha* [all mean auspicious]. He is *Śiva* because he possesses beautiful qualities such as omniscience and the like; the suffix *ac* is applied here because the group beginning with *arśas* (*arśādi*) is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

By way of the figure of speech *hetvalaṅkāra* (poetic cause) or through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), omniscience and the other [perfections] are twofold—distinguished as the limbs (*aṅga*) and the imperishables (*avyaya*)—as established in the *Śivapurāṇa* and the *Āgamas*. As it has been said:
"Omniscience, contentment, primordial awakening..."
O wise ones, the knowers of the ritual declare that the six limbs of Maheśvara are: sovereignty, eternality, unimpaired power, and infinite power, O All-pervading One.
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forbearance, fortitude, the power of creation, self-awakening, and indeed the state of being the presiding controller.
"These ten indeclinables always abide in Śaṅkara. Thus [it is said].

Although qualities cannot exist in Paraśiva because he is partless (*niṣkala*), as stated in the Śruti: "He is actionless, partless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless," and according to the Vātulaśuddha: "O Mahāsena, the principle of Śiva is proclaimed to be partless," nevertheless, for the sake of creation—

"Because it is the cause of the arising of all principles (tattva) for the world, the body is assumed by its own will for the benefit of yogins. Likewise, in that very same [text]: "For the sake of recitation and worship for yogins, ascetics, men of knowledge, and even mantra-practitioners, the partless (niṣkala) becomes possessed of parts (sakala)."

The designation [of Śiva as "Śubha"] is made by taking up the qualities fashioned by the supreme Śakti who rests upon Him, according to the words of the *Vātulaśuddha*. Alternatively, Śiva is "Śubha" because of his auspiciousness (*śobhanatva*). And this auspiciousness consists in the purity characterized by the absence of the three impurities known as *āṇava*, *kārmika*, and *māyeya*, which reside in all living beings.

Purity (*śuddhatva*) is *saṇam*. *Aṇu* is the individual soul (*jīva*). Its beginningless connection with ignorance (*avidyā*), which brings about the state of being a soul, is the *āṇava-mala* (the atomic impurity). Or, the *kārmaṇa-mala* (the karmic impurity) consists of the impressions (*vāsanā*) that are the fruit of beginningless karma. [The *māyīya-mala* is the notion that] when the conditions for the empirical usage "it exists" and "it shines" are present, one thinks "it does not exist" or "it does not shine."

When the totality of conditions for empirical transaction (*vyavahāra-sāmagrī*) is absent, there is neither existence nor manifestation; thus, this obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), which consists in the state of being unfit for empirical transaction, is known as *māyīya-mala*. This is well-established in all the Śiva-āgamas. Due to the absence of these three kinds of impurities, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—which is not subject to karma—is omniscient and pure.
It is possible, as it has been stated in the Vāyusaṃhitā:
"Alternatively, the Lord is the singular mass of all auspicious qualities without exception."
He is called Śiva by the virtuous who know the true meaning of the principle of Śiva.
"Because it is by its very nature free from the connection with the stains of beginningless impurity, and because its essence is absolutely pure, it is therefore called Śiva. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in another passage of that same work, it is said: "The pure one shines as Śiva.

It is also stated in the *Vātulaśuddha*: "Because of his purity, he is called Śiva. Alternatively, Śiva is so called because "everything rests (*śete*) within him," since Paramaśiva, like the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) which is the cause of all things, serves as their substratum.

Because he is the support of the world. [The word] *asvatantra* (dependent) is formed correctly through an irregular *uṇādi* derivation (*nipātana*) from the verbal root *tan* with the prefix *pra*, applied to words such as *śarva*, *nīghṛṣva*, *riṣva*, *laṣva*, *śiva*, *paṭva*, and *prahva*. He who, being one, presides over every womb, in whom this [world]...

"He perceives the universe through true discernment; having realized that Lord, the boon-granting God who is worthy of praise, he attains this ultimate peace"—so says the Śruti. Alternatively, He is called Śiva because "he is tranquil" (śāmyati).
According to the Jainendra Vyākaraṇa sūtra, "śivādayaśca," the form [Śiva] is derived by adding the suffix *kvanip* and applying the elision (*lop*) of the vowel.

The meaning is "changeless. This is because of the Vedic scripture: "Actionless, partless, tranquil; three-eyed, blue-throated, perfectly peaceful. Alternatively, [the term] *śiva* is derived from the root *vaś* (meaning "to desire") with the suffix *ac*, followed by a transposition of letters (*varṇavyatyaya*) according to the rule for *pṛṣodarādi* compounds, whereby the vowel *a* [is replaced].
And when the substitution of the vowel *i* occurs, the form is *śiva*. According to the statement of the learned: "The word *siṃha* is derived from the root *hiṃs* (to injure);

*śiva* is traditionally remembered [as derived] from the root *vaś* (to desire); and *kaśyapa* is established through the transposition of phonemes, as in the case of *paśyaka* (one who sees)," its meaning is "the locus of His will. This is so even though [the suffix] is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

Since the grammatical rule *kṛd* prescribes that the agenthood [denoted by a *kṛt* suffix] consists in being the locus of an effort (*kṛti*) directed toward the meaning of the verbal root, it follows that in the present case, the suffix *ac* (as in *jña*, etc.

cannot have "locus" as its meaning; nevertheless, because there is no effort whose object is cognition and so forth, the agent-suffixes following roots that denote cognition and the like [do not signify an agent].

In such expressions as "he knows," "he desires," and "he exerts effort," since [the self] is universally accepted as the indicator of the locus [of these states], they ultimately resolve into being the locus of desire. And that desire is indeed non-different from the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) of Śiva, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). For it is heard in scripture: "His supreme power is indeed manifold and innate."
And because of the scriptural statement, "the activity of the power of knowledge," it is also stated in the *Vātulaśuddha*:
"In that Śiva, however, is the supreme power (*parā śakti*) arising from a thousandth part [of the Absolute];
from a thousandth part of the supreme power, the primordial power (*ādiśakti*) arises."
From a thousandth part of the primordial power (Ādi-śakti), the power of will (Icchā-śakti) arises;
from a thousandth part of the power of will, the power of knowledge (Jñāna-śakti) arises.
From a thousandth part of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti) arises;
thus it is said: "The supreme Śaiva power is the Command (ājñā), whose nature is consciousness (cid-rūpā) and which belongs to the Supreme Lord."
When Śiva remains [in union], by means of her who has become his instrument,
there arises within him the supreme power called Will (Icchā), mounted upon the circle of his lap;
she is renowned as Mahālakṣmī, dark-hued and enchanting to all.

This is also because of the statement in the Śivapurāṇa. However, while it must be stated that Paramaśiva, who has the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) as his substratum, is himself directly the substratum [of the other powers], the statement that he is the substratum of the power of will (icchāśakti)—which can only be somehow justified through non-difference from her—is made. Alternatively, Śiva is so called because he desires the welfare of the world (*vaṣṭi lokahitam iti śivaḥ*).
The derivation of the form is as before. Because he constantly promotes the undertaking of all goals for those humans who desire auspiciousness, he is therefore called Sadāśiva.

Thus it is stated in the Mahābhārata. Alternatively, he is called Śiva because he makes (karoti) what is auspicious (śivam); this form is derived from the root *śiv* with the suffix *ṇic* (indicating "he performs that") followed by the *ac* suffix (*pacādyac*). And so says the Śruti: "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the maker of auspiciousness; one should abandon everything else. It is also said in the Mahābhārata:
"All Dānavas and gods are equal to me;
I am Śiva to all beings, and therefore, O gods, the Śiva-principle is mine. Thus it is said. Here is the summary verse for this:

In Him the world rests; He desires it, bestows the highest good upon His creatures, and attains peace; He is the limit of the entire multitude of auspicious qualities, possesses the power of will, and remains eternally pure by His very nature.
"Salutation to that Supreme One whose life-story explains the name of Śiva. Thus [it is said].
The word "Śiva" possesses its intended meaning (tātparya) regarding as many meanings as have been shown; for when it is employed for the purpose of a hymn, the inclusion of praise in its many forms—
namely, the inclusion of meanings appropriate to that function within the words found in various remaining verses of poetry— is indeed a merit.

Thus, it is entirely appropriate that the presentation of these etymological meanings (*yogārtha*) by means of conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*) is intended to demonstrate the uniqueness of those etymological meanings, as if they were conventional.
This applies even to purely etymological terms such as *bhaktavatsala* ("affectionate toward devotees") and the like.
From the very fact that the reading is conjoined with conventional names, it is quite clear that [the term] intends to convey a meaning common to both [conventional and etymological] applications.
Thus, in this context, there are words such as *bhaktavatsala* ("affectionate toward devotees") which are directed toward a unique etymological meaning.

The intention is that [his] self-interest is unique. Although there are others who are likewise affectionate toward their devotees (*bhaktavatsala*), nevertheless they are not as affectionate toward their devotees as Śiva is; for, when providing a justification based on the view that his affection is of a different kind, there would be an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) of distinction, which consists in describing that very thing as being otherwise.

This is the figure of speech called *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) characterized by non-difference (*abhedaka*) as previously defined. Furthermore, when the support [of the statement] is established through the perspective of concealment (*apalāpa*), asserting that "only Śiva possesses affection for his devotees (*bhaktavātsalya*), and no one else whatsoever possesses it," even though there is a connection (*yoga*), the absence of connection (*ayoga*) is expressed;
thus, the figure of speech called *sambandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of relation), as defined above, is also suggested.

This is the general direction. In all these names, because the various wondrous sentiments (*rasa*) suggested therein serve as adjuncts to the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) of love directed toward the Supreme Lord, they should be understood as instances of the *rasavat* figure of speech.
Among them, in this particular name, there is the single figure of speech known as *śleṣa* (punning), which rests upon multiple meanings.

For the definition of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is that it has as its locus both the subject being described and the subject not being described. And this is the first type [of *śleṣa*], because its scope is restricted to a single phoneme (*varṇa*). Furthermore, according to the etymological derivation "He in whom the world lies" (*śete 'smin jagat*), that which is well-known as the "world" (*jagat*)—extremely vast as it may be—lies within Him, existing therein without obstruction.

Thus, by implication, this is the figure of speech *adhikālaṅkāra* (excess). For its definition states: "When there is an excess of the substratum over the thing contained within it, that too is considered [adhikālaṅkāra]. Therefore, because it is based on such a state of possessing pervasive magnitude, it gives rise to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of wonder (*adbhuta*).

Because it serves as a constituent of the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) consisting of delight directed toward the Supreme Lord, there is the figure of speech *rasavat* (possessing flavor), for its definition is that "when flavor (*rasa*) functions as a subordinate element, it is the figure *rasavat*. In the justification of the use of the word *śiva*— which denotes auspiciousness—
in the sense of "one who brings about welfare" (*śivaṅkara*) through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of signifying its cause, there is the figure of speech *hetu* (cause).
Some declare that the identity of the cause and the effect constitutes the definition of "cause" (hetu); therefore,

it cannot be argued that because the word *śiva* denotes auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), its gender would necessarily be neuter when used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) for its cause, rather than masculine, for there is no established rule regarding the gender of the primary meaning (*śakya-liṅga*) for words used in a figurative sense.

For in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ), even though that [gender] exists there in some instances, it is universally accepted that there is no such restriction when words expressing qualities (guṇavacana) imply a relation to a substance (atvartha-lakṣaṇā), nor when all [words] imply a connection with a male (puṃyoga-lakṣaṇā). Furthermore, in the case of a connection with a male... [the rule does not apply].

[Objection: It is the *prakṛti* that possesses the feminine characteristic; however, it must be stated that the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) itself denotes the female gender related to the meaning of the *prakṛti*. If that were the case, then since the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) [denoting possession] in the sense of "belonging to this" would not otherwise apply, its introduction by the suffix *ṅīṣ* would result in the sublation of that [secondary suffix]. Nevertheless, [the form] *prāṣṭī* [is derived as follows].

Because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the forms ending in *taddhita* suffixes could not be established. Therefore, when the base itself (*prakṛti*)— by virtue of its association with that [suffix]—
occurs through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote a female related to it, then [the rule applies] to that which is feminine.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that for this [word *strī*], the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by its own force (*svārthika*), as prescribed under the heading of the feminine gender (*stryadhikāra*).

This is clearly set forth in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *puṃyoga* rule: "A word for something may be applied to what is not that thing in four ways: because of identity with it (*tātsyāt*), because of possessing its qualities (*tāddharmyāt*), because of proximity to it (*tatsāmīpyāt*)," and so forth.

This is stated by the passage beginning with "due to their coexistence" (*tatsāhacaryāt*), and it is also clear in the *Padamañjarī*. Furthermore, there is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of these three; or rather, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) characterized by the entry of multiple figures into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*).
Even though two figures may exist in the very same instance of combination because of the application of two definitions, [it is still considered a case of commingling].
The commixture (*saṅkara*) of these two occurs through their entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*). For example:
"By means of basins for the trees constructed from moonstones, which have received floods of oozing moisture from the embrace of the moon..."

Because the watering of the trees had been rendered fruitless due to the lack of respect for the causal conditions [of water], the forest of Damayantī was fashioned there as if from the hearts of her friends;

herein lies the figure of speech *udātta* (the sublime), consisting of a description of a magnificent reality— the depiction of the overflowing of crystal basins caused by their connection with moonlight.

Because there is the presence of both the figure of speech *asambandhe sambandharūpātiśayoktiḥ* (poetic fancy consisting of a relation where no relation exists) and [the *śiva* word-play], there is a *saṅkara* (commixture) characterized by their entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*). However, in this case, although the *rasavad-alaṅkāra* (sentimental ornament) exists in the connection "He lies here, therefore the world is Śiva," within that connection there is another connection.

Furthermore, while *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs by being distributed [over multiple meanings], and the figure of speech *hetu* (poetic cause) occurs only in relation to a specific connection [between cause and effect], there is indeed a disparity; nevertheless, the commingling (*saṅkara*) through the entry into a single expressive word remains entirely unimpeded.
For instance, even in the verse cited:

The unity of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) in which two ornaments are being blended is not the cause of the aforementioned blending (*saṅkara*). For if that were the case, the designations would have been "blending through the entry into a single expressive word" (*ekavācakānupraveśa-saṅkara*),
"blending through grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya-saṅkara*), and so forth, rather than [the current ones].

Although it is constituted by the identity of the expressive word (*vācaka*), however, the very factor that causes the aforementioned commingling (*saṅkara*) is the identity of the single [word] that presents the relation serving as the locus for the two figures being commingled; for this alone conforms to the meaning of the term "interpenetration of a single expressive word" (*ekavācakānupraveśa*). And that—

In some cases there is identity of relation, while in others there is its difference; this is another matter. In the present context, within a single expressive word-form "Śiva," *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs by virtue of being the locus for two relations presented by that word.
Because they reside in a single relation presented by that [word], the figures of speech *rasavat* and *ālambana* have entered into [the structure] as subordinate elements.

It is indeed appropriate that there be a commingling (*saṃkara*) through the entry of both [the *rasavat* and the *alaṃkāra*] into a single expressive word; let it be, however, that the commingling through the entry of a *rasavat* figure and another figure into a single expressive word occurs even partially. Enough of this digression following upon a digression.

And this [name] is established by Śruti; for it is well-known from many Śruti passages such as: "Obeisance to Śiva and to the one more auspicious than Śiva," "Therefore Śiva is omnipresent," and "Neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone is absolute. Furthermore, His majesty is also established by Śruti, as in: "Or even if he be a Caṇḍāla..."
For the Śruti declares: "One should utter the word 'Śiva,' one should converse with him, and one should eat together with him.
That two-syllabled name, when uttered by a mountain, swiftly destroys the sins of men even through a single incidental mention.
Alas, you, being other than auspicious, hate that Śiva, whose fame is pure and whose command is inviolable!
The two-syllable mantra "Śi-va," joined with the salutation "Namaḥ," is sufficient as a mantra ordained for the destruction of great sins and for the sake of liberation.

From such passages in the Śruti, Bhāgavata, and Purāṇas, those who know the Śiva-āgamas employ the term "jewel of living beings" (jīvaratna) for this very name and for the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara-mantra) composed of the name of Śiva. Therefore, for those who perceive Śiva in their hearts together with that Power (Śakti), there is eternal peace, and not for others.
According to the method described in the Śiva Purāṇa,

the superiority of this name is established by its being the proponent of Śrī Sāmba Śiva— who transcends all principles (tattvas) and is the cause of all auspiciousness— thereby making it the most excellent of all.
Even from the employment of such names of Śiva in conjunction with the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī), [great merit is obtained].

Furthermore, [it consists of] the letters Na, Ma, Śa, Va, Ya, and Ra, which are non-different from the forms of the Tāraka (Om), the Staff, the Earring, the Half-moon, and the Bindu— these being Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, who constitute the parts of the Praṇava and with whom one has attained identity.
By virtue of its refinement, the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī) shares a structural similarity with the *praṇava*, which expresses the supreme reality (*paratattva*);
and the *praṇava* itself consists of six forms— namely, the letters *a*, *u*, *m* (bindu), *nāda*, *kalā*, and *sattā*—
and is composed of six *kalās* known as Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, Śāntyatītā, and Uttarā.

[This belongs] to that which consists of the six powers known as the supreme consciousness— namely action, knowledge, will, and so forth— and which possesses the form of the six *sādākhya*s: the *sādākhya* of action (*karma-sādākhya*), the *sādākhya* of the agent (*kartṛ-sādākhya*), the *sādākhya* of the embodied (*mūrta-sādākhya*), the *sādākhya* of the unembodied (*amūrta-sādākhya*), the *sādākhya* of Śiva (*śiva-sādākhya*), and the *sādākhya* named *mahā-sādākhya*.
To him whose nature consists of the six faces named Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna, and Gopya;

and who possesses the form of six hands called Sucitta (Good Mind), Subuddhi (Good Intellect), Sumanas (Good Thought), Sujñāna (Good Knowledge), Nirahaṅkāra (Free from Ego), and Sadbhāva (True Being).
[He is] of the nature of the sixfold devotion consisting of faith, steadfastness, attentiveness, equanimity, bliss, and direct experience;
and he is of the nature of the sixfold liṅgas known as the conduct-liṅga, the guru-liṅga, the Śiva-liṅga, the *cara*-liṅga, the grace-liṅga, and the great-liṅga.
[Salutation] to that which consists of the sixfold limbs: [the devotee], the one graced by Maheśvara, the one whose life-force is the *liṅga*, the refuge, the unity, and the form;
[to that which consists of] the six sense organs in the form of the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, ears, and mind;
and [to that which consists of] the six objects in the form of fragrance, taste, form, touch, sound, and satisfaction.
[He is] the one whose nature consists of six limbs known as omniscience, eternal satisfaction, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, the state of being unimpeded, and infinite power;
[he is] the one whose form consists of the sixfold path (adhvan) composed of phonemes, words, mantras, worlds, principles (tattva), and kalās;
[and he is] the one [residing in] the mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūraka, ... [chakras].
[This is] the abode of the six cakras designated as the command of the purified hatas,
and the dwelling place of the six elements known as blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen;
[it is so described] because it possesses both collective and individual forms, as do the others.
Since other mantras lack such an extraordinary degree of majesty, the five-syllabled mantra alone possesses supremacy over all.

For this very reason, the five-syllabled mantra is conventionally designated as the "Jīvaratna" (the jewel of living beings). This is due to its beginning with the *praṇava* (OM), its association with the word *namaḥ*, and its Vedic character.

[He is] one who has mastered the fourfold classification of mantras— namely *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*— along with their four intermediate subdivisions as taught in the treatises on mantra such as the *Śāradātilaka* and *Prapañcasāra*, which reveal the mantras and deities of the gods;

and [he is one who knows] the ten types of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) regarding the states of debtor and creditor within the grids of the planets, lunar mansions, and elements, as well as defects such as those of sleep and so forth.

Its supremacy over all else is also due to its independence from discursive thought (*avicāra*). Even for children, at the very first moment of beginning their education, the authors of treatises such as Kamalākara have prescribed that the instruction of the five-syllable mantra *oṃ namaḥ śivāya*— ending in *namaḥ* and preceded by the *praṇava*— must be performed.

Because [the text] beginning with "vinīya" prescribes that even women and Śūdras may be taught the Vedic recitation in its inverted order, and because it prescribes that [this mantra] is to be chanted by all,
and because it possesses meaning through the connection of action and its factors (kriyākāraka), therefore, [it applies] specifically to the five-syllabled mantra.
"Supremacy over all" and "all is delightful"—this is the contemplation on the five-syllable mantra.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the section on debate within the *Śrīvīraśaivānandacandrikā*.]
[The Tenth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
In ancient times, it was clearly established within the assembly hall of the Pramathas, such as Basaveśa and others, by one named Kalaketu Brahmā, who was possessed of virtuous conduct.
O venerable Guru, having drunk in from the hollows of my ears the majesty of the eight enclosures (aṣṭāvaraṇa) as proclaimed by you, I have become filled with joy in manifold ways.
In some way, there is the refutation of even those non-Vedic doctrines that are not contradictory [to reason],
by means of arguments imbued with the meaning of the Vedic scriptures.
O King, demonstrate to me in due order how that was performed; may your wisdom nourish our satisfaction.
Having obtained such skill of intellect through the grace of Mahādeva,
I shall first begin with the refutation of non-Vedic doctrines.

Since the entire range of objects of knowledge is established through direct perception and universal experience, even in my own view, [the truth] is found within the Vedas, scriptures, and so forth, in accordance with my own [position].
Having fabricated a pretext for the sake of enticing others.
O most excellent of the virtuous, please express some opinion of your own that is worthy of laughter;
how indeed could there be such a feat of illusion here?
In its own nature, this is the accomplishment of what is desired by you.
O King of Kings, with a mind free from doubt, I declare that such is the well-expounded doctrine of the Lokāyatas as it was being propounded by the eminent Bhṛṅgin.
It has not yet become an object for the path of my ears.
Among those, there are three non-Vedic systems of thought, distinguished as Lokāyata, Ārhata, and Bauddha.
Therein, the Cārvākas, who are synonymous with the Lokāyatas, assert the following: "Earth, water, fire, and air are the four elements;
there is nothing else. By their very nature, jars and other such things are merely transformations of those [elements]. Infancy..."

The body itself—distinguished by the states of infancy, youth, and old age—is the self; there is no self distinct from it. If one were to admit that there exists a self separate from the body, then someone distinct from the body would be perceived being led away by the messengers of Yama while crying out, like a man being led away by the king’s soldiers.

Since [a self] is not perceived, the body itself is the self. Consciousness arises spontaneously within the body—a transformation of a collection of inert elements—just as red color arises from the combination of betel nut, leaf, lime powder, and saliva.
Living while existing is itself the natural cycle of transmigration; it is not dependent on anything else, even for one who does not desire it.

Liberation, which is of the nature of death, is attained by itself; therefore, a wise person should not exert himself in vain for its sake. Only things such as jars, which are perceived through direct observation, are real.
That which is unseen is not accepted [as real] precisely because it is not seen—this is also the view of others.
That which consists of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) is not conventionally designated as "seen," because there is a contradiction between being seen and being unseen.
Nor [is it so designated] on account of its being the cause of the observed variety in the experience of pleasure and pain, which are its effects.

It must be said that the postulation of an unseen force (adṛṣṭa) in the form of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) is not logical, because the diversity in the experience of pleasure and pain is established solely through the power of specific intrinsic natures (svabhāva-viśeṣa), without any dependence on the postulation of such a merit and demerit which, like the horn of a hare, is a mere fiction.
For this very reason, there is whiteness in the crane, blackness in the crow, greenness in the parrot,
a variety of colors in the peacock's plumage, the fifth note in the cuckoo, the red crest on the cock,
the presence of eyes on the ears in serpents, and a long neck in the camel.

This is established solely by virtue of the specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) [of things]; otherwise, one would have to postulate many distinct types of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) as the root of those various diversities. Thus, [this applies] to solidity in earth, coldness in water, and upward flaming and hot touch in fire.

Furthermore, regarding the touch of wind as being neither hot nor cold, we perceive no cause other than its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, one should not even postulate an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) consisting of merit and demerit, fashioned by prescribed and prohibited actions. That which is desired is the prescribed action; that which is undesired is [the prohibited].

That is prohibited action. An unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by these two types of actions is not perceived. It is claimed that there exists another world called heaven and hell, distinct from this world which is the means for the direct experience of pleasure and pain, and serving as the locus for the experience of pleasure and pain.

This is merely a fabrication of the cunning. The enjoyment of fine food, young women, linen garments, sandalwood, and the like—along with a favorable location—is heaven; whereas being beset by enemies, disease, hunger, and other calamities, or being in an unfavorable location, is hell. If water located at a distance were the sacred bathing site (*tīrtha*), and if images made of clay, wood, stone, copper, and so forth were the deity.
In that case, even a fish would attain purity by bathing in a sacred ford; even a crane would be liberated there through meditation; even a mute would become a sage by practicing silence;
even a jackal would become a knower of the Self through chanting; and even a bear [would become pure] due to the absence of clipping its claws and hair.
One may attain celibacy; even a moth, by entering the midst of a blazing fire, may achieve the great vow;
even a tortoise, through the absence of sexual union, may reach mastery over the senses;
even a serpent, by subsisting on air, may become a yogi; and even those who are deaf and so forth [may likewise attain perfection].

By turning away from listening to songs, instrumental music, and the like, they may attain a state of dispassion; [others] may attain the state of an ascetic by eating sand like a pigeon, by drinking drops of water like a *cātaka* bird, by eating fruit like monkeys and others,
by grazing on grass like cattle and others, and by feeding on grains like ants.
Furthermore, by drinking blood, aquatic creatures; by committing incest, beasts, birds, and wild animals; and by eating what is forbidden to eat, humans would incur rebirth in hell.
Yet, on this basis alone, one should not postulate merit and demerit as the causes of their pleasure and pain.

Therefore, one should not undergo useless exertion through austerities such as restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), vows (*vrata*), and fasting, which are achieved by means of bodily suffering. For this very reason, there exists a certain self distinct from the body,
and it [attains] heaven through specific meritorious actions.

By those who concoct such inconsistent arguments— claiming that one goes to hell due to the performance of evil deeds, or attains the earth through a mixture of merit and sin; and who, while being in fact nihilists, are rogues who consider themselves believers, feeding on the sweets of hope that heaven and other realms exist at the end of the body.

The truth-telling Cārvāka is treated as a nihilist (*nāstika*). Just as even a highly skilled artisan cannot turn a pot into a cloth, so too a deceitful person cannot, by mere whim, make us—who speak things as they truly are—into nihilists. Even though...

Although heaven and such things, being beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition known as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), do not exist at all, nevertheless— relying on the principle that "one should instruct another by means of what is already established for that other person"— and accepting the afterlife as it is accepted by others,
and accepting the authority of verbal testimony (*śabda*) as it is accepted by others, the identity of the body with the self (*dehātmatva*) is established.

For instance, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with "Indra indeed went forth from among the gods, and Virocana from among the asuras," and having stated that he dwelt in studentship for thirty-two years, it says, starting with "That which is the Self," [describing how] they prepare the body of the deceased with food, clothing, and ornaments.

For by this [passage] ending with "they think they will conquer that world," Virocana is shown to have acquired the knowledge of the body as the Self upon hearing [it]. Likewise, in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], there is the statement: "This Self, this is the tail, the support," and "Of this Self, half indeed is the wife. Similarly, in the passage concerning the Śūlagava sacrifice:

In the *Karma* [Purāṇa], by the passage beginning "To him whose head is that [which is worshipped] in the body of a porpoise," the very body is designated by the word "Self" (*ātman*). Likewise, according to the followers of the Mādhva school, the conscious body (*cid-deha*) alone is established as the Self. Similarly, for those who assert "All is the Self," based on the scriptural teaching of universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*), [the Self is present] even in objects such as jars.

Because its meaning is sublated, the notion of selfhood terminates at the mere body; otherwise, there would be the consequence of invalidity, as in the case of such statements as "stones float. [This is evident in] such cognitions as "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am happy," or "I am miserable."
The [scriptural statements] that it is "neither atomic nor gross, neither short nor long" and so forth, which are sublated by direct perception,

must be understood as being like the non-difference [of the Self from the body], which is sublated by the perceptual experience of difference. If it were accepted that the Self is distinct from the body and is beginningless, then for that [Self], whose nature is eternally liberated, transmigratory existence would be adventitious.

What is its basis? If cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) were also beginningless, then like the self (*ātman*), it would follow that cyclic existence is eternal. If, on the other hand, it is the stream [of existence] that is beginningless, then there would be no destruction even during the dissolution (*pralaya*).
If the dissolution itself were also beginningless as a stream, then the stability of the world would never occur at all.

For it is so stated in the Smṛti: "When the time for reabsorption arrives, all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state at the end of the [current] Brahmā. Thus, at the time of liberation from previous Brahmās who have passed away, [the liberated souls enter].

Since it must necessarily be asserted that infinite souls are liberated simultaneously, and since— according to your own reasoning— it is impossible to assert that liberated souls can again enter into the cycle of existence (*saṃsṛti*), the current state of *saṃsāra* itself is difficult to establish. This is especially so if many souls from the past have already been liberated.

Even if it were granted that for the Brahmas in Satyaloka and other realms there is merely the experience of their own bliss, and even if such a state were admitted to be a result of ritual injunction (*vidhi*), it must still be accepted that their liberation is not yet universal, nor is the concomitant state of liberation necessarily attained; for the existence of *saṃsāra*, which obstructs the liberation of infinite living beings, persists. This would be the case for those of short lifespan.

Even though living beings have repeatedly performed hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption— which serve as the means for liberation— preceded by the observance of prescribed conduct consisting largely of physical austerities throughout their many past and endless births, along with both gross and subtle forms of worship;
Because liberation is non-existent, even if those means [of attainment] exist hereafter, there would be no liberation at all;

for such a liberation would be like the mere scent of a sweetmeat. For this very reason, since it would follow that the liberation of one entails the liberation of all, there would be no liberation even for a single individual, such as Vasiṣṭha or Vāmadeva.
Since liberation in the form of identity with that single Brahman— which is replete with all means of attainment— is easily accessible even to the deluded who act according to their whims,
therefore all the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth, which set forth those specific means of attainment [are necessary].

The established position is that [the self] is merely a fabrication of the cunning. Therefore, since many refutations remain active against the view that the self is distinct from the body, it is proven that the body alone is the self and nothing else;
for even if the authority of the Vedas and other scriptures were accepted, they would result in fruitless exertion, as one could act according to one's own whims.

The delusion that a fraudulent person has established the authority of a teaching whose content is contradicted by direct perception serves merely to deceive the world. For this very reason, the statement of the Purāṇas—that "in each Manvantara, a different Śruti is ordained"—is perfectly consistent. Moreover, in every Manvantara...

The deities such as Indra, who are honored through virtuous rites consisting of fire-offerings, worship, and meditation— namely the Munis, Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, who appear differently in the [Manvantaras] beginning with Svāyambhuva— their respective illuminating mantras must be recited individually; thus, the Ṛgveda is indeed composed of ten maṇḍalas by Viśvāmitra and others.
Furthermore, the claim that the Veda was composed by others such as Vedavyāsa and Kaṇāda-Gautama,
rather than by the Supreme Self, is a false statement. Since this Veda contains matters contradicted by direct perception, how could it be said to have been uttered by the Self?

Having begun with the statement, "In the case of a Brahmin, one should offer [the oblation] into the hand of a goat, into a clump of *darbha* grass, or into water," it concludes with, "In this way, his *agnihotra* is performed even in the fire itself";
thus, the goat, the hand of a sheep, the clump of *darbha* grass, and the water are all alternatives distinct from the [sacrificial] fire.

The demonstration that [the Vedic injunctions] are sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists of: (1) the claim that the sacrificer, equipped with sacrificial implements, goes to heaven once burnt;

(2) the attainment of heaven as a means of accomplishment, like the production of abundant fruit for trees burnt by a forest fire, based on the offering of oblations burnt in the fire; and (3) the statement, "The divine cows indeed carry [the sacrifice] while lying on their backs."

[The Upanishads contain] such statements as "the cows move on their backs," "O stones, hear!"—which ascribes the quality of being a listener to stones—and "He who is handless and footless is swift, a grasper; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears"—thus describing things that are logically impossible. Furthermore, [it is said that] gods such as Agni and Indra do not exist; if they did exist...

They would perish like the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) if they were bodiless; how could they consume the oblation? If they consist of sound-forms, then having consumed the oblation, how could they be the givers of fruit? If they consist of object-forms, then [the mantra] "Svāhā to the waters! Svāhā to the plants! Svāhā to the trees! would be the oblation.

How could insentient things such as the recipient (sampradāna) and water bestow a fruit? In that case, due to the arrival of the deity of water within the fire, the fire would be extinguished; the medicinal herbs and other materials would be consumed by the flames; and if water and the like were not present, there would be an absence of a recipient, resulting in the futility of the ritual action. Likewise, for Śarva...

Since everything in the formula "svāhā" and so forth constitutes the recipient (*sampradāna*), who is the giver, what is the oblation, and to whom would the fruit be given? Therefore, deities that are not objects of direct perception do not arrive, they do not consume the oblation, and they do not bestow the fruit; thus, the notion that heaven results from sacrifice is mere hope. Consequently, all of this...
The truth is that action is for the purpose of burning away the oblation alone, not for the sake of the fruit of heaven.

Likewise, if a deity were to exist in wooden, stone, or metal images and the like, would that deity be limited or unlimited? Not the first [alternative], because it is impossible for it to be simultaneously connected with all physical forms; for if it were present in one image, it would be worshipped by that person alone, and not by everyone in every house.

The worship would be fruitless. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because since the presence of the deity is inherently established (*sahajasiddha*), rituals such as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) accompanied by specific refinements would be redundant. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that a specific form of self-conception (*abhimāna-viśeṣa*) is established by consecration alone, in the case of insentient images and the like.

How could a deity whose nature is volition (cetanā) conceive the thought "Who am I"? For if that were the case, it would follow that it would engage in activities such as coming and going, just like a human being. [This would be so] if one were to conceive the thought "I am the king" with respect to a painting possessing its own form.

Because such a cognition does not depend upon consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), nor do people perform the consecration of a painting. If it is argued that consciousness arises through consecration, like fire produced by the friction of wood, then all food that has been offered should be eaten; otherwise, it would remain as before.

The scoundrels perform useless worship of existing images made of clay, stone, or wood solely for their own enjoyment; likewise, the deceivers perform daily and occasional rites such as *śrāddha*, which provide satisfaction to the ancestors,
solely for their own enjoyment— for when one person has eaten here, the belly of another is not filled.

It is filled. When a Brāhmaṇa who is living, or one who has already eaten, is present, the stomachs of one’s own ancestors and others would be filled. Furthermore, food and other offerings given after a long interval to those who died in another year would become a source of satisfaction; in this very same way, it is for a lamp that is burning.
One should provide ghee, oil, and so forth from the previous year or the year before that for the increase of the lamp’s flame.

Therefore, just as Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s performance of the *śrāddha* and other rites was rendered futile upon hearing that the sons of Pāṇḍu had been burned in the house of lac, so too are other *śrāddhas* and such rites performed with intent for the class of ancestors (the *pitṛs*).

What is being done is futile. For those intent on protecting their own kin, even though they are capable of violence, it is called the "dharma of non-violence" (*ahiṃsā-dharma*); yet violence itself is indeed dharma. Therefore, even by the Veda (*śruti*), various forms of violence are enjoined. [Examples include] Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna... [killing his mother].

It is directly perceived that Arjuna killed his teacher Droṇa, Kṛṣṇa his uterine brother, and Indra the demon Vṛtra even after granting him freedom from fear; likewise, Kārtavīrya slew Jamadagni for the sake of the cows, and so forth. Therefore, for one who is capable, violence alone is the supreme duty. The same applies to falsehood.

This is the law: for there is the scriptural injunction, "One should speak a falsehood as witness where the execution of those belonging to the [four] castes would otherwise occur. Thus, the command "one should not speak a falsehood" is merely a general admonition; for the sake of the matter at hand, one should indeed speak a falsehood—as Karṇa did for the sake of the Brahmāstra, Yudhiṣṭhira for the sake of victory, and [Duryodhana] for the sake of the destruction of the Kauravas.
For it is well known that Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya spoke nothing but falsehood for the sake of Subhadrā;

likewise, theft too is dharma. The notion that "non-stealing is dharma" is merely a fabrication of those obsessed with protecting their own property. One should accomplish one's desired ends even by means of theft.

Indeed, Indra stole Yuyu; Śambara carried off Pradyumna; Citralekhā [stole] Aniruddha; the ten-faced Rāvaṇa abducted Sītā; and people intent on the concealment of their virility embrace celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
One who embraces the vow of celibacy for a period of forty-eight years is a *brahmacārī* in the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*).
Because of the teaching on the practice of unchaste women, they abandon [their vows]. Likewise, those unable to support a family desire to remain without possessions.
Therefore, [sages] such as Agastya, Saubhari, and Jaratkāru, having abandoned the state of non-possession, [resumed household life].
They refrained from taking wives. Thus, for the poor whose bellies were emaciated by hunger, the giving of gold, land, cattle, clothing, and polished food has been extolled.
Travelers unable to endure the fatigue of the road praise the construction of temples, ponds, wells, tanks, gardens, water-stations, and shelters.

It is not even the case that great merit accrues to the doer by providing water for drinking to animals, birds, wild beasts, and so forth in ponds, wells, tanks, and the like; rather, if animals should happen to fall into those ponds, wells, tanks, and such places through negligence, then for as many hairs as there are on the bodies of those animals, for that many years the doer goes to hell.

In this regard, [the following cases are mentioned]: if a person sleeping in a temple dies due to the collapse of loose stones from that temple; if a Brāhmaṇa who built the temple dies; if a man who ate there dies from indigestion, or from a bone stuck in his throat, or from overeating; and likewise for the giver of the food. Thus...

Since robbers greedy for the wealth of the owner might even manufacture weapons that cause death, the giver of wealth, clothing, and so forth would— like the maker of the weapon— be liable for sins such as cow-slaughter or the killing of a Brahmin, as they would be the instrumental cause of that death.
Thus, in the sixty-first chapter of the Sambhava Parvan, regarding the vow of chastity devised by Śvetaketu for the sake of protecting his mother, Pāṇḍu said to Kuntī:
"Now I shall declare this ancient dharma; listen to it from me."
The Purāṇa was seen by the sages, the best among all upholders of dharma.
"O fair-faced one, it is said that in former times women were unconfined;
O lady of lovely smiles, they moved about according to their own will and were independent."
When they were transgressing against their husbands while still in their youth, O fortunate one, let there be no half [of the merit];
for that indeed is the eternal law.
And even creatures born of the animal realm, O knower of dharma, O lady of beautiful hips, O dark-eyed one, observe that very dharma exactly as prescribed.
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, even today among the Northern Kurus, the law of women’s lack of restraint persists; for that indeed is the eternal dharma.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor are beautiful-eyed women ever satiated with men.
Thus, for women who are afflicted by thirst, there is no such thing as approaching an improper man; this applies to every single individual, O lady of pure smiles.
Indeed, upon seeing a man here in secret— whether it be a son, a grandson, or likewise a brother— the womb then becomes moistened with desire.
"O auspicious one, this is the natural state of women; it is not produced by any external cause. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, in the *Pārāśarasmṛti*:
"When the husband has disappeared, died, renounced the world, become impotent, or fallen [from his caste], in these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women. Thus it is said.
In this context, it is not a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*), but rather that very [rule] which must necessarily be observed;
for since the *Pārāśara-smṛti* pertains specifically to the Kali age, it is impossible to conceive of it as having another age as its subject matter.
Even though Śvetaketu stated that if a woman goes to another man by transgressing her husband, [the sin] belongs to the women from the very beginning...
It has been stated that "there would be the sin of killing an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā)," but even that is only accepted on the basis of reasoning;

for if one were to pass over many menstrual periods, many instances of killing an embryo would result, and there would also be the interruption of progeny. Furthermore, it would entail the abandonment of such acts as the immolation of a Brāhmaṇa, which are prescribed by the Śruti.

What fault is there in abandoning what was stated by Śvetaketu? Likewise, there is no fault even in not following the practices taught by other sages. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the Veda on the grounds that "a woman does not obtain two husbands," for that is accepted as being merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda). Elsewhere...

For in the Śruti itself, it is heard that Gāyatrī is the wife of the Vasus, Triṣṭubh the wife of the Rudras, Jagatī the wife of the Ādityas, and Aruṇvatī the wife of the Ṛṣis. Likewise, the fact that Draupadī had five husbands is well known, as is the fact that Svadhā is the wife of the Pitṛs.

It is heard in scripture that Soma, Gandharva, and Agni hold the status of being wives in common with all women. Likewise, the rules regarding forbidden sexual intercourse (*agamyāgamana*) are merely contrived by incompetent people— for instance, Candra [approached] the wife of his guru,
Viśvāmitra [approached] Menakā, Vasiṣṭha [approached] Madayantī, and Dīrghatapas [approached] a Śūdra woman.

Parāśara approached Satyavatī, and Vyāsa approached a Śūdra woman. Nor should it be said that sexual intercourse with a forbidden woman is a fault only in the Kali age and not in other ages; for no such restrictive rule regarding the subject matter is heard in the Veda.

The claim that "the seizure of a Brahmin’s property leads to sin" is likewise charming only when left unexamined; for in ancient times, the entire earth was given by Bali to Vāmana, who was a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), and that very same earth was later given by Paraśurāma to Kaśyapa as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
It is precisely because of this that the earth became well-known by the name *Kāśyapī*.

The status of being a thief of Brahmin property (*brahmasvāpahāritva*) is established. Because of the rule that "whatever belongs to someone is intended for that person's own fruit," every religious merit (*dharma*) performed by anyone on the earth would belong to Kaśyapa. Nor can it be argued that there is no fault in the aforementioned objection because that land was not given by Kaśyapa to others; for what [is the nature of that land]?

Was it given by Kaśyapa to the Kṣatriyas or to the Brāhmaṇas? It cannot be the first, because Kṣatriyas are unfit to receive gifts. Nor can it be the second, because the previously mentioned fault remains as it was, since there would be no cessation of the sin of seizing the property of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmasva*). Furthermore, according to the scriptural statement, "The property of a Brāhmaṇa is [to be guarded] like one's own sons and grandsons."

Because we observe the severance of the lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth among Kṣatriyas who are intent on seizing the property of Brahmins; likewise, even the division of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) is imagined by foolish people. For instance, from Vivasvat, the son of Kaśyapa...
How could Vaivasvata Manu, born of the daughter of a divine artisan, be a Kṣatriya?
And how could Harita and others, born in such a lineage of Manu, be Brāhmaṇas?
Furthermore, how was the king named Āśmaka born from Madayantī by Vasiṣṭha?

How could Yadu, born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) from the Kṣatriya Yayāti and the Brāhmaṇa maiden Devayānī, be a Kṣatriya? Or how could Kakṣīvanta and others, born of a Śūdra woman, be Brāhmaṇas? And among the two sons of the king named Vena, how was one a Niṣāda?

How could another, Pṛthu, have been a Kṣatriya? Or how was the son of Jamadagni a celibate student (brahmacārī)? And how did he perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), even though he was ineligible for it? Furthermore, despite the absence of his elder brother’s marriage, how did his younger brother Bhīmasena take Hiḍimbā as his wife? And [how did] Viśvāmitra [accept] Triśaṅku, who was a Caṇḍāla?
Or how did he employ [them] in sacrifice? Therefore, even the division of castes and stages of life (varṇāśramavibhāga) is not to be respected.
Many rules are heard of in the world; even those who are attentive abandon some of these rules.
Even by Brahmā it is impossible to perform them in their entirety; therefore, falling away [from them] is inevitable.

Only a Śūdra is truly virtuous. Those Jains and Buddhists who have been deceived by Keśava, as well as people tricked by rogues, having fallen into an unbearable crisis, perform futile vows out of devotion.

In our Cārvāka doctrine, however, there is no such rule. Since in other doctrines one hears of many rules, the possibility of sin arises if they are not practiced, resulting in a fall; thus, in those systems, liberation never occurs. But in our doctrine:
Because such restrictive rules do not exist, there is no possibility of sin arising; thus, liberation occurs even for one who does not desire it.

A materialist (Lokāyata) who maintains an equal vision toward women—such as Brahmins and others—who are to be addressed by the terms "sister," "mother-in-law," "daughter-in-law," or "wife," is distinguished from other practitioners of religious observances (samayin). This very point was also stated by Manu:

By the statement, "Even after committing a hundred improper acts, wives, sons, and others must be supported," the performance of even a hundred improper acts is permitted for the sake of maintaining one's own dependents—wives, sons, and so forth; therefore, by the logic of *kaimutya* (how much more so), the performance of improper acts for one's own sake is established as being even more forbidden. Consequently, [this applies] for as long as one lives.

Even if one incurs debt for the sake of experiencing pleasure, that pleasure should be enjoyed; there is no subsequent attachment to suffering after the abandonment of the body, because liberation— in the form of the absence of rebirth— has been attained since the body that experiences pleasure and pain has been reduced to ashes.
Therefore, for those devoid of intelligence and human effort, there is the lifelong performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, the study of the three Vedas with their auxiliary limbs,
the observance of the vows of renunciation such as the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the wearing of sacred ash and *rudrākṣa* beads,
and the wearing of white clay, *gopīcandana*, *tulasī*, and jewels.

"It is established that [the self] exists solely for the purpose of procuring the means of life. This is nothing more than a delusion intended to confuse the ignorant. To begin with, the identity of the body with the self is utterly impossible; if the body itself were the self, then regarding an object that has come within the range of vision during childhood—

If that which has entered the path of experience during the state of youth were not to arise as a memory in the state of old age, it would be because bodies possess arising and destruction through their processes of growth and decay;
for the body of an old man is mutually distinct from the bodies of childhood and so forth. And yet, this is not the case.

It must be stated that even though these [bodies] are distinct from one another, because impressions produced by each preceding body give rise to impressions in the second and subsequent bodies, the recollection of what was experienced during childhood immediately following it in youth and so forth is possible; this is evident from the observation of constant increase and decrease [in the continuum].
If one were to admit the arising of a distinct mental formation (*saṃskāra*) for each of those [moments] that perish every instant,
then the postulation of infinite mental formations would result in great theoretical complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, if the body alone were the self,
then a child's engagement in activities such as suckling milk would not occur, because [such activity requires] the cognition that it is a means to achieve a desired end.
This is because, at that time, there is no experience of [the act] as a means to a desired end, which serves as the cause for engagement.
Nor should it be said that for you— who maintain the existence of a self distinct from the body— it is difficult to account for engagement in activities such as suckling at the breast.
For activity is possible through the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the living being, which is produced by experience in a previous birth,
and through the resulting knowledge that [the action] is a means to a desired end in the form of a memory. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so,
other things experienced in a previous birth would likewise be remembered.

This is because there is an absence of anything to awaken those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). However, in the case of an infant’s drinking of breast milk and so forth, it is postulated that the unseen force of destiny (*adṛṣṭa*)—which sustains life—is precisely what awakens the seed of memory. Therefore, one must accept that the self (*ātman*) exists as something distinct from the body. On this point, the words of the *Gītā* serve as authoritative proof:
Just as a person, having cast off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new,
so too, having cast off worn-out bodies—
"The embodied one takes up other new [bodies]," so it is said.

Nor should it be said that establishing the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda-prāmāṇya*) against a nihilist (*nāstika*) who does not accept any means of knowledge other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is as impossible as describing a specific fragrance in a sky-flower; for [this argument applies] to one who denies the validity of words...

We ask you: is the statement "your word is not a means of valid cognition" (a) a means of valid cognition or (b) not a means of valid cognition? Not the first; if it were a means of valid cognition, then the validity of words would already be established. Not the second; if the statement "words are not a means of valid cognition" is itself not a means of valid cognition—
Even then, the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda*) is already established. Likewise, inference (*anumāna*) is also a valid means of knowledge:

"The body is not the self, because it is visible, because it possesses form, and because it is material, like a jar. Furthermore, by such inferences as: "The body has a seer distinct from itself, because it is visible, like a jar."

Since it is established that the self is not of the nature of the body and is distinct from the body, the self is indeed other than the body. Nor should it be said that the aggregate of the vital breaths, the senses, and so forth is itself the self,
for [this would be untenable] in the case of those who are blind, deaf, lame, or otherwise deprived of individual senses.

Because that [body] is a composite, it would follow that it is not the self. Nor should it be argued that the inference "the body is not the self" and so forth is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), on the grounds that it is sublated by direct perceptual experience such as "I am a child," "I am stout," or "I am thin";
