for [one also perceives]: "I am a child, not a youth, nor an old man," and "I am a youth, not a child, nor an old man."
This is because [the notion] "I am old, not young, nor a child" is sublated by direct perception,
and because there is recognition [in the form]: "I, who experienced my parents in childhood, am the same I who now experiences my grandchildren in old age."

Because the self is established as distinct from the body that persists through stages such as childhood, it is appropriate to sublate the cognition of the body as the self by treating it as an error; for this [establishment] is supported by a favorable logical argument (*anukūlatarka*) to the effect that if the self were not distinct from the body and so forth,
then the aforementioned recognition would not occur.

By means of proofs such as "because it is visible," the Self is established as distinct from the body, beginningless, and imperishable. Furthermore, because of recognition—such as "I who saw previously am the very same one who heard [it]," and "I am that very same one who remembers now"—the aggregate of the senses is not the Self; for what was seen or heard by one cannot be [remembered] by another.

Because remembrance would otherwise be impossible, it must necessarily be asserted that the Self is of the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa), the witness of all, and distinct from the five sheaths (pañca-kośa), in accordance with the scriptural text: "Therefore, there is another inner Self different from this one consisting of food."

"An ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain; impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed into a pit. According to this statement, one who is shrouded by ignorance is not independent regarding pleasure and pain, but is dependent upon the impulsion of the Lord in accordance with their good and evil deeds.
It is established that a living being is one who experiences the pleasure and pain of heaven and hell.
As for the objection that a sacrifice such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, once perished, cannot be the cause of a result occurring at a later time— that is incorrect.

For just as memory arises through the medium of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) even when the prior experience has ceased, so too is the accomplishment of all human goals achieved through the medium of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, [which is based] upon one's own prior experience.
Just as one’s own memory is produced by one’s own [past] impressions, so too it is only one’s own previously acquired virtuous karma that bestows its fruit upon oneself;

furthermore, the diversity of pleasure, pain, and so forth is based on the diversity of karma. Nor should it be argued that there could ever be a lack of sequence or an occurrence of events without cause, for things such as a jar do not arise in the absence of a cause.

Furthermore, because memory does not arise prior to its conditioning (*saṃskāra*), and because heaven does not arise prior to the performance of rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, [the cause must exist before the effect]. If it were produced first, it would not be produced later either.
Nor is there a contradiction regarding priority and posteriority in the sense that "it is produced from itself. Therefore, [the production] is independent of a cause.

The arising of an effect [from itself] is illogical. Furthermore, "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) means its own existence; for it is not possible for something to be born from itself. If there were another cause, then it is established that this is simply the diversity of karma.

If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone were the cause, then due to the absence of causal variety, there would be only uniformity in pleasure, pain, and so forth; or else, that [uniformity] would have to exist at all times. Therefore, the occasional variety of pleasure and pain experienced by the self must indeed correspond to the karma of living beings.

As for the claim that the doctrine of the self as the body (dehātmavāda) is established solely on the basis of Vedic statements such as "this tail is the supreme self," that too is not so; just as the word *gopati* ("lord of cows") applied to the sun does not refer to cattle, and just as in the expression "the pot has clay as its self" (*mṛdātmā ghaṭaḥ*), it refers merely to the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

This term "Self" (ātman), though employed here as denoting the nature of the sheaths beginning with the "consisting of fire," is determined at the conclusion to reside in the Brahman that is the tail; therefore, it does not refer to the body as the Self. Consequently, even though the body is called the "Self," it is not conscious.

As for what was also said—that if liberation has not occurred for the self, which is distinct from the body, throughout beginningless saṃsāra, then liberation could not occur later either—that is incorrect; for just as a body that was never previously produced can now be produced, so too the production of liberation, which was previously unproduced, is possible now. By this, [the objection is refuted].
Since liberation would likewise entail arising and perishing just as the body does, the claim that "liberation is the destruction of the body" is refuted; furthermore,
because of the usage of the expression "the calf is liberated when its bonds have fallen away," the terms "liberated" (*mukta*) and "dead" (*mṛta*) are not synonymous.

As for the claim that at the time of death no one other than the body is perceived by the relatives through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this must be addressed: it is impossible to reject the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of inference (*anumāna*), which is distinct from direct perception.
Furthermore, contradiction (*vyāghāta*) cannot be the reason for the invalidity of inference, for a contradiction cannot be established by mere words alone. Nor...

There is a contradiction due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because even in the case of the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl, there is an absence of validity due to such deviation. Therefore, the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as "that which has an unseen cognition as its instrument" implies an instrument that is free from defects. In this way, the Veda (*śruti*) is indeed a means of valid cognition with respect to its own meaning; by this, [the arguments] fabricated by the crafty [opponents] are refuted.

The claim that [the Veda] is "known" (veda) is refuted; for the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa has aphorized that Brahman has the scripture as its source. Since it has been established that the capacity of a word to generate knowledge—even regarding an object that is absolutely non-existent—is the very nature of its authority, and since there is an absence of defects, its validity is secured. For this very reason...
The authority of the Veda regarding Dharma, which is characterized by injunction (*codanā*), has been explained in detail by the Bhaṭṭācāryas.
Consequently, this Veda is authorless (*apauruṣeya*); Śiva and others are its rememberers (*smartāraḥ*), not its authors (*kartāraḥ*).
Its authorlessness consists in its being a word that is not produced by the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence serving as the cause for its application.

The passage beginning with "This was His breath—the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, and the Samaveda; from that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Rig-verses and Saman-chants were born"—also refers merely to [the Lord's] role as the rememberer (smartṛtva). That very quality of having such scripture as its source was also aphorized by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa. As for what was stated...

As for the claim that "the Veda is fabricated by rogues" or that "it is different in every Manvantara," and so forth— that is not so; for [those texts] merely establish that Śiva and others are the rememberers (smartṛs) of the mass of Vedas, which exists throughout each Manvantara and is divided into three or four parts.

For the sake of accomplishing study in accordance with the respective ages (*yuga*), the great seers (*maharṣi*) who are qualified, such as Vedavyāsa and others, having divided [the Veda] by the grace of the Supreme Lord, reveal it; they do not, however, produce it anew. Nor is it the case that [the Veda is non-eternal], because of the scriptural statement, "The Vedas are indeed infinite," and because of the designations such as "The Āruṇa" and "The Kāṭhaka," [which occur] in every *manvantara*.

It must be stated that what is being described is the origin of the Veda; however, statements such as "the Sāma-śākhās are a thousandfold" are intended to demonstrate the multiplicity of branches as established by such declarations, and do not concern their actual origin.
Furthermore, designations such as "Kāṭhaka" refer to the suffix denoting the reciter (*proktṛ*). And thus, [it is] inherently...

The Veda is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) and is stainless, because it is independent of other means of knowledge. Since the Vedas are eternal and free from defects, their authority is established. Consequently, there is no room for doubt regarding the lack of authority in the Veda. Thus, its status as a valid means of knowledge is established by virtue of its not being dependent upon a speaker.

The Veda possesses a state of being most highly esteemed (*abhyarhitatva*). In the case of that which is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), however, its validity depends upon other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).

In the absence of other means of knowledge, the very status of being of human origin is not even accepted. That which is of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*) is indeed a valid means of knowledge, even in the absence of being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*). Now, it might be argued that the validity of the Veda is established through partial correspondence with other means of knowledge.
If it is argued that the authority of the scriptures spoken by the Buddha and the Arhats is established because of partial agreement [with other sources], this is true; however,

it is not established that every portion of the Veda is authoritative simply because of partial agreement with rituals such as the *kārīrī*, for [the Veda] is self-evident (*svataḥ*) in its authority due to its being unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) and its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*).

It is called "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) because it is that which is most worthy of honor; for partial agreement cannot establish validity, otherwise even the words of a deceiver would attain validity due to partial agreement.
Regarding the matter of agreement, some [points] stated in the Veda are indeed stated in the Buddhist scriptures and elsewhere as well. And yet—

It must be stated that what was taught by the Buddha was merely restated by the Veda; for in the world, people become possessors of jewels only after obtaining them from a mine of jewels, and they do not become mines of jewels by obtaining them from elsewhere. Likewise, all systems of doctrine subsist upon portions of the Veda, for the eternal Veda does not [subsist upon them].
Since we and others have never seen an omniscient being anywhere, it is impossible for the Buddhist scripture to have its root in an authoritative omniscient person;
nor can the hypothesis that such a person existed ever be refuted. Furthermore, the Buddha’s omniscience does not follow from his production of scriptures.
Because the two Buddhist scriptures are mutually dependent. Furthermore, that which is non-omniscient does not know that omniscience;

and that which is omniscient is not perceived by anyone. Therefore, the authority of his words is not possible [for others]. This is because, in the case of the fundamental knowledge—which is free from attachment, aversion, and so forth—it would be like the words of another.

Since the Vedic subject matter is established as being devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*), the teaching therein is produced by another, brought forth like a reflection; it is through mere proximity, like that of a man [to] a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), that omniscience arises. In this way, the soul’s cognition is merely dependent upon the senses and other such factors.

Knowledge regarding subtle, supersensible, and other such objects cannot be established without scripture; and scripture itself cannot be established without an omniscient being. By this, the notion of an eternal scripture is refuted. Thus, once the authority of the Vedas alone is established, the regulations concerning the duties, conduct, castes, and stages of life are likewise validated.

They bestow the fruits of heaven and liberation. The statement, "In fire alone his *agnihotra* becomes offered," is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning a residual ritual duty; nevertheless, it is not absolutely non-authoritative with respect to its own literal meaning, because it can be categorized in three ways—as a restatement of qualities, as a descriptive statement of fact, or as a commendatory declaration.
And likewise, there is also the composition of those who are learned: "In cases of contradiction, there is figurative praise (guṇavāda), restatement (anuvāda), and restriction (avadhāraṇa);

as well as the statement of an existing fact (bhūtārthavāda). Thus, arthavāda is considered to be threefold. For example, in the passage "The sacrificial post is the sun," the meaning is that the post possesses the quality of purity like the sun. Similarly, [in the passage] "Fire is the remedy for cold," [it is a figurative praise].

The restatement of a meaning already well-known in the world is useful for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*). "Medhātithi slew Indra," and so forth, is an explanatory passage concerning an established fact (*bhūtārthavāda*). This same principle should be applied to the authoritative cognition of established facts regarding both mantras and names.
Thus is the authority of those [Vedic portions] that are subordinate to an action (*kāryaśeṣa*). But as for the Vedāntas, which are not subordinate to anything else—

In the Supreme Self, whose essence is consciousness (*cidātman*), the awareness of universal identity possesses the highest degree of validity, independent of anything else. Therefore, the authority of mantras and *arthavādas* in conveying their respective meanings is possible according to the manner previously described. Thus, [the text continues]: "equipped with the sacrificial implements, [he goes] to heaven..."

In the phrase "he should go," the connection of the self with the sacrificial implements is mediated through the body; this is consistent because the self's body functions as a metaphorical vehicle for attaining heaven, much like a chariot.
As for what was stated regarding [the origin] "from the plants" and so forth—that is not [the case], since a corporeal form is heard in scripture in passages such as "Purandara, thunderbolt in hand."

The fivefold nature of a deity consists of the enjoyment of oblations (*havis*), sovereignty, graciousness, and the granting of boons; this is accepted by Bādarāyaṇa and others because it is established that the presiding deities (*abhimāna-devatā*) have medicinal herbs as their object. Due to their possession of sovereignty, the deities [are capable of such actions].
Because there is an absence of burning and visual perception [of such results].

As for what was said—that when a Brahmin is harmed due to indigestion, or when an animal falls into a well and so forth, the sin belongs to the one who performed that act—that is incorrect; for merit is traditionally recorded in the drinking of water and in the giving of food.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural teaching on the extreme merit [of such acts], and because of the traditional injunction that evil deeds accrue to either the animal or the Brāhmaṇa in the event of its slaughter,
merit and sin do not exist merely through fallacious reasoning. Moreover,
the taking of another husband by a woman is forbidden for Brāhmaṇas in the Kali age.

It is like the case of [the sage’s] obtaining [his wife]. The non-restraint of women must be abandoned because they are not protected by the great multitude, as seen in Gautama’s abandonment of Ahalyā due to her husband’s curse; Bhīṣma’s rejection of Ambā due to his father’s word; Rāma’s slaying of his mother; and the procreation of a son by the brother-in-law, and so forth—due to the extraordinary power (*tejoviśeṣa*) of those individuals.

This is of little consequence, because there is a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) stating that "there is no transgression. For it is heard in scripture that fault lies in purposeless violence; thus, even killing should not be performed, as seen in the case of Balarāma’s circumambulation of the earth to pacify the fault of killing the Sūta and the Paurāṇika, and in the memory of Daśaratha’s grief for his son caused by the killing of the sage’s son.

By false speech, Karṇa [fell] due to the curse of Jamadagni’s son; likewise, by [falsehood], Dharmaputra beheld hell; by the theft of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), the Vasus entered the womb of human beings;
and by the misappropriation of what was given, Nṛga attained the state of a lizard in a blind well.

From Indra’s loss of luster due to the violation of Ahalyā; from Nahuṣa’s attainment of the state of a serpent due to his desire for Śacī; from the destruction of the ascetic power of Saubhari and others due to their attachment to wives;
from the simultaneous death of the Yādavas due to the excess of drinking; and from excessive indulgence with women—

Due to Vicitravīrya’s being seized by consumption; due to the Pāṇḍavas’ loss of their kingdom through the vice of gambling; due to Kalmāṣapāda’s attainment of the state of a Rākṣasa through the vice of hunting;
due to Devāpi’s fall from grace through his reviling of the Vedas, the gods, and the twice-born; and due to Śantanu’s transgression of the agreement with Gaṅgā.

Since it is established in various Purāṇas—such as through the story of Draupadī’s abandonment, the injury done to her, and the humiliation of Jayadratha—that violence and the like must not be committed, let this suffice for the details.
As for what was said, that "even after committing a hundred improper acts, [the king] must be supported," etc., that is incorrect; for when protection is mandatory, [one must act].

Because the intended meaning has been determined; and because of the prohibition, "Even in times of dire distress, one must not resort to the livelihood of a Śūdra"; and because the argument that for one whose every means of subsistence have failed, the loss of life constitutes a justification—thereby permitting the consumption of food-leavings and kuluttha beans prepared through the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances—is refuted. Therefore, it is not [permissible].

It is established that one may act according to one's own will. This is the conclusion here: because of such scriptural declarations as, "Speak the truth, practice dharma, do not neglect your private Vedic study," and so forth; and because of the passage in the Kaṭhavallī:
"Regarding this man who has died, there is doubt: some say he exists, others say he does not exist."

"Instructed by you in this knowledge, this is the third of the boons. Thus questioned by Naciketas, Yama replied: "The wise man, having realized through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self that God—who is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret cave of the heart, situated in the depths, and ancient—becomes tranquil."

He abandons both joy and sorrow. The wise one is neither born nor does he die; this person has not come from anywhere, nor has anyone ever become anything at all. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, he is not slain when the body is slain.

Existing in the midst of ignorance within the body, though wise themselves, they consider themselves learned. Wandering about like the blind led by the blind, these deluded ones go astray. The world beyond does not reveal itself to the fool who is intoxicated by the delusion of wealth.
The fool, who thinks "this world exists but the next does not," falls again and again under my sway.

Because it has been established by such passages as these: "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—departing there, people who know Brahman go to Brahman. Smoke, night, likewise the dark fortnight, and the six months of the southern solstice—there [they go to] the lunar world..."

"The yogi of light, having reached it, returns. Thus, [the text describes] the travel by way of the path beginning with light for those yogis who meditate upon Brahman, as well as the travel by way of the path beginning with smoke for those devoted to the performance of the true dharma such as sacrifices, and for others distinct from these.

For it is frequently heard in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other texts that those devoted to unrighteousness— such as violence, theft, and adultery— experience various kinds of terrible torments in hell corresponding to their respective actions. Therefore:

The practice of dharma enjoined by the Śruti, Āgama, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas must be accepted as the means for attaining the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), while the practice of what is prohibited therein must be accepted as the cause of all evil. Therefore, the Lokāyata doctrine, which contradicts this, should not be adopted by those seeking the highest good; thus all is clear.

[Thus ends the section on] the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*), which are distinguished by one hundred and one unsurpassed divisions arising from the churning of the ocean of the Śāmbhava Āgama— attained through the grace of the venerable Toṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the beginningless, stainless, and mobile Aparā [form of the Goddess].
[This work was composed] by the eminent teacher Śrī Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows the mass of bliss arising from tasting the nectar of the realization of ultimate reality;
[it concerns] the seizure of the seven constituents of the enemy of the sole hero who causes a tumult among ten million Yādava Murāris, [and] the [conquest of] the western ocean...

*Śrīmadbhagavad
The Tenth Chapter in the Section on Debate.
[The Eleventh Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O you who are preeminent in virtue, by your words the entire doctrine of the Lokāyatas has been set forth,
as well as the refutations thereof.
Having heard this, my mind became filled with wonder.
Indeed, its refutability is due precisely to its contradiction with the Vedas and the Agamas;
for you have imagined that [scripture] to be based on another tradition.
It is held that on this earth the Arhat is the god who set [the teaching] in motion;
and even by you, the name "Omniscient One" is applied only to Śiva.
Since non-violence, truthfulness, abstention from theft, and so forth— which are always written and recited at the beginning of the *Amarakośa*— attain the state of being rooted in your scripture;
Furthermore, how could these many phenomena taught in the scriptures of the Jina continue to exist in the future?
Having spoken thus, Bhṛṅgī began to speak further regarding the Buddha who had been struck down by Krama:
"O King, listen; I am attentive and joyful."
I speak this praise out of an excess of affection.
The Ārhata followers, also known as Jains, establish their doctrine in this manner: there are two categories of reality, namely *jīva* (the soul) and *ajīva* (the non-soul).
The *jīva* is conscious, co-extensive with the body, and possesses parts.
The *ajīva* is of six kinds; among these, the first is the mountain and so forth.

There are five [categories] known as influx (*āsrava*), restraint (*saṃvara*), destruction (*nirjarā*), bondage (*bandha*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). That by which the soul flows toward sense objects is called *āsrava*; it is the aggregate of the senses. That which restrains or holds back the senses is *saṃvara*, which is discernment (*viveka*). That by which desire, anger, and so forth are completely worn away is *nirjarā*.

Asceticism (*tapas*) consists of practices such as plucking out the hair, climbing onto heated stones, non-violence, wearing the five types of impurities, carrying a peacock feather, eating from the hollow of the hand, and nakedness; it results in the shedding of *karma* (*nirjarā*). Bondage (*bandha*) is the succession of births and deaths brought about by the eightfold *karma*. Four of these are the destructive *karmas* (*ghātikarmāṇi*), which are specific forms of evil.
Furthermore, there are four acts of non-malice which take the form of specific merits. The definitive knowledge that "the entire universe is exactly of this nature" is absolute.
The notion that bathing, climbing heated stones, and so forth—as taught by the Jina—do not constitute Dharma is a misconception.

Perverted knowledge (*viparīta-jñāna*). The knowledge that the slaughter of sacrificial animals prescribed by the Vedas and so forth is *dharma* is scriptural knowledge (*ājñānika*). The cognition that all philosophical systems (*darśanas*) are equal is conventional knowledge (*vainayika*). These five are the means of bondage. [They are to be avoided] by virtuous persons who possess faith and right knowledge.

Right conduct (*samyak-cāritra*) consists of the observance of rules such as the renunciation of violence while they are being practiced. Right view (*samyag-darśana*) is faith directed toward the categories of reality (*tattvārtha*). Right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is the accurate cognition of the categories of reality. These three constitute the means to liberation; they alone are called the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*).

Restraint (*saṃvara*) is the cessation of the aggregate of the senses denoted by the term "influx" (*āsrava*); its cause is right protection. That [protection] is threefold: protection of the mind, protection of speech, and protection of the body. When activity is restrained through such protection, restraint arises; and from restraint comes the shedding of karma (*nirjarā*).

It arises; it is of two kinds: that produced by its own natural maturation, and that produced by the power of austerity even at an improper time. Thus, when the cessation of bondage produced by the eight aforementioned types of karma occurs through such nirjarā, [the soul] having swallowed—

Liberation is the attainment of one's true self through the upward movement of the soul— which has been freed from all previously accumulated karma— just as a seed shoots upward after its husk is split open by contact with the heat of the sun during full maturation; it is the abode of infinite knowledge and infinite qualities.

The subject matter is the Supreme Self; and the purpose, in terms of conventional usage, is the thorough knowledge of the nature of the six substances, the five existential categories, the seven principles, the nine predicaments, and the path to liberation; and in terms of the ultimate standpoint, it is [the realization of the self].

Self-cognizing knowledge consists of the tasting of the nectar of bliss, whose sole characteristic is the unchanging supreme bliss arising from the self-awareness of one’s own stainless and pure soul. Furthermore, by means of supreme certainty, there is the attainment of the happiness of the established doctrine of the innate self, which is the fruit of that knowledge and is inseparable from the infinite qualities of absolute self-knowledge.

The venerable teachers, the supreme Arhats, have established the designations of perception, inference, and scripture. There exists a world beyond; there are the heavens, beginning with Acyuta and ending with Preraṇā, situated one above the other, and above those are the celestial palaces (vimānas).

There are three [terraces]. Above that is the liberation-stone (*mokṣa-śilā*), composed of light. Therein indeed is the Blessed One, whose form is that of a liberated soul, possessing the ten powers (*daśabala*) consisting of the nature of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, tranquility, power, skillful means, aspiration, and wisdom.
Having performed his labors,

he was endowed with the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā)— consisting of the divine eye, the divine ear, the recollection of past lives, knowledge of the minds of others, and the power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya)— and was thus a conqueror of Māra, the vanquisher of all the world.

The glorious Ācārya, Upādhyāya, and Sādhu Parameṣṭhin shines brilliantly like the Pārijāta tree in the midst of the celestial trees. These seven categories (sapta-padārtha) are established by means of the logic of the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī-naya):
"it may be that it exists," "it may be that it does not exist," and "it may be that it both exists and does not exist."

It may be inexpressible; it may be both existent and inexpressible; it may be both non-existent and inexpressible; and it may be both existent and non-existent and inexpressible—this is the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*). Its meaning is as follows: the word *syāt* expresses a slight degree [of truth] and is an indeclinable particle resembling a verbal suffix. For there are four types of opponents:

There are those who maintain that existence is real (sadvādins), those who maintain non-existence (asadvādins), those who maintain both existence and non-existence (sadasadvādins), and those who maintain the indeterminable (anirvacanīyavādins). Furthermore, among these,

there are those who maintain that what is real is indeterminable (sadanirvacanīyavādins) and those who maintain that what is unreal is indeterminable (asadanirvacanīyavādins), having adopted views that are mixed with the doctrine of indeterminability while still maintaining the conceit that their objects are real.

And those who maintain that [reality] is both existent and non-existent yet indescribable; thus there are three types. Against these seven types of proponents, seven types of responses should be employed. A proponent of existence (sadvādī), having approached a Jaina, asks: "Is there liberation in your doctrine? To this, the Jaina replies: "It may be that there is. [Likewise, one should address] a proponent of non-existence...

Against one who maintains that [the world] does not exist, it may be said: "It exists"; against one who maintains both existence and non-existence, it may be said: "It both exists and does not exist"; against one who maintains that it is inexpressible, it may be said: "It is inexpressible"; and against one who maintains both existence and inexpressibility, it may be said: "It both exists and is inexpressible."

Against one who maintains that [the world] is non-existent and indescribable, [the response would be]: "It may be non-existent and indescribable. Against one who maintains that it is existent, non-existent, and indescribable, [the response would be]: "It may be existent, non-existent, and indescribable. By this much, all proponents, becoming despondent, fail to provide a further answer. Therefore, for him—

Because the logic that establishes the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) exists, the seven categories, beginning with the soul (*jīva*), are established. Therefore, our doctrine— being unassailable due to the presence of the fourfold requisites (*anubandhacatuṣṭaya*)— should be accepted.
Such is the methodological path of the tenets of the Arhats.

The Buddhists, who wear their lower garments untucked and are clad in saffron robes, maintain that there are two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): direct perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna). Furthermore, they assert two categories: the external and the internal.
Of these, the external consists of the earth, mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth; the internal consists of mind (citta) and mental factors (caitta).

This entire world consists of these two collections alone. Among them, the atoms are the cause of the external collection; and those atoms are of four kinds: some are solid and are called earthy, others are moist and are called watery, others are hot and are called fiery, and others consist of motion.

[The elements] belonging to air. From those four kinds of atoms, which have simultaneously aggregated, the external collection arises; and for the internal collection, the five aggregates (*skandhas*) are the cause:
the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).

And the aggregate of mental formations; thus are the five aggregates. Among them, sounds, touches, and so forth, when examined by the mind, constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); the manifestation thereof is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*);
the suffering produced thereby is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*); and names such as "Devadatta" constitute the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).

The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of these constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). From these five aggregates, which have come together as a mass, an internal complex arises. Within these aggregates, the word "self" (*ātman*) is proclaimed; yet in reality, the self is merely the form of the momentary, self-luminous store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

All phenomena are indeed momentary. These are the twelve sense bases: the eye base, ear base, nose base, tongue base, body base, mind base; and the six objective bases: the form base, sound base, odor base, taste base, tangible base, and mental-object base.

The body, the sense faculties, and the cognitions are momentary; the proof for this is that the body, the sense faculties, and the cognitions do not persist beyond a single moment. Like the flame of a lamp, the aggregates proceed, lingering for but a moment.
The mind arises perceptibly; as it arises, it perishes.
Once perished, it does not return, yet it arises again and again.
The Buddhist scripture is fourfold according to the capacity of its audience;
the Buddhist Sautrāntika taught that external objects are perceivable by direct perception.
The Vaibhāṣika proclaims that the external object is to be inferred from the form of cognition;
here, the Yogācāra asserts that there is only consciousness and nothing else.
"The Madhyamikas know reality to be neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor distinct from both; it is completely free from the four extremes. Thus [it is said].

The omniscient Buddha—the abode of all-encompassing sovereignty, virtue, fame, glory, dispassion, and liberation—composed this treatise as the means for attaining liberation; therefore, this treatise is to be accepted.
Such is the system of doctrine of the Buddhists, which contradicts the Vedic scriptures.
Having heard these words concerning the doctrines of the Arhatas and the Sugatas as spoken by Bhṛṅgin,
Śīlavān proceeded to refute them all.
O Bhṛṅgin, place these words of mine in your heart; by doing so once, you shall become composed.
Tell me, O Blue-throated One, how could equanimity arise?
Of the two epithets, "Moon-Like" and "Moon-Crested."
Here, the first is the Ārhata doctrine and the last is the Saugata doctrine; these two are presented in sequence,
[established] by means of reasonings joined with the Vedas and the Agamas.
I revile and disparage it within my mind.
Having thus spoken in the assembly,
those words uttered by the virtuous one were completely refuted; now, therefore, I shall state the erroneous doctrine.
O King, listen, having fixed this in your mind.
To this we reply: this admission is not tenable. Why? Because of the impossibility [of contradictory attributes] in one [substratum].

For it is impossible for contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence to coexist simultaneously in a single substratum (*dharmī*), just like cold and heat. As for these seven categories that have been determined—namely, that there are only these many and they are of such a nature—[this is untenable].

They may be exactly as they appear, or they may not be so at all; for otherwise, a cognition whose form is undetermined—whether it be thus or not thus—would be invalid, just like a cognition of doubt.
[Objection: But surely, since an object consists of multiple aspects, the cognition that arises must have a determined form.

"It ought not to be non-authoritative, like doubtful knowledge. We say: "No," for for one who asserts that non-exclusivity (*anekāntatva*) is unrestricted across all things, even a definitive determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) would—since it is no different from other things—be "perhaps existent" (*syād asti*).
Due to the onset of conceptual constructions such as "it may exist" or "it may not exist," there would be a state of non-determination.
In this way, for both the determiner and the result of determination, existence would belong to one alternative and non-existence to the other alternative.
This being the case, how could the Teacher (Tīrthakara), who is himself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabhūta*), [be so]?

How could one be able to teach when the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the knower (*pramātṛ*), and the act of knowing (*pramiti*) have not been determined? Or else, how could those who follow his intention proceed toward the object taught by him if its nature remains undetermined?
For it is only when there is a determination of the certainty of the result that everyone [proceeds] to the performance of the means for attaining it.

The world proceeds without confusion, and not otherwise. Therefore, one who composes a treatise whose meaning is undetermined would have speech that is as unreliable as that of a drunkard or a madman; likewise, on this view, the number five of the five astikāyas would itself be subject to doubt, being questioned whether it exists or does not exist.

In the alternative case, however, it would not be so; consequently, the number [of categories] would either become deficient or excessive. Furthermore, it is impossible for these categories to be inexpressible.
If they were inexpressible, they could not be mentioned; yet they are mentioned, and thus to say they are "inexpressible" is a contradiction.
And when they are being spoken of, they are either apprehended in that very way or they are not apprehended;
likewise, the fruit of such apprehension— right vision (samyagdarśana)— either exists or does not exist,
and similarly, its opposite, wrong vision (asamyagdarśana), also either exists or does not exist.

To prattle "it exists" or "it does not exist" would belong to the category of the intoxicated or the insane, not to the category of one who is to be convinced. Furthermore, there would be existence in one alternative and non-existence in another; likewise, permanence in one alternative and impermanence in another—such being a state of uncertainty.

There would be an impossibility of worldly activity; furthermore, there would be the consequence that the natures of the soul and other categories, which are established from beginningless time and determined by their own scriptures, would not be as they are determined.
Thus, since the two contradictory properties of existence and non-existence cannot coexist in a single substratum such as the soul or other categories, [if it were] existent...
Furthermore, because a non-existent property cannot exist within a single entity, and because existence is impossible for that which is non-existent,
this doctrine of the Arhatas is incoherent. By this,
their various assertions of non-absolutism— such as being both one and many, eternal and non-eternal, distinct and non-distinct, and so forth— are refuted.

These points must be considered. Furthermore, what was stated—namely, that after asserting there are two categories of entities, the first is the conscious soul (*jīva*), which is of the same size as the body and distinct from the body—that is utterly inconsistent.
For if the soul were of the same size as the body, it would possess intermediate dimensions like the body itself, and consequently, it would be composed of parts (*sāvayavatva*).

Because of the pervasion that "whatever has parts is impermanent," it would follow that [the self] is impermanent; nor is this a desirable consequence, as it would entail the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Furthermore, when the self enters the bodies of elephants and so forth due to the diversity of karma, it would possess the dimensions of those [bodies].

There would be no entry into the subtle bodies of ants and the like. If it is argued that the reason [being composed of parts] is unproven because there is no restrictive rule stating that "whatever possesses intermediate dimension is composed of parts," we say no;
for if something were not composed of parts, it could not possess intermediate dimension, just as in the case of space (*ākāśa*).

Thus, because there exists a cogent argument that subverts the opposing position, furthermore, since one must admit that living beings possess infinite parts even within a single lifetime, it would have to be postulated that those parts undergo contraction during childhood, and [subsequently] expansion during youth of those parts previously contracted.
An expansion of the soul's parts would have to be postulated; for it is impossible to conceive that the soul's parts, which are contracted and limited solely by the body, could be infinite.
Now, when one attains a large body through a change of birth within a single lifetime, some of the soul's parts—

If it is argued that some [atoms] approach and others depart during the formation of the subtle body (*tanuśarīra*), we say no, because this would entail the soul (*jīva*) being subject to modification.
For if the soul were constantly being filled and depleted by the arrival and departure of constituent parts, it would follow that the soul itself is non-eternal and changing.

Because the state of being subject to modification (*vikriyāvatva*) cannot be avoided. Nor can it be accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), for that would entail the consequence of impermanence (*anityatva*), like a piece of leather.
Nor should it be argued that even there it is an accepted consequence, for the very admission of bondage and liberation (*bandha-mokṣa*) would be contradicted;
[otherwise] the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is enveloped by the eightfold karma (*karmāṣṭaka*), like a gourd, [would be untenable].
For one submerged in the ocean, there is an upward movement due to the severing of bonds.
Furthermore,
because it is admitted that parts which arrive and depart undergo coming and going, it possesses the nature of decay.

The gods would possess selfhood like that of a body; consequently, some persisting constituent part would have to be the self, yet it cannot be identified as "this is it. Furthermore, it must be explained from where the incoming constituents of the living being emerge, and where they dissolve when they depart.
For [the soul] would neither manifest from the elements nor dissolve into the elements, because the living being (*jīva*) is non-material (*abhautika*).

Nor can any other substratum for the parts of the souls be established—whether common or uncommon—due to a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) remains thus undetermined.
The self would then be subject to change. This is because its constituent parts, which come and go, would possess an indefinite dimension.

Therefore, due to the occurrence of such defects, it is not possible to maintain that the self undergoes the successive arrival and departure of parts even in a sequential manner. Furthermore, regarding the final dimension of the living being existing in the state of liberation—
Since permanence is asserted by the Jains,
there would follow the consequence of permanence for the first and middle dimensions of the soul as well; thus, there would be the consequence of non-distinction [between them],
resulting in nothing more than the dimension of a single body.

There would be no attainment of other bodies that are either increased or decreased in size. Alternatively, because the final dimension of the soul (jīva) is fixed, the soul would have to remain of a fixed dimension even during its prior states;
consequently, without distinction, it would always be either minute or large.

The soul must be admitted to exist; it is not of the same size as the body. Therefore, like that of the Sautrāntikas, the doctrine of the Ārhats (Jainas) is also inconsistent and should be disregarded.

In this way, the Buddhist doctrine also is not tenable. Is there some other conscious entity that serves as the cause for the production of the aggregate of atoms and aggregates, or do the atoms themselves simply congregate?
Even in the first case, is that conscious entity permanent or momentary?

If permanence is admitted, it constitutes a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*), because all phenomena are admitted to be momentary and permanence is not admitted. Furthermore, if they are momentary, it is impossible to say that something which has not yet attained its own nature at first subsequently brings about the production of a composite aggregate.

If they were of the nature of the second [category], how could the mental factors (*cetanā*), the aggregates (*skandha*), and the atoms (*aṇu*) coalesce into specific forms without a directing consciousness? Therefore, the two-fold collection is illogical.
Furthermore, that which was stated—that all entities are momentary—is utterly inconsistent.

Because there is a lack of evidence. First of all, perception [is not such evidence], because it would contradict the recognition "This is that very Devadatta. Nor [can it be argued that perception is inconclusive] like the cases "This is that same lamp-flame" or "This is that same Gurjarī woman," where—since the object is merely the non-difference of the genus (jāti) and the identity of the individual (vyakti) is not established—the [recognition] [does not prove identity].
If it is argued that [the cognition] would be invalid, then there would be the recognition "this is of the same class as that";

there would be a recognition based on the individual (vyakti), such as: "This very Devadatta who was seen in the city of Pāṭaliputra, I see him now in Māhiṣmatī. For time and space [are related] only to the individual.

Because a universal (*jāti*) lacks such a relationship by virtue of being directly connected [to the individual], and furthermore, if it is claimed that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has the universal as its objective support, then— given that even the universal is momentary according to your own view— the postulation of a justification for recognition would be utterly inconsistent. Nor is there inference (*anumāna*).

Because there is an absence of a probans (liṅga) pervaded by that [thesis]; nor is it the word [itself], because according to your own system, since even that cannot endure due to its momentariness, its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is utterly impossible.
Therefore, the Buddhist doctrine is contrary to scripture, worldly experience, and perception; thus [it is known] by learned people.
It is simply not to be respected by those following the Vedas; let the elaboration cease here.

[Thus, from the venerable Tōṇṭada Siddheśvara—the incarnation of the moving Śiva who is beginningless, stainless, and supreme; who attained the grace of the ocean of the Śāmbhava Āgama churned by him; and who [revealed] the sixfold...]
In [this work] composed by the eminent teacher Śrī Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows a mass of bliss through the tasting of the nectar of the *Alasudhā*,
[it concerns] the Lord of the Western Ocean— who was the sole hero among those who raised a great clamor against ten million Yādava-Murāris—
and the preceptor who established the pure Vedic doctrine of Advaita, Keladi...

In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, within the section on debate (*vādakāṇḍa*), follows the exposition of the doctrines of the Arhatas and the Sugatas, composed as an ornament for the king of the earth, Basava— who delights the heart of Mallāmbā, the lawful consort of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth, who is like the full moon in the milk-ocean of the lineage of Sadāśiva Rāyanāyaka.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Refutation of That."
[The Twelfth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
Immediately after, O Guru, what did Bhṛṅgin say then?
Or what was correctly answered there by Śīlavat? Tell me.
O King, whose exceptional and abundant eloquence has surpassed even the lords of the gods through your own intellect, please attend to this entire matter in its completeness.
It produces that sense of wonder within the mind.
Indeed, it was previously refuted that the views designated as Ārhata and Saugata are contrary to the system of the Nigamas and Āgamas; this is precisely what you have stated.
By this, your desired goal does not attain fulfillment.
Now I shall set forth another opinion,
which is conducive to the investigation of the meaning as understood through the Vedas;
O you who are foremost among those of virtuous conduct, please proceed.
Having heard this, may you rejoice for a long time.
Thus, the doctrine favored by the Mīmāṃsakas, which was joyfully set forth at the outset by the eminent Bhṛṅgin,
has here been refuted.
One who possesses virtue speaks of each such thing as it has been seen.

Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into Dharma. Dharma is proposed as the subject to be investigated by way of its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its essential nature (*svarūpa*), its instruments of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and its results (*phala*). Among these, the means of valid cognition consist of injunctions (*codanā*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, and names. The definition of Dharma is: that which is the object to be accomplished by an injunction.

In that context, *codanā* (an injunction) consists of the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), and gerundive (*tavya*) suffixes, such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. *Arthavāda* (explanatory passage) is of four kinds: censure (*nindā*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), the deeds of others (*parakṛti*), and ancient history (*purākalpa*). Among these, an example of censure is: "One should offer oblations of wild- sesame gruel (*jartila-yavāgvā*)."

Regarding the oblation of wild- sesame gruel (*jartilayavāgū*) prescribed by the sentence "One should offer it with gruel of *gavīdhuka*," they say: "Wild-sesame and *gavīdhuka* are indeed not [proper] oblations. By this censure, the excellence of the oblation of goat's milk is established. As for the praise: "Vāyu, indeed..."

The passage beginning with "The deity is the swiftest" (*kṣepiṣṭhā devatā*) and so forth establishes the excellence [of the rite] by indicating that an action whose deity is swift will indeed bestow its fruit immediately. Regarding the previously enjoined sacrifice to Vāyu as its deity, Vaṭku Vārṣṇi said: "Cook beans for me."

*Parakṛti* (the deed of another) consists of such [passages] as "He makes the eastern sacrificial shed," which serve as reminders of matters to be performed in former times (*purākalpa*). *Mantra* consists of such [passages] as "They grasped this rein of the Truth. *Karmasamākhyā* (the name of a ritual action) consists of such [terms] as "Vājapeya" and "Śyena. Thus...

The authority of *śruti* is fourfold. The authority of *smṛti* is twofold: consisting of the *Dharmaśāstras* and that which determines ritual practice (*prayoga*). The *Smṛtis* of Manu and others constitute the *Dharmaśāstra*; the *Śikṣā*, *Kalpa*, *Vyākaraṇa*, and so forth, are those that determine linguistic usage. Custom (*ācāra*) is twofold: the custom of linguistic usage and...

And [the third is] the practice of the application of meaning. Among these, the first is the use of correct words dependent upon the understanding of grammar; the second, however, is the spring festival and so forth, which are contrary to the Dharmaśāstras. Thus, the means of valid knowledge regarding dharma have been set forth.
Among those, the fallacious authorities (*pramāṇābhāsa*) consist of the scriptures of the Jainas, Buddhists, Cārvākas, Pāñcarātras, Pāśupatas, Śāktas, Kaulas, Vāmas, and so forth. Now,
one might object that since some cultured persons (*śiṣṭa*) accept the Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata, and other such systems as authoritative...

If it is argued that [this practice] possesses the status of a semblance of valid authority (*pramāṇābhāsatva*) because it is performed by certain refined persons (*śiṣṭas*) who follow its prescribed conduct, we say no;
for they are considered non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*) due to being censured in the *Dharmaśāstras*, *Purāṇas*, and other such texts. As it has been said:
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"The Kāpāla, the Pāñcarātra, the Yāmala, the Vāma, the Ārhata,
and other such [systems] are indeed for the purpose of delusion."
Thus, by means of their engagement with these treatises, they delude men here;
for these treatises, rooted in illusion, lead to their delusion in future lives as well.
In the Parāśara Upapurāṇa,
O Sage, some praise the Pāñcarātra, some the Bhāgavata,
some praise the Śākta, and likewise some the Vāma.
O Great Sage, whatever other treatises exist that are in contradiction with the Veda— which is indeed unauthored and possesses intrinsic authority— [are to be rejected].
Endowed with faith, the twice-born embrace those very [practices] and perform them as great sins when the end of the age has arrived.
And in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"Those who subsist on excrement, those who have skulls as their ornaments,
the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, others, and likewise the Pāñcarātras."
Likewise, all other evil-minded ones are worshippers of the Asuras;
by the word "pāśa," the Vedic dharma (trayīdharma) is intended, because it protects the world.
Because they fragment that [Veda], they are therefore called *pākhaṇḍas* (heretics).
And in the *Sūtasamhitā*:
"O believers, the paths such as the *Pāñcarātra* have their root in the Veda."
For these are not independent; therefore, they are based on the root of delusion.
In that very same context, in another section, there is the inclusion of non-Vedic systems such as the left-hand Pāśupata and others;
the Pāñcarātra and so forth are also causes for the non-arising of knowledge.
Likewise, in another section of the *Kūrma Purāṇa*,
it is stated: "In that Kali age, there will be Brahmins and Kṣatriyas who follow the left-handed Pāśupata conduct as well as the Pāñcarātra."
When knowledge and ritual action have ceased and the world has become inactive,
insects, mice, and snakes will show themselves to human beings.
There exist thousands of such statements; they are not written here for fear of prolixity.

Furthermore, according to the principles of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā, the Pañcarātra and similar systems are not authoritative. This was stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Ācārya in the *Virodhādhikaraṇa*: "Those which are not accepted by those learned in the three Vedas..."
Those [teachings] which fall into the shadow of doctrines mixed with something of the truth,
which are intent on worldly gathering, honor, gain, and fame, which are contrary to the Three Vedas, and which have visible results such as mere outward beauty;

They are composed based on perception, inference, analogy, presumption, probability, and traditional authority; they establish the foundations of dharma and adharma as accepted by the Pāñcarātras, Pāśupatas, Śākyas, Nirgranthas, and others; and they contain a few mantras and medicinal herbs capable of effecting human healing, subjugation, eradication, and derangement.

And those external [scriptures] which, by the power of demonstrating occasional successes, teach other matters that consist mostly of a livelihood— faintly perfumed with the scent of limited truths such as non-violence, truthful speech, tranquility, self-restraint, compassion, and charity— which are in agreement with the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
These [scriptures] are based on the practice of barbarian customs and the consumption of impure food;

it is precisely because of this that their lack of authority is established through both scriptural testimony (*śruti*) and logical reasoning (*darśana*). For if their invalidity were not established by disregarding them, others might think, "It is impossible [to invalidate them]."

"Those of equal vision [should act] because of beauty, ease, and the stated reasons, and due to the influence of the Kali age, lest they fall into the delusion that the animal sacrifice mentioned [in the Veda] should be abandoned. For as long as those who are utterly opposed to the established path of the Three Vedas have not been refuted, the purification of Dharma cannot be attained. Thus [it is said].

If it is argued: "Even though the Pāñcarātra and other such systems are non-authoritative because they contradict Śruti and Smṛti, let there still be authority for those portions that are not contradictory," [the response is: "If it is argued that what is not contradicted is authoritative provided it does not conflict with the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa)—this is the meaning of the Sūtra."
Objection: To this, the reply is "not so, because of the limited extent of the scripture" (*na śāstraparimāṇatvāt*).

This means that the scripture is finite. For it is said: "The auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the expansion of Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*)."
Because it is established that the scripture (*śāstra*) is limited in scope. For Dharma, as measured by just anyone, will not yield its fruit;
rather, Dharma is that which is measured by the Vedas, the Smṛtis rooted in them, the Purāṇas that augment them, and their auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*).
Therefore, even if tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth—which are not contradicted by Śruti and Smṛti—are present there [in the *Śunaka*], [they do not constitute Dharma].
Like milk drawn into a bellows, it is both unenjoyable and unreliable.

Even regarding those duties well-known in the world, such as non-violence and truthful speech, the prescription of dharma must be carried out by citing the words of Manu and others at the time of its formulation; it is not [to be done otherwise].
However, [this is not the case] with those [works] composed and revised by people of the present day.
As it was said by the Teachers:
"In the form of a counter-mask, [the commentary] has as its object the meaning of the earlier treatises."
Whatever else is performed, that is not authoritative with respect to Dharma. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, because it is established by such Vedic texts as, "May I become a bearer of the divine nectar of the Vīramāheśvara doctrine," and "O Brahmaṇaspati, your purifier is spread out; salutation to Brahman,
may there be retention for me," and because it is not included within the Pāśupata [system], it is indeed authoritative, and not otherwise.

[The subject matter] is the domain of fallacious means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*). Therefore, the first chapter has as its primary purpose the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the second chapter concerns the differentiation of *dharma*.

For instance, [the means of differentiation include] difference of words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṅkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), name (*saṃjñā*), change of context (*prakaraṇāntara*), and so forth.

[It is] the agency in establishing the distinction between the essential natures of dharmas. In that regard, in the case of "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), "he gives" (*dadāti*), and "he offers oblations" (*juhoti*), the distinction between actions is established through different words (*śabdāntara*). In cases such as "he sacrifices the fuel-sticks" (*samidho yajati*) and "he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt" (*tanūnapātaṃ yajati*), the distinction between actions arises from repetition (*abhyāsa*). In cases such as "he offers three oblations" (*tisra āhutīr juhoti*), [the distinction arises] from number (*saṅkhyā*).

Distinction of rites (*karmabheda*): In such passages as "The *āmikṣā* [curd-mixture] belongs to the Viśvedevas," there is a distinction of rites due to a qualifying attribute (*guṇa*). In such passages as "Now this is the Jyotis," or "Now this is the Viśvajyotis," there is a distinction of rites due to a name (*saṃjñā*).
In such passages as "He performs the Agnihotra for a month," there is a distinction of rites due to a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*). Thus...
It has been stated that the second chapter establishes the distinction between ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
Now, it is stated that the third chapter establishes the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*). For instance:

"Direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyāna*) are the means of proof regarding the status of being a subordinate element."

In such cases as "One should worship the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse," the status of being subsidiary to the worship of the Gārhapatya is established by direct statement (*śruti*). In such cases as "O Soma, enter me" (*bhakṣehi mā viśa*), the application of the mantra— extending up to the words "may [he] be satisfied" (*tṛpyatu*)— to the acts of taking up, looking at, and consuming the Soma is determined by indicative power (*liṅga*).

In such passages as "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa," the determination that the sacrifice is to be performed by the giver is established through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). The application (*viniyoga*) of the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*), after-sacrifices (*anuyāja*), the butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*), and so forth, to the New and Full Moon sacrifices is established through context (*prakaraṇa*). [The mantra] "Both Indra and Agni... [is applied through position].

Thus, by means of the sequence characterized by proximity of place (*sthāna-sādeśya*), there is an application (*viniyoga*) of these mantras— beginning with "indrasya tvā bāhubhyām" and so forth— in the *aindrāgneyīṣṭi* and other rites. This applies to those mantras accompanied by ritual formulas, such as "indrāya rājñe sūkaraḥ," which are found in the immediate vicinity of the fire-piling (*agnicayana*).
The fact that certain rites constitute parts of the Aśvamedha sacrifice is established by the designation "Aśvamedhika. Such is the subject matter of the third chapter.

The subject matter of the fourth chapter is as follows: first, an investigation into what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is conducted in order to distinguish their application (*prayukti*). [Examples include: the rule regarding the acquisition of property; the rule "one should not look at the rising sun";
and the specific quality of the animal in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal. These are for the sake of the sacrifice.

Then follows the inquiry regarding whether [the acts] serve human ends (*puruṣārtha*). Following that is the inquiry into what constitutes a motivator (*prayojaka*) and what does not, in passages such as: "He pours curds into hot milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas, and the whey (*vājina*) for the Vājins.
Then follows: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of gold hears no evil report."

In such passages, there is an investigation into the injunctions regarding results (*phala-vidhi*) and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Following that, in cases such as "One should sacrifice with the Rājasūya" and "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," there is an investigation into whether [the latter] serves as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) for the purpose of indicating time (*kāla*), or as a primary act (*pradhāna*). Such is the investigation of the fourth chapter.

Immediately following this, in the fifth chapter, an investigation into *krama* (sequence) is undertaken. First is the investigation into the sequence of the Vedic text (*śrutikrama*), as in the passage: "The Adhvaryu priest, having initiated the Gṛhapati, initiates the Brahman," and so forth. Next is the investigation into the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*), as in: "He offers the Agnihotra; [he cooks] the barley-gruel..."

In cases such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), there is first the consideration of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), as in "he sacrifices the fuel-sticks" (*śamīdhmo yajati*) and so forth. The order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*) applies to the animal sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati. The order of the principal (*mukhyakrama*) is as follows:

first the performance of the ritual procedure for the vegetable offering, and thereafter the performance according to the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the purpose (*artha*), the order of recitation (*pāṭha*), and the order of performance (*pravṛtti*).
An investigation into the relative strength and weakness of the means of determining sequence, beginning with direct statement;
thus concludes the fifth chapter.

Then, in the sixth chapter, there is first an inquiry into the eligibility of gods, animals, and humans; then an inquiry into the eligibility for the Niṣāda-Sattrayāga sacrifice; then an inquiry into the eligibility for obligatory, occasional, and optional rites; and after that—
The investigation of eligibility regarding substitutes; thereafter, the investigation of eligibility for the *abhyudayeṣṭi* sacrifice;
thereafter, eligibility based on the cause of disconnection (*apaccheda*); then, eligibility for the *sārasvata-satra* and other rites;
and then, eligibility for the *viśvajit* sacrifice. Thus, the investigation of eligibility has been conducted by means of the sixth chapter.

The subject matter of the seventh chapter is the extension of general rules (*sāmānyātideśa*). First, there is the investigation of the *pāriplava* (the revolving recitation) regarding the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*); then, the extension of injunctions (*vidhyatideśa*) in such passages as "these very Brāhmaṇas are the five oblations"; and thereafter, the extension of auxiliaries by way of their function (*kāryamukhena*). Thus...
The Seventh Chapter.

Investigation of the Eighth Chapter: First, the extension of specific details (*viśeṣātideśa*); then, the investigation into how sacrifices such as the *saurya* have the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as their archetype; then, how the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice has the *savanīya* animal sacrifice as its archetype;
and how the *savanīya* has the group of eleven animals (*paśvaikādaśinī*) as its archetype.

The *ekādaśinī* (the group of eleven animals) serves as the archetype for groups of sacrificial animals (*paśugaṇa*). Sacrifices whose deities are unspecified have the *soma* sacrifice as their archetype. The *soma* sacrifice serves as the archetype for sacrifices such as the *atirātra*, the *vājapeya*, and the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and others.
The twelve-day sacrifice is of two kinds: the *ahīna* and the *satra* sacrifice. It is characterized by having a single performer and multiple *sutyā* days.

It involves many sacrificers and numerous *sutyā* days. The *dvirātra*, *trirātra*, and so forth have the *ahīna-dvādaśāha* as their archetype (*prakṛti*). And for the *satras*, the *satra-dvādaśāha* serves as the archetype.
This applies to the sacrificial sessions (*kratu*) accomplished over a year, such as the *kuṇḍapāyināmayana* and others.
The Gavāmayana serves as the archetype (prakṛti). All animal sacrifices (paśu) are modifications (vikāra) of the Sānnāyya offering.
Sacrifices to a single deity are modifications of the Āgneya sacrifice; those to two deities are modifications of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice. Such is the subject matter of the eighth chapter.

Now, the subject matter of the ninth chapter is stated: the acceptance of the definition of words such as *ulūkhala* (mortar), *musala* (pestle), *dṛṣad* (lower millstone), *upala* (upper millstone), *vrīhi* (rice), and so forth, as denoting the means for producing the *apūrva* (transcendental result). Following that is the investigation into their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to the deity.

Then follows the deliberation on the modification of threshing and so forth; then, in the second pāda, the deliberation on the modification of the Sāman; then the deliberation on the modification of the *adhrigu* injunction. Thus concludes the ninth chapter.

Then follows the investigation of the tenth chapter: first, the extension (*atideśa*) of ritual elements (*padārtha*) by way of their function (*kārya*); then, the cessation of threshing in the *kṛṣṇala* oblation; the cessation of cutting the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) when it is provided by the patron himself; the sublation (*bādha*) of *kuśa* grass in cases such as "the sacrificial grass consists of *śara* grass"; and [finally] the modification (*parivṛtti*) of the archetypal injunction (*codaka*) in the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice and others.

From the omission [of the *nañ*], there follows the sublation of the auxiliary members (*aṅga*) other than the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. Subsequently, the status of the deity (*devatātva*) is established as the referent qualified by a word ending in the dative case. Thereafter follows the investigation into the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Following that are the principles of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), the maxim of "not-censure" (*na-hi-nindā-nyāya*), and the maxim of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*). Thus.
The Tenth Chapter.
Then, in the eleventh [section], there is the investigation of tantra. Tantratva is the performance of subsidiary elements (aṅga) once for the sake of multiple primary objectives.

Next, in the twelfth [section], there is the investigation of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). "Incidental application" means that even those auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) which are performed without being specifically enjoined for it, yet fall within the context of the primary rite (*tantra*), serve as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) to the primary rite when they have been performed in connection with the performance of the principal injunctions.
Thus, Mīmāṃsā, consisting of twelve chapters, has been briefly described.

In this regard, although the section concerning deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*) is not required for the determination of the meaning of other scriptural passages from the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas— since it is accepted by all disputants as such— nevertheless,
Mīmāṃsā is extremely contradictory regarding the nature of the deity and consciousness, much like the doctrine of *sphoṭa* in the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*).

Such indeed is their intended meaning: that the deity is an object qualified by a word, and that the deity is simply a word ending in the dative case. This is utterly untenable. For instance: "They grasped the right hand of Indra," "Vajrahasta Purandara," "Sahasrākṣa."

In cases such as "Gotrabhid Vajrabāhu" [where Indra is addressed], "The thirty gods attained their status through three [sacrifices]," "Vajrabāhu slew Vṛtra," and "Vidura chose [the path]," [Indra and others] are clearly perceived as sentient beings. Likewise, in passages such as "Agni, whose face is ghee, whose source is ghee, the bull, is kindled; like a horse that carries the gods... [the deity is perceived as sentient].
Nor should it be argued that because fire lacks the manifestation of sentience, there is no validity [in its being considered sentient];

for even when this is the case, in such [Vedic] passages as "He has four horns, three feet," and so forth, the feet, heads, and hands— which possess qualities unique to sentient beings— are clearly understood even by children.

Because they are objects of cognition, the sentience of the deities certainly exists. Furthermore, in the mantra: "Obeisance again and again to the golden-armed one, to the golden-hued, to the golden-formed, to the Lord of gold, to the Lord of Ambikā, to the Lord of Umā, to Paśupati," [the Lord] appeared as a woman in that very space.
"O Uma, daughter of Himavat, who shines so brightly"— thus, by the *Kenopaniṣad*,
Uma is clearly established as the daughter of Himavat and as female; and [the text] "Salutation to Rudra, the Bountiful One" makes known her husband Śiva as conscious and, therein, as male.
Furthermore, how can it be asserted that the One who is perceived even within other mantras as being compassionate is insentient? Nor [is it the case] that,
although a mantra of the Upaniṣads may have as its purport a deity with form for the sake of meditation, [it follows that the Supreme Self is not sentient].

It must be stated that the mantras which are constituent parts of ritual acts (*karmāṅga-mantra*) do not possess such [independent] reality; for even in the case of the *Śatarudrīya*, which is itself a constituent part of a ritual act, there is a clear perception of them as being directed toward a conscious entity in such mantras as "The poor one, Nīlalohita, the blue-necked, the deep-red one," and so forth. Nor is there any need to accept a deity distinct from the word [itself].

It should not be argued that even in cases such as "Svāhā to the sound *īṅ*," "Svāhā to the teeth," and "Svāhā to the jaws," this would entail the acceptance of deities distinct from the words themselves;
for while such [deities] may be accepted in certain instances due to the force of sublation (*bādhaka*), there is no evidence for accepting them in all such cases.
Otherwise, in cases such as "an animal with a black neck for Agni" (*āgneyīṃ kṛṣṇagrīvīm*), there would be no ritual immolation (*ālambhana*) of a female animal.

Furthermore, since the feminine gender in words such as *nadī*, *kādambinī*, *khaṭvā*, and *vīthī* is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), it is necessary to accept the same principle in the present case as well. [Examples include: *siṃhaḥ*, *siṃhī*, *kukkuṭaḥ*.

If it is argued that in cases such as *kukkuṭī* (hen), because gender and so forth are understood through suffixes like *ṅīp*, the sacrifice must therefore be of a female animal alone, then let this same logic be applied to the present case as well. Furthermore, the expression of numbers— singularity, duality, and plurality— would also not be possible through case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Because there is deviation [from the rule] in cases such as *dārāḥ* (wife/wives), it is nothing but the prattle of a fool to claim that an object which has been set aside by a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) in one instance must necessarily be accepted even in an uncontradicted context. Therefore, in expressions such as *īṅkārāya svāhā*, even though there is no deity, [the term is used]; likewise in *vajrahastaḥ purandaraḥ* and so forth.

There is indeed no contradiction in establishing that deities possess consciousness. Nor does the acceptance of divine consciousness contradict the fact that the words *agni*, *vaiśvānara*, and *vahni* are listed as synonyms in the *Amarakośa*—as in "Agni, Vaiśvānara, Vahni"—given that in the *Āgneya-puroḍāśa* sacrifice, [the mantra] "This for Vaiśvānara... [is recited].
It should be stated that there is no contingency of accepting [the deity] as "mine" and so forth, because even though the words differ, the referent is one;

for even in the position that accepts a deity distinct [from the mantra], since the deity is defined precisely by its qualification through the word, there is no room for over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Now, [it may be argued that] the mantra [functions] by way of recollecting the object to be performed...

If it is argued that, even though the constituent part of the ritual (*kratvaṅga*)— namely, its own enjoining statement which forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction for the performance of the non-ritual [subsidiary] and has as its purport the primary sacrifice assisted by itself— also intends the sentience of the deity, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) in the primary injunction caused by this difference in purport; we say no, because such a result is acceptable.

Nor should it be said that a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is a fault; for only a split of the sentence consisting in the repetition of an injunction (*vidhyāvṛtti*) is a fault. To explain: there are two kinds of split of the sentence—those occasioned by the repetition of an injunction and those occasioned by a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*). As in the case of "He sweeps the house" (*gṛhaṃ sammārṣṭi*), etc.

With respect to the act of sweeping directed toward the house, since it is necessary to enjoin even the singularity inherent in the house, both [the house and its singularity] are enjoined through the very repetition of the injunction; thus, uttering [the word] twice becomes a fault. However, when there is a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*), [it is not so].

There is no repetition of the sentence at all. For example, in the case of the statement, "The cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni (Āgneya) is unswerving on the new moon and full moon days," once it is accepted that this is an injunction for a sacrifice qualified by substance, deity, and time, [there is no repetition] of that which has a qualified intention.

Since there is an intention (*tātparya*) even regarding the qualifiers of an injunction, there is no fault of repeating the injunction even when the intentions differ. Likewise here, although there is an intention toward its own literal meaning for the mantra— which is a verbal form that constitutes a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) together with the subsidiary-injunctions— there is no fault of the injunction being repeated.

If it is objected that, if consciousness is admitted for the deity, then— since the deity would be inherently primary like a king— the deity could not be a subordinate element (aṅga) of the sacrifice by way of being the means of accomplishing the sacrifice, as a material substance (dravya) is; we say no, because even though the sacrificer is the enjoyer of the fruit and is thus primarily everything, he is nevertheless implied as the agent by the injunction "one should sacrifice" (yajeta).
Just as that which is capable of accomplishing its own purpose can be a subsidiary element of a sacrifice, so too is it possible here.

[Objection: Is it not the case that where there is the status of being a subordinate member (*aṅgatva*), there cannot be the status of being a primary element (*pradhānatva*), as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; and where there is the status of being a primary element, there cannot be the status of being a subordinate member, as in the case of the *soma* sacrifice? How, then, can both of these contradictory states be accepted here? [Response: No, because this cannot withstand logical analysis (*vikalpāsahatvāt*). To explain: regarding the presentation of another...
