Regarding this, what is being asserted: that there is no status as a subordinate (*aṅgatva*) with respect to anything other [than the principal], or that there is no status as a subordinate with respect to that very thing toward which it has the status of a principal (*pradhānatva*)? In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, because even though the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites are principals with respect to the fruit, they possess the status of subordinates with respect to the Jyotiṣṭoma itself. It is not the second case.
Because there is deviation [in the application of the rule] in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the *paśupuroḍāśa*, the final *prayāja*, and so forth;
for the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice is performed after the principal sacrifice has been completed, following the offerings to Agni and to Agni-Soma.

Furthermore, because it serves as a *pratipatti* (disposal) consisting of the expenditure of the sacrificial offering (*havis*) by those who require its removal to another location due to the congestion of that place,

the sacrificial substance (*haviraṅga*), being of the nature of a sacrifice (*yāgarūpa*), possesses primacy (*pradhānatva*) since that which is of the nature of a sacrifice is accomplished through the material provided by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). It is exactly so.

By the statement, "The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) of the animal sacrifice also belongs to the same deity as the animal," the deity of the animal serves as a reminder; thus, because the deity is that which accomplishes the sacrifice, it possesses primacy even as a subordinate quality of the animal sacrifice. The same applies to the final fore-offering (uttama-prayāja).

By virtue of the mantra "Svāhā to Agni, Svāhā to Soma," although these [oblations] are subordinate because they are for the sake of the deities through the medium of recollecting them, they also possess primacy according to the principle that every sacrifice must be accomplished by means of a deity. All of this applies without distinction to the *āśrayis* (the substrates).
It is clearly stated in the fourth chapter [of the *Tantravārttika*] that "the meaning is understood as the state of being six.

Therefore, since it is possible to accept even a contradiction on the basis of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction whatsoever here in accepting the subordinate status (*guṇatva*) of the deity with respect to the sacrifice, even though the deity is the primary element (*pradhānatva*).

[Objection: Even if one accepts that the deity possesses consciousness, how can it be the primary [agent]? Since it must necessarily be stated that it is merely subordinate because it brings about the sacrifice—[Response: No, because at the very moment when its consciousness is established, its status as the primary agent is also established. Sacrifices and the like, however, are merely auxiliary parts of the ritual action (*karma*). For example, in the world:

Service to servants and the like is for the sake of the king because it brings about the favor of the sovereign; similarly, rites such as sacrifices are for the sake of the deity by way of propitiating the presiding deity. Nor should it be asked how there can be an establishment of a matter cognizable through scripture by means of a worldly analogy without a formal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for [it is established] by one who is satisfied...
"Thus Indra satisfies him with progeny and cattle; having drunk the ghee and the sweet, pleasant milk of the cow,

may he protect this man as a father protects his son"— since there exist numerous such authoritative scriptural passages (*mantra* and *arthavāda*), where could an action that has perished possibly bear fruit?

Furthermore, because there exist Purāṇic statements such as "without the propitiation of the Supreme Person," and because the efficacy of divine grace in producing results is also evident from worldly usage— such as "Paśupati is pleased with him" or "a son has been born to him"— the Vedic mantra-text also expresses this same meaning.

"O Bountiful One, be gracious to our offspring and to our progeny. The meaning of this is as follows: although one should say "mīḍhvan," the form "mīḍhvaḥ" is a Vedic (chāndasa) form derived from the root *miha*, meaning "to sprinkle.
O Śiva, you who are moist with compassion (*dayārdra*), [be gracious] to our *toka* and *tanaya*—that is, to our offspring in the form of sons. Offspring...
"Tokam" means "the two of them together. According to Amara, "ātmaja," "tanaya," and "sūnu" also mean son. "Mṛḍaya" means "make happy.
This is the second person singular, active voice, imperative mood of the causative form (*ṇijanta*) of the root *mṛḍ* (meaning "to gladden").
The meaning is: "O Compassionate One, gladden us by procreating a male offspring. [This refers to] that which is produced through action.
Only the grace of the Supreme Lord produces the fruit of a son, and not inert action alone.

Furthermore, from the designations "this is the village of the deity" and "this is the field of the deity," the primacy of the deity is established, rather than its being subordinate. Although it may be considered subordinate by virtue of being the means for accomplishing the sacrifice, even that does not [diminish its primacy].
There would be a loss of primacy for the deity.

Now, one might object: "If the sentience of deities is accepted, then when sacrifices are being performed in many locations and the deities such as Indra and others—who are each of a single form—are invoked simultaneously, how is it possible for them to go to those places, given the contradiction? To this, we say: no.
For those who have attained the grace of the Supreme Lord through the performance of specific austerities and particular sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*),
and who have thereby acquired unsurpassed sovereignty, it is possible for them to simultaneously assume a manifold array of bodies.

There is no contradiction, because it is possible to move to many locations simultaneously. Alternatively, it is observed in the world that a single king can be the intended object of salutations performed by many soldiers at once; likewise [it is possible] for those who have each assumed a separate body.

There is no contradiction, because it is possible for the gods to be the intended recipients (*uddeśyatva*) of sacrifices performed by multiple agents. If it is argued that all of this constitutes a contradiction regarding the ritual action (*karman*), [the answer is] "no," because we observe multiple forms of reception (*pratipatti*). This very point was raised as an objection and resolved in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* of the *Uttaratantre*. Therefore, the statement that there is no consciousness in the deity is [a denial] of heaven...

This [claim] is as devoid of reasoning and contradicted by many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the statement that [heaven] consists of unsurpassed bliss. If it is asked, "How is it contradictory for heaven to be the object of unsurpassed joy?", we reply: no; for the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* (1.2.9–10) states: "Thinking the sacrifice and the gift-offering to be the highest, the deluded know nothing higher than that; they go to the world of the moon, the peak of heaven... and so forth.
"Having experienced the fruits of their good deeds, they enter this world or one even lower.

By reflecting on such scriptural passages as, "Having dwelt there until their merit is exhausted, they return again by that very same path," it follows that even in heaven, the hundred-eyed Indra experiences no peace, being fearful of his eventual fall. They...

Furthermore, by reflecting on such Smṛti passages as, "Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, when their merit is exhausted, they enter the world of mortals," how could it be possible for the bliss of heaven— which, immediately after its own experience,
becomes a cause of misfortune just like the pleasures of saṃsāra— to be an object of unsurpassed delight? It is not so.
It cannot be argued that this [pleasure] is called "unsurpassed" because, in comparison with other pleasures,

there is no evidence for the existence of a superior pleasure, and because it appears to those experiencing it at the time of its own perception as being unsurpassed due to its intensity, even though it is subsequently accompanied by affliction.

Because it cannot withstand critical analysis: is this [state] called "unsurpassed bliss" because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a bliss greater than this, or because it appears as such to those who experience it?
In the first case, since the fruit of the *dahara-vidyā* and other meditations consists of various desired forms such as non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*), [the objection does not hold].
Because many means of valid cognition exist, there is a loss of the absolute certainty regarding heaven.
For instance: "Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise;
endowed with that world of the fathers, he is magnified. Having said this, immediately thereafter, in the very same manner:
"Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of the mothers, if he becomes desirous of the world of brothers, if he becomes desirous of the world of sisters..."

"He becomes one who desires the world of women, he becomes one who desires the world of friends, he becomes one who desires the world of perfumes and garlands, he becomes one who desires the world of song and instrumental music"— having said this, and having stated that immediately after each such [desire], his mothers arise by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), and so forth, by that...

In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the fruit is set forth as follows: "Endowed with the world of the mothers, he is magnified," and so forth. Furthermore, in that very same text, it is said: "Whatever desire he may have, whatever region or portion of land he desires, that arises for him by his mere volition (saṅkalpa); endowed with that, he is magnified. He...

He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold, four-fold, five-fold, eight-fold, nine-fold. There is that lake Airammadīya, there that Aśvattha tree Soma-savana, there that unconquerable citadel of Brahmā, the golden hall built by the Lord. There is the Person, Mānava; he leads him to Brahman.
And he does not return again, he does not return again—this is great sovereignty: the reunion with parents, sisters, brothers, sons, wives, and friends experienced and lost in that birth;
the power to assume a multitude of diverse bodies; and the attainment of whatever is desired through mental meditation.

The attainment of such utterly marvelous happiness— consisting of wandering through one's own desired lands, attaining a form similar to that of the worshiped Lord, dwelling in His proximity, possessing the power of creation like Him, and non-return [to saṃsāra]—

renders the nature of happiness belonging to that heavenly bliss (svarga) merely a semblance of happiness when compared to it, given the existence of this [higher] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Because it is impossible to state [otherwise]. Not the second [alternative], because it would entail that the pleasures produced by scratching an itch are unsurpassed pleasures (*niratiśaya-sukha*), since at the time of experiencing them, the pleasure of scratching an itch is experienced precisely as being unsurpassed. Therefore, the doctrine that heaven (*svarga*) is unsurpassed—
"It is a deluder of the foolish; thus it is to be disregarded"—all this is entirely consistent.

[Thus, from the venerable Ṣaṭsthalanirṇaya, which is distinguished by the one hundred and one unsurpassed sections produced by churning the ocean of the Śāmbhava Āgama— attained through the grace of Toṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the mobile Aparā form of the beginningless and stainless [Śiva]...]

In [this work] composed by the eminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows a mass of bliss through the taste of nectar, [it concerns] Keladi Sadāśivarāya— the sole hero among the millions of Yādava-Murāris, the plunderer of the seven constituents of the enemy king, the sovereign of the western ocean, and the preceptor who established the pure Vedic doctrine of Advaita.

In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, within the section on debate (*vādakāṇḍa*) and the instruction of Basava— the joy of the hearts of the people and the Indra of the earth— concerning Mallāmbā, the lawful consort of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth and the full moon in the milky ocean of the lineage of the Leader,
this is the twelfth chapter, titled "The Manner of Describing and Refuting the Mīmāṃsaka Doctrine."
[Chapter] ||
[The Thirteenth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O true Guru, tell me: what did Bhṛṅgin then begin in that assembly, and what answer was given by Śīlavat at that time?
O King, ocean of all branches of knowledge, moon that causes the nectar of learning to swell,
O illustrious one, listen to these words of Bhṛṅgin and Śīlavat.
The Mīmāṃsaka position, though based on scripture, has been refuted by reasoning and through valid means of knowledge; yet, by that much alone, the establishment of your own position is not achieved.
I shall now proclaim another doctrine consistent with the purpose of the Smṛtis;
listen, O foremost of the virtuous, to this teaching which asserts that the Unmanifest is the agent.
Thus, I shall state in its entirety and in due order the refutation of the Kapila doctrine as it was initiated by Bhṛṅgīvara in the assembly and proclaimed by Śīlavat.
The followers of Kapila, moreover, describe it thus:

the unmanifest (*avyakta*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) known as form, taste, smell, touch, and sound—these are the primal natures (*prakṛti*). It is called "unmanifest" because it is not manifested [as a specific object], unlike a jar, a cloth, or similar things.
Through its derivation, the wise declare this to be the Pradhāna— without beginning or middle, beyond the Mahat, eternal, subtle,
the mark, insentient, without beginning or end, and likewise characterized by productivity.

For this unmanifest (avyakta) is indeed partless, one, and common to all; this very unmanifest is designated by synonymous terms such as *pradhāna*, *brahma-bahudhānaka*, *akṣara*, *kṣetra*, and *tamaḥ-prasūna*. Intellect (*buddhi*), however, is "thus and thus, and not otherwise," like "this is indeed a cow."

"It is not a horse; this is indeed a post, not a person"—such is [the nature of] determination (*adhyavasāya*). From determination arises activity toward cows and other objects. The qualities of this intellect (*buddhi*) are knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—these are its four *sāttvika* forms; while non-virtue, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty [are its *tāmasa* forms].
There are four forms characterized by *tamas*, and thus there are eight forms in total.
Dharma is that which is not opposed to the *Śruti*, the *Smṛti*, and the conduct of the virtuous (*śiṣṭācāra*), and which possesses auspicious characteristics; it is the opposite of *adharma*.
Right knowledge (*samyagbodha*) regarding the true nature of the elements is [the cause of liberation], whereas attachment to objects such as sound and the like is ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Ignorance is the opposite of knowledge. Dispassion is the opposite of passion. Sovereignty, consisting of the eight qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā), is the opposite of non-sovereignty.
Unrighteousness is the opposite of righteousness; it is characterized by inauspiciousness and is contrary to the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous.

Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the non-comprehension of things as they truly are, which is the opposite of knowledge (*jñāna*). Non-detachment (*avairāgya*) is attachment to objects such as sound and the like, which is the opposite of detachment (*vairāgya*).
Lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*) is the absence of powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth, which is the opposite of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

The fruits [of the qualities] are: ascending progressively by means of knowledge of dharma, dispassion, sovereignty, and their causes; the cessation of the activity toward liberation; unimpeded movement; and descending by means of adharma and so forth.
Thus, there are eight forms of the intellect (*buddhi*): mind (*manas*), thought (*mati*), intellect (*buddhi*), renown (*khyāti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

*dhṛti* (fortitude) and *prajñāna* (knowledge) are used as synonymous terms. The ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is said to be the conceit expressed in such thoughts as "I hear," "I see," "I taste," "I smell," "I touch," and "this person has been killed by me. It is of three types: the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi*.

By these synonymous terms, it is indeed the *ahaṃkāra* that is designated. The subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell. Among these, from the subtle element of sound, there is the perception of sound in general.
However, there is no perception of specific sounds such as udātta, anudātta, svarita, kampita, or the notes ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, and so forth.

Likewise, there is perception of the general quality of touch belonging to the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra), but not perception of specific touches such as soft, hard, cold, or hot. Similarly...

From the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), there is the perception of the generality of form, but not the perception of specific forms such as white, black, green, or yellow. Likewise, from the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), there is the perception of the generality of taste, but not the perception of specific tastes such as pungent or bitter.
From the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*), there arises the cognition of the universal property of smell (*gandha-sāmānya*),

but not the cognition of specific smells characterized by fragrance or foulness. These subtle elements are the non-specific [causes], the material causes (*prakṛti*) of the gross elements, and are the atoms that serve as objects of experience.

These are designated by synonymous terms. Thus, the eight primary natures (prakṛtis)—known as the unmanifest (avyakta), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and the subtle elements (tanmātras)—have been established. Now, there are eleven organs: the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, and mind.
The great elements known as earth, water, fire, air, and space, along with these, constitute the sixteen transformations.

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects of the five sense organs, beginning with the ear. Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure are the functions of the organs of action, beginning with speech.

The objects of the five [senses] are their respective domains; the objects of the mind are its conceptualizations, discriminations, and so forth. The senses, which are instruments of a transformative nature, are designated by synonymous terms such as *khāni*, *niyatāni*, *padāni*, *ārayaḥ*, and *akṣāṇi*. They function by way of sustaining [their objects].
Earth is that which assists the other four elements and is endowed with the five qualities known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; likewise,
those [qualities] existing in the state of cohesion assist the other four elements.

Water is endowed with four qualities known as sound, touch, form, and taste; fire, functioning through the state of digestion, assists the other four elements and is endowed with three qualities known as sound, touch, form, and taste; and air, functioning through the state of conveying, assists the four elements other than itself.

Air possesses sound and touch; it functions by providing space and assists the other four elements that are distinct from itself. Space possesses the single quality of sound. The elements are the particulars, the modifications, the forms, the bodies, and the physical structures; they are classified as calm, terrible, or deluded.

They are designated by synonymous terms. Thus, there are sixteen transformations. [The Self] is beginningless, subtle, all-pervading, conscious, devoid of qualities, eternal, the seer, the enjoyer, the agent, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), stainless, and characterized by non-procreation; it is so called because of its antiquity, because it dwells in the city (*puri*), and because it functions as the domestic priest (*purohita*).

He is called the *puruṣa*. Because he is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, he is without beginning (*anādi*). Because he is partless and beyond the reach of the senses, he is subtle (*sūkṣma*). Because everything has been attained by him and there is nothing further for him to go to, he is all-pervading (*sarvagata*). And because he possesses the perception of pleasure, pain, and delusion, he is conscious (*cetana*).
Because the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* do not exist in it, it is "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*).
Because it is uncreated and unproduced, it is "eternal" (*nitya*). Because it perceives the transformations of *prakṛti*, it is the "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*).
Because of its conscious nature and its cognition of pleasure and pain, it is the "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*).

Because of its indifference and lack of qualities, it is a non-agent (*akartṛ*). It is a "knower of the field" (*kṣetravit*) because it knows the field as it pertains to its own qualities, or because it knows that which pertains to the qualities within the fields. It is "stainless" (*amala*) because it possesses no auspicious or inauspicious karma. Because it is seedless, it produces nothing at all; thus, it is "devoid of the nature of procreation" (*aprasavadharmā*).

Thus, this Sāṅkhya Puruṣa is designated by synonymous terms such as Ātman, Pumān, Bahula, Jantu, Jīva, Kṣetrajña, Nara, Kavi, Brahma, Akṣara, Prāṇa, and Aja. In this way, there are twenty-five principles (tattvas): the eight primary natures (prakṛtis), the sixteen transformations (vikāras), and the Puruṣa.
And so it has been said by the traditionalists:
"Root-nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolution;
the group of sixteen is only evolution; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolution."

"One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life he is devoted to—whether he has a shaven head, matted hair, or a topknot—is liberated; there is no doubt about this. Thus it is said.

If this Puruṣa were the agent, then he would perform only auspicious deeds and not inauspicious ones; nor is the threefold state observed in him. Rather, it is established that the agency over all moving and non-moving beings belongs solely to the qualities of Prakṛti—sattva, rajas, and tamas. Regarding this, those who know the tradition say:

The literature known as Dharma, the practice of restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), and thorough discernment; knowledge, sovereignty, dispassion, and illumination—this is the sattvic state of being.
Passion, anger, greed, slander of others, extreme ferocity, lack of contentment, distorted appearance, and harshness— this is well known as the mode of activity characterized by *rajas*.
Insanity, intoxication, despondency, atheism, addiction to women, sleep, laziness,
cruelty, and impurity— this is the tamasic disposition.
Therefore, the Puruṣa is declared to be a non-doer, even while engaging with these qualities of Prakṛti,
because his vision is contrary to rajas and tamas.
"I am doing this," thus the ignorant person conceives [this thought]. Thus [it is said].

Even though one is incapable of bending a blade of grass, if one says, "All this has been done by me," one becomes deluded through ego-inflation and acts like a madman. Regarding this, there is a scriptural authority (*āgama*):
"All actions whatsoever are performed in every way by the qualities (*guṇas*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*)."
One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."
Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this immutable Supreme Self,
O son of Kuntī, does nothing and is not tainted, even though it dwells within the body.
And he who sees that actions are being performed in every way by nature alone, and likewise sees the Self as the non-doer—he truly sees. Thus it is said.

There are many puruṣas because of the diversity of pleasure, pain, and delusion; of mixture and purification; of the rules governing actions; of birth and death; and because of the distinctions between the worlds, stages of life (āśrama), and social classes (varṇa). If there were only one puruṣa, then when one is happy, all would be happy; and when one is in pain, all would be in pain.
If one were deluded, all would be deluded; if one were confused, all would be confused; if one were pure, all would be pure;
if one lacked proficiency in the instruments, all would lack proficiency in the instruments; and if one were born... all.
If there were only one [Self], when one is born all would be born, and when one dies all would die; yet this is not the case.
Therefore, because of the diversity of forms, wombs, dispositions, destinies, bodies, and marks, the Sāṅkhya teachers maintain that there are many Puruṣas.
Kapila, Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Pañcaśikha, Patañjali, and others describe [it].
By the etymological derivation that "the three qualities" (*traiguṇya*) are simply the "triad of qualities," *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* themselves are called the triad of qualities. Among these,
[the quality of *sattva*] possesses infinite varieties characterized by clarity, lightness, joy, contentment, forbearance, satisfaction, and so forth.

In brief, *sattva* is of the nature of happiness. *Rajas*, which has endless varieties, is summarized as being of the nature of suffering, characterized by grief, torment, perspiration, paralysis, agitation, anger, hatred, and so forth.
[And *tamas*] has endless varieties, characterized by concealment, obstruction, loathsomeness, dejection, heaviness, laziness, sleep, negligence, and so forth.
In brief, darkness (tamas) consists of delusion (moha). Regarding this, those who know the tradition say:

"One should know sattva to be illuminating; one should know rajas to be the instigator; one should know tamas to be destructive. This is the triad of qualities (traiguṇya), designated by its name. Thus it is said.
Presided over by the Puruṣa who is beyond the unmanifest Mahat, the intellect (buddhi) arises;
from the eightfold intellect, the ego (ahaṅkāra) arises;
and from the threefold ego—distinguished by the characteristics of the *vaikārika*, *taijasa*, and *bhūtādi*—it proceeds in succession.

The sequential emergence of the sense organs from the *vaikārika* [sāttvika-ahaṅkāra], the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) from the *bhūtādi* [rājasa-ahaṅkāra], and the sense organs and subtle elements from the *taijasa* [tāmasa-ahaṅkāra] is called "transmigration" (*sañcara*). Then, the dissolution of the gross elements into the subtle elements,
of the subtle elements, the sense organs, and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) into the ego-sense, and [of the ego-sense into the intellect].

When the intellect (*buddhi*) has dissolved into the unmanifest principle (*avyakta-tattva*) from whatever cause it arose, and remains until the final dissolution (*pralaya*), this is called "re-absorption" (*pratisañcara*).

The intellect is the internal self (*adhyātma*); that which is to be known is the elemental sphere (*adhibhūta*); and Brahmā is the presiding deity therein (*adhidaivata*). The ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is the internal self; that which is to be identified with is the elemental sphere; and Rudra is the presiding deity therein.

The ear is the internal; that which is to be heard is the elemental; space is the deity therein. Likewise, the skin, that which is to be touched, and the wind; the eye, that which is to be seen, and the sun;
the tongue, that which is to be tasted, and Varuṇa; the nose, that which is to be smelled, and the earth; speech, that which is to be spoken, and fire.
The Indras are those from whom one must receive with the hand; the Viṣṇus are those to whom one must go on foot; the Mitras are those to whom one must discharge through the anus;

the Prajāpatis are those who are to be gladdened by the organ of generation. [This refers] to the triad of instruments consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and the threefold internal organ, distinguished as the organs of knowledge and the organs of action.
And the internal, elemental, and divine aspects are to be known. Thus they have said:
"He who knows the principles (tattvas) as they truly are—their natures as qualities (guṇas) and their divine counterparts."
"Having been liberated from evil and having gone beyond attachment to defects, he enjoys the qualities, but he is not enjoyed by the qualities. Thus it is said.

The five forms of higher cognition (*abhibuddhi*) are: higher cognition itself, the activity of the intellect, the conceit of agency, desire, and the sense of "what is to be done. Higher cognition (*abhibuddhi*) is the cognition directed toward an object; the activity of the intellect (*buddhikriyā*) is the determination that "this is to be done";
the conceit of agency (*abhimāna*) is the egoic activity of thinking "I do it"; desire (*icchā*) is longing; and volition (*saṅkalpa*) belongs to the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*).

Action (*kriyā*) consists of the observation and hearing of objects such as sound and so forth, which is the function of the cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya*); and action consists of speaking and so forth, which is the function of the active faculties (*karmendriya*).

Thus, these are the five higher cognitions (*abhibuddhi*). [The others are] fortitude (*dhṛti*), faith (*śraddhā*), happiness (*sukha*), the desire to know (*aviditṣā*), and the desire to investigate (*vividiṣā*).
There are five sources of action;
they are established in speech, deed, and intention, by which one protects [the self].
Having them as its culmination and having them as its foundation—this indeed is the characteristic of fortitude (*dhṛti*).
Freedom from envy, celibacy, performing sacrifices,
officiating at sacrifices, austerity, giving gifts, receiving gifts, and offering oblations are recorded as the characteristics of faith.
He who, seeking happiness, practices learning, ritual action, and austerity,
and is constantly devoted to expiation— this is proclaimed as the path to happiness.
The desire to know is like one fainting from the smoke of poison; yet for those who meditate, this very desire to know is the source of wisdom.
Regarding this, they say: "Unity and diversity, as well as this eternal insentience—"
"For that desire to know (vividiṣā) is indeed to be understood as the subtle effect which is capable of being agitated. Thus [it is said].

The desire to know (vividiṣā) that brings about the destruction of cause and effect is the natural disposition. Fortitude, faith, the desire for pleasure, and the desire to know—these four lead to bondage; the desire to know leads to liberation. These are the wombs of action.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, the one called udāna, and vyāna—
these are the five vital airs within the bodies of embodied beings.
The wind that presides over the mouth and nose is called *prāṇa* because of its functions of breathing forward and departing;
the wind that presides over the navel is called *apāna* because of its functions of drawing down and moving downward;
the wind that presides over the heart is called *samāna* because of its functions of equalizing and assimilating.
The wind presiding over the throat, because of its upward movement and its departure [from the body], is udāna;

the wind presiding over the joints, because of its dispersal and its yawning, is vyāna. These are the five winds. [Furthermore, there are the fivefold ego-sense (ahaṃkāra): vaikārika, taijasa, bhūtādi, sānumāna, and niranumāna.

The five types of agents of action (*karmātmānaḥ*) are to be understood in order as: the performer of auspicious actions, the performer of inauspicious actions, the performer of deluded actions, the performer of auspicious-and-deluded actions, and the performer of inauspicious-and-deluded actions. Ignorance (*avidyā*) has five sections (*parva*): darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), great delusion (*mahāmoha*), gloom (*tāmisra*), and blinding gloom (*andhatāmisra*). Among these, "darkness" (*tamas*) refers to [the state regarding] the eight [objects].

The conceit of identifying as the Self those which are not the Self— namely, the eight *prakṛtis* designated as the unmanifest (*avyakta*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*)— is the eightfold delusion (*aṣṭadhāmoha*) consisting of the conceit that one has attained the eightfold sovereignty of powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*). This occurs when one turns away from the ten objects of experience, both perceptible and revealed by scripture.

The conceit "I am liberated" is the tenfold *mahāmoha*. The arising of suffering for one who is obstructed by the eightfold supernatural powers (*aṇimā* etc. and the tenfold objects such as sound is called the eighteenfold *tāmisra*. [This occurs] regarding the eight powers and the objects.

When death has occurred, despair is called the eighteenfold *andhatāmisra*. Thus, this ignorance (*avidyā*), which consists of five sections, becomes sixty-fourfold: the eleven obstructions of the senses and the seventeen obstructions of the intellect. This power (*śakti*) is thus twenty-eightfold, as follows—with respect to the ear:
Deafness, numbness of the tongue, leprosy on the skin, blindness of the eyes,
loss of smell in the nose, muteness of speech, lameness of the feet, crippledness of the hands, upward displacement of the rectum, impotence of the generative organ, and insanity of the mind. Now...

There are seventeen obstructions of the intellect (*buddhi*), which are the opposites of contentment (*tuṣṭi*). For example: the conviction that "Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) does not exist" is an infinite [delusion]; likewise, the state of ignorance such as "I am ignorant" is a play of darkness (*asat*);
similarly, the non-perception of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) due to superimposition, and the [belief] that the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) truly exist [only through such superimposition].

The view that [the elements] are the true causes is a lack of insight; the engagement with the subjects taught in the Vedānta, namely "All this is indeed Brahman," is unsurpassed; engagement in protection is well-crossed;
the engagement in wealth by one who sees no fault in its depletion is leading; and the power of enjoyment is the state of being bound in saṃsāra.

For one who does not perceive the faults of violence and so forth, the undertaking of enjoyments is called *anuttamāmbhasikā*. Now, the eightfold opposites of the perfections (*siddhi-viparyaya*): the manifestation of the notion of oneness through delusion regarding diversity and pride is called *atāra*;
grasping a contrary meaning from merely hearing the words, such as "one who knows diversity is liberated," is called *asutāra*.

Having heard [this], one who has practiced erroneously and possesses knowledge of diversity is considered unliberated; for even though one is intent upon study, hearing, and higher knowledge, the accomplishment of the knowledge of the twenty-five principles does not occur due to either dullness or being impaired by false scriptures— such ignorance is "dark beyond darkness."

Even for someone overcome by internal suffering, if there is no agitation regarding cyclic existence and no desire to know [the truth], the attainment of knowledge does not occur. That lack of knowledge is invalid as a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). In this way, these two—being intensely joyful and being delighted—should be understood.

Lack of certainty even when instructed by a friend is ignorance (*ajñāna*); it is unpleasant and constitutes improper speech. For one who is ill-fated and turns his back on the Guru, there is no attainment of knowledge; that is ignorance, which is always devoid of joy. Thus, these eight reversals of attainment (*siddhi*) are to be understood as non-attainments (*asiddhi*). Likewise:

The reversal of the sixty-four perfections (*siddhi*), the seventeen obstructions to intelligence (*buddhi-vadha*), and the eleven obstructions to the faculties (*indriya-vadha*)—thus incapacity (*aśakti*) is described as being of twenty-eight kinds.
Now, contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is ninefold: one who is satisfied having realized Nature (*prakṛti*) to be the ultimate reality;...
One attains equanimity. The technical designation for that contentment is *ambhas*.

Another, having realized the intellect (*buddhi*) as the ultimate reality and being fully satisfied, [attains a state] whose designation is *salila* for that contentment. Yet another, having accepted the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) as the ultimate reality and being fully satisfied, [attains a state]...

The designation for that contentment is *āpaḥ* (water). Another person, having determined that the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are the objects of enjoyment from the perspective of ultimate reality, becomes fully satisfied; the designation for that contentment is *vṛṣṭi* (rain).
Thus, there are four internal types of contentment. In all four of these as well, there is no liberation.
This is due to the absence of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

On the other hand, for outsiders (*bāhya*), there are five contentments (*tuṣṭi*) regarding the enjoyment of objects, arising from seeing the defects in their acquisition, preservation, decay, attachment, and injury. A renunciant (*pravrajita*) is contented because he perceives the defect in the acquisition of wealth.

For him there is no liberation, because of the absence of knowledge of reality; that is called the fifth contentment, "the son. Another, having seen the defects in the protection of wealth, becomes a renunciant and is contented. For him also there is no liberation, because of the absence of knowledge of reality; that is the sixth contentment.
The seventh contentment is called *suparā*. Another person, having seen the fault of decay in material objects, becomes a renunciant and is content;

yet even for him there is no liberation because of the absence of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). That is the seventh contentment, called *sunetrā*. Still another, having seen the fault of attachment to material objects, desists from them and is content.
Even for him there is no liberation, because of the absence of knowledge of reality; this is called the eighth contentment, "the wheel of the maidens.
Another person, however, having turned away from external objects upon seeing the faults such as violence caused by the pursuit of wealth, is contented.

Even for one who has gone forth [into the religious life], there is no liberation due to the absence of knowledge of reality; that is the ninth contentment, called *uttamāmbhasikā*. Thus end the nine contentments.

Now, the eight accomplishments (*aṣṭasiddhi*): among those things that have become the true nature of reality (*tattvabhāvabhūta*), the mere hearing of the sound is the first, *Tārā*. Among those things that have become the true nature of reality, the non-apprehension of the object is the second, *Sutārā*. Having dispelled internal suffering, [the third is] among those things that have become the true nature of reality...

Knowledge arises, and that is the third accomplishment, called Tāratārā. That knowledge which arises through study regarding the elements in their true state is the fourth accomplishment, called Pramoda.
That knowledge which arises after having dispelled suffering pertaining to the physical world [is the fifth].

When knowledge arises after having dispelled the suffering pertaining to the divine realm (*ādhidevika*) regarding those things that have become the true nature of reality (*tattvabhāva*), that is the fifth accomplishment (*siddhi*), called "The Joyful" (*pramuditā*). When knowledge arises after having dispelled [the suffering] regarding those things that have become the true nature of reality, that is the sixth accomplishment, called "The Exultant" (*pramodamānā*).

That knowledge which arises from the cessation of association with those who are affectionate regarding the principles of reality is called the seventh, *ramyakā*. That knowledge which arises from a guru who has been fully satisfied by service and gifts regarding the principles of reality is the eighth perfection (*siddhi*).
It is called "Ever-Joyful. Thus are these eight accomplishments (*siddhi*). Now, the ten root meanings:
existence, oneness, being subject to decline, subservience to another, otherness, and lack of agency.
In union and in separation, many men remain; such is the persistence of the body and its remaining function.
The meaning of this is as follows: because composite objects exist for the sake of another, the existence of Puruṣas is established.
Because she has accomplished her purpose, like a dancer who has finished her performance, her cessation occurs; thus, its state of being subject to disappearance is established.
Because there is transformation of various distinct forms, the Manifest is the effect of this [Unmanifest]; therefore, by virtue of being an object, the existence of Pradhāna is established.

Siddham. By the phrase "caused and impermanent," its unity is established. By the phrase "by means of various methods," its being for the sake of another is established. By the phrase "composed of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, and objective," its distinctness is established. And by the phrase "and from that, through inversion," its lack of agency is established. [This is] for the purpose of the Puruṣa's perception and for the purpose of liberation.

Thus, the establishment of the connection [of the Self] with the Pradhāna is achieved; and since its purpose has been fulfilled upon the dissolution of the body, the establishment of their disconnection follows. Furthermore, the plurality of Puruṣas is established by the passage beginning with "birth, death, and the instruments," and so forth.

Now, the creation of grace (*anugraha-sarga*): having produced the external [elements] from the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and seeing sons suitable for the arising of meditation through the creation of grace, Brahmā created the creation of grace from those subtle elements. Now, the fourfold creation of beings (*bhūta-sarga*).
Therein, there are eight types of birth: that of the *piśācas*, *rākṣasas*, *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, *indrās*, *prajāpatis*, *saumyas*, and *brahmas*. There are five classes of animal births:
domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, and immobile beings. Domestic animals range from buffaloes down to mice.

The material creation consists of birds ranging from the *garuḍa* down to the mosquito; wild animals ranging from the lion down to the jackal; reptiles ranging from the serpent-king *śeṣa* down to the leech; stationary beings ranging from mountains down to grass; and the human species, which is of one kind, ranging from the Brahmin down to the *cāṇḍāla*.
This is the mandala of saṃsāra.

Now, bondage is threefold: *prakṛtibandha*, *vaikārikabandha*, and *dakṣiṇābandha*. Among these, *prakṛti* is eightfold. For one who conceives of the *prakṛtis* as being the Supreme (*paratvena*), that is called *prakṛtibandha*. [This refers to] worldly ascetics (*pravrajitānām laukikānām*).

The "transformative bondage" (vaikārika-bandha) is said to belong to those who are dominated by the sense organs born of transformation, who are engaged with objects such as sound and the rest, whose senses are unsubdued, who lack knowledge, and who are deluded by desire—
namely, householders, students, mendicants, and forest-dwellers.

For those whose minds are afflicted by desire, who act out of pride, and who bestow sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), it is called "bondage through the sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā-bandha*). And it has been said:
"By means of both the material bond (*prākṛta-bandha*) and likewise the modified bond (*vaikārika-bandha*)."
Bound by the third [debt] through sacrificial fees, a living being transmigrates.

Now, liberation is threefold: liberation is threefold due to the abundance of knowledge, the subsiding of the afflictions of the senses and speech, and the total destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). And it has been said:
"The first liberation is through knowledge; the second is from the exhaustion of passion."
But the third [type of suffering] arises from total destruction; thus has the definition of liberation been explained.

Now, there are three kinds of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*): perception (*dṛṣṭa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*). That which consists of the objects of the sense-faculties as they are directly perceived is perception. When rain is inferred from the rising of clouds, water from the presence of cranes and the like, fire from smoke, that is inference. [Regarding] Indra...
"The king of the gods, the Northern Kurus, and the golden Mount Meru"—such is the authoritative statement (āptavacana). And it has been said:
"He who is devoted to his own duty and is free from attachment and aversion..."
One who possesses knowledge, is endowed with virtue, is trustworthy, and is likewise one whose nature is to be known.
Now, suffering is threefold: internal (ādhyātmika), external (ādhibhautika), and celestial (ādhidaivika).
Among these, the internal is twofold: bodily and mental.
Bodily suffering arises from an imbalance of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman), such as fever, dysentery, cholera, and so forth.

Mental suffering consists of desire, anger, greed, delusion, envy, and so forth. Now, that which arises from other beings is called *ādhibhautika*. The suffering arising from humans, domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, and stationary objects is *ādhibhautika*. That which arises from divine beings is *ādhidaivika*. [This includes] Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Vināyakas, and so on.

Suffering caused by the possession of malevolent spirits is superhuman (ādhidaivika). Thus, for the renunciant who is overwhelmed by these three kinds of suffering, the desire to know (jijñāsā) arises. Through that desire to know, there comes the realization of the true nature of reality. From the intensification of that knowledge, the subsiding of the passions of the senses occurs.

Furthermore, from the cessation of the delight in the sense organs comes the destruction of all merit and demerit; and from the destruction of merit and demerit, liberation (kaivalya) for the person (puruṣa) results—this is the established doctrine (siddhānta) propounded by the sage Kapila.

To this it is replied: By the passage beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* teaches that Brahman alone— denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*) and heard of as the cause existing prior to the entire phenomenal world— is [the subject], and not the *pradhāna*, because the *pradhāna* is insentient.

For it is impossible to establish, by means of the scriptural passage beginning with "Then he saw," that the act of seeing— which is a quality of consciousness consisting of an observation conducive to the production of the effect about to arise— is [the cause].
Now, it might be argued that transformation into the form of the world is appropriate for the insentient *pradhāna* alone, and not for the sentient [Self].

For transformation—like milk abiding in the state of curds, or like a lump of clay in the state of a jar—is the assumption of another form through the abandonment of the previous state. And such [transformation] is impossible for the changeless sentient [Self].

It would contradict logical reasoning to claim that a transformation in the form of a modification of the cause is possible for the Supreme Lord; for in another scriptural passage, "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring similar to herself," she is described as being inferable from her red and other colors.
It is heard in the Sāṅkhya system that this capacity to produce many offspring belongs to *prakṛti* by virtue of its homogeneity;

in accordance with that, here too, it is precisely the *pradhāna*, denoted by the term "Being" (*sat*), which functions as the cause by existing prior to the world. For this very reason, [it is not the cause] due to the absence of *tamas*.
Due to the conjunction of *rajas* and *sattva*, it is logical that there is a sequential possession of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

Thus, agency (*kartṛtva*), which consists in possessing the knowledge and action conducive to an effect, is established in the case of *prakṛti*. Therefore, because it is so stated in scripture and in accordance with the previously mentioned principle of transformation (*pariṇamana*), [agency belongs] to *pradhāna* alone.

If it is argued that the status of being the cause of the world is thereby established, we say no; for since this would be cognizable through inference alone, it would contradict the attribute of "seeing" (īkṣati), and because Prakṛti— which arises from the Supreme Lord and occupies the thirty-first position among the thirty-six principles— is insentient.
Furthermore, this is established in the Sūtras and Bhāṣyas by the argument "like the cups, because there is no distinction.

Agency is also not tenable [for the Self] by virtue of possessing the power of action and the power of knowledge through the forms of *rajas* and *sattva*, because it is impossible for *sattva* and *rajas* to be connected with *māyā*, which consists of the three *guṇas*, in the absence of *tamas*. Nor is it the case that...

It must be stated that when there is a distinction due to the predominance of *rajas* and *sattva* and the non-predominance of *tamas*, the connection with the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is possible for *pradhāna*; [otherwise],
it is merely the state of equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇas*), namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Because [it] is accepted as being primordial nature (prakṛti).

As for what was said— that if one accepts the transformation of the changeless conscious principle into the form of the world, it would result in its becoming subject to modification— that too is not so; for the Supreme Lord possesses subtle powers of consciousness and non-consciousness, which are synonymous with the powers of knowledge and action that are incapable of being divided into name and form.

Sovereignty is causality; the state of being an effect belongs to that very Supreme Lord in His possession of the powers of knowledge and action, known as the gross powers of consciousness and unconsciousness which are fit for the differentiation of name and form. Thus, the objection that it is impossible for the changeless [Brahman] to undergo transformation is refuted.
This alone is our distinction from the Advaitins.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in passages such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sad eva somyedam agre āsīt*), the absence of distinctions in the reality that is pure Being (*sanmātra*) is determined by the restrictive particle *eva*? And if it is thus devoid of distinctions in its causal state, how can one understand its association with the subtle world (*sūkṣmaprapañca*)? [Reply: No, for the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "Being alone" (*sad eva*) does not...

In Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sat*), [the term "Being"] serves to exclude specific qualifications; however, it excludes the doctrine of non-being as the cause, which is heard in such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-being (*asat*); from that, Being was born. Furthermore, in passages such as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," there is no absence of qualification, because of the word "was" (*āsīt*).
A specific action is understood; by the word "first" (agra), a specific time is denoted;

by the force of the restriction "only one," another agent is excluded by precluding any other presiding deity over the phenomenal world; and by the term "without a second" (advitīya), the status of being the material cause of the universe is understood.

Because it is appropriate to establish causality for that which precedes the effect and serves as the locus of unity; therefore, since the dual status of being both the instrumental and material cause—which consists in being a non-different source—is impossible without the specific attributes of omniscience and omnipotence, both omniscience and infinite power are established. Furthermore:

For this entity denoted by the word *sat*, which existed prior to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and consists of both a base meaning and a suffix meaning, it is not possible for it to refer to a single reality without its being of a dual nature consisting of the relationship between attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*).
This is because it is appropriate that the word *sat* denotes two distinct entities through its base and its suffix.

"Śakti and Śiva are expressed by the base and the suffix of the word 'Sat' (Being); through their state of equilibrium as Consciousness-Brahman, they constitute the self of the entire universe"— according to this traditional teaching, the *liṅga-tattva* (the principle of the subtle body) is precisely that which is characterized by consciousness and activity, which are synonymous with the subtle *cit* (consciousness) and *acit* (non-consciousness).
The established reality is that the reality denoted by the term "Sat" (Being) is the non-different efficient and material cause of the entire universe.

[Objection: Surely it is established that the cause of the world must be conscious, because the act of seeing—which consists in the contemplation of the entire universe—is impossible in the non-conscious *pradhāna*. This is so because in the immediately following textual passage of the Śruti, "That fire thought," and "Those waters thought, 'May I become many, may I procreate,'" thinking is heard as belonging to fire and water.
If it be argued that the term "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) applied to the Pradhāna by the word "it" (tat) is secondary, because a secondary sense of seeing is possible for the Pradhāna, we say no;

for at the time of the conclusion, in the passage "That is the Self, That art thou, O Śvetaketu," the word "Self" (ātman), which denotes a conscious being, is heard. Therefore, the "seeing" in the case of fire and water is not secondary.
However, because the character of being a sign (*liṅgatva*)— which has a non-different efficient and material cause (*abhinnanimittopādānakāraṇa*)— continues to apply,

"seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) remains primary in that intended sense. Consequently, it is improper to establish that the non-conscious world-cause is of the nature of Being (*sad-rūpa*) by accepting a figurative "seeing" on the part of a conscious agent.
Because at the time of the conclusion, the agent of seeing is established as being conscious by means of the word "Self" (ātman).

If it be argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) itself, as denoted by the term "Being" (*sat*), is the cause of the world, we say no; for liberation is taught as being preceded by reflection upon the object denoted by the term "Being," in the words: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall attain [the goal]."
The actual state of affairs is that the causal principle of the world, being the nature of the *liṅga*, is indeed distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), because it constitutes its very body.

Furthermore, liberation for one who abides in the individual soul (*jīva*) is not intended by the doctrine that the Pradhāna is the cause. Liberation is taught as the non-difference from the referent of the word "Being" (*sat*), according to the text "That [is] the Self; thou art That" (*tat tvam asi*). And that [liberation] must be realized only by one who abides in the subtle body (*liṅga*). Moreover, there is the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one.

It is asserted that through the knowledge of the reality of the gender (liṅga) denoted by the word "Sat," there arises knowledge concerning all sentient and insentient entities as being its effects; this is expressed by such passages as, "By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known. [This refers to] the Pradhāna.

That [theory] is not tenable regarding the causality of the world, because it is impossible for the conscious Self to have as its cause the insentient *pradhāna*, given that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is of the nature of consciousness. Now, one might argue: "If the insentient *pradhāna* is known to be the cause of the world, then all its effects—which are the locus of insentient modifications—are also known, just as [when the cause] clay [is known]."

If it is argued that this is like the knowledge "this is made of clay" regarding a jar or other objects which are known to be its effects, [we reply: no; for having begun with, "O gentle one, understand from me at the end of a dream," [the text continues]: "When a person here is said to be 'sleeping,' then, O gentle one, he has become united with Being (*sat*); he has gone to his own self (*svam apītaḥ*). Therefore, they say of him 'he sleeps' (*svapiti*), because he has gone to his own."

Since the dissolution of the self, which has attained union with the Existent, even in that [state]— as declared by the scriptural passage ending with "he becomes merged in the Existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1)—
is not possible in the insentient *pradhāna*, it must therefore be the sentient *liṅga-tattva* (the causal body) alone.

It is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being). For this very reason, in such passages as "The Puruṣa is indeed Rudra; Sat-mahas, obeisance, obeisance," its status as the Supreme Principle (liṅgatattva) is recorded in the sacred tradition. Furthermore, because of the concluding statement beginning with "From the Self, the ether [was born]," the fact that the object denoted by the word "Sat" is the cause of the world is likewise recorded in the sacred tradition.

Therefore, since an insentient primordial nature (jaḍaprakṛti) cannot logically be the cause of the world, it is beyond dispute that only the conscious being denoted by the term "Sat" is the cause of the world.
[Thus,

the incomparable essence of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*), which is non-different from the one hundred and one unsurpassed stages produced by churning the ocean of the Śāmbhava Āgama— obtained through the grace of the venerable Toṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the beginningless, stainless, and mobile Aparā— ]

In [this work] composed by the eminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows a mass of bliss from tasting the nectar of awakening, for Keladi Sadāśivarāya— the sovereign of the western ocean, the remover of the seven constituents of the enemy hero who was the sole protagonist in the tumultuous conflict against ten million Yaḍavamurāris, and the teacher who established the pure Vedic doctrine of Advaita.

In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, within the section on debate (*vādakāṇḍa*), in the instruction of Basava— the thunderbolt for the earth and the joy of the heart of Mallāmbā, the lawful consort of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth and the full moon in the milky ocean of the lineage of the Leader.
The Thirteenth Chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Sāṅkhya Doctrine and the Method of its Refutation."
[The Fourteenth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O illustrious Guru, tell me then what was undertaken by Bhṛṅgin;
and you should also recount that which was censured by the virtuous Śīlavat.
O Protector of the Earth, having thus analyzed the doctrine set forth by Bhṛṅgin,
I shall state the refutation of it as expressed by Śīlin.
Having heard each of those things, O Bhava, be joyful.
O you of such character, that position which was propounded by me— that primordial nature (prakṛti), designated as the unmanifest, is the creator of the world—
has been refuted today by your faults.
For that which is insentient possesses no agency.
That primordial power, celebrated in the Vedas as Tripurā, Umā, and the Mother of the Universe—
her alone, the agent of the primary cause of creation and so forth, [I worship].
I shall set forth this doctrine which they proclaim.
How can that Śākta doctrine be refuted? Or rather,
I shall observe the particularity of your inspired intuition, O virtuous one, just as I have previously observed the various tenets of those respective schools.
This is not, at first glance, fit to be refuted.

Desiring to know what that cause of the manifestation of the universe is— which is established by a multitude of various Smṛtis beginning with "From whom [it arises]"— they remember it as having a nature dependent on many lords.

In this regard, since the status of being a creator and so forth belongs only to those who possess an incomparable and inexpressible power (*anirvācya-śakti*) and not to others, it is the Supreme Sovereign (*parameśvarī*) alone— who is established in manifold ways through the Śrutis,
Āgamas, and other sources— as the cause of the entire universe. Thus, it is heard in the *Śrī Navārṇopaniṣad*:

All the gods indeed approached the Goddess and asked, "Who are you, O Great Goddess? She replied, "I am the embodiment of Brahman. Through such statements as, "From me proceeds the universe consisting of Prakṛti and Puruṣa; I am both the void and the non-void; I am the Self, I am the entire universe," [she establishes] her nature as the Supreme Brahman.
For it is also heard [in scripture] that the Supreme Lord, having entered into the phenomenal world which is the effect, is the producer [of that world].

Nor should it be said that the Supreme Lord alone, as delimited by primordial matter (*prakṛti*), is the creator of the universe, and not the supreme power (*parā śakti*) alone; for it is stated: "One should know Māyā as primordial matter, and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā."

Since the scripture has established that even the Lord, though delimited by primordial nature (*prakṛti*), possesses the status of a creator, there is no inconsistency [in our position]. Furthermore, in the *Saptaśatī* of the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*,
Aparājitā said to the smoke-crested Īśāna:
O messenger, O Blessed One, go to the side of Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Speak to Śumbha and Niśumbha, those two exceedingly arrogant Dānavas:
"Let Indra obtain the three worlds, and let the gods be the partakers of the sacrificial offerings."
Beginning with these words:
"Since Śiva himself was appointed as a messenger by that goddess,
she therefore attained renown in this world as Śivadūtī."
This is because, through such passages, Śiva’s status as the messenger of the Bhagavatī is established;

furthermore, for that very reason, the Goddess establishes her own non-duality by stating, "In this world, I alone am one; who else is my second? Nor does the phrase "who else is my second" imply... [text truncated]
It should not be said that by the word "other" (*apara*) used in the feminine gender, the non-existence of only a power distinct from oneself is indicated,

rather than the non-existence of individual manifestations of Śiva and others as males; for according to the Śruti, "I am neuter, I am male, I am female, I am stationary, and I am moving," there is the [non-dual] reality of the entire range of entities undivided by femininity, masculinity, and so forth.

This is because it establishes that [the Goddess] is not distinct from Him. Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad* and other texts, since they perceive His omnipresence;

for by such statements as "She who is the mother of all beings from Brahmā down to an ant," it is heard that She is the mother of Viṣṇu, who is included among all things. As it is said: "The Goddess who [resides] in all beings..."

And because of the statement, "She exists in the form of the Mother"; furthermore, because the Goddess’s role as the agent of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of this world is established by Brahmā himself in the passage: "O you who consist of the universe, you are the form of emission in creation, the form of maintenance in preservation, and likewise the form of withdrawal at the end of this world. Nor is it [the case that...].

It cannot be said that there is no rule regarding whether the general statement "the world evolves from that Brahman" implies that the controlling power (niyantṛtva) must be understood as supreme; for, according to the *Śruti*, in the first chapter (*prathama-adhyāya*) of the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā), under the section on names (*nāmadheya-pāda*),

in the discussion concerning the passage "The gravel is anointed" (*aktāḥ śarkarāḥ*), because a substance is fit for anointing [only when it is another substance], [it is established that the word 'anointed' denotes a quality].

Just as when it is established that "the collyrium [should be made] from one of ghee, oil, or fat," the supplementary statement "ghee indeed is light" indicates a preference for ghee, so too here there is a preference for the Goddess (Devī), since everything is subordinate to her. Furthermore, scripture (āgama) is an authoritative means of knowledge regarding agency, which has been demonstrated by Śruti to have another [higher] purpose.

And such a nature as consisting of the Śruti belongs to the Goddess alone, because it is established [in scripture] that "the Goddess who resides in all beings in the form of the Śruti. Furthermore, the representation of Viṣṇu and others as agents by means of the Goddess herself in the form of the Śruti must be accepted as being of the nature of an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), because she is independent.

Inference (*anumāna*) is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this regard: this world has a single deity as its creator, because, while not being produced by anything other than that [deity], it is produced by that [deity]. Just as smoke, which is not produced by anything other than fire, is produced by fire alone;
much more could be deliberated upon, but we desist for fear of prolixity. This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

To this it is replied: as for what was stated—that the statement of the *Navārṇopaniṣad* alone is the proof for Śakti’s agency—that is not so; for in that very text it says, "My womb is within the waters, in the ocean. By this, it is established that "my womb"—meaning my cause, the Supreme Lord—resides within the waters, that is, in the midst of the water.

Because the Goddess is perceived to lack independence; furthermore, even though Īśāna acts as the messenger of the Goddess, there is no contradiction in Śiva being the presiding authority over the Goddess. "The matted-haired Śambhu, the Lord, was performing penance nearby; the Blessed Śambhu said to him, 'O son...'"
"Protect my abode, named Ānandakānana, which increases my love," and so forth;
thus, that Īśāna, having been liberated by the Supreme Lord himself, installed a great *liṅga* there and performed supreme austerity— such is the praise of Jñānavāpī in many ways.

Because the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* refers specifically to a particular class of attendants (gaṇas) known as Īśāna; nor should it be argued that the status of being the creator of the world’s manifestation and so forth is contradictory, for [it is said]: "O highly fortunate one, create all this multitude of living beings according to their own karma, just as before, under my authority and nourished by my vital energy."

For it is possible that the Blessed Goddess, impelled by the very word of Śiva, is the cause of creation. Nor is there any contradiction with the [relevant] *adhikaraṇa* (section of the Brahma-sūtras), because once it is established that all the Śruti texts devoted to the Goddess have another [divine] meaning, there is no sublation of their referring to the Lord (*Īśvara*) either. Furthermore, inference is not a valid means of knowledge [in this context].
Since being anything other than that [the Supreme Lord] is unestablished, it falls under the fallacy of the "unestablished" (asiddha) reason;

furthermore, because scripture declares that the world originates from the Supreme Lord alone as qualified by power (*śakti*), and because there are many proofs for Śiva’s status as the creator of the universe, the conclusion is that everything is logically consistent. This is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
[Thus,
from the venerable Tōṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the moving form of the beginningless and stainless Aparā,
and who obtained the grace of the Śāmbhava Āgama ocean churned by him— producing the unsurpassed division of one hundred and one *sthala*s...]
In the *Yaḍavamurārikoṭe*, composed by the eminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya— who bestows a mass of bliss through the savor of nectar—
[therein is described] the seizure of the seven constituent parts of the enemy of the sole hero Kolāhala, the lord of the western ocean, who was pure in his Vaidya lineage...

In the instruction of Basava, the thunderbolt for the earth, who brought joy to the heart of Mallāmbā— the lawful wife of Vīrabhadra Dharaṇīndra, the full moon in the milk-ocean of the lineage of Keladi Sadāśivarāya Nāyaka, the preceptor who established the doctrine of non-dual monism (advaita).
In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, within the section on dialectical inquiry (*vādakāṇḍa*),
the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Method of Describing and Refuting the Śakti Doctrine."
[The Fifteenth Chapter in the Section on Debate of the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
Having heard from me the establishment of the doctrine called Śākta by the Guru today, as well as the refutation of the objections raised against it,
[it was] demonstrated by me according to the view of the Great Sage.
Tell me truly what happened immediately thereafter.
O King, that which was proposed by Bhṛṅgin was refuted even by Śīlavat;
I shall explain that to you in detail, step by step.
Contemplate this, O you of pure self-awareness!
Even those who abide in other philosophical systems do not claim that the power [of causality] can belong to anything other than the Possessor of Power as the cause of the world;
indeed, they all declare that there is only one Supreme Being.
You are such a self; your intellect is like that.
O Bhṛṅgin, quickly tell me in detail what other such doctrine there may be; I shall examine it,
for among all doctrines, there is none that is without obstruction.
In this [state], there is a specific capacity for investigation.
I declare that such a nature,
as well as knowledge, will, and action— these too,
along with omniscience, are indeed accepted where [the Sugata exists].
In my view, the Great Lord alone is the agent.

However, those who follow the doctrine of Gautama state as follows: [the categories are] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), tenet (*siddhānta*), members of a syllogism (*avayava*), deliberation (*tarka*), ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), discussion (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

"The attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*). This is the first aphorism of the *Nyāya* system. That which exists in something is its "reality" (*tattva*). Knowledge of that [reality] depends upon the triad beginning with "enunciation" (*uddeśa*).

An "enunciation" (*uddeśa*) is a word that generates a cognition whose qualifier is merely the delimitor of the state of being the object of definition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). In a sentence of definition (*lakṣaṇa-vākya*),...

Furthermore, because the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence possesses a qualifier that is distinct from the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is there over-extension with respect to the portion denoting the definiendum within the definition-statement itself, since that too functions as a subject (*uddeśa*). For this very reason, the *Ṭīkā* states: "In each individual definition, the subjects (*dharmin*) are indeed already indicated."
Nor is the separate mention [of the subject] thus rendered useless, because its purpose is to exclude a number that is either too few or too many. Alternatively,
an *uddeśa* (enunciation) is a word that generates the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) which serves as the cause for stating a definition (*lakṣaṇābhidhāna*).
A definition is a statement of a property that is co-extensive with the delimitor of the object to be defined.

Investigation (*parīkṣā*) is an inquiry whose result is either the establishment or the refutation of a definition. Among these, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is an instrument of valid knowledge (*pramā*). Valid knowledge is a cognition that accords with reality (*yathārtha-anubhava*).

A cognition is "in accordance with reality" when it does not have as its qualifier (*prakāra*) something that does not reside in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). For example: "This is a jar. For in this case—

In the cognition "This is a jar," the jar is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The property of being a cloth (*paṭatva*) and so forth, which subsists in things other than that [jar], does not exist here as its qualifier (*prakāra*), because here only jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) is the qualifier, and that [jar-ness] subsists in the jar. [This is not the case] in the error "This is silver."
Since silverness—which does not reside in the piece of mother-of-pearl that serves as the substantive—is merely a qualifier (prakāra), there is no over-extension [of the definition].

And being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) consists in being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of a relation that is appearing; and that [relation] is the connection between the perceived qualifier and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), which is the state of being an object of cognition dependent upon that [connection].
Causality is the state of belonging to a class of things that invariably precede [the effect] and are not established otherwise [than as causes].

The term "belonging to a class" (*jātīya*) is included to exclude the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a staff standing in a forest; however, it would result in over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a donkey used for that same purpose.
The term "not otherwise established" (*ananyathāsiddha*) is for the purpose of exclusion. Being "not otherwise established" means the absence of being established otherwise.

There are three kinds of being established otherwise: (1) when the prior existence of one thing is perceived only along with another, it is established otherwise by that [other]; as, for example, the color of a thread [is established otherwise] by the thread itself, or the "staff-ness" [of a staff] by the staff.

Otherwise, when an effect can be produced by that which is already established as an invariable antecedent, its coexistence [with that antecedent] constitutes another form of "being otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhi*). For example, the donkey in relation to this jar;
for [the donkey's presence] is otherwise established with respect to other jars, distinct from those delimited by the property of being this particular jar.

Because this jar can arise from a staff and so forth that have already been established as antecedent conditions. When the prior existence of something with respect to one thing is understood only after its prior existence with respect to another thing has been known, it is "otherwise-established" (anyathāsiddha) with respect to the former; for example, space with respect to a jar. To explain: with respect to the jar...

The causality of space (ākāśa) must be apprehended as its nature of being space (ākāśatva). And this "nature of being space" is not a genus (jāti), because it subsists in only one thing. Rather, the nature of being space is the state of being the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of sound.
Furthermore, causality is constituted by the property of being invariably antecedent to the effect. And thus, with respect to sound—

If its status as a prior entity is already apprehended, then there is "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) with respect to the jar, because its status as a prior entity is apprehended [independently] of the jar.

Furthermore, that cause is threefold, distinguished as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). That in which the effect inheres when it is produced is the inherent cause; for example, threads are the inherent cause of cloth.

An *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) is that cause which, while being inherent in the same object as either the effect or the [other] cause, is the cause [of the effect]. For example, the conjunction of threads is the non-inherent cause of a cloth, and the color of the threads is the non-inherent cause of the color of the cloth.
A cause distinct from both of these is a *nimittakāraṇa* (instrumental cause), such as the shuttle, loom, and so forth, for a cloth.

And those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are fourfold, distinguished as perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), and verbal testimony (*śabda*). Among these, perception is a cognition that does not have another cognition as its instrument (*jñānākaraṇaka*). It is twofold: determinate (*savikalpaka*) and indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*). Therein, a cognition possessing a qualifier (*saprakāraka*) is determinate; [a cognition] devoid of qualifiers (*niṣprakāraka*) is indeterminate.

Knowledge is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). The instrument for that [knowledge], which is perception (*pratyakṣa*), is also sixfold, distinguished as the nose, tongue, eye, ear, skin, and mind. Their objects are, respectively, odor, taste, form, sound, touch, and pleasure and so forth. [The contact is] conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Conjunction with the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), inherence in what is conjoined with the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in what is inherent (*samavetasamavāya*),
and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
The cause of perceptual knowledge is the contact between the sense organ and its object, which is of six kinds. Thus has perception been explained.
Inference (*anumiti*) is a cognition produced by a knowledge of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) which has pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its qualifier.
The instrument (*karaṇa*) of that [cognition] is inference (*anumāna*).
