[The definition of the probandum is: the probandum (*sādhya*) which is not the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the locus of the means (*sādhana*) and which is non-co-located with the counter-positive [of that absence].

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the state of being non-separable. That inference is of three kinds, distinguished as positive-negative (*anvaya-vyatirekin*), purely negative (*kevala-vyatirekin*), and purely positive (*kevala-anvayin*). For example: "The mountain possesses fire because it has smoke";
"The living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth"; and "A jar is denotable [by words]."
And "because of being an object of cognition" (prameyatvāt). Thus is the inference.
Comparison (upamiti) is the cognition of an object qualified by its similarity to a cow; the instrument of comparison (upamāna) is the means of producing that cognition.

A word that arises from the knowledge of the reality of its own meaning is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). The cognition of the word is the instrument (*karaṇa*); the recollection of the word-meaning is the intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*); and the knowledge of the sentence-meaning is the result (*phala*). Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhi*) are the auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*). Word is of two kinds.
It is both worldly (*laukika*) and transcendental (*alaukika*). For example: "Cows are in the cow-pen," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma.
It is clear from the root text that *arthāpatti*, *anupalabdhi*, *sambhava*, and so forth, are included within these [categories] as appropriate.

The objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) are twelvefold: self, body, sense organs, objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation. Among these, the self (*ātman*) is that which possesses the universal property of selfhood (*ātmatva*). It is twofold: the Lord (*īśa*) and the non-Lord (*anīśa*). The Lord is that which possesses eternal knowledge; the non-Lord is that which possesses non-eternal knowledge.
The body is that which possesses a genus residing only in its ultimate constituent parts, like the mental conjunction that produces cognition.
Being a substance that does not originate another substance, the body, which is itself composed of parts, is of two kinds: born from a womb (*yonija*) and not born from a womb (*ayonija*).
That which arises from the union of semen and blood belongs to those such as ourselves and is *yonija*. That which is independent of these is *ayonija*.

The definition of a sense organ (*indriya*) is that which serves as the substratum for the conjunction of the mind (*manas*) with the instrument of knowledge that does not produce recollection—such as the divine sage Nārada and others.
And that [sense organ] is of six kinds: the olfactory organ is composed of earth (*pārthiva*), the gustatory organ is composed of water (*āpya*), and the visual organ is composed of fire (*taijasa*).
The auditory organ is ether; the tactile organ is composed of air; the mind is the internal organ that grasps the self.
Form, taste, smell, touch, and sound are the objects. However, the Vaiśeṣikas assert that there are seven categories: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence.
Substance is the substratum of qualities. These are nine: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind.
Earth is that which possesses smell; water is the substratum of cold touch; fire is the substratum of hot touch;
[and ether] is formless.

Air is the substratum of touch; space has sound as its quality; time is to be inferred from the opposite qualities of priority and posteriority; direction is to be inferred from non-restricted priority and posteriority; the self possesses the universal property of selfhood (ātmatva); the mind is the sense organ that is the means for the apprehension of pleasure and so forth. As for the qualities:

Color, taste, smell, touch, sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, weight, fluidity, viscidity, mental impressions, merit, and demerit [are the qualities]. Action is that which possesses a genus pervaded by existence and not residing in eternal substances.
The five types of action are throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion.

Universality (*sāmānya*) is eternal, one, and inherent in many; it is of two kinds: the higher and the lower. Particularity (*viśeṣa*) is that which resides in ultimate eternal substances. Inherence (*samavāya*) is an eternal relation. Non-existence (*abhāva*) is that which is distinct from existence (*bhāva*).

Non-existence is of two kinds: mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*). The latter is threefold: antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Intellect (*buddhi*) has been described; the internal organ (*manas*) has also already been described. Volitional activity (*pravṛtti*) is an impermanent effort that produces unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). Volitional activity consists of the initiation of speech, intellect, and body.

Thus says the Sūtra. The exertion of recollecting the names of Śiva is the initiation of speech; the effort conducive to the remembrance of Śiva is the initiation of the intellect; and the effort directed toward the ritual bathing of Śiva and so forth is the initiation of the body. Faults—namely passion, hatred, and delusion—are the causes of worldly activity.

Pretyabhāva (rebirth) is the conjunction with a subsequent body immediately following the disjunction from a previous body. Phala (fruit) is experience. Duḥkha (suffering) is an object of knowledge that is connected with pain, provided it is distinct from the self and liberation;
according to the moderns, suffering is that which possesses the universal property of "suffering-ness" (*duḥkhatva*).
Liberation (mokṣa) is the destruction of suffering that does not coexist with the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of suffering having the same locus as itself.
However, the destruction of present suffering is necessarily simultaneous with the prior non-existence of future suffering;
therefore, there is no liberation during the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). Furthermore, this [liberation] is to be accomplished through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).

And by the power of the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra), having understood even that accumulation of merit and demerit gathered throughout beginningless previous existences whose time of fruition was indefinite, he completely casts it off by creating various bodies and experiencing [the results] therein at that very time.

For meditative absorption (*samādhi*) possesses an inconceivable excellence of power. Some maintain that there is equal primacy between the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and ritual action (*karman*). Others hold that actions serve as causes for liberation by means of the knowledge of reality. In reality, however, it is the knowledge of reality alone that is the cause of liberation through the destruction of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*); as for ritual action, [it serves as a subordinate aid].

It is otherwise established by its being exhausted in producing the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition that apprehends a mutual contradiction between two properties residing in a single substratum (*dharmin*). It is threefold:
born from common properties (*samānadharmaja*), born from uncommon properties (*asamānadharmaja*), and born from conflicting testimony (*vipratipattija*). [This occurs] according to one’s desire...
The purpose of that [activity] is its motive (*prayojana*).
It is twofold: primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*). The first consists of pleasure and the absence of pain;
the means to achieve those is the secondary. An object determined as possessing the status of being the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*)...

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*). It is of two kinds, due to the distinction between similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). A tenet (*siddhānta*) is an object established as authoritative and accepted within an illustration (*udāharaṇa*).

And it is fourfold, due to the distinctions of the tenets of all schools (*sarvatantra*), specific schools (*pratitantra*), contextually restricted tenets (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*), and implied tenets (*abhyupagamasiddhānta*). For example, [the existence of] odor and so forth...

The doctrine that "the sense organs have objects" is a tenet established across all systems (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*). A doctrine contrary to other systems is a tenet specific to a particular system (*pratitantra*); for example, the Naiyāyikas' position on the non-eternality of sound is not accepted by the Prābhākaras. A tenet established through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is a tenet established by implication (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*).

Just as when the fact of having an agent has been established in the case of earth and so forth, omniscience is [established] in the case of God; an *abhyupagamasiddhānta* (a tenet accepted for the sake of argument) is a point that, though established in relation to a dependent [system], is accepted as applicable to an independent [system]. For example, the Naiyāyikas accept the status of the mind as a sense-faculty, which was established by the Vaiśeṣikas.

Nyāya is a statement that generates a verbal cognition which serves as the motivator for the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), which is the final cause of inference. Through the five constituent statements—beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*)—as a single syntactic unity, there arises the knowledge of the meaning of the great sentence.
Thereafter, there arises a mental cognition (*mānasa-jñāna*) in the form: "there is the possession of fire in that which is qualified by smoke. Thereafter...
"The cognition 'that which possesses smoke pervaded by fire' is the mental consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*); from that, inference arises.
A "member" (*avayava*) is a sentence that produces the verbal cognition which, in turn, generates the cognition produced by the *nyāya* (syllogism).
This is because it is accepted that the cognition of the meaning of the great sentence follows immediately after the cognition of the meaning of the constituent parts. And these [members are...]

The thesis, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion. A thesis is a statement that generates a desire to know the grounds for its assertion. A reason is a statement incorporated into a formal argument (nyāya) that possesses a term characterized by an ablative case ending.

The statement of an example is the *udāharaṇa*. The statement of the application (*parāmarśa*) is the *upanaya*. The statement of the proven conclusion (*sādhya*), which is determined by the connection with the mark (*liṅga*), is the *nigamana*. Reasoning (*tarka*) is the attribution of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) through the attribution of the pervaded (*vyāpya*). Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the determination of the true nature of the object.
*Vāda* (debate) is a discussion undertaken for the purpose of determining the truth. *Jalpa* (wrangling) is a discussion between those desiring victory, wherein both parties employ means of proof.

*Vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is that which lacks the establishment of one's own position. The nature of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is the possession of that property by virtue of which, when it is known, there is a rule that inference does not occur. And these [fallacious reasons] are:

There are exactly five [types of fallacious reasons]: the deviant (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣa*), the unestablished (*asiddha*), and the sublated (*bādhita*).

Deviance (*savyabhicāratva*) consists in possessing a limiting condition (*upādhi*) that is incompatible with the certainty that the reason resides only in what possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat-mātra-vṛttitva-niścaya-virodhi-hetvābhāsatā*). And it is of three kinds, based on the distinction between the common (*sādhāraṇa*), the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), and the non-conclusive (*anupasamhārī*).

The common (sādhāraṇa) [inconclusive reason] is that which occurs in both the similar class (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), as in: "Sound is eternal, because it is knowable" (prameyatvāt). Counter-thesis (satpratipakṣatva) is the state of a logical mark whose effect is obstructed by the presence of another mark of equal strength. Strength, moreover, consists in pervasion (vyāpti) and being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā).

For example: "The earth and so forth are without an agent because they are not produced by a body," and "The earth and so forth have an agent because they are produced. A reason (*hetu*) that lacks either pervasion (*vyāpti*) or presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
And that is of three kinds, distinguished as: unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), and unestablished in its pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*).

The unestablished due to the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) is, for example: "The young woman is made of gold and possesses a wealthy owner, because she is adorned with various ornaments. The unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) is, for example: "The beloved possesses hands and so forth, because she is a human being. The unestablished due to the lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*) is, for example: "The mountain possesses fire, because of blue smoke."

The "unestablished due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*) can also be "conditioned" (*sopādhika*). For example: "Sacrificial violence (*yāgīyā hiṃsā*) is a means to demerit (*adharma*), because it is violence, like violence outside of a sacrifice. Here, "being prohibited" (*niṣiddhatva*) is the condition (*upādhi*). A condition is that which, while being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*), is not a pervader of the probans (*sādhanāvyāpaka*). [Furthermore,] there is the absence of the probandum in the subject (*pakṣe sādhyābhāvaḥ*).

Sublation (*bādha*) is, for example: "Fire is not hot, because it is a product. Quibble (*chala*) is the statement of a refutation by shifting the intention of the words to something other than the speaker’s intended meaning; for example, when it is said, "Devadatta has nine wives," [the opponent objects]: "He has only one wife; how could he have nine wives with so much effort?"
Thus: an answer employed with the intention of establishing a probans without relying upon pervasion (*vyāpti*) is a *jāti* (futile rejoinder).

For example: "If this [sound] is non-eternal because of its similarity to a cloth due to its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), then why is it not eternal precisely because of its similarity to space due to its being cognizable (*prameyatva*)?"

A point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is the cause of defeat; defeat (*nigraha*) is loss. For example, when one has employed the argument, "Sound is impermanent because it is a quality perceived [by the senses], like a pot," and this is refuted by the opponent through the contradiction of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the abandonment of the thesis—such as subsequently asserting, "In that case, the pot is impermanent"—constitutes a point of defeat.
The followers of Gautama maintain that liberation results from the knowledge of the reality of these sixteen categories;
the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that liberation results from the knowledge of the reality of seven categories.

Here it is investigated: first of all, that which was stated in the Gautama-sūtra beginning with "the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition" is indeed inconsistent. For instance, [the categories] are:
self, body, sense-faculties, objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation.

Since the other fifteen categories accepted by him— beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— are included within the fourth category of "objects of knowledge" (*prameya*), as defined by the term "object of knowledge" (*prameya*) in the aphorism that classifies the objects of knowledge.

Since the number sixteen is unestablished due to the absence of a separate existence apart from the objects of cognition (*prameya*), knowledge is likewise unestablished; consequently, the attainment of liberation [based on that] is as unreal as a flower in the sky.
Furthermore, [the categories such as] self, body, sense organs, objects, intellect, mind, activity, and so forth— [The original text continues with the critique of these categories.]
That which was stated in the aphorism defining the divisions of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) is also inconsistent;

for within the object of cognition named "object" (*artha*), which is included among the categories to be divided such as "self" (*ātman*) and so forth, there are the three preceding [categories]— the self and so on— as well as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest.
Because the eight other categories of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), which consist of qualities (*guṇa*) and will be analyzed later,
are included within their respective [appropriate] categories according to their nature, this sūtra would be rendered purposeless (*ānarthakya*).
There is an inconsistency in the classification. [Objection: But surely, the categories are the six padārthas;

therefore, the mention again of the self (*ātman*) and so forth—already enumerated in the *prameya-sūtra*—is for the sake of providing a knowledge of the classification that pertains to the nature of the objects of cognition (*prameya*), which consist of the six categories. Furthermore, in the *prameya-sūtra* itself, later on...

This is an enumeration of the self and other categories that are about to be analyzed; and it is stated a hundred times that "wholesome advice must be spoken" in order to illuminate the self's preeminence by virtue of its fitness for liberation through the knowledge of its distinction from other entities.
If it is argued that this is an "enunciation" (uddeśa) according to the logic stated by Śabarasvāmī in his Bhāṣya, we say no;

for since the self’s superiority and its fitness for liberation have been established through the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth— by means of the discrimination between the insentient and the sentient— your own technical definition of "enunciation" as the repeated division of what has already been divided is contradicted.

Because it constitutes an obstacle to the study of the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Āgamas, it indeed brings about demerit. Likewise, in the Rāmāyaṇa, the Blessed One stated: "In the same way, those fools who consider themselves learned, having encountered the science of logic (*vīkṣikī*) within the preeminent treatises on Dharma, propound it as useless."

This was established by Vālmīki. By this, the following view is also refuted: that even in the first aphorism (*sūtra*), the separate mention of doubt (*saṃśaya*) and the other categories included within the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is necessary because they are useful for debate (*vādakathā*) employed for the ascertainment of truth (*tattvāvadhāraṇa*). Furthermore:

In the aphorism beginning with "pramāṇaprameya," the formation of a *dvandva* compound is untenable; for Pāṇini, in the rule "arthe dvandvaḥ," teaches the *dvandva* compound only in cases where there is a difference between the referents (*padārtha*) of the constituent words. Nor can it be argued that even in the absence of a difference between the referents, a *dvandva* may still occur by taking the difference between the delimiters of the referents (*padārthatāvacchedaka-bheda*) as the basis.
Or rather, it must be stated that [the rule] is applicable, because otherwise the sūtra prescribing *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for items of identical form would result in being redundant.

This is because in examples such as "ghaṭāḥ" (pots), although there is a plurality of individual objects (*padārtha*), the property that delimits the objecthood (*padārthatāvacchedaka*)—namely, "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*)—is one;

thus, the condition for the application of the rule is absent. Furthermore, the *ekaśeṣa* is an exception to *dvandva* (copulative compound) and applies only in those instances where *dvandva* would otherwise have occurred.

Because it must be stated [otherwise]. Nor should it be argued that the Sūtra is not redundant because, in cases of multiple meanings such as the word *saindhava*, since there is a difference in the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the word-meanings (*padārtha*), the rule for "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) applies there; for if that were so, then [the redundancy would apply] to both the rules for *dvandva* and its exceptions.

Accepting that the application [of the rule] occurs sometimes due to a difference in the categories (*padārtha*) and sometimes due to a difference in the delimiters of the categories (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), Pāṇini’s sūtra is also conducive to establishing the proofs for the compound formations that demonstrate his own technical system of sixteen categories.
It is improper to associate this with a defiled state of existence or with deluded faith.

It has been stated that the self attains liberation through the knowledge of the reality of the sixteen categories. Now, as for that self, is it of atomic dimension or of intermediate dimension? Not the first.

If [the self] were of atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), it would follow that it is imperceptible, because of the absence of largeness (*mahattva*). Nor should it be argued that there is no such fault, since largeness is a cause only for external sensory perception when [an object] possesses manifested color (*udbhūta-rūpa*); for that would involve the fault of over-complication (*gaurava*) regarding the delimiting property of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), [as one would have to define it] as "being perceptible" and "having largeness."
Because of parsimony regarding the relationship between cause and effect; for if that were not the case, the consequence of the self being imperceptible would be unavoidable.
Now, although magnitude is observed in air, it is nonetheless imperceptible [to the external senses];
likewise, even though the individual soul (jīva) is imperceptible to the external senses, because it is perceptible to the internal sense, its dimension is atomic.

If it is argued that [the atom] must exist [as perceptible], we say no; for there is no rule that wherever there is magnitude (*mahattva*), there must necessarily be perception (*pratyakṣa*). Rather, it is said that magnitude is a cause for perception. Thus, because an atom lacks magnitude, it is not perceptible. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.

Because that which is of intermediate dimension is pervaded by impermanence; however, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it must be stated that [the self] is all-pervading (*vibhu*). Furthermore, whatever substance arises in another location for our enjoyment must be said to be produced by our unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); since our unseen merit resides in our own self, its...

If [the soul] were limited, then because there would be no conjunction of the self with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) at the location where the object arises, how could it be possible for that object to serve as the basis for experience?
Therefore, one must assert that even at the location where the object arises, there is a conjunction of the self with the unseen force. By means of that—
The accomplishment of mastery [is established]. And that [self] is distinct for each body due to the variety of mutual pleasure, pain, and so forth;

it is eternal because of its all-pervasiveness. It is perceived by mental direct perception as "I. In case of dispute, it is inferable from signs such as cognition; it is the substratum of qualities such as knowledge.
If it is argued that liberation results from the knowledge of the reality of the sixteen categories regarding such a self, we say no;

for there must be either a difference or a non-difference between the qualities such as cognition and the self. It cannot be the latter [non-difference], because it would entail the impermanence of the self, since it would be non-different from impermanent cognitions and so forth.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the destruction of its all-pervasiveness, because it would be non-different from cognition and other qualities that are limited in scope. Nor is the first position tenable; for if there were a difference [between the self and its qualities], then—just as in the case of a jar and a cloth—the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) would be impossible, resulting in the qualities belonging to something else.
Consequently, since it would not be the substratum of qualities such as cognition, it would follow that the self is insentient (*jaḍatva*).
Furthermore, that which was stated regarding the self’s distinctness in each body and its omnipresence is untenable.

For instance, it is impossible for that which is distinct in each body to be all-pervasive. If there were omnipresence, then distinctness in each body would not be possible; such is the nature of omnipresence.

Because it has been stated that [the self] is in conjunction with all corporeal substances; if that were the case, one would have to assert that every self is connected to a single body. That is not possible, for when one [self] is connected [to a body], another is either connected by way of that same delimitation or not. If it is not, then...

If it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the destruction of [the soul's] omnipresence. If they were connected, then because of the conjunction of infinite selves in a single place, the body itself would be destroyed. Furthermore, since the conjunction of all selves exists within a single body, when one experiences pleasure, all would experience pleasure; when one experiences pain, all would experience pain.

It might be argued that because the connection of all selves exists with respect to all bodies— and since pleasure, pain, and so forth are observed by the selves only through the limitation of their respective bodies— there is no occurrence of a confusion of experiences, as the conjunction of the mind is also distinct for each body. But this is not so.

Because the conjunction with the mind is equally present for all [souls]. Nor should it be argued that there is no contingency of confusion regarding experience because of the rule that whatever body is produced by a particular *adṛṣṭa* belongs for experience to that very soul alone; for even in this case, there is no such restrictive rule that "this *adṛṣṭa* belongs to one person and not to another. Not so.
It cannot be argued that there is no such fault because the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by an action belongs only to the one who performed that action;

for since an action arises in connection with all selves, it is impossible to establish a restriction that it belongs to one alone and not another, and thus the resulting confusion of experiences (*bhoga-sāṅkarya*) is unavoidable. Furthermore, if the selves were all-pervading...

The departure, movement, and so forth are untenable [for the Self]. Nor should it be argued that because the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) persists as long as ignorance lasts, its departure, movement, and so forth belong to it alone, while these are merely attributed to the Selves by metaphorical extension through that medium; for this contradicts the scriptural text: "As he departs, the vital breaths (prāṇas) depart after him."

It would contradict [the scriptures] to say that the soul's movement occurs first and the movement of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), characterized by the vital breaths, occurs afterwards. Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that the movement and non-movement pertaining to the body are merely metaphorically attributed to the soul; rather, it is the soul itself whose movement and arrival are heard of in scripture, not that of the insentient [body] alone.
[This refers] to the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). For this very reason, [the scripture states]: "There are these two persons in the world who pierce the solar orb:

the wandering mendicant disciplined in yoga, and he who is slain facing the enemy in battle. Thus, it is logical that the Self alone is the piercer of the solar orb. As for the restriction regarding objects of enjoyment located in another place, however—

We shall demonstrate more thoroughly later on that [the world] arises through the power of the determined capacity of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara). As for the claim that the self is an object of mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) in the form "I am," that is trivial; for, as follows, being an object of mental perception means—
It is the state of being the object of a mental cognition produced by the mind (*manojanya-jñāna*). It must be stated that this is a mental cognition which illuminates "I.

If that were the case, then since it is invisible as an object distinct from that [cognition], and since if it were non-distinct from it there would be the faults of impermanence and contradicting established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*), [the self cannot be so]. Furthermore, regarding the self, first of all, [it is expressed as] "I."

Because it is accepted that when [an object] is the object of mental cognition (*mānasajñāna*), the cognition functions solely as the illuminator of itself; likewise, because cognitions of jars and so forth are similarly restricted to themselves alone, they are, for that very reason,
like those who are blind regarding the nature of others and objects other than themselves— distinct from one another and not cognizing one another.

There would also be no differentiation of cognitions from one another, nor, even through the internal synthesis of those differentiated cognitions which take the form of determinate judgments (*vyavasāya*), would there be a differentiation in the form of subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*). This is because the self, like a jar, would fall within the category of the object of cognition (*grāhya*) and thus lack the status of being the subject of cognition (*grāhaka*). For whatever [is an object],...

This is because of the rule that whatever is an object of knowledge possesses insentience (*jaḍatva*). Nor should it be argued that although objects such as jars, which are objects of knowledge produced by the external senses, are insentient, the self is not so because it is not an object of those [senses], and thus there is no aforementioned defect since the self is an object of mental cognition alone and lacks insentience. [Reason: Because of the rule that whatever is an object of knowledge possesses insentience. Nor should it be argued that although objects such as jars, which are objects of knowledge produced by the external senses, are insentient, the self is not so because it is not an object of those [senses], and thus there is no aforementioned defect since the self is an object of mental cognition alone and lacks insentience.

Even if pleasure and the like have that [consciousness] as their object, as do remembered objects such as jars, their insentience (jaḍatva) remains; thus, the consequence of their being insentient is indeed unavoidable. If this were accepted, then since it is a fixed rule that an insentient thing—like a jar—is never a substrate for the arising of knowledge through inherence, the attainment of liberation through the knowledge of the reality of the sixteen categories would be impossible.

We do not know whose [it is]. Furthermore, even if one accepts that the self (*ātman*) is insentient (*jaḍa*), the defects of its being eternal and its being a mere fiction—according to the reasoning employed by the Śākyas—are not abandoned. Moreover, mental cognition (*mānasajñāna*) having the self as its object is simply not tenable. Why? Because the mind (*manas*), being atomic (*aṇu*), is partless (*niraṃśa*), whereas the self (*ātman*), being all-pervading (*vibhu*), is infinite.

Because these two are partless, a conjunction between these two partless entities is simply not possible, since conjunction is necessarily non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti). Thus, due to the impossibility of a conjunction between the self and the mind, there would be an absence of the cognition produced by it; consequently, the manifestation of the self as "I" (ahaṃkhyāti) would not occur at all. The same applies to the mind's [conjunction] with a sense organ.
Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also not possible, because conjunction resides in two things (*dviniṣṭha*), whereas the mind is partless (*niraṃśa*).

Even in the case of external perception, sense-object contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*) is not required. For instance, it is indeed the case that there would be contact between the parts of the sense organ and the whole object, as well as between the parts of the object and the whole sense organ.

The relation [of conjunction] is not possible. Why? Is the sense organ composed of parts (*sāvayava*) or partless (*niravayava*)? Not the first; if it were composed of parts, would the part of the sense organ itself be composed of parts or partless?

If that part were also composed of parts, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, because a part possesses the nature of being a constituent (*avayavin*), there would be a conjunction between the constituent and the whole (*avayavin*).
It is not possible. Likewise, the connection of a part of the object with the sense faculty is also not possible;
for since a part of the object also possesses parts, it is itself a whole, and thus there is no connection between two wholes.
Therefore, the parts of the sense faculty and the object are themselves partless. This applies successively to each preceding [part] in relation to each succeeding one.

Since they must be admitted to be partless by virtue of not possessing constituent parts, it follows that conjunction between two partless entities is untenable; for conjunction, by the rule of its being a pervasive occurrence (*vyāpyavṛtti*), necessarily exists only in a single location.

Because there is no division of space or time for two partless entities. It is not the second [alternative]: if the sense organ were partless, it would be impossible to speak of its conjunction with parts. Does the sense organ—leaving aside the physical ball (golaka)—go to the location of the object, or does the object come to the location of the ball? Not the first.

Otherwise, one would fall into the state of being blind and deaf; furthermore, since the sense organ has already reached [the object], even sensation would be cut off. Nor is the second [position] tenable: for objects such as the star Arundhatī, the Pole Star (Dhruva), and the lunar mansions travel seven hundred thousand yojanas in an instant, reaching the region of the eyeball and then departing again instantly.

Because it is highly unreasonable due to its contradiction with all empirical experience— since that fixed celestial sphere (*dhruvamaṇḍala*) and the rest remain in their own respective places— it should be understood that the claim "perception is knowledge produced by the sense organs" is untenable. Consequently, one should consider that inference and other means of knowledge rooted in this [definition] are likewise as non-existent as a flower in the sky.

By this, the proof of God (īśvara) is also cast far away, because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to establish him. Let it be granted for the sake of argument that there is inference; nevertheless, an inferential cognition (anumiti) is not possible here, because such a cognition depends upon the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti), and the nature of that [pervasion] cannot be known. To explain:

Indeed, the nature of pervasion (vyāpti) must be understood through its definition (lakṣaṇa). However, if the definition were stated as being common to both valid and fallacious reasons, there would be no knowledge of pervasion at all.
Therefore, the definition must be stated as being common to all valid reasons; this being the case:

Prior to the statement of the definition, at the stage of the formal enunciation (*uddēśa*), it is not possible to state the definition as being contained within a valid reason (*saddhētu*) without first possessing knowledge that distinguishes between valid and invalid reasons; for there would be no knowledge of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*).
If one were to investigate by what such knowledge of the object to be defined is produced, it must be said that it arises from the definition itself.

The knowledge of the definiendum (lakṣya) is required for the sake of knowing the definition (lakṣaṇa). The purpose of the definition is precisely the knowledge of the definiendum by way of its exclusion from other things.
Therefore, there arises the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya). Even if another definition were stated in that case, [the same problem would persist].
There would be the fallacy of circularity (*cakraka*) and other defects. Therefore, because there is no knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), inference is not possible.
If it is argued that inference is possible because the pervasion is grasped through the repeated observation of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of smoke and fire in the kitchen, we say no.

According to the principle that "the cognition of one related member causes the recollection of the other related member," there is simply the recollection of the fire-related member from the cognition of the smoke-related member; it is not, however, as you have stated, preceded by the repeated grasping of pervasion (vyāpti) in the form: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire," as previously observed in the kitchen.
It is an inference because it is correctly experienced. Nor should it be argued that if this were so, there would be the cognition "I remember," rather than the conventional usage "I infer";
for such usage belongs only to the Naiyāyikas, not to everyone.

Because ordinary people generally lack the knowledge of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), the reflective awareness of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), and so forth, they employ the linguistic expression "I do not infer"; however, since it is established by the experience of all that this [inferential cognition] is indeed of the nature of memory, there is no fault.

Therefore, due to the absence of knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no inference. Furthermore, it is claimed that God is established by the inference: "The earth and so forth have a creator, because they are effects, like a pot. What, indeed, is this so-called "establishment"? Is it the operation of a producer (*kāraka*) or the operation of a cognizer (*jñāpaka*)? Not the first, because [the earth] would not be produced by the eternally established Supreme Lord.

Because the operation of a causal agent is impossible. Not the second [alternative]: in the Supreme Lord, whose luminosity is undivided, even the operation of a cognizer—consisting of the activity of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is limited by space, time, and so forth as taught—is impossible through inference. Moreover:

Because God would be cognizable by a limited mental cognition (*mānasikajñāna*), the consequence of His being insentient (*jaḍatva*) and so forth would be unavoidable. Furthermore, the very production of an inference (*anumāna*) is not possible, because the inferrer (*anumātṛ*) is unestablished.
If it is argued that [the inferrer] is established by the notion "I," we say no; for that notion of "I" is of the nature of a mental cognition.

Because its being the object of that [cognition] is not perceived as distinct from it; for if there were no difference between them, defects such as impermanence would follow due to the restriction that words, cognitions, and actions endure for only three moments. Furthermore, because that [object] is absent at the time of cognitions such as "this is a jar" and during states like sleep or fainting, it cannot be inferred by inference.

It must be stated that [the Self] is known by the marks of qualities such as cognition; however, we do not know by what means it is inferred, because that very [Self] is unestablished. Furthermore, is it something whose manifestation depends on another (*parādhīnaprakāśa*) or is it self-manifesting (*svaprakāśa*)?
Not the first, because that which depends on another for its manifestation shares the same status as a jar and thus cannot be an inferer.

It cannot be the second [alternative]: [is it] insentient like the light of the sun and so forth, or self-luminous, or the independent consciousness-light that illuminates it? Not the first, because it would again fall under the maxim of "dawn at the mill. Not the second, because it would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), since [the opponent does not admit] the luminosity of consciousness (*citprakāśa*).

This is because the self is accepted as being of the category of *guṇa* (quality), whereas [consciousness] is accepted as being of the category of *dravya* (substance). If it is argued that the self is not insentient (*jaḍa*) because it is accepted as being endowed with the attribute of consciousness (*ciddharma*), even though it is distinct from the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), we say no; for like a jar or other objects, that which is distinct from consciousness is devoid of the attributes of consciousness by virtue of its inherent relation (*samavāya*). Thus, it remains insentient.

In brief, [the object] is subject to insentience because it is the object of inferential knowledge, which consists of the activity of a limited internal organ, and because it is beset by the refutations proclaimed by the Śākyas.

By this, the Vaiśeṣikas as well are refuted. For they indeed assert that there are exactly seven categories (padārtha), namely: substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), action (karman), generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), inherence (samavāya), and absence (abhāva).
That too is untenable, because it has already been refuted by the very method used for the refutation of the sixteen categories.
In particular,
they describe the definition of substance as "that which is the substratum of qualities.
Being the substratum of qualities means being a locus that is not the absolute non-existence of qualities.

Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that there is no lack of over-extension (*avyāpti*) with respect to a jar delimited by its first moment, because color (*rūpa*) is also the locus of qualities such as number (*saṅkhyā*) and form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, since one says "yellow is distinct from blue," blue, yellow, and so forth are also loci of the quality of separateness (*pṛthaktva*); thus, the definition is overly extensive (*ativyāpta*). Nor [is it restricted] to color and the like...

It must be stated that number, separateness, and so forth are perceived as residing in substance alone, through the relation of inherence in a single substratum; for it is equally easy to argue the opposite, and there is a lack of evidence [for your claim]. Nor should it be argued that the very fact that qualities cannot otherwise be accounted for (anyathānupapatti) serves as the proof for the non-acceptance of qualities in a quality, because [this argument] is merely a definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
Once the knowledge of the object has arisen through the mouth [of the definition], there is indeed the distinction that "this substance possesses this quality.

Prior to that, let there simply be the determination "this is a quality"; how could there be the application of a reason such as "because qualities are not admitted within a quality," since there is an absence of knowledge regarding its own nature? The distinction would have occurred even earlier.

If [the nature of the categories] were already known, then the statement of their definitions would be entirely useless. Nor should it be argued that the purpose of a definition is solely the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a category, because at the time of the initial enumeration (*uddeśa*), the knowledge of the essential nature of the categories has already occurred. Otherwise, without such knowledge of the essential nature of the categories...

Because the knowledge of the division of categories is impossible without the knowledge of the division of the objects themselves, and because the knowledge of the essential nature of an object is impossible without the knowledge of its division, such mutual dependence leads to defects such as circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, the cognition arises that there are two forms within a single jar; in that case—
The number two does not reside in the jar, because the number two is absent in a single jar.

Therefore, since the number two appears as residing solely in the color [and other qualities], the definition of substance as "that which is the substratum of qualities" is over-extended (*ativyāpta*) to color and the like. By this same reasoning, the definition that "substance is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)" is also [invalidated].

This [position] is to be understood as refuted, because number, distinctness, and other qualities are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of form and the rest. Nor should it be argued that number and so forth are perceived in form and the rest by way of a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*); for if that were the case, it would follow that substance and quality [would likewise be identical].
Let there be only a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*), since inherence (*samavāya*) will be refuted due to a lack of evidence.
If it is argued that "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is a universal (*jāti*), we say no; for there is a lack of evidence for the existence of such a universal.
Nor is it the case that the very cognition of a recurring form—"this is a substance, this is a substance"—across all substances [proves its existence].
The proof [for the existence of universals] regarding substances, qualities,

and actions is that a uniform cognition (anugatākāra-pratīti) would not arise in relation to them without a property consisting of the very nature of substanceness, qualityness, and actionness; and it must be stated that, by the method of elimination (pariśeṣa), that property is nothing other than a universal (jāti).

Since the occurrence of a uniform linguistic usage is possible through the postulation of a single word as the expressive unit, it is improper to postulate a universal (*jāti*) on the grounds that such usage would otherwise be inexplicable. Furthermore, [this applies] whether by way of being the delimiting factor for conjunction,
the delimiting factor for disjunction, or the delimiting factor for being an effect.
And it should not be argued that the existence of a universal (*jāti*) is established by its being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the states of being the sublated and the sublator;

for some property must be admitted as the delimiting factor in each respective case, but not a universal. This is because the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between a universal and its individual instances has already been refuted, and inherence is as non-existent as a flower in the sky.
Because it will be stated [later], and because here too, the property of being denoted by a single word exists in conjunctions (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.

Therefore, the definition of the essential nature of substance (*dravya*) is untenable. For this very reason, the claim that "the nature of a quality (*guṇa*) is to possess a genus while being distinct from substance and action" is also incorrect, precisely because the essential nature of substance [remains unestablished].

Since it is impossible to know [the substrate], it is all the more impossible to know its difference from it, according to the maxim that "a painting can only be completed when the wall exists. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated more thoroughly later in the section on the refutation of the Mādhva doctrine that even the nature of difference itself cannot be known.

Likewise, it is impossible to assert that [the self] is differentiated by action, because the doctrine of difference will be refuted later on. Therefore, the nature of the quality cannot be known through such a definition. What is this?

The claim that "action-ness" (*karmatva*) consists in being one or another of the five types beginning with upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) is also incorrect. According to such scriptural passages as "He created all this," and by the etymological derivation that "that which is acted upon is action" (*kriyata iti karma*), the entire universe is an object of action;
therefore, the restriction that there are only five types of action is not tenable. If it is argued that action-ness is a universal (*jāti*), then regarding its existence...
Because it has been demonstrated that there is no means of valid cognition [for such a thing]. Furthermore, what is meant by "universal" (*sāmānya*)?

If it is said that a universal is "eternal, unitary, and subsisting in many," that is incorrect; for this definition over-extends (*ativyāpti*) to *inherence* (*samavāya*), since that too is admitted to possess those same characteristics. Nor can it be defined as "subsisting in many while being eternal."

It must be stated that "inherence" means existence by way of the relation of inherence; since that [relation] is being refuted, this definition is untenable. Furthermore, as it has been shown that there is no proof for the existence of a universal (*jāti*), what is meant by "particularity" (*viśeṣa*)? [It refers to] eternal substances...

Indeed, a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is accepted as that which differentiates one thing from another. If, when asked what differentiates it from itself, one says it is its own nature, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
If it depends on another, there is the consequence of fallacies such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore:

Because of parsimony (*lāghava*), eternal substances are themselves the differentiators; thus, there is no dependence on another differentiator, and consequently, the existence of *viśeṣa* (particularity) is not established.

Even if an inherence (samavāya) were to exist, we see no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it. Nor is the qualified cognition "this is a jar" a cognition whose objects are the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation, simply because it is a qualified cognition.
Just as by the inference "the man is stick-bearer" (*daṇḍī puruṣaḥ*), some kind of relation is established;

yet conjunction (*saṃyoga*) cannot exist between a quality and its possessor (*guṇaguṇin*), because conjunction is restricted to two substances (*dravya*) and because there is an absence of inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*). [Furthermore,] it would involve the postulation of countless individual natures (*svarūpa*) as being relations.

The establishment of inherence (*samavāya*) as one [entity] follows from parsimony (*lāghava*) rather than prolixity (*gaurava*). It must be stated that this inherence is accepted as being exactly one for the pair of quality and qualified, part and whole, action and agent of action, genus and individual, and for the particularities (*viśeṣa*) and eternal substances. However, if inherence were one, there would be the cognition of color in air, because of the inherence of touch [there].

Furthermore, because the inherence of color is one and the same; nor should it be argued that even though the relation exists, there is no perception of the possession of color due to the absence of the related entity (color), for if that were so, it would not be a relation at all, since a relation must reside in its relata. Therefore, in the case of air...

The cognition of possessing color would indeed occur. If it is argued that even though inherence (samavāya) is one, there is no inherence characterized by color in air, we say no; for there would be a difference between the inherence characterized by color and the inherence characterized by touch.

To claim that "the establishment of a single inherence follows from parsimony" would result in a contradiction of one's own statement and a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*). For indeed, it was on the grounds of parsimony that a single inherence was accepted; if there were multiplicity, how could there be parsimony? In that case, there would be great prolixity (*gaurava*). To explain: inherence, being accepted as a distinct category for each individual substance, [would become manifold].

When the question arises as to by what relation [inherence] exists in a jar or the like, since conjunction is restricted as a relation only between two substances, there can be no conjunction between the relation and its relata. Nor can it be inherence, because there is no further inherence for inherence; for if one were to accept such a thing, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.

And thus, since there is no other recourse, the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*) alone must be accepted as the refuge. This being the case, the assumption of two distinct properties (the universal and the relation) constitutes an excessive complexity for you alone. [Objection: But surely, in a single jar, there are certain qualities such as color, etc., and certain universals such as "jar-ness," etc., which are all perceived together?

If it is argued that, because postulating a relation of essential identity (svarūpasambandha) involves complexity (gaurava), a single inherence (samavāya) is accepted as residing in each respective category for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), we say no; for then the sense organ of sight, which perceives the color residing in that object, would also perceive the odor residing therein.

Because inherence is one, the inherence of fragrance—which is non-different from the inherence of color—is present in the region of the eye. Nor should it be said that the inherence delimited by color is distinct [from] the inherence delimited by fragrance; for otherwise, the same fault would recur.

Since it must indeed be the case that [the effect] arises at dawn, one should resort to the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*) alone for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*); inherence (*samavāya*) is not accepted due to its complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, it is impossible even to ascertain the nature of the reason cited as "because it is a qualified cognition" (*viśiṣṭabuddhitvāt*). To explain: [The opponent might argue: "In the case of a qualified cognition such as 'this is a staff-bearer' (*daṇḍī*), there is no relation between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*, i.e., the staff) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*, i.e., the person) other than inherence; therefore, inherence exists. [We reply: This is not so. For in the case of a cognition such as "this is a staff-bearer," the relation between the qualifier and the qualificand is simply conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is a quality (*guṇa*) residing in both the staff and the person. Consequently, since the relation between the qualifier and the qualificand is established by something other than inherence, the existence of inherence is not proven by this example. Moreover, in the case of a cognition such as "this is a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), the relation between the qualifier and the qualificand is identity (*tādātmya*), because the qualifiers "blue" and "lotus" are identical with the single substance that is their substratum. Therefore, the reason "because it is a qualified cognition" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it applies to cases where the relation is either conjunction or identity, rather than inherence. Thus, the existence of inherence cannot be established. Furthermore, if inherence were a distinct entity, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), as one would have to postulate another inherence to connect inherence with its relata. Hence, inherence is not a real entity. As it has been said: "Because of parsimony, one should accept only the relation of essential identity. One should not accept inherence due to its complexity. Moreover, the very nature of the cited reason cannot even be known. Thus ends the section on the refutation of inherence.

As for this "distinctness" (*viśiṣṭatva*), is it non-different from the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and their relation (*tatsambandha*), or is it different? It cannot be the second [option], because if it were different, then upon being told "bring the man with the staff" (*daṇḍinam ānaya*), it would follow that one must bring something other than that [man], precisely because it is distinct from him. Nor can it be the first; for if it were non-different from each of the qualifier and so forth individually, [the following would occur].

There would have to be a distinct cognition [of the relation], because it is not distinct from the individual natures of those [relata]. Nor can it be said that the relation resides in the aggregate, for that would entail the fault of circular reasoning (*ātmāśraya*), since the very nature of that [aggregate] would be the relation itself.
What is this so-called "non-existence" (abhāva)? If it is argued that it is "being distinct from existence" (bhāvabhinnatva), then what is this "existence-ness" (bhāvatva)?

If it is argued that it is "being cognizable through a cognition whose mode is affirmation" (vidhimukhapratyayavedyatva), [we reply] no; for in the case of the cognition "there is no jar on this ground," even the jar is cognizable through a cognition whose mode is negation (niṣedhamukhapratyayavedyatva).
Because it would not be an object of a cognition that does not represent it [as such], it could not possess the nature of being an existent (*bhāvatva*).

Nor should it be argued that the absence of the absence of a jar is not identical to the jar, but rather something distinct; for in this very same sequence, its absence would also be distinct, leading to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And it is not the case that...
It must be stated that the absence of the absence of a jar is distinct [from the jar], whereas its [the jar's] absence consists of the locus itself;

for by the same reasoning through which the absence of the absence of a jar is accepted as being distinct, its [the jar's] absence must likewise be accepted as distinct. If that were the case, an infinite regress would result.

Nor should it be said that the absence of the absence of a jar is not admitted to be distinct solely due to the fault of infinite regress; rather, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), let the absence of the absence of a jar be admitted as being simply the jar itself, since there is complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating an additional absence. Here, on this ground, only the jar exists; the absence of the jar—

"No," for since the absence of the absence of a jar appears as non-different from the jar itself, there is a contradiction with experience. By this, the definition that "non-existence is the object of a cognition qualified by the meaning of the negative particle" is also cast far away;
for the jar, which is the nature of the absence of the absence of a jar, possesses the status of being the object of a cognition qualified by the meaning of the negative particle.

In that case, there would be the state of being non-existence (*abhāvatva*). In the cognition "the absence of a jar exists," since even the absence is the object of a cognition not delineated by the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), it would not possess the state of being non-existence. Nor should it be said that "being existence" (*bhāvatva*) is simply "existence" (*sattva*);
for what is called "existence" is either existence as its own nature (*svarūpasattva*) or being qualified by the universal "existence" (*sattāviśiṣṭatva*).
Not the first, because there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*), since the existence of intrinsic nature (*svarūpasattva*) persists even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*).

Not the second, because there is under-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, since it is accepted that the triad beginning with universals is devoid of further universals (*niḥsāmānya*). Therefore, the state of being an entity (*bhāvatva*) is difficult to ascertain.

The state of being different from that is even more difficult to ascertain in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*). Nor should it be argued that "non-existence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*); for it can only be asserted that "non-existence-ness" is an indivisible adjunct when one has already cognized a positive entity (*bhāva*) as distinct from it. This remains the case even now.

Because there is no distinction between the categories of existence and non-existence, they describe some among the seven or sixteen technical categories (*padārtha*) as eternal and others as non-eternal. The atoms (*paramāṇu*) of earth and so forth, as well as the five beginning with space (*ākāśa*), are eternal; whereas those consisting of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so on are [non-eternal].

The effects consisting of bodies, sense organs, and objects are impermanent; the qualities such as color and so forth are also impermanent. Even among those, the quality residing in the atoms of water and the other elements is eternal, whereas that which resides in an effect is impermanent. Action is also impermanent.
The triad beginning with generality (sāmānya) is exclusively eternal. Among these, from the atoms of the impermanent categories...
They describe the process of origination as follows: God is the efficient cause, and the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings is likewise so.
Thus, by the power of the unseen merit and demerit of living beings and through the will of God, motion arises in the otherwise immobile atoms;
from motion comes disjunction (*vibhāga*); from disjunction comes the destruction of the prior conjunction; and from that—

Regarding the production of subsequent conjunctions: it is claimed that, in sequence, a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) arises from the conjunction of two atoms; from three such dyads, a triad (*trasareṇu*); and from four triads, through the sequence of tetrad (*caturaṇuka*) and so forth, the world consisting of the great earth and other elements arises. This is incorrect.
For instance: Does conjunction exist by pervading its own substratum, or does it exist without pervading it?

Not the first, because the magnitude of dyads and so forth would be impossible; for conjunction pervades its own substratum, and thus two atoms would result in having only a single dimension [due to partial overlap].
Due to the impossibility of conjunction, there would be only atomhood (*paramāṇutā*) and not duality-of-atoms (*dvyaṇukatā*). Nor is the second [alternative] possible:

for a non-pervasive conjunction is impossible between two partless atoms, because, being partless, they lack any spatial or temporal division. [Objection: But surely, by the power of God’s will, even two partless [atoms could conjoin]?
If it is argued that the conjunction of two atoms is possible, [we reply: Is God independent or dependent?
If he were independent, then because of his lack of dependence on the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings and on the conjunction of atoms, [creation would occur constantly].
If there were dependence on those, then because of being subject to them, the consequence would be the loss of his independence. Without depending on anything else...

Indeed, agency (*kartṛtva*) is itself autonomy (*svātantrya*). For this very reason, it was stated by the venerable Pāṇini: "The independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*). If [the self] were not autonomous, then because of its dependence on another, the consequence would follow that it is not the Lord (*anīśvara*), just like a potter who is dependent on fixed materials. This applies even to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) regarding the conjunction of atoms...

Nor can causality belong to that [pradhāna] either, because it is insentient (*jaḍa*). If it is argued that causality is possible through the will of God, that is inconsistent, as has already been demonstrated previously.
If the production of an effect were to occur through the independence of the insentient alone, then even a lump of clay would [be a creator].

One should produce a jar by means of the potter’s mantra. [Objection: But surely, in a desolate forest or similar place, the production of a sprout from a seed is observed even without the activity of a conscious agent; will it not be the same here as well?
[Reply: No; for in that case, does the seed produce a sprout that already exists or one that does not exist?

Not the first, because it is impossible for that which is already established by itself to be produced. Not the second, because if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a mango tree could arise from a jackfruit seed. Therefore, even in that case, the production of a sprout does not occur through the independence of the insentient seed; rather, it is solely due to the will of the Lord (*īśvara*).

Because [the Lord] acts as a director. Now, if it is argued that in all cases, when the world arises from atoms due to the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of living beings, let the will of God alone be the director—[we reply: no;
for according to your own view, God would lack independence, being dependent on fixed objects like a potter, and would thus be insentient (jaḍa).
Furthermore, because [this] has been demonstrated; moreover, by such scriptural passages as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second.
It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It found no delight, therefore one who is alone finds no delight.
It desired a second," and so forth, [it is shown that] prior to creation, there was only the Lord.

Because of the statement that [Brahman] is the cause of the world, and because of the exclusion of any other entity by means of the particle *eva* and so forth, it is understood that its very independence—characterized by not looking to the face of anything else—is intended.
Therefore, the view that the world arises from atoms under the influence of the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings is incorrect. Something else is now considered.

If it is argued that the production (*utpatti*) of jars and the like is their relation to the first moment, we say no; for a relation must reside in two things (*dviniṣṭhatva*). Since the jar does not exist at the first moment, that definition is untenable. Nor should it be said that the definition is tenable because the jar exists at the first moment; for if [it were so] at the first moment...

If the pot already exists, then its production would not occur at all, because it is already established. It is your own position that the pot exists after its production, whereas prior to it, the pot does not exist; for you have stated that the pot, being previously non-existent, is produced by means of clay, a staff, a wheel, water, a cloth, and so forth. Therefore, at the moment of production—

It is incorrect to say that production (*utpatti*) is the relation with the first moment due to the absence of the jar; furthermore, even the production of the jar is not possible according to your own position, because production must have a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Since the jar does not exist prior to its production, there would have to be a production that is without a counter-correlate.

The meaning is that there would be the production of something from no objective basis (*nirviṣayaka*). How could the existent (*sat*) be born from the non-existent (*asat*)? This contradicts the Śruti;

and "the existence of the non-existent is not found" contradicts the Smṛti. Therefore, the eternal nature of the jar must indeed be accepted. [Objection: But then, by such Śrutis as "from which [all this arises]," etc.—
Furthermore, through the experience of a jar, the origination of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) characterized by that jar is perceived;

this [origination] would not be possible. If that were the case, there would be no relationship of cause and effect between Brahman and the phenomenal world, because the entire phenomenal world characterized by the jar would also be eternal. If you say this, we reply: no, for in the Śruti—
The word *jāyante* (they are born), for its part, refers to manifestation (*āvirbhāva*), because there is no other possible recourse.

Since it is stated that the root *janī* means "manifestation," it is understood that "arising" (*utpatti*) is "manifestation" (*āvirbhāva*), because arising—defined as the connection with the initial moment—has already been refuted. Manifestation, then, is as follows:
By means of clay, a staff, water, a wheel, a cloth, and so forth, the jar— which previously existed in a subtle form beyond the range of both sense faculties and as identical with its own self—
is [manifested] in a gross form such that it becomes an object for both sense faculties.

Thus, it is established by the authority of Śruti, Smṛti, and experience that [the effect] is indeed a manifestation; for the production of what is non-existent is impossible, as this has been determined through both scripture and reasoning. The position that the non-existent is produced is utterly inconsistent, because it would lead to the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of even non-existent things like a hare’s horn being produced. Therefore...

The causal relationship between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is also possible, since the nature of its origination has been demonstrated. As for the pot characterized as previously described, its "abiding" consists in its stability—uncontradicted until the desire to withdraw [the world]—due to its possession of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Likewise, its destruction is also not [non-existent].
It is not destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), but rather concealment (*tirobhāva*) alone; for it is recorded in tradition that "invisibility is disappearance.

It is an abiding in a state of identity with the subject (*pramātṛtādātmya*), having transcended both sense organs due to the blow of a mallet or similar causes, existing in a subtle form and devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

It must be considered as follows: if the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the object were destroyed, there could be no memory regarding it, because memory is necessarily characterized by having an object. The same applies to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, since arising and destruction possess counter-correlates (*sapratiyogika*), these two [terms] refer respectively to manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and concealment (*tirobhāva*).
This is to be reflected upon. As it has been stated in the venerable *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
"The two whose expansion constitutes space (the heavens and the earth) and time (day and night) are my powers of manifestation and concealment regarding the multitude of objective entities."
In this way, even the definition of liberation (mokṣa) stated by you is not tenable. To explain:
liberation is defined as the absolute cessation of suffering. Regarding this, it is investigated:
the absolute destruction of the twenty-one kinds of suffering, characterized by the absence of any suspicion of their recurrence—
The destruction of its essential nature— that is to say, its annihilation— is indeed what you maintain to be liberation (*mokṣa*). However, in that case,

since pleasure and pain would fall within the category of the six objects by virtue of being objects of mental cognition (*manojanya-jñāna*), it would be untenable for [the categories] to possess the number twenty-one.

Nevertheless, since the mind is admitted to be eternal, its destruction is impossible, which leads to the undesirable consequence that liberation cannot occur. Furthermore, even upon the destruction of cognition and pleasure, it follows that the self would persist in a state of insentience like a stone. If you accept this as a desired conclusion—

And likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the self] being non-eternal. If it is argued that even for an insentient entity, eternality is possible as in the case of space, we say no; for that too is non-eternal. "From the Self, space was produced. From this [Self], breath, mind, intellect, and the senses are born. Space, air, light, water, and earth—the support of the universe."
Since the origin [of the world] is heard in such scriptural passages as "She who upholds" (*dhāriṇī*), there is no need for further elaboration.

Therefore, in the systems of Gautama and Kaṇāda, the distinction between the insentient and the sentient is not possible; nor, by means of that, is the division between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) possible; and consequently, the determination of bondage and liberation is also not possible.

Since this has been demonstrated, one should consider that these two systems were composed for the purpose of deluding people. For this very reason, their censure is heard in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other texts. Thus, for example: "This wisdom is not to be attained through reasoning," according to the Śruti; and "Because reasoning is unstable," according to the Vyāsa-sūtra.

"Reasoning is unstable, the scriptures are diverse, and the opinions of the great sages are also diverse; the truth of Dharma is hidden in a cave [of the heart]. The path is that which has been trodden by the great men"—this was the speech of Dharmarāja to the Yakṣa in the Mahābhārata. [One should avoid] those who rely on mere reasoning and those who act like herons.

"One should not worship [the teacher] even with mere words," so says Yājñavalkya. "They know a man who is always attached to *ānvīkṣikī* (logic) to be like a dog," such is the speech of Vyāsa to Śuka in the *Padma Purāṇa*. [One should not teach] to the envious, nor to the crooked, nor to one who has been burnt by his own actions, nor to one burnt by the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*).

And it should be told to a slanderer as well. To summarize, the statement of the Śaiva Tantrikas is that [an unfit disciple] would be cruel, of little learning, addicted to vice, ungrateful, hypocritical, a widow, devoid of devotion to the Guru, full of envy, prone to addiction, attached to worldly status and the like, and a mere logician (tārkika).
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Method of Describing and Refuting the Tarka Doctrine," in the section on debate within the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*.]
[The sixteenth chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O Guru, having heard your excellent refutation of the Tarka doctrine, my heart has become filled with joy.
After that, whose doctrine was undertaken by Bhṛṅgin?
And tell me how that was refuted by Śīlavat through reasoning.
O best of the virtuous, you have great pride because of your reviling of the Tarka system;
I shall speak of the even greater Yoga system.
I observe how you refute [this] through reasoning.
To Bhṛṅgin, who had spoken thus, Śīlavat immediately replied:
"O Bhṛṅgin, listen; I shall declare the esteemed doctrine of Yoga."
I shall corrupt it; behold it right here!
"O King Basava, listen thus: I shall respectfully relate the astonishing words of Bhṛṅgin and Śilina."

Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (*citta-vṛtti-nirodha*). The meaning of the word *citta* is the abiding of the seer, the *puruṣa*, in its own nature as pure consciousness alone. The mind is called the "whole" (*avayavī*) consisting of a collection of fluctuations. A fluctuation (*vṛtti*) is a transformation of the mind into the form of a jar or other objects. And that fluctuation—

It is twofold, being both afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*). Furthermore, these are fivefold through the distinctions of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), error (*viparyaya*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), sleep (*nidrā*), and memory (*smṛti*). Among these, valid cognition is non-deceptive knowledge (*avisaṃvādijñāna*). And that is threefold through the distinctions of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*).

Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the mind, primarily characterized by the ascertainment of the specific aspect of an object— which consists of both general and particular features— arising from the coloring of the mind by an external thing through the gateway of the sense organs.
Inference (*anumāna*) is the determination of the signified (*liṅgin*) through its sign (*liṅga*) in the form of a generality, based on the apprehension of their relationship.
Scripture (*āgama*) is the word of a reliable person (*āpta*). Misconception (*viparyaya*) is knowledge that arises regarding an object as being a certain way when it is not so.

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a variety of misconception. In expressions such as "Devadatta’s blanket," the distinction determined by the genitive case—which does not exist [in reality]—is nevertheless [present] in expressions such as "consciousness is the essential nature of the person."

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the determination [of an object] through superimposition. Sleep (*nidrā*) is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that proceeds by abandoning all objects due to an excessively intensified state of *tamas*. Memory (*smṛti*) is the ascent of an object experienced through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) into the intellect by way of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Among these, [there are] the means of valid cognition, error (*viparyaya*), and conceptual construction.
The waking state consists of these very [modifications] when they are being dissolved through the power of experience; that is the dream state. Thus are the fivefold functions.

The Pātañjalas, who infer the insentient nature and the state of transformation established in the Sāṅkhya system, describe it as follows: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (*citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ*). The meaning of the word *citta* is the abiding of the seer, the *puruṣa*, in his own nature as pure consciousness. At any time other than that of yoga, [the mind remains active].
It has the form of a jar and so forth. Just as the moon appears to be moving when the waves of water are moving,

in the same way, for those whose mental modifications have ceased their outward inclination through practice and dispassion, the mind also abides in its own cause— the mind itself— in the form of latent power (*śakti*), due to the inward-turning of its modifications.
