Cessation (*nirodha*). Effort is the exertion toward the state of transformation wherein [the mind], having its fluctuations suppressed, abides in its own essential nature. Practice (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated fixing of the mind in that very state. That same practice, when cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with great zeal, becomes firmly established; it is to be observed right here [in this life].

For one who has become dispassionate through seeing the bitterness of transformation in sound and other objects of the seen world, as well as in the heard world such as the realms of the gods, there arises the discernment: "These are under my control; I am not under their control.
This is *vairāgya* (dispassion). Such is *yoga*, distinguished by the categories of *samprajñāta* (cognitive) and *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive).

Concentration (samādhi) is of two kinds. That particular form of cultivation (bhāvanā) is called *samprajñāta-samādhi* by which the true nature of an object is known (*prajñāyate*)— that is, known clearly (*prakarṣeṇa*)— due to being free from correct doubt and error.

That samādhi is fourfold, distinguished as *savitarka*, *savichāra*, *sānanda*, and *sāsmita*. Meditation (*bhāvanā*) is the repeated fixing of the mind upon the object of meditation (*bhāvya*) by excluding all other objects. The object of meditation is twofold: the Lord (*īśvara*) and the principles (*tattva*). These principles are further divided into two types based on the distinction between the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*).

The twenty-four principles are insentient, while the Puruṣa is sentient. Among these, when contemplation (*bhāvanā*) proceeds by taking the gross elements and the sense organs as its objects, through the synthesis of preceding and succeeding moments and the blending of the mental impression with the word and its meaning, then it is the *savitarka* concentration. In this very same focal object—
When contemplation (*bhāvanā*) proceeds devoid of the mental recitation of words and the synthesis of the preceding and succeeding [moments],

then it is *nirvitarka* (non-discursive) samādhi. When contemplation proceeds by taking as its object a subtle thing— characterized by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— as delimited by space, time, and specific qualities (*dharma*), then [it is *nirvicāra*].

[The former] is with deliberation (*savicāra*). The cultivation performed upon that very same object of focus—without the delimitation of place, time, or qualities, and by way of the manifestation of the mere substratum (*dharmimātra*)—is the concentration without deliberation (*nirvicārasamādhi*). These are the concentrations on the grasped (*grāhyasamādhayaḥ*). However, when the *sattva* of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is permeated by even a trace of *rajas* and *tamas*, [it is otherwise].

When that [sattva] is cultivated, because the power of consciousness (citiśakti) exists in a state of subordination, there arises from the intensification of the cultivated sattva— which consists of pleasure and light— the *samādhi* accompanied by bliss (*sānanda*). Those who have fixed their resolve upon this very *samādhi* do not perceive the other principle, namely, Pradhāna and Puruṣa.

Because they are free from the ego-identification with the body, they are designated by the term "bodiless" (*videha*). This is the attainment of grasping (*grahaṇa-samāpatti*). Beyond that, when a meditative cultivation proceeds by taking as its object pure *sattva* that is not overwhelmed by even a trace of *rajas* and *tamas*, then, regarding that object of perception—the *sattva*— [The text continues: ...the mind becomes one with it. This is the attainment of the grasped (*grāhya-samāpatti*). In this state, the distinction between the seer and the seen disappears; there is only the light of knowledge, and the mind is absorbed in that alone. This is called the "great" (*mahā-*) attainment. By means of this attainment, the yogi becomes capable of entering the bodies of others and of perceiving objects beyond the reach of the senses. Thus ends the description of the attainments. Now, concerning the supernormal powers (*siddhi*s) arising from the practice of *samādhi*: [the text continues].
Because the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) becomes subordinated and its emergence results in a state where only pure existence remains, this samādhi is called "with self-sense" (*sāsmita*).
Furthermore, one should not suspect that there is no difference between egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and self-sense (*asmitā*);
for where the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) perceives objects through the mental imprint of "I," that is egoism (*ahaṅkāra*).

Asmitā is that state in which, when the mind has become inward-turned through the reverse process of dissolution and is merged into its own nature (prakṛti), only pure existence shines forth. In this very samādhi, those who are satisfied with the primordial nature (prakṛti) and do not perceive the Supreme Self, the Puruṣa, [remain] in their own causal state within the mind.

When [the mind] has reached dissolution, they are called "those dissolved into nature" (*prakṛtilaya*). For those who, having known the Supreme Puruṣa, proceed with meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), this discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is said to be "having grasped the meditative absorption" (*gṛhītasamāpatti*).
In that state of cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*), all four stages likewise persist in the form of latent potencies (*śakti*).

In that regard, the abandonment of each [preceding stage] for the sake of the subsequent one constitutes this four-stage *samprajñāta* (cognitive) samādhi. The *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive) samādhi is preceded by the practice of the cause of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*) and consists of residual latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). This is the meaning: it is called "cessation" (*virāma*) because one ceases [from mental activity].

The "cessation-sign" (*virāma-pratyaya*) is that which is both cessation and a sign; its repeated instillation in the mind is practice (*abhyāsa*). In that state, whatever mental modification (*vṛtti*) arises, it is continuously negated by means of the formula "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), until only the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) remains; this is non-cognitive absorption (*asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*). It is not [otherwise].
In that state, because nothing is perceived, it is the seedless (*nirbīja*) samādhi, which is "without cognitive awareness" (*asamprajñāta*).
The transformation of the mind (*cittapariṇāma*) is fourfold, distinguished as: emergence (*vyutthāna*), the commencement of samādhi, one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*), and cessation (*nirodha*).

Among these, the stages of the mind known as the "distracted" (*kṣipta*) and the "stupefied" (*mūḍha*) constitute emergence; the stage of the "distracted-and-concentrated" (*vikṣipta*) is [the commencement of samādhi].
The commencement of *samādhi* arises from the predominance of *sattva*. However, when one-pointedness has been restrained, it reaches the ultimate stage.

Furthermore, there are *saṃskāras* for every transformation. In that regard, the *saṃskāras* produced by the state of emergence are counteracted by the *saṃskāras* born of the commencement of *samādhi*; those [latter] are [counteracted] by those born of one-pointedness, and those [in turn] by...

By the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced through cessation, both those impressions and their own nature are destroyed. Just as lead, when heated while mixed with gold, consumes both itself and the impurities of the gold, so too do the impressions born of cessation consume both the impressions born of one-pointedness and themselves. Thus...
In brief, the essential nature of yoga and its means should be understood.

Now follow the means in detail, preceded by a demonstration of the practice of yoga. Those known as the "bodiless" (*videha*) and the "dissolved-in-nature" (*prakṛtilaya*) were previously mentioned; because they do not perceive the supreme reality, their samādhi—though it arises—is based on worldly existence (*bhava*). Beyond this, [there is] the knowledge of reality.
And for the sake of this— namely, that one who desires liberation must apply effort toward its cultivation—
it has been taught that for yogins other than those who have attained dissolution into the body-less state (*videha*) or dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*),
samādhi is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and discernment. Regarding that subject of yoga:

Clarity of mind is faith (*śraddhā*); vigor is enthusiasm (*utsāha*); mindfulness is the non-forgetting of what has been experienced; concentration is one-pointedness; and wisdom is the discernment of that which is to be known. In this regard, through faith, vigor arises; the practitioner becomes enthusiastic regarding the object of yoga. For one who possesses enthusiasm...
Memory arises with respect to objects experienced in the past; through that recollection, the mind becomes concentrated.
One whose mind is concentrated correctly discerns the object of meditation.
These are the means for cognitive (samprajñāta) concentration. Through the practice of that, and beyond it—

From dispassion (*vairāgya*), the state of non-cognitive absorption (*asamprajñāta*) arises. Now, for those yogins who possess the aforementioned means, there is a distinction based on the difference between their means. The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that is the cause of action is more stable. For yogins possessing intense momentum (*tīvrasaṃvega*), meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is near at hand, as is its fruit.

It arises quickly. Furthermore, for those who do not desire results such as the pleasures of sense objects, the dedication of all actions to the Supreme Lord is the supreme means. Through that devotion to the Lord, the attainment of *samādhi* occurs.

The Puruṣa, being untouched in all three times by afflictions such as ignorance, by actions consisting of prescribed, prohibited, and mixed forms, by the results of action in the form of birth, lifespan, and experience, and by latent dispositions (āśayas) which are specific types of formations (saṃskāras) called "impressions" (vāsanā), is therefore distinguished and capable of exercising lordship.

By the mere will of the Lord, He is capable of uplifting the world. For all individual selves, there is a connection with mental afflictions and the like through the mere conceit of victory and defeat belonging to the combatants, just as one has such feelings toward a master. However, for this Lord, there is no such thing as pleasure, pain, or the like.

The distinction of the Lord from ordinary persons is that He does not [possess] the notion "it does not exist. And His sovereignty of such a kind arises from the excellence of *sattva*; and the excellence of *sattva* arises solely from preeminent knowledge.
Furthermore, there is no mutual dependence between these two—knowledge and sovereignty—because they are independent of one another. These two...
Since knowledge and sovereignty exist within the nature of Īśvara as beginningless entities, His connection with that kind of nature is likewise beginningless;
for the conjunction and disjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are impossible apart from the will of Īśvara.
Just as the mind of other living beings— which has transformed into the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion—

becomes conscious when it is reflected in the stainless, sattvic body of a yogin that resembles the self of dharma through the transfer of the shadow of consciousness (*cicchāyā*), it is not so for the Lord; for His [consciousness] is purely solitary.
The sattvic transformation is characterized by excellence and exists as an object of experience through a beginningless connection;
therefore, by virtue of being distinct from other persons, he alone is the Lord (Īśvara). Nor is there a plurality of Lords, for if they were equal, [there would be no distinction].

Because their intentions are diverse, the very production of an effect is untenable; even though there is a variation of excellence and deficiency, that which is most excellent is indeed the Lord. Just as smallness and greatness are observed in atoms and space, so too the mental qualities such as knowledge and the rest are seen to exist in varying degrees of intensity.

In some cases, they bring about a state of unsurpassed excellence; and that in which these qualities such as knowledge are unsurpassed is Īśvara. Thus, the possession of unsurpassed knowledge is the seed of omniscience.
Because of His supreme compassion, His sole purpose is the favoring of living beings during the dissolution of individual kalpas and the great dissolution of all.

His resolve is: "I shall deliver all transmigrating beings without exception. Whatever is desired by someone is that person's purpose. He is the teacher and instructor even for the first creators, such as Brahmā and others, because he is not limited by time due to his beginninglessness. And of him...

The *praṇava* is the signifier (*vācaka*). The relationship between these two as signified and signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is eternal; it is manifested through convention (*saṅketa*), but it is not created by anyone. The meaning is that, just as "this is his father" or "this is his son" is manifested by someone [but is not created], it is not so [in the case of the *praṇava*]. [This applies] to that which consists of three and a half morae (*mātrā*).

The proper utterance of that *praṇava* is its recitation (*japa*), and the repeated fixing of the Lord—who is expressed by it—in the mind is the means for one-pointedness. Through the practice of that recitation and meditative cultivation, the result arises: knowledge of the inward-facing consciousness and the absence of the obstacles to be described hereafter.

Disease, languor, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of renunciation, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability are the obstacles that distract the mind. Disease is fever and the like, caused by an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Languor is the mind's lack of serviceability. [Doubt] has both alternatives as its object.

Knowledge is doubt; yoga is that which is to be accomplished, or it is not—such is its nature. Negligence (*pramāda*) is the habit of non-exertion, an indifference toward the means for accomplishing meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Laziness (*ālasya*) is heaviness of body and mind, the cause for the absence of engagement with the object of yoga. Non-abstinence (*avirati*) is the state of the mind being joined with sense objects.
Perverted cognition is erroneous perception.

Due to some cause, there is an absence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is the state of not having attained the stage [of dhyāna]. Even when the stage of concentration has been attained, the non-abiding of the mind—that is, its instability—therein is the lack of stability. By these [factors]...
Together with the distractions of the mind, there are five [factors]: suffering, mental distress, trembling of the limbs, and inhalation and exhalation.

Suffering is characterized by affliction. Mental distress is a state of dejection of the mind. Trembling of the limbs is the shaking of the body. Inhalation is the connection of the vital breath with the external air.

The exhalation of the abdominal air is *praśvāsa*. These [breaths], occurring along with the distractions (*vikṣepa*), are to be restrained through practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). Now, as another means for the restraint of those distractions, the mind should again [be directed] toward a single chosen reality (*tattva*).
One should perform re-entry; by the power of that, one-pointedness arises and becomes free from distraction.

The preparatory cultivation that brings about the mental formations is fourfold: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Among these, loving-kindness is friendliness, compassion is pity, and sympathetic joy is gladness.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is not to be despised. Just as one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward those who are happy, thinking, "Excellent, may they remain happy," rather than feeling envy; and toward those who are suffering, one should cultivate only compassion (*kṛpā*), thinking, "How indeed might these beings be liberated from suffering," rather than remaining indifferent; and toward those who possess merit, one should feel only joy through rejoicing in their merit.

One should not, however, harbor hatred toward those who possess merit, thinking, "What are these people? Regarding those devoid of merit, one should cultivate only equanimity—neither approval nor hatred. In this way, through the preliminary practice of friendliness and the other [immeasurables], the mind becomes serene by means of cultivating friendliness and so forth, which serve as the antidotes to hatred, attachment, and the like.
The mind in which serenity has been generated becomes fit for concentrations such as *samprajñāta*.
There is also another method: by means of a specific effort applied to the abdominal air, its expulsion outward according to a measured duration, which is designated as *pracchardana* (exhalation).

One-pointedness of mind is accomplished through *recaka* (exhalation), through *pūraka* (inhalation) by filling the internal and external air, or through *kumbhaka* (retention) consisting of the restraint of the filled air, also known as *vidhāraṇa*.
Now, the preliminary limb of *samprajñāta-samādhi* is as follows:
the mental modification (*manovṛtti*) that bears fruit in the form of [the perception of] smell, taste, form, sound, and touch brings about one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).
For example, for one who fixes the mind on the tip of the nose, the consciousness of a divine fragrance arises; likewise on the tip of the tongue.

The consciousness of taste at the tip of the tongue, the consciousness of form in the middle of the tongue, the consciousness of touch at the root of the tongue, and the consciousness of sound at the base of the tongue—
this consciousness arising through the respective doors of the sense organs regarding their respective divine objects,
leads to one-pointedness of mind. Therein, the sattvic illumination becomes increasingly excellent.

In that [state], that luminous activity (*jyotiṣmatī pravṛtti*), through the power of practice consisting of the nature of bliss, brings about one-pointedness of mind free from sorrow, which is a transformation of *rajas*. This is the meaning:
for one who meditates on the mental essence (*cittasattva*) within the center of the hollowed lotus of the heart, resembling the tranquil Ocean of Milk.
Through the light of wisdom, when all mental fluctuations have ceased, stability of the mind arises; this is one form of yoga.

For one who is free from passion, even the mind becomes a cause for stability; it is the knowledge of the Self whose external sensory functions have subsided, which—by means of the mind alone—has as its object the state of being an enjoyer in the dream-like condition, or the object of deep sleep, and is thus freed from [the waking] support.

It serves for the steadiness of the mind. When an object as intended—whether external, such as the moon, or internal, such as the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*)—is meditated upon, steadiness of the mind arises. For the yogi who cultivates steadiness of the mind through these means, by way of meditating on subtle objects, [the mind reaches] down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
Mastery is the fruit. The mind of one who cultivates this [object] is not obstructed.

Thus, for the conditioned mind whose fluctuations have ceased, there arises a gradual state of abiding in and being absorbed by that [object] with respect to the subject, the instruments of perception, and the objects—namely, the self, the senses, and their domains.
And there is a transformation into that form: just as a stainless crystal takes on the appearance of whatever it rests upon, so too the stainless mind,
through its coloring by various objects of meditation, attains the state of having those very forms.
Now, meditative absorption (samāpatti) has been said to be fourfold. Sound is that which is perceivable by the sense of hearing, or it is of the nature of a sphoṭa.

Meaning consists of the universal (jāti) and so forth. Cognition is a modification of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) in which the quality of sattva predominates. Conceptual construction (vikalpa) has the definition already stated. Meditative absorption mixed with these is "with deliberation" (savitarka).

When the memory of words and their meanings has dissolved, there occurs the non-discursive (nirvitarka) meditative attainment, which— by virtue of the manifestation of a clearly perceived objective form that has arisen— is as if devoid of its own nature because the aspect of cognition has become subordinate; it has as its objects the subtle elements (tanmātras), the internal organs, and so forth.

Savicārā [meditation] is that which possesses the manifestation of subtle objects as delimited by space, time, qualities, and so forth, being twofold insofar as it has both word and object as its domain and is accompanied by conceptualization of word and object. Nirvicārā [meditation] is that which possesses the manifestation of the mere substratum consisting of the internal organ and the tanmātras, devoid of space, time, qualities, and so forth.

The attainment without deliberation (*nirvicārā samāpattiḥ*). This attainment regarding subtle objects has as its objects the specific *liṅga* (the principle of ego), etc.; the non-specific *liṅga*, the *tanmātras*, and the sense organs; and the *liṅga*-only, which is the intellect (*buddhi*).

And it has as its object the primary principle (pradhāna), which is without marks (aliṅga). There is nothing subtler than this. These aforementioned attainments (samāpatti) exist together with a seed; thus, it is "seeded" (sabīja) cognitive concentration (samprajñāta-samādhi). Accordingly, compared to the discursive (savitarka) attainment which has gross objects, the non-discursive (nirvitarka) attainment possesses primacy. Even more than that—

From that [state] comes the savicāra [samādhi] whose object is subtle; from that, too, comes the nirvicāra [samādhi] which is free from conceptual construction. When that [nirvicāra] becomes pure through the power of intense practice, *adhyātmaprasāda* (inner clarity) arises.
The mind, freed from the latent impressions of the afflictions, becomes fit for a steady flow. Thus...

When there is firmness in the form of confidence of mind (*cittavaiśāradya*), one bears *ṛta*—that is, truth—and it is never obscured by error; thus, the wisdom that "bears *ṛta*" (*ṛtambharā prajñā*) arises therein. And from that light of wisdom, seeing everything as it truly is, the yogi attains supreme yoga.

The wisdom derived from scripture and inference has the general as its object; for words and logical marks lack the capacity to apprehend particulars, unlike the sense organs. This wisdom, however, which arises from proficiency in non-discursive [insight], is distinct from those two.
Because its object is specific. For in this wisdom, even the particulars of things that are subtle, concealed, or remote appear in a perfectly clear form.
Therefore, the yogi must exert supreme effort toward that very wisdom alone; it is by means of that wisdom that [the goal] is produced.
It obstructs other formative forces (saṃskāras), both those born of emergence and those born of meditative concentration;
it renders them incapable of performing their own functions.

Now, as for the non-discerning [samādhi]: when discerning [samādhi] has dissolved and all mental modifications have dissolved into their own cause, that modification which arises from residual impressions alone—
in which [modification], through the exclusive exclusion "not this, not this," the seedless samādhi occurs— is that in which [the yogi abides].
The person, established in his own true nature, becomes pure. Therefore, having here stated the definition of yoga as it pertains to this context,
the explanation of the terms "cessation of mental fluctuations," the definitions of its two means— practice and detachment— and the nature and distinction of those two means, [the author proceeds].

Having described the primary and secondary divisions of yoga through the distinction between *samprajñāta* (cognitive) and *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive), and having extensively demonstrated the means preceded by the presentation of the practice of yoga, [the author] proceeds to demonstrate the easy means regarding Īśvara.

Having determined the nature, the means of knowledge, the power, the methods of worship, and the fruits [of the Self], [the author] has extensively explained the distractions of the mind along with their concomitants such as suffering,

and the means for their cessation, including the practice of the single principle (*ekatattvābhyāsa*), friendliness (*maitrī*) and so forth, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth, and cognitive absorption (*samprajñāta*).

Having described the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)— along with their characteristics, their fruits, and their respective objects— by means of definitions such as "the practice whose object consists of previously unperceived constituent parts," and by way of a concluding summary;

Having thus concluded the exposition on both conscious (*samprajñāta*) and unconscious (*asamprajñāta*) [samādhis], it has been stated that the seedless (*nirbīja*) samādhi is preceded by the seeded (*sabīja*); such is the system of the first chapter of the *Yogapātañjala*.

Thus, yoga with its means has been explained for one whose mind is concentrated. Now, the practices for accomplishing yoga preceded by the practice of its means are set forth even for one whose mind is in the state of emergence (*vyutthita*): "Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute *kriyā-yoga*. Austerity..."
Austerity consists of the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, self-study (*svādhyāya*) which is the recitation of mantras such as the *praṇava*,
and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*), which is the dedication of all actions to that Supreme Teacher without regard for their fruits. These constitute austerity (*tapas*).

When practiced, [the yogic limbs] beginning with *yama* weaken the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as ignorance that reside in the mind, thereby assisting meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The five afflictions are ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live.
Ignorance is delusion; it is the conceit of selfhood in what is not-self. That...

It is the ground for the production of the fourfold afflictions— namely, egoism (asmitā) and the others— which are distinguished as dormant, attenuated, interrupted, and active. Among these, those afflictions that reside in the soil of the mind and do not initiate their own effects due to the absence of an awakening stimulus are "dormant" (*supta*), such as the afflictions existing in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) during childhood.
In the absence of the auxiliary cause of awakening, they are not manifested.

For yogins who possess practice, these [latent impressions]— whose capacity to produce their effects has been weakened by the cultivation of the respective antidotes to ignorance and so forth— remain situated in the mind as mere residual traces.
Subtle entities are incapable of initiating their own activity without an abundance of causal conditions;
those whose power remains suppressed by some powerful affliction are termed "interrupted," such as attachment in the state of aversion,
or aversion in the state of attachment.

In the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), those noble [impurities] which, having attained the proximity of their auxiliary causes, bring about their own effects, are the adversaries of yoga; in them, even though ignorance (*avidyā*) remains as the fundamental basis for each of these four types, it is perceived through its continuity. And while that [ignorance] is false, [the following occurs...]

Once they have been turned back by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), there is no further sprouting for those [impressions] which are like burnt seeds; therefore, one should first apply effort toward their eradication.
In this regard, the general definition of ignorance (*avidyā*) is the appearance of something as what it is not (*atasmiṃstaditi pratibhāsa*).

The conceit of permanence regarding impermanent things such as pots; the conceit of purity regarding impure things such as the body; the conceit of happiness regarding objects that are suffering; the conceit of selfhood regarding the body which is not-self; the delusion of merit regarding what is non-meritorious, and the delusion of purpose regarding what is purposeless, and so forth.

Asmitā is the identity of the powers of seeing and the instrument of sight. The power of seeing is the Puruṣa; the power of sight is the sattvic transformation in the form of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), unoverpowered by rajas and tamas.
These two exist in the relationship of the enjoyed and the enjoyer, and the insentient and the sentient.

And *asmitā* (egoism) is the conceit of a single identity between two things that are absolutely distinct in nature; for example, although *prakṛti* is in reality devoid of agency and enjoyment, she conceives "I am the agent" and "I am the enjoyer"—this is the affliction consisting of *asmitā*. For one who knows pleasure, [attachment] arises toward the means of pleasure preceded by the recollection of pleasure.

Lust is greed in the form of craving. For one who has experienced suffering, that affliction characterized by hatred is the anger consisting of revulsion toward the means of attaining it, preceded by the recollection of that suffering.
Fear is that which takes the form of dread, arising from the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of having experienced the suffering of death in a previous birth.

The affliction known as *abhiniveśa* (clinging to life) arises spontaneously; it takes the form of a continuous attachment day after day, occurring in everyone from the lowest worm up to Brahmā, without any apparent cause, in the form of the thought, "May I not be separated from my body, sense-objects, and so forth. Such is the nature of this state of *vyutthāna* (emergence).

Since they are of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*), those who desire to practice one-pointedness must first eliminate the afflictions. Those subtle afflictions that persist in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are to be abandoned through reverse transformation (*pratiloma-pariṇāma*). As for their gross forms, which have already initiated their effects—*yāḥ*... [is the beginning of the description of those].

The fluctuations consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion are to be abandoned by means of meditation (*dhyāna*) characterized by one-pointedness of mind alone. By the mere practice of purifying the mind, those gross fluctuations cease, just as thick, gross dirt is removed from cloth and the like.

It is removed by mere washing; however, that which is subtle therein must be removed by various means such as heating and so forth. Actions in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), whether auspicious or inauspicious, which are to be accomplished through afflictions (*kleśa*) and are to be experienced in this life or in another birth, [are likewise removed].

[They are] the producers of results. When the afflictions (kleśas) characterized as described above remain unsubdued, the maturation (vipāka) of karmas occurs, consisting of birth, lifespan, and experience. Birth refers to being human and so forth;
lifespan is the connection with a single body for a long duration; and experiences refer to sense objects and the sense faculties.

The meanings of the word *bhoga* (enjoyment) are the experience of pleasure and the experience of pain, according to the grammatical analysis as the object (*karman*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), or the state (*bhāva*).
These are the latencies of karma accumulated upon the ground of the mind since beginningless time.

They initiate effects characterized by birth, lifespan, and experience. Birth, lifespan, and experience initiated by meritorious karma have happiness as their fruit; those initiated by non-meritorious karma have suffering as their fruit.

This twofold division is relative to all living beings. However, for the yogin who has fully understood the discrimination [between the self] and the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, [there is no such duality].
Every means of enjoyment that is perceived is nothing but suffering, like food mixed with poison.
For a yogi who is extremely refined is agitated by even the slightest trace of suffering; just as the eye experiences great pain from the mere touch of a thread of wool, whereas no other limb does.

Because objects being enjoyed give rise to an increase in craving according to their respective natures, because the suffering caused by failing to obtain them is unavoidable, and because they serve as the means for other forms of suffering, they possess the very nature of suffering; this is what constitutes the "suffering inherent in change" (*pariṇāma-duḥkhatva*).

Since hatred toward that which obstructs the means of pleasure persists at all times while those means are being enjoyed, the suffering of pain (tāpa-duḥkhatā) is difficult to avoid even during the experience of pleasure;
for when objects both desired and undesired are present...

The experience of pleasure and the experience of pain, as they arise, initiate a corresponding formative impression (*saṃskāra*) within their own field; and from that formative impression, there again occurs the experience of such sensations.
Thus, because the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is not severed due to the production of boundless formative impressions, everything is indeed suffering.

Furthermore, due to the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*— namely, the functions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* which arise in the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and are mutually opposed by way of being the subduer and the subdued—
all of these are characterized as suffering because they are invariably accompanied by pain. This is the intended meaning.
For the discerning person who desires an absolute and final cessation of suffering,
all objects appear as being of the nature of suffering until the four aforementioned causes [of suffering] are eliminated.
Therefore, the ripening of all karma is indeed of the nature of suffering.

The nature of that which is to be abandoned is now stated, since the means for attaining right knowledge— which cuts off the aforementioned ignorance that is the root of the afflictions— consists in the ascertainment of what is to be avoided and what is to be adopted. Because the past has already passed away and the present being experienced cannot be relinquished, it is only future suffering [that must be abandoned].

This is to be abandoned. That conjunction of the seer, whose nature is consciousness, with the intellect, which is the object of sight—a conjunction characterized by the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed preceded by the non-discrimination [of the two]—is the cause of suffering, which is the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of the transformations of the *guṇas*.
Through its cessation, there is the cessation of the cycle of existence. [The functions of the *guṇas* are] illumination, activity, and inertia.

The nature of the perceptible is as follows: luminosity (*prakāśa*) is the attribute of *sattva*; activity (*kriyā*), which takes the form of engagement, is the attribute of *rajas*; and stability (*sthiti*), which takes the form of restraint, is the attribute of *tamas*. These three constitute its essential nature.
Earth and the other elements, as well as the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such as smell, are each twofold, distinguished as gross and subtle.
The sense organs are threefold, distinguished as the cognitive organs (*buddhīndriya*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The effect of the visible object (*dṛśya*) is its transformation, which is non-different from it in its essential nature, appearing in the form of both the perceiver and the perceived.
Its purpose is experience (*bhoga*) in the manner described, and its fruit is the cessation of transmigratory existence preceded by discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*).

Thus, for this [Prakṛti], which consists of the transformation of various states and forms, and which is both to be abandoned and the object of perception, there are four stages. Among these, the gross elements and the sense organs are the specific (viśeṣa) stages;
the subtle elements and the internal organ are the non-specific (aviśeṣa) stages; and the intellect (buddhi) is the mere indicator (liṅgamātra).

The unmanifest is without marks (*aliṅga*). Thus, because the unmanifest, whose nature consists of the three *guṇas*, is recognized as the underlying continuity everywhere, these four stages of the *guṇas* must necessarily be known at the time of yoga.
The *puruṣa*, being pure consciousness alone, is pure due to the absence of transformation and so forth, and is well-established.

He perceives cognitions colored by objects through the absence of reflection and other such processes. The Puruṣa’s status as a seer exists merely by its proximity to the intellect (buddhi) when that intellect has already become colored by an object.
This is what is called the production of the Puruṣa’s state of being an enjoyer with respect to the nature of the "seen" (dṛśya), which possesses the characteristics previously described.

The purpose [of the *pradhāna*] consists precisely in the abandonment of its own self-interest. For the *pradhāna*, when it proceeds, does not proceed by depending on some purpose of its own; rather, it proceeds with the thought, "I shall accomplish the experience (*bhoga*) of the *puruṣa*.
If this is so, and the accomplishment of the *puruṣa*'s experience is indeed the purpose, then once that has been accomplished—

In that case, with respect to that which is purposeless, [the intellect] would cease its activity; and since that [intellect] would be devoid of transformation, all perceivers, due to its purity, would be free from bondage. Consequently, there would be the cessation of saṃsāra—if this is what is thought here, [the following is the response]:

Although it has ceased its activity and is lost with respect to a particular person who has achieved their purpose through the attainment of experience culminating in discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), nevertheless,
because it is common to all persons, it remains active with respect to others. Therefore:

Because the *pradhāna* is common to all enjoyers, it can never be destroyed; nor does the liberation of one lead to the liberation of all. This is because the powers of the subject (*svāmin*) and the object (*sva*), which are established as the perceiver and the perceived through their observed natures as the seer and the seen, [remain distinct].
The perception of its own nature is the cause of that [consciousness], as is its innate state of being the enjoyer.

Union is not something distinct from the very nature of the object of enjoyment; for there can be no union between those two—being eternal and all-pervasive—that is distinct from their own natures. Indeed, what constitutes the state of being the object of enjoyment for the enjoyed, and [the state of being the enjoyer] for the enjoyer...
The state of being an enjoyer is established as beginningless; that itself is the conjunction (*saṃyoga*). The cause of that conjunction is ignorance (*avidyā*).

When there is the non-existence of that ignorance—which has been uprooted by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) which is opposed to its own nature—there is also the non-existence of its effect, namely the conjunction. Of that [conjunction]...
And there is the abandonment of the visible object. This is the intended meaning: its abandonment is not possible in the manner of discarding a material substance;
rather, when discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has arisen, the conjunction caused by non-discrimination ceases of its own accord.
It is precisely this cessation of conjunction that is designated as the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the Puruṣa. Thus, regarding this conjunction...

The essential nature, the effect, and the cause have been explained. The discriminative knowledge that "the qualities (guṇas) are one thing and the Puruṣa is another" is the means for the relinquishment of the object of vision (dṛśya).
This occurs through the dissolution of ignorance by the power of cultivating its opposite.

The inward-turned transition of the intellect (*buddhi*), which has ceased its conceit of being a knower and an agent and is no longer overwhelmed by the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, is discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). When that discernment proceeds in a continuous stream, isolation (*kaivalya*) indeed occurs through the cessation of the objective world's mandate.
For the person in whom discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has arisen, wisdom (*prajñā*) becomes sevenfold at the final stage (*prāntabhūmi*).

For that one who has produced knowledge of discrimination, wisdom—which consists of the discrimination of what is to be known—becomes sevenfold at the final stage, at the limit of all stages of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that possess an object of support (*sālambana*). Therein:

The form of liberation from duty is fourfold: "I have known what was to be known; there is nothing further to be known"; "My afflictions are exhausted; there is nothing further to be exhausted"; "Knowledge has been attained by me";
and "Discriminative discernment has been reached by me"—thus, by the cessation of other mental modifications.

In that state, such wisdom alone arises. Such wisdom is the stainless knowledge regarding the objects of action, which is called "liberation from action" (*kāryavimukti*). Liberation of the mind (*cittavimukti*) is threefold:
"My intellect has accomplished its purpose; the *guṇas* have had their authority removed, like stones fallen from a mountain peak."

They will not return to existence again; for when the *guṇas* are oriented toward dissolution into their own cause, since the root cause called *moha* no longer exists and these [guṇas] are devoid of purpose, how could there be any further sprouting?
And my *samādhi* has become second nature; while that exists, I am established in my own true nature.

Such is the threefold liberation of the mind. Thus, when this sevenfold wisdom of the ultimate stage has arisen, a person becomes solitary with respect to the limbs of yoga that are to be described hereafter.

Through practice preceded by knowledge, there arises an illumination of knowledge in the form of a sattvic transformation, which progressively diminishes the impurity characterized as afflictions— the veils over the light of the mind and the self— and gives rise to discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*).
Now, the limbs of yoga:

The eight [limbs] are restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). Among these, some, such as concentration and the others, are internal limbs because they directly assist absorption, while others, such as restraint and observance, are external.

They assist concentration by means of uprooting discursive thoughts such as violence, which are its opposites. When mastery of posture (*āsana*) is attained, there is stability in breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); thus, each subsequent stage serves as an aid to the one preceding it. In this regard, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), truthfulness (*satya*), non-stealing (*asteya*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*) [are the yamas].

The five restraints (*yamāḥ*) are as follows: violence (*hiṃsā*) is an action intended for the purpose of depriving a living being of life, and it is the cause of all misfortune; its absence is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). Truthfulness (*satyam*) is the correspondence of speech and mind with reality. Non-stealing (*asteyam*) is the absence of taking what belongs to another. Celibacy (*brahmacaryam*) is the restraint of the sexual organ.

Non-acceptance of the means of enjoyment is non-possession (*aparigraha*). These are the restraints (*yamas*). Non-violence and the other restraints are those that are not limited by caste such as Brahminhood, by places such as sacred fords (*tīrtha*), by times such as the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, or by circumstances such as the purpose of serving a Brahmin.
These are called the "Great Vows" (*mahāvrata*). They are as follows: "I shall not kill a Brahmin; I shall not kill anyone at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*);

I shall not kill on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight]; I shall not kill anyone except for the sake of the gods or Brahmins," and so forth. Thus, apart from these four types of restrictions...
"I shall not kill anyone, anywhere, at any time, for any reason whatsoever"—thus they are unrestricted.

This should be applied accordingly to truthfulness and the other [vows] as well. When undertaken in this way without limitation, proceeding in a general sense, it is called the "Great Vow" (mahāvrata).

The five observances (niyamas) are purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord. Purity is twofold: external and internal. External purity is the cleansing of the body with earth, water, and so forth;
internal purity is the cleansing of the impurities of the mind through friendliness and other such qualities.

Contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) is satisfaction (*tuṣṭi*). The remaining [terms] have been explained previously. Regarding the cultivation of the counteragent (*pratipakṣabhāvana*) for the obstruction of discursive thoughts (*vitarka*): "discursive thoughts" (*vitarkas*) are so called because they are thought over; they are violence and the like which are obstacles to yoga. When an obstruction occurs upon the cultivation of their counteragent, then yoga [is established].

It is easy [to understand] that these—non-violence and the others—are limbs of yoga. Furthermore, those [opposites], such as violence, are of three types—performed, caused to be performed, or approved—and thus constitute nine varieties. Greed, anger, and delusion are the causes of these nine; greed is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Anger (*krodha*) is a mental state characterized by a burning nature that uproots the discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

Delusion (*moha*) is the conceit of selfhood in that which is not the self. Thus, actions such as violence, which are individually distinguished by their specific types of performance, are divided into three categories according to their causes—delusion and the rest. Furthermore, these are further divided according to their different states.

They are of three types: weak, medium, and intense. The weak are dull, being neither intense nor medium. The medium are neither dull nor intense. The intense are sharp, being neither medium nor dull. These...

The yogi must effect the abandonment of those [faults] which result in suffering, ignorance, and infinite consequences, by means of the cultivation of their opposites. Thus, for one who cultivates non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), even natural enemies such as snakes and mongooses abandon their hostility; the meaning is that even those who delight in violence relinquish their habit of harming.

For the yogi who practices truthfulness, the fruits of rituals such as the Agniṣṭoma and others arise. For one who practices non-stealing, divine jewels present themselves. For those who observe celibacy, unsurpassed power arises. Through stability in non-possessiveness, [one gains knowledge] regarding future births: "Who was I? Of what nature was I? What actions did I perform?"

Through inquiry, one comes to know everything correctly. Now, as for the fruits of the observances (*niyama*): for one who possesses purity (*śauca*), there arises a sense of revulsion even toward one's own limbs through reflection on the nature and causes [of the body], such that [one thinks], "This body is impure; no attachment should be placed upon it. For this very reason, there is non-association with others who possess bodies.
Furthermore, the purification of *sattva*, which consists of luminosity and bliss, is non-overpowering by *rajas* and *tamas*.
It is cheerfulness, a mental joy through the absence of weariness. It is the steadiness of the mind upon the objects of the senses, which is one-pointedness; this is the conquest of the senses.

The turning away of the senses from their objects toward the Self, and the fitness or capability of the mind for the vision of the Self—these are the five fruits for one who practices purity (*śauca*). This is the sequence: from the purification of the *sattva* comes cheerfulness; from that, one-pointedness; from that, mastery over the senses.

Therefore, through the excellence of contentment regarding the fitness for the vision of the Self, an internal bliss manifests for the yogi. Asceticism, when practiced thoroughly, [purifies] the body and the senses by means of the destruction of the impurities of the mind characterized by afflictions and the like.
It bestows success and excellence. When one's study—characterized by the recitation of intended mantras and so forth—is being perfected, there occurs union with the desired deity;
the meaning is that the deity becomes manifest. This [is] regarding the Lord.
From that, a special kind of devotion arises, which is the manifestation of the previously described concentration (*samādhi*).

For when that Blessed Lord, the Sovereign (*Īśvara*), being pleased, removes the afflictions that act as obstacles, he awakens the concentration. When the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), staff posture (*daṇḍāsana*), cross-legged posture (*svastikāsana*), and so forth, become motionless—
When it becomes comfortable and non-disturbing, it then attains the status of being a limb of yoga.

Furthermore, there is another means for that very [posture]: through relaxation of effort and through final attainment, that posture becomes steady and comfortable by means of relaxation of effort and final attainment. Regarding the mastery of posture:

When steadiness is attained, there are no obstacles to concentration; the yogi is not afflicted by the dualities such as cold and heat, hunger and thirst. When steadiness of posture is achieved, the breath control (prāṇāyāma) caused by that [steadiness] becomes capable of being practiced. And that—
It is characterized by the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation. Inhalation, which functions externally, is *recaka*;

exhalation, which functions internally, is *pūraka*; and the internal suspension of movement is *kumbhaka*. This threefold [breath control] is designated as "long" and "subtle" when it is marked by space, time, and number.

It occurs as characterized by location, such as the nose, the *dvādaśānta*, and so forth; as characterized by time, such as having a measure of thirty-six *mātrās* and so forth; and as characterized by number, in the form "performed this many times" and so forth. The external object of the breath is the nose, the *dvādaśānta*, and so forth; the internal [object]...

The "objects" are the heart-cakra, the navel-cakra, and so forth; having drawn these two objects toward oneself and reflecting upon them, the cessation of movement in the form of a pillar-like state is the fourth prāṇāyāma.
From that prāṇāyāma, the obscuration in the form of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that veils the luminosity residing in the *sattva* of the mind is removed.
The meaning is that it (the affliction) is thereby diminished. Furthermore, another result is the fitness of the mind for the *dhāraṇās*.
Now, as for *pratyāhāra*: it is called *pratyāhāra* because the senses are withdrawn (*pratīpam āhriyante*) from their respective objects.
This refers to the eyes and other senses being withdrawn from their respective objects, such as form and so forth.

Association (*samprayoga*) is functioning with a directedness toward that [object]; its absence is remaining in one's own essential nature alone, having abandoned that directedness. When this [absence] exists, the sense organs become mere imitators of the essential nature of the mind.
And as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is practiced, the sense organs become subject to control, just as follows:
The meaning is that even when being led toward external objects, they do not go [there]. Thus,

having described the *kriyā-yoga*— which is a constituent limb (*aṅga*) of yoga characterized by the first quarter [of the Yoga Sūtras] and has the fruit of attenuating the afflictions (*kleśa*)— [the author now proceeds] to state the enumeration, nature, cause, field, and fruit of the afflictions.
Having spoken thus, and having explained the classification, nature, cause, and fruit of actions,
the nature and cause of their maturation (vipāka) have been stated. Then, because afflictions and the like are to be abandoned,
and because abandonment is impossible without knowledge, [the nature and cause] of knowledge [are now discussed].

Since [the path] depends upon the treatise (*śāstra*), and since the treatise possesses a fourfold structure (*caturvyūhatva*) by way of making known the causes for abandoning what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and adopting what is to be adopted (*upādeya*), and because the nature of that which is to be abandoned cannot be established apart from its abandonment, the fourfold structure is presented together with abandonment.

Having explained each [limb] together with its respective cause, and having analyzed the nature of the limbs of yoga— beginning with *yama*— which exist as internal and external causes for discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) that serves as the material cause, along with their results;
Having stated the enumeration of the postures (*āsana*) and so forth, which culminate in concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and exist in a relationship of mutual assistance toward one another,
their respective characteristics were set forth, followed by the statement of their results. This, then, is yoga.

The intention of the *Sādhanapāda* is as follows: having attained the state of a seed through the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), it has sprouted through posture (*āsana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); it has flowered through sensory withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), and it will bear fruit through meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and absorption (*samādhi*).

Thus, in order to determine the three previously mentioned ancillaries beginning with *dhāraṇā*, and to define them by first stating the designation "saṃyama" for the purpose of demonstrating the external, internal, and other types of accomplishments (*siddhi*), he begins as follows. Therein, the essential nature of *dhāraṇā* is thus:

Dhāraṇā is the stabilization of the mind upon locations such as the tip of the nose or the navel-cakra. This is practiced by one who possesses self-restraint (yama) and observances (niyama), has mastered posture (āsana), has eliminated the distractions of the vital breath (prāṇa), and has withdrawn the aggregate of the senses, whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) has been perfumed by the cultivation of the mind through friendliness and other virtues.

In an unobstructed place, with the body erect and the pairs of opposites conquered, the yogi must effect the stabilization of the mind for the practice of *samprajñāta* samādhi upon the tip of the nose or other such points.

Now, regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*): when the mind is held upon an object, the uninterrupted flow of that very object—which has been made the focal point through the maintenance (*dhāraṇā*) by way of avoiding dissimilar transformations of the mental continuum—is meditative concentration. That same meditative concentration appears as the mere object itself.

That samādhi becomes as if empty of its own nature. When meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and absorption (*samādhi*) operate upon a single object, that is *saṃyama*. Through the practice of *saṃyama*, the birth of discernment regarding that which is to be known occurs. This *saṃyama* is distinguished by its objects, whether gross or subtle.

When the fluctuations of the mind have become steady, the application [of practice] should be undertaken. Among the five preceding [limbs], beginning with restraint (yama), the triad beginning with meditation (dhyāna) is internal; yet even that is external to the seedless [samādhi]. When the quality consisting of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of emergence has vanished, [then it becomes internal].

When the form of the activity of cessation manifests, and the mind is perceived as persisting in both states by virtue of its nature as the substratum (dharmin), then that state is designated by the term "transformation into cessation" (nirodha-pariṇāma). This is so despite the fact that the functioning of the guṇas is characterized by mobility.

Even if there is no immobility of the mind, it is nevertheless said that there is stability in such a transformation. Its fruit is described as follows: through the previously mentioned formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of cessation, that mind becomes tranquil in its flow;
by having abandoned distraction, the mind becomes transformed into a continuous stream of similar moments. Now...
The transformation of meditative concentration (*samādhi-pariṇāma*) consists of the grasping of various objects, which is a property of the mind (*citta-dharma*);
likewise, one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*), which is a similar transformation directed toward a single object, is also a property of the mind.
The transformation of meditative concentration is the waning of the former and the arising of the latter. Now—

The transformation of one-pointedness is a specific modification of the mind that is indeed concentrated; it is a single cognition whose flow has become tranquil and entered the past path, while another has arisen and is manifest in the present path— both being characterized by the state of a concentrated mind.

The transformation into one-pointedness is the persistence of the mind— when it is concentrated— in a continuous sequence of two similar cognitions, which are alike because they have the same form as their object;
this occurs with respect to gross and subtle elements that exist through the distinctions of the characteristics of intellect and action.

Transformation (pariṇāma) should be understood as being threefold, according to the distinctions of characteristic (lakṣaṇa), state (avasthā), and substance (dharma). The transformation of characteristic (dharmapariṇāma) is the assumption of another characteristic by a persisting substratum (dharmin) upon the cessation of its previous characteristic; for example, when a substratum characterized as clay abandons its characteristic of being a lump [of clay].

The transformation of attributes (*dharma-pariṇāma*) is the acceptance of another attribute, such as the form of a jar. Now, the transformation of temporal phases (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*) is as follows: that very same jar abandons its future state, accepts its present state, and, by abandoning that [present state], assumes its past state. Furthermore, the transformation of conditions (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) is likewise [of that same jar].

Because of the continuity between the first and second similar moments of a jar; and because the functioning of a quality does not exist for even a single moment without undergoing transformation. Now, as for the definition of the substratum (*dharmin*):
the substratum is that which conforms to qualities (*dharmas*) that are past, present, or yet-to-be-designated.
Now, the supernormal powers (*siddhi*) are described by way of demonstrating the objects of the aforementioned *saṃyama*:

through *saṃyama* upon that triad of transformations previously mentioned—distinguished as changes in quality (*dharma*), temporal characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*)—the yogin gains knowledge of the past and the future. This is the intended meaning: * **Change in Quality (*Dharma-pariṇāma*):** For example, when clay ceases to be a lump and becomes a jar; the lump is the previous quality and the jar is the subsequent quality. * **Change in Temporal Characteristic (*Lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*):** When the jar exists in the present, it abandons its future temporal character and assumes its present one. * **Change in State (*Avasthā-pariṇāma*):** As the jar gradually undergoes new states such as newness, oldness, and so forth. By practicing *saṃyama* on these three types of transformation, the yogin attains knowledge of the past and the future. The underlying intention is as follows: [text continues]

When one practices *saṃyama* with freedom from distraction, thinking: "In this substratum (*dharmī*), this attribute (*dharma*)— possessing this characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and this state (*avasthā*)— having come together from the future time-path, performs its own function in the present time-path, and then enters the past time-path," then [the knowledge of the three times arises].
Whatever has passed away or has not yet arisen, all that the yogi knows.

In linguistic usage, there is a confusion of word, object, and cognition because they are mutually superimposed; although distinct, they are produced as a single form within the intellect. This is the true nature of the word, namely its capacity to denote; this is the true nature of the object, namely its being denoted; and this is the true nature of cognition.

Having established the distinction that "this is the quality of being a manifester," through *saṃyama* upon that distinction, knowledge of all sounds arises; with this very intention, one knows everything, such as: "This sound was uttered by this particular living being."

From the direct realization of formative forces (saṃskāra), there arises knowledge of past births; thus one remembers everything that is past, thinking, "In this way that object was experienced by me," or "In this way that action was accomplished by me."
For one who has grasped another's mind through a sign such as the color of the face and so forth, knowledge of that other's mind arises from *saṃyama*.

Because of the restraint [arising from the knowledge] that "there is form in this body," when the power of that form— which consists in its being perceivable by the eye— is suppressed and obstructed through the force of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), such that there is no conjunction between the eye and light, the yogi’s invisibility occurs; the meaning is that he is not seen by anyone.

Through *saṃyama* upon karma, which is twofold—being either with or without external pressure (*sopakrama* and *nirupakrama*)—there arises the knowledge: "At this time and in this place, my separation from the body will occur"; or [this knowledge arises] from portents (*ariṣṭa*) pertaining to the self, to other beings, or to the divine.

Knowledge of the separation from the body arises. Among these, the internal signs consist of such things as the failure to hear the sound of air within the chest when the ears are plugged. The external signs consist of such things as the sudden appearance of deformed persons. The celestial signs occur quite unexpectedly—

The perception of objects such as heaven, which are otherwise impossible to see, [is attained]. For one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon the moon, knowledge of the stars is perfected. For one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon the Pole Star (*dhruva*), the foremost of luminaries, there arises knowledge of the motion of the stars. These, ending with the knowledge of time, are the external perfections (*bāhya-siddhi*).

But as for the internal [objects], when a yogin has performed *saṃyama* upon the sixteen-spoked wheel called the navel (*nābhi*) situated in the middle of the body, knowledge arises regarding the bodily arrangement— that specific configuration of the channels (*nāḍī*), humors (*dhātu*), and other constituents.
For one who has applied restraint to the pit of the throat, hunger, thirst, and the like cease.

Below the hollow of the throat is the channel called *kūrma*; for one who has performed *saṃyama* upon it, stability of the mind arises. In the skull of the head is the aperture known as the *brahmarandhra*;
because it is the support of light, it is "light. For one who has performed *saṃyama* there, the vision of perfected beings (*siddhas*) occurs.
*Pratibhā* is a cognition that arises suddenly, independent of external signs, produced by the mind alone, and non-erroneous;
when *saṃyama* is practiced upon it, there dawns the "saving" (*tāraka*) knowledge of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which precedes it. The heart is the core of the body.

A specific location within that [heart]—inside a small, downward-facing lotus—is the seat of the *sattva* of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). For one who has practiced *saṃyama* there, knowledge of one's own and others' minds arises. *Sattva* is a specific transformation of *pradhāna*, consisting of luminosity and happiness; it is the *puruṣa*.
The enjoyer is of the nature of the presiding subject;

because those two possess the respective natures of the enjoyed and the enjoyer, and because they are conscious and unconscious, their state of being utterly unmixed is their distinctness—this is the meaning. That which is the non-distinction of the cognition regarding those two is the failure to manifest them as separate.
Therefore, the notion of agency belongs to the *sattva* alone; the experience (*bhoga*) of the perceptions of pleasure and pain belongs to the *sattva*.

The purpose of another (*parārtha*), which is independent of its own interest, has the purpose of the *puruṣa* as its motive. Consequently, that which is "for one's own sake" (*svārtha*)—which has the mere nature of the *puruṣa* as its object—is [the state] in the *sattva* when egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) has been abandoned, wherein there is the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*).
When transference occurs for one who has practiced restraint, knowledge concerning the Puruṣa arises.
Therein, the Puruṣa, established in Sattva, knows that very knowledge which has itself as its object; however, the Puruṣa, as the knower, does not itself become an object of that knowledge.
Because of the consequence that [the knower] would become an object of knowledge, and because there is an absolute contradiction between the knower and the known;
therefore, from the practice of *saṃyama* upon the *puruṣa*, even for one who has emerged from meditative absorption, various forms of knowledge arise.
Among these, "intuitive" (*prātibha*) is the aforementioned knowledge; through its manifestation, one perceives subtle objects and so forth.

One perceives sound; auditory knowledge arises from the sense of hearing, and from that refined [knowledge], one knows divine sound—that which exists in heaven. Knowledge arises from the sense of touch;
by practicing *saṃyama* upon that, divine knowledge regarding the object of touch is born.

The mirror is the knowledge born of the sense of sight; through *saṃyama* upon it, divine knowledge of form arises. Taste is the knowledge born of the sense of taste; through *saṃyama* upon it, consciousness of divine flavor arises. News is the perception of smell; upon that—

Through self-restraint, a divine fragrance is experienced. These aforementioned perfections (*siddhis*) become obstacles for one who is progressing toward excellence; this is the meaning. In that state, by giving way to joy, wonder, and so forth, *samādhi* becomes slackened. Upon emerging from it, however, one returns once more to the state of worldly activity.
The *siddhis* (accomplishments) arise because they bestow distinguished fruits.

Due to the pervasiveness of the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*citta*), which are nonetheless contained within the body by the power of determined karma, that very consciousness which arises in the form of the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is what constitutes [the experience] in the body.

Bondage is now described. When, by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the collection of karmas known as merit and demerit—which are the causes of bondage—attains a state of relaxation, and when there occurs the perception of that movement of the mind which flows from the region of the heart toward the objects through the gates of the senses; [this is the process of binding].
This is the channel for carrying the mind (*cittavahanāḍī*); by means of this, the mind flows.

And since this is distinct from the channels that carry *rasa*, *prāṇa*, and so forth, when one knows how to move [the mind] between one's own body and another's body—whether that other body be dead or living—[one attains mastery].

He enters by means of the gateway of the movement of consciousness. When the consciousness enters another body, the sense faculties also follow it, just as honey-bees follow the king bee. Then, having entered another body, this yogi conducts himself through it just as he did through his own body, because—
The cause for the contraction of the experience of the all-pervading *citta* and *puruṣa* is karma, which acts as a dominant factor;
if that [karma] is cast off by means of *samādhi*, then through its own sovereignty, the accomplishment of experience occurs everywhere.
The simultaneous uprising of the functioning of all the senses is like the flame of a grain-husk fire. That—

That which is denoted by the word *jīvana* (life) receives its designations through the distinctions of its functions, such as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth. Among these, it is called *prāṇa* because it leads the air (*vāyu*) from the heart out through the openings of the mouth and nose.

In this same way, the designations of apāna and the other breaths are also to be inferred. Therein, through restraint (*saṃyama*) upon udāna, or through the cessation of the other vital airs, even when immersed in water or similar substances, the yogi rises up like a tuft of cotton.
Through mastery over the samāna breath, because the fire becomes manifest and free from obstruction, the yogi appears as if blazing with radiance.

It appears as follows: through *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, there arises a divine ear capable of simultaneously perceiving subtle, obstructed, and distant sounds. Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, [one attains mastery] over light objects such as cotton wool.

Having cultivated that meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), which is characterized by becoming one with its object, the yogi— having attained extreme lightness of body— first moves through water according to his desire, then gradually proceeds by means of a web of spider-silk threads, and finally travels through the sky at will, moving among the rays of the sun.

The activity of the mind outside the body, independent of the body, is called *mahāvidehā* (the great bodiless state); it is so named because it occurs through the firm removal of the ego-identification with the body. Through *saṃyama* upon that [state], there is the destruction of the veil over the light. Now:

For the sake of attaining the seeded (*sabīja*) and seedless (*nirbīja*) samādhis useful for one's own realization, there are various means: when one has performed *saṃyama* upon the specific qualities (*dharma*)— such as grossness and so forth— which consist of the five particular states of the five elements beginning with earth, mastery over the elements (*bhūtajaya*) occurs, and the elements become subject to his will.

The meaning is that they come into being. For instance: the gross form of the elements, which is perceived as possessing specific shapes, and their own essential natures (svarūpa), have respectively as their effects the characteristics of odor, cohesion, heat, motion, and the provision of space. And [their] subtle [forms] are, respectively—

The subtle elements (tanmātras), such as odor and the rest, are established as the causes of the gross elements. The pervasive qualities (guṇas) are perceived everywhere as being inherent, by virtue of their nature as illumination, activity, and inertia.
Their "possessiveness of purpose" (arthavattva) consists in the power residing in those very qualities to bring about experience and liberation.

Thus, by practicing *saṃyama* upon each of these five elements as they are distinguished by their specific characteristics and states, the yogi becomes a master of the elements (*bhūtajayī*). For example: having first performed *saṃyama* on the gross form, and subsequently on the subtle form—in this sequence, for one who has thus practiced *saṃyama*—
The natures of beings conform to one's intentions, like cows following their calves.

Now, the fruit of mastery over the elements (*bhūtajaya*): therein, *aṇimā* is the attainment of the form of an atom; *mahimā* is greatness; *laghimā* is the attainment of lightness like a tuft of cotton; *garimā* is heaviness;
*prāpti* is the power of touching the moon and so forth with the tip of a finger; *prākāmya* is the non-obstruction of one's will.
Sovereignty (*īśitva*) is the state of being the lord over the body, the internal organ, and the [external] world; mastery (*vaśitva*) is omnipotence everywhere;
and because all beings follow him, they do not transgress what he has said—these are the powers beginning with *aṇimā*.
Yogins who have mastered the elements (*bhūtajaya*) and are devoted to the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) come into being. Now, regarding the perfection of the body:

the perfection of the body consists of beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine firmness (*vajrasaṃhananatva*). Beauty, grace, and strength are well known. Adamantine firmness refers to the fact that his body possesses a compactness as hard as a diamond (*vajra*).
They manifest. Through *saṃyama* upon grasping, essential nature, self-sense, inherence, and purposefulness, mastery over the senses is attained.

Grasping is the activity of the senses directed toward objects; essential nature is their common quality of luminosity; self-sense is the accompaniment of the *ahaṃkāra*; and inherence and purposefulness are as explained previously.

By performing *saṃyama* on these five states of the senses as previously described, one becomes a conqueror of the senses. Thereafter, there is the attainment of unsurpassed movement for the body like that of the mind, known as "swiftness of mind" (*manojavitva*);
the acquisition of the functioning of the senses independently of the body, known as the "state of being without organs" (*vikaraṇabhāva*); and mastery over all things.
Mastery over the primary matter (pradhāna). These three perfections manifest for one who has conquered the senses.

Now, regarding the conquest of the internal organ: for one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon that pure, *sāttvika* transformation, there arises a discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, which consists in the mere knowledge of the distinctness of the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, as well as sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience. This occurs when the *guṇas* [have been mastered].
Through the loosening of the conceit of agency caused by that [samādhi], for the yogin established therein,
there arises through samādhi both the presiding over all states of being and omniscience;
that is, the mastery over all modifications of the guṇas and all states of being, like a master.

The state of being the presiding subject (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*) is the knowledge of these very [guṇas]—which exist as subjects characterized by being quiescent, arisen, or undesignatable—as they truly are; this is omniscience. And when the supreme consciousness of mastery (*vaśīkāra-saṃjñā*) has been attained regarding these, it is called the perfection (*siddhi*) named "Free from Sorrow" (*viśokā*) in this treatise. Now...
Through the successive stages [of the *bhūmikās*], and by means of detachment (*vairāgya*) from those as well, there is isolation (*kaivalya*) upon the destruction of the seeds of the defects.
When detachment arises for the yogi regarding this sorrowless perfection (*siddhi*),
then, through that, there is the destruction of the seeds of the defects— namely passion and so forth— which are ignorance and the rest.

And there is the absolute cessation of suffering; for that person, when the mandate of the *guṇas* has been fully accomplished, there is abiding in one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). To such a yogin, the gods become offerers of invitations;
they present divine women, elixirs, and the like, but he should not entertain wonder or attachment toward them.
Through *saṃyama* on the transformation of moments in their sequence, discriminative knowledge arises.
The causes of distinction between objects are genus, characteristic, and location; where distinction cannot be determined due to some deficiency, [therein...]

From restraint (*saṃyama*), the realization of differentiation indeed arises. By the power of the aforementioned *saṃyama*, the knowledge produced in the final stage (*bhūmikā*) enables the yogi to cross over the unfathomable ocean of *saṃsāra*; thus, its name is significant in accordance with its meaning.

It is called "the liberator" (tāraka). And that [knowledge] has as its object all principles (tattvas) existing in every way—having as its objects all subjects beginning with Mahat, and existing in all states through various transformations consisting of the distinctions of gross, subtle, and other bodies; thus it has everything as its object in every respect.

Because there is no sequential order for this [citta] in grasping the entirety of the various states, transformations, and the conditions of deficiency or excess, it is "non-sequential" (akrama). The meaning is that it perceives everything simultaneously, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.
The result is thus described: when the purity of the *sattva* of the mind and the *puruṣa* are equal, there is isolation (*kaivalya*). This refers to the *sattva* of the mind.

Purity (*śuddhi*) is the entry into one's own cause through the cessation of the conceit of being the agent of all; it is the absence of imputed experience for the *puruṣa*. When the purity of both [the *puruṣa* and *prakṛti*] is equal, isolation (*kaivalya*) arises for the *puruṣa*;
the meaning is that liberation occurs. Thus, this is the internal means.

Having described the three limbs of yoga and assigned them the designation of "saṃyama," and having established the threefold transformation for the purpose of demonstrating the objects of saṃyama, he has shown the supernatural powers (siddhis) arising from the strength of saṃyama— pertaining to the past, future, and present— in order to generate confidence in samādhi.
