The Lord Vāsudeva, who is the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), is the embodied one (*śarīrī*) and the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

Since the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the substantive are not excessively different, the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is indeed one. Knowledge of this qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita-jñāna*) is the means to liberation. Sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) do not [refer to a mere identity].
[These statements] are not intended to convey non-difference of essential nature (*svarūpābheda*), but rather are intended to convey qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*).

Therefore, the elision of the genitive case in "that" (*tad*) means "you belong to Him"; the meaning of the sentence is: "You belong to that Blessed One," or "You are the body related to that Blessed One."

According to the logic of the "box of substitutes" (*pratinidhipeṭikānyāya*), the cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl has real silver as its object. By that example, it is possible to establish through inference that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indeed real. All non-dualistic (*advaita*) scriptural texts are merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), whereas the dualistic (*dvaita*) scriptures [are literal].

All [knowledge] is indeed ultimate; therefore, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) arising from the sequence of hearing the scriptures of the Blessed One, the Vedas that accord with them, and the Dravidian Vedas which expound the Blessed One— being focused on qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*)— is not merely [empirical].

The means to liberation, however, are the five purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and other such Vedic rituals taught in the scriptures of the Blessed One that are not in conflict with them, as well as the nature of the Blessed One,
which is fivefold, distinguished as the *arcā*, *vibhava*, *vyūha*, *antaryāmin*, and *paravāsudeva*.

And liberation consists in the attainment of the same form as the Lord (sārūpya) in the non-material Vaikuṇṭha above the shell of the mundane egg, for the eternal Śeṣa, the eternal servant, who has attained all non-material enjoyments; such is the view of the followers of Rāmānuja.

That is utterly untenable. For it has been stated in the opening verse of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "That which is, in ultimate reality, the nature of absolutely pure knowledge, yet appears as the nature of objects through erroneous perception"—referring to that which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, and without eyes.

And by the Śruti: "That which is without ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, and exceedingly subtle— [that] the wise behold as the source of all beings"— it is established that the Blessed One is of the nature of knowledge, bliss, and existence.
Since there is no existence of a physical form at all, the conceptualization of an image (arcā) and so forth as having an essential nature is utterly lacking in authority.

Even regarding that image, the conceptualization of it as the essential nature of the Blessed One is extremely trivial; for [the Lord] "dwells in the fire of the Brahmins, dwells in the heart of the yogis, and in images for the unawakened—everywhere."

By the statement "by one who sees with equanimity," since you are not yet awakened, it is indeed appropriate to conceive of non-difference from the Blessed One in the image. Nor should it be asked, "In that case, how can the cognition of the Blessed One be directed toward Śālagrāma stones and the like? For this is due to the majesty of the scripture.

To the extent that a vision consisting of superimposition (āroparūpā dṛṣṭiḥ) directed toward non-difference from the Blessed One is produced, does his true nature (tattvam) thereby become established? No, because it contradicts direct perception (pratyakṣavirodhāt). For a Brahmin who is mentally conceived as a father during a *śrāddha* rite does not thereby actually become a father. However, according to scripture, a specific course of action (*pravṛttiviśeṣa*) may indeed result.
"Let it be done, or rather, prosper; for by that much, its true nature does not become [established].
As for what was said—that the incarnations such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are forms of the Blessed One—we have no dispute with them regarding their being a portion (aṃśa) of Him."
This is because there exist numerous statements from the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas.
As it is said in the venerable Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa: "Requested by the gods who desired the slaying of Rāvaṇa, who had been exalted [by power], the eternal Viṣṇu was born in the world of men."

As for what was stated— that Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Vāsudeva, and Aniruddha are the lords of the manifestations (vyūha) and are indeed Blessed Lords (bhagavat)— that is utterly unacceptable. Are the manifestations the multitudes of individual souls (jīva-rāśi) with Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others as their presiding lords, or are they also Blessed Lords themselves who have those [souls] as their presiding lords?

As for the claim that Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others [are also supreme], it is not the first case; for if Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe, were to assign the status of "Lord of the World" to those sovereigns who remain near him—just as one might conceive of minor lordships within one's own various manifestations (vyūhas)—then his status as the Supreme Lord would be lost. Furthermore, in your own system, Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, does not possess the lordship over the direction of Īśāna.

Just as in that case, so it should be stated here as well; for by the statement of the *Atharvaśikhā*, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra— they are all produced from Him," and by the statement of the *Māṇḍūkya*, "They consider the Fourth to be the cessation of the manifold world, auspicious, non-dual, whose essence is the realization of the one Self," there is a distinction between the causal Rudra and the effected [Rudra].

Because it is impossible for the Rudra who is an effect to possess limited authority; for in your own view, since you accept that Nārāyaṇa alone is the cause of the world, he cannot be accepted as having both the nature of an effect and a cause—so how could this be possible?
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because it is utterly inconsistent for something to fall upon itself. Furthermore:

Regarding Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others as well, is there any gradation of excellence or are they equal? It cannot be the first [alternative], for what discerning person would assert that one and the same entity possesses a degree of excellence over itself? Nor can it be the second, since you yourselves have accepted that in the Rāma incarnation, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna were all indeed manifestations of the Blessed Lord.

It must be stated that a gradation is likewise accepted here as well, because in the case of the incarnations and so forth, there is a distinction of forms, such as the Lord’s assumption of an ordinary human form for the sake of protecting the boon granted by Brahmā to the Rākṣasa.

Even if the acceptance of a gradation of natural states (*prākṛta-taratama-bhāva*) were possible, such an acceptance by the Lord in His non-natural state (*aprākṛta-daśā*) is utterly inappropriate. Therefore, the conception of the Lord’s true nature (*svarūpa*) in the corrupt *Pāñcarātra* is simply incapable of being sustained. Consequently, for the sake of determining the Lord’s true nature:
The followers of Rāmānuja must be pure Vedic *śiṣṭas*;
likewise, even for those who have not had the *cakrāṅkana* (branding with the discus) performed upon them, [the practice] remains a means for attaining the highest good in the hereafter.
Furthermore, regarding the *Pāñcarātra*, its lack of authority has already been stated in the *Bhāṣya*; it is not mentioned here because it is well known in the world.

Not the second [alternative], because it contradicts the statement of the Pāñcarātra that "the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the stainless one, alone is the ultimate reality. Furthermore, in the non-material Vaikuṇṭha, the Vaiṣṇavas who are knowers of the Dravidian Vedānta and purified by the five sacraments [reside] in the supreme abode.

If it is argued that they "attain the supreme equality" as stated in the Śruti— "the stainless one attains the supreme equality"— and thus they worship the Supreme Vāsudeva, then the inferiority of Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others is clearly established.

Regarding what was stated—that the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) is a form of the Blessed Lord—it is replied as follows: This is indeed the intention of you Rāmānujas: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, and who controls the earth from within—He is your [Self]."

In such scriptural passages as "The Self, the Inner Ruler, the Immortal," the Lord's state as the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) and His relationship as the body and the embodied (śarīra-śarīribhāva) are established. In the world, there is no practice of treating the body and the embodied as being absolutely distinct; rather, the body is a qualification [of the embodied].

The Blessed One is the qualified [subject]; the Śruti texts such as "That thou art" and "I am Brahman" are intent upon qualified non-duality (viśiṣṭādvaita). The meaning of the non-difference Śrutis—such as "That thou art," "Thou art that," and "Thou art His body related to the Blessed One"—is established when there is repetition.

According to the principle that "the meaning becomes more extensive," since the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa repeatedly teaches the Antaryāmin as the "body" (*śarīra*), it is consistent only with qualified non-dualism (*viśiṣṭādvaita*). This wish would be fulfilled if the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa were intended by Rāmānuja to establish the relationship between the soul and the body (*jīva-śarīra-śarīribhāva*).

Furthermore, the state of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*) is secondary; there is no primary intention (*tātparya*) regarding the state of being the inner ruler. Rather, it concerns the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīvabrahmaikya*) alone.

The status of being the inner ruler is merely restated (*anūdyate*), while the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman is what is enjoined (*vidhīyate*). Therefore, one must necessarily maintain that the intention of the scripture lies precisely therein. For instance: "He whose body is the earth... (*yasya pṛthivī śarīram*).

Having stated, "The sun is whose body," it is subsequently heard: "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. To Maitreyī, this instruction is given that the one who is the inner controller and the immortal is "this Self" (ātman), your very own nature. Therefore, just like the statement "That thou art," this is indeed an instruction of non-difference.

This is the final conclusion, and not merely [the relationship] of body and embodied one, nor the state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmitva*). Nor is it [the case] that "he whose body is the earth, whose body is the sun, whose body is the wind, whose body is the self (*ātman*);
who, dwelling within all, controls all from within; of whom all is the body."

Since this very [relationship] is observed through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) regarding the nature of the body, and because when there is repeated practice the meaning becomes more extensive rather than diminished— let alone being merely figurative— it must be stated that, according to this principle, the relationship between the body and the embodied is indeed the intended object of the teaching; and so it is.

Since the repetition [of the term] is also observed following each statement "the body, the body" with the words "this is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal," the maxim "for when there is repetition" applies equally even to the instruction regarding the non-difference of essential nature (*svarūpa*). However—

When investigated more thoroughly, it is determined that precisely because the sentence concludes immediately after the instruction "That is your Self," the intended purport (*tātparya*) is indeed the teaching of non-difference. This is evident from the sequence: "He whose body is the Self, he whose body is the earth... followed by "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal."

Because of this instruction— and because there is no completion of the sentence immediately after the word "body"— it is firmly determined that the relationship between the body and the embodied one, as well as the relationship of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), are being restated. Therefore, as in the passage, "He has entered here up to the tips of the nails," there is indeed non-difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-abheda*).
The specific manner of expression is highly esteemed;

however, since you lack knowledge of the particular intention behind such a statement, it is indeed appropriate for you to conclude that the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* has as its purport nothing other than the state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmitva*).

As for the claim that the sentences "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) intend a qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) by accepting the elision of the genitive case in *tasya tvam asi*, that is stated out of a lack of understanding regarding your intellect; it is not [established] from the elision of the genitive. For if the elision of the case-ending were accepted here—

In that case, even in the preceding statement, "That is the Truth, That is the Self," one would have to resort to the elision of case-endings or provide various other interpretations of the sentence-meaning for the sake of confusing those who are unlearned. Therefore, [this must be understood] through the cognition of a common substratum.
When the meaning is thoroughly investigated, that which is true is the Brahman denoted by the word "That," and He is the Self—He who is this subtle essence;

"all this has that as its self. Because of this reference to what precedes and follows, it is understood that the purport of the sentence lies solely in the non-duality of essential nature (*svarūpādvaita*), namely: "Thou art That [Self], the Supreme Self, that Brahman."

Furthermore, since the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* culminates in non-duality (*advaita*), and because, according to the aforementioned reasoning, there is no intended meaning (*tātparya*) for qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*), the sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) have their intended meaning unassailably established in the sense they convey. Moreover, it is said: "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another... (*yatra hi dvaitam iva bhavati tad itara...*).

"He sees the other. But where everything has become the Self for him, how could he see whom? According to this scripture, duality appears to be unreal. For where there is, as it were, duality—in reality, duality does not exist—duality, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, is an object of the intellect within the sphere of empirical usage.

The purport of this scripture is established by its own internal sense (*svarasataḥ*), and it is certain that duality is unreal based on the statement from the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "Those who hold to duality see what is untrue. Therefore, by the subsequent portion—"But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?"—it is precisely non-duality (*advaita*) that is intended.
It is stated without any deception; therefore, non-duality (advaita) has been firmly established. Furthermore, the unreality of duality can also be easily demonstrated through inference.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the unreality of duality must be established by accepting the analogy of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—arguing that, according to the logic of the "substitute-basket," silver truly exists within the shell—that is extremely weak. For instance, in the case of a substitute such as wild rice (*nīvāra*), only a few particles of grain (*vrīhi*) are present; therefore, [the argument fails].

Just as the production of a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is accomplished [by means of other materials], so too here, if there were actual parts of silver, one could likewise produce a bracelet, a crown, or the like from them. Therefore, the assertion that silver is real has become an unreal statement. Furthermore, for ordinary people, the silver in mother-of-pearl is merely phenomenal (prātītika), as evidenced by their experience; thus, the silver in mother-of-pearl is not real.

As for what was said regarding the reality of dream-objects— that is, just as the emission of the final vital element (*caramadhātu*) and so forth, being real effects, must necessarily be produced by real causes, so too is the sexual union with a dream-maiden and the like real.

The claim that "it is like that" is incorrect; for since we observe the arising of curiosity toward a real person from the sight of unreal silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, such a rule lacks probative force.
Nor should it be argued that even in that case there is no violation of the rule because the cognition whose object is the silver in the shell is itself real.
Since it is impossible to assert the intrinsic reality of cognitions without their being colored by objects,

and since it is more appropriate to assert their unreality due to their not grasping an object, the rule that "a real effect must be produced from a real cause" is indeed violated. Furthermore, when [one perceives] a man with black teeth...

By the statement, "He sees him, and then he slays him," a real death occurs through the vision of a man with black teeth who is actually unreal. In that case, there is indeed a violation of your own rule, because the man is unreal.
As for what was said regarding the creation in the intermediate state—"For it says [the scripture] creates chariots, yoked horses, and paths"—it refers to this.

To claim that the statement "it creates" expresses the reality of the creation in dreams is inconsistent, because the subsequent sūtra— "But it is mere illusion (māyāmātra), because its nature is not fully manifested"— establishes its unreality. Furthermore, the sūtra "mere illusion" [is not intended to mean...].

Indeed, it is the rule that the statement of the *siddhānta-sūtra* follows immediately after the *pūrvapakṣa-sūtra*. How could there be such a transposition here? Nor is this an opening with the *siddhānta*—as in the case of [the sūtra] "Vaiśvānara [is Brahman], because of the distinction of the common term" (*vaiśvānaraḥ sādhāraṇaśabdaviśeṣāt*)—following the statement "In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says" (*sandhye sṛṣṭirāha hi*).

It should be stated that, just as in the case of the sūtras beginning with "Because of sound and so forth, and because of being established within," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented by the sūtra "It is mere illusion" (*māyāmātram*); [the opponent might argue] that here too it is not so,
but this is not correct, because there is instruction regarding such a vision, because of impossibility [otherwise], and because they also record him as a person (*puruṣa*).
This is clear because there is no sūtra providing an answer to this objection; however, since only the sūtra "But it is mere illusion,

because its nature is entirely unmanifest" exists, the sūtra "For [the scripture] declares creation" (*sṛṣṭir āha hi*) is therefore a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa-sūtra*) establishing the reality of dreams.
"It is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*) because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety"— this will be explained later.

For those whose intellects are endowed with straightforwardness, the portion "because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety" constitutes the *siddhāntasūtra* (concluding aphorism) that declares the unreality of dreams.

It shines forth. However, just as you, with your crooked intellect, have thrown such statements as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) into confusion, so too do you throw even the Sūtras themselves into confusion by treating a Pūrvapakṣa-sūtra as a Siddhānta-sūtra.
Since this depends upon a perversion of wisdom, the wise should remain indifferent to it. Therefore—

The formal inference— "Duality is not ultimately real because it is an object of perception, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell"— is indeed possible. As for the claim that perceptuality is impossible in the case of illusory silver due to the absence of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*),
that is trivial, for in the case of the phenomenal appearance (*prātibhāsika*), [the conditions are met].

Even in the absence of the emergence of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), it is accepted that [the object] is either the object of an ignorant modification (*avidyāvṛtti*) or is manifest to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsya*). Furthermore, even though the sky is not perceptible, its impurity is known in common experience.
In that case, how can there be a resolution for you venerable proponents of *satkhyāti*, given that the sky does not exist as something present before one?
Because it is impossible to apprehend [them]. Just as there are no parts of silver in mother-of-pearl, what parts could exist in space?

In this matter, silence on your part alone is appropriate. Therefore, because error is of various kinds, it is impossible even to state a single form [for it]. Nor can it be argued that although it is perceptible, it lacks ultimate reality (*apāramārthikatva*).

It should not be said that the doubt regarding the lack of a probative force (*aprayojakatva*) is being raised; for there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*) against the contrary position: if duality were unreal, then it would not possess the quality of being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), just as consciousness (*caitanya*) does not. Furthermore, if difference...

How can there be a cognition of the ultimate pillar and jar? For the purpose of cognizing the difference between the pillar and the jar, the cognition of the jar is necessary, because the cognition of an absence depends upon the cognition of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
Furthermore, the cognition of the jar that generates the cognition of its absence is not non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), but rather conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

It must be stated that [the cognition] has as its qualifier the state of being a pot characterized by the exclusion of other things and possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth; for the sake of knowing that property as the differentiator of the pot from non-pots, the difference of the pillar from the pot must be apprehended in the pot;
and for the sake of knowing the difference of the pillar from the pot, the knowledge of the counter-correlate—the pillar—is necessarily required.
And likewise, for the sake of knowing the difference of the jar from the pillar, the knowledge of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), the pillar, must necessarily be asserted;

and for the sake of knowing the difference of the jar, the knowledge of the jar in the pillar is necessary—thus there is a mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya). Furthermore, if difference were not the very nature (svarūpa) [of the things themselves], [it would be untenable].

If it is said that "difference" is a distinct entity from the pot, then a difference must be asserted for the pot as well, and for that [difference] as well, and for the difference of that [second difference] as well; thus there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, there is no logical justification for duality (*dvaita*); those who hold to duality are seers of what is unreal.

This concludes a brief exposition on the refutation of distinctions such as "that which is sublated by valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇaniṣiddha*) and so forth. Therefore, it is fully established that non-duality (*advaita*) alone is the ultimate reality.

As for the claim that actions are a means to liberation, that too is extremely weak; for among the internal means such as *yama*, *niyama*, and *prāṇāyāma*, which are themselves internal means for *nididhyāsana*— the direct realization that is the proximate cause of liberation— [actions do not hold such a status].

At the time of practicing *prāṇāyāma*, the performance of ritual action (*karman*) is irrelevant; for ritual action is not a visible means (*dṛṣṭa-sādhana*) like *prāṇāyāma*, but rather an invisible one (*adṛṣṭa*). Since the purpose can be accomplished through visible means such as *prāṇāyāma* and the like, what is the use of rituals that serve only invisible ends? Furthermore, [regarding] *yama*:
"Name" refers to the Vedic rites, both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*); "restraint" (*niyama*) refers to virtues such as compassion and the like.
Having indeed renounced all such ritual actions, one must engage in the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*).
Otherwise, in the absence of any activity other than that which has Brahman as its object, how could the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) come to be?

Now, it may be argued that there is no relevance whatsoever for ritual actions (*karma*) in the inquiry into Brahman; on the contrary, the performance of rituals is actually an obstacle, because the practice of rituals destroys the single-minded application to the activities of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, which are the means for attaining direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). Therefore:
Prior to the desire to hear [the scriptures], the utility of ritual actions lies in the accomplishment of mental purity (*citta-śuddhi*).

Those qualities designated as "restraints" (*niyama*), such as compassion and the like, are included within the qualifications of the seeker (*adhikāri-viśeṣaṇa*) such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*). And this is appropriate; for by means of this [purity], there is an absence of obstacles to hearing [the teachings].

Mental reflection (*manana*) occurs; thereafter, when meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*) is to be produced through mental reflection, the postures (*āsana*) and other practices prescribed in the Yoga Śāstra must be performed, each preceding one serving as a visible cause for the succeeding one. For instance, posture (*āsana*) is a limb of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Through *prāṇāyāma*, practiced according to the authoritative teachings of the Yogaśāstra, there occurs the cessation of hunger, thirst, sleep, lethargy, and other obstacles that hinder the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the Brahman which is to be meditated upon.

Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) consists in bringing the ten faculties, including the five vital breaths, under one's own control; from withdrawal, concentration (dhāraṇā) directed toward an object with qualities becomes uninterrupted;
then, by setting aside heterogeneous mental impressions, [dhyāna arises].

There occurs *nididhyāsana*, which consists in the continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions (*sajātīyapratyayapravāha*). Then, just as one who is separated [from an object] may have a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of a beloved woman through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of her image, so too does the direct perception of the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahma*) arise.
Immediately thereafter follows the direct perception consisting in the realization of the Brahman without attributes (*nirguṇa*).
Furthermore, a mental modification (*vṛtti*) of undivided form becomes the remover of ignorance.

Thus, for one who possesses the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), has renounced all obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*), and is engaged in hearing, reflecting, and so forth upon the subject of Brahman— where could there be any attachment to the performance of ritual action?
Therefore, the statement that "action is the means to liberation" is merely a delusion of ordinary people who are ignorant of such spiritual treatises on yoga.
As for the scriptural passage beginning with, "Performing actions here, one should desire to live a hundred years," and so forth—
This concerns exclusively the householder who is not attached to the inquiry into Brahman.

As for the claim made by the Udak-kūla Rāmānujas— that purification of the mind must be accomplished through daily and occasional rites accompanied by the five purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāras*)— that is extremely weak;
for [the duties of] both Vedic and Tantric traditions coexist in one place, just like the duties of the various stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*).

Because it is impossible for [all] to remain [in the Vedic path], they postulate various ritual acts based on the capacity of the qualified person to perform them in their entirety. Likewise, there are scriptural statements such as:
"For men who have utterly strayed from the Vedic path, the Pāñcarātra and other paths are indeed beneficial in the course of time. And so forth.

They say that those who are unworthy of the Vedic path enter the way of Tantra. For this very reason, the Rāmānujas of the Southern Bank (Dakṣiṇakūla), having abandoned the path of the Śruti, exist in a state of mixture with the five sacraments (pañcasaṃskāra) and the Dravidian compositions (Draviḍaprabandha). By this, there arises knowledge of the meaning of both the Dravidian Vedas and the Kevala Vedas.

The claim that [the Vedas] are the means for liberation is refuted; for if liberation can be achieved by one means, another means would be redundant. Furthermore, it is possible to accept both Vedas according to the difference in the qualifications of the aspirants. For this very reason, the traditional saying that Nammāḷvār and others, who were expounders of the Dravidian Veda, were Śūdras, is also justified.

As for the claim that liberation is merely *sārūpya* (attainment of similarity) and not *sāyujya* (union), based on the scriptural statement, "The stainless one attains supreme equality," because it is impossible for the individual self— who is an eternal servant and an eternal subordinate— to be in union with the Lord, who is the sovereign master, independent of all, and the Lord of Lakṣmī; that argument is extremely weak, for in that [state] where...

"Multiplicity, as it were, comes into being. By such scriptural passages as "That thou art" and "I am Brahman," and by such traditional texts as "Know me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata" and "Those who perceive duality see what is unreal," [the non-duality of the Self is established].
And by the sūtra, "The non-difference from That [is established] on account of words such as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa)," once the non-duality of Brahman is established—

wherein pure consciousness alone is real and modifications are unreal like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell— it follows that the limited knowledge existing in the individual soul (jīva) [does not belong] to Vāsudeva.

Since the possession of omniscience and the status of Lord of Fortune (*lakṣmīpati*) are merely conventional and inappropriate to speak of in the state of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), union (*sāyujya*) is possible. For this very reason, the Śruti states:
"The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself; being Brahman, he merges into Brahman. Now, [one might object]: by Brahman...

If the soul's attainment of *sāyujya* (union) is accepted, how can the enjoyment described in such scriptural passages as "eating, playing, and rejoicing with women, or with chariots, or with kinsmen, or with friends" be possible?
Therefore, let liberation be accepted as *sārūpya* (attainment of similarity in form) alone; for in that case, these scriptural texts regarding enjoyment are logically consistent.

If this is argued, we say no; for according to the principle of the Sūtra, "The worshipper [is independent] like Vāsudeva, except for the activity of the world, on account of the context," one who possesses the capacity for all actions other than the activity of the world— being entirely independent like Vāsudeva—
attains the fruit of the *ahaṅgraha* meditation upon death at Prayāga, just as one attains universal sovereignty.

Because liberation does not consist in the arising of all enjoyments, for according to such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma*) and "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma*),

liberation is precisely the state of abiding in the immutable consciousness that is the pinnacle of being, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). For this very reason, [it is] together with Brahman...

The assertion that for those who meditate on Brahman with attributes (saguṇopāsakas), there is liberation together with Brahman after remaining until the end of the Brahmā-kalpa— based on the Smṛti stating "When the time of reabsorption arrives, they all go to the end of the Supreme" and the Śruti stating "they are all liberated from the highest immortality"— is indeed inconsistent.

If liberation is thus defined as similarity [to the Lord], and that consists in attaining all non-material enjoyments fashioned by the Blessed One in the extraordinary Vaikuṇṭha above the mundane eggshell, then—
by once again attaining saṃsāra, which is denoted by the very term "non-material"— it is a case of "dawn at the mill."
By logic, it is clear that liberation in that state is impossible; on the contrary, there would only be bondage.

For instance, how could the attainment of all enjoyments be possible for Vaiṣṇavas who are non-material beings in the non-material Vaikuṇṭha, given the absence of the means for enjoyment? [The answer is: there are non-material young women, and with them—
There would also be non-ordinary enjoyment (*aprākṛta-sambhoga*), and through the birth of a non-ordinary embryo, the birth of a non-ordinary son, and so forth—all such things would occur.
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault? [the answer is: because even mere pleasure is invariably accompanied by suffering.
Since the pervasion is established, if one accepts the enjoyment of non-material young women, there would also necessarily be the suffering born from separation from a non-material wife; alas, alas!
Thus, like the description of the meaning of such statements as "That Thou Art," even the description of liberation has been rendered utterly confused.

Now, one might object: "In that case, how is it said that you attain enjoyment through such passages as 'he becomes desirous of the world of women' and so forth? For even there, these same defects are equally present. We reply: No, because meditations on the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman have as their ultimate purpose the realization of the unqualified (nirguṇa) Brahman.

Even though obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites performed without desire (*niṣkāma*) for the sake of purifying the mind produce various results— such as the nourishment of the body and the removal of diseases— even if they generate such fruits,
those fruits are merely intermediate; therefore, they do not constitute liberation (*mokṣa*).

For the Advaitins, the establishment of liberation is possible because liberation consists in the nature of undivided existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*); because even for them, those means of enjoyment are not required within the bliss of one's own nature; because there is no possibility of obtaining objects again [once they have been abandoned]; and because liberation is distinct from the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

Because the fruits of meditative worship (*upāsanā*) are described as being distinct [from liberation], and because the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*) is described as being distinct from worship, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in our view; indeed, all such inconsistencies belong solely to Rāmānuja. This is the whole point.
Delightful.

[Thus, from the venerable Tōṇṭada Siddheśvara— the incarnation of the mobile form of the beginningless and stainless Aparā, and who obtained the grace of the Śāmbhava Āgama ocean churned by him— arose this work divided into the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*), which are distinguished by one hundred and one unsurpassed sections.]
In [this work] composed by the eminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows a mass of bliss from tasting the nectar of the *latattva*,

[it concerns] the preceptor who established the pure Vedic Advaita doctrine, the sovereign of the western ocean, the remover of the seven constituents of the enemy of the solitary hero who caused a tumult among ten million Yādava Murāris.

In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, within the section on debate (*vādakāṇḍa*), under the instruction of Basava— the joy of the heart of Mallāmbā, the lawful consort of Vīrabhadra Dharaṇīndra, who was like a full moon in the milky ocean of the lineage of Keladi Sadāśivarāya Nāyaka, and who was a thunderbolt to the earth— [ends here].
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Rāmānuja’s Doctrine and the Method of Its Refutation."
[The nineteenth chapter in the section on debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā] ||
The doctrine of Rāmānuja was presented by the Guru, and therein a refutation was made,
consisting of statements and counter-statements spoken by Bhṛṅgin and Śilī.
Having heard what was translated by you, my heart became filled with joy;
for various doctrines proceed through diverse methods of exposition.
Tell me, Bhṛṅgin, what happened immediately after that, or what did Śīlin do? My mind desires to know both of these things.
Listen, O King, I shall relate the unfolding of their dialogue,
which proceeded in the assembly in the form of objections and replies.
Having placed Śiva and Viṣṇu upon the scale, one who is virtuous has weighed them; now,
in order to know [the result] of these two—
And [the practice of] elevating and disparaging.
If you have here, at every step, refuted the nature of the Supreme Brahman by adopting the very methodology belonging to that [dualistic] school,
this will not suffice to inspire full confidence in my heart.
May you exert yourself separately to suppress his prosperity.
O Bhṛṅgin, listen specifically to this as I endeavor to clarify Śiva’s status as the supreme reality and to refute the exaltation of Hari,
through the weaving together of the words of numerous Vedas, Āgamas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas.
Apply your mind with focused attention to these arguments that blossom forth from hundreds of sound reasonings.

The manner of investigating the supreme mystery— that the Supreme Brahman is indeed Śiva, who is to be worshipped through a special devotion awakened by the investigation of the secrets of all the Vedas and Āgamas, and who is the essential heart known by those proficient in the Vīraśaiva doctrine— is as follows.

That which is well-known from the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas is now set forth, preceded by the refutation of the objections conceived by opponents: "From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; into which they enter when they depart."

"In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, the object to be inquired into is designated by the word *brahman*: 'Seek to know That; That is Brahman. When the question arises as to what its nature is, it is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: 'What is the cause? What is Brahman? From whence were we born? By what do we live? Wherein do we abide?'"
"And established in what do we abide amidst pleasure and its opposite?
Beginning with such questions, [the text addresses] certain sages who discourse on Brahman and understand that Brahman alone is the cause of the world, yet do not know it specifically.

When the inquiry for the purpose of determining that [Brahman] has commenced, a doubt regarding Brahman as the general cause is stated in the form: "What is the cause there? That very same doubt concerning the cause is expressed by the five statements beginning with, "From where have we been born? and so forth.

It has been elaborated in five ways according to the distinctions of its effects, its production, its maintenance, and so forth. In that regard, in the fifth statement, "the established rule for those who know Brahman," the word "by whom" (*kena*) is to be supplied;
there is mutual communication among those very ones who reflect, "This is Brahman. Alternatively, "brahmavidām" is in the genitive case. But if this is so—
The investigation of specific particulars is without support, because the very premise that "Brahman is the cause" remains unestablished;

for it is possible that effects have either other causes or no cause at all. To dispel this doubt and to demonstrate the establishment of the subject (*dharmin*) of one's own inquiry, the following [scriptural passage] is immediately recited.
"Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the womb, and the person—these are to be considered.
It is the conjunction of these [that produces results], and not from the self's own power; for the self is also not the master over the causes of pleasure and pain.
By "chance," the position that there is no cause is meant. Thus, [the various views] are [presented] by way of their meanings.

For those who were unable to reach a definitive conclusion, yet desired such a conclusion through the grace of Gaurī, the presiding deity of the knowledge of Brahman, and who sought her grace by meditating upon her, there arose the definitive realization that, by her grace, the cause of all— that Brahman— is indeed Śiva; this is the meaning intended to be demonstrated by them.
"Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities;
[they saw] Him who alone presides over all those causes, which are joined with Time and the Self.
Such is the subsequent context. For in the following mantras therein, the *kṣara*...
The Pradhāna is the immortal and imperishable Hara; therefore Śiva is omnipresent. Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe.
[We know] Maheśvara, the wielder of Māyā; him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the supreme deity among deities, the Lord beyond all lords—him we know.
The God, the Lord of the World, who is worthy of praise.

Furthermore, there are statements from the *Atharvaśikhā* and other texts that serve as witnesses for the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, which—by means of names such as Hara, Śiva, Rudra, and Maheśvara mentioned in passages like those cited above—establishes that the statements regarding the cause of the universe have Śiva as their ultimate referent. [The *Atharvaśikhā* states: "All this is Śarva-Brahman..."
Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the sense organs are produced from Him, along with the primary elements;
He is not the cause of causes, but is the meditator upon the Cause. Endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of All, Śambhu dwells in the midst of space as the object of meditation.

Impelled by the mantras of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, which are supported by such statements from the Atharvaśikhā as these, all causal passages— employing general terms such as "Being" (sat), "Self" (ātman), and so forth— establish that Śiva alone is the cause of the world, the Supreme Brahman.

In order to dispel the suspicion that the cited scriptural passages have other intended meanings, many corroborative statements in the form of Purāṇic declarations are also presented. For instance, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, there are such corroborations beginning with "What is the cause, O Brahman? and so forth.
Having assembled, those high-souled sages, expounders of Brahman,
engaged in many discussions based upon the knowledge of the Self.
What is the root of this world? Is it indeed our very self, or could it be the Lord (Īśvara) who is the cause of all existents?
While they were thinking thus, relying upon the practice of meditation,
the Great Goddess Gaurī, daughter of the Mountain King, appeared before them.
Having begun thus, they were gazed upon by the consort of the Supreme Lord;
within that [vision], they beheld the God who is the cause of all.
"They behold Śambhu, the Seer, the Ruler, Rudra, the Great, the Ancient Puruṣa. Thus [it is said].
In the Śiva Purāṇa as well: "In ancient times, certain sages who were seekers of liberation and exponents of Brahman, their minds filled with doubt, reflected thus: 'How [is this]? "
What is the cause, from where were we born, and by what do we live?
Where is our firm foundation, and by whom have we been brought to growth?
By whom do we perpetually abide in pleasures, whether our own or those of others?
And by whom was this inviolable order of the universe established?
Does time, inherent nature, necessity, or chance prevail?
Are the primary elements, the womb, the person, or perhaps their union the supreme cause?
Because time and the like are insentient, and even though the self is sentient,
it is investigated [as to its nature] because it is overwhelmed by pleasure and pain and lacks mastery over itself.
Absorbed in the yoga of meditation, they beheld the sovereign power of the Lord,
which directly severs the bonds, though it remains deeply concealed by its own attributes.
With their bonds severed by her, they beheld Mahādeva, the possessor of power and the cause of all causes, with divine vision.
"He alone presides over all causes without exception, including Time and the Self, together with my own immeasurable power," and so forth.
The *Atharvaśikhā-upabṛṃhaṇa* in the *Śiva Purāṇa* also states: "Since all this— beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—
is first brought forth together with all the elements and the sense organs."
And he who is the meditator upon causes is the meditator upon the supreme cause;
he is never produced from anything else at any time.
"Endowed with all sovereign powers, he himself is Sarveśvara by name;
Śambhu, dwelling in the midst of space, is to be meditated upon by all who seek liberation. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, corroborative texts from the Śiva Purāṇas and other sources should be seen which establish that even the Atharvaśiras, Kaivalya, and other Upaniṣads provide the defining characteristics (liṅgas) of Brahman, such as Śiva being the sole and absolute cause; such statements exist both in terms of their literal wording and their underlying meaning.

By being in syntactic unity with the root scriptures (*mūla-śruti*), they establish the unwavering supremacy of Śiva even for those root scriptures; being themselves powerful according to the "lion-in-the-forest" maxim (*vanasiṃha-nyāya*), they determine that the state of the Supreme Brahman, the cause of the universe, belongs exclusively to Śiva alone, as opposed to the Purāṇas of other deities.
The greater number of *Śiva-purāṇas* is also a reason for their preeminence;
as it has been said:
"In the eighteen Purāṇas, Śiva is described by ten."
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is proclaimed to have four [arms], and Brahmā two.

Thus, by means of the aforementioned number of Purāṇas and by the number of texts such as "the Śaiva [Purāṇa] has one hundred thousand verses" and "the Skānda [Purāṇa] has one hundred thousand verses," the Vedas and their supplements (Upabṛṃhaṇas), having entered into a relationship of mutual benefactor and beneficiary, [establish] that of Śiva...

The state of being the Supreme Brahman is established; or rather, because the words *brahman*, *ātman*, *sat*, *akṣara*, and so forth— which are heard in the causal passages of the world found in the *Muṇḍaka*, *Aitareya*, *Chāndogya*, and other Upaniṣads— are used in grammatical apposition with words such as *Śiva*, which are well-known in the *Nighaṇṭu*.

Similarly, in the *Pūrvatantre*, within the section on names (*nāmadheya-paṭalikā*), in passages such as "they praise with the *ājya*s," "they praise with the *pṛṣṭha*s," "they praise with the *bahiṣpavamāna*s," and "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrā*," the words *ājya*, *pṛṣṭha*, *bahiṣpavamāna*, *citra*, and so forth [denote] the acts of praising (*stuvate*) and sacrificing (*yajate*).

Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting hymns (*stotra*), sacrifices (*yāga*), and so forth, it is accepted that [the term *yajñāyajñīya*] denotes a hymn and a sacrifice. On this point, Pārthasārathi Miśra states:
"Because of the avoidance of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) which possesses coreferentiality."

The designation as a name alone is thus justified. For this very reason, it was established in the second chapter, in the *Aghora-agnihotra* section, that in cases such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), there is no denotation of the oblation (*homa*) and so forth because of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, among those factors that result in something being a name...

Even when etymological derivation (*yaugika*), syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), being named after that (*tat-prakhya*), and designation by that (*tad-vyapadeśa*) are distinct [grounds for determining a name], it is established that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) alone,
as the pervasive factor in all cases, is what brings about the status of being a name. Therefore, in the present case as well, since words such as "Brahman" denote Śiva—
It is indeed logical that [the word] denotes Śiva by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with well-known words such as "Śiva" and so forth.

Now, one might object: "How can words such as *sat*, *ātman*, and *akṣara*, which are heard in a general sense, stand in grammatical apposition with words such as *Śiva*, whereby they could be considered names here according to the logic of the previous Tantra?
This is not so; for [it says]: "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Person, dark and tawny..."
"Salutation indeed to the one with upward-flowing vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), the three-eyed one (virūpākṣa), who possesses universal form (viśvarūpa).

In this mantra, because words such as "Truth" (ṛta) and others stand in grammatical apposition with the word "Virūpākṣa," the word "Brahman" refers to Śiva. In exactly the same way, [it is said]: "Beyond that is the Supreme Brahman, the Great One."

Just as [the Upanishads state]: "Knowing Him—the Lord who is hidden in all beings, the one who envelops the universe—they become immortal"; for here, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *īśa* (Lord), which is established by well-known lexicons (*nighaṇṭu*). It is exactly thus.
"Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being;
free from sorrow, one beholds Him, the desireless, the majesty of the Creator, through the grace of the Ordainer.
Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Lord" (*īśa*), the word "Self" (*ātman*) refers to Śiva. It is exactly so.

In the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, they consider non-dual Śiva (śivādvaita) to be the fourth state, according to the passage: "That is the Self; that is to be known. Likewise, in another place it says: "The fourth is without measure, beyond empirical usage, the cessation of phenomenal expansion, auspicious, non-dual—the syllable Om itself is the Self."

Furthermore, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Śiva," the word "Self" (*ātman*) has Śiva as its referent. As it is said: "When there was darkness, there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone existed. That is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent [splendor] of Savitṛ, and that is wisdom."

Therefore, in the passage "from which the ancient [path] has issued forth," the word *akṣara* refers to Śiva because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *Śiva*. And thus,
all general terms that establish the world as the cause [of creation] refer specifically [to Him].

The conclusion rests upon Śiva. Regarding the final section of the sixth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], which states, "Or rather, it is the goat, because of the wording of the mantra," it is revealed in scripture:

"One should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In this regard, there arises a doubt: does the word "animal" (*paśu*) refer to all [animals] such as cows and so forth, or only to the goat? As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), in the injunctive sentence—

Since it is impossible to restrict the word *paśu*— which, based on Vedic revelation (*śruti*), is common to cattle, horses, and other animals— the conclusion is that it denotes all [animals]. However, the established position (*siddhānta*) is that because the word *chāga* (goat) occurs in the wording of the mantra, "Of the goat's omentum and fat," the word *paśu* must, by virtue of that, be restricted to the specific [goat].
This is the conclusion. Likewise, in passages such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), the reference is to Śiva.
This is in accordance with the statement, "Brahman alone is the eldest of beings; who then could rival him?
(Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1), which implies that there is no one equal to Śiva, as expressed in the mantra: "O Rudra, there is indeed none other than you" (Atharvaveda Saṃhitā 11.2.1).

It is established that [the world] does not exist [independently]. For it is heard in scripture: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: 'Shall I now create the worlds? He created these worlds:
water, light-rays, death, and the waters. And: "Under the governance of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī..."

"The sun and the moon remain held apart"—this refers to his status as the sovereign ruler of all. Likewise, in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web], and as herbs arise upon the earth," and so forth; thus, all such scriptural passages concerning the cause of all things refer to Śiva.
The conclusion.

Is it not stated in the Mahābhārata that Yudhiṣṭhira is a great tree consisting of Dharma— Arjuna its trunk, Bhīmasena its branches, the two sons of Mādrī its abundant flowers and fruit, and Kṛṣṇa, Brahman,
and the Brāhmaṇas its root? Thus, Yudhiṣṭhira is described as having Brahman as his root by way of being a tree.

By designating Śrī Kṛṣṇa as "Brahman," the Blessed Vyāsa has clearly stated Kṛṣṇa’s nature as Brahman through the force of this epithet; for, by mentioning Kṛṣṇa and the Brāhmaṇas separately, he accepts that the Veda and austerity— which are insentient— are included among sentient beings.

Because it would contradict the context, although the word "brahman" may refer to the Veda or austerity, it is not appropriate to understand those two here; rather, it must refer to something else entirely,
like the root situated at the base of a tree.
In the presence of Yudhiṣṭhira, who was concealed by the state of being a king, it is proper to accept only that which is the actual cause;
and since Viṣṇu alone is such [the cause], this is the heart-intent of Vyāsa. Therefore, Nārāyaṇa alone is the referent of the word "Brahman.
Nor is there any contradiction with the hymn to Śiva composed by Nārāyaṇa in the Droṇaparvan, which speaks of "form" (rūpa) and "light" (jyotis).

"Sound, ether, wind, touch, taste, water, smell, earth, desire, dharma, and Brahman—the Brāhmaṇas and all this, both the stationary and the moving, have originated from you. Even when the word *brahma* is used in conjunction with the word *brāhmaṇa*, it is observed that it refers to the Veda; why should it not be so here as well?

It might be argued that [the word "syāt" should be supplied]; however, in that case, because of the association with non-sentient entities such as "form" (rūpa) and "light" (jyotis), and because there is no context of predominantly sentient beings, it is appropriate that the reference there is to the Vedas by virtue of contextual fitness. But here, since the list of sentient beings—namely Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, and the Brāhmaṇas—is read as the actual meaning, Kṛṣṇa alone is the source.

If it is argued that [the term] is denotable by the word "Brahman," it is not so; for in the passage "Kṛṣṇa, Brahman, and the Brāhmaṇas," since the word "ca" (and) seen subsequently in the sense of conjunction is capable of being determined in that very way, if it were intended to refer to Kṛṣṇa, the conjunction would not be obtained, and thus it must refer to Śiva.

The first stage of the proponent’s argument is that, because the previously mentioned accumulation of qualities pertaining to Kṛṣṇa is obtained here, it is indeed appropriate to determine that the word "Brahman" used in this context refers to Śiva.
Now, the first stage of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Is it not the case that in such scriptural passages as 'Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman,
Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate reality, Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, the Self (*ātman*),
Nārāyaṇa is the highest,' Nārāyaṇa is designated by the word 'Self' (*ātman*) as being the supreme Brahman?"

Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is also present; because other terms such as "Being" (*sat*) and "Syllable" (*akṣara*) are also largely established [as referring to him] in the *Subāla* and other Upaniṣads;
and because the statements heard in general that establish the causality of the universe [point to] Nārāyaṇa.

This is the conclusion. Furthermore, by reflecting upon the scripture which states, "Whatever exists in this entire world, whether it is seen or even heard, Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that, both within and without," it is heard that Nārāyaṇa is all-pervasive. Thus, [it is established] in the Aitareya Upaniṣad.

By the designation of the word "ātman," and by the designation of the word "brahman" in the *Brahmasūkta*— such as in the passage "Brahman gave birth to the gods"— there are heard the supreme divine attributes of being the cause of the universe, being all-pervasive, being the Lord of all, and so forth.

Since it is possible for [the lineage] to culminate in Nārāyaṇa, how can it culminate in Śiva? Nor [does the text say] that he first brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha; rather, "Soma flows, the progenitor of thoughts, the progenitor of heaven... [and so on].

It should not be argued that his status as the progenitor of the entire universe is established by the statement in the *Brahma-nārāyaṇa* [section], "The progenitor of the earth, the progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu," because this merely establishes that Śiva is the creator of Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa; for in the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*, it is said: "He who [is the source] of the gods... [and so forth].

"In the beginning, before [all else], Rudra, the great seer, superior to all, beheld Hiraṇyagarbha being born; may that god unite us with auspicious mindfulness"—thus [it is said] in the mantra of that very third chapter of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "He who is the first of the gods..."

"In the mantra: 'In the beginning, Rudra, the great seer, superior to all, beheld Hiraṇyagarbha being born; may that God unite us with auspicious mindfulness,'" [it is stated] in that very third chapter of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "He who was the first of the gods..."
Because in the mantra, "Rudra, the great seer, who is superior to all, beheld Hiraṇyagarbha as he was being born;
may he endow us with auspicious understanding," there is heard only the act of beholding by Śiva— who is himself born— as directed toward Hiraṇyagarbha as his object.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for Hiraṇyagarbha to be born— given that he is established by the lexicon as having the name "Self-Existent" (Svayambhū) and "Four-Faced" (Caturānana)— the author provides an etymological derivation of the term *janayāmāsa* by treating it as containing the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in its own sense;
thus, by changing the case ending, he accepts Hiraṇyagarbha as the agent [of the action].
Through a thorough examination of other scriptural passages (*śruti*), it is established that Hiraṇyagarbha is indeed self-born.

For this very reason, Manu has demonstrated his non-origination from another by stating, "In him, Brahmā himself, the Grandfather, appeared," and so forth. Therefore, Hiraṇyagarbha is not born from Śiva.

It is indeed possible. In the same way, it is not possible for Viṣṇu to be born from Śiva. Furthermore, the mantra "Somaḥ pavate" (Soma flows) reveals the Soma plant and is not intended for Śiva. Moreover, because the *pāvamānī* verse recited in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* lacks an application in the ritual rules (*sāmavidhi*) as a hymn to Rudra—unlike those found in the *Rudrasaṃhitā* and other such texts—[it does not establish his identity].

Because it is impossible to assert that Śiva is the Supreme (paratva), and because it is therefore impossible to establish Śiva as the cause of the universe by way of being the progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha and Viṣṇu, the first position of the opponents is that all scriptural passages concerning the cause of all things culminate in Nārāyaṇa.

As for the proponents of the Siddhānta: in the statement of the *Atharvaśikhā*, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are produced," the fact that the gods beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu are created is clearly heard. As for the cause:
"Śambhu, the Lord of All, endowed with all sovereignty, is to be meditated upon in the midst of space"—
since this establishes that Śiva alone is the cause of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the rest, as seen in such passages as: "Soma flows,
the progenitor of thoughts," and "He brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning."

Since that very same meaning is being recognized [in other texts], how can one assert that in the Taittirīya mantra "yo devānām" and the Śvetāśvatara mantra, there is only the self-origination of Hiraṇyagarbha and not his being created by Śiva,
and that the mantra "somaḥ pavate" refers merely to the plant?

It is possible [to argue this]. Furthermore, upon examining the mantras of the *Taittirīya* and *Śvetāśvatara*, in the passage stating that "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra are produced from Him," one must necessarily admit the self-origination of Brahmā; therefore, he cannot be [said to be] created by Śiva.
It must be stated that it is accepted that even Viṣṇu, who is mentioned alongside him [Brahmā], is not created by Śiva;

if that were so, then Rudra, Indra, and the others would likewise not be created, because they too are mentioned alongside Brahmā just as Viṣṇu is. Nor can this be an unintended consequence (iṣṭāpatti).
It is like falling into the mouth of a venomous serpent while fleeing from the fear of a scorpion;
for [He] has been established as the cause of all in the Subāla, Mahā, Nārāyaṇa, and other Upaniṣads, as well as in the Viṣṇupurāṇa and other texts.

Since equating Viṣṇu with Indra on the basis of a reading identical to that of Hiraṇyagarbha would be an object of extreme ridicule, therefore— even against one’s will— a clear-minded and supreme Vaiṣṇava, purified by the five sacraments (*pañcasaṃskāra*), must necessarily accept that Rudra and Indra were created [by him] in this passage. If so, then...

Let it be admitted that even Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa are created beings. Nor should it be argued that because Indra’s inclusion among the class of individual souls (jīva) is extremely clear in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, Śiva’s status as his creator is what is accepted in this passage, and not that of Viṣṇu and Brahmā.

Why is this "half-old-woman" approach (*ardhajaratīya*) being accepted? Therefore, according to the maxim that "a word uttered once conveys its meaning only once," if a sentence is intended to convey the state of being created in Śiva, let it be accepted as such in all instances;
otherwise, let it be abandoned. Or rather, within a single sentence, for one [meaning]...
The claim that there is a state of being created in one part and a state of not being created in another is merely the prattle of a deluded person; therefore,

having accepted the state of being created for all [entities] here, for the sake of this very point, one must accept the state of being created in such passages as "He first generated Hiraṇyagarbha" and "Soma flows," and not otherwise.

By reflecting upon the two mantras, one must accept that Brahmā and Viṣṇu are created, and that these two mantras alone have this as their meaning; otherwise, the previously mentioned defect would remain as it was. Furthermore, regarding the mantra "Soma pavate":

If one were to accept that the word *latā* is subordinate (*paratva*), then there would be an acceptance of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for many words denoting "produced" (*janita*)— as stated repeatedly in the passage beginning with "of cognitions produced" (*matīnāṃ janitā*)— without any underlying cause. Therefore...

Since the primary meaning must necessarily be accepted, it should be admitted that the word *soma* in this mantra refers to Śiva; for such is seen in another mantra as well, in the statement "Obeisance to Soma" (*namaḥ somāya ca*). [As stated] in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*:
Soma is the progenitor and lord even of the intellects, of heaven, of earth, of Agni, of Sūrya, of the wielder of the thunderbolt,
and indeed of Viṣṇu himself.
In the Kālikākhaṇḍa, it is said:
"Soma is the Lord who engenders Heaven and Earth, Indra and Agni, the Sky, Yama, Varuṇa, and the Moon."
Thus, by means of corroboration from the Purāṇas and other sources, the second stage [of the argument] establishes that the Supreme Lord must indeed be accepted as the progenitor of Viṣṇu.
Now, according to the opponent’s summary of the purport of the four Vedas,
[the word "soma"] refers to the plant-essence by way of a secondary application (*gauṇavṛtti*) to Maheśvara.
By a certain Ṛgvedic verse, the status of being the progenitor was attributed to Viṣṇu;
yet that [status] ought to belong to you alone in its primary sense,
and not to Indra, nor to the lotus-born Brahmā, and certainly not to Murāri (Viṣṇu).
But surely, according to the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad, which states: "Puruṣa, indeed, was Nārāyaṇa; he desired, 'May I create offspring.
From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā is born; from Nārāyaṇa, Rudra is born," and so forth, [it says]: "In the beginning, there was indeed only one Nārāyaṇa; neither Brahmā nor Īśāna existed."

By the *Mahopaniṣad*, beginning with "Neither the Agniṣṭoma nor these two, heaven and earth," and by the *Subālopaniṣad*, beginning with "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here—rootless and without support; from this, these creatures are born; divine, unique, the god Nārāyaṇa"—it is [established] that of Nārāyaṇa alone...
Since [the scriptures] declare that Śiva is the creator of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and since they establish that Brahmā and Rudra are born from Him,

how can Śiva’s status as the cause of the universe be accepted on the basis of His being the creator? On the other hand, there are [scriptural passages] that establish Nārāyaṇa as the object of creation.

All such statements are merely figurative. For this very reason, even Kālidāsa, in the third canto of the *Kumārasambhava*, establishes the origin of Brahmā with the verse: "Brahmā, whose body was born [from him], having joined his self to Brahman. Now, one might object that in the *Subālopaniṣad* there is only the primacy of Nārāyaṇa.

It has already been established that, since the conceptualization of Śiva as a creator is impossible on those grounds, how can his status as a created being be asserted? Nor is it the case that the status of Brahmā and Īśāna as created beings is indicated by the scriptural hearing of their priority even over Brahmā and Īśāna, in passages such as "Neither Brahmā nor Īśāna, nor Agni and Soma... and so forth.

It must be stated that [the first position] cannot establish creatorship by mere primacy alone. Likewise, in common usage—as in "Yajñadatta was the first; at that time Caitra and Maitra were not yet present"—only the primacy of Yajñadatta is indicated, while only the state of being produced immediately thereafter is understood regarding Caitra and Maitra.

One cannot, on this basis alone, postulate a relationship of produced and producer therein; rather, by the statement "Nārāyaṇa existed," the primary and initial origination of Nārāyaṇa is understood, followed by the subsequent origination of these two, Rudra and Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, since the sequence is not intended to be significant...

If it is argued that—since the production of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśa has been established [in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*], and since there is a requirement for their sequential order—the sequence of production is appropriately set forth in the passage "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; neither Brahmā nor Īśāna" (Mahopaniṣad 1.1)—we say no. For [the text continues] "From Nārāyaṇa, Rudra was born... [and so on].

This is because it is clearly heard in the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad* that Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa, stating "he was born"; and since the *Subālopaniṣad* must be interpreted in accordance with this, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) proponent's third stage of argument is that Śiva’s status as an object of creation is established.

Now, the fourth stage of the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*): By the statement of the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; he has no progenitor, nor is there any lord over him," it is established that Śiva alone is the cause, and there is no other cause for Śiva.

Since there is an explicit scriptural denial [of the origin of Rudra], how can the birth of Śiva from Nārāyaṇa be accepted on the basis of the statement "Rudra was born from Nārāyaṇa"? Nor can it be maintained that the scriptural statement "Rudra was born from Nārāyaṇa" is merely figurative because he is not its cause.

It is stated [in scripture]: "Soma flows, the progenitor of thoughts," and by the two statements, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra— they are all brought forth," as well as by the statement negating any other cause for Śiva, "Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa."
Because the statement itself must be interpreted otherwise.

As for the manner of that alternative interpretation: it is because it is more appropriate to say that [the deities] arise from Viṣṇu for the sake of making him accessible through devotion (*bhakti*). Furthermore, those [beings]—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—[are not independent].

In this very context of the phrase "they are fully produced," let it be understood that Viṣṇu’s birth from Śiva is merely figurative, intended to demonstrate the accessibility of the Lord to his devotees; for since Viṣṇu’s status as being created by Brahmā is also seen in other Purāṇas, such as the Viṣṇupurāṇa and the Mahābhārata, [it follows that] Śiva himself is likewise subject to being born.

It must be stated that what is primary is that which is to be spoken; for one whose devotion is manifest, it is only for the sake of his accessibility (*saulabhya*) that an incarnation is established as authoritative. When the doubt arises as to whether the descent (*avatāra*) of Śiva or Viṣṇu should be postulated for the sake of accessibility to the devotee, [it is concluded] that it is indeed Śiva’s.

It is appropriate to state that his manifestation is for the sake of accessibility to devotees; for instance, the manifestation of Śiva even from Hiraṇyagarbha is heard of in the Viṣṇupurāṇa and other texts. In the Upaniṣads, the manifestation of Viṣṇu is heard of.
It is reasonable to conclude that in many instances, manifestation is intended for the sake of accessibility to devotees.

Even by others, having observed the birth of [the Lord] from many such as Vasudeva, Daśaratha, and Kāśyapa during his incarnations as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth, it is accepted that the birth of the Blessed Nārāyaṇa is not ultimate, for the sake of accessibility to his devotees. Even in the world, [it is seen that] for a sovereign king who has many dependents...

They say that the King’s accessibility to his dependents is demonstrated by his coming to their homes out of a particular affection for those who rely on him; however, this is not the case when they come together in one place, because such accessibility to dependents would remain unmanifest [in that context] and because such an interpretation would be inappropriate. Therefore, since it is heard in scripture that Nārāyaṇa arose from Śiva alone—

Since there is no scriptural statement regarding the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha from him, the conceptualization that Nārāyaṇa was born for the sake of accessibility to devotees is indeed untenable. Furthermore, in the passage stating "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra— they all emanate forth," if one were to accept their manifestation merely for the sake of accessibility to devotees...

It would have to be accepted that even for Brahmā, Indra, and others, there is an incarnation for the sake of being easily accessible to their devotees; for otherwise, the fallacy of the "half-old woman" argument (*ardhajaratī-nyāya*) would follow, as it is more appropriate to interpret the meaning of words heard within a single sentence according to a uniform principle. Furthermore, in the passage: "Puruṣa, indeed, Nārāyaṇa, desired... [and so forth].

Indeed, since this [statement] is capable of being construed as a restatement (*anuvāda*) due to its connection with the word "ha" (indeed), the fact that Śiva is produced—which is heard in the text, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all brought forth"—must be construed as the original injunction (*purovāda*).
Nor should the reverse be suspected, for it is heard: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all brought forth."

Thus, since it is impossible to assume the status of a *purovāda* (a prior statement providing the basis for a subsequent one) because the fact that "Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa" is not heard in the sentence concerning as many objects as there may be,
for this very reason it was established in the *Pūrvatantra*.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the injunction "He takes eight [spoonfuls] in the *upabhṛt*" is an original prescription (*purovāda*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the eightfold-oblation of clarified butter previously enjoined, the sentence "That which he takes in the *upabhṛt* is for the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s" is indeed the original prescription; it means that "that which he takes in the *upabhṛt*, he takes for the *anuyāja*s."

The statement is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*). By that same logic, upon hearing the word "ha" (indeed), it is appropriate to assume that the sentence from the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad* is figurative (*aupacārika*) precisely because it is reiterative.

For this very reason, it has been established in the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā) that there is no fault in using a secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) in a reiteration. [Objection: But surely, "not indeed here..."?

"In the beginning there was only the Supreme Kiñcana (the One), rootless and supportless; from Him these creatures are born—the divine, singular God Nārāyaṇa. Thus, in the Subāla Upaniṣad, after describing the non-existence of all deities other than Nārāyaṇa prior to the emergence of the phenomenal world, [it establishes] the oneness of Nārāyaṇa.

Because he is established as the cause of the entire world, Nārāyaṇa alone is the Supreme Brahman; for, in his address to the gods, Śiva spoke such words as, "I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is no other whatsoever distinct from me," preceded by a negation of all other deities.
It cannot be argued that because the state of Śiva is described [in the Subāla Upaniṣad], it is logical that he alone is the cause of the world;

for this would contradict the Saubāla Śruti. Nor can it be said that since it is impossible to describe him as the cause of all things in both places while first negating everything else, one of them must necessarily have a figurative meaning—[the answer being] no, because of the Subāla...

It should not be said that [the text] is appropriately centered on Śiva in accordance with the statements of the *Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad*; for, according to etymological definitions such as "The waters are called *nārāḥ*, and the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara; their abode (*ayana*) is in them, and for that reason he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa," it refers to a specific deity.

Since the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* applies specifically to the word *saṃjñā*, and because it is appropriate that this passage is devoted to describing Viṣṇu alone as the cause of all— as he is established by the *Subāla-śruti* and his status as the cause of the universe is determined by the force of the unique scriptural mention of *Nārāyaṇa*— the word *Śiva* found in the *Atharvaśiras* [must refer to him].
The fourth stage of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is that, because Nārāyaṇa alone is appropriately supreme, he alone is the cause of the world.

The proponents of the Siddhānta, however, maintain that because the grammatical rule prescribing the *ṇatva* [nasalization] in the word "Nārāyaṇa" applies only when it is a proper name— as seen in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*— the statement in the *Atharvaśiras* must, in accordance with the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, refer to Viṣṇu alone; thus, "I am the one."

Furthermore, there is an inconsistency in the use of the first-person pronoun (*aham*) in the phrases "for the first month" (*prathamamāsam*) and likewise "I am thus" (*tathā vartāmi*) and "I shall be" (*bhaviṣyāmi*).
For instance [it is said]: "The gods, indeed, went to the heavenly world.
Those gods asked Rudra: 'Who are you? He replied: "I alone."

"I am the first month; I both exist and shall exist, and there is no one else whatsoever distinct from me"—thus he entered the innermost of the inner, and he entered the interval between the quarters. "I am that eternal and non-eternal Brahmā; I am the eastern one, I am the western one"—so it is heard. In that regard, [it concerns] Rudra.

At the time of the beginning of creation, it is logical that the teaching of universal identity is made with reference to its own self, as it abides in the state of being the cause of all things; for this conforms to the rule [of Pāṇini] prescribing the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*) in the sūtra "when there is coreferentiality with 'we', the first person is used" (*asmatsāmānādhikaraṇye'smadyuttamaḥ*).

Is it not the case that the teaching of universal identity, as in "I am indeed the Sun," is a teaching of universal identity intended to refer to the Supreme Self who dwells within one's own self? For it is precisely because of the Supreme Self that the status of being the cause and so forth is well-known. [If so,] how can there be such statements as "I alone existed first"?

To eliminate doubt, it is the very word of Rudra [that says]: "He entered from within, even deeper within. Therein, the term "He" (saḥ) refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman), because He is present in the intellect (*buddhi*). According to the manner stated in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*, the Supreme Self, who dwells within all bodies, [enters] by means of presiding over the bodies of gods, humans, and so forth.
