Since it is accepted that [the Self] is denotable by all words— just as it is denotable by words such as "god" and "human"— and because in the preceding statement, "I alone existed in the beginning," the word "I" was introduced as referring to the Supreme Self residing within one's own body, the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who is within the sun" is as follows: He...

The meaning is that the Supreme Self entered the class of individual souls (jīva), which are even more internal than the vital breaths and so forth, by way of being their inner controller (antaryāmin). If it is argued that, therefore, the teaching regarding Rudra’s status as the cause of all is intended with reference to the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, we say no; for that [teaching] belongs to Rudra himself in the "Antarādi" passage.

There is no contradiction in the intent of the passage being to explain the entry [of the Self] by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all; likewise, the preceding statement is also devoted to establishing that Rudra alone is the cause of all. Nor does it follow that, if this were the case and the statements beginning with "He who is within the sun" (*so 'ntarāditye*) were accepted as being words of Rudra, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the form "I entered" (*ahaṃ prāviśat*).

It must be stated that there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me, because the completion of Rudra’s speech is understood immediately thereafter by the particle *iti*. Furthermore, since "he entered" (*praviśat*) is a verbal form belonging to the scriptural passage beginning with "He who is within the sun," its application is logically consistent. Nor is it the case that after the phrase "he entered," there follows "I am eternal and non-eternal... [and so on].

It must be stated that, by following the sequence of Rudra’s speech as indicated by "ityādi" (and so forth), the completion of Rudra’s discourse is not established; otherwise, if the context of Rudra’s speech were interrupted in the middle by a Vedic statement (*śrutivacana*), one would have to expect [the phrase] "she spoke again" (*punaḥ sābravīt*) and so on, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of having to supply such missing words (*tadadhyāhāraprasaṅga*).

Immediately after the completion of the entire speech of Rudra, because there is no need to supply ellipses such as "he said" (*so 'bravīt*) for the connection with "that [person] within the sun" (*so 'ntarādityāt*), nor is there any fault in a non-adjacent connection (*vyavahitānvaya*),
since in your own view as well, the word *iti* connects to the conclusion of the entire speech of Rudra.

This is because the fault of syntactical connection with an intervening element (*vyavahitatvānvaya*) is equal [in both cases]. Nor should it be argued that the particle *iti* may be construed in its own place as having the sense of a reason (i.e., "because"), for the context would then be consistent with the statement: "Upon entering into the Supreme Self, I alone existed first. This cannot be said, [for] [it refers to someone] other than Rudra.

Because there is no word that establishes the supreme self (paramātman). Nor should it be argued that the word "that" (sa) refers back to the supreme self present in the intellect, just as in expressions such as "dyed by that" (tena raktaṃ), the word "that" refers to a substance such as lac-dye present in the intellect; for [in that case], by that...

In passages such as "the red," because there is a reference to multiple unstable meanings, there is a disparity with the illustrative example; therefore, in cases like "He who is within the sun," the word *tat* (that), which refers to a single stable meaning, cannot refer to something merely present in the intellect. Furthermore, since the Supreme Self is denotable by all words, [I am... [the text continues].
It must be stated that the word "he" (saḥ) refers to the Supreme Self;

for otherwise, there would arise the fault of a discrepancy between the subject and the predicate (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the question and answer, namely: "He questioned Rudra," and "He replied. Nor can it be argued that the word "Rudra" also refers to the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, such that no fault of discrepancy would exist between the question and the answer.
It must be stated that this is because the culmination [of all things] in the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) was not previously understood by the gods.

For it is only when the Supreme Self is known as the cause and so forth that the doubt does not arise: "How is it that you say, 'I alone existed first'? Therefore, as a response to that [doubt], [the text says]: "He [is] within the innermost... (*so'ntarād antaraṃ*).

Because there is no response stating "He entered," the scriptural statement "Then he from within" must indeed be understood as establishing Rudra alone as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*); thus, in that mantra, he speaks with reference to his own self:
"I alone was in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall be in the future."

Because of the use of the first person plural verb ending (*ceti*), and because the single term *Nārāyaṇa* refers to Śiva through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is Śiva alone who possesses the status of the Supreme Brahman, as he is the cause of all.
As for the statement from the *Mahābhārata*: "Viṣṇu is the self of the Lord Bhava of immeasurable splendor," [it is explained as follows:]

Therefore, this [objection] is trivial; for, as in the case of the word *ātman* in Viṣṇu’s statement in the Mokṣadharma— “Therefore, I first worship Rudra as my very self” (*tasmādātmānamevāgre rudraṃ sampūjayāmyaham*)— the intended meaning may reside in either a primary sense or a figurative one regarding non-difference.

But surely, by reflecting on the *Saubāla* Śruti— "The unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable (*akṣara*), the Imperishable into darkness (*tamas*), and darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity"— it is described that at the time of creation and so forth, the unmanifest and the rest, in due order, become unified within the Supreme Nārāyaṇa; therefore, [this belongs] to Nārāyaṇa alone.

The state of being the Supreme Brahman is thus appropriate; for likewise, because it is heard in other Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth that Nārāyaṇa alone is the impeller of darkness (*tamas*), he alone is the Supreme Brahman. Nor [is there any contradiction], for it is said: "When there was darkness, there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being—Śiva alone existed. That is the Imperishable; that is the most excellent [state] of Savitṛ."

And because it is established that "the ancient wisdom issued forth from him," and since Śiva alone is presented as the cause of all by virtue of being the impeller of darkness (*tamas*), he alone must be declared the Supreme Brahman;
for even the *Śvetāśvatara* mantra is devoted to Nārāyaṇa. To explain: "When there was darkness... [and so on].

In the Śvetāśvatara mantra, the phrase "when [it] comes" (*yadā*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the darkness (*tamas*) that arrives at a specific time; it depends upon the statement from the Subālopaniṣad: "That which brings about its own manifestation dissolves into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); the Unmanifest into Darkness (*tamas*); and Darkness becomes one with the Supreme Deity (*paraṃ devaṃ*)," because a restatement necessarily requires a prior statement (*purovāda*).

Because he is established as the presiding deity over that darkness, that mantra also ultimately refers to Nārāyaṇa alone, in order to conform to the preceding statement (*purovāda*). If it is objected: "Why should the Maitrāyaṇīya scriptural passage, 'Darkness alone was this in the beginning,' not be the *purovāda* here?"—the answer is no; for even that [passage]...
Because a general scriptural statement must terminate in a specific one established by another scripture—such as the *Saubāla-śruti*—there is no lack of distinction.

Thus, the word "Śiva" occurring in the mantra "Śiva alone is [the cause]," although it may denote another deity through its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) as "the Auspicious One," must be applied to Nārāyaṇa through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Or rather, [it refers to] Śarvāṇī here.

In such passages as "These beings arise from space alone; they merge back into space," the mention of causality—indicated by the employment of the particles *ha* and *vai*—must, in accordance with its preceding statement, refer to Nārāyaṇa; thus, even words like "space" (*ākāśa*), though denoting insentient things, [refer to Him].
In some way, the application [of the term] to Nārāyaṇa is accepted. What burden is there in accepting its application there, given that it is extremely remote as a designator of another deity?
Furthermore, because [the name] occurs among the thousand names in the passage "Sarvaḥ, Sarvaḥ, Śivaḥ, Sthāṇuḥ," [it applies] to Nārāyaṇa.
The application of the word "Śiva" is thus justified. Therefore, the opponent maintains that the mantra-upaniṣad refers to Nārāyaṇa alone, and that he alone is the cause of the world.

The proponents of the Siddhānta, however, maintain that by examining other mantras such as "For there is only one Rudra, no second stands beside him," "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe," "The Great Lord who possesses Māyā," and "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords," it is established that the Mantra-upaniṣads refer entirely to Śiva.

It is understood [that this is so]. Furthermore, because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the *Puruṣasūkta* mantras such as "I know this great Puruṣa," the mantra and the Upaniṣad are devoted to Nārāyaṇa. Since there is a difference in what is propounded by both, [the text] excludes others through the two [mantras], stating: "There exists no other path for going."
It should not be argued that this is impossible because it cannot be determined to be a means to liberation;
for, precisely through the recognition of the Śvetāśvatara mantra, it is appropriate that the Puruṣasūkta has Śiva as its ultimate referent.

Now, one might object: since the opening verse "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads" refers to Hari as the Puruṣa because he lies within this body designated as 'puruṣa', the letter *śa* here is used by way of transposition for the letter *ṣa*.
Likewise, both the word "Bhagavān" and "Puruṣa" may apply to Vāsudeva without any limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*).

By the citation of the word *puruṣa*— whose exclusive devotion to Nārāyaṇa is understood from the Purāṇic statement "Sanātane"— in the middle of the Vedic passage, "I know this great Puruṣa," [it is established that] he possesses that name as understood from the Kalpasūtra: "One should worship Mahādeva or the Mahāpuruṣa."

By the mention of the term "mahāpuruṣa," [the text] establishes that it refers to the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa) who is the subject of the Puruṣasūkta; and as being part of a single syntactical unit with that [sūkta], at the end of the immediately following section which begins with "adbhyaḥ sambhūtaḥ," it states: "Hrī and Lakṣmī are his two wives."

Furthermore, because the mark of being the Lord of Lakṣmī is traditionally taught in the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa—"This is Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is the creator; he is the one desired by Uśanas"—and because this Vārāha-mantra is recited in the Puruṣavrata as the Vaiṣṇavī Saṃhitā, it is said that "one who employs this [mantra] pleases Viṣṇu."
By its inclusion in the Vaiṣṇava Saṃhitā,

and by its application to the Vaiṣṇava rite of propitiation (śānti) within the Atharvavedic section on the eighteen great propitiatory rites (mahāśānti), specifically among those rites dedicated to various deities where the Puruṣasūkta is prescribed for the Vaiṣṇava rite;

By the application [of the Puruṣasūkta] to the worship of Nārāyaṇa in the *Smṛtis* of Śaunaka and others; by the observation of hymns to Viṣṇu through the method of the *Puruṣasūkta* in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other texts; and by the Kalpa-sūtras stating, "The sacrificer worships with the *Puruṣa*, that is, with Nārāyaṇa," and "Then the worship with the two *Nārāyaṇa* [verses]," and so forth.
If it is argued that the *Puruṣasūkta* has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme object because of the designation "Nārāyaṇa" and common usage, [we reply:
in this very Upaniṣad it is stated: "That which is higher than that is formless and free from suffering;
those who know this become immortal, while others indeed encounter only suffering."

"Having all faces, heads, and necks, dwelling in the secret cave of all beings, the Blessed Lord is all-pervasive; therefore, O Śiva, you are omnipresent. By the recitation of this mantra, Śiva is established as being superior to Nārāyaṇa, who is propounded in the *Puruṣasūkta*.

Since the final purport of this [passage] culminates in this very point, therefore the mantra "yadā tamaḥ" establishes the causality of Śiva by virtue of his existence at the time of the beginning of creation, which is characterized by a particular state of *tamas*. As it has been said: "yadā tamaḥ..."

The claim that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) is true; for passages such as "In the beginning, this was indeed darkness alone," "Prajāpati alone was this in the beginning," and "There was neither day nor night" can function as prior statements (*purovāda*).
Therefore, the passage beginning with "Neither day nor night" is not a restatement, because at that time there was a connection with those specific conditions.

Because nothing [else] is understood as that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*); and neither the absence of the distinction between day and night nor the absence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of existence and non-existence is the thing to be enjoined, since both of these are already understood from the two preceding statements cited as the *pūrvavāda*.
For a sentence that proceeds to enjoin something after having restated something else does not require another statement for the sake of that restatement.

It would reach its fulfillment and attain its fruitfulness by concluding with the very meaning already obtained from the preceding statement (*purovāda*). And thus, if the word "Śiva," setting aside its general reference to the Supreme Lord, were to conclude specifically with Nārāyaṇa as obtained from the preceding statement, then [the verse] "When there was darkness... [would apply].

Should a statement that has been raised to establish something and has reached halfway through its course simply rest right there? For we do not perceive any meaning not already established by the preceding injunction (*purovāda*) in the case of the word "Śiva" functioning as a synonym for Nārāyaṇa; therefore, according to the opponent's view, this very sentence would be purposeless.

Therefore, at the time of the beginning of creation, among those passages that lead to [the understanding of] *tamas*, its presiding deity is sometimes referred to by the word "Nārāyaṇa," sometimes by the word "Prajāpati," and sometimes by the general term "Paramātman. Because two contradictory specific attributes are heard therein, the final conclusion remains undetermined.

In order to demonstrate that those [entities] appearing during emergence possess a single object, [the author] restates the *tamas* (darkness) pertaining to the time of the beginning of creation— which was obtained from them— and by means of the word "Śiva," he attributes to it the status of the Supreme Lord as its presider, which was not previously obtained from them; thus, the meaningfulness of that [word] must be explained.

Therefore, having set aside that [objection], one must state that the word "Nārāyaṇa," which stands as the subject of the preceding statement (*purovāda*), has its application (*vṛtti*) in Śiva alone.

For it is better to accept the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a single word than the meaninglessness of an entire sentence. And this is accepted in the *Pūrvatant*ra (Mīmāṃsā) regarding the animal sacrifice: "There are eleven portions of the animal; he cuts off two [portions] from each. In this case, the word "animal" (*paśu*) is taken to indicate the specific parts of the animal.

Although, in order to avoid the redundancy of the restating injunction—which prescribes two portions (*avadāna*) when they are already obtained through the general rule—it might be argued that in the sentence "If the sacrificer is one who takes four portions, the omentum (*vapā*) should be treated as if it were five-portioned," the word *vapā* must be taken as indicating (*lakṣaṇā*) all animal-offering materials (*pāśukahavis*) in common with the heart and other parts; nevertheless, this is so: [The text continues: "For indeed..."

In order to accomplish the five-fold cutting (*avadāna*) for the heart and other organs, since the preliminary spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the subsequent sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) are present, there would otherwise follow three cuttings for the heart and so on; however, by the rule that "only two portions of the sacrificial substance (*havis*) should be cut," the completion of the required number is achieved through the increase resulting from the spreading and other acts, and thus that [rule] becomes meaningful. It is stated thus.

By this method, the first half-verse beginning with "tama" establishes that certain causal statements, such as "In the beginning, this was indeed one [mass] of darkness," ultimately culminate in Śiva; likewise, in the second half-verse...

The portion beginning with "That Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6): "Just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of the same nature emerge, so, O gentle one, various beings are born from the Imperishable and into it they also merge"— this is the portion [of the mantra] beginning with "tat savitur vareṇyam."

In the Supreme Person residing in the center of the solar orb, the Sāvitrī verse—describing Him as "He who impels our intellects"—expounds the mark of His being the inner controller of all, which is invariably associated with His status as the cause of the universe; thus it says: "And from Him [the Puruṣa] proceeded the ancient wisdom. Then He thought: "tadaikṣata."
"May I be many, may I procreate"—he thought, "Let me now create the worlds"; he desired, "May I be many, may I procreate"; "By austerity Brahman is built up; from that food is born.

By such words as "contemplation" (*īkṣaṇa*) and "vision" (*prekṣaṇa*), [the text refers to] the Creator's observation of the multitude of things to be created at the time prior to the initial creation.
It establishes that the causal statements of the *Chāndogya* and other Upaniṣads culminate in Śiva; thus,
this mantra reveals that all causal statements have Śiva as their subject matter.

As for the argument that [the Puruṣasūkta refers to Viṣṇu] because of the recognition of the *Puruṣasūkta*, that is refuted by the *Garbhaśrāva* [mantra]. This is because, through the recognition of the *Śrīrudra* mantras such as "O Rudra, that form of yours which is auspicious" (*yā te rudra śivā tanūḥ*) and "Do not harm our offspring" (*mā nastoke*), it has Śiva as its ultimate referent. Furthermore, the statement "There is no other path for going" (*nānyaḥ panthā ayanāya*) occurs in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* as well.

Because [Śiva] is heard [in the Veda], because his status as the means to liberation is established, and because the word "Īśāna" is heard in the passage "the Lord of immortality," the *Puruṣasūkta* in reality has Śiva as its supreme subject. Furthermore, this is confirmed by the determination in the Sūtra "By the word itself it is measured" (*śabdādeva pramitaḥ*) that the text refers to Brahman due to the hearing of the word "Īśāna."

Furthermore, the word *puruṣa* is not denotative of Nārāyaṇa alone; for, by virtue of its general denotative power—as in the rule "the words *puruṣa*, *ātman*, and *mānava* denote the self"—it is appropriately connected to a specific deity. This is analogous to the section concerning *barhis* and *ājya*, where words such as *barhis* and *ājya*, which denote unrefined darbha grass and clarified butter respectively, [are understood to refer to the refined forms].

Because a specific power [of the word] is not admitted; for the word *pṛṣṭha*, which is established in the *Citrādhikaraṇa* as the name of a particular hymn (*stotra*), has its conventional usage in certain instances such as "they attend with *pṛṣṭhas*" through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and this fact having been made known, [the purpose of the argument is fulfilled]. As for the water, it reached the seasonal [sacrifice]; of those [waters]...

For all Mīmāṃsakas accept that an etymological explanation (nirvacana) found in an explanatory passage (arthavāda), such as "the wind turned on its back," possesses the capacity to specifically determine the meaning of a term like *vāmadevya*.
Therefore, since the word *puruṣa* lacks a specific [conventional] power [for this particular context], it must rely on its general power.

Because the specific conclusion is established by means of the *Śvetāśvatara* mantra, it is logical that [the text] has Śiva as its ultimate referent. For this very reason, the claim that the term "Mahāpuruṣa" refers to Nārāyaṇa is refuted. Furthermore, even the status of being the Lord of Lakṣmī—[as seen in the passage] "to Śrī..."—[is explained].

The goddess Ambikā is the Lakṣmī who consists of stone; upon her [lap] is mounted the supreme Śakti of Maheśvara, known as Mahālakṣmī, dark-complexioned and enchanting to all. Thus, according to both the *Ghṛtasūkta* and the supplement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) to the *Śivapurāṇa*, the Liṅga of Śiva alone is proclaimed.
The designation "Nārāyaṇa" is also appropriate for the *Puruṣasūkta* because Nārāyaṇa is its seer (*ṛṣi*).

Furthermore, its application (*viniyoga*) in the worship of Nārāyaṇa is entirely justified, just as the application of the mantra beginning with "Agnirmūrdhā" (which is dedicated to Agni) is justified in the worship of Aṅgāraka. Otherwise, [it would not be so].

"One should worship the Giver of Wealth, who possesses universal form, with the Puruṣasūkta"—because of this application (viniyoga), there would otherwise be the contingency of [the sūkta] being subordinate to something else. Likewise:
"With the Jyeṣṭhasāman, with the three-fold chant, with the Devavratas, with the meritorious Rathantara, and with the Puruṣasūkta."
The fact that [the Puruṣasūkta] refers to Śiva is established even by the statement from the Liṅga Purāṇa which enjoins its application for the consecration (abhiṣeka) of Śiva.

Therefore, since the Puruṣasūkta has Śiva as its referent, and because the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad also has Śiva as its referent due to the recognition of those mantras, all statements concerning the cause of the universe must be interpreted in accordance with it.
The established conclusion is that Śiva alone is the supreme reality.

Now, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): In the *Mahopaniṣad*, by means of the passage beginning with "Verily, there was only one Nārāyaṇa; there was no Brahmā, no Īśāna, no Agni and Soma, nor these two, heaven and earth," the state of being produced (*janyatva*) is established for Brahmā, Īśāna, Agni, Soma, heaven, and earth, preceded by the negation of their existence.

Having described [the state of] Nārāyaṇa alone, who is without companion, as existing at the time of the beginning of creation as the cause of all, it is further explained that because negation is stronger than affirmation,
and because it is impossible for Īśāna to be described as the cause of all, it is Nārāyaṇa alone [who is so].

It is logical that, at the conclusion of all statements regarding the cause, it is precisely that [Brahman] which possesses the nature of the Supreme Brahman. For this very reason, according to the maxim of the goat and the animal, those passages establishing the state of being the cause of all— such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"— by means of terms such as *sat* (Being), *ātman*, and *akṣara-brahman* (the Imperishable Brahman), [refer to Him].
Since it is logical that all doctrines concerning the universal cause culminate in Nārāyaṇa alone, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme Brahman.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: in such scriptural passages as "Verily, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," the statement that Nārāyaṇa is the creator of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) refers, in certain instances, to Nārāyaṇa— who was first produced from Paraśiva at the beginning of a particular *kalpa*— as being the creator of the phenomenal world other than himself.
Because it can be so construed, it is not contradicted in any way by the acceptance of Paramaśiva as the supreme cause;
for [the passage] "Nārāyaṇa alone existed" is followed by "He appeared, the dispeller of darkness."

Furthermore, according to the *Mānavīyopabṛṃhaṇa*, at the time of the beginning of creation, prior to the emergence of Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the others, it is understood that Nārāyaṇa alone, without a second, arose from Paramaśiva.
This is in accordance with the sequence of the creation of the elements, senses, and so forth, as set forth in the *Mahopaniṣad*, [which describes him] in the midst of the waters.

Since the entire body of meanings beginning with "In the created universe, the four-faced Brahmā was created by Nārāyaṇa" is also clearly evident in the words of Manu, it is established— without contradicting any Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇa, or other sources— that Paramaśiva is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world; therefore, Śiva alone is the Supreme Brahman.

And thus says a Vedic mantra: "The supreme Brahman is Truth, Reality, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, whose seed is drawn up, the three-eyed one; salutation indeed to the one of universal form. For by the explicit mention of the name "the three-eyed one" (*virūpākṣam*) in this mantra, [it is said]: "Having paid homage to Mahādeva, the Truth..."

In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, within the context of the salutation to Śiva, there is the application [of the mantra] "Truth, O Lord"; and in the *Baudhāyana Sūtra*, beginning with "Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the water from the feet of Mahādeva," it states that one should cause [the disciple] to consume [the water] with the mantra "Ṛta, Satya, the Supreme Brahman," thus establishing its application in the consumption of the water from Śiva’s feet.

"Alternatively, one should know the Supreme Self, whose form is supreme bliss, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, through the instruction of the Guru. O Gārgī, that Brahman is within the city of Brahman, in the midst of the space of the small lotus [of the heart].
Through practice, the virtuous perceive Him; you too should act likewise. Thus it is said in the *Yogayājñavalkya*.

Since this [passage] clearly establishes its focus on Śiva by way of being syntactically one with the preceding section—thereby providing the specific form of the object of meditation for the *daharavidyā* taught in that earlier section—it is evident that its ultimate purport is Śiva.
Therefore, when it is established that Paramaśiva is the cause of the universe in accordance with these mantras, [the text continues]: "There was indeed one..."
The established conclusion is that even the statement of the Mahopaniṣad, "Nārāyaṇa existed," is not contradicted.

But surely, in the *Mahopaniṣad* it is heard that Rudra originates from Nārāyaṇa: "Then again, Nārāyaṇa, desiring something else, meditated with his mind; while he was absorbed in meditation, from his forehead a three-eyed person with a trident in hand was born"; likewise in the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*.

Because it is heard in scripture that "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa" and "Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa," the status of Nārāyaṇa as the supreme cause is established for Rudra. For this very reason, it is stated in the Mahābhārata: "Brahmā, Sthāṇu, Manu, Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, Dharma, Tapas, Dama," and so forth.
"Those twenty-one who were born are remembered as the Prajāpatis; they honor the eternal ordinance of that God.
This is because it is stated that Brahmā, Śiva, Dakṣa, Manu, and others follow the ordinance established by the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa.

Of these two as well, Brahmā is the elder, because his birth is heard of first in the very scriptural passage cited immediately above, which serves as its corroborative expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*): "These two, the best of the wise, are born from my grace and my wrath;
shown the path by me, they are the agents of creation and dissolution. This is Brahmā, the teacher of the world."
The Lord is the creator of the world from the beginning; he is indeed your mother, your father, and your great-grandfather.

"Rudra, who arose from his forehead, shall be his younger brother; instructed by me, he will become the bestower of boons upon all beings. Since it is thus stated that Śiva is the younger brother of Brahmā, and since the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other texts establish that Brahmā himself originated [from Nārāyaṇa], therefore, [this applies] to Nārāyaṇa.

Because He is the cause of all causes and is therefore supreme, and because even Brahmā, Śiva, and others are dependent upon Him, He alone should be worshipped and sought for refuge by those desiring the stable goal of human life; for the Atharvaṇa Śruti states: "He who, in the beginning, creates Brahmā... and "The cause should be meditated upon. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3) and (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18).

The prima facie argument is that this is because of the Śvetāśvatara mantra-verse: "To him who imparts the Vedas as well as [himself], to that God, who is the light of self-knowledge, I, seeking liberation, go for refuge."

As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): the descriptions in the *Śrutis* and *Smṛtis* such as "the three-eyed, trident-bearing Puruṣa was born" regarding Rudra being created by Nārāyaṇa—all of that refers to his manifestation from Him in the form of the Saṃhāra-Rudra during specific *kalpas*. And I...

This is made clear by the statement of Śiva granting a boon to Nārāyaṇa in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "At the end of the kalpa, when you have departed, I shall become your son, born of my wrath, bearing a trident and possessing a terrible form. In this very manner, the Kumāra appeared upon the lap of the Lord.

Regarding the description of the manifestation of Rudra from Brahmā in passages such as "Nīlalohita," that too is intended to show his manifestation for the sake of Brahmā’s grace, by demonstrating the means for the creation and expansion of the world; thus it is said: "The Great Lord Nīlalohita was designated by the Supreme Lord as [Brahmā’s] son."

"Having become [the son], he favors Brahmā," according to the statement of Vāyu: "The God is without beginning or end, endowed with consciousness and other qualities; He under whose control are all cognitions and the instruments [of action] without exception;
His sovereignty is endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* and is not artificial; for the sake of creation, He is the Son of Brahmā."

As stated in the *Bhārata*: "The Lord has arisen from the forehead," it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the statement regarding Rudra's subordination should be understood in this very way as referring either to the portions (*aṃśa*) of Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa, or specifically to Rudra in his incarnations (*avatāra*).
Is it not stated in the Taittirīya Śruti: "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate reality.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, the Self; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme. Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditator;
meditation is Nārāyaṇa, the supreme. Whatever exists in this entire world that is perceived..."

It is also heard [in scripture]: "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without," and so forth; by such passages, the status of Nārāyaṇa alone as the Supreme Brahman is clearly established. Nor [should it be argued] that by resorting to a genitive compound (*pañcamī samāsa*) in the phrase "the Supreme Brahman from Nārāyaṇa" (*nārāyaṇāt paraṃ brahma*), [it refers to] one who is superior to Nārāyaṇa...
It must be said that the status of Paramaśiva as the Supreme Brahman is to be established, because in the Mahopaniṣad,

within the section expounding the Supreme Brahman, the reading is demonstrated through the word-division "Nārāyaṇaḥ paraṃ brahma" (Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman), and [this status is established] in order to bring about consistency with that [text].
By the rule *śu-pām suluk-pūrvasavarṇā-āc-chē-yā-ḍā-ḍyā-yā-jā-laḥ*, when the elision (*luk*) of the nominative case-ending is applied according to Vedic usage,
the phrase "Nārāyaṇa" results in the final intended meaning being "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman. This remains so even though the term "nārāyaṇaparaṃ brahma" is a compound word (*samasta-pada*).
Because, according to the *niṣādasthapati* maxim, only a coordinate (*samānādhikaraṇa*) compound is to be accepted;
for in the *niṣādasthapati* section, since there is no burden [of complexity] in taking [the compound] as a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the case-meaning,
a coordinate *tatpuruṣa*— that is, a *karmadhāraya*— is preferred over a non-coordinate *tatpuruṣa*.

This is because it establishes that the *karmadhāraya* compound alone, as proven by such scriptural instruction, is the most highly esteemed. Furthermore: "I alone am the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Reality, O Grandfather;
I alone am the Supreme Light, and I am the all-pervading Supreme Self."
Furthermore, because this mantra is supported by the *Liṅgapurāṇa* through a statement of the Lord addressed to Brahmā which establishes Nārāyaṇa’s status as the Supreme Brahman,
it is impossible to assume a *vyadhikaraṇa-tatpuruṣa* compound. Therefore, Nārāyaṇa alone is the Supreme.
"Brāhmaṇa" is the designation for that very one who possesses the preeminence over all deities.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the demonstration of Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman in passages such as "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman" is due either to his non-difference from Śiva obtained through Śiva’s grace,
or because it aims at the state of being [Śiva] attained through the realization of non-difference from Paramaśiva; thus, it refers to Śiva alone.
It is primarily intended to describe the nature of the other. Since it is impossible for those two— bound within a single Vidyā by the relationship of the object of worship and the worshipper,

and thus characterized as primary and subordinate— to actually possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman, the description of that subordinate state must be understood according to the principle of the section concerning the contradiction of qualities between the primary and the subordinate (*aṅgaguṇavirodhādhikaraṇanyāya*).
Because it must be interpreted primarily [as the principal]; this was established in the section concerning "the conflict between the quality of a subsidiary and its purpose" (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*),
where it is stated that among the options for the initiation periods (*dīkṣā*) of the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) and others,
whether it be the *dīkṣaṇīyā* or the *somayāga*, whichever [is performed] after the *iṣṭi*...

It has been determined that, since it is impossible for the priority [of the *dīkṣiṇīyā*] to be established by the direct statement (*divākya*), and because it is appropriate to favor the principal rite in the necessary *soma*-sacrifice, it is logical to abandon the priority of the subordinate *dīkṣiṇīyā* itself. In the same way, [it is said]: "The Supreme Brahman is beyond Nārāyaṇa."
Even if one resorts to a *vyadhikaraṇa-tatpuruṣa* compound, there is no fault;

for, according to the principle of the section on "the quality of the subordinate" (*aṅgaguṇādhikaraṇa-nyāya*), the determination of meaning is guided by conformity with the principal element. Furthermore, in another Śruti it is stated: "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman."
It should not be argued that because the study [of the text] is seen through word-by-word division (*padaviccheda*), a compound with the ablative case (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is inappropriate;

for in another Vedic scripture, *nārāyaṇaḥ paraṃ brahma*, by the application of the rule *supāṃ suluk* etc., the ablative case ending in *nārāyaṇāt* is understood as a substitute (*svādeśa*) for the nominative, such that the meaning is "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman beyond [all else]."

This is because it is possible for the Śruti to establish a single meaning [in both passages]. Nor is there a contradiction with the statement from the Liṅga Purāṇa, "I alone am the Supreme Brahman," for that occurs in the context of a mutual dispute between Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa prior to the manifestation of the Great Liṅga, wherein each claimed, "I alone am the most excellent."
Immediately after what has been recited,

for the sake of quelling that dispute, may all fear be released from me as I behold Mahādeva Paśupati, who has appeared within the great *liṅga* manifested there; you two have been brought forth [by him].

Formerly, from my two limbs, there arose two of great power; O Viṣṇu, I myself am divided threefold under the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Bhava. Though the Supreme Lord is partless, he manifests through the qualities of creation, preservation, and dissolution.

The established conclusion is that Śiva’s status as the cause of all is proven by the Vedas; for the collection of statements regarding the excellence of Brahman— induced by the instruction on reality beginning with "O Viṣṇu, abandon your delusion"— serves only to establish the nature of that [excellence] as it truly is.

But surely, in the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa*, during the description of the acceptance of the deities to be sacrificed to at the *dīkṣiṇīyā* sacrifice, it is established that Agni is the lowest of the gods and Viṣṇu the highest, with all other deities situated between them. Thus, the inferiority of Agni is set forth.

Having described all other deities as being intermediate, since Viṣṇu is heard to be supreme— by the scriptural statement that "Viṣṇu is the highest"— it is Viṣṇu alone who is the ultimate cause, and not Paramaśiva, who is distinct from him, who is the ultimate cause. Of Viṣṇu...

Because it contradicts the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*, which establishes the state of supremacy [of Viṣṇu]. Nor is the statement, "Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods, Viṣṇu the highest," a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) regarding the *Dīkṣiṇīya* sacrifice; for it has been established that in cases of contradiction, there may be figurative speech (*guṇavāda*), or restatement (*anuvāda*) when the fact is already determined. An explanatory passage is considered to be of three kinds: based on a factual reality (*bhūtārthavāda*), based on a quality (*guṇavāda*), or based on a restatement (*anuvāda*). Since these distinctions apply, the passage in question cannot be a mere explanatory praise.

According to this principle, since [the passage] must be interpreted as being for the purpose of praise (*stāvakatayā*), it has no *tātparya* (intentional focus) regarding its own literal meaning; therefore, because the description of Viṣṇu’s supremacy is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), it lacks *tātparya* regarding its own literal meaning.

It should not be argued that there is a contradiction in establishing the supremacy of Paramaśiva; for while it is not a matter of objective reality that fire is inferior or that all other deities are situated between them, one may nevertheless say, "Fire is the lowest of the deities,
Viṣṇu is the highest of the deities, and having grasped both of these, one is initiated."
If the *Dīkṣiṇīyā* sacrifice in the *Soma* ritual were not established as having the purpose of securing (*parigraha*) all the deities for whom one is about to sacrifice,

then— given that this is not established— the *Anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel) would not need to be performed for the purpose of securing the deities of the *Soma* subsidiaries, as established in the previous section of the *Tantra* under the sūtra: "And for the purpose of securing [the deities], the *Iṣṭi* comes first, because it is for that purpose."

The *Dīkṣiṇīyā* [offering] was determined in the *Saṅkarṣaṇakāṇḍa* on the basis of the conclusion that, for the purpose of securing the deities who are to be sacrificed to, the very act of securing all deities is accomplished by incidental extension (*prasaṅga*) through that *Dīkṣiṇīyā* alone.

Because of the scriptural statement regarding the assumption of another deity through conjunction with the *saṃskāra*s, it is established by the *adhikaraṇa* that the fire prescribed for the *dīkṣiṇīyā* sacrifice in the *Soma* ritual is to be maintained for the sake of the *Soma* sacrifice as a whole; there is no removal of the fire for each individual rite.
Thus, the *dīkṣiṇīyā* [is part of that maintenance].

Because there would be a contradiction of the established conclusion—that [the fire-altar] results from the conjunction of the refinements of ten million presiding deities—the statement "Agni indeed is of the gods" cannot be a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). Therefore, Viṣṇu is the supreme;
such is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that although the statement "Agni is the lowest of the deities, Viṣṇu is the highest" has a figurative meaning due to its contradiction with many extremely powerful scriptural passages, it retains its own literal sense insofar as there is no contradiction regarding the portion that establishes the *dīkṣiṇīyā* as being for the purpose of securing the deities.

Because it is possible to accept [their] validity. Nor should it be argued that, in the absence of a superior-inferior relationship between Agni and Viṣṇu, the inclusion of all deities would not be established due to the impossibility of grasping them from both sides;
for even if one were to grasp them from both sides by treating those two as the lower and upper limits, the aforementioned lack of proof remains just as it was.
For when there is a sacrifice to deities who constitute the lower and upper limits, the inclusion of other deities situated between them is not established.

If it is argued that, by the force of the scriptural injunction, all deities are included through the inclusion of both [limits], then it follows that by the force of the same injunction, all deities would have to be grasped through the sacrifice to Agni and Viṣṇu; such is the extent of the argument. In that regard:

And just as in the statement, "One offers with a winnowing basket, for by it food is prepared," the mention of the winnowing basket's quality of being a food-preparer serves as a praise and not as an indication of its utility as a means for the oblation (*homa*),
so too here is the mention of the inferiority and superiority of the two [deities], Agni and Viṣṇu.
Since it functions as a praise, it is not tenable that it is conditioned by the acceptance of another deity; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

In reality, the words *avama* (lowest) and *parama* (highest) here do not refer to inferiority or superiority, as seen in the mantra: "Agni was the first of the deities, and Viṣṇu was the highest among those who have come together."

This is because the fact that the *dīkṣiṇīyā* serves the purpose of securing the deities is established precisely by the clarification provided through the words "first" and "last"; and in that context, the word "last" (*uttama*) is used just as in the passage: "He recites the first three times and the last three times."
Because of its co-occurrence with the word "first," and because it stands in opposition to "first" as being "subsequent";

for in numerous mantras and brāhmaṇas— such as "Agni is the first of the deities" and "The gods have Agni as their mouth"— the priority of Agni is established, and thus [the meaning of] the word *avama* [is determined].
And because the conclusion of the intended meaning (tātparya) necessarily follows from this, the word "supreme" (parama) refers to what comes after.
Since the impossibility of accepting the deity to be described [later] is established by that alone,
even though Viṣṇu is a subsequent deity, Paramaśiva remains the supreme cause.
The established conclusion is that, due to the absence of contradiction, Paramaśiva alone possesses the nature of the Supreme Brahman.

Now, one might object: since the author of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā-sūtras, by formulating the aphorism "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*), has defined Brahman as the cause of the world's origin and so forth, his intended meaning culminates in Nārāyaṇa alone;
therefore, it is logical that Nārāyaṇa alone is the cause of the world. And thus:

"First, that Lord Nārāyaṇa created the waters; then the Blessed One himself created Brahmā from those waters. Such passages establish the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that, in accordance with the defining characteristics [of the texts], Nārāyaṇa alone is the cause of the world.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that in the *Mahābhārata*— composed by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā-sūtras*, for the purpose of proclaiming his own intended Supreme Brahman— it is Śiva alone who is the cause of the entire universe and possesses the nature of the Supreme Brahman, as demonstrated in both the *Bhīṣmaparvan* and the *Sabhāparvan*.
This has been established by the voice from his own throat; for it is said:
"Therein the eternal Lord of Beings, having created all the worlds, is worshipped with fierce splendor, surrounded by thousands of spirits."

By such words describing Maināka, and by the statements in the Śāntiparvan that "the Lord is conscious and the agent," it is established that this Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, is the imperishable source of all principles.
He knows the ordinances of all principles; he is the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
From his right side, the Lord created Brahmā, the source of the worlds;
likewise, from his left side, he created Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the worlds.
"And when the end of the age had arrived, he then created the Lord Rudra"—by these words from the *Anuśāsana-parvan*, [it is said]:
"I am Brahmā, as well as Kapila and Ananta; in ancient times, we were all exceedingly heroic sons of Brahmā."
All [beings] have been produced from you by the God of gods; you are the Lord of all, the causal self, and the one worthy of praise.

Thus, by means of these words from the *Harivaṃśa* occurring within the *Śivastotra* composed by Kṛṣṇa, the definition of Brahman established in the *Janmādyasya yataḥ* section— namely, that Śiva alone is the cause of all— is made manifest. Therefore, Paramaśiva alone is the supreme cause.
Regarding the descriptions in certain Śruti texts, Purāṇas, and the Mahābhārata that establish Nārāyaṇa as the supreme cause,
the ancients maintain that these incarnations, such as Kṛṣṇa and others, belong to Nārāyaṇa himself through his non-difference from Paramaśiva.
We, however, say this: this Nārāyaṇa is indeed distinct from Paramaśiva;
yet, the description of the attributes of the Supreme Brahman (Parabrahman) is thus appropriately established in him. As it was stated by Sudarśanācārya:
"He is called the Self (Ātman), and He is the Supreme Reality (Parama-tattva)."
"The supreme light is the lotus-navelled Supreme Lord;
the practitioner, whose sole delight is in the contemplation of Him and who possesses no other state of being, becomes like Garuḍa through the contemplation of Garuḍa. Thus it is said.

Nor should it be suspected that this is the reverse— that Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme cause, while Śiva’s status as the supreme cause is merely a description established through the contemplation of him as Nārāyaṇa;
for, regarding the cause of the world, there is the hearing of many contradictory specific attributes pertaining to various deities, so [of whom could it be said...]?

Regarding the question of the causality of the world, it is proper to determine that [causality] solely in accordance with those scriptural passages (śruti) whose primary intent is to ascertain a specific deity, because a scripture that has no other purpose is more authoritative.
For this very reason, when the performance of the Āgneya and Agniṣṭoma sacrifices in their respective order is required on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī), [the sequence must follow the scripture].

In the sequence of the *śruti*, the order of the recitation of the mantras alone is the regulator for the purpose of remembering the items to be performed; it is not the order of recitation of two *brāhmaṇa* passages, which have fulfilled their function by enjoining that which contradicts [the mantra order]. Thus, "but in case of conflict, it shall be according to the mantra."

This has been determined in the fifth section (*adhikaraṇa*); likewise, in the present case as well, the Upaniṣads such as the *Subāla* and others— having fulfilled their purpose by establishing the existence of the Creator, the multitude of created objects, the sequence [of creation], and so forth within the sections on cosmogony— [are not intended to establish the non-existence of the Self].
Even though, by the force of scriptural passages denoting specific individual deities, there arises the cognition of another deity as the cause,

[the inquiry] proceeds for the purpose of extracting the Creator-Brahman from the form of a specific deity, taking for granted the existence of a creator and other attributes established by other scriptural passages.

Because the *Mantra-upaniṣad* provides a powerful demonstration that Paramaśiva— designated by such terms as Hara and Śiva— is the cause of the world’s origin and so forth, it is established that Paramaśiva alone,
as the cause of the universe, is determined to be the Supreme Brahman. By this...

The opponents' conceit—that the use of the term "Nārāyaṇa" in the sections on creation is powerful—is dispelled. Nor can it be argued that the repetition of the term "Nārāyaṇa" in various sections on creation is more forceful;
for even though the word "Nārāyaṇa" is repeated many times in the sections on creation, [it remains subject to other interpretations].
Because [the term "Nārāyaṇa"] can occur as a word for the vital breath, space, the Imperishable (akṣara), and so forth— just like the case of words referring to Nārāyaṇa—
and because it is weak when in conflict with a Śruti that has no other purpose; furthermore, because in the *Atharvaśikhā* it is stated,
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra— they are all produced," and so on, regarding Brahmā and the others...

And because there is no contradiction or suspicion of reversal by demonstrating the specific relationship of cause and effect between Paramaśiva [and Nārāyaṇa]; for the demonstration of Paramaśiva as the cause of the universe does not have Nārāyaṇa as its object by casting Nārāyaṇa into the category of effects on the grounds of hearing of his birth.
It is possible to connect [the passage] in this way. Nor should it be argued that because Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra are produced from him,
the word "Viṣṇu" mentioned between Brahmā and Rudra refers to those who are his incarnations, such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.

Because there is a lack of authoritative evidence. Furthermore, even the mantra "When [there was] darkness" (tamaḥ), by demonstrating that the direct causal statements have Śiva as their object, clarifies that the teaching of Nārāyaṇa’s causality in the Subālopaniṣad and other texts also has Śiva as its object. For this very reason...
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the fact that the *Bhagavad Gītā*— which establishes Kṛṣṇa’s causality in manifold ways— is actually devoted to Śiva is explained to Pārtha:
"That divine, supreme knowledge has been understood by you exactly as it is."
Hṛṣīkeśa himself spoke with affection to the eternal one.
"Go, go to your own place; you ought not to grieve.
Worship Śiva, the refuge of those who seek shelter, with supreme devotion. Thus [he spoke].
Regarding his divine knowledge, there is a statement by Vyāsa at the conclusion of the *Īśvaragītā* in that very same work:
"The blessed Lord Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the son of Devakī, himself directly imparted this supreme [teaching] to Arjuna."
Clarifying the statement of Vyāsa, which describes that very work as a commentary on the meaning of the *Īśvaragītā*, [he says]:
"The Lord Śiva, whose characteristics are truth and so forth, is the cause of all;
neither Viṣṇu, nor Viriñci, nor Indra, nor any other person [is the cause]."
O best of beings, the Vedas and the Purāṇas, such as the Mahābhārata and others,
indeed always speak while holding Śiva together with Ambā in their hearts.

And so forth. By a thorough examination of the *Parāśara-upapurāṇa*, [the author] clarifies that all discourses on causality concerning other deities found in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other texts actually pertain to Śiva;
therefore, [it follows that] even those passages which establish the causality of other deities...

The culmination is in Paramaśiva. It is not that the passages establishing Śiva as the cause culminate elsewhere in Nārāyaṇa or others; rather, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the intention of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the Sūtras, is that Śiva alone, by virtue of being the cause of the entire universe, constitutes the state of the Supreme Brahman.
Now, at the beginning of the *Mānava-dharmaśāstra*, it is said:
"This [universe] was then enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without defining marks, beyond reasoning, indescribable, as if entirely asleep.
Then the Blessed Self-existent One, the Unmanifest, whose power had been aroused, made this manifest, beginning with the great elements."

The dispeller of darkness appeared. Desiring to bring forth various creatures from his own body, he meditated and first created the waters; into them, he cast his seed. That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun. Within it, Brahmā himself was born, the grandfather of all the worlds.

Beginning with these words, [it continues]: "The waters are called *nārāḥ*; the waters are indeed the offspring of *nara*. Since they are declared to be his *ayana* (abode), he is remembered as *Nārāyaṇa*. By this statement, [he is established] as the progenitor even of the Grandfather (Brahmā), the source of the entire world.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the name *Nārāyaṇa* is etymologically explained as the Supreme Person who is the cause [of all], it is logical that Nārāyaṇa alone possesses the status of being the cause of the world.

However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: in the statement "He appeared, the dispeller of darkness" (*prādurāsīt tamonudaḥ*), the term "dispeller of darkness" (*tamonudaḥ*) contains the suffix *kvip*.

When it is said that "the word emerged in the ablative case," and there arises an expectancy for another agent of the act of birth— asking "from what?"— then, in accordance with that expectancy, at the time denoted by the word "thence" (tataḥ), which follows the dissolution, [the emergence occurs] from Paramaśiva, who is the presiding impeller of darkness.

Because the first manifestation of Nārāyaṇa [is described], the conclusion is reached that Śiva alone is the cause of the world. Nor is there any contradiction, for when the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule "ig-upadha-jña-ā-pi-kṛ-bhyaḥ kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.135) due to its having an *ik* vowel as its penultimate (*ig-upadha*), the word *tamonudaḥ* ending in *a* becomes a nominative singular form.
It must be stated that this is an epithet of Nārāyaṇa as one who is about to manifest;

for it is impossible for him to be the presiding lord of darkness prior to the manifestation of Nārāyaṇa, who is himself established only after that manifestation. Therefore, Nārāyaṇa [arises] from Paramaśiva, the dispeller of darkness.

From the phrase "He appeared" (*prādurāsīt*), it is understood that the purport of Manu’s intention is that Paramaśiva is the progenitor of Nārāyaṇa. For this very reason, at the conclusion of the *Mānava-dharma-śāstra*, there are these words: "One should know Him as the ruler of all, subtler than the subtlest, golden-hued, and perceivable by the intellect in deep sleep."

"The Supreme Person. Having thus determined the Supreme Person, his forms are well-known as established by the statement: "Pervading all beings with five forms, he perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay."
The five known as the Brahmās are supreme; they belong to Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is the refuge of all worlds.

Thus, because the *liṅga*— which pervades the entire multitude of living beings— is established either by means of the fivefold forms beginning with Sadyojāta according to the statement of the *Ādityapurāṇa*, or by means of the pentad of earth and the other elements contained within the group of eight forms, Śiva alone exists in his supreme state (*parabhāva*).

And because this is the ultimate intent of the [author's] mind, even Yājñavalkya the Yogin— the preeminent among the authors of the Dharmaśāstras— states: "Having superimposed the wind upon the earth and conjoined it with the letter *la*,
one should meditate upon Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, in his four-armed form."

One should retain [the breath] for five *ghaṭikās*; through this retention (*dhāraṇā*), one shall attain perfection. Having projected the vital air (*vāyu*) into the water-element (*vāruṇa*) and conjoined it with the syllable *na*, one should retain [it] for five *ghaṭikās*—[visualizing it] resembling pure crystal, clad in yellow garments, and infallible (*acyuta*). One is liberated from all sins. Furthermore, having projected the vital air into the fire-element (*vahni*)...
Endowed with the letter *repha*, it is devoid of the *varada* [mudrā] and the *rudra* [seed-syllable], resembling the rising sun.
With these and other [verses], having superimposed wind upon space and endowed it with the letter *ha*,
one contemplates Mahādeva in the form of the *bindu*, Sadāśiva whose form is the void (*vyoma*).

Meditate upon Him who is fixed in the mind— resembling pure crystal, adorned with the crescent moon as His crest, possessing five faces, gentle in appearance, ten arms, and three eyes; whose hands illuminate all weapons, who is adorned with every ornament, whose body forms half of Umā’s, who grants boons, and who is the cause of all causes.

"One should maintain [the meditation] for even a moment; he alone is said to be liberated in the three worlds by those who are learned," thus it is established after describing the maintenance [of meditation] upon all beings from Brahmā down to Paramaśiva.
This is what is meant here, O Gārgī, best among the knowers of Brahman: that the forms of the effects, beginning with Brahmā, reside within one's own...

"Having withdrawn [the world] into its own cause, one whose mind is disciplined should then unite the self with the Supreme Lord. Thus, he has established that Paramaśiva alone is the cause of all; therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that Śiva alone is the cause of the universe.

But surely the Gaṅgā, the river of Viṣṇu’s feet, was held by Śiva? Regarding this, they say: "First was the water in the vessel for the ritual observances of the Primordial Grandfather (Brahmā); afterwards came the purifying water from the feet of the Blessed One who reclines upon the serpent."
Furthermore, here is seen the divine Bhāgīrathī, the daughter of the great seer Jahnu, who destroys all impurity and is the jewel adorning the matted locks of Śambhu.

Thus, the Gaṅgā, who flows from Viṣṇu’s feet, is in some places described as being in the form of water released from the water-pot of Brahmā, residing in Satyaloka, for the purpose of washing the lotus-feet of Trivikrama when they are extended upwards. In other places, however—
It is described as water flowing outward from the aperture of the upper cosmic egg, which was pierced by Viṣṇu’s foot.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa also: "When the shell was split by the spreading foot of Viṣṇu, [water flowed] from the sky..."
Then Kuṭilā fell from the edge of Viṣṇu’s foot, and from her came Kuṭilā.
"O Sage, she became famous in the world by the name Viṣṇupadī. Thus [it is said].
In the Sabhāparva of the Mahābhārata:
"Flowing forth from that opening, the river Pāvanī, the consort of the ocean, fell there at his feet and entered the ocean, the sea of worldly existence. Thus it is said.

In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, however, it is described thus: "Then, from the breaking of the egg, there fell a great mass of cool water, frequented by hosts of those who have performed meritorious deeds. In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* as well: "Above the northern region of the sages, Dhruva is situated."
This is the divine third station of Viṣṇu, radiant in the sky.

Having begun thus, it is said: "Then, O Brahmin, flows forth that river which removes all sins—the Gaṅgā, tawny with the anointing of the limbs of the celestial nymphs. Having issued from the foot of Viṣṇu and bathing the orb of the moon, the Gaṅgā indeed falls from heaven into the city of Brahmā on all sides."

Issuing from the stream of the nail of the big toe of Viṣṇu’s left lotus-foot, she whom he constantly bears upon his head day and night with devotion— from her [the Gaṅgā], the Seven Sages, devoted to the practice of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), remain, their matted locks being washed by the garlands of her waves.

She whose continuous flood of water has bathed the lunar orb, which consequently bears an ever-increasing radiance night after night; she who, having fallen from the summit of Mount Meru and emerged from the lunar orb,
flows in four directions for the purification of the world— she is Sītā.
Cālakanandā and Cakṣurbhadrā are established as one and the same,
characterized by movement through the divisions of the four directions; even Śarva bore her division known as Cālakanandā upon his head with affection for more than a hundred years.
"And the bone-fragments that issued from the mass of Śambhu’s matted locks, having purified the heavens, led the sinful sons of Sagara [to heaven]. Thus it is said.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa as well:
"The station of Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe, which is supported by Dhruva—
from that [station] the goddess Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, has issued forth."
Having entered that source of nectar, the support of the waters, the moon—
which purifies the world— encounters the continuous stream of the sun’s rays as they revolve.

Having begun with the statement, "And she fell upon the back of Meru and then went forth in four directions," and having described Sītā's arrival at the eastern ocean, [it continues: "In the same way, the river named Alakanandā flows from the Gandhamādana mountain in the south."
Having gone to Merupādavana, the Nandana grove that delights the gods.
Having purified Lake Mānasa with her great force,
she went from Mānasa to the beautiful mountain peak from the king of mountains.
And from there, having purified all those mountains where they rejoiced in the south,
they reached the great mountain Himavat.
There Śambhu, whose banner is the bull, supported her and released her;
the Lord had been propitiated by Bhagīratha through fasts, hymns of praise, and right conduct.
There, having been released by Śarva, she entered the salt ocean in seven ways; then, in the east, she indeed became threefold, known as Mahānadī.
Following Bhagīratha's chariot, [the Ganges] flowed with a single stream toward the south.
Thus it has been described in the Kedārakhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"By mere resolve alone, the unborn Lord Vāmana grew;
the earth was pervaded by Viṣṇu, the sovereign Viṣṇu, with a single step."
Even that heaven was pervaded by that great-souled one,
who remained in Satyaloka, just as the world of men is pervaded by water.
From the water that arose from contact with his feet was born Maṅgalamaṅgalā, the remover of sins,
by whom the three worlds were made pure.
And by which all the Sagaras were made prosperous.
"And by whom the matted locks of Śambhu were filled at that time by Bhagīratha. Thus [it is said].

In the *Mahābhārata*, it is described as follows: "From the foot of Viṣṇu, from Śiṃśumāra, from Dhruva, from Soma, from Sūrya, and from Viṣṇu in the form of Meru, [the Gaṅgā] descended onto the head of Śiva and then onto the Himālaya mountain. Therefore, the bearing of the Gaṅgā by Śiva is a cause for his diminution.
This is the discourse of fools who, like frogs in a well, chatter contentedly upon hearing only five or six syllables.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the bearing of the Gaṅgā cannot be accomplished by any other means; this is understood from the words of the Gaṅgā addressed to Bhagīratha in the *Mahābhārata*: "O illustrious one, I shall do as you say; there is no doubt in this matter.
However, my speed as I fall swiftly from the sky is difficult to sustain; none in the three worlds is capable [of it]."
"O King, no one else is able to sustain her except for Nīlakaṇṭha Maheśvara, the best of the gods," and so forth.
It is also understood from the words of Brahmā addressed to Bhagīratha in the *Rāmāyaṇa*:
"O King, the earth will not be able to endure the fall of Gaṅgā; indeed, [Maheśvara] is the one to sustain her."

"O Hero, I see no one other than the Wielder of the Trident [who can do so]. In the *Bhāgavata*, however, it is understood from Bhagīratha’s words addressed to Gaṅgā as she asked: "O King, there is no one capable of withstanding my momentum as I fall upon the surface of the earth; otherwise, having pierced the surface of the earth, I shall go to the subterranean realm (rasātala)."
"One should maintain the power of the Blessed One, for Rudra is the self of all embodied beings; in him this entire universe is woven, like a cloth upon its threads. Thus it is said.

And this holding back of the Gaṅgā was not only for the sake of enabling Bhagīratha’s ancestors to cross over, but also for the sake of protecting the world by preventing the destruction of the earth through the force of the Gaṅgā;
it is said to be for the purpose of refilling the ocean that had been drunk by Agastya and which thus benefits all.

For in that Āraṇyaparvan, while Brahmā was contemplating a means to refill the ocean— which had been swallowed by Agastya yet remained beneficial to all as a purifier of the world— Bhagīratha was told that he would bring down the Gaṅgā to deliver his ancestors, and that by her the ocean would be refilled.
"Embodied beings shall become free from fever; thus it has been declared and explained at length.

In this way, the bearing of the Gaṅgā—which cannot be accomplished by any other—was performed by Śiva for the sake of protecting the world, and not because he himself required purification by the Gaṅgā; rather, he bore her for the benefit of the world. Thus, for the sake of helping the world...

Even though Śiva performed the bearing of the Gaṅgā, had it been from the Viṣṇupadī [the celestial river], then Śiva would have become truly auspicious by bearing upon his head that sacred water (tīrtha) flowing from the stream issuing from her feet. [For] she who has issued from Viṣṇu’s foot flows, flooding the orb of the moon.

There would thus be scope for such statements as these. However, the distinction is that this [act of] bearing refers to the Gaṅgā Haimavatī, who was propitiated by Bhagīratha and resides in the world of the Four-faced One (Brahmā). As it has been said:
Even Gaṅgā, flowing from the foot of the Enemy of Madhu, was not indeed borne upon the head by you while you wore the elephant-hide;
rather, she was [brought] for Bhagīratha, who was intent on propitiating her.
"Having granted the boon, she flowed forth from the abode of the Hundred-Holder (Indra). Thus [it is said].
The point here is this: there are two Gaṅgās. One is the daughter of Himavat who flows in the world of Brahmā;
she was brought from the world of Brahmā to the earthly realm by Bhagīratha through a certain portion of her self.
The other originates from the foot of the Blessed One, who manifested his three strides with legs extended upward; she falls downward from that height.

In one part she is situated in the sky as a source of utility for the gods; in another part, divided into four by the wind, she flows above Mount Meru and in three directions from the city of Brahmā, falling down and entering the oceans of the east and the other quarters. Thus it is said in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:
"White-limbed, with eyes like lotus petals and dark, curly hair;
wearing white garlands and garments, she is crooked and intent on the recitation of names. Thus [it is said].
Having praised Umā, the eldest daughter of Himavat, it was said: "The ascetic woman, possessing the luster of the moon's rays, was led by the Divākaras, the Rudras,
and the Vasus to the world of Brahmā."
Then all the deities said, "O Brahmā, you ought to explain what this woman will give birth to— a son who shall be the slayer of Tāraka?"
Then the Lord of the Gods said, "This poor ascetic woman is not capable of bearing the splendor of Śiva; let this wretched girl be released."
Then, O Nārada, the crooked and enraged Kuṭilā said to Brahmā:
"O Blessed One, I shall strive in such a way that the [weapon] of Śarva, which is so difficult to overcome, [may be neutralized]."
I shall maintain this splendor; listen likewise, O best of beings, for I have propitiated Janārdana through well-performed austerity.
O Grandfather, just as I shall sustain that power of Hara, so shall I act, O Lord;
what I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.
Then, O great sage, the blessed Grandfather Brahmā, the Lord of all, being enraged, commanded Kuṭilā, who was exceedingly fierce.
Since you, O crooked woman, have not remained within my word regarding this evil deed,
therefore you shall be consumed by my curse this very day.
O sage, having been thus cursed by Brahmā, the daughter of Himavat,
consisting of water, flowed with great speed and flooded the world of Brahmā.
Seeing that river with its waters risen,
the great-grandfather bound it firmly with the verbal bonds of the Ṛg, Sāman, Atharvan, and Yajus.
"O Brahman, that daughter of the mountain remained bound exactly as she was, consisting of water and flooding the pure matted locks of Brahmā. Thus it is said.

In this context, the Gaṅgā herself is mentioned under the alternative name "Kuṭilā," as stated in the Rāmāyaṇa: "O Rāghava, these two daughters of the King of Mountains, honored by the world— the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, and the goddess Umā."
Because the word "Gaṅgā" was seen in place of the word "Kuṭilā" in the verse concerning Umā, the daughter of Himavat and the eldest [of the goddesses].

Then all the gods, desiring to accomplish a divine purpose, requested the eldest daughter from the lord of mountains— the river Gaṅgā who flows through the three paths. Himavat, in accordance with righteousness, gave his daughter, the purifier of the worlds.
Out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds, [he brought] the Gaṅgā, who flows according to her own will, [down to earth].
Then the gods, who work for the welfare of the three worlds, having accepted [the boon],
took up the Gaṅgā and departed with their inner selves fulfilled.

This is because the aforementioned account of her crooked course is presented in summary form within the *Rāmāyaṇa* itself regarding Gaṅgā. Thus, first of all, the primordial Gaṅgā of the Himavat, having attained a state of non-attainment (*asiddhitva*) due to a curse from Brahmā, reached the earth out of deference to the devotion of Bhagīratha and became the "Three-pathed One" (*tripathagā*).

This has been described with authoritative evidence. However, the other Gaṅgā, Viṣṇupadī, is in some places said to be the water released from the water-pot of Brahmā residing in Satyaloka for the purpose of washing the lotus feet of Trivikrama when they are extended upwards; thus, since two Gaṅgās are established, [the objection does not apply].
Since it has been stated that Gaṅgā resides upon the head of Śiva, there is no room for the doubt that she has been pierced through.

Now, let this be so; nevertheless, at the time of the Gaṅgā’s emergence from Viṣṇu’s foot, the Haimavatī situated on her path became mixed with her. Therefore, the following doubt—that she is called "pāvanī" (purifying) because she was held by Śiva upon his head—is refuted by establishing that her purifying nature arises precisely from her connection to Śiva’s head.
O Rāma, at the words of Viśvāmitra,
Śivā fell from the sky onto the auspicious head of Śiva;
and that goddess Gaṅgā, who is exceedingly difficult to restrain, reflected thus.
"I shall indeed enter Pātāla, seizing Śaṅkara by the current.
Knowing his arrogance, the Blessed Lord Hara became enraged.
Then the Three-eyed Lord resolved to cause her intellect to disappear;
that meritorious [intellect] fell upon the holy head of Rudra.
There, the celestial sages, gandharvas, and those dwelling on the surface of the earth touched the water fallen from the body of Bhava, thinking it to be purifying. Thus [it is said].

In this context, by the words "in Śiva," "on the head of Śiva," and "on the meritorious summit of Rudra," the supreme auspiciousness and supreme purity of Śiva’s crown are expressed; thus, it is established as the final conclusion that Śiva alone possesses the sovereignty over all deities.

Now, an objection may be raised: since it is established in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other texts that the one residing in the center of the solar orb is the object of the Gāyatrī mantra and is therefore the object of all worship, Nārāyaṇa alone must be the one denoted by that mantra.
For instance: "Now, that golden person who is within the sun... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6).
"He is seen with golden beard and golden hair, entirely golden down to his fingernails; as a lotus flower is reddish-yellow like a monkey's buttocks, so are his eyes," and so forth.

According to this scriptural passage, it is established that only the one residing within the solar orb is prescribed as the object of meditation. Therefore, the one to be meditated upon therein is...

It is Viṣṇu alone, and not Śiva; for the term *puṇḍarīkākṣa* (lotus-eyed) refers to Nārāyaṇa both by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and etymological derivation (*yoga*). Furthermore, because of the natural force of the dual number in *akṣiṇī* (two eyes), it refers exclusively to Nārāyaṇa and not to Śiva, who is well known to possess three eyes. Moreover, regarding the word *puruṣa*, [it refers to] the Puru...

Because he lies within this body, which is a mere designation (*saṃjñā*), the Person is Hari; here, the letter *śa* is used interchangeably with the letter *ṣa*. Thus, both the word "Bhagavān" and "Puruṣa" apply without qualification to the eternal Vāsudeva—this is according to the perspective that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme.

In accordance with the established corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), it is Viṣṇu alone who is to be meditated upon as residing within the solar orb; for this very reason, it is he alone whose status as the subject of the *Gāyatrī* mantra is logically justified. For this same reason, he is "to be meditated upon always" (*dhyeyaḥ sadā*).

It is also consistent [with scripture] that Nārāyaṇa, situated in the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, makara-earrings, a crown, and necklaces, possessing a golden body, and holding the conch and the discus.

Nor should it be argued that the object of meditation is that which resides in the center of the solar orb, and that this is simply the deity in the form of Sūrya who presides over that orb; for it is not established in lexicons and other authorities that the word *āditya* denotes the deity who presides over the orb.
Since words ending in the nominative case are naturally understood as referring to objects distinct from that [the sun], they do not refer to the sun itself. Nor can the word *āditya*,
which denotes the one who presides over the orb, be applied to a single part of that orb, namely the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), by means of the potsherd.

One should not argue that, just as in the case of the injunction "he scatters husks," one must accept a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a single part and thereby accept that words ending in the nominative case refer to the deities presiding over those parts; for when the primary meaning is possible, resorting to figurative indication is improper. Furthermore, in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa, regarding the one who is in the sun...

"Standing, He controls from within the sun; the sun does not know Him. If the word "sun" (āditya) were to denote the individual soul (jīva) who identifies with the solar orb, then this very scripture would serve as the authority for the fact that the object of meditation is distinct from it; how then could [the passage] refer to the sun? Therefore, [it refers to] the Sun—[not the individual soul].

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that Nārāyaṇa alone is the one to be worshipped as the Sun situated in the center of the maṇḍala; therefore, by virtue of being the subject expounded by the Gāyatrī mantra, he alone possesses the status of being the supreme among all.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that [the Lord within the sun] is he who is "copper-colored, ruddy, and tawny, most auspicious; he who glides along, blue-necked and deep red"—for by these two verses, it is Śiva alone, denoted by the term "blue-necked," who is presented as residing within the solar orb. Therefore, [it refers to] "he who is within the sun."

Even according to the Śruti text, "The golden person is seen," this [text] refers exclusively to Śiva, by virtue of the recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of the term "tāmra" from the Śruti passage [cited earlier]. Furthermore, just as upon hearing the word "nīlagrīva," the words "Nārāyaṇa" and so forth— which are well-known in lexicons and other sources— [are understood to refer to Śiva].

In that regard, since [the word "eye"] is not heard there, how can it be determined that [the reference] is to Nārāyaṇa as the supreme? Nor should it be argued that the dual ending in "akṣiṇī" is untenable; for a dual number does not merely indicate duality, nor is it capable of establishing that a third eye does not exist. Indeed, the fact that Devadatta has two sons does not imply that he has no third son.

In the phrase "the two righteous ones," it can be determined that there is no third son; however, it is sufficient to produce the certainty that the third son is unrighteous. Similarly, here too, while the two eyes of the Supreme Lord are like lotuses, the third—

The determination that [the space] is filled with garlands of flames of fire arises from the dual number. Therefore, there is no obstacle whatsoever to its referring to Śiva. As for what was said—that because the word *puruṣa* refers to Nārāyaṇa, how could Śiva possibly be the object of worship—that is utterly inconsistent. For it is said: "Righteousness (*ṛta*) is truth (*satya*)."
"By the two Vedic passages, 'We know the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, who is dark and tawny;
