we meditate upon the Great God, the thousand-eyed Puruṣa,' and by the mantra contained within the Pañcabrahma-mantras, 'We know that Puruṣa...'; [it is said] 'Rudra is indeed the Puruṣa; salutations, salutations to the Great Being.'"
By the *Tvaritarudra* mantra: "The Person, the size of a thumb, who rests upon the thumb—the Lord of the entire world, the Master, the Sustainer of the universe—He is pleased.
And by the *Taittirīya* mantra: "The Person, the size of a thumb, He is the Ruler of what has been and what is to be. He is that very one.
Furthermore, since the *Kaṭhavallī* mantra, "He who is the Lord of this [world] from the beginning," establishes that the word *puruṣa* refers to Śiva—

both by its designation as a name and by the principle of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term "the sole source of life"— how could it possibly refer to Nārāyaṇa? Nor can it be argued that the word *puruṣa* denotes both the Self (*ātman*) and a human being (*mānava*).

It must be addressed how it can be asserted that the word "man" (*manuṣya*), which denotes a human being common to all, refers to Śiva when it appears in the *Nighaṇṭu*. This being the case, [the same applies to] words such as "breath" (*prāṇa*), "ether" (*ākāśa*), "light" (*jyotis*), and "Vaiśvānara," as found in the *Nighaṇṭu*, the *Kāvya*, and other texts.
[The following sūtras establish that certain terms refer to Paraśiva: "Ākāśa [is Brahman] because of its characteristic mark";
"Vaiśvānara [is Brahman] because of the distinction of the common term"; "Jyotis [is Brahman] because of the mention of the feet"; for this very reason.

Otherwise, there would be no determination [of the subject] as being the Supreme Lord based on the sūtras of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, such as "Prāṇa" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.23) and so forth. Now, in determining the meaning of a word,
just like a lexicon, the introduction, the conclusion, repetition, and other unique indicative marks (*liṅga*) are also determinants of the meaning.

Regarding the word *ā*: for it has been established by the commentator Ācārya Vācaspatimiśra in the *Bhāmatī* that when there is repetition (*abhyāsa*), there is indeed an increase in the meaning; it does not become diminished, much less does it become figurative (*upacarita*). Therefore, it is not the case here...

The claim that [the term] "determiner of word and meaning" is merely a delusion of a few people ignorant of the true nature of words and their meanings, establishes that the word *puruṣa* refers exclusively to Śiva. As for the argument that, by the power of yoga, the phrase "in this body known as *puruṣa*" refers to Nārāyaṇa, that too is extremely weak; for one beholds the *puruṣa* who dwells in the city (*puri*).

Thus, because the general definition [of the word] has been determined by the scripture itself to have Śiva as its referent through the previously mentioned criteria of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth; and because, in the event of a conflict with the etymological interpretation found in Smṛti, the principle of the *adhikaraṇa*— "it would be unreliable, for there is no inference when [the scripture] exists"— [applies], the [Smṛti] is dependent upon the scriptural definition.

Due to its weakness, it is simply not to be respected. Precisely for this reason, by the force of numerous scriptural passages, the word *Nārāyaṇa* found in the verse "He should always be meditated upon as abiding in the center of the solar orb" is determined to mean Nārāyaṇa himself;
for in the case of the term *nārāyaṇī*—meaning "the wife of Nārāyaṇa"—it is like [the terms] *upādhyāyī*, *kṣatriyī*, or *āryī*, which denote the female counterpart of the male.

Śiva alone is the one denoted by the word Nārāyaṇa. For this very reason, Purāṇic statements such as "the blue-throated, three-eyed Lord with Ambā, situated in the midst of the solar orb, the medicine for the world," are also consistent when referring to Śiva. Therefore, it is Paraśiva alone who resides in the center of the solar orb.
Since He alone is the subject matter expounded by the Gāyatrī, Śiva alone possesses the state of being supreme over all.

Now, one might object: "Even if it is established by scriptural discourse that Śiva is the object of worship as residing within the solar orb, how can he be the one propounded by the Gāyatrī? Rather, it must be Nārāyaṇa alone.
This doubt arises only for those who do not fully understand the meaning of the word "Gāyatrī. As for him who...
"May the divine Savitṛ impel our thoughts toward that excellent *bhargas* which is beyond the sphere of *dharma*";
since this is the etymological interpretation (*nirukti*) of the seer, and because the object of worship exists within the solar orb (*ādityamaṇḍala*), this constitutes the meaning of the *gāyatrī*.
Since this has been definitively established, what dispute can there be regarding the fact that Śiva alone is the one propounded by the Gāyatrī?
[Objection: But surely it is Nārāyaṇa who is propounded by the Gāyatrī;
for instance, in the section beginning with "The light [is Brahman] because of the mention of its feet" (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa), the Supreme Brahman is that which is denoted by the word "light."

Having stated, "Because of the designation 'caraṇa' (foot)," and in response to the inquiry "Where is the designation 'pāda' (quarter)? [it is said]: "In the preceding section, this very thing was declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: 'Such is His greatness; yet the Puruṣa is greater than that; all beings constitute but one quarter of Him.'"

If it is argued that [the Brahman] is not [meant here] because the previous section dealt with the designation of the three feet and this section deals with the designation of the meter (*chandas*), we say no;

for, according to the Sūtra, "Because there is a statement regarding the fixing of the mind [on it], and because such is seen [in scripture]," the Gāyatrī is established as the object of meditation in the passage:
"The Gāyatrī, indeed, is all this being, whatever exists here. Thus, it is the Gāyatrī that is presented as the object of worship.

Having raised the objection as to how that which is denoted by the word "light" (jyotis) can have the Supreme Lord as its referent, it must be stated that the Supreme Lord alone is the object of worship by means of the Gāyatrī;
this is because of the recognition of the Puruṣasūkta mantras, and because the Puruṣasūkta has Nārāyaṇa as its primary referent.

Since the mantra thus recognized must necessarily be devoted to that [deity], the Gāyatrī cannot have Nārāyaṇa as its supreme object. Furthermore, because of the Nirukta’s statement, "The god Savitṛ is for us," which refers to him in a general form, there is no exclusive devotion to Śiva; rather, it is the goat [that is meant].

On account of the words of the mantra—according to the principle of the sixth section on the penultimate [letter], supported by the reasoning stated previously—the supreme referent is Nārāyaṇa alone; we do not perceive any indicative marks or statements that point toward Śiva as the referent.
Furthermore, regarding the word *bharga*: the root *bhṛñ* means "to sustain," *ramu* means "to sport," and *gamal* means "to go."
Thus, because the word *bharga* is derived from three verbal roots (*dhātu*) and, by virtue of its reference to Vāyu, possesses the nature of Viṣṇu;

nor is it the case that the derivation of the word does not occur from three roots at all— for since it is derived from the root *bhṛj* (meaning "to burn"), it ultimately refers to Rudra alone as the cause of dissolution, and not [to Viṣṇu].

It should be stated that [the word *bharga*] refers exclusively to Viṣṇu; for, just as the word *adbhuta*— derived from the two verbal roots *ad* (meaning "to eat") and *bhū* (meaning "to exist") established by the grammatical sūtra *adi-bhū-bhyām ḍutac*— is applicable to Viṣṇu, so too is the word *bharga*.

If it is argued that, therefore, because the Gāyatrī is devoted to Viṣṇu, it is established that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, then this must be considered as follows: what was asserted— that the verse "tāvānasya mahimā" (so great is His majesty) is devoted to Viṣṇu on the basis of its recognition as part of the Puruṣasūkta— is inconsistent, [given] the Puruṣasūkta’s...

Since it has been determined in many ways that the [text] recognized in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* refers to Śiva, there is no possibility of its referring to Viṣṇu due to the recognition of those mantras;
therefore, the Gāyatrī mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa passage, "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," is not [that same Gāyatrī].

[The Gāyatrī] is devoted to Viṣṇu, yet it is devoted to Śiva. Furthermore, the fact that the Gāyatrī impels the intellect is heard in scripture; this, however, is a unique characteristic (liṅga) of Śiva alone. For it is said: "That syllable is the most excellent [quality] of Savitṛ, and from it the ancient wisdom has issued forth."

This [verse] establishes that it is Śiva alone who impels wisdom, preceded by a recognition of the meaning of the Gāyatrī. Likewise, in another mantra: "He who first generated Hiraṇyagarbha—may He endow us with auspicious understanding"; and "Behold Hiraṇyagarbha being born—may He [endow] us..."

"May He unite us with auspicious intellect; may that God unite us with auspicious mindfulness"—through such mantras, it is established by the power of repeated practice that Śiva alone is the impeller of the intellect. As for what was stated—that because the word *bharga* is derived from three verbal roots, it refers to Viṣṇu—[that is refuted].

That too is rooted in a complete ignorance of the boundaries established by the grammarians (*vaiyyākaraṇa*). For instance, the derivation of a single word from three verbal roots (*dhātu*) has never been observed anywhere in grammar; however, the formation of the word *adbhuta* occurs because the suffix *ḍutac* is prescribed for the root *bhū* when the particle *aditi* is used as an attendant word (*upapada*). Thus it is said of that [word]: [it is derived from *aditi* and *bhū*].

There is no accomplishment whatsoever from two elements. Furthermore, regarding the fact that the Gāyatrī has Śiva as its ultimate referent, there are corroborative statements in the third part of the Himavat-khaṇḍa, in the second chapter of the *Śivarahasya*:
"In ancient times, Gāyatrī performed supreme and most formidable penance."
Śambhu was pleased by that austerity and by his supreme devotion.
Thereafter, the Blessed Lord Bharga, the cause of creation and the other cosmic processes,
spoke to her with words that were exceedingly clever and profoundly deep, like a thundercloud.
"O Goddess, you have certainly performed severe penance for ten thousand kalpas;
therefore, I am pleased with you—choose a boon according to your desire."
Among the bestowers of boons, I am the most excellent, the granter of the boons you desire;
what is there that cannot be given by me here? I am now pleased by your ascetic penance.
Having heard those words, she prostrated herself on the ground like a staff;
then, assuming the form of Gāyatrī, she was overwhelmed with tears of joy.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Bharga, destroyer of saṃsāra; O renowned ocean of compassion, grant me the boon I desire.
The scripture states that a mantra is unfit for recitation in the absence of the state of Śiva;
Śaṅkara awakens the intellect of the divine Savitṛ.
May that very Lord, the effulgence who impels our intellects,
[grant] the supreme knowledge of the shining Sun-god.
He who impels [the world] is the Universal Self; he alone is the most excellent Śiva. Who else indeed could impel that excellence of the Sun?
Whether for us or for others, he is indeed Śaṅkara, who is Bharga;
the greatness of this very word "Bharga" is heard in the Vedas.
Because he burns away saṃsāra, he is Bharga; he is the bestower of heaven and liberation.

Based on such corroborative statements as these, it is established that the word *bharga* refers exclusively to Śiva; thus, the conclusion is that Śiva alone is the subject matter expounded by the Gāyatrī.
Now, it is established that Paramaśiva is denoted by the syllable *praṇava*:
Prajāpati brooded over the worlds; from them, as they were being brooded upon, that which is knowledge flowed forth;
he brooded over that [knowledge]; from it, as it was being brooded upon, these syllables [emerged].
They flowed forth; he brooded over them, and from them, thus brooded upon, the syllable *oṃ* flowed forth.
Just as all leaves are pierced by a pin, so is all speech pierced by the syllable *oṃ*. "The syllable *oṃ* is indeed all this"—thus it is because of its being the essence of all Vedic speech.

Furthermore, because it is established as the locus of the dissolution of all speech, and because the *praṇava* is supreme among all words due to its being the most venerable, Śiva is that which is expressed by it; thus, Śiva alone is supreme. [As it is said: "Making the Self the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill..."
"By the practice of churning through meditation, one may see the God as if hidden"—
thus, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad,
because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with terms such as Śiva, Rudra, and Maheśvara, [the text] has Śiva as its ultimate referent.
Because the word "Deva" is used to establish that the Praṇava denotes Śiva alone, who is renowned in the world, Śiva’s status as the supreme of all is affirmed.

But surely, it is Viṣṇu alone who is denoted by the Praṇava; for [it is said]: "Viṣṇu, whose body is adorned with a shining crown, armlets, bracelets, necklaces, and jeweled waistbands, and whose chest, feet, and hips are graced by ornaments, and whose limbs are embellished by a beautiful breast-jewel and great makara-shaped earrings."

Since the verse on the meditation upon the *praṇava* exists precisely as having Viṣṇu as its referent— because in various Upaniṣads there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "Brahman" and "Self," as in "The *praṇava* is the bow, the Self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target," and [as in] "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa"— [it follows that he is Viṣṇu].

Since, according to the statement of the Gītā, the word *ātman*— which denotes the *praṇava* (the syllable *Oṃ*)— can also apply to Viṣṇu, and because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Brahman" in the passage, "The designation of Brahman as *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat* is considered to be threefold," the words *Oṃ*,
*Tat*, and *Sat* refer to Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*).

Since it is possible for that which is to be expressed to be denoted [by a word], Nārāyaṇa alone is the referent of the word *praṇava*. For this very reason, the statement of the learned also comes to pass: "The conscious portion, all-pervading, stainless, free from conceptual construction, desireless, and formless, is accessible through the syllable *oṃ*. Therefore, the status of being the referent of the *praṇava* belongs to Viṣṇu alone.
In the *Rāmāyaṇa* it is said: "You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call, you are the syllable *oṃ*, and you are Prajāpati.

Therefore, since it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the one denoted by the *praṇava*, his status as the supreme of all is proven—if this is argued, it is replied here: "That which is proclaimed as the sound at the beginning of the Vedas and is established at the end of the Vedas—of that [sound] which is merged into primordial nature (*prakṛti*), he who..."

In the Taittirīya Śruti, it is said: "The Vedas, beginning with the Praṇava, O Sage, are firmly established in the Praṇava. Furthermore, by the statement of Manu: "That which is not preceded and followed by the Oṃkāra perishes at the beginning and end of the Vedas," [the Supreme Being] must necessarily be understood as the referent of the Praṇava that is recited.

Because it is the teaching of Śiva alone, who is denoted by the term Maheśvara, and because it is established by the previously cited Śvetāśvatara mantra that Śiva alone is what is expressed by the *praṇava*,
[he is so designated] through the general forms of the words *brahman* and *ātman* in their respective Upaniṣads and in the Gītā.

The *praṇava* being recited refers exclusively to Śiva. And regarding the phrase "of him who is dissolved in *prakṛti*": he who is beyond *prakṛti*—that is, beyond the form (*ākāra*)—is Maheśvara, the Great Lord; for in expressions such as "this is prior" (*idam pūrvaḥ*) or "that is beyond" (*tatparaḥ*), when the word "beyond" (*para*) is heard, that which is expressed as being beyond is the Great Lord.

Thus, by explaining the meaning— supported by the Smṛti that the syllable *ākāra* denotes Viṣṇu— it must be stated that the Praṇava denotes Viṣṇu alone and not Śiva; for, in this way, through such a strained interpretation, the word *para*, which according to the limits of lexicography (*kośamaryādā*) signifies "excellent," would be made to refer to Śiva.

Furthermore, since the word *maheśvara* can appropriately refer to Śiva—as evidenced by the statement of the learned Kālidāsa that "Maheśvara is indeed Tryambaka and no other"—it is utterly improper to resort to a circuitous interpretation for the sake of establishing your own position. And thus, its meaning is as follows: of him...
The genitive case in "of Viṣṇu" (viṣṇoḥ) is used in the sense of the ablative, referring to Viṣṇu who is dissolved into the letter 'A', which is the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the Praṇava;
this is like the expressions "he makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya svaruṃ karoti*) or "he takes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpāt svarum upādatte*).
Scripture itself states that He who is beyond and superior to Viṣṇu is indeed Maheśvara.

Since it declares that Śiva is denoted by the word *praṇava* and possesses superiority over Viṣṇu, Śiva’s status as the most excellent of all is established through His being the referent of the word *praṇava*. Even therein, He is to be understood as the *nāda* consisting of the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*), which is superior to the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m* that denote the forms of the manifested effects.

Because it is established that "Śiva" is the fourth [state], consisting of half a mora, beyond conventional usage, the cessation of phenomenal expansion, non-dual, and indeed the syllable *oṃ*, Śiva alone is what is denoted by the word *praṇava*. For this very reason, a corroboration is also heard in the *Śaiva Purāṇa*:
The syllable Om (praṇava) is the designator of that Śiva, the Supreme Self;
the letter A is the great seed, the quality of passion (rajas), and the four-faced creator.
The syllable *U* is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the womb; it is the essence (*sattva*), the protector Hari.
The syllable *Ma* is the person (*puruṣa*), the seed; it is darkness (*tamas*), the destroyer Hara.
The Nāda is the Supreme Person, the Lord, devoid of qualities, inactive, and auspicious;
thus, by these three measures alone, everything is threefold.
Having denoted the self that is Śiva, it awakens [the soul] by means of the half-mora;
for this Praṇava is indeed Śiva, or Śiva is remembered as the Praṇava.
"There is no absolute difference between the signified and the signifier anywhere.

Because Viṣṇu is described as being of the nature of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), and because Paramaśiva transcends that by being signified by the fourth half-mora (*mātrā*), he is the supreme among all. For this very reason, the venerable Puṣpadanta [said]:

O You who transcend all transformation, You express the three Vedas, the three modes of conduct, the three worlds, and even the three gods by means of the three syllables beginning with the letter 'na';
and by subtle sounds, You encompass Your fourth state.
O Giver of Refuge, the syllable "Om" praises you both collectively and individually.

Thus it has been well said. As for what was stated—that [Brahman] is "to be reached by the syllable Om," that "the syllable Om is Prajāpati," and so forth in the Viṣṇubhujaṅga, Rāmāyaṇa, and other texts—all of that is indeed favorable to our position, as it refers to Viṣṇu, who is denoted by the letter *Ā* which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *praṇava*. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

There is no contradiction. As for what was stated—that the verse on the meditation on *praṇava* has Viṣṇu as its referent—that is also consistent because it concerns meditation on the deities presiding over the letters of the *praṇava*, just like the meditations on the *vyāhṛtis*, the *gāyatrī*, and so forth. By that much alone, [it refers] to Śiva himself.

Regarding the fact that He is the controller of that which is denoted by the *praṇava*, the *praṇava* indeed signifies the Supreme Brahman; for the *praṇava* is the supreme state, and through its union [it is] directly Paraśiva. By reflecting upon such numerous authorities, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that Śiva alone, who is denoted by the *praṇava*, is the highest of all.

Now, the consideration of the *tāraka* (the saving mantra): Indeed, for a living being desiring to die at Maṇikarṇikā in Kāśī, it is taught by the Śruti that "when his vital breaths are departing, Rudra explains the *tāraka* Brahman. Thus, the *tāraka* is the unique cause of liberation.

In response to the inquiry as to what its form is, [he said]: "To you who are about to die and are staying half-submerged in the waters of Maṇikarṇikā, I shall impart the mantra known as the Tāraka-Brahman. 'Śrī Rāma, Rāma, Rāma'—this indeed is called the Tāraka. Therefore, Janakīnātha is certainly the Supreme Brahman."

By reflecting upon the statements in the *Padmapurāṇa* regarding the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava, as well as through such authoritative sources as, "The bull-bannered Lord [Śiva] muttered the mantra of Śrī Rāma in Kāśī for a thousand *manvantaras* through recitation,
fire-offerings, worship, and so forth," he attained the fortune of liberation for those seeking release.

Indeed, for a living being residing in Karṇālaṅkāra— who dwells in the half-water of Maṇikarṇikā, which is the primary sacred field (kṣetra), and who is the right ear of the multitude of seekers of liberation dwelling in Vārāṇasī— the mantra taught by the Supreme Lord is itself proclaimed by the Śruti.

"I [speak] to Pārvatī, who is the most intimate inner self, for the purpose of determining the meaning of the word *tāraka*— which was not yet determined— by the Supreme Lord himself, in accordance with the short *Jābāla Upaniṣad* which states: 'The Blessed Lord Rudra taught the saving *brahman*.'"

Since the status of the Rāma-mantra alone as the "Tāraka" (the Savior) is established by Purāṇic statements that determine the meaning of the Śruti— beginning with "O Diśās, [teach] the mantra known as Tāraka-Brahman," and concluding with "Indeed, 'Śrī Rāma, Rāma, Rāma' is called the Tāraka"— [it follows that] the mantra of Śrī Rāma [is to be recited] in Kāśī...
And because it establishes that Śiva is a worshipper [of the Praṇava], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that Viṣṇu alone is the supreme of all.

However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since it is proven by authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) that the Praṇava alone possesses the quality of being the "savior" (*tāraka*), the claim that any other mantra is the savior is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*); thus, it is established that the Praṇava alone is the savior.
For instance,

[the nature] of the *praṇava* is established by the statements of the *Atharvaśikhā* and other Upaniṣads, by the words of authoritative persons following them, and by the statements of the *Śivarahasya* and other Purāṇas which serve as their supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*).
In Vārāṇasī, it is clearly established that [the teaching] takes the form of the *tāraka* mantra as it is being imparted at the time of death,
and that it likewise takes the form of the *tāraka* mantra when accompanied by its individual constituent, the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*).
To explain:
The breeze, fragrant with musk and the pollen of flowers,
born from the upper garment on the left breast of Pārvatī,
removes the exhaustion of death from people.
At the time of the instruction on the Praṇava in Madhikāśī.
Fools whisper into the ear, "Recite the name of Śrī Rāma," for those who know the Vedas do not say so;
you alone, O Maheśvara, are indeed the Savior established by the Vedas.
In Kāśī, you alone are the perpetual teacher of the Praṇava.

In Kāśī, Śiva, the supreme, describes the five-syllabled savior-mantra (*pañcākṣara-tāraka*) as being thus endowed with the *praṇava*, that jewel among the crest-jewels of the Vedas; out of reverence for this,
Kāśī has been propitiated by the entire multitude of silent ascetics, beginning with Dūrvāsas.
This very city of Śiva, which rests upon Śambhu, has been resorted to by the maiden of liberation.

Thus, because the word *praṇava*— in its form as a collective whole (*samaṣṭi*)— is determined to be the "savior" (*tāraka*) through such scriptural passages, Purāṇas, the words of the learned, and the *Śivarahasya*, the *praṇava* alone is the savior.
Since it consists of six syllables, among its six forms, the letter *ṅa* has the shape of the savior, and the letter *ma*...

The staff (*daṇḍa*) is described as follows: the letter *śa* is shaped like a ring (*kuṇḍala*), the letter *vā* is like a half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the letter *ya* is like a mirror (*darpaṇa*), and the *praṇava* is of the nature of light (*jyotis*). By reflecting upon such statements, [one understands] the forms of the *tāraka-daṇḍa*, the *kuṇḍala*, the *ardhacandra*, and the *darpaṇa*, which constitute the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the *praṇava*.
Because the letters *na*, *ma*, *śi*, *vā*, and *ya* are taught as a collective whole (*samaṣṭi*),

and because there is no difference between the *praṇava* and the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*) in their forms as both the collective and the individual, it is established that the five-syllabled mantra, like the *praṇava*, possesses the quality of being a "savior" (*tāraka*).

Nor should it be argued that since the *rāma-mantra*— "Śrī Rāma, Rāma, Rāma"— is declared to be the savior (*tāraka*) when recited three times, how can the *praṇava* (Oṃ) possess the quality of being the savior? For [the *rāma-mantra*] is that in which they delight...

For it is said in the Umāsaṃhitā: "Indeed, at the end [of practice], yogins [rest] in the true bliss that is the self of consciousness (cidātman). Thus, by the word *rāma*, the Supreme Brahman is denoted;
for according to the rule "in the sense of location and instrument," [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*), as in: "Yogins delight (*ramante*) in this."

Furthermore, because the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed by the sūtra in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and because instruction [regarding this] is observed among those in the fourth stage of life (*turyāśrama*) who are practitioners of yoga seeking liberation, it is the *praṇava* alone that denotes that [state]. Otherwise,
[there would be no such realization for one] born of Daśaratha and Kausalyā [who, despite his status, suffered] through separation from Sītā.

If Rāma were the referent of the word *tāraka*— being like an ordinary human who was extremely distressed and subsequently obtained the Pāśupata weapon through the initiation of Virajā by the power of Agastya’s instruction—
it would result in a contradiction with many Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇa texts. Furthermore, if it were [the case] that [this applies] only to the name Rāma...
If, on the strength of the previously mentioned authorities, the quality of being a "savior" (tārakatva) were to be accepted [for Rāma],

then, because Rāma is non-different from Nārāyaṇa, by virtue of the instruction of his mantra, all those desiring to die would attain identity of form with Nārāyaṇa after death, and not identity of form with Śiva. Furthermore:
"I am a hare, I am a mosquito, I am an elephant, formerly I was a human"—

thus do the newly initiated devotees of Śiva dwelling in the city of Kāśī converse with one another. Even when the common mark of Śaṅkara is applied to the people residing in Vārāṇasī, there remains on their heads the scar from the blow of Arjuna’s arrow.
This would contradict many authoritative proofs, such as [the statement] "It reveals the Ancient Lord" (prācīnamīśam), and so forth.
Therefore, the Tāraka mantra is indeed the Praṇava, and that which is expressed by it is Paramaśiva alone; thus, Śiva’s status as the supreme of all is beyond dispute.

Regarding the "selection of the Pāśupata": indeed, by virtue of the traditional lexicographical authority (*abhidhānakośasmṛti*) which states that Śambhu is the Lord (*īśa*) and the Master of Beasts (*paśupati*), the term *paśupati* is well-known as a name unique to Śiva. Furthermore, it is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*), like the word *paṅkaja* ("lotus"). Consequently, because the conventional sense emerges, there is also the manifestation of the meaning of the sacrifice; thus, [the phrase refers to] the beasts...

Based on the etymological derivation that "the Lord is Paśupati," it must be stated that *pāśupatya*— devotion solely to Śiva— is established through the power of yoga (*yogabala*). Just as the capacity to produce a lotus, though common to grass and other plants,
is understood specifically as the lotus alone due to the greatness of yoga, so too is this *pāśupatya* perceived as adventitious (*āgantuka*) through the majesty of yoga.

Regarding the doubt as to whether [the state] is innate (*sahajasiddha*) or not, through an examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is established that it is indeed adventitious (*āgantuka*).

Since this adventitious Pāśupata state is to be attained from one who has transcended oneself, it follows that one's own inferiority and the superiority of the giver of the Pāśupata initiation are proven; such are the synonyms for the term "Paśupati."

Words such as *Śambhu* and others also denote the Reality that transcends all. Regarding this, there is a scriptural authority (*śruti*) in the second section of the sixth book of the *Yajurveda*: "He said, 'I choose a boon:
let me alone be the lord of cattle'; therefore, Rudra is the lord of cattle"—this is indeed the scripture itself.
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is that the statement "it was chosen as a boon by Rudra" implies that Śiva’s Pāśupata [vow] was merely adventitious and induced by another.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that before this sentence comes into operation, [the bridegroom] must already have been chosen;

otherwise, the statement "he said" would be untenable as a description of a past event (*bhūtārthavāda*). Therefore, wherever this sentence is recited in successive previous kalpas from time immemorial, from each of those instances...

From this very statement—that "one must possess the Pāśupata [discipline] which was established previously"—it follows that the Pāśupata is beginningless (*anādi*). In the same way, the eternality (*nityatva*) of sacrifices, oblations, and so forth, which are presented as having been obtained through the granting of boons by various deities, must be supported; otherwise, [the system would lack authority].
Otherwise, the non-eternality of all Vedic rituals would follow, resulting in a collapse of dharma and adharma due to the differences between kalpas; therefore,
by means of making known the connection with those respective deities and rituals as eternally established, [the mantra]— as heard in proximity to them— [serves its purpose].

The explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning the choice of the bridegroom is for the purpose of praising ritual action; likewise, this [passage] also has the purpose of praising ritual action by means of proclaiming the state of being eternally established as Paśupati. In this very way, even the extreme degradation that might otherwise accrue to Viṣṇu in various contexts [is avoided].

This must be avoided; otherwise, there would result an extreme degradation of Viṣṇu, who—according to scripture—is heard to have been brought by the gods through their own will to occupy the middle part of the arrow that was prepared for the destruction of Tripura, with the mantra: "They prepared the arrow; Soma is its barb; Viṣṇu is its feathers; [Indra] the people."

It would be impossible to prevent [the attainment]. Therefore, this [statement] is for the purpose of praising the ritual action, because it serves as the means for obtaining the *pāśupata* boon. In this regard, the essential point is this:
liberation, which consists in the removal of the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), is dependent upon the performance of the *pāśupata* vow.

Furthermore, the performance of that [practice] depends upon the knowledge: "We, such as gods and humans, are cattle (paśu), and Śiva is the Lord (pati) of us who are cattle. Because of the absence of the performance of the Pāśupata vow, there is an absence of the knowledge of reality; therefore, for the world, liberation itself does not exist.
Having reflected thus, Śiva himself, the benefactor of all the worlds, under the pretext of choosing [him as his bridegroom],
made manifest his own eternally established state of being the Lord of Creatures (Pāśupatya) for the sake of universal renown;
this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

The Refutation of Rudra’s Possession of the Quality of Tamas: Now, one might object that because the Taittirīya Śākhā records, "He wept; because he wept (arodīt), that is the nature of Rudra (rudratva)," and since weeping is the etymological basis for the application of the word *rudra*, and since that [weeping] is rooted in the quality of tamas, Rudra must be characterized by tamas (*tāmasatva*).

Because the activity of preservation is conditioned by the quality of *sattva*, Viṣṇu possesses the nature of *sattva*. Therefore, it is logical that Viṣṇu, who impels *sattva*, is the Supreme Brahman. Rudra, however, effects the dissolution of the entire universe by employing *tamas* as his instrument; thus, he is characterized by the employment of the quality of *tamas*, which brings about cruelty.

It is well known as a defect; therefore, because he is overcome by darkness like an ordinary person, Rudra performs improper acts such as the burning of Tripura, the slaying of Jalandhara, the severing of the fifth head of Brahmā, and the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice— acts which constitute the suppression of deities.

He is seen as such; for this very reason, he is designated as Rudra, Bhīma, Ugra, and Paśupati. Accordingly, his dwelling in cremation grounds, his lordship over the spirits of the deceased, his smearing with ashes, his wearing of bone garlands and heron feathers, his drinking of poison, and [his presence] during the twilights—these are observed.

Since conduct such as dancing— which generates the agitation of Bhadrakālī and others— and nakedness are observed, which correspond to an overwhelming state of *tamas*, it is not logical that Rudra possesses the nature of the Supreme Brahman; rather, because qualities such as protection are seen which are conditioned by *sattva*, only Viṣṇu possesses the nature of the Supreme Brahman.
"It must be stated" is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

Now, even if we accept that the state of being *tāmasa*—which is the attribute of the Saṃhāra-Rudra—is also an attribute of Paramaśiva, we shall establish that it lacks the nature of a defect. In this regard, what is it that is being proposed as a defect in the state of being *tāmasa*: is it the possession of the quality of *tamas* which brings about cruelty? Or...
Nor is it being overcome by darkness like an ordinary person; for the former is not a fault. To explain:

in order to provide rest for a time to living beings who are utterly exhausted from wandering back and forth in the great forest of saṃsāra, [the Lord] brings about a state of deep sleep for them all.
Desiring to withdraw the world, Mahādeva assumes darkness as an instrument for that withdrawal; just as one might,

in order to relieve the pain of a long-standing wound and bring comfort to people who are suffering intensely— deprived of sleep and food— assume a state that causes some temporary discomfort in order to remove the pain of the wound.

A physician intending to cut a wound takes up a surgical instrument as a necessary means for that purpose; yet the mere taking up of the instrument does not cause him to be characterized by cruelty, but rather serves as an indicator of his supreme compassion, thinking, "This [patient] is to be protected. This very point has been stated in the Śiva Purāṇa:

For it is stated: "In the case of a physician who knows the cause [of the disease] and inflicts injury upon the patient, there is not even the slightest cruelty; the compassionate one is merely the applicator of the instrument. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because [the relationship between] darkness and its overpowering effect...

This is because [the Lord] is not observed to possess the cruelty toward objects that is inappropriate for one who is awake due to the power of sleep; nor should it be argued that [acts such as] the burning of Tripura do not exist, for they are indeed appropriate. For instance, restraint (nigraha) is of two kinds:
that which has the purpose of favoring (anugraha), and that which does not have that purpose. The first is of three types:
[The purpose] is directed toward those who are to be favored, those who are not to be favored, and both.
Among these, the first is the restraint of disciples and others for the sake of following right conduct; that, moreover, is indeed a merit.
The second is not a fault if it results in the favoring of many more; [for instance], when one person is brought to his end.
For one who acts wickedly, the welfare of many is secured; for there is the saying that "killing in such a case bestows merit.
This is as in the case of hunting, the killing of tigers and the like, and the killing of thieves. It is for the sake of benefiting both [the public and the offender], just as it is said:
"But those men who, having committed sins, have been subjected to punishment by the king, become stainless..."

The virtuous and those who have performed good deeds go to heaven. Thus, among those who are faultless, any instance of punishment inflicted by Śiva—whether it be the punishment of his own sons or even the punishment of Brahmā and others—is indeed appropriate to the object of that punishment.
As it is said in the Śiva Purāṇa: "Furthermore, whatever punishments are shown even toward Brahmā and the other gods..."

These [deities] were also created by the form of Śrīkaṇṭha solely for the benefit of the world. Indeed, there is no doubt that the sovereignty of this staff belongs to Śrīkaṇṭha; Śiva presides over the form known as Śrīkaṇṭha while sporting. Brahmā and the others, though possessed of faults, have been restrained by him as was appropriate.

Consequently, they too became free from sin and thereafter were liberated from their feverish distress. Even the restraint of the wise is not to be despised in its true nature; for this very reason, punishment meted out by kings toward those deserving of it is praised.

And so forth. Regarding what was stated—that there is the designation "the fierce one" (*ugra*) and so on—it must be said in response: the word *ugra* also exists as a term for the subsequent [deity]. This is because we hear of the state of being fierce and the state of being commanded: "He is fierce; may I be fierce among those born. Furthermore, from the root *gam* with the prefix *ut*, it arises as the subsequent [deity].

In the sense of "he exists" (*bhavati*), the word *ugra*—formed with the suffix *-rap* according to the *Uṇādi* sūtra beginning with "rudrendra"—is a conventional term (*nipātita*) denoting Śiva’s status as the supreme of all. The word *bhīma*, although it denotes that which causes fear, nevertheless brings about his excellence; for this entire world, whatever it may be, [depends] upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
"Whatever moves has issued forth; great is the fear, the raised thunderbolt—those who know this become immortal.
By means of this mantra, the quality of being the supreme Brahman, the controller of all, is established as the cause of fear for the entire world.
Therefore, because this Rudra is the impeller of *sattva* and so forth, his state of being characterized by *sattva* belongs to *sattva* alone.
Regarding the term "pravartaka" (the initiator), as set forth by Śvetāśvatara:
"O best of brahmins, within Rudra there is the quality of *sattva* and without there is *tamas*;
within Viṣṇu there is *tamas* and *sattva*, and without there is the quality of *rajas*."
All that exists both within and without belongs to that Prajāpati;
whiteness is born from the quality of *sattva*, and passion is born from the quality of *rajas*.
One should know in brief that [the body] born from the quality of darkness (tamas) is black;
one should meditate on the white form of Rudra, the black form of Viṣṇu,
and the red form of Brahmā for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.
By such statements as these,
all the gods would become of mixed caste (saṅkara), Purandara would be a śūdra,
Pitāmaha would be a vaiśya, and Hari would be a kṣatriya.
The Blessed One Rudra is a Brāhmaṇa, the highest of all.
And by such statements as these:
"The Lord dissolves for us that which is suffering or the cause of suffering;
therefore, Śiva, the supreme cause, is called Rudra by the virtuous."
Because you cause all living beings to weep at the time of their end according to your will,
you are therefore called Rudra by the wise and the best of sages.

By means of such corroborative statements from the *Skānda*, *Liṅga*, and other Purāṇas as previously cited, through the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of names denoting Him, and by the statement in the *Prapada-Brāhmaṇa*— "Among the gods I am Brāhmaṇa; among men I am [the self]"— it is established that Śiva alone is *sāttvika* and Viṣṇu is *tāmasa*.
Since it is established that Śiva alone possesses the status of a Brāhmaṇa and Viṣṇu possesses the status of a Kṣatriya,
it is beyond dispute that Śiva alone is supreme over all.

Now, regarding the state of being concluded with a salutation (*namaskāraśeṣitva*): "Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—Rudra who has entered all beings, to that Rudra let there be salutation! All is indeed Rudra;
to that Rudra let there be salutation! Thus, according to the Taittirīya Śruti and other passages, [the mantra ends] with "salutation to him."

"Salutations to the Lord of the gods, the Master of the Gaṇas; salutations be to Sthāṇu eternally, and salutations to that one who possesses the excellent bow; salutations indeed to the destroyer of Tripura and to the destroyer of Bhaga. Through such statements from the final chapter of the Droṇaparvan and other sections of the Mahābhārata, the salutation is directed toward Śiva alone.
The state of being a remainder is being demonstrated.

Now, is it not the case that Viṣṇu is celebrated in this verse, "I offer salutation to the great Viṣṇu," as well as in the mantra: "Oṃ" is one syllable, "namaḥ" is two syllables, "nārāyaṇāya" is five syllables, and thus "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" consists of eight syllables? In this way...

According to the Purāṇic statement, "Just as water fallen from the sky goes to the ocean, so too does salutation to all the gods go toward Keśava," [it follows that] even salutations intended for various specific deities [ultimately reach Him].

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that Viṣṇu alone is the most excellent among all, because it is established that [the breaths] go exclusively to Viṣṇu, and because by means of the specific mention of the prāṇas and so forth— which illustrates the *kaimutika* logic— the fact that Viṣṇu alone is the recipient of salutation (*namaskāra-śeṣitva*) is made clear.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: since in all the *Rudra-sūkta* hymns contained within the Vedas, one observes a sequential recitation of synonyms for Śiva ending in the dative case preceded by an act of salutation (*namaskāra*); whereas, although such [synonyms] exist occasionally in the mantras of Viṣṇu throughout the three Vedas, they do not occur with such frequency.

When there is repetition, the meaning becomes more extensive and never less; let alone the possibility of it being a figurative meaning—according to this principle, the status of being the object of the salutation belongs to Śiva alone, not to Viṣṇu. Nor does the Purāṇic statement that "the salutation of all the gods goes to Keśava" [apply here].

It should not be argued that the previously stated reasoning is refuted by the demonstration that even the salutations directed toward various deities such as Śiva have Viṣṇu alone as their ultimate destination; for in the Taittirīya [Āraṇyaka], it is said: "To whom there is salutation—that is the head;
Dharma is the crown of the head; Brahmā is the upper jaw; Yajña is the lower jaw; and Viṣṇu is the heart."

In this meditation on the divine Śiṃśumāra, whose limbs consist of all the deities as prescribed in the Taittirīya recension, while the individual names of other deities are indeed mentioned in the descriptions of those respective limbs, [the author], instead of taking the name of Śiva— which ought to have been prescribed for the purpose of describing him as a specific limb— does not mention it.

By means of the figure of speech *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), having established the state of being the recipient of salutation (*namaskāraśeṣitva*) as a unique attribute of Śiva, [the author] very clearly demonstrates through direct statement (*śruti*) itself that this state of being the recipient of salutation is distinguished from others by the phrase "to whom [even] the head does not bow."

The Purāṇic statement that "water falls from the sky," which contradicts such scriptural [Vedic] testimony, does not convey its own literal meaning because it is weak according to the principle of the *adhikaraṇa* rule— "In case of contradiction, there should be no reliance [on the Smṛti], for when [the Veda] exists, there is inference [of its basis]. Thus, by restricting the scope of the word "all" (*sarva*), [it is concluded that] it is not so.

Just as in the injunction "one should not harm any living beings," one postulates the exclusion of violence performed in sacrifice, and just as when the giving away of all one's possessions is enjoined in the Viśvajit rite by the rule "one should give away all one's wealth" (sarvavedasa),
one postulates the exclusion of oneself, one's sons, one's wife, one's maneless lion, one's enemies, horses, and so forth; so too [in this case].

For it is logical to conceive of [the deity] as being distinct from the manifestation of Śiva. Nor should it be argued that Viṣṇu’s status as the recipient of the salutation (*namaḥ-śeṣitva*) is heard in the mantra, "I offer salutation to the great Viṣṇu," because at the beginning of that mantra, it says, "Salutation to Brahman,
salutation be to Agni, salutation to the herbs," and so forth.

Since Viṣṇu is also seen to be worthy of salutation by virtue of being common to Brahmā, Agni, the Earth, medicinal herbs, and so forth, it has not been stated that Viṣṇu alone possesses the status of being the object of the salutation (the *śeṣin*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Caturvedatātparya-saṅgraha*:
We have heard that some offering has been made to the deities; yet, apart from you, there is no one else who can receive that which is the ultimate ground of all salutations.
Indeed, no one else is able to accept it.
"To wear here the crown brought by the thief. Thus [it is said].
By this, it is established as the final conclusion that even the salutations heard in mantras dedicated to other deities are directed toward Śiva alone.

When the churning of the Ocean of Milk had been commenced by all the gods and asuras together, and when the wish-fulfilling cow, the desire-granting tree, the Kaustubha gem, Lakṣmī, the thought-jewel, Uccaiḥśravas, the nectar-rayed moon, and the nectar itself had emerged therein,
a competitive spirit arose due to the extreme height of their greed.

While those various delightful objects were being seized by Nārāyaṇa, Purandara, and other deities as if they were ordinary men, [Śiva] beheld the Kālakūṭa poison— which was produced immediately thereafter, which strikes terror into the world, and which quells the pride of all the gods— within Nārāyaṇa and the other deities.
When their limbs were scorched by the garlands of flames from the poison, they fled while even forgetting themselves; yet,
finding no other refuge, they took shelter solely in the lotus feet of Śiva.

The supremely compassionate Supreme Śiva, who delights in his own self, seeing Nārāyaṇa and the others worshipping him, took the approaching Kālakūṭa poison of terrible form in his hand like a rose-apple fruit and swallowed it.
Thus, the supreme excellence belongs to Śiva alone, as is well known from all the Purāṇas, such as the Bhārata, Rāmāyaṇa, Skānda, and Liṅga.

Is it not the case that Śiva’s drinking of poison does not manifest his greatness, but rather reveals the greatness of Viṣṇu alone? For instance, in the *Tantrabhāgavata*, having seen that terrible-looking great poison appear, [Śiva] meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa.

In his heart, he meditated upon the one whose banner is Garuḍa. Having encapsulated the auspicious, Anuṣṭubh-metered mantra of Acyuta, Ananta, and Govinda with "Oṃ" and "Namaḥ," Hara recited it. By the power of the three names of Viṣṇu, who is indeed omnipresent, that poison which was capable of destroying the world became digested.
Through the consideration of such authorities as the *Mīmāṃsā* and others,

and because it is clearly established by the power of chanting the names Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta, Ananta, and Govinda— which are unique to Nārāyaṇa— that "Śiva bears the poison," this [text] demonstrates the relationship of the worshipped and the worshipper between Nārāyaṇa and Śiva.
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it becomes clear that Nārāyaṇa alone possesses the state of being supreme over all.
As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is stated in the *Śaivadharmasaṃhitā*:
"In ancient times, all the gods and demons together churned the Ocean of Milk,
making Mount Mandara the churning stick and Vāsuki the rope."
Therefore, the great poison Kālakūṭa became [the means] for the sake of purification;
then, seeing that, all the gods, led by Śakra, [acted].
Confused, helpless, and deprived of their senses, the great asuras fled;
their weapons, garments, and armor were scorched, their limbs were burnt, and their eyes were singed.
Beholding one another, some gods and dānavas spoke to each other,
all of them burning intensely like forests consumed by a forest fire.
Crying out "Alas! Alas! with vulgar cries, those gods and deities emerged, breathless, shattered, and stripped of their necklaces and ornaments.
Having begun thus:

"The entire host of gods, headed by Purandara, their limbs scorched by the garland of fierce flames from the Kālakūṭa poison produced during the churning of the Ocean of Milk, became terrified and looked about for a protector."

Then, having approached a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of saving their own lives, Brahmā— himself unable to protect the gods— considered Viṣṇu to be their savior; accompanied by those gods and led by Brahmā and Indra, he, fearing the fire of poison and unable to protect the deities, went to Kailāsa.

Being entreated by Viṣṇu who had returned, the omniscient leader of the Gaṇas, Nandīśvara, standing at the gate of Kailāsa, beheld them and spoke with eyes possessing the luster of blue lotuses to the gods headed by Śatakratu, along with the Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas: "For what purpose have you come, O highly fortunate ones?"
The beings were agitated in their minds: "The eightfold divine sovereignty has been bestowed upon you."

By him, your sovereignty has been overturned; you, led by Śakra, though once lords of the three worlds, are now all indeed freed from feverish affliction. So too are the gods, including Nārāyaṇa, along with Indra, Varuṇa, and the serpents.

"Why then are you so agitated by fear, like deer tormented by a lion? What is the sorrow, what is the distress, or from where has this fear come? You ought to explain all of this quickly and according to the facts," and with such words he questioned them.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, while the ocean was being churned by the gods led by Brahmā and the Śuras and Asuras at the request of Nandīśvara,
[there appeared] that which resembled a serpent or a bee, and was like a dark blue cloud.

A terrible poison appeared, possessing a radiance like the fire of universal destruction (*saṃvartāgni*). As that poison rose up, with a luster equal to the fire of time (*kālānala*), Viṣṇu’s body—previously reddish-white from being scorched by it—attained a black hue. Seeing Janārdana, whose body had been reddish-white, now turned black, all [beings] then...

"We have come to Śaṅkara for refuge out of fear,"—with such words they entreated him. Then Śailādi, together with the gods including Nārāyaṇa, went into the presence of Śiva and informed him of the purpose of the gods' arrival. Thereupon, led by Viṣṇu, they praised and prostrated before Śiva.

They reported the affliction caused by the Kālakūṭa poison. Then, having heard their words and looked upon the gods, the Lord Paraśiva, the ocean of compassion, remembered the terrible poison, which possessed a radiance like the fire at the end of an eon. As soon as the Lord remembered the poison, it was instantly swallowed by him.
Then his palm shone like a lotus with a bee upon it;

by the mere recollection of this, while the Kālakūṭa poison was held in his hand, the Blessed One Padmasambhava, having paid homage, spoke to the Omniscient One for the sake of the worlds: "Drink that!"

Out of a desire for the world's welfare, Śaṅkara, the storehouse of compassion, being thus entreated by Brahmā, accepted his words with the simple reply, "So be it. He then drank the entire terrible Kālakūṭa, the great poison, which resembled a dark blue cloud, just as one might drink nectar. Thus was that horrific substance swallowed by him.

Thus, since it is very clearly understood in many Purāṇas that [Śiva] drank the Kālakūṭa poison in order to make the world free from fear, and because this is likewise found in the Itihāsas such as the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, Śiva alone is to be served and sought for refuge by all.
As for what was said— that the poison was digested through the power of chanting the three names "Acyuta," "Ananta," and "Govinda"—
that is extremely weak; for the meaning is that Śiva, while recollecting the three names preceded by meditation on Nārāyaṇa, held the poison, and it attained the state of being digested.

Because these three cited verses are not found anywhere in the well-known Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, they must have been fabricated by those very [authors], like the Bhāllaveya-śruti and other such texts. Furthermore: "O Govinda, whatever great names you possess, those alone are my names; no deliberation is required here."

In the *Harivaṃśa*, during Kṛṣṇa’s journey to Kailāsa, by means of the Lord’s speech to Viṣṇu, it is stated that the eternity of names such as Acyuta is established through the etymological derivation of their components; furthermore,
it is Śiva alone who impels all living beings toward action in accordance with their karma and causes them to know [the truth].

On the strength of all the previously cited statements from the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas, it is possible [that these names refer only to Him], and not to anyone else. Therefore, by reflecting on the meaning of those three names and by the force of the authoritative evidence, it is logically sound that their final conclusion rests in Him alone; thus, because even these three verses have Śiva as their ultimate purport, [there is no contradiction].
There is no inconsistency whatsoever. Thus, the meaning is established as follows: *acyuta* means devoid of falling away (*cyuti*);

*ananta* means devoid of end (*anta*). By the etymological derivation "he who finds (*vindati*) the *gā*s (cows)," he is the agent of experiencing the auspicious and inauspicious karma performed by all living beings.

"Having realized that 'I am that Brahman which illumines the manifold world of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth,' one is liberated from all bonds. And: "In the three abodes, whatever is the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoying—He who is distinct from these, the Witness, pure consciousness alone, is indeed Sadāśiva."

Furthermore, because of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad’s scriptural statement regarding isolation (*kaivalya*), "A certain timid person resorts [to Him] thinking 'He is unborn,'" and its further statement, "O Rudra, with that face of yours which is auspicious (*dakṣiṇa*),
protect me eternally," it is heard that eternity and the status of being the witness of all belong to Śiva alone, and not to Nārāyaṇa, who is other than Him.

Since the Śruti declares that "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra are all produced from him," thus establishing his manifold state of being born, there is no room for doubt that the three names refer to Nārāyaṇa;
rather, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that they refer exclusively to Śiva.

Now, did not the Blessed One, the eminent sage Vālmīki— who, by virtue of a boon from the Lotus-seated Lord, possessed the faculty of knowing the meaning of all the Vedas— compose that great epic poem called the Rāmāyaṇa, which consists of the life-story of Śrī Rāmacandra? In that great poem...

By means of describing the qualities of Śrī Rāmacandra, [the author] has clearly established that very Śrī Viṣṇu’s state as the Supreme Brahman, being the cause of all things. For instance: "Yogins delight in the infinite, true, blissful Self of Consciousness"; thus, by the word 'Rāma', he is designated as the Supreme Brahman.
Thus, in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, which consists of the life-story of Rāma and which establishes his nature as the Supreme Brahman through the words of the *Umā-saṃhitā*:
"You are the goddess Śītā-Lakṣmī; you are the god Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, and Prajāpati. For the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa, you have entered a human body here. I know you to be the imperishable slayer of Madhu."

He is pleased because he is established as the "best of gods" in the *Bālakāṇḍa* during the hymn composed by Paraśurāma, and because it is stated in the first canto of the *Ayodhyākāṇḍa*: "Requested by the gods who desired the slaying of Rāvaṇa, the eternal Viṣṇu was born in the world of men. Thus he is gratified.

Furthermore, because it is established at the time of the conclusion that "Rāma is indeed Viṣṇu, the eternal," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that Rāma is none other than Viṣṇu, and he alone is the Supreme Brahman.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: since the *Rāmāyaṇa* is the first epic poem (*ādikāvya*) and thus a supreme work of literature (*uttamakāvya*), its expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is Rāma’s attainment of the state of Brahman; yet, by means of the function of suggestion (*vyañjanāvṛtti*), its implied meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*) is Śiva’s very state of being the Supreme Brahman. This [is evident] at the time of his arrival and entry into Agastya’s hermitage.
It has been clarified in various places by the words of Śrī Rāmacandra and by the words of poets.

For it is said, after describing the entrance into Agastya’s hermitage: "In this place, the gods along with the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis constantly attend upon Agastya, who is restrained in his diet. And there, it is stated: "Therein is the abode of Brahmā; therein is the abode of Lakṣmī."
And likewise: the abode of Viṣṇu, as well as the abode of Indra and that of Vivasvat.

"The place of Soma, the place of Bhaga, as well as that of Kubera, the places of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and likewise the place of Vāyu"— by such [passages], the locations of those who attend upon Agastya have been described;
and thus, for those dwelling in his hermitage, it was like being among the gods.
The abode of Śiva has not been mentioned. Therefore, by highlighting that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others alone are the worshippers of Agastya, and not Śiva, the greatness of Śiva is revealed.
Thus, Śiva is the one to be propitiated through the masses of ascetic penances of Agastya, who is himself worshipped by all the gods.

Thus, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), this is established. Consequently, since it is proven that the other gods are themselves worshippers of Śiva, it follows that Śiva’s superiority over them is perceived as absolute;
this is the meaning. Furthermore, when Rāmacandra sent Śatrughna for the purpose of slaying Lavaṇa...

In order to slay him, he gave [Rāma] a certain weapon in the form of an image of Hari and described its power: "O Satrughna, this arrow was not released by me previously while seeking the death of Rāvaṇa, lest great terror should arise among living beings. Having thus described the arrow as being of such a nature...

Even while bestowing [the boon], Śrī Rāmacandra said: "When the trident that was extracted from his own spear by Śiva and placed in Lavaṇa’s hand is present, he cannot be conquered by any means whatsoever; therefore, at the moment the trident is no longer in his hand, he must be slain with an arrow while he is being obstructed. Having thus instructed him, [he gave the boon].
Rāma said: "The task of the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha is indeed difficult to overcome," and so forth.
Thus, he further manifested that Śiva alone is the Supreme Brahman; in this way, the preeminence of Śiva is established.
Then, seeing those two who were intelligent and well-versed in the Vedas, [he spoke] for the purpose of augmenting the Vedas...

The Lord taught that very [truth] in this manner; thus, by establishing that the *Rāmāyaṇa* serves to supplement the Vedas, it is proven that when the poetic work of the *Rāmāyaṇa* has Śiva as its intended meaning through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanāvṛtti*), it possesses the status of being taught by the Vedas— therefore, Śiva alone is the supreme cause.
The established conclusion.

Now, in the Bhagavadgītā, which is the very essence of the Mahābhārata, at the commencement of the instruction regarding the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra to Pārtha, [it is said]: "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion (māyā), as if they were mounted on a machine."

"Go to Him alone as your refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata; by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode"—thus was it taught by the Blessed Kṛṣṇa. Likewise: "I seek refuge in that very Primeval One from whom the ancient course of activity has issued forth."
When there arises the inquiry as to what is the object of the surrender (*prapadana*) being performed by the Blessed One, [the Lord] says:

"But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self, the imperishable Lord who, pervading the three worlds, sustains them. Having said this, [it is shown that] that which is to be worshipped is not something other than Himself, but rather His very own essential nature.
For it has been established [by Me]:

"Since I have transcended the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama (the Supreme Person). Thus, by virtue of My own transcendence of both the perishable and the imperishable...

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that because the state of being supreme is established for those two [the sun and the moon] by means of them, it is logical that Viṣṇu alone possesses the nature of the Supreme Brahman.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: because the word *īśvara*, which is a name unique to Śiva, is recorded in the verses previously cited and elsewhere; and because everything, including the manifestation of the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) and so forth, must be explained either through non-difference from Śiva or through a connection with Śiva.

Because the name of the Lord (Īśvara), heard first under the designation "Puruṣottama," must be followed as the primary one due to its superior power; furthermore, Arjuna—who had vowed, "I stand with my doubts dispelled; I shall do your bidding"—remained devoted to the worship of Śiva for as long as he lived.

It is understood that in the *Gītā* as well, Kṛṣṇa has taught that Śiva alone—possessing all supreme attributes and being the one to be sought as a refuge by those desiring liberation—is to be taken as such. By this, following the statement "Go to Him alone for refuge," and beginning with "Hear again from Me my supreme word, O Śarva, which is the most secret of all... (18.63), it is established.

The doubt that the instruction "abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone," and the subsequent vow "I shall do as you say," refer to Viṣṇu, is hereby dispelled. For, in that case, Arjuna would have abandoned the worship of Śiva and performed only the worship of Viṣṇu.

Because it would entail the obligation [to perform both], he performed only the worship of Śiva throughout his life, not the worship of Viṣṇu; for there is a scriptural injunction regarding his lifelong devotion to the worship of Śiva. As for the claim that all the offerings prepared for the daily evening worship of Śiva were offered to Kṛṣṇa—

That statement also intends to convey that Śiva-nature exists within the form of Kṛṣṇa, and thus [the offering] was made with the thought of worshipping Śiva. Likewise, it is stated that when Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna went to Kailāsa, Arjuna saw all the offerings near Śiva; and he [saw] that entire offering.
Desiring his own ethical conduct, he saw that [the fruit] offered to Vāsudeva in the vicinity of Tryambaka was superior:
"Those people who worship Me with undivided thought, for those who are ever-devoted, I provide for their acquisition and preservation. Come to Me alone for refuge. But their fruit is finite."

Knowing the words of the Blessed One beginning with "That occurs for those of small intellect," Arjuna abandoned other deities and performed the worship of Śiva alone for as long as he lived; of this there is no dispute.
Therefore, because the Gītā is the essence of the Mahābhārata, it is clear that Śiva alone is the one propounded by the Gītā.
The established conclusion is that Śiva alone is what is propounded by the Bhārata.
Is it not so that, by reflecting upon Vedic statements such as "Agni is the first among the deities," "Agni is all the deities," and "These two,

Agni and Soma, are indeed the two kings of the deities; Agni is the mouth, the first among the deities," the primacy of Agni among the deities, his universal nature (*sārvātmya*), and his status as the controller of the deities are established?
Because of the recitation of marks of Brahman such as "thatness" (*yattva*) and so forth, Agni alone is the cause of the universe and is to be meditated upon as Brahman;
for all Vaidikas accept that the service of Agni alone is the means of deliverance (*tāraka*). Likewise:
"The Sun is the soul of that which moves and that which stands; you are the traverser, the all-seeing, the light-maker, O Surya."

"O Sūrya, you illuminate the entire universe as the medicine for all to see," and so forth; since such Vedic passages declare that the Sun is the self of the universe and the illuminator of all, he alone is the one to be meditated upon and sought for refuge. For this very reason, in the passage "That Sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods," he is described as honey, being the means of sustenance for all the deities.
The definition [of Brahman] is shown by such statements as "dependent on rising and setting" and "the daily dissolution of all living beings,

which rises taking away the vital breaths," and so forth. Furthermore, the Sāvitrī mantra reveals the Sun (Savitṛ), and it brings about the status of a Brāhmaṇa through the purificatory rite of initiation (upanayana).
This is well known. Therefore, the Sun alone is the Supreme Brahman. Likewise:

"We invoke you, Gaṇapati, the Lord of hosts, the seer among seers, possessed of most exalted fame, the eldest king of sacred hymns, O Brahmaṇaspati; hearing us, sit upon your seat with your protections."
Because Gaṇapati is traditionally declared to be the Eldest King (*jyeṣṭharāja*) and the Lord of Prayer (*brahmaṇaspati*), it is logical that his supremacy alone is appropriate.

Furthermore, in the first chapter of the *Gaṇeśa Purāṇa* within the *Skanda Purāṇa*, it is stated: "He who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), free from ego (*nirahaṅkāra*), beyond conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), formless (*nirākṛti*), free from affliction (*nirāmaya*), and effortless (*nirīha*)—he is called Gaṇeśa; he is formless (*arūpa*)."

He is possessed of form and likewise assumes manifold forms; His true nature is accessible through devotion and His true nature is accessible through knowledge. For the sake of the welfare of all moving and non-moving beings, He manifests through names and forms.
When at times the dissolution occurs and the three worlds have become a deluge, He lies in yogic sleep, formless and transcending the qualities (guṇas).

Without support, a mass of consciousness and bliss, eternal, self-luminous, and consisting of the universe—that majestic one performed an act of observation, holding it before him: "There is nothing here distinct from me; why then should I fear? Having joined those [energies], being alone, I shall become manifold through the nature of the world. Thus he thought.

"Having reflected, He first created Rajas, Sattva, and Tamas; thus endowed with these three qualities, He became known by the names Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. By this collection of statements from the Ādi Purāṇa and other sources, it is established that Gaṇeśa—who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), formless (nirākāra), and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda)—exists prior to the dissolution of the universe, and is therefore the progenitor of Brahmā and the other gods.

Thus, its status as the Supreme Brahman is established by virtue of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe. [Objection: "Is there anyone higher than Indra? Indra is higher than the universe; Indra is the king of what has been traversed and what remains to be traversed"—since such scriptural passages declare Indra to be the highest of all, it is more logical that he alone possesses the nature of the Supreme. Thus [the opponent argues].
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that this doctrine of the supremacy of various deities is dependent upon the specific qualifications of their respective practitioners.

Furthermore, since it is accepted that the omnipresent Supreme Lord is denotable by all words through His presiding over all bodies, this is merely a description of another aspect of the Supreme Lord’s majesty.
Just as excellent elephants, horses, ornaments, and so forth are common property for the ministers and others.
"Whatever being is possessed of glory, beauty, or power, know that to have sprung from but a fragment of my splendor"— by reflecting on the meaning of this passage from the *Bhagavad Gītā*,
[the Lord] is described as having the specific nature of the Supreme Lord. However, the common causality of the world...

By examining the collection of mantras from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad and other sources, it is established that supremacy belongs to Paramaśiva alone; therefore, there is no transcendence for others who possess various powers, such as Agni, Sūrya, Gaṇapati, Indra, and so forth. Rather, [it belongs to him].
The established conclusion is that it is logical for Śiva alone to possess the state of being the supreme among all and the state of being the ultimate.

Therefore, by means of the aforementioned arguments, supported by the logic of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā which determine the meaning of the statements of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Āgamas, it is established that the causality of the origin and so forth of the universe belongs to Śiva alone; [therefore], to him alone...

The nature of another is logical. Nor should it be argued that Nārāyaṇa alone is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world, and not Śiva, because the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad* declares the origin of Brahmā, Rudra, and others from Nārāyaṇa, stating: "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa; Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa."

Although there are scriptural accounts of the emergence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra from one another by taking into account their distinctions as the embodiments of the qualities (guṇas) who have entered into the sphere of activity,
[they are in fact] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra appointed to the fivefold duties consisting of creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace.

Since no birth whatsoever is heard of for Paraśiva, who is designated by the terms Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Mahāliṅga, he alone possesses eternity and the state of being the cause of all. Thus it is said in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā of the Śaiva tradition:
"Those three, whose nature is causal, were born directly from Maheśvara, the source of the universe of moving and non-moving beings."

They are the causes of creation, preservation, and destruction; presided over by His power, they are eternally capable of performing their respective functions. All three were previously assigned by the Father to their three respective duties.

Brahmā exists for creation, Hari for protection, and Rudra for dissolution; yet all three, out of mutual rivalry and desiring to surpass one another, propitiated the Supreme Lord, the Impeller, through austerity. By the grace of that Parameṣṭhin, they attained the state of being his very self.

In a former kalpa, Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa created Rudra; in another kalpa, Brahmā, who is identical with the universe, again created Rudra and Viṣṇu. Furthermore, the Lord Viṣṇu created Rudra and Brahmā; and again, Brahmā created Nārāyaṇa, and Bhava (Rudra) created Brahmā once more.

"In this way, in age after age, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are born from one another, each desiring victory over the other. With reference to the specific events occurring at the end of each respective age, various [accounts] have been composed by the great seers; the wise man is not deluded therein. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the Mṛgendrottara of the Śaiva Āgama, there is the statement of Guṇirudra:
"By those seventy-one [Manvantaras], a Manvantara of a Manu is to be known;
by fourteen of those Kalpas, a day of Brahmā is considered."
In this interval, Śakras die and are born again and again three hundred times; sixty such days constitute a year for him.
The lifespan of Brahmā lasts for as many hundreds of years as there are atoms in those [worlds];
a hundred years of his life is equivalent to a single month of Hari.
A hundred years of such months constitutes the duration of Hari’s stay;
it lasts as long as my month of Mādhava comes to its end.
A period of one hundred years for me, corresponding to the birth and life of Hari, constitutes but a single day for His Lord; by that measure, a hundred such days would equal one year for me.
At one time, we were born again and again;
yet, through a mere blink of Sadāśiva’s eye, even that [existence] was then brought to an end.
When that which is the subtlest part of another attains dissolution therein, for that Śiva, the Supreme Self, there is neither birth nor death. Thus it is said.

Therefore, because He is the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe and is eternal, Śiva alone should be meditated upon, worshipped, saluted, and taken as refuge by those seeking liberation who desire the eternal fruit; thus, everything is beyond reproach.
[Thus,
from the venerable Tōṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the moving form of the beginningless and stainless Aparā,
and who has obtained the grace of the Śāmbhava Āgama ocean churned by him— producing the unsurpassed division of one hundred and one *sthala*s...]

In the work composed by the eminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya— who bestows a mass of bliss from tasting the nectar of the *latattva*— for Keladi Sadāśivarāya, the sovereign of the western ocean, who is the sole hero among the "Yādava Murāri Koṭe Kolāhalas," the remover of the seven constituents of his enemies, and the preceptor who established the pure Vedic Advaita Siddhānta.

[The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Establishment of Śiva’s Preeminence," in the section on Debate within the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, which is the instruction of Basava— the joy of the hearts of the people and the Indra of the Earth— concerning the consort of Vīrabhadra, the Dharaṇīndra who is like the full moon in the milk-ocean of the lineage of the Leader.]
[The Twentieth Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O venerable Guru, you have established through the words of the virtuous Bhṛṅgin the superiority of Śiva and the inferiority of Viṣṇu, as declared by the Vedas and the Āgamas.
Having heard the nectar-like essence of words issuing from the lotus of your mouth, I have become swollen with bliss; what more could Bhṛṅgin possibly say?
O Lord, please now tell me in due order the prima facie arguments and the established conclusions composed by Śīlin; I wish to hear them at this time.
That very [reality], which has been seen many times and to great effect, should now be revealed here;
for the supreme state of Śiva is based upon the root of the Tantras.
The practices of the Vīraśaivas, which involve the wearing of the *liṅga*, have been established therein;
thus, the authority of those Tantras is not tenable.
O Bhṛṅgin, whatever you seek to destroy, I shall quickly accomplish that.

Now, having established the lack of authority of the scriptural statements teaching the wearing of the *liṅga*— on the strength of a multitude of Smṛti and Purāṇa passages such as "the leading of those fallen from the Vedic path into the path of Tantra"— it has been supported that the wearing of the *liṅga* is Vedic by virtue of the authority of the Śruti.
If the lack of authority of the scriptures were admitted, then none of the Vīraśaiva practices, such as the wearing of the *liṅga*,
would be performed by those who follow the Vedic tradition and its established lineages. This is not the case.
This is an admitted consequence, because there exist numerous statements by those who follow that [tradition] establishing the authority of the Āgamas.
For instance, in the Sūtasaṃhitā:
"The son of Satyavatī is the author of the eighteen Purāṇas..."
Just as the Lord Maheśvara is the source of the various divisions beginning with the Kāmika;
In the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*: "Because they establish the same meaning, there is identity between the Veda and the Siddhānta;
the wise should always know that the authority of these two is equal."
Alternatively, according to the *Kriyāsāra* and the *Śivaniśvāsa-śruti*,
