those Śiva-scriptures emerged directly from the mouths of Śiva himself; they are superior [to others].
The Nigamas and Āgamas spoken by Śiva have mutually non-contradictory meanings;
it is only by those of limited intellect that mutual contradiction is imagined.
The authority of both the Nigamas and the Āgamas should be understood without distinction by those who perceive reality, on the basis of the instruction of the supreme authoritative teacher.

Thus, because the authority of the Āgamas must be accepted by the learned— as they establish the duties of the castes, stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), and so forth, which are not contrary to the Vedas, and because they have the Supreme Lord as their sole author who is omniscient— all the practices prescribed in the Āgamas [are authoritative].
It is established that [this] is to be performed according to the Vedic injunctions.
Is it not the case that the knowledge prescribed in the Veda bestows both enjoyment and liberation,
whereas the knowledge taught elsewhere is not a means for liberation?
Knowledge derived from the Śruti alone bestows the fortune of liberation; nothing else does so.
Thus it is stated in the Śruti: "Those who have ascertained the meaning through the realization of Vedānta."
Because the scriptures differ from the Vedas, that knowledge does not bestow liberation.
The deliverance of those who follow non-Vedic paths occurs through adherence to the Tantric way;
this was declared by the omniscient Śiva himself to Pārvatī as she listened.

"Because the Goddess is female, and because [her teaching] conforms to her, that which is non-Vedic has been spoken," and so forth— by such authorities, it is established that knowledge alone arising from the Vedānta is the means to liberation. Having kept in mind the lack of qualification for women regarding knowledge derived from the Śruti, [the author addresses] Gaurī...

Instruction has been given specifically for those returning [to the path]; therefore, knowledge produced by the Vedānta alone is the direct means to liberation, whereas for those qualified as women, Śūdras, and others, knowledge produced by the Āgamas and other sources serves as a means only through a gradual succession.

It must be stated that after attaining a birth suitable for the knowledge produced by Vedānta, liberation is generated through the gateway of the knowledge produced by Vedānta once again. Furthermore, it is not consistent that knowledge produced by scripture (āgama) is a means to liberation, because scriptures are delusive treatises. For instance, in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
And you, O mighty-armed Rudra, compose treatises of delusion;
O great-armed one, demonstrate what is untrue as being true.
"Make yourself manifest and make me unmanifest"—
by this statement from the Purāṇa, it is established that the scripture which sets forth the superiority of Viṣṇu, whose essence is *sattva*,
is the means for attaining liberation for those human beings whose internal organs are defiled by the faults of the Kali age.
Since it is unfit for those devoid of purity of mind, the intent here is that one should compose a scripture that establishes one's own superiority while negating the superiority of others; thus,
because the Āgamas composed by Rudra are delusive scriptures, the practices prescribed therein [are likewise unfit].
It is understood that [the practice] is not to be performed according to the Vedic injunctions, and that the knowledge produced thereby lacks the quality of being a means to liberation.
Furthermore, the scriptures lack authority because they are not included among the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
For it is said: "The limbs [of the Veda], the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara,"
The Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and Arthaśāstra—
these four are declared to be the Upavedas immediately following [the Vedas].
The sacred tradition declares that the wielder of the trident is himself the original author and the seer of these eighteen branches of knowledge, which follow diverse paths.

Thus are the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). Among them, it is first not included within the *Ṛgveda*, because it lacks the quality of teaching matters useful for the group of *hotṛ* priests. Nor is it included within the *Yajurveda*, because it lacks the quality of being restricted to use by the group of *adhvaryu* priests. Nor is it included within the *Sāmaveda*.
Because it does not state matters required by the group of Udgātṛ priests; nor in the Atharvaveda, because it lacks the quality of being solely devoted to rites of sorcery (*ābhicārika*);
nor in the Upaniṣads, because, despite being composed in the form of either mantra or brāhmaṇa, they lack the status of an authoritative scripture (*āgama*) for establishing Brahman.

This is because the distinction between these designations is clearly perceived. The Upaniṣads present a fourfold classification of meditation: meditation on identity (*sampad-upāsanā*), meditation on symbols (*pratīka-upāsanā*), meditation with the grasping of the self (*ahaṅgraha-upāsanā*), and meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇa-upāsanā*).

Among these, in the case of meditation on identity—such as "One should meditate on speech as a cow"—one regards speech and so forth as being [the object of meditation] while they are already present there.

The uninterrupted contemplation of identity with the Cow is the meditation on attainment (*sampad-upāsanā*). In meditations on symbols (*pratīka-upāsanā*) such as "One should meditate on space as Brahman" and "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman," because space, the mind, and so forth lack intrinsic existence, [they are not to be contemplated as identical with Brahman].

The uninterrupted contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of identity with Brahman regarding things that have been made [into symbols] is *pratīkopāsana* (symbolic meditation). "This person who is seen in the eye—this is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman. They call him 'the one who gathers all blessings' (*saṃyadvāma*); he is indeed the leader (*vāmin*)."

This very one, through the continuous meditation "I am the Lord characterized by the qualities of being the humble, the all-pervading, the possessor of the power of light, and the one who brings together all desires," and having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful, the sage goes forth.
In the context of the phrase "the source of beings" (*bhūtayoni*),

the meditation on the "I" (*ahaṅgrahopāsanā*) consists of the uninterrupted contemplation: "I am Brahman, known as Sadāśiva, distinguished by such qualities as being accompanied by Umā, being the Supreme Lord, possessing sovereignty, having three eyes, and having a blue throat."

Nor should it be argued that, because here Brahman— qualified by attributes such as having a blue throat— is presented as an object of meditation distinct [from the self], and because there is an absence of the word "I" (aham) and an absence of intended meaning [to that effect], how can this be of the nature of *ahaṅgraha* meditation?

Because this very Upaniṣad later establishes that the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self is the means to liberation, stating: "Having realized that which shines forth as the manifold expansion of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, is Brahman—I am That—one is liberated from all bonds. [Any state] distinct from these three...
Nor is it meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇopāsanā), because there is no exposition of such a form of meditation. Nor is it among its ancillaries (tadaṅgeṣu);

even there, it is not in the *śikṣā*, because that lacks the exposition of the sequence for the pronunciation of Vedic syllables, accents, and prosodic measures (*mātrā*). In that regard, [it is] in the *vrajana*.
If it is accented (udātta) and uttered together with the vowel *a*, as in "stutam," "dhṛtam," "ghṛtena," "ūrdhvam," "havyapūrvaḥ," and "anta āhutam"—this refers to the phoneme (*varṇa*).

In the case of the term *dvādaśāhīnasya* ("of the twelve-day Ahīna sacrifice"), because the suffix *kha* is prescribed by the rule *ahnaḥ khaḥ kratau* when it denotes a collection of days (*ahargaṇa*), there is an oxytone accent (*antodāttatvam*). [The word] *ahīna* is not [formed] with the negative particle *nañ*, as in *na hīnaḥ = ahīnaḥ*.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because there is an absence of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, the vowel *i* situated after the letter *h* becomes *svarita*. Thus, one should utter the phonemes neither too clearly nor too indistinctly. Like a vessel full of milk, the wise person should pronounce [the words] according to their understanding; as for the *cāṣa* bird—

"The crow speaks with one mora (mātrā), the brāhmaṇa with two moras; the peacock cries with three moras, and the mongoose with half a mora. Since this [instruction] concerns the subsidiary limb (*aṅga*) consisting of phonetics (*śikṣā*), it does not appear in the *Kalpasūtras*.

Because it lacks the capacity to prescribe the sequence and the specific methods for the performance of the constituent and subsidiary rites of the Śrauta rituals; nor because grammar (vyākaraṇa) lacks the aim of producing words by means of the analysis of euphonic combinations (sandhi), compounds (samāsa), roots (prakṛti), and suffixes (pratyaya); nor [does it apply] to prosody (chandas).
Because it lacks the focus on the rules governing the meters, phonemes, and morae of Vedic and worldly literature;

nor because it lacks the focus on explaining the meanings of words for the purpose of understanding the sense of the *ṛc* verses as found in the *Nirukta*; nor because it lacks the function of determining the times for the performance of duties enjoined by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* as found in the *Jyotiṣa*; therefore, it is not [one of these].
It is included within the *vedāṅgas*, but not among the four *upāṅgas*. Even there, it is not included in *mīmāṃsā*,

because [the latter] consists of the investigation of dharma as declared by *śruti* and *smṛti*, along with its definition, its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its essential nature, its instruments, its application, its sequence,

its eligibility (*adhikāra*), its extension (*atideśa*), its modification (*ūha*), its sublation (*bādha*), its systematic performance (*tantra-anuṣṭhāna*), and its incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

Because it lacks the focus on [the six] foundations; nor in the Uttara-mīmāṃsā, because it lacks the focus on the inquiry into Brahman, its definition, its means of proof, its reconciliation of contradictions, the removal of objections, its instruments of knowledge, and its fruits; nor in the Nyāya-vistara.

Because it lacks the capacity to produce the intellectual skill required for the investigation of categories (padārtha), which is constituted by the application of worldly maxims conducive to determining the meaning of the Vedas;
nor [is it found] in the Purāṇas.

This is because [this work] lacks the focus on describing the creation and dissolution— whether primordial, occasional, or constant— as well as the origin of deities, the genealogies of Manvantaras and royal dynasties, and the greatness of sacred fords (tīrtha) and holy sites (kṣetra), which are characteristic of the Dharmaśāstras; nor does it appear anywhere within those Dharmaśāstras.
Because they consist of scattered explanations presented as established facts within various other contexts, their Vedic foundations are obscured;

furthermore, they lack the intent to expound upon the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), customary practices, ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), penance (*prāyaścitta*), charity, propitiatory rites (*śānti*), works of public utility (*pūrta*), legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), yoga, and so forth. Therefore, they are not included among the *upāṅgas*.

Nor is it found in the Upavedas; even there, it is not in Āyurveda, because that consists of three sections—diagnosis, treatment, and measures conducive to preserving the body—and thus lacks the quality of being a means for achieving a visible fruit. Nor is it in Dhanurveda.

It is not concerned with the art of music (*gāndharva*), because it does not aim to demonstrate the agility required for physical exercises useful in subduing enemies— such as piercing targets, fixing arrows, raising and striking weapons— or the mastery of the three scales (*grāma*) and melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*) differentiated by the various sequences of ascending and descending through the seven notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*.

This is because [the Veda] lacks the intent to convey aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and so forth through the performance of dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*)— such as hand-movements, eye-glances, and head-motions— along with the rhythmic beats (*tāla*) of *cañcatpuṭa* and other types, the various musical instruments like the *mṛdaṅga*, and the application of passion mixed with the imagined primary passion (*pradhānarāga*), all of which correspond to the time and place [of the performance].
Nor [is it found] in the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*),

which deal with the collection of taxes, the protection of the subjects, the seven constituent elements of sovereignty such as the means of policy (*sāma*) and the king himself along with his ministers,

the circle of twelve kings beginning with the enemy, the six measures of foreign policy, the three powers, and the three aims of life (*trivarga*), nor with the knowledge of these and the conduct corresponding to them.
Because they lack the intent to establish [the truth],
and because they are not included within the Vedas, their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), their secondary limbs (upāṅgas), or the Upavedas, the Āgamas are not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, inference (*anumāna*) is also a means of establishing this point: the Vedas are not a valid authority (*pramāṇa*) because they do not set forth matters not already stated in the Vedas; wherever there is the quality of setting forth matters not already stated in the Vedas, there is a lack of validity, as in the case of the *Pāñcarātra* and *Pāśupata* tantras, for therein—

The lack of authoritative status [of these texts] is established because they propound matters contrary to the Vedas, such as the branding of the body with heated wheels, lingas, and tridents. Nor can it be argued that this reason is "counterbalanced" (satpratipakṣa) by the following counter-argument: "The scriptures are authoritative because they propound dharma as declared in the Vedas, just like the Smṛtis."
Is it the state of expounding some portion of the meaning taught in the Veda, or the state of expounding the entirety of the meaning taught in the Veda?
Not the first, because there is a deviation [from the rule] in the Buddhist scriptures, which expound dharmas taught in the Veda such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and truthfulness (*satya*).
Nor the second, because the state of expounding the entirety of the meaning taught in the Veda does not exist in the Smṛtis, as seen in the illustrative example.
The reason is unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*). Therefore, if it is argued that even by means of inference the Āgamas are not a valid authority (*pramāṇa*), it is said in response:

the validity of the Vedas and the Āgamas must be stated without distinction, because they were composed by the Supreme Lord, the ultimate authoritative person (*paramāpta*). [This applies equally to] the eighteen Purāṇas...
The author is the son of Satyavatī, just as the Lord Maheśvara is the author of the various divisions beginning with the Kāmika.
Because, according to such statements, the fact that God is the creator is established.

The identity between the Veda and the Siddhānta arises from their exposition of a single goal; therefore, the wise should always recognize that the authority of these two is equal. Because they proclaim the dharma of the Veda, the Śiva-āgamas are called "Siddhānta"; because they do not contradict what lies outside the Veda, they are said to be "concordant with the Veda. Therefore, [there is no difference] between the Veda and the Āgama.
Because both possess the commonality of being composed by the supreme authoritative [teacher],
because they share the commonality of propounding dharmas such as the mantras of the five-syllabled [formula], the rudrākṣa, the ash, and the stages of life (āśrama) as taught in the Vedas,
and because they share the commonality of contradicting the conduct prescribed by the systems outside the Veda, such as those of the Buddhists and the Cārvākas.

The authority is equal. In reality, however, it must be stated that the authority of the Āgamas is indeed greater than that of the Śruti. For instance, such is the authority of the Śrutis, which are the very breath of the Supreme Lord.
The authority of the Āgamas— which, emerging from the mouth of the Lord of Cedi, are uttered with the movement of the palate and lips, and are capable of conveying meaning— is indeed supreme.

As for the claim that knowledge derived from the Āgamas cannot be a means to liberation because it is non-Vedic, that is not so, since it is impossible to define what "non-Vedic" actually means. Furthermore, the assertion that the instruction of Śiva to Pārvatī serves as evidence for the non-Vedic nature of the Āgamas is utterly inconsistent. For instance, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka [Upaniṣad]:

In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the fourth chapter, Yājñavalkya instructs his wife Maitreyī, saying: "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. From this teaching of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*nididhyāsana*), it might follow that these are non-Vedic; likewise...

In the Gārgī-brāhmaṇa, regarding the statements addressed to Gārgī such as "By the command of this very Imperishable (akṣara), O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand," and so forth, their non-Vedic character would follow, because the act of instruction directed toward a woman is identical [in both cases]. Therefore, instruction directed toward a woman is an indicator of non-Vedic status.
Such a statement is to be disregarded because it causes delusion in the ignorant. Thus concludes the demonstration of the authority of scripture.
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Establishment of the Authority of the Āgamas," in the section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā.]
[The Twenty-first Chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O Lord of Teachers, having heard the debate between Bhṛṅgin and Śīlavant regarding the scope of the authority of the Tantras as proclaimed by you, I have become filled with joy.
What did the virtuous Bhṛṅgin undertake immediately thereafter? What was answered there in full? I have a great curiosity to hear all of that.
"Listen, O King Basavendra, whose intellect shines with the sharpness of a blade of kusha grass; I shall speak—listen to the words established by the discourse between those two."
Relying upon the scriptures of Śiva, the teachings of the Śaiva Purāṇas, and the words of the sages,
you have established the preeminence of Śiva.
In that regard, you have now established the authority of the scriptures;
however, the authority of the Śaiva Purāṇas is not tenable therein.
If you are able to ward off this thunderbolt blow, with your self fixed upon the devouring of the great defect of tamas-ness.
Then we consider him blessed and the foremost among eloquent speakers;
for the killing of mosquitoes does not lead to the manifestation of prowess.
O Bhṛṅgin, you boast again after having merely performed easy tasks;
for the virtuous remain silent while performing deeds that are difficult to accomplish.
Now, you must establish the quality of tamas in the Purāṇas.
I shall refute that as well; behold my skill in reasoning.

Now, one might object: since the Śaiva Purāṇas are characterized by the quality of tamas (tāmasatva), how can the Vīraśaiva duties taught therein—such as the wearing of the *liṅga* and so forth—be authoritative? To explain: the creator of the Purāṇas is the four-faced Brahmā, who in some kalpas is predominant in sattva, while in others he is predominant in rajas.
In some [traditions], it is by *tamas*. When he is intensified by *sattva*, he composes the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas;
when intensified by *rajas*, the Brāhma Purāṇas; and when intensified by *tamas*, the Śaiva Purāṇas. Thus, the Śaiva Purāṇas were composed by Brahmā while blinded by the quality of *tamas*.

The Purāṇas are collections of sacrificial lore; indeed, they were composed by Vyāsa in ancient times as such collections. Furthermore, one should not entertain the delusion that they lack authority due to mutual contradictions, because such a claim is unproven and because it is stated therein that the Purāṇas have a single unified purpose.
A contradiction with another means of knowledge is indeed difficult to establish. If you ask, "What then is the interpretation of that statement?
listen:
[beings] are mixed, and they are of the nature of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Since the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), understood as an effect, is incapable of possessing the status of being the cause of the world— as established by the scriptural text, "Indeed, all these beings arise from ether alone"— that [causality] must ultimately terminate in the Supreme Self who dwells within it (the *antaryāmin*); thus, there is no contradiction with the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
It should not be said that there is a contradiction with scripture, for the opposite could just as easily be asserted:

the status of being the cause of the world, which is heard in the *Atharvaśiras* in reference to Viṣṇu as an effect, failing to find its proper application there, ultimately culminates in the Supreme Śiva, who is his inner controller (*antaryāmin*).
In reality, however, there is no contradiction with the Śruti in any Purāṇa;
for while the Śruti passages such as "Brahmā from Nārāyaṇa" intend to describe the mutual origination of the forms of the Guṇas,
the Śruti passages such as "all this [proceeds] from Paramaśiva" intend to describe their origination from Paramaśiva— this has been explained in detail.
This has been established by Appaya Dīkṣita in works such as the *Śivārkamaṇidīpikā*.
As for the claim that [the scripture] lacks authority because it contradicts itself, that too is refuted by this very [argument]:
the emergence of Rudra from Nārāyaṇa refers to the Guṇirudra, whereas the emergence of the three forms (trimūrti) [refers to the primordial manifestation].
Since this is intended as a systematic determination regarding the subject matter of Paramaśiva, there is not even a scent of self-contradiction.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the meaning stated by us is not supported by other Purāṇas accepted as authoritative,
that too—

This is trivial; for the fact that Śiva is the progenitor of Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa and their object of worship—as propounded in the *Śivapurāṇa*—which others might merely envy, is already universally accepted even in the *Mahābhārata*, which states: "He created Brahmā from his right side."
For the sake of the creation of the world, the Lord likewise [created] Viṣṇu from his left side for the protection of the world;

and because it has been elaborated in such passages as: "Since Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and you, along with the immortals, always worship his Liṅga together with Śakti, he is indeed most worthy of worship. Furthermore:

Furthermore, because the meanings declared in the Śiva Purāṇa are expounded in detail within the Pādma Purāṇa—in the dialogue between Śiva and Rāghava favored by you—as well as in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa and the Śivarahasya-pāda; and as it has been stated:
"The divine Purāṇa-saṃhitā, endowed with the majesty of the Liṅga."

The claim that the *Laiṅgya* [Purāṇa] lacks authority because it was composed with an insistence on the majesty of the *Liṅga*, initiated by a question focused on specific details, is also not tenable; for there is no such thing as "insistence" other than the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of words, and the intended meaning is the most preeminent factor.

If [you claim] that this is the cause of validity, how can it be presented as a contradictory reason for invalidity? On the contrary, where there is no firm conviction (*āgraha*), that [cognition] might even be sublated by another means of valid cognition; however, where there is no firm conviction at all, that is sublated in every respect, or one would experience an internal conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And yet...

It should not be argued that although there is an insistence on the praise expressed by the word "māhātmya" (greatness), there is no authority regarding its constituent elements, such as [Viṣṇu's] being the progenitor of Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa; for since even they (the opponents) already know the mere praise, it is precisely regarding those constituent parts that their inquiry arises, and [the text] serves as the answer to that.

For that which has come forth as the ancient [tradition] possesses authority precisely because it possesses *tātparya* (intentional focus). Nor do we say "because of possessing *tātparya*"; rather, following the maxim that one should not produce a divergence of understanding when questioned by those desiring to hear the greatness of the *liṅga*, [the scripture] conceals the true state and acts solely in accordance with what is to be refuted.
It should not be said that because [the Purāṇas] proceed [with narratives], their intent lies merely in praise and thus they lack authority regarding the literal meaning;

for when one who has not realized the truth asks about reality in the Purāṇas—which are composed for the purpose of explaining the truth—even if one asks with a distorted understanding, [the answer is given]: "What you have asked is not so."

This must be stated as the true nature of reality (*vastutattva*); for if one were to abandon that and admit a different course of action, it would follow that the Purāṇas are treatises of delusion (*mohaśāstra*). This is so even though Maitreya asked only in general terms what the cause of the world is.

Therefore, by Parāśara— who was long acquainted with his nature, who knew it well, and who understood his devotion to Viṣṇu— the [text] was produced from the presence of Viṣṇu in accordance with that [devotee's] capacity, following the maxim that one should not cause a disturbance of the intellect.

Furthermore, since it has been stated [in the text] beginning with "the world," the opposite view could also easily be maintained. Moreover, even if that were the case in the *Laiṅgya*, in the *Śaiva* [Purāṇa], when the ṛṣis residing at Prayāga asked Sūta:
"By the power of unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa), you have come into our sight; yet, performing no meritorious act whatsoever... [the text continues].
You ought not to go in vain. Therefore, [listen to] this Purāṇa, which is more meritorious than the best, which consists of sacred narratives joined with knowledge,
which has liberation as its sole fruit, which is excluded from improper conduct,
which demonstrates the causes of the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the worlds, and which is the entire essence of the Vedānta.

"Make us hear it today. Since the discourse has begun with this general inquiry, the authority [of the scripture] must be stated by you as well; furthermore, it is precisely by you that the authority of the *Bhāgavata* must be established. For therein lies the question of the sages to Sūta: "O Sūta, do you know?"

"Blessings upon you! The Blessed Lord, the Master of the Sātvatas, has been born from Devakī through Vasudeva for the sake of his intended purpose. It behoves you now to describe that very purpose to us who desire to hear it,"—since this refers specifically to a particular matter, he [the Lord], having received this praise...

Since their intense devotion toward the Blessed One is manifested through the four verses beginning with "ghorām," and since even prior to that, when requesting the author, their specific dedication to the *Bhāgavata*— the abode of aesthetic rasa— was already revealed by the words "Alas, the *Bhāgavata*, the dwelling place of rasa," it proceeds by way of that [dedication].

In this context, it is difficult to avoid the charge of being unauthoritative. As for the claim that the *Kūrma-purāṇa* and others are notorious for having lost their original repositories (*naṣṭakośatva*), that too is baseless;

for the *Brāhmī-saṃhitā*, which consists of six thousand verses and is currently in circulation, is certainly not lost, as it is included within the seventeen thousand verses known from the statement of the *Matsya-purāṇa*.
If it is argued that this portion consisting of eleven thousand verses, which exceeds the *Brahmasaṃhitā*, has been lost, let it be so; who says "no"? For we do not cite the statements found therein.
As for the *Saṃhitā* that is currently being heard, there is nothing within it resulting from the loss of anything other than itself.

There is a seed of doubt: since that other portion has been lost, this Saṃhitā too must have been lost in the same way, because there is no restrictive rule for the loss of some parts while others remain.
If it is argued that the [text] being heard must be a fabrication by someone and thus unreliable, we say no, because that is not a decisive reason.

Neither for you nor for me is there even a sesame-seed’s worth of lack of confidence regarding Pāṇini’s grammar on account of the destruction of the prophecies concerning Indra and others; moreover, this being the case, the loss of seventeen thousand verses out of the twenty-three thousand [verses] known from the statement of the Fish incarnation in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa—
If there were six thousand verses already existing, a lack of confidence would inevitably arise that is difficult to avoid.

As for the claim that the work is subject to suspicion of interpolation due to its extreme prolixity—that cannot even withstand a critical inquiry when analyzed; for instance, what exactly constitutes "extreme prolixity"? Is it intrinsic?

Is it the state of having more text, or is it being perceived as possessing a number greater than the established number? In the first case, there is no proof of the desired point because this would apply equally to all Purāṇas. In the second case, however, the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*), for he who...

If one objects that the full number of verses as calculated is not found and thus the text must have its manuscript lost, then for the sake of that very objector, how can such an excessive extent, as previously described, be established?
Whether this [extent] or some other be the case, in any event, does that [excessive length] exist within the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas?
If that is not so, why do you pointlessly delude others? Let this matter rest for now.

As for the claim that the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* is authoritative because it is free from the seven defects mentioned in the *Śivapurāṇa*, the part consisting of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is correct, but the part consisting of the reason (*hetu*) cannot withstand scrutiny;
for instance, regarding what was said to establish the first distinction, namely the nature of the speaker’s qualities:
Because he possessed knowledge of the ultimate reality of the deities obtained through the boons of Pulastya and Vasiṣṭha,
and because his greatness was indicated by the use of the term "incarnation" (*avatāra*) even in the Śiva Purāṇas regarding his own birth,
Parāśara is superior to the four-faced Brahmā, who is the speaker of the Śiva Purāṇas and belongs to the *tamas* mode.

Let us examine this: is the "speaker" (*vaktā*) here intended to be the poet who composed the work, or is it one fashioned by the poet within his own composition as the speaker of the subject matter he intends to convey?
In the first case, [there is the contradiction] that the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas are proclaimed to have been composed by the four-faced Brahmā, who is overflowing with the quality of goodness (*sattva*).

Because you yourself have proclaimed that the description of Parāśara’s excellence is irrelevant to the subject at hand; and in the second case, the inconsistency of the claim that the speaker of the Śiva Purāṇa suffers from the defect of being *tāmasa* is quite evident, for Matsya, Kūrma, Śiva, and others are indeed recorded as its speakers. And thus:

To whom would the claim not be a cause for laughter— that the Viṣṇu Purāṇas differ significantly from the Śiva Purāṇas solely because the former are narrated by Parāśara, who is himself worshipped by those such as Pulastya (the benefactor of Parāśara), while the latter are narrated by those who worship Śiva? And as for that [claim]...

The greatness [of the Lord] was established through the use of the term "incarnation" (*avatāra*) regarding His birth; yet even that was for His own satisfaction. Is there the conceit that the word "incarnation" is capable of expressing the birth of the Great Ones?
Or is it because, despite being common to all, it is used specifically in that context? It is not the first case.
This is because there is an absence of a lexicon, grammatical treatises, and so forth that could establish the word's power [of denotation].

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because it is unproven; for those who were consumed by the curse of Gotama, [it was said]: "All of them shall descend into wombs such as those of Brāhmaṇas and others."

Even in the case of the emergence of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*), the term "point of entry" (*avatārapada*) is employed; if it is argued that this usage is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), then the opposite could equally well be asserted. As for the second point of distinction—that [the Purāṇa] conforms to direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*)—that too is common to all Purāṇas, as has already been stated.
This has been explained. As for the third distinction—that there is no self-contradiction—that very point is unestablished (*asiddha*). For in the *Bhāgavata* itself it is said:
"O Giritra, that supreme light is not accessible even to all the world-protectors, to Viriñca, or to the lords of the gods, Vaikuṇṭha. Where [that light resides]...

Because it establishes a matter that contradicts the excellence of the Lord—which is the subject matter of the entire work—by stating that "Rajas, Tamas, and Sattva are not Brahman, which is devoid of all distinctions.
Furthermore, since the absence of actual contradiction is common to both [theories], there would be a distinction in their discourse regarding that. And as for what...
We have already stated that the fourth distinction, which consists in its agreement with other Purāṇas, is also common [to other texts]. Furthermore, as for the fifth and sixth distinctions— namely,
beginning with a general question and the absence of the "sheaths" (kośas)— these too are partially unestablished and lead to over-extension.

And this has already been stated previously. Furthermore, as for the seventh point of distinction—that [the scripture] is not overly prolix—that too has already been declared impossible to explain. Therefore, enough of this frantic pursuit of a gnat; let us desist. Thus, it is established that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is indeed self-evident.
"Of all the Purāṇas," thus [it is said].

[Thus ends the section on the six stages (*ṣaṭstha*), distinguished by one hundred and one unsurpassed divisions produced from churning the ocean of the Śāmbhava Āgama, which was obtained through the grace of the venerable Toṇṭada Siddheśvara— the incarnation of the mobile form of the beginningless, stainless Aparā.]

To Keladi Sadāśivarāya—the sovereign of the western ocean, who uprooted the seven constituents of the enemy of the lone hero [who caused] a tumult among ten million Yādavas and Murāris; the preceptor who established the pure Vedic Advaita Siddhānta; and the eminent teacher who bestows the mass of bliss from tasting the nectar of the reality of *latatattva*—[this work was composed] by Maritoṇṭadārya.

In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, within the instruction of Basava— the joy of the hearts of the virtuous and the Indra of the earth— composed by Vīrabhadra, the full moon of the milky ocean of the lineage of leaders and the lawful consort of the Lord of the Earth;
in the section on debate, this is the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Darkness (Tāmasatva) of the Śaiva Purāṇas."
[Chapter] ||
[The twenty-second chapter in the section on debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O illustrious Guru, exalted by the perfection of knowledge regarding the six stages (ṣaṭsthalajñāna),
you have indeed refuted the claim that the ancient Śaiva scriptures are characterized by darkness (tāmasatva).
Now, having heard these words spoken so correctly by you, who are possessed of virtuous character, my heart is satisfied; what more, then, could I begin with joy?
What has been answered by Bhṛṅgin and Śīlin for me today?
My heart desires to hear it; please speak now out of compassion.
O King Basavendra, your intellect is subtle-sighted;
listen as I relate in due order the words that ought to be spoken by those two.

O foremost among those endowed with virtue, you have joyfully explained the authoritative scripture of the ancients along with its reasoning, for the purpose of dispelling the quality of darkness (tamas).
Your desired conclusion is not established by that [argument] alone; rather, I shall establish it precisely through that great Śaiva doctrine which is accepted by the teacher Śrīkaṇṭha.
"We shall see your power; do not harbor pride as you did before.
Hearing these words of Bhṛṅgin, he laughed and spoke again:
When the ocean itself is being swallowed, how insignificant are the drinking of ponds and rivers?
I shall now proceed to refute this doctrine asserted by you.

Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. The word *atha* (now) signifies immediate succession; that is, it means "after the study of the Vedas," because the study of the Vedas is relevant to the subject at hand. Therefore, since the study of the Vedas has been completed, an inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken. [This follows] after the inquiry into Dharma.

Because the inquiry into Brahman is useful for the inquiry into Brahman, the latter is commenced immediately after the former. Now, [the texts state]: "The *ṛta* and *satya* are the Supreme Brahman"; "Thence, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Greatness"; "As the one hidden in all beings according to their classes, the sole enveloper of the universe, the Lord. That [Brahman]— (Aligned with the provided text structure: ...because it is useful for the inquiry into Brahman, the inquiry into Brahman is commenced immediately after that. Now, [it is said]: "The *ṛta* and *satya* are the Supreme Brahman"; "Thence, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Greatness"; "As the one hidden in all beings according to their classes, the sole enveloper of the universe, the Lord"—that [Brahman].

"Having known [Him], they become immortal; beholding the Supreme Brahman, one goes [to Him] by no other means"—since the status of Śiva as the Supreme Brahman is evident through such statements supported by the context, one might ask: "What remains to be deliberated? If this is asked, the answer is: No; for some say that the individual soul (jīva) is Brahman, while others say that Nārāyaṇa and others are.
Regarding the term "Brahman," the inquiry into Brahman is commenced for the purpose of refuting that [notion].

If it is objected: "Since the sūtra *athāto dharmajijñāsā* has already stated that the study of the Veda is useful for the inquiry into Dharma, thereby providing an answer as to its utility for other inquiries as well, for what purpose is it stated again in *athāto brahmajijñāsā*?"— it is not so.

It is stated separately that "the inquiry into Brahman (brahmavicāra) must be performed. Since this [latter] proposition is already effectively established by that [former] proposition, for what purpose is this repeated proposition? [For example:

"Now, therefore, follows the definition of the subsidiary" (athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam), or "Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into that which serves the purpose of the sacrifice and that which serves the purpose of the person" (athātaḥ kratvarthapuruṣārthayor jijñāsā).

A formal proposition (pratijñā) must be stated for the purpose of initiating a new subject matter, just as in the statement, "Now, therefore, follows the definition of the subsidiary elements" (*athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*). It must be explained how this is called a proposition regarding a new subject matter;
[the answer is that] there is no difference [between them] because the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā and Uttara-mīmāṃsā constitute a single system.
Alternatively, since this is a single treatise, it is logical to maintain that this is the commencement of another subject matter.

"The source from which there is the birth and so forth of this [world]"—the state of being the cause of the world's birth and so forth is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman, and that is possible in Sāmbaśiva. According to the Vedic revelation: "Soma flows, the progenitor of prayers, the progenitor of Indra, the progenitor of Bṛhaspati, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu. Thus [says] the Śruti. Who...
"Rudra, the great seer, who is the source and origin of the gods and superior to the universe,
brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning; may he endow us with auspicious intelligence"—
since these two Vedic passages establish that Rudra is the cause of Viriñci, the creator of all, and Viṣṇu, the protector of all.

The fact that [He] is the cause of all is indeed established. By the statement, "Extremely subtle within the midst of the waters, the creator of the universe, possessing manifold forms," the status of being the direct creator of the universe is set forth;
therefore, too, the fact that Sāmbaśiva is the cause of the world is indeed established. And it is not merely that "Soma flows."
It might be argued: "Since the mantra refers to the *soma* creeper, how can it be said to refer to Śiva? To this we reply:

because the meaning of the scripture is clearly recognized in the *Atharvaśikhā*, which states, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all produced from Him," it is impossible to deny that [the mantra] refers to Him.
The establishment of His being the cause of all is achieved because He is the means for determining Viṣṇu and others as causes.

And that Brahman, known as Sadāśiva, is not non-different from the individual soul (jīva); for by perceiving the Self and the Impeller as distinct, one, being favored by Him, thereafter attains immortality. "The Knower and the Unknower, the two unborn ones, the Lord and the Unlord. "The infinite Self is indeed of universal form and a non-agent. "Two birds, inseparable companions and friends, [perch] upon the same..."

They both embrace the tree; of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the *pippala*, while the other looks on without eating. When he perceives the other as the Lord, beloved, and understands His greatness, he is freed from sorrow. Drinking the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, they have entered the cave.

"In the highest supreme goal; those who know Brahman, the five-fire sacrificers, and those who have thrice kindled the fire-sacrifice speak of shadow and light. For the one unborn [Self] lies down beside her while enjoying her, but another unborn [Self] leaves her once her enjoyment has been experienced"—through such scriptural passages, the clear distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) is established.

Since they are perceived as distinct, how could non-difference be established? Nor should it be argued that non-difference is established by such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), for [the scripture says]: "He whose face, head, and neck are everywhere; who dwells in the cave of the heart of all beings;
who is the Lord pervading all, therefore Śiva is omnipresent; whose hands and feet are on every side."
He has eyes, heads, and faces on every side; He possesses ears everywhere in the world, and stands encompassing all.

The God who is in fire, who is in the waters, who has entered the entire universe, who is in the herbs, and who is in the trees—to that God, salutation after salutation. To Rudra who is in fire, who is in the waters, who is in the herbs—[to that Rudra, salutation].

He has entered into all beings; let there be obeisance to that Rudra. Having eyes on every side, a mouth on every side, arms on every side, and feet on every side, he blows together heaven and earth with his arms and wings.

Through a thorough consideration of such scriptural passages as "The one God, creating... and others, because Śiva manifests as the indwelling soul (*śarīrin*) of all, the statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) have as their purport precisely the qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*). Indeed, this is simply the knowledge of Śiva as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all.
It is the means for attaining liberation. And thus it is heard in the branches of the Śvetāśvataras:

"Then, having known that which is beyond, the supreme Brahman, the great one, who dwells hidden in all beings according to their classes, the one Lord who encompasses the universe—having known Him, they become immortal. Therefore...
The knowledge of duality alone is the means to liberation.

To this it is replied: That which was stated—that the knowledge of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita-jñāna*) is the means to liberation—is utterly untenable. For instance: "Having realized that 'I am that Brahman' which illumines the manifold world (*prapañca*) of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, one is liberated from all bonds."

By the Śruti on Kaivalya beginning with "Thus," and by the Māṇḍūkya Śruti—"The fourth is without measure, beyond empirical usage, the cessation of the phenomenal world, auspicious, non-dual; the syllable Om is indeed that. The Self alone enters the Self by means of the Self"—it is evident that the non-duality of Śiva alone is what is intended by statements such as "That thou art."

The primary purport must necessarily be stated as being solely for one's own benefit. Nor is the scriptural text "That Brahman, I am" non-dualistic; rather, even if duality were authoritative, this text is intended for the practice of meditation on non-difference, meaning that one should perform the meditation on non-difference during worship. Thus...

Even the Māṇḍūkya Śruti does not have as its purport the non-duality of Śiva; for in the preceding section it states: "It is neither inwardly cognitive, nor outwardly cognitive, nor cognitive of both, nor cognitive, nor non-cognitive;
it is unseen, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without characteristics, the essence of the realization of the one Self."

It should be stated that this is presented as an alternative position, based on the passage: "They consider the fourth state to be the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), auspicious (*śiva*), and non-dual (*advaita*). For while it is possible for there to be an auspicious non-duality consisting of pure consciousness (*niṣkṛṣṭacaitanya*) distinct from the *viśva*, *taijasa*, and *prājña* states, [it is not possible for such a non-duality to exist within those states themselves].

The phrase "of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña, who are the possessors of identification with their respective states" introduces an alternative view therein; however, this is not the case in the non-dualism of Śiva (Śivādvaita). For this very reason, the Kaivalya Upaniṣad declares: "Whatever is to be enjoyed, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoyment within the three abodes—I am the witness distinct from these, pure consciousness, the eternal Śiva."

Thus, because Sadāśiva— who is distinct from those possessing the ego-identifications of waking and other states— and who is undivided consciousness, is fit for non-duality, [the text] establishes his non-difference from the individual soul (jīva).
Therefore, by the authority of the Māṇḍūkya Śruti, the non-duality of Śiva alone must be accepted, in accordance with the Kaivalya Śruti.

And it has already been stated by the previously cited [passage]: "Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of non-duality, that Śruti is intended merely for such worship," because there would be contradiction with many preceding and subsequent Śrutis if the non-duality of Śiva were not accepted.

For instance: That which is the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe, more subtle than the subtle, eternal—that reality alone is you; you indeed are that. "I am that non-dual Brahman.
More minute than the minute, I am that very one; likewise, I am the Great One, this wondrous universe. I am the Ancient One.

"I am the Person, I am the Lord, I am golden-hued, I am the very form of bliss"— since this is taught as having non-duality (*advaita*) alone as its intended meaning, how can it be said that statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) are merely figurative? Furthermore, [regarding] the non-difference of the individual soul from Śiva...

Having firmly established that the attributes of the Supreme Lord belong to the individual soul and that the attributes of the individual soul belong to the Supreme Lord, [the author] declares this as an established truth through such statements as:

"He alone, whose self is deluded by Māyā, having assumed a body, performs all [actions]," and so forth. Nor does the word *sa* (he) refer back to the previously mentioned individual soul as being identical to Māyā.

It should not be said that the term "living being" (jīva) refers to the Supreme Lord, nor that—having taken the established non-difference of the living being [from the Lord] as a premise—the possession of the attributes of a living being is predicated [of Him]; for [the scripture says]: "Making the Self the lower fire-drill and the Praṇava the upper fire-drill," thus [referring to] the Supreme Self.

Because there was previously not even a trace of the individual soul (*jīva*) apart from its meditation as non-different from the *praṇava*, it likewise declares the established fact that the individual soul has no connection with the attributes of the Lord: "The individual soul who sports in the three cities—from him indeed is born this entire manifold [universe]; from him is born the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."

"Mind and all the senses. Now, if it is argued that because of the statement, "Having thus known the form of the Supreme Self, which dwells in the cave, is partless and non-dual," the purport of this Śruti is precisely such knowledge and not non-duality—[we reply: that [non-duality] refers to the meditation upon Brahman, which possesses a second, as being non-dual.

Due to the absence of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*) and through a careful consideration of what precedes and follows, the intended meaning of the scriptural passage here—namely, "dwelling in Brahman, one attains Brahman"—is, on the contrary, necessarily established as non-duality by another scriptural text; thus, duality is not proven. "You are female, you are male... [and so forth].

"Whether as a youth or even as a maiden, you, when aged, walk with a staff"—according to this ancient Vedic revelation, [the Self] appears through the qualities of all the senses yet is devoid of all senses; it is the Lord and Ruler of all, the refuge and friend of all. Within the city of nine gates, the embodied soul, like a swan, sports outside.
"The Lord of the entire world, both the stationary and the moving; handless and footless, yet swift and a grasper;

He sees without eyes and hears without ears"—by this subsequent Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad passage as well, the non-duality of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) is clearly perceived; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in statements such as "That thou art."
As for what was said—that duality is established as authoritative by the Śruti text, "Two birds, inseparable companions"—likewise, in the Gītā it is also stated:
"There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable; the perishable consists of all beings."

The claim that "the immutable (akṣara) is called the unchanging (kūṭastha)" is untenable; for in the Paiṅgī-rahasya-brāhmaṇa, both the individual soul (jīva) and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) are explained as being distinct from one another, and thus the duality favored by you lacks scriptural authority. Indeed, it is thus:
The explanation of the Paiṅgi-rahasya-brāhmaṇa: "He who eats the sweet" refers to the *sattva*;

"without eating he gazes" means that another, not eating, looks on. These two—the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*—are respectively the knower and the ignorant; by means of the former, one sees the dream. Now, as for this bodily witness (*upadraṣṭṛ*),...

Thus, since the distinction has been clearly established as being solely between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is not even a scent of the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman (*jīva-brahma*). Furthermore, the statement from the *Gītā*, "There are these two persons in the world," is merely an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the previously explained scripture (*śruti*); it does not intend to establish a difference between the individual soul and the Lord (*jīveśa-bheda*).

However, [the statement] refers specifically to the distinction between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, because non-duality is firmly established in that very same context by the verse, "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) in all fields, O Bhārata," the statement "These two" possesses the very same purport as previously stated. By this, all scriptural passages concerning duality are also answered.

As for what was said— that the statement "Now, therefore, the definition of the subsidiary" (*athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*) does not mark the beginning of a different treatise, but rather the commencement of another section within a single, multi-faceted treatise, just like the statement "Now, therefore, the desire to know that which pertains to the ritual purpose and the human purpose" (*athātaḥ kratvarthapuruṣārthayor jijñāsā*)— that is extremely weak.

Since it is observed everywhere that a difference in subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), and author (*kartṛ*) necessitates a difference in treatise (*śāstra-bheda*), a distinction between the two treatises must necessarily be accepted here as well.
The subject matter of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* is ritual action (*karman*), while the subject matter of the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* is Brahman.
Furthermore, the purpose of the two is distinct:
in one case, the purpose is heaven resulting from performance by means of knowledge of Dharma accompanied by the logic of the "thousand-fold subject" (*sahasrādhikaraṇanyāya*);
in the other, the purpose is liberation through perfect knowledge by means of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth. It is exactly thus.

The difference in authorship is evident to all people. Since both [systems] thus possess distinct authors who serve as the grounds for the difference between the two treatises, how can their non-difference be established? Nor should it be argued that their unity is created by the fact that they consist of logical inquiry (*nyāyavicāra*); for, in that case—

There would also be unity among the *prayoga-śāstras* of Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Āśvalāyana, and others, because the method for presenting the sequence of performance is identical. [Objection: Let it be so; who says otherwise?
[Response: As *prayoga-śāstras*, those *sūtras* possess precisely that unity. For this very reason, they are called *kalpa-sūtras*.

Their designation is also one and the same. Likewise, in the verse enumerating the fourteen fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*)—namely, "the six auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and the four Vedas"—the term "auxiliary sciences" includes the six *aṅgas*, and among them, all the ritual manuals (*prayogaśāstra*) are recited as a single *aṅga*. For this very reason:

If it is argued that [the Mīmāṃsāsūtra] is a manual of ritual practice (prayogaśāstra), then, just as in that section [of the Śābarabhāṣya], the investigation into its authority or lack thereof was conducted by accepting the unity of all the sūtras; so too here.

If it is argued that there is no difference between Pūrva-mīmāṃsā and Uttara-mīmāṃsā, we say no; for unless there is a difference in the subject matter to be established, it is impossible in any way to claim the identity of the two systems merely on the basis of the unity of their method of inquiry. Otherwise, there would be no distinction even between Śikṣā and Vyākaraṇa. Therefore, the difference lies solely in the difference of subject matter and the difference of purpose.

It must necessarily be stated that these two are the factors that cause the division of a treatise (*śāstra*). Furthermore, a difference in authors is a factor causing the division of a treatise only in a secondary sense, not in a primary sense; for even though the Lord Patañjali is the single author of the treatises on Yoga, Medicine, and Grammar, the division of those treatises is extremely clear. In the present case as well...

However, because the three—subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), and agent (*kartṛ*)—are distinct, their difference must indeed be stated. Now, let there be a difference between *Śikṣā* and *Vyākaraṇa*, even though they are identical in their mode of teaching words, since a difference in subject matter and purpose exists between them; for the subject matter of *Śikṣā* is the true nature of Vedic sounds.

The subject matter: Since there is a distinction, the subject matter of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the true nature of worldly and Vedic words. Nor should it be said that there is no difference in purpose;
for a single correct word, when properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) in the heavenly world, [granting] mother and father...
"By the statement of the venerable commentator (Bhagavadbhāṣyakāra), 'He who investigates these words, and he who meditates upon them—

both of them are performers of meritorious deeds and piercers of the solar orb,' as well as by the Purāṇic statement, 'One who knows the division of even the smallest vowel-measure and is expert in the sequence of phonemes [attains this] through grammar..."

Since it is heard that the fruit of training consists in attaining the status of a teacher such as Vyāsa, according to the statement, "One who knows the specific distinctions of the *padakrama* should go to the assembly of teachers," there is indeed a difference in their fruits. Therefore, the distinction between the two is well-established. Now, [one might object]:

If it is argued that although there is a difference in the results (*phala*) in the present case, how can there be a difference [in the means] since the object—the true nature of the meaning of the Vedic sentences—is one, we reply: no; for just as grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), despite the unity of the object consisting of the true nature of the Vedic syllables, serves to distinguish the true nature of worldly phonemes and to distinguish Vedic phonemes according to its respective perspective (*mati*).

Furthermore, you speak of a distinction between the two *śikṣās* (the *pūrva-mīmāṃsā* and the *uttara-mīmāṃsā*). Since that very distinction can be easily stated on the basis of their respective natures—the former consisting of an inquiry into the meaning of the sentences of the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) and the latter consisting of an inquiry into the meaning of the sentences of the later section (*uttarakāṇḍa*)—it follows that the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā* and the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā* do not constitute a single treatise (*eka-śāstra*). Moreover, [there are other reasons].
The subject matter of the sentences in the earlier section (pūrvakāṇḍa) is ritual action (karma), while the subject matter of the sentences in the later section (uttarakāṇḍa) is Brahman;

thus, a distinction between their respective objects is evident through the difference in their modes and qualificands. It was previously stated that [the Upanishads] exist as distinct from the subjects of Phonetics (śikṣā) and Grammar (vyākaraṇa).
Therefore, there is no identity between the two treatises consisting of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā.

Moreover, even if the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā were identical insofar as they both consist of an inquiry into the meaning of Vedic sentences, how could they be non-different when their distinctness is extremely evident through the principle of what is applicable and what is not applicable?

For the purpose of investigating the *Uttara-tantra*, all the principles (*nyāya*) of the *Pūrva-tantra* are required, whereas the principles of the *Uttara-tantra* are not [required] in the *Pūrva-tantra*. Therefore, since such a distinction exists, what scholar would assert that the two scriptures are one? Consequently, there is no single scripture (*eka-śāstrya*).

The claim that [the two systems belong to] the Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsās is entirely without justification. Furthermore, since all remaining points have already been effectively refuted by the refutation of the Rāmānuja school, we have set them aside and left them unaddressed here, following the maxim of "grinding what is already ground. Thus, everything is consistent.
[Thus,
from the venerable Tōṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the mobile form of the beginningless and stainless Aparā,
and who obtained the grace of the Śāmbhava Āgama ocean churned by him— [this work] which is divided into the one hundred and one unsurpassed *sthala*-divisions...]

In [this work] composed by the eminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows a mass of bliss from tasting the nectar of the reality of *latatattva*, for Keladi Sadāśivarāya— the lord of the western ocean, the sole hero who caused a tumult among ten million Yādavas and Murāris, the seizer of the seven constituents of the enemy, and the teacher who established the pure Vedic doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*).

In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, within the section on debate (*vādakāṇḍa*) in the instruction of Basava— the joy of the hearts of the people and the Indra of the earth— concerning Mallāmbā, the lawful consort of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth and the full moon in the milky ocean of the lineage of Nāyakas,
this is the chapter titled "The Exposition of the Nīlakaṇṭha Doctrine and its Refutation."
The Twenty-second Chapter.
[The twenty-third chapter in the section on debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O Lord Śrī Toṇṭadācārya Cakravartin, supreme among gurus!
First, the Nīlakaṇṭha-mata was commenced by Bhṛṅgin, and after that [the other].
Having heard that refutation of [the opponent's] views, spoken by the virtuous one according to the path of the Vedas and Agamas,
from the lotus of your mouth, my heart became filled with joy.
Furthermore, what did those two begin? I have a desire in my heart to hear this;
O ocean of compassion, O high-minded one, explain it to me.
O illustrious King Basava, leader of the lineage of monarchs!
Your skill in intellect is exceedingly difficult to find, even among gurus.
That which I must explain regarding those two, insofar as they consist of debate, I shall now fully declare to you; let it be heard with careful attention.
The philosophy of the venerable Śaṅkara’s non-dualism is in accord with numerous scriptures,
is served by hosts of great sages, is renowned, and bestows supreme liberation.
Moreover, how are you able to find fault with that Śaiva [tradition], which is endowed with the Purāṇas, the Smṛtis, and the Dharma, upon this earth?
"When that [enemy] was slain and I had begun [my work], your fleeing was indeed real;
nevertheless, saying 'let there be no fear for you,' I gave you the gesture of granting safety."
Then, when Bhṛṅgin— who was like a lion to the elephants of all the established conclusions of the philosophical systems— said, "O virtuous one, I give it to you upon your head," [he accepted it].
That answer was spoken by Śīlavat, the foremost among the devotees of Śiva;
it is being repeated by you, O Bhṛṅgin of evil mind, merely according to your own understanding.
Therefore, today you shall now exert yourself to witness your prowess;
see my speech properly, if indeed you possess the capability.
As long as you continue to refute what has been said by me, you speak with such joy;
state, therefore, the established tenets of that system, and hear therein its refutation.

Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. The word "atha" (now) signifies immediate succession. "Atha" means immediately after the attainment of the fourfold qualification; "ataḥ" (therefore) means because the attainment of those qualifications has occurred; thus, "brahmajijñāsā"—the investigation concerning Brahman—must be undertaken. And the fourfold qualification is as follows:

Discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, detachment from the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, the perfection of tranquility and the other [means], and the desire for liberation. What is called "investigation" (vicāra) is a specific activity consisting of hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana). Hearing is [the process] for one who has understood the connection between words and their meanings, [consisting of] the Upanishads along with their supporting texts, as received from the mouth of a teacher.

Reflection (*manana*) is the operation conducive to the generation of the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence; it consists of the continuous stream of thought regarding that very same heard object—
the non-dual reality— which has been contemplated through the *sūtras*, *bhāṣyas*, and *vārtikas* along with supporting arguments,
and which has been brought about by the sequence of *yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, *pratyāhāra*, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*.

The knowledge that brings [liberation] near; the resulting partless mental modification (*akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti*) is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), which is the means for liberation in one's essential nature (*svarūpa-mukti*) consisting in the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna-nivṛtti*). Its fruit in this life consists of cattle, sons, friends, wife, house, fields, gardens, wealth, gold, vehicles, silken garments, and so forth.

Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the absence of longing for both [this world and the next], such as rebirth in the hereafter, immortality, or the state of knowing reality. Tranquility (*śama*) is the restraint of the internal sense-faculties;
self-control (*dama*) is the restraint of the external sense-faculties; and the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) is the longing for emancipation.

Since such a perfection of the fourfold means occurs only in the fourth stage of life (*turīyāśrama*), those belonging to the fourth stage alone possess the primary qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*); however, because householders (*gṛhastha*) are qualified for obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*), they possess only a preliminary qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. For this very reason:

The view of Bhagavatpāda is that there is a scriptural injunction stating, "One should perform the hearing [of the scriptures] when [the moon is] in Śravaṇā. However, some [hold that] because the rule for renunciation in times of distress is established by the statement, "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone," [renunciation is not mandatory].

They say that, like the *prayāja* and other such rites, [the practice of *agnihotra*] possesses the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by way of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*), and thus householders also possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

In response to the inquiry as to what the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman is, the definition of Brahman is stated by the aphorism: "That from which the origin and so forth of this [world proceed" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*). Being the cause of the world's origin and so forth is its *taṭastha-lakṣaṇa* (indirect or circumstantial definition). Its *svarūpa-lakṣaṇa* (essential definition), however, is existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānandatva*). Now, one might object: what is the purpose of a *taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*?

What is this distinction being made between the "definition of essential nature" (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*)? If it is argued that it must necessarily be stated in a single form, we say no; for the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman contradicts many *smṛtis*, and as such, it will be refuted in the *Samanvaya* Sūtra. Likewise, it is stated: "The non-difference from That [Brahman] follows from the words regarding 'origin' (*ārambhaṇa*) and so forth."
Furthermore, since it will be stated in the Sūtra that the world is not to be relished, the world is false;
consequently, a definition composed of such [worldly] elements would lack ultimate reality and would merely characterize Brahman in a conventional sense.
Therefore, to avoid this, the essential definition (svarūpalakṣaṇa) is stated as being distinct [from the worldly definition].

And when the inquiry arises as to what the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that Brahman is, the Sūtra "Because it has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*) establishes that Brahman has the scripture as its means of valid cognition, and not perception or other such means of valid cognition; for even in that regard, because Brahman is beyond the senses, it is not perceptible, just like space (*ākāśa*). For this very reason...

Because there is no perception of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and because [the subject] lacks occurrence [in the example], there is an absence of a probans (*liṅga*) pervaded by that; and because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), neither general inference (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa-anumāna*) nor inference by elimination (*pariśeṣa-anumāna*) is possible. Therefore, it must be stated that scripture alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And thus says the Śruti: "One does not perceive that Great One without the Veda."
"But I ask you about that person who is known from the Upaniṣads."

Now, how can Brahman have the Veda as its source (*śāstrayonitva*), given that the scriptural texts of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) do not have Brahman as their primary purport? Nor [can it be argued] by reflecting on the scriptural passage, "I ask you about that person who is known through the Upaniṣads" (*tantvaupaniṣadaṃ puruṣaṃ pṛcchāmi*).

It must be stated that although Brahman is not an object of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) of the Vedas, it possesses the status of having the scripture as its source (*śāstrayonitva*) by virtue of being established through the authority of the Upaniṣads.

In response to the doubt that it is difficult for Brahman to have the Vedas as its source (*śāstrayonitva*) because the scriptures— consisting of meditations on attributes (*sampad-upāsanā*), meditations on symbols (*pratīka-upāsanā*), and meditations involving identification with the Self (*ahaṅgraha-upāsanā*)— do not establish non-dual Brahman, the aphorism *tattu samanvayāt* determines that the Vedāntas indeed have non-dual Brahman as their subject matter.

The intention here is as follows: "But that [Brahman] has the scripture as its source. The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of indicating the rejection of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). "[It is known] from the harmony" (*samanvayāt*); that is, because of being correctly concordant (*samyaganugatatvāt*).
Correct concordance consists in the fact that the Vedic texts regarding Brahman form a single unified statement through their introductory and concluding sections.

In some cases, [the meaning is understood] through a unique mark (*liṅga*) not shared by others and through repetition; for instance, in accordance with the question regarding the supreme instruction of the *Tattvamasi* and other scriptures—
namely, "Have you asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known?"— there follows the corresponding reply.

Because the question is appropriately framed, and because it would be inexplicable without the non-difference of the knowledge of all things from the knowledge of Brahman, it is determined that in the concluding statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), non-duality alone is expressed in its primary sense. Otherwise, [it would not be so].

Otherwise, there would be a lack of syntactic coordination between the preceding and following contexts. For this very reason, in the second chapter of the *Pūrvatantra*, in the section titled "The Upāṃśuyāja should be like the Paurṇamāsī," it is stated:
"Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice for the sake of avoiding insipidity (*ajāmitva*)."

By accepting the status of these sentences— beginning with "Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to in a whisper for the sake of non-repetition; Agni and Soma are to be sacrificed to in a whisper for the sake of non-repetition"—
as mere restatements (anuvādaka) out of a desire for syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) due to their inclusion of the *tavya* suffix, [the author] [relies on] the *upā...* located at the beginning.
Even the statement "he performs the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice in the interval," which is a description in the present tense,
is accepted as being injunctive; for this very reason, in the first chapter, within the section on names (*nāmadheya-peṭikā*),

in the section titled "Those preceded by [other injunctions] are not for the purpose of injunction, because their capacity [for injunction] exists in the traditional recension" (*pūrvavanto 'vidhānārthās tatsāmarthyaṃ samāmnāye*).

The sentences beginning with "When a son is born, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," and continuing with "Insofar as it consists of eight potsherds," and so forth, are *arthavādas* intended to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the initial sentence concerning Vaiśvānara.

That has been accepted. By that same principle, here too, non-difference is accepted in order to establish the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the preceding and the subsequent [passages]. In this very way, in the subsequent section [of the Brahmasūtras], "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition," it is stated: "Brahman is the tail, the support."

"That which is non-dual is Brahman alone; he indeed becomes non-existent if he knows 'Brahman is non-existent. But if he knows 'Brahman exists,' that is one bliss of Brahman. 'Teach me, O Venerable One, about Brahman. 'Seek to know Brahman through austerity; austerity is Brahman. [He] understood: 'Food is Brahman. Breath..."
"Brahman," he understood; "Mind is Brahman," he understood; "Consciousness is Brahman," he understood;
"Bliss is Brahman," he understood—thus it is taught through repeated practice. For when one perceives even the slightest difference in this [Brahman], then fear arises for him.
It is also heard in scripture that dualistic cognition (*dvaitavijñāna*) is a cause of harm even in the midst of the practice of Brahman.
Likewise, in the section [of the Brahma Sūtras] beginning with "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark" (*ākāśastalliṅgāt*), regarding the passage "What is the goal of this world?
'Ether,' he said," if the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) were intended to refer to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), then that which is supreme... [would not be established].

The Udgītha is most excellent; "this very one is infinite"—such qualities as infinity, being heard in scripture, are marks (liṅga) that are not shared by anything else. In this very way, all the Upaniṣads have their systematic unity (samanvaya) in Brahman alone, which is non-dual.
Up to the conclusion of the first chapter,

it is established that certain Upaniṣadic passages are intended to teach the meditation on the "I" (*ahaṃgraha-upāsanā*) for the sake of favoring those of dull intellect, in order to lead them toward the realization of non-dual Brahman (*advaita-brahma*). For example:

"This golden person is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair," and so forth. Therefore, the Vedāntas have their systematic unity (*samanvaya*) in non-dual Brahman. [Objection: But surely there is another [Self] because of the mention of difference; for there is a mention of difference, and both [the Upanishads] speak of the embodied self as well.

They are studied as distinct. However, [the opponent argues: "Because of the impossibility [of identity], the embodied soul is not [the Self]; for two Selves have entered the cave, as is seen from that," and so forth—in these passages, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is clearly propounded by the author of the Sūtras.
Therefore, if it is argued that the distinction alone is the intended meaning of the Sūtra-author, we say: no.

"Non-difference from that [the cause] follows from the word 'origin' (ārambhaṇa) and so forth; for this very reason, there is the comparison with the reflection of the sun and so on; and as the carpenter [is both free and bound], so too [the soul]; but it is mere illusion (māyāmātra), because [in reality] its true nature is unmanifest"—in these and other such sūtras, non-difference is clearly expressed by the term "non-difference" (ananyatva) and by the comparison using the example of the sun's reflection.

Since the non-duality of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is established by the statement that the soul is a reflection in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), difference is certainly not the intended subject of the Sūtra-author; thus, non-duality alone is proven.
That which is stated by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya and his foremost disciples, the proponents of Advaita—
that Brahman is non-dual and the entire world other than it is illusory (*mithyā*);
and that in this system the word *mithyā* is intended to mean "indescribable" (*anirvacanīya*), not "non-existent" (*asat*).
And the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the effect consists in its being incapable of being defined as either existent or non-existent as something distinct from its cause.
And silver in a mother-of-pearl shell [is so] in relation to its own material cause, the mother-of-pearl.
Because it is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) from that [Brahman] and a transformation (*pariṇāma*) from ignorance (*ajñāna*), it is impossible to define as either existent or non-existent;

likewise, the world (*jagat*) is also indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) because it is an illusory manifestation from Brahman—its own material cause—and a transformation from Māyā, which is of the nature of ignorance regarding that [Brahman]. If so, then [regarding] the world...

When the objection is raised that [the world] would lack the status of being something to be accepted—just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—we accept three levels of existence: illusory (prātibhāsika), such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell;
