empirical (vyāvahārika), which is the world; and ultimate (pāramārthika), which is Brahman. And thus, regarding the world...

Although the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) is the same as in the case of silver appearing in a mother-of-pearl shell, the additional factor of "empirical reality" (*vyāvahārikatva*) has been introduced; however, by that much, there is no loss of its falsity (*mithyātva*). In this regard, [the scriptures state]: "There is no multiplicity here at all";
"Now follows the instruction: 'Not this, not this'"; and "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; it is simply clay."

Let it be granted that the Śruti passage beginning with "Truth" (satyam) is the authority for the claim that Brahman is non-dual and the material cause of the world; however, regarding those points, there is no dispute between us Vīra-Māheśvaras—who are proponents of non-duality—and you followers of the venerable [Śaṅkara] Bhagavatpāda. All else is different.

It is not capable of producing the blossoming of joy in our minds; for instance, what is the proof for the postulation of two types of material causes—namely, the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmopādāna*) and the illusory material cause (*vivartopādāna*)? It is certainly not the Sūtra, because the Sūtra is authoritative precisely because it is favorable to our own position, as it speaks of "self-creation" (*ātmakṛti*).

Regarding the phrase "because of transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*): even in the Śruti, there is the statement, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," which demonstrates a conformity precisely with the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*). This is further supported by Smṛti texts such as: "Just as gold is accepted as one and undivided despite the differences of bracelets, crowns, earrings, and so forth; likewise, [the Self remains one] through the conceptualizations of gods, animals, humans, and castes. Etc.

Furthermore, because the analogy of the golden earrings (*svarṇakuṇḍala*) is evident; moreover, in your view there is the postulation of two material causes (*upādāna*), whereas in our view there is the postulation of only one material cause—thus, the collection of scriptural and traditional (*smṛti*) statements from our side is supported by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore:

Is a distinct "apparent existence" (*prātibhāsika-sattā*) accepted here? No, for both you and we find two levels of existence sufficient. For instance, there is nothing at all apart from Brahman and the world;
Brahman alone is ultimately real (*paramārtha-sat*), whereas the world, though empirical (*vyāvahārika*), is not ultimately real.

For example, although there are worldly conventions such as "an earthen jar," "with respect to the clay," "fetch water with the jar," "the jar has become cracked," "look at the jar," or "the jar is destroyed," yet with respect to the jar,
the clay alone is ultimately real. [This is] because of the clay.
Even though there is a continuity with the jar, the earth does not persist in its entirety within the jar, because it is absent from the cup (śarāva).

Therefore, for both you and us, the two types of existence alone are sufficient; anything beyond this is simply not capable of withstanding logical scrutiny. Furthermore, regarding the claim that the world is "indescribable" (anirvacanīya), we see no logic in that either.
This is because, through differentiation, it is possible to designate [the same substance] as a "bracelet," "earring," or "pendant" in relation to gold.

Nor should it be argued that even so, bracelets and the like can still be designated as "existent" in relation to gold; for there is also the cognition of existence in such expressions as "an existent bracelet" (*sat-kuṇḍalam*) and "an existent necklace" (*sad-graiveyakam*).

Because it arises as a distinct entity. Even so, if only the existence of the clay itself is perceived there and not something distinct from it, then the cognition should be "the clay is existent," but not "the earring and so forth are existent.
In that case, how can you be a proponent of non-duality (*advaitavādin*)? [For you admit] that "the earring exists as distinct from the gold."
If you say, "Even though you know non-duality, you speak as if there were duality," then we shall state the secret; listen attentively.
Duality is of two kinds: one consists of mutual negation (*anyonyābhāva*), while the other is spatial or structural (*vaibhāgika*).
Among these, we do not first assert the former kind of difference between the world and Brahman, as the Madhvites do, but rather the second.

Since the world is a manifestation (*vaibhāgika*) of Brahman, and thus only a manifested differentiation (*vaibhāgika-bheda*) exists, there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*). For instance, an earring exists only as a differentiated state of gold and so forth. If it were said that [the earring] does not exist [as such], then the cognition "this is an earring" would arise even with respect to a necklace, because [it is the same] gold.

Because it exists there just like the earring; therefore, what need is there to say that some difference also exists between the gold and the earring? You yourself have stated that this very difference is conventional (*vyāvahārika*). Now, you too must admit that from my two material causes (*upādāna*) there must be two differences; in that case, there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating duality.

If it is argued that this [conclusion] is likewise unavoidable for you as well, we say no; for, unlike my own conceptualization, your conceptualization lacks universal acceptance and is therefore not admissible. Nevertheless, even by the logicians (tārkika), clay is accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*) of a jar, whereas mother-of-pearl is not accepted as the illusory material cause (*vivartopādāna*) of silver.

Likewise, since mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is also accepted [by them], and they also accept disjunction (*vibhāga*), our entire position is now established. Nor does it follow that your hypothesis is invalid simply because others do not accept that disjunction is identical to mutual non-existence.

It should be stated that [the object] is "universally accepted. While the opponents accept the substratum possessing the property of division, we, the Vīraśaivas, postulate merely its "distinctness" (bhedatva); however, for you, the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins), it is the shell and the silver that are not mutually agreed upon.

In that case, you have accepted two assumptions not favored by others: the relationship of material cause and effect between the body and its cause, and the status of the mother-of-pearl as the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the silver;
furthermore, the assumption of "apparent reality" (*prātibhāsikatva*) is entirely unaccepted by anyone. Therefore, my own hypothesis alone is superior.

Objection: If the insentient phenomenal world (prapañca) is accepted as non-different from Śiva, then the world would possess consciousness just like Brahman; furthermore, the distinction between the insentient and the sentient would not exist, because everything would be a transformation of the conscious Brahman. Reply: This is not so, for by the power of His will, [Brahman] manifests in the form of both the sentient and the insentient.
Since transformation is possible from Brahman, why then should illusion (māyā) be postulated?

As for the objection that if the world were of the nature of a transformation of consciousness (*cetanapariṇāma*), it would follow that the world itself is conscious—that too has already been refuted by the author of the Sūtras himself in the passage beginning with "But it is seen" (*dṛśyate tu*). Indeed, the meaning of that Sūtra is as follows: in the world, the birth of a conscious scorpion from non-conscious cow dung is observed.
Therefore, the creation of the insentient world by a sentient being does not entail any logical fault; thus, there is no room for any inconsistency within this system of thought.

But surely, if the doctrine of transformation (pariṇāmavāda) is accepted, there arises the contingency of defects such as the total destruction [of the cause] or the contradiction of its being partless, because such is observed in the world. For milk, when transforming into the nature of curd, attains identity with it only through the destruction of its entire essence and so forth. Therefore—

If it is argued that the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) is untenable, we say no; for the theory of transformation alone constitutes the intended meaning of the Sūtrakāra, as evidenced by the Sūtra "But [the relationship between Brahman and the world] is like that of a serpent and its coils because both designations are used" (2.1.27), and the Sūtra "And [the objection regarding the impossibility of such a relationship] is refuted by the example of stones and so forth" (2.1.24). It is for this very reason that the analogy of the serpent and its coils is stated in the Sūtra.
And the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) has been formulated with reference to the analogy of milk and curd.

Now, by the power of the will-force (icchā-śakti), transformation occurs— whether in the form of the insentient or the sentient— without the consequence of exhausting its entire essence, just like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) or a desire-granting tree (kalpavṛkṣa).

If it is argued that the analogy of the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) is inconsistent for you proponents of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), because the power of will is absent therein, we say no; for even by you, it is accepted that prior to every undivided mental state (*akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti*), the will of the Supreme Lord acts as the regulator. Thus, for the gods...
Because it is impossible for an insentient entity to produce such manifestations without the will of those devotees;

and since the movement of a mere insentient thing is inconceivable without the impulsion of a conscious being, it is appropriate to maintain that in every instance where such a thing would otherwise be inconceivable, the process is carried out solely by His will. For this very reason, [it is said] of the Supreme Lord...
The state of being the inner controller of all has been declared in the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa.

If it is objected that, since the Supreme Lord alone is the inner controller of all and His will alone governs every effect, the scriptures that enjoin injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered useless— the answer is no; for, like rain, the will of the Supreme Lord is the governing factor for all effects, just as it is for all crops.

In general, just as specific seeds are the cause for the production of their respective sprouts, so too are specific karmas the cause for the experience of pleasure and pain by specific souls; thus, there is no fault such as partiality, cruelty, or the futility of the scriptures that enjoin and prohibit [certain actions].
In the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda), everything is indeed most excellent.
[Thus,

the venerable] *Ṣaṭsthalanirṇaya*, which is distinguished by one hundred and one unsurpassed stages (*sthala*) produced from churning the ocean of the Śāmbhava Āgama— attained through the grace of Toṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the supreme mobile form of the beginningless and stainless [Lord]— ...

To Keladi Sadāśivarāya— the sovereign of the western ocean, the upholder of the pure Vedic non-dual (advaita) doctrine, the remover of the seven constituent parts of the enemy of the sole hero who caused a tumult among ten million Yādava Murāris, and the disciple of the preeminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya, who bestows the mass of bliss from tasting the nectar of the reality of the *la* syllable.

In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, within the instruction of Basava— the joy of the hearts of the people and the Indra of the earth— beloved wife of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth and the full moon in the milk-ocean of the lineage of Nāyakas,
this is the section on debate titled "The Exposition of the Advaita Doctrine and the Method of its Refutation."
The Twenty-third Chapter.
[The twenty-fourth chapter in the Section on Debate within the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā]
O Lord of Teachers, you have now related what was spoken by Bhṛṅgin—
the established doctrine of the Advaita school— and after this, its refutation.
Having heard everything that Śīlin had spoken, supported by the logic of the Nigamas and Āgamas, I became filled with joy due to the weight of my compassion.
After that, a conversation indeed took place between Bhṛṅgin and Śilī;
O high-minded one, please relate it as my heart desires to hear it.
Listen, O King, I shall speak today of what Bhṛṅgī said to Śīlin:
"All the doctrines held by Śīlin are renowned throughout the earth."
Those which are non-Vedic here, as well as those which are indeed Vedic,
that have been spoken by me have now been refuted by you.
What do you consider to be the most excellent, or what does my mind wish to know? Tell me that, so that I may conduct myself in accordance with it, endowed with humility.
Having heard these words of Bhṛṅgin, Śīlin spoke to Bhṛṅgin:
"O Bhṛṅgin, listen today; I shall state a doctrine that is the ultimate answer to all."
The Vīraśaiva doctrine is the most excellent on earth in this world,
just as Śiva is the supreme among all the gods.

The supreme excellence of Vīraśaivism is established by means of a refutation of various doctrines, namely those of the non-Vedic Lokāyata, Arhat, Sugata, Vaidika-Gautamīya, Kāṇāda, Kāpila, Pātañjala, Jaiminīya,
Vaiyāsika, Viśuddhādvaita, Mādhva, Rāmānujīya, and others.

The Vīraśaiva, who is devoted to the doctrine of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) characterized by the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) between his own *liṅga* and body; who is endowed with the knowledge of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*) divided into one hundred and one varieties; who is initiated into the threefold Vīraśaiva initiation; and who is dedicated to the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) and the five conducts (*pañcācāra*), is the most excellent of all.
For it is said in the Pārameśvara-tantra:
"O Goddess, he who has my power (*vibhūti*) on his forehead, my linga upon his throat, and the wearing of rudrākṣas upon his body— he is myself, without a doubt."
In the Śāṅkara-saṃhitā:
"He who, having placed his own chosen liṅga upon the seat of his hand, directs the movement of his mind toward absorption in it..."
O dear one, he whose soul is free from desire for the multitude of external activities—he indeed is a Vīraśaiva. Thus [it is said].

Now, it may be argued that the supreme excellence of the Vīraśaivas—who are single-mindedly devoted to the threefold liṅga and the eightfold surrender—is not possible, due to the absence of corresponding arguments and proofs.
To explain: in the world, within the creation of Brahmā, there are four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
There are four stages of life (āśramas), well-known from the Śrutis, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas. Among these, they are not included within the category of Brāhmaṇas,

[since the latter] consist of the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), the birth ceremony (jātakarman), the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa), the first outing (upaniṣkramaṇa), and the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana)...
The sixteenth [chapter] concerns the four sets of observances consisting of the *śiśucūḍā*, *upanayana*, *vedavrata*, and *prājāpatya-saumyāgneya-vaiśvadeva*;
the *samāvartana*; marriage; the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*);

the *aupāsana*, *sthālīpāka*, *vaiśvadeva*, *sarpabali*, *īśānabali*, *aṣṭaka*, monthly *śrāddha*, and other rites known as the seven *pākayajñas*; and the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), the *agnihotra*, and so forth.

The seven types of *haviḥ-yajñas* are known as the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the Animal Sacrifice (*paśubandha*), the Four-Monthly Sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, the *Sautrāmaṇī*, and the *Agniṣṭoma*.

The seven designations for the sacrificial sessions (*saṃsthā*) are the *Agniṣṭoma*, *Atyagniṣṭoma*, *Ukthya*, *Ṣoḍaśin*, *Atirātra*, *Āptoryāma*, and *Vājapeya*. [These pertain to] the bodies of the Brāhmaṇas.

There are forty ritual observances (*saṃskāras*) and eight personal virtues (*ātmaguṇas*), namely: compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of longing;

as well as the specific means of livelihood consisting of sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, studying, teaching, giving gifts, receiving gifts, and gathering gleanings and alms, and so forth.
And which [are the *yamas*], since they are established as the duty (*dharma*) of Brāhmaṇas in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇas*, and *Itihāsas*,
and because these are not practiced by the Vīraśaivas,
just as [the lineages] named Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Agastya [are established] among the Brāhmaṇas.
Due to the absence of lineage (*gotra*) and ancestral branches (*pravara*) indicative of a specific descent,
[this applies to] those Brahmins who follow the Taittirīya Yajurveda branch composed by Āpastamba, Bodhāyana, Bharadvāja, Satyāṣāḍha, Vaikhānasa, and Agniveśya,
and who adhere to the six authoritative *Sūtras*; as for those following the Ṛgveda branch...

Of the Āśvalāyana-sūtra; of the Śrauta-sūtra of Drāhyāyaṇa, which follows the Kauthuma branch of the Sāmaveda; of the Gṛhya-sūtra of Jaimini, which follows the Talavakāra branch; and of the Kātyāyana-sūtra and others, which follow the first Yajurvedic branch, the Vājasaneyi.

And because there is an absence of relationship with those [classes] considered most venerable; nor [is it so] for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, due to the absence of the previously mentioned sacraments, gotra, sūtras, and śākhās, along with sacrifice, study, and giving.

There is no inclusion [of these] among the Śūdras, because of their service to the three higher castes, eating the remnants of food from a slave, subsisting on his property, performing *śrāddha* rites without mantras, performing the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), and the performance of birth-impurity rites (*sūtaka*) and other such acts performed by slaves belonging to specific castes.

Because the duties of Śūdras do not apply; nor among those of mixed origin, because designations such as Mūrdhāvasikta, Ambaṣṭha, and Pāraśava do not exist [among them]. Therefore, they are not included within the [four] castes.

This is because the sequence of studying and teaching the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas—which establish the duties (*dharma*) of the [four] castes—is not observed among the Vīraśaivas. Furthermore, upon considering such statements as, "One is born a Śūdra by birth; one is born a twice-born (*dvija*) by action," birth alone is common to this human being without distinction.

For it is heard in the scriptures that even one born into a family of Brāhmaṇas or other [castes] incurs a state of fallenness (*pātitya*) in the absence of the primary sacraments (*saṃskāra*), such as the initiation (*upanayana*). For that very reason, there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) even to hearing the Vedic knowledge; thus it is said:
"If he hears the Veda, his ears are to be filled with molten lead and lac; if he recites it, his tongue is to be cut out."

For it is stated in the *Gautamīya-dharma-sūtra*: "In the event of [unauthorized] retention [of Vedic texts], there shall be corporal punishment; one who seeks equality in sitting, lying down, speech, or on the path is to be fined.
Furthermore, it cannot be argued that—on the analogy of the *niṣādasthapati*—there is an entitlement to hear the Vedic sciences even in the absence of initiation (*upanayana*) and other such rites.

It must be stated that this entitlement to hear the sacrificial mantras (*yājamāna-mantra*), which is obtained through an injunction such as "one should cause the *niṣādasthapati* to sacrifice," does not apply here because no such injunction exists in the present context. Nor is there an entitlement for the wife to hear Vedic sentences even in the absence of her initiation (*upanayana*), [as in the case of] the wife...
Regarding the phrase "he causes [her] to recite," there is no perception of an injunction concerning the act of reciting similar to an injunction for the ritual procedure itself. Furthermore,
since the wife's status as an agent is already established by the specific injunctional sentences heard in such passages as, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."

Furthermore, since agency is restricted by the Vedic statement, "One must not transgress in respect of dharma, artha, and kāma," there is no perception of such [a restriction] for the subject in this context through either Śruti or Smṛti—just as there is for a wife. Nor should it be argued that initiation (upanayana) should be postulated for the purpose of Vedic study, because [the Smṛti states]: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year."

Since the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is prescribed for the three social classes alone—specifically for the Kṣatriya in the eleventh year and the Vaiśya in the twelfth—and since study consists of the acquisition of syllables which culminates in the performance of the duties taught therein through the medium of understanding their meaning; and furthermore, because among the Vīraśaivas no performance of the rites enjoined by the Vedas is observed. Nor is it the case that...
It must be stated that there exists no Vedic ritual such as the wearing of the *liṅga*,
because no mantra or brāhmaṇa text prescribing such wearing is observed. Otherwise,
even those not included among the three twice-born castes would possess the qualification for Vedic knowledge.

Therefore, the Vīraśaiva doctrine is non-Vedic, and the Vīraśaivas who follow that path are likewise non-Vedic; consequently, their superiority is not tenable. Nor [is it tenable] because the *Atyāśramopaniṣad* states: "He fully proclaimed to those beyond the stages of life (atyāśramins) that which is supremely pure and cherished by the assembly of sages."

It should be stated that from hearing [the scriptures] regarding the Vīraśaivas, they are called *atyāśramins*. For those who possess an *āśrama* are *āśramins*; and those who have transcended the *āśramins* are *atyāśramins*, [referring thus] to the ordinary *āśramas*.

Because after practicing for some time, a transgression must eventually be expected; thus, since Vīraśaivas lack the status of being members of a formal stage of life (*āśramin*), it is impossible to establish their status as "those beyond the stages of life" (*atyāśramin*).
On the contrary—

For even the practice of Vīraśaiva initiation— which is contrary to the performance of rites established by the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas, and involves practices such as observing impurity (sūtaka)— is observed among them. Therefore, among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, each subsequent group is inferior to the preceding one, and the Śūdras are inferior to them.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because the established rule that those inferior to them are "mixed castes" (*saṅkara*) is supported by authoritative evidence, the superiority of the Vīraśaivas serves only to satisfy their own inner circle and is not in accordance with valid authority (*pramāṇa*).

To this, the following reply is stated: "There is no superiority of the Vīraśaivas, because of the absence of reasoning and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that regard, is there an absence of reasoning regarding superiority, or an absence of means of valid cognition, or an absence of both? It cannot be the first [alternative], for [superiority] is not established when unsupported by means of valid cognition.

For although mere reasoning may serve as a means for worldly excellence such as wealth, lordship, and so forth, in regard to supramundane excellence, it is reasoning alone when conjoined with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is the decisive factor. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because we do not accept that mere valid cognition—even when conjoined with the principles of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā—can by itself be a means for attaining excellence. As, for example:

In such passages as "The sacrificial post is the sun; the *prastara* grass-bundle is the sacrificer; Agni is indeed the Brahmin; cattle other than cows and horses are not truly cattle," there is no establishment of meaning through mere means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) devoid of logic.
Nor is it the third [alternative], because [the meaning is established] by many means of knowledge accompanied by reasoning (*yukti*).
Because there exist [scriptures] composed by the Supreme Lord, the most authoritative one; for instance, in the latter part of the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā:
"Animals are superior in intelligence to worms, insects, and moths."
Humans are superior even to animals; among them, the twice-born are the most excellent.

Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; among the Brahmins, those whose intellects are fixed on sacrifice; among those whose intellects are fixed on sacrifice, the performers [of the rites]; and superior even to them are the renunciants.
Among them, the wise are the best; among them, the worshippers of Śaṅkara are the best;
and among them, O fortunate one, those who are united with my Liṅga as their own body are the most excellent.
One who possesses knowledge of the six stages (ṣaṭsthala) becomes superior even among those whose limbs are attached to the Liṅga;
there is nothing superior to that, at any time, throughout the three worlds.
"He is to be saluted and always honored by those who seek to conquer cyclic existence;
to him gifts should be given and from him they should be received, for he is to be worshipped just as I am."
Is this not indeed untenable? For the statements beginning with "superior by means of wisdom," which are intended to demonstrate excellence and deficiency according to the gradations of knowledge,
were addressed solely to the Vīraśaivas at the stage of initiating the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
This is because, by examining whether or not [the Śūdras] are included within the [four] castes (*varṇa*), one merely establishes their relative superiority or inferiority;

for the statements in the *Śāṅkara-saṃhitā*—beginning with the words "O twice-born ones" (*dvijātayaḥ*) and establishing a progressive superiority—must be applied as referring specifically to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). Thus, regarding them...
Even when demonstrating excellence through a gradation of *dharmatās*, the conclusion rests upon the mere excellence of the Vīraśaiva dharma;

therefore, it is appropriate to determine that the purport of the authoritative texts (*pramāṇas*) lies in establishing the superiority of the Vīraśaiva dharma as well, which pertains to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). Thus, for those belonging to the Vīraśaiva caste...

If it is argued that this is not so because there is no utility for the cited statements regarding the question of "in which caste is he included," and otherwise because it would contradict the established text proving that he is not included among the castes—
[we reply: even though he is not included among the three twice-born castes (*traivarṇika*), [he is still considered a Brahmin].

This is because there exist many Āgamas and Śrutis consistent with them that establish the existence of a non-material Brahman-spirit who is superior to the three social classes (*varṇas*). For instance, it is said in the *Suprabhedāgama*:
"There exists the abode of the stainless state, whose form is Being, Consciousness, and Bliss."
It is free from conceptual construction, formless, and devoid of every defect.
Having thus begun and described the supreme reality of Paramaśiva as transcending the three forms (trimūrti):
"The Supreme Brahman, named Śiva, desiring to create the universe,
assumed a certain form manifested through the dawning of bliss."

Having thus described the relationship between the attribute (*dharma*) and the possessor of the attribute (*dharmī*) as attained through divine play (*līlā*), [the text continues] with the description of the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) arising from that connection with the attributes: "divine, non-material, eternal, blue-throated, three-eyed, crowned with the crescent moon, pure, resembling pure crystal," and so forth.

Having described His essential nature as that which is to be worshipped by means of the forms of the *guṇas*, and having established— by virtue of being the substratum of non-material qualities and by virtue of His eternally auspicious nature— that there exists a power distinct from Him which constitutes the inherent cause for the creation of all worlds, [he describes] he who, through the assistance of that [power], was the first among the gods.

Having first described the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha as established by such Śruti passages as "Rudra, the great seer, superior to all," and having then set forth the instruction in the entirety of Vedic knowledge as understood from such Śruti passages as "He who in the beginning created Brahmā and delivered the Vedas to him,"...

Then, when that Hiraṇyagarbha, desiring to emit the universe, had spoken of the knowledge concerning creation through the veil of Māyā and had prayed to Tryambaka for the means of fashioning the entire world, he was told by that Hiraṇyagarbha: "The creation must be performed by you alone; having seen it [the way], [act accordingly]."
"Requested thus, 'I too shall create by virtue of that same nature,' Śambhu said:"
He created beings equal to himself in appearance, who were omniscient and omnipotent,
their minds perpetually flowing with supreme awakening and bliss.
Having created the Pramathas, who are capable of performing the rites of universal creation and dissolution,
he established the cycles of the social classes and stages of life among the hosts of Pramathas.
Then the Lord taught them extraordinary and virtuous conduct;
consequently, all those born of that lineage have maintained their vows through devotion to Śiva.

Thus, by demonstrating that the Vīraśaivas originated from those very Pramathas who were born directly from Śambhu, their supreme excellence is understood, as they arose prior to the members of the three [upper] castes.

Indeed, Śrī Basaveśvara— the incarnation of Nandīśvara authorized by the venerable Supreme Lord, whose heart was single-mindedly intent on establishing the five-fold conduct (*pañcācāra*) and the eight extraordinary enclosures (*aprākṛtāṣṭāvaraṇa*) for the Vīraśaivas—
[was born] to Mādāmbā and one named Mādhava, who were born into a family of Brahmins devoted to the conventional (*prākṛta*) dharma.
Having accepted the status of a son, he manifested himself there; then, after residing in the home of his mother and father until the age of eight, he subsequently practiced the Vīraśaiva dharma—
this being heard in literary works such as the Basaveśvara Purāṇa and others concerning him.

If it is argued that since attachment to ordinary conduct is observed [in him], how can his conduct be considered non-ordinary, we say: no; for Nandīśvara is an extraordinary incarnation of the venerable Supreme Lord, who is the most intimate to the Goddess, and who has attained omniscience.
May Indra and the other gods, their crowns shattered by the repeated blows of the staffs of the threshing pestles on the threshold of your abode,
become [your devotees]; may we, having attained the state of Piśācas, resort to your presence.
"Why do we not seek the sovereignty of the immortals, O Lord of the Pramathas?"—
thus addressed by all the gods led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as the Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Nāgas, and Yakṣas;
you who shine resplendently as the cause of both favor and restraint, O guardians of the quarters, proceed forward!

"O clouds, leave the sky! O serpents, go to the netherworld or enter the surface of the earth! O Brahmā, raise your own abode far away! This is a crisis for us as our lord Śambhu dances"—by such words [did Nandin issue] this expulsion that may protect us. And so forth.

A certain Brahmin named Mādhava, who desires a son for me on this earth, is performing penance; his wife, whose mental faculties are fixed upon you, practices the same observances as you, O Nandīśvara, who possesses a preeminent skill in transforming the entire phenomenal world that is not shared by any other.

"O Śrī Vīramāheśvara, having attained the status of their son upon this earth, O Wise One, establish firmness therein through various amusements for your son regarding those who have set out upon the path of heresy. Thus [it was said].
In accordance with the verse stated in the *Basaveśvara Purāṇa*: "Whenever a decline of the Śaiva dharma occurs,

at that very time this incarnation of the Gaṇeśas [appears] upon the surface of the earth," and according to the statement in the *Śaṅkara Saṃhitā*, he appeared for the sake of favoring the world and with the desire to uphold the Vīraśaiva doctrine.

Since Basaveśvara—who has performed his divine play (*līlāvatāra*) through another form—arose as a deity, there is no requirement for a specific gender when referring to him, as there is no dependence on a substantive. It is exactly like this: for example, the venerable Śaṅkarācārya, the establisher of Advaita, is called "Śaṅkara" (the Benevolent One).

For it is well known that Vyāsa is traditionally remembered as Nārāyaṇa himself, and according to the statement in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*— "Śaṅkara will incarnate together with four disciples"— it is established that those who have attained non-difference from the venerable Supreme Lord are heard to have taken birth in the prohibited land of Kerala. It is exactly thus.

Patañjali, who was also Ādiśeṣa, descended by the name Patañjali for the sake of favoring the world through the propagation of the knowledge of the Yoga-pādas and other sciences, falling into the joined palms of a Brāhmaṇī named Goṇikā in the form of a seven-year-old boy.
The greatness of Cidambaram is heard [in tradition]. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vajrasūcī*:
"From a doe, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was born; from Kuśa grass, Kauśika; from the back of a hare, Gautama; from a female jackal, Vasiṣṭha;
from an anthill, Vālmīki; from Urvaśī, Vyāsa; and from a pitcher, Agastya was born of a fisherwoman's daughter."

Because it is heard in scripture that Viśvāmitra was born as a Kṣatriya and Nārada as the son of a slave-girl, and likewise because it is heard that there is no fault even when Viṣṇu and others are born into castes lower than their own for the sake of showing favor to the worlds of the gods; so too in the present case.
For those who possess the initiation that is without a formal locus— such as the Pramathas and their descendants by Śrī Sāmbaśiva,

as well as Basaveśvara— there is no possibility of defects such as caste, even though they were born into low-born families; therefore, for the sake of blessing the world, wherever it may be, [the descent] of Basaveśvara, who is an incarnation of the Supreme Lord, [occurs].

Even though birth occurs through human procreation, for those Vīraśaivas born into the extraordinary Brahmin lineage who have transcended the system of castes and stages of life (ativarṇāśramin), there is not even the slightest stain of such doubt;
thus, everything is entirely favorable.
The origin of the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes is declared in the Puruṣasūkta: "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth;
the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) was made from his arms; that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya;
from his feet the Śūdra was born," just as [the castes arose] from the Virāṭ-Puruṣa.

Likewise, because their origin is heard [in scripture], and because there is the exposition of the duties pertaining to the various stages of life (*āśrama*) and so forth— mediated by both the observance and the transgression of the castes and stages of life well-known from the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Itihāsa* taught by them— of those Brāhmaṇas.

Furthermore, the adherence to the dharmas proclaimed therein by the Vīraśaivas— by virtue of their status as extraordinary (aprākṛta) Brāhmaṇas— is the following of the dharmas taught in the divine Āgamas, from the *Kāmika* to the *Vātula*, which are self-evident authorities originating from the activity of the palate, lips, and other organs of the Supreme Lord who created them.
The distinction is that [the scripture] consists of those portions that do not contradict the scriptures that establish the duties to be performed by oneself.

Now, since Vedic knowledge is of the highest importance, and because the *Āpastamba-sāmānya-sūtra* states that "the collection of dharmas consisting of the sequence of the Agniṣṭoma and other rites prescribed therein is enjoined by the three Vedas," [one might argue] that even in the absence of such [rites] in the Āgamas, they should be performed by Brāhmaṇas.

If it is argued that [the Vedic path] should be primarily practiced, and that the religious duties such as temple construction, festivals, and consecrations taught in scriptures not contradictory to it should likewise be followed, we say no; for their subject matters are distinct from the sequence of the five conducts (*pañcācāra*) and the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) to be practiced by the Vīraśaivas.

Because the sequence of the one hundred and one stages, beginning with *piṇḍa* and ending with *jñāna-śūnya*, along with the entire collection of doctrines, is described in the Āgamas as being primarily to be practiced,
and because those Vīraśaiva doctrines are presented in a distributed manner throughout various Śrutis; [therefore, they are authentic].

It is established that where the sequence of certain practices is being described, the study of those [texts] and so forth is primary; however, the adherence to other authorities is to be done without contradicting one's own respective practice.

As for that which was previously described— namely, that [the *sāttvika* creation] is devoid of sacraments such as *garbhādhāna*, and consequently devoid of the *vedavrata*s such as the *prājāpatya* contained therein— that is incorrect;
for by demonstrating the variety of non-material (*aprākṛta*) manifestations, it is established that those [beings] included within the non-material creation...
Because of that lack of dependence. And so it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"Human beings are traditionally held to be of two kinds: pure (*viśuddha*) and natural (*prākṛta*).
Those who have undergone the *śiva-saṃskāra* are pure; others are considered natural."
Indeed, the regulation of the duties of the castes, stages of life, and so forth is considered to be twofold:
one was ordained by Śiva, and the other was proclaimed by Brahmā.
The dharma of those who abide in the stages of life (āśrama) prescribed by Śiva consists of devotion to the dharma spoken by Śiva;
for those who are devoid of the Śiva-consecration (saṃskāra), the dharma is remembered as that of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Thus has the distinction between the ordinary and the extraordinary been shown.
Furthermore, that description regarding the non-existence of the *gotra-sūtras* and so forth is also superficially attractive;

for instance, because there exist four founders of lineages (*gotra-pravartaka*), who are leaders of the Pramathas—namely Reṇuka, Dāruka, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and Gajakarṇa—who were born from the mouth of Sadāśiva. By this, [the objection] is refuted.

The claim that there is no qualification for the study of Vedic knowledge and so forth is refuted by the very fact of the miscarriage [of the fetus]. This is because his superiority even over the Brāhmaṇas is established precisely by his non-natural (aprākṛta) nature. As for the argument that he does not belong to any stage of life (atyāśramitva), that too is charming only when left unexamined; for he follows the "Hermitage of Hara" (Harāśrama) at the stage of full spiritual maturity.

Because even the transgression of that [duty] is possible; for, as stated in such passages as, "Devotion to Śiva arises in those men who have perfected themselves over many births, who follow the Śruti and Smṛti, and whose sins have been exhausted," it is possible both to follow the stages of life (*āśrama*) in previous births and to transgress them.
If it is objected: "How can the *pramathas*, who are eternally liberated (*nityamukta*), be the founders of lineages (*vaṃśapravartaka*)?", we say no;

for, just as in the cases of Agastya, Vasiṣṭha, and others, it is possible for them to establish lineages for the sake of favoring the world and for the sake of propagating the Vīraśaiva tradition. Nor is this...

Since the continuation of a lineage is rooted in women, and since the Pramathas—being eternally liberated due to the impossibility of passion, hatred, and the like—have no requirement for the performance of ritual acts, it might be asked: "In the absence of the taking of wives, how can there be the production of a lineage? [To this we reply: even for those who are eternally liberated...
In the section concerning the Dahara-vidyā, by stating "Now, if he should desire the world of women," and so forth,
the taking of a wife is shown for the purpose of demonstrating complete independence; likewise, in the present context,
[the mention of] the progenitors of the lineages (gotra) is for the purpose of demonstrating the complete independence of the Pramathas as well.

This is because Reṇuka and others, who were the originators of the four Vīraśaiva traditions, were born from the taking of wives. Nor should it be suspected that nowhere is the taking of wives by the Pramathas heard of; for in the Purāṇas, it is stated that Nandikeśvara had a wife named Suyaśā.

Because it is so heard [in scripture]. Regarding this matter, there are also mantras. In the section concerning the offering of forty-four oblations within the *īśānabali*, which is included among the seven types of *vākaya* sacrifices, [it says]:
"To the Graha who touches the water, svāhā! To the Grahi who touches the water, svāhā! To the Dvārāpa who touches the water..."

"dvārāpāya svāhā | dvārāpyupaspṛśo dvārāpyai svāhā. Regarding this, [the commentator] states in the *Īśānabaliprayogavivaraṇa*: "The one named Dvārāpa is Nandīśa; his wife is Dvārāpī, with the feminine suffix *ṅīp* applied according to the rule *puṃyogādākhyāyām*. Her name is well-known in the Purāṇas as Suyashādevī."

Because of the examination [of the lineage]. And thus, since a succession of progeny is possible through the taking of wives by the founders of the *gotras*, such as the teachers Reṇukācārya and others, those [teachers] are the founders of the *gotras* for the Vīraśaivas. Nor [is it the case that] for the founders of the *gotras*...
Among them, since some have not even heard of taking a wife and others lack the authority to take a wife, it must be explained how the continuity of the lineage (gotra) is maintained;
for just as the succession of sons, grandsons, and so forth constitutes the means of perpetuating a lineage, [so too must there be another means].
This is because it is possible for the continuous stream of disciples and grand-disciples to establish a connection of lineage (*gotra*). For this very reason,

since a Kṣatriya lacks the possibility of attaining the status of a Brāhmaṇa himself and thus lacks eligibility for [Vedic] ritual acts, the King should choose his *pravara* by means of the *pravara* of his domestic priest (*purohita*).

This is because the statement of the Āpastamba Sūtra declares that disciples who are Kṣatriyas, by virtue of being officiating priests (*yājaka*), possess the lineage (*gotra*) of their venerable Brahmin preceptors. Furthermore:
"Reṇuka, Revaṇa, Rudra, the Sage Nīla, and Maheśvara..."
Ghaṇṭāsiddha, Sāraṅga, Vṛddha, Agastya, Guru, and Guru.
Triśikha, Aṣṭajaṭa, Pañcavarṇaka, Siddhaśāsana—
these and others of great fortune were born from the Mahāpuruṣa.
Following this description of the lineage of disciples of Reṇukācārya and others, [it continues]:
Dāruka, Marula, Amāya, Cālavāṇḍa, Mahātapas,
Jyotirmati, Guru, Cikka, Vyāghra, Kantha, and Bṛhadvasu.
Nārakaṇṭha, Patsyakaṇṭha, Muktakaṇṭha, Mahāmuni,
Ekādaśaśikha, the Yogin, and he who bears the name Mallikārjuna.
By these and other such statements, the tradition of the Dāruka lineage has been declared.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, as well as Eka, Rāma, Muṇḍī, Guheśvara, Sutāra, Tāraka, Muktā, Nūpura, and Purāṇaka.
These and others are said to be born of the lineage of Ghaṇṭākarṇa.
Gajakarṇa, Triraṅguṣṭha, Mañcaṇa, Saṅgama, Avyaya,
Kalyāṇapaṇḍita, Keśin, Mādhava, Śrīpati, and Prabhu.

The lineage of Gajakarṇa is declared by such passages as "Mallikārjuna and others emerged from the mouth of Vāmadeva. Therefore, the relationship of progenitor and progeny, as well as the relationship of teacher and disciple, among Reṇuka and the others, exists as far as possible.

This has been clearly stated in the root scriptures (Mūlāgamas), and it is also explicitly set forth in the Kriyākāṇḍa. Therefore, because the Vīraśaivas— who are non-worldly Brāhmaṇas— possess [distinct] lineages and so forth, their status as the most excellent is established.
As for the claim that the status of being an *atyāśramin* is impossible for Vīraśaivas— given that in the word *atyāśrama*,

the prefix *ati-* signifies "transcending," and thus implies possessing a specific dharma obtainable through a specific knowledge arising subsequent to the performance of the duties of the [four] stages of life (*āśrama*)— [that is not so].

As for the claim that this is due to impropriety (*anaucitya*), that is not so; for according to the grammatical sūtra *svatī pūjāyām*, and because the word *svati* is listed among the indeclinables (*avyaya*)—along with *tu*, *hi*, *ca*, *sma*, *ha*, *vai*, and *pādapūraṇe*—it is heard in usage as having the sense of excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*). Therefore, in the present context...

Even if the sense of "transcending" (atikramaṇa) is impossible, the sense of "excellence" (prakarṣa) is possible. Thus, an *āśrama* that is preeminent is an *atyāśrama*; those who possess such an *atyāśrama* are *atyāśramins*. Alternatively, those who possess an *āśrama* are *āśramins*; those who are preeminent among *āśramins* are *atyāśramins*.

Thus, since the state of being an *atyāśramin* (one who has transcended the stages of life) is possible among the Vīraśaivas through this description of its meaning, the word *atyāśrama* applies— by way of both etymological derivation and conventional usage (*yogarūḍhi*)— to the specific religious duties practiced by the Vīraśaivas, just as the word *paṅkaja* (lotus) does.
Its superiority, however, arises from its being taught by Maheśvara prior to the creation of the non-ordinary *pramatha* attendants.
Accordingly, there are scriptural statements (*āgama*) such as:
"The one who has transcended the castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśramī*) is declared to be the Guru for all who possess the qualification."
He shall become the most excellent among others, just as I am the Supreme Person.
One who transcends the castes and stages of life is said to be the direct teacher of teachers;
the five-syllabled supreme knowledge leads to the attainment of the light of Śiva.
The syllable Oṃ is the Praṇava, the subtle and supreme seed of all sciences;
because it is the reality, one should purify all principles without exception by means of the Praṇava.
One should dust the body with ashes using the mantras beginning with "agniriti" and so forth;
one should contemplate within oneself Śambhu, the Lord,
the supreme Śiva, who is peaceful and accompanied by Umā.
They call this the practice of the hermitage, characterized by limbs smeared with ashes and manifesting all-encompassing radiance.
The *liṅga* is Śiva, the field (*kṣetra*) is the body; their union is the support.
Therefore, one who is joined with the *liṅga* and the body is indeed a transcendent ascetic (*atyāśramī*).
O Sage, he who is established in this crest of the Vedas proclaimed the Pāśupata;
some wise ones call this the "Crest-vow" (Śirovrata), others call it the "Beyond-āśrama" (Atyāśrama), some call it the "Great Vow" (Mahāvrata), and others call it the Śāmbhava or Aiśvara.
By this statement,

[the author] refers to the Supreme Lord accompanied by the recitation of the jewel-like five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī-mantra-ratna*) preceded by the *praṇava*, as well as the smearing with ashes consecrated by mantras such as "Agni" and the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* and *rudrākṣa*.

The connection between the *liṅga* and the body, distinguished by a specific worship that permeates all that is to be slain, is the *atyāśrama*; one who possesses this is an *atyāśramin*. This very vow is called the *pāśupata*, the *śirovrata*, the *atyāśrama*, the *mahāvrata*, and the *śāmbhava*.

Because it is established in the Upaniṣads as "belonging to the Lord" (aiśvara), it is proven that the status of being a "transcendent ascetic" (atyāśramin) belongs exclusively to the Vīraśaivas, and that they alone possess supreme excellence. Now, [one might object]: in the compound *atyāśrama*, [the term] refers to an "asceticism that has transcended" (*atiśayita āśramaḥ*), and in the compound *atyāśramin*, it refers to "ascetics who have transcended" (*atiśayitā āśramiṇaḥ*); thus, the meaning of the prefix *ati-* is "excellence" (*prāśastya*).

When there is a connection with either the duty (*dharma*) or the possessor of the duty (*dharmī*), for the sake of accomplishing the state of being a praiseworthy ascetic (*praśastāśramitva*), as many duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) as are to be performed must be undertaken. These include the forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and so forth established by the Vedas.
Their sequence is to be understood from the Śruti, Smṛti, Kalpasūtras, and other such sources. Of these...
If it is argued that because [the Vīraśaivas] are not seen among the [standard] Śaivas, their status as having transcended the stages of life (atyāśramitva) is all the more untenable, we say no;
for practices that transcend the castes and stages of life exist through the Ūrdhvavaktra [tradition],
and they indeed rejoice as manifest Mahādevas within the Āgamas.

By reflecting upon the scriptural statements taught in the *Kriyāsāra*, it is established that while being born from the upper face of the Supreme Lord, the *Āgama-moda* is the dharma of the highest stage of life (*atyāśrama*); furthermore,
this is established in its entirety because the scriptures teach the five conducts (*pañcācāra*), the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*), and the reality of the six sites (*ṣaṭsthala-tattva*).

Because following that [tradition] and the arising with the face turned upward are not observed elsewhere— such as among Brāhmaṇas and others— and because their correct performance of these [rites] according to the rules and as appropriate is seen only among those belonging to the Vīraśaiva caste, it is they alone who possess the status of *atyāśramin* (those beyond the stages of life), and it is with reference to them [that this is said].

The *Mantropaniṣad* has also been set forth. Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Kāmikāgama*: "Those born from the fifth mouth of the Five-faced One (Śiva) are superior; those of the fifth [caste] are dearer to me than all other castes, for they are my devotees," this—supported by the previously cited statement—[establishes that those] born from the face of Īśāna are therefore [superior].

Due to their birth from the fifth face, the supreme status of the Vīraśaivas— those known as the "Fifth" who transcend all castes and are observed to be devoted to extraordinary (aprākṛta) duties such as those of the Brāhmaṇas and others— is beyond dispute.
And they, distinguished by the various forms of the manifestation-free [realization] of the universal and the particular,

being endowed with the ninefold devotion known as hearing, chanting, serving at the feet, worshiping, bowing, servitude, friendship, and self-surrender, [practice] that which is distinct from the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such [austerities].
Austerity (*tapas*) consists of the emaciation of the body fashioned for the sake of Śiva who occupies that station.
Ritual action (*karma*) to be performed consists of activities conducive to the worship of Śiva who has taken his place, other than the *agniṣṭoma* and similar sacrifices.

Japa is the repeated recitation of mantras— such as the Praṇava, the Pañcākṣarī, and the Śrīrudra— that have Śiva as their sole object and are distinct from the Vedas that enjoin rituals like sacrifice. Dhyāna is the continuous, uninterrupted contemplation focused exclusively on Śiva, excluding the mental visualization of the forms of other deities.

Knowledge is precisely the realization of the reality of the six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*), which is the primary subject matter taught in the *Āgamas* such as the *Kāmika*, and which is distinct from the analytical investigation of the meanings propounded by other scriptures.
Such fivefold worship of Śiva alone constitutes the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*); those who are devoted to that [are the true practitioners].
The mental contemplation directed toward the sun of consciousness— designated as the *prāṇaliṅga* shining within the space of the heart—

is itself the *sandhyāvandana*. Those who possess this [contemplation] offer as an oblation the objects known as sound and so forth, by means of the instrument of the mind, which has as its locus the internal light consisting of the *prāṇaliṅga*.

The offering (*homa*) is indeed the act of surrender; those devoted to that [surrender] possess the eleven virtues known as truth, forbearance, compassion, purity, self-restraint, gentleness, austerity, renunciation, celibacy, contentment, and uprightness; they are attached to these, feeling desire for devotees and anger toward those intent on unrighteousness.

Greed regarding the worship of Śiva, delusion toward Śiva, pride toward those other than devotees, and envy toward those who have turned away from the path of Śiva’s devotees— these are the factors that bring about the application of the six internal enemies (ariṣaḍvarga) to their respective objects.
[Furthermore,] cooking for the sake of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama constitutes a violation of the vow of a devoted wife.

The gathering of male and female servants and others who bear the insignia of the Lord; residing within a house marked with the insignia and mudrās; subsisting on grain and wealth marked with that same insignia;
and the bestowing of gold, silver, garments, ornaments, and other gifts upon the devotees of Śiva.
With substances purified by acceptance preceded by the touching of ashes, one performs the worship of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama;

this constitutes the sixfold state of being a true devotee toward the Guru, consisting of servitude, heroic servitude, attendance, heroic attendance, abiding by the covenant, and remaining within the tradition.

Practicing the sixfold vow, which consists of: knowledge of [the self] as non-different from Śiva; the dissolution of the mind in one’s chosen *liṅga*; the experience of bliss in the mobile [liṅga]; full comprehension of the eleven kinds of grace; and the fulfillment of devotion.

There are six types of conduct (*ācāra*): the conduct of signs (*liṅga*), the conduct of good behavior (*sadācāra*), the conduct of service (*bhṛtyācāra*), the conduct of Śiva (*śivācāra*), the conduct of the Gaṇas (*gaṇācāra*), and the conduct of the covenant (*samayācāra*). Those endowed with these possess the sixfold form consisting of freedom from anger, truthful speech, forbearance, non-divisiveness regarding property, favoring others, and the offering of substances to worthy recipients.
The two kinds of ethical conduct (*śīla*) are [non-violence and truthfulness]. The fivefold observances (*niyama*) are non-anger, service to the guru, purity, moderation in food, and vigilance.

[The eightfold supernatural powers are] the grace of the Guru, the grace of the *liṅga*, the grace of the *jaṅgama*, the grace of the *prasādin*, the grace of nourishment, the grace of the *samaya*...

There are eleven kinds of *prasāda* (serenity/tranquility), categorized by the distinction between impure knowledge (*asāda-jñāna*) and pure knowledge (*prasāda-jñāna*), including the absence of the sense organs (*jñānendriya*), the absence of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the presence of pure essence (*sadbhāva-prasāda*), and the clarity of pure knowledge (*prasāda-jñāna*). These are further distinguished by the water from the feet of the Guru, the water from the bathing of the *liṅga*, the water for immersion, the water for touch, the water for concentration, the water of truth, and so forth.

While partaking of the ten kinds of water from the feet, "knowledge" consists of the contemplation of identity with the Great Liṅga, which is the nature of the Supreme Reality; therein, within that Great Liṅga, is the immersion of the mind.

Bathing consists of establishing a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions preceded by the suppression of heterogeneous impressions; the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* consists of non-contact with effects produced by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Thus are established internal bathing, smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*), and wearing [the marks]; as for external ones, however—

Constantly performing, according to rule, the fivefold special rites of bathing, smearing the body with ashes, and wearing them as ash-ornaments— produced from the various forms of ritual action consisting of the primary, secondary, and tertiary ashes (bhūti, bhasita, and bhasma), which serve as protection—
[they restrain] the mind, intellect, ego, consciousness, and the senses of hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
Of the fourteen organs of form— those characterized by conduct and so forth—
and of the fourteen objects known as doubt, certainty, pride, memory, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure.
For the purpose of attaining the experience of grace from that very liṅga, its internal wearing consists in bearing it in the form of that liṅga itself;
whereas the external [wearing] consists of Rudrākṣas,
which are divided into thirty-eight varieties produced from the three eyes of the Supreme Lord— representing the sun, moon, and fire.
Performing the wearing of the six [sacred marks] according to the prescribed rule,

the internal [practice] consists of the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra while contemplating the identity— expressed by the word "one" (a-ya)— between the body (aṅga) denoted by the word "obeisance" (namaḥ) and the Liṅga denoted by the word "Śiva"; the external [practice], however, is as follows:

The recitation of the five-syllable mantra by way of mental, whispered, or audible utterance— preceded by the radiance of a rudrākṣa rosary used for easy counting, which takes the place of the garland of the alphabet (mātṛkā) beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *kṣa*, which is difficult to count— while practicing both [the visualization and the recitation] in this manner, results in invincibility throughout the three periods of time.

That very *sattva* is the Guru; that very *cittva*, which is the state of illuminating everything by being independent of any other light, is the *liṅga*. The internal mobile [form] is the indivisible bliss (*akhaṇḍānanda*) which is the ground of rest for the gradations of worldly bliss; whereas the external mobile [form] is one endowed with the five seals (*pañcamudrā*).

Eternality (*nityatva*) consists in being neither the counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) nor the counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*); that itself is the internal grace (*prasāda*). The external grace, however, takes the form of the remains of food offered to the Guru and the *liṅga*, and is known by the names *śuddha*, *siddha*, and *prasiddha*.
The internal *pādodaka* is the state of perfection consisting in conjunction with all embodied forms; the external, however, is threefold, distinguished as *liṅgodaka*, *pādodaka*, and *prasādodaka*.
One whose heart is single-mindedly intent on the performance of duties to be practiced, conjoined with such mental contemplation [should perform the rite].

The limb of yoga is characterized by the contemplation of the identity (*aikya-yoga*) between one’s own self, the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama* (the living teacher), through the triad of initiation consisting of piercing (*vedha*), mantra, and ritual action (*kriyā*).
It is further characterized by the transformation into the bliss of accepting that which has been offered as grace (*prasāda*), because it is the supreme object to be attained.

"Bhogāṅga" (the limb of enjoyment) refers to [the body]; "tyāgāṅga" (the limb of renunciation) refers to the state of having abandoned the body, mind, and wealth through non-deception regarding the Guru, the Liṅga, and the mobile [deities]. Thus, the gross, subtle, and causal bodies constitute the limbs of renunciation, enjoyment, and yoga.
Having accomplished this, [the Guru] bestows upon them that which is perceivable by the subtle faculty of the eye (*dṛkkalā*),
consisting of all six components— namely the downward-turning vessel (*adhovṛtta-khaṇḍikā-vṛtta-gomukha-nāla-golaka*)—
which serves to avoid the undesirable results of accumulated karma (*saṃcita-karma*) that constitutes the cause of various future births related to one's own [past] connections.

External worship consists of performing the sixteen-fold offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra) after attentively fixing the Liṅga— denoted by the word "iṣṭa" because it bestows the desired goal through its identity with the Great Liṅga (Mahāliṅga)— within the gross body, which is denoted by the term "tyāgāṅga," at any one of the six locations.

By means of breaking the twenty-one knots situated within the spinal column (kaśerukā-daṇḍa) produced by the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu)— which is termed *kumbhaka*— and thereby turning the Kuṇḍalinī upward,
[one reaches] that which resides within the pericarp (karṇikā) located in the center of the four-petaled lotus, distinct from the eight-petaled unstruck (*anāhata*) lotus situated in the heart.

The *prāṇaliṅga*— which is the very nature of consciousness distinguished by the life-force (*prāṇaśakti*) possessing the luster of coral the size of a thumb— is to be grasped by the mind; it consists of both the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*),

and is adorned with the garments of discernment between the inert and the conscious arising from the waters of the consecration characterized by forgiveness, and with the ornaments of truthful speech.

Faith (*śraddhā*) consists of the cessation of desire preceded by the knowledge of the instability of enjoyments pertaining to this world and the next; it takes the form of *vairāgya* (dispassion), which is characterized by turning away from other objects like flower garlands; it takes the form of *samādhi*, which is the dissolution of the mind preceded by such detachment; and it takes the form of firm conviction (*akṣata-dṛḍha-viśvāsa*) known as *nirahaṃkāra* (absence of egoism), which is the absence of the conceit "I am this" (*aham-iti-abhimāna*).

The gong known as *mauna* (silence), which consists of the cessation of worldly objects, verbal usage, and the offering of food (*naivedya*)— characterized by the absence of the knowledge of the phenomenal world rooted in delusion— and which takes the form of a lamp consisting of partless, non-conceptual knowledge that removes ignorance regarding the root of all things.

By means of sixteen internal offerings— conceived as mental states, untainted, and consisting of salutations in the form of an intellect that offers objects such as scent and the like, that bestows freedom from attachment to worldly objects such as betel, wives, and sons, and that discerns the identity of all phenomenal expansion with that [Self]— he [should worship].

Internal worship consists of the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga*; and through the dissolution of the mind, abiding in identity with that which is beyond qualities (*nirguṇa*), formless (*nirākāra*), partless (*niṣkala*), higher than the highest (*parātpara*), and whose nature is satisfaction—that is the worship of the Stainless One (*nirañjana*).
Those who are intent upon the practice of these three kinds of *liṅgas* [attain liberation].

And thus, the previously mentioned triad of marks constitutes the reality of Paraśiva, whose sole form is the manifestation of the root *praṇava*; because it appears independently of any other instrument, it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*);
and because it acts independently of any other cause, it is autonomous (*svatantra*).

Because it exists independently of any other substratum, the Supreme Reality of Paraśiva— characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, and encompassing all substrata— having entered into the play of the relationship between the worshiped and the worshiper,
is slightly agitated before the emergence of the waves of existence, like the ocean characterized by its surging billows.

It occurs as follows: then, through the states of deficiency and excess, a twofold nature arises between the two which have attained mutual integration (*anyonyasamarasībhūta*) and are independent (*svatantra*), self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), and quiescent (*śānta*). Among these, that which has attained the state of excess [pertains] to independence and self-luminosity.
The very consciousness of Śiva, which has entered in the form of the root *praṇava* through the process of resonance (*pratisphuraṇa*), becomes the *liṅga-tattva*.

When its self-luminosity has become diminished, the very consciousness of Śiva that has entered in that same manner becomes the *aṅga-tattva*. In that context, the *liṅga-tattva* is indeed that [consciousness].

The *bhāvaliṅga*, which consists of the process of the reflection of *saccidānanda* (Being-Consciousness-Bliss), is threefold: the *prāṇaliṅga* and the *iṣṭaliṅga*. Furthermore, each of these three types of *liṅga* is twofold. Among them, the *bhāvaliṅga* is indeed the *mahāliṅga*.

The *prasādaliṅga* is of two kinds. The *prāṇaliṅga*, however, is of two kinds: the *jaṅgamaliṅga* and the *śivaliṅga*. The *iṣṭaliṅga* is also of two kinds: the *guruliṅga* and the *ācāraliṅga*. Thus, the category of *liṅgas* is sixfold.

The very power of self-existent self-luminosity is that which, within these sequential signs (*liṅga*), constitutes the *kalā* known as *śānti*, *atītā*, and *uttarā*; it is the form of the *praṇava*, a synonym for the *cit-śakti* (consciousness-power), which serves as the material cause for the subtle expansion of the world of cause and effect.
The Kalā of Śāntyatīta, consisting of the letter *ya*, which is another synonym for the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*) whose nature is bliss;
the Kalā of Śānti, consisting of the letter *vā*, which is another synonym for the Power of Direction (*ādi-śakti*) characterized by orientation (*aunmukhya*);
and the Kalā of Vidyā, consisting of the letter *śi*, which is another synonym for the Power of Will (*icchā-śakti*) characterized by subtle activity (*sūkṣma-kriyā*).

The state of sixfold nature consists of: the *kalā* of the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) composed of the letter A, which is a synonym for the power of outward-directed knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*); and the *kalā* of cessation (*nivṛtti*) in the form of the letter Na, which is a synonym for the power of gross exertion and action (*sthūla-udyama-kriyā-śakti*).

He worships. And thus, the Great Liṅga (mahāliṅga), because its nature is the heart characterized by the synthesis of all categories of existence, is called the "faceless" (agopyamukha) even though it has the form of the pure synthesizer. However, the pentad of liṅgas beginning with Prasāda [is associated] respectively with sound and the other [objects].

The unmanifest five faces known as Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, which consist of the forms of those who discern distinct objects, are so called. Such is the pure discerning subject (*anusandhātṛ*) of the principle of *liṅga-tattva*, characterized by the perception of difference that culminates in non-difference, according to the analogy of the waves of the ocean.

Because it is the cause of favor by way of its nature as form (*rūpatva*), it is indicated as being worthy of worship (*upāsya*). Thus, the reality of the limbs (*aṅgatattva*) is threefold: the limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*), the limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), and the limb of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*). Each of these is also twofold. The limb of yoga is divided into two: oneness (*aikya*) and refuge (*śaraṇa*). As for the limb of enjoyment, however—
"Prāṇaliṅgin, Prasādin"— thus, the characteristic of a devotee of Maheśvara consists in the limb of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*).
In this way, when the manifestation of the sixfold limbs reaches a state of diminution, that very power (*śakti*) is called *samarasabhakti*, *ānandabhakti*, *anubhavabhakti*, and *avadhānabhakti*.
[He assumes] the form of the sixfold devotion— namely, *naiṣṭhikī-bhakti* (devotion of steadfastness) and *śraddhā-bhakti* (devotion of faith)—
the state of the sixfold internal organ characterized by feeling (*bhāva*), knowledge (*jñāna*), mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*),
and the form of the sense organs of cognition such as the ear and so forth.
The state of being the six categories characterized by sound and the rest, as well as their objects;

the state of being the form of the six-syllable mantra that expresses them; the state of being the nature of the organs of action, such as speech, which serve as the means for ritual action; and [their] subtle form—
Having attained the state of being the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the five elements beginning with ether (*kāśa*),
as well as the state of the sixfold form of the hands known as *sadbhāva*, *sujñāna*, *sumanas*, *nirahaṃkāra*, *subuddhi*, and *sucitta*,
it becomes the *aṅga-tattva*. Of such a *aṅga-tattva*...

Although [the Self] possesses a nature consisting of contracted powers such as consciousness (cit), which are fashioned by the playful power (*līlā-śakti*) of Maheśvarī, it is nevertheless called the "worshipper" because, through its association with subtle forms and adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the mental space (*mānasa-vyoman*), it assumes the form of the subject of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-pramātṛ*), characterized by the bestowal of differentiation based on the division that constitutes upward emanation (*ūrdhva-sṛṣṭi*). Thus...

And the principle of refuge (śaraṇatattva) is a limb of the principle of the sign (liṅgatattva), while the sign of the refuge is the vital breath (prāṇa). Between these two, there is a state of mutual aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya) according to the analogy of the seed and the tree. Thus, the sign is indeed the refuge, and the refuge is indeed the sign. Of such a refuge...

Because it possesses the recognition of one's own Self (svātmapratyabhijñāna) attained through the weighty glance of one's own self-reflection (svavimarśa), this very mind is the great liṅga in the form of the Praṇava;
it is characterized by the non-apprehension of all objects— such as sound and so forth— which are the respective domains of each external sense organ, such as the ear and the rest.

Because it is turned inward as a means of realization (*sādhana*), and because the teacher’s speech—the scripture consisting of *nāda*, *sunāda*, and *mahānāda*—is the cause of grace (*prasāda*) characterized by favor through the sequence of *paśyantī* and the others, which take the form of intention, determination, and utterance;
therefore, the ear alone, as the instrument for perceiving sound, is the sign of grace in the form of the letter *ya*. This applies to both the stationary (*cara*) and the moving (*jaṅgama*).
Because it is synonymous with that [Supreme Self], the skin, pervading all limbs,
is the mobile liṅga consisting of speech (vāk), since it is the means for the cognition of sensations such as cold; indeed, the Great Light itself has entered the eyeball.
Because it is the means for illuminating all existing forms and objects, the eye itself is the Śivaliṅga composed of the syllable *Śi*.

Since the Guru is the embodiment of the mantra, the six-syllabled mantra (*Ṣaḍakṣarī*) itself has attained the nature of the six flavors, such as sweet and so forth; therefore, the tongue itself is the means for tasting the flavor of the recitation of such a mantra.

The *makāra* is the *guruliṅga*. Because it is the support for the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) through the two channels named *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, and because it consists of the nose itself— which, through the process of evacuation (*recana*) in the form of purification of the body that serves as the cause for performing virtuous deeds, and through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) arising from that sequence— is the *ācāraliṅga* consisting of the syllable *nakāra*.

It is said: thus the characteristics of the *liṅga* are to be understood. Now, one who possesses devotion characterized by affection for the marks of Śiva—such as ashes, rudrākṣas, and so forth—and for those who have taken refuge in Śiva, through the realization of the identity of the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama*, is indeed a devotee; he is Śiva himself.
Maheśvara is indeed one who possesses steadfast devotion, characterized by the realization that [the Lord] consists of the Śrīguru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama;

he is one whose devotion is vigilant and free from forgetfulness regarding the fivefold conduct (*pañcācāra*)— the first of which consists of the five modes of behavior defined by the water from the feet of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama, as well as the sacred ash (*prasāda*), Rudrākṣa beads, and Mantras.

The *prasādī* is one who, even when afflicted by disease and the like, adheres strictly to the rule of accepting only the grace of the water from the feet (*pādodaka-prasāda*), and does not accept medicine offered at the *liṅga*; for him, the *liṅga* alone is the life-force (*prāṇa*), and the life-force alone is the *liṅga*.
One who possesses such contemplation is indeed a *prāṇaliṅgin*. Such a *prāṇaliṅga* himself becomes the Lord (*pati*),

having attained the state of being the consort (*satī*)— realizing that for the True One (*satī*) there is no other reality— and thus, having abandoned association with any other consort, he is filled with the bliss of union with his own power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
Relying upon the path of cessation, one who is endowed with devotion, knowledge, and dispassion alone is called a refuge.

By the cessation of such thoughts regarding a virtuous husband, being devoid of the appearance of other objects and turning away from conceptual construction, one contemplates that everything is of the nature of Śiva.

Just as in the union of fire and camphor, oneness is indeed the state of becoming a single fusion within the Great Liṅga that faces inward; thus, the stage of the limbs (aṅgasthala) is to be contemplated. In this way, the relationship between the sixfold liṅgas—beginning with conduct—which are differentiated by the distinctions of the sixfold conduct, is to be contemplated.
Regarding this point, there are the words of the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā:

"The sign of conduct (ācāraliṅga) is called the nose; it rests upon the plane of devotion (bhaktasthala), is endowed with the power of cessation (nivṛttikalā), and is the instrument for perceiving smell."
The Guru-linga, known as the tongue, is situated in the station of Maheśa;
it is conjoined with the power of Vidyā and is the means for perceiving form.
The mobile linga known as the skin, which rests upon the station of the Prāṇalingin,
is endowed with the power called Śānti and is the means for perceiving touch.
The Prasādaliṅga is known as the ear, taking refuge in the station of Śaraṇa;
it is endowed with the Śānti and Atīta Kalās and is the instrument for perceiving sound.
"The mental [form] is the Great Liṅga, which takes its resort in the station of unity (aikyasthala);
it is endowed with the states of Śānti, Atīta, and Uttara, and is the means for the apprehension of all. Thus [it is said].

In this context, although the mind (*mānasa*) and the others function as instruments (*karaṇa*), they are designated by the term "indicative mark" (*liṅga*) because the cognitive attribute of smelling and so forth— which belongs to the conscious self— is dependent solely upon them as the means for apprehending and appropriating objects such as odors. Furthermore, the definition of a devotee (*bhakta*) and so forth is found in the Skanda Purāṇa.
In the Śaṃkarasaṃhitā: Right conduct, devotion to Śiva, single-minded focus on the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama*,
and the power [of devotion] toward the sectarian marks and the refuge— this is the unsurpassed station of the devotee.
One who possesses purity of disposition should avoid the wives of others and the wealth of others;
with a self disciplined by devotion to the *liṅga*, he is established in the great abode of Maheśvara.
Having experienced happiness through the object offered to the Liṅga while remaining composed,
and avoiding that which is not offered, one reaches the supreme state of grace.

In the wind whose nature is prāṇa is the liṅga; in the liṅga is prāṇa well-established. There is neither pleasure nor pain—the dual pair—there; that is the station of the one established in prāṇa-liṅga.
My husband is the *liṅga* and I am Satī; thus, the Lord himself is present.
There is no worldly pleasure [greater than this]; it is the supreme place of refuge.
"The six waves are not six entities, nor does the eightfold worship exist;
there is no objective state, only identity with one's own innate mark (*nijaliṅga*), like the union of fire and camphor. Thus it is said.

And thus, since the stage of the limbs (aṅgasthala) is included within the stage of the Liṅgas, there is the single reality of the Great Liṅga called Mahāsāda, which is endowed with the Kalās known as Śānti, Atīta, and Uttara; and there is the pentad of Kalās residing in the remaining five Liṅgas.

In brief, the five forms of Sādākhya— namely Śiva-sādākhya, Mūrta-sādākhya, Kartṛ-sādākhya, Rūpa-sādākhya, and [the fifth]— together with the [other] principles (tattvas), constitute the eleven liṅgas. This being so, the Great Liṅga (mahāliṅga) of the partless, solid liṅga-principle is called "Mānasa" and is inward-turned.

The intended meaning is that the five *prasādaliṅgas* are the five external faces, while the five *sādākhyas* are synonymous with [the faces] beginning with Īśāna. Now, furthermore, regarding that Great Lord...
