In the play of manifesting the gross five [elements], through the power of the *nivṛtti-kalā*— which is synonymous with the *ācāra-liṅga* and *niṣkriya-śakti*— there arises the *māyā-tattva*, which is synonymous with *prakṛti* and consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; this serves as the fundamental cause of the twenty-three principles beginning with *ahaṃkāra* and ending with the earth (*bhūmi*).
In that regard, consciousness itself, having entered into the *sāttvika* and other [guṇas], is designated by the names Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
Residing within these, there are respectively Fire, Sun, and Moon;
and there are four divisions known as Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. This fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*) was created by me.
This is because of the statement in the *Gītā*: "He created [the world] according to the divisions of qualities and actions.

One should not raise the objection as to how the four castes can arise from the three qualities (*guṇas*), for there is the Vedic revelation: "Rudra, the Great Seer, is superior to the universe; Rudra is indeed the Puruṣa; Obeisance, obeisance to him who is Being and Greatness."
From the quality of *sattva* arises the birth of Brahmā, who is a portion of Rudra and whose nature is consciousness entered by the quality of *sattva*.

Because it is mixed with what is called the quality of *rajas*, from that same portion of *sattva* arises the birth of the Vaiṣṇava Kṣatriya. From the *tamas* portion contained therein arises the birth of the Vaiśya, who is a portion of Brahmā.
From the quality of *tamas*, the Śūdra was born as a portion of Indra. The other gods are *saṅkara* (mixed castes).
And it is said in the *Parāśaropapurāṇa*: "All the gods are *śaṅkara*; Purandara is a *vṛṣala* (Śūdra);
Pitāmaha is a Vaiśya; Hari is the supreme Kṣatriya; [Brahmā is] the Brāhmaṇa."
The Blessed Lord Rudra is the highest of the high among all; for Rudra, who has become Brahman, his status as a Brāhmaṇa is not born of any cause.

If it be objected: "But since it is heard everywhere in the Purāṇas that Viṣṇu is Sāttvika and Rudra is Tāmasa, how can the stated conclusion be established?"—the answer is no, because the statements regarding the Sāttvika and Tāmasa natures of Viṣṇu and Rudra are based on their limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of preservation and dissolution; by their very nature, however, [they are equal].
Viṣṇu is characterized by *tamas*, while Rudra is characterized by *sattva*. As it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*:
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of *prakṛti*; joined with these, the one Supreme Person here assumes the forms of this [triple nature]."

For the sake of maintenance and so forth, there are the designations Hari, Viriñci, and Hara; indeed, among these, the auspicious results belong to the person whose nature is characterized by *sattva*.
O Girijā, that supreme light— unattainable even by the guardians of all the worlds, by Viriñci, Vaikuṇṭha, and the lord of the gods— is free from both rajas and tamas.
"Sattva is not that Brahman which is devoid of all differentiation. Thus [it is said].

In this context, in the first verse, through the figure of speech *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence), it is clearly perceived that Viṣṇu’s nature as *sāttvika* and Rudra’s nature as *tāmasa* are determined by their respective functions of protection and so forth.
This is evident from the statement "O Mountain-dweller, [this] is not yours" addressed to Rudra on the occasion of the emergence of the fierce Kālakūṭa poison.

According to the sequence of words spoken by Brahmā, it appears that the state of possessing the quality of *tamas* for Vaikuṇṭha and the state of possessing the quality of *sattva* for Rudra—who is synonymous with Surendra—are natural;
this is because Rudra is white in color and Viṣṇu is black in color. Regarding this point:

In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Whiteness is born from the quality of *sattva*, passion is born from the quality of *rajas*, and blackness is born from the quality of *tamas*; thus one should know it in brief."
He whose being consists of illusion (māyā), whose body is the quality of darkness (tamas),
and who exists for the dissolution of the three forms (trimūrti)— he is Rudra, and no other.
Likewise: "He whose body is directly Tamas and whose quality is Sattva, for the sake of protecting the three forms [of the gods], is Viṣṇu and no other."
In this regard, all beings from Brahmā down to the smallest insect are possessed of the three impurities (*mala*). Viṣṇu is a *pralayākala*;
because he is devoid of *kalā*, he is eternally ignorant, possessing only the single impurity of *māyā* for the purpose of dissolution.

A *mantra*, however, is characterized by the manifestation of the limbs of renunciation that reach the upper limit; because it is distinguished by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the impurity of karma alone, it is a *mantra*.

The manifestation of the limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga), however, is called Mantreśvara because it consists in the state of being oriented toward the exhaustion of the latent impressions of the karma-mala.

The manifestation of the limbs of yoga (yogāṅga), moreover, is called Mantramaheśvara because it consists in having attained the exhaustion of the latent impressions of the karma-mala. Thus, these are the six kinds of subjects (pramātṛ).

The distinction is this: the manifestation of the partless, compact *liṅga* is the vibration of the "I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhaṃsphuraṇa*), which is full and free from the emergence of impurity (*anutpannamalollāsa*).

In this context, it should be understood that the category of *aṅga-tattva* (the auxiliary principles), which consists of the manifold diversity (*prapañca*) characterized by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and is an effect of *māyā*, comprises twenty-five items. Herein, the triad of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) are the effects of *sattva*; the five organs of action (*karmendriya*) are the effects of *rajas*.
It should be understood that the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the five gross elements (*bhūta*) are characterized by *tamas*. Regarding this,

because of the Lord’s statement, "At the end of many births, the one possessed of knowledge takes refuge in Me," [it occurs] in this present life through the power of virtuous deeds such as the worship of Śiva accumulated over many previous births.
Thus it is established that only someone who, by the power of the Guru’s glance alone, attains such knowledge of Brahman in its six aspects becomes liberated.
Now, for one who has taken refuge in the Brahman characterized by the aforementioned six planes,

the six syllables beginning with 'A', starting from Gopī and ending with Sadyojāta— namely, Muditā, Jyotis, Bindu, Ardhacandra, Kuṇḍala, Daṇḍa, and Tāraka— become the six elements themselves and thus attain the status of being its limbs.
Upon its limb, which consists of the six *praṇavas*, the desired *liṅga* remains firmly established. Indeed, on its pedestal is the *ācāra-liṅga*;

in the enclosure of the *khaṇḍikā* is the *guru-liṅga*; in the circle is the *śiva-liṅga*; at the *gomukha* is the *jaṅgama-liṅga*; in the place of the *yoni* is the *prasāda-liṅga*; and in the *golaka*—

Because these six kinds of *liṅgas* manifest in their respective locations as the "Great *Liṅga*," a devotee there, with faith and devotion, takes a fragrant substance in the hand of a pure mind and, while recollecting the *nakāra* mantra, [offers it] to the *ācāraliṅga*, which is endowed with the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
Having offered it through the gateway of the olfactory organ and become an enjoyer of its grace, there occurs a transformation.

For the devotee of Maheśvara, having placed the substance of mercury (rasa) into the hand of Subuddhi with firm devotion toward the Guru-liṅga endowed with the power of knowledge, and while recollecting the mantra of the letter *Ma*, offers it through the gateway of the gustatory organ.

Having accepted His grace, one becomes transformed. One who possesses such grace, through vigilant devotion toward the Śiva-liṅga endowed with the power of will, takes hold of the object of form with a hand free from egoism,
while recollecting the Śikha-mantra by means of the sense organ of sight.
Having offered it and become an enjoyer of its grace, one becomes subject to transformation.

One who possesses the *jaṅgama-liṅga* endowed with the power of being a bearer of the *prāṇa-liṅga*, having grasped the object of touch with the hand of *sumanas* through the experience of devotion, while recollecting the syllable *vā*, offers it into the mouth of the sense of touch;
becoming a partaker of its grace, he becomes a transformed soul (*pariṇāmī*). As for the one who has taken refuge:

By means of the hand of excellent knowledge, one who has grasped the word and its meaning through the blissful devotion toward the *prasāda-liṅga* conjoined with the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), while recollecting the mantra beginning with the letter *ya*, offers it into the mouth of the sense of hearing; having consumed that *prasāda*, he becomes transformed. As for unity, however, it occurs through the devotion of *samarasa* toward the Great Liṅga conjoined with the Consciousness Power (*cic-chakti*).
Holding the object of satisfaction with the hand of true being, while recollecting the Praṇava mantra, one offers it into the mouth of the mind; being satisfied by its grace, one becomes transformed.
In this very sequence, we shall describe the ritual procedure for the offering of mixed substances:

edible food and the like for the *ācāra-liṅga*; drinkable items such as milk and the like for the *guru-liṅga*; chewable items such as cakes and dumplings for the *śiva-liṅga*; and lickable items such as lentil soup and the like for the *jaṅgama-liṅga*.

Having offered all these things—the lickable substances, elixirs, and so forth—to the *prasādaliṅga*, and then to the *mahāliṅga*, one becomes a partaker and enjoyer of that *prasāda*. Now, regarding the offering of mixed items (*miśrārpaṇa*):
the offering of roots, tubers, fragrances, and so on, to the *ācāraliṅga* contained within the *ācāraliṅga*.

Having offered fragrant substances such as tree bark and the like to the *guruliṅga* included within the *ācāraliṅga*; having offered fragrant buds and the like to the *caraliṅga* included within the *ācāraliṅga*;
and having offered fragrant fruits and the like to the *prasādaliṅga* included within the *ācāraliṅga*.

Partaking of that grace, one becomes subject to transformation: [one offers] sweet flavor to the Ācāraliṅga contained within the Guruliṅga; astringent flavor to the Guruliṅga contained within the Guruliṅga;
and pungent flavor to the Śivaliṅga contained within the Guruliṅga.

Having offered the sour taste to the mobile liṅga (caraliṅga) within the guru-liṅga, the bitter taste to the grace-liṅga (prasādaliṅga) within the guru-liṅga, and the salty taste to the great liṅga (mahāliṅga) within the guru-liṅga,
one becomes happy by partaking of that grace. [Likewise, one offers] to the conduct-liṅga (ācāraliṅga) within the Śiva-liṅga...
Yellow form for the Guru-liṅga within the Śiva-liṅga;
white form for the Śiva-liṅga within the Śiva-liṅga; green form for the Caraliṅga within the Śiva-liṅga; red form for the Prasāda-liṅga within the Śiva-liṅga; blue form for [the same].
Having offered all this to the Great Liṅga within the Śiva-liṅga and partaking of that grace,
one becomes happy. [One offers] the rough touch to the Ācāra-liṅga within the Jaṅgama-liṅga,
and [the offering] to the Guru-liṅga within the Cara-liṅga.

To the mobile Śivaliṅga contained within the mobile liṅga, [offer] a soft touch; to the mobile jaṅgamaliṅga contained within the mobile liṅga, a warm touch; to the mobile prasādaliṅga contained within the mobile liṅga, a cool touch;
and to the mobile liṅga itself, a mixed touch.
Having offered all that to the Great Liṅga residing within the Ācāra-liṅga, one becomes happy as an enjoyer of its grace.
[One offers] the sound produced by cymbals and the like to the Ācāra-liṅga residing within the Prasāda-liṅga,
and the sound produced by the lute strings to the Guru-liṅga residing within the Prasāda-liṅga.
To the Śivaliṅga contained within the Prasādaliṅga, [he offers] the sound of drums and the like produced by striking with a staff;
to the Jaṅgamaliṅga contained within the Prasādaliṅga, the sound produced by flutes and the like;
and to the Prasādaliṅga contained within the Prasādaliṅga, the sound of songs and the like.
Having offered all this sound to the Great Liṅga contained within the Prasāda-liṅga,

one becomes blissful while partaking in its grace. [One offers] the satisfaction of fragrance to the Ācāra-liṅga contained within the Mahāliṅga, and the satisfaction of form to the Śiva-liṅga contained within the Mahāliṅga.
Having offered the satisfaction of touch to the mobile liṅga contained within the Great Liṅga,
the satisfaction of sound to the grace-liṅga (prasādaliṅga) contained within the Great Liṅga,
and total satisfaction to the Great Liṅga itself contained within the Great Liṅga, one becomes an enjoyer of its grace.
He becomes truly delighted. [He offers] to the Ācāra-liṅga at the time of contact with the objects of the senses;
to the Guru-liṅga at the time of the cognition of those objects; to the Śiva-liṅga at the time of the knowledge in the form of the ascertainment of the object;
to the Jaṅgama-liṅga at the time of the satisfaction born from that ascertainment of the object; and to the Prasāda-liṅga...

Having offered the time for attaining the determined reality to the Great Liṅga, and the time for experiencing bliss immediately following the attainment of that determined reality to the Liṅga, he becomes one who enjoys the experience of the Liṅga and is filled with supreme bliss.

For one who has thus surrendered their refuge and whose consciousness is dissolved into Brahman, there arises the state of being composed of the six-syllabled mantra that expresses it: "O Goddess, the syllable *oṃ* is the face;
the two syllables *namaḥ* are the two arms; the syllable *śi* shall be the middle of the body; and the two syllables *vāya* are the two feet."

From the base of the pedestal (pīṭhapāda) up to the knees is said to be the middle; from there to the heart it is circular, and likewise to the throat it is cow-faced (gomukha). From the midpoint between the eyebrows to the end of the neck is the linga-throat, and the head is the linga-peak. According to this statement, such is also the case for that body.

Because it has the nature of the *mantra-liṅga*, there is absolutely nothing further to be practiced. And he, having thus become merged in oneness with the great dense *liṅga* (mahāghana-liṅga) and being nourished by uninterrupted indignation (*amarṣa*), remains [in that state].
Only one who possesses such knowledge of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*) is truly supreme. This is the very meaning.
This has already been clearly stated in the collection of citations from the *Sūtasamhitā*, beginning with "from worms, insects, and moths.
Therefore, he alone is liberated; he alone is worthy of universal veneration; he alone is supreme over all. He alone...

And He is to be approached through all means such as seeing, touching, and worldly interaction. Regarding this matter, the authorities (pramāṇas) should be consulted by those possessed of intelligence in the penultimate section of the Kriyākāṇḍa; thus, everything is consistent.
O illustrious Guru, by means of the words issuing from your lotus-like mouth, you have composed, through the form of debate, refutations and ornaments for all philosophical systems,
complete with logical reasoning.
Indeed, those [teachings] were heard from Bhṛṅgin and Suśīlin.

Having heard this preeminent doctrine, enriched by the greatness of the Śrī Vīraśaiva tradition and constituting the very essence of all the Vedas and Āgamas, [the world was moved] by waves from the ocean of milk consisting of joy.
I experienced the unsurpassed pleasure of swinging on a swing.
And he was renowned in the world, O King Basava, for his wisdom, his forbearance, his worship of Śiva,
his profundity, and his capacity for exposition.
Your fame rests in your fortitude and your majesty.
The ocean of milk assumes the state of white silken garments upon his waist and chest; the celestial Ganges becomes a pure bodice upon his forehead;
the sky takes on the beauty of his hair; and the stars all around him appear like flowers.
Of the fame-woman of King Basava, who pervades the quarters of the horizon.
Upon her feet with their throbbing golden buds, there are golden tinkling bells at both her ankles;
at the limit of her waist is a small row of bells fixed to her girdle;
around her neck are strings of gold and gems; and upon her hands are two shimmering golden bracelets.
The universes shine forth as the jewels in the hair of the Fame-bride of the steadfast King Basava.
O King Basava, the brilliant crystal linga is indeed the reflection of your fame;
the rain-cloud is the vessel for your consecration, the stars are garlands of flowers, the sun and moon are the two lamps, and the entire sky is the incense. All this world is [your offering].
For the wise, the offering is constant praise, and the goddess of speech is the sound of the bell.
[Thus,
from the venerable Tōṇṭada Siddheśvara, who is an incarnation of the mobile form of the beginningless and stainless Aparā,
and who obtained the grace of the Śāmbhava Āgama ocean churned by him— resulting in the division into one hundred and one unsurpassed *sthala*s...]

In [this work] composed by the eminent teacher Maritoṇṭadārya— who bestows a mass of bliss from tasting the nectar of the reality of *latatattva*— [it concerns] Keladi Sadāśivarāya, the lord of the western ocean, who was the sole hero capable of raising a tumultuous roar against ten million Yādavas and Murāris, the remover of the seven constituents of state from his enemies, and the teacher who established the pure Vedic doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*).

In the *Vīraśaivānandacandrikā*, within the section on debate (*vādakāṇḍa*) in the instruction of Basava— the joy of the heart of Bāhubalī and the Indra of the earth— this is the [chapter] titled "The Exposition of the Excellence of the Vīraśaiva Doctrine and the Excellence of the Śiva-devotees Established therein," concerning Mallā, the lawful wife of Vīrabhadra, the lord of the earth, who was like the full moon in the milky ocean of the lineage of leaders.
The twenty-fourth chapter.
[The Section on Debate is completed.]
